rewrite: Although generally unreactive under normal circumstances, hydrogen still combines with a wide range of elements. With highly electronegative elements like the halogens or oxygen, it carries a partial positive charge. Conversely, when bonding to less electronegative substances such as metals and metalloids, hydrogen assumes a partial negative charge, forming compounds commonly called hydrides. Notably, its bonds with fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen enable a special noncovalent interaction—hydrogen bonding. This medium-strength force occurs between molecules and is essential for the structural stability of numerous biological molecules.

input: In 1877, Thomas Edison invented the phonograph. Unlike the phonautograph, it was capable of both recording and reproducing sound. Despite the similarity of name, there is no documentary evidence that Edison's phonograph was based on Scott's phonautograph. Edison first tried recording sound on a wax-impregnated paper tape, with the idea of creating a "telephone repeater" analogous to the telegraph repeater he had been working on. Although the visible results made him confident that sound could be physically recorded and reproduced, his notes do not indicate that he actually reproduced sound before his first experiment in which he used tinfoil as a recording medium several months later. The tinfoil was wrapped around a grooved metal cylinder and a sound-vibrated stylus indented the tinfoil while the cylinder was rotated. The recording could be played back immediately. The Scientific American article that introduced the tinfoil phonograph to the public mentioned Marey, Rosapelly and Barlow as well as Scott as creators of devices for recording but, importantly, not reproducing sound. Edison also invented variations of the phonograph that used tape and disc formats. Numerous applications for the phonograph were envisioned, but although it enjoyed a brief vogue as a startling novelty at public demonstrations, the tinfoil phonograph proved too crude to be put to any practical use. A decade later, Edison developed a greatly improved phonograph that used a hollow wax cylinder instead of a foil sheet. This proved to be both a better-sounding and far more useful and durable device. The wax phonograph cylinder created the recorded sound market at the end of the 1880s and dominated it through the early years of the 20th century.
rewrite:
Thomas Edison’s invention of the phonograph in 1877 introduced a device that could both record and reproduce sound, distinguishing it from earlier instruments like the phonautograph. There is no documented proof, however, that Edison’s work directly derived from Scott’s phonautograph, despite the similarity in their names. Edison initially experimented with a wax-impregnated paper tape, envisioning a “telephone repeater” akin to the telegraph repeaters he had developed. While these early tests convinced him that sound could be physically captured and replayed, his records suggest he did not achieve actual sound reproduction until months later, when he first used tinfoil as a medium. In this pivotal experiment, tinfoil was wrapped around a grooved metal cylinder; a stylus, vibrated by sound, indented the foil as the cylinder turned, allowing the recording to be played back immediately.

An article in Scientific American that publicized the tinfoil phonograph cited Marey, Rosapelly, Barlow, and Scott as inventors of recording apparatuses—yet emphasized that their devices could not reproduce sound. Although Edison also created phonograph variants using tape and disc formats, and many potential applications were imagined, the tinfoil model remained too rudimentary for practical use. It captivated audiences briefly as a novel demonstration, but its limitations were evident. A decade later, Edison unveiled a significantly improved version employing a hollow wax cylinder instead of foil. This new design produced better sound, was far more durable and functional, and ultimately launched the commercial recorded sound market in the late 1880s. The wax cylinder phonograph went on to dominate that market well into the early twentieth century.

input: San Diego County has one of the highest counts of animal and plant species that appear on the endangered species list among counties in the United States. Because of its diversity of habitat and its position on the Pacific Flyway, San Diego County has recorded the presence of 492 bird species, more than any other region in the country. San Diego always scores very high in the number of bird species observed in the annual Christmas Bird Count, sponsored by the Audubon Society, and it is known as one of the "birdiest" areas in the United States.
rewrite: San Diego County ranks among U.S. counties with the most endangered animal and plant species. Its diverse habitats and location on the Pacific Flyway support a recorded 492 bird species, surpassing any other region nationally. The area consistently achieves high counts in the Audubon Society's annual Christmas Bird Count. Consequently, San Diego is renowned as one of the "birdiest" places in the United States.

input: At the same time, these movements were influenced by, and in some respects continued, philosophical thought within the Vedic tradition as reflected e.g. in the Upanishads. These movements included, besides Buddhism, various skeptics (such as Sanjaya Belatthiputta), atomists (such as Pakudha Kaccayana), materialists (such as Ajita Kesakambali), antinomians (such as Purana Kassapa); the most important ones in the 5th century BCE were the Ajivikas, who emphasized the rule of fate, the Lokayata (materialists), the Ajnanas (agnostics) and the Jains, who stressed that the soul must be freed from matter. Many of these new movements shared the same conceptual vocabulary—atman ("Self"), buddha ("awakened one"), dhamma ("rule" or "law"), karma ("action"), nirvana ("extinguishing"), samsara ("eternal recurrence") and yoga ("spiritual practice").[note 24] The shramanas rejected the Veda, and the authority of the brahmans, who claimed they possessed revealed truths not knowable by any ordinary human means. Moreover, they declared that the entire Brahmanical system was fraudulent: a conspiracy of the brahmans to enrich themselves by charging exorbitant fees to perform bogus rites and give useless advice.
rewrite: Alongside Buddhism, the philosophical movements of this era encompassed a range of thinkers: skeptics like Sanjaya Belatthiputta, atomists such as Pakudha Kaccayana, materialists including Ajita Kesakambali, and antinomians like Purana Kassapa. The most significant groups in the 5th century BCE were the Ajivikas, stressing fate's rule; the Lokayata (materialists); the Ajnanas (agnostics); and the Jains, who focused on liberating the soul from matter. These diverse movements, while influenced by and in some ways extending earlier Vedic thought found in texts like the Upanishads, collectively rejected the Vedas and the authority of the brahmans. They dismissed the Brahmanical system as a fraudulent scheme, accusing brahmans of enriching themselves through exorbitant fees for false rites and useless counsel, claiming a monopoly on revealed truths inaccessible to ordinary people. Despite their differences, many shared a common conceptual language, employing terms such as atman ("Self"), buddha ("awakened one"), dhamma ("law"), karma ("action"), nirvana ("extinguishing"), samsara ("eternal recurrence"), and yoga ("spiritual practice").

input: In DC circuits and pulsed circuits, current and voltage reversal are affected by the damping of the system. Voltage reversal is encountered in RLC circuits that are under-damped. The current and voltage reverse direction, forming a harmonic oscillator between the inductance and capacitance. The current and voltage will tend to oscillate and may reverse direction several times, with each peak being lower than the previous, until the system reaches an equilibrium. This is often referred to as ringing. In comparison, critically damped or over-damped systems usually do not experience a voltage reversal. Reversal is also encountered in AC circuits, where the peak current will be equal in each direction.
rewrite: In under-damped RLC circuits, voltage reversal occurs as the system oscillates. Here, current and voltage can reverse direction multiple times, creating a harmonic oscillator between the inductance and capacitance. Each oscillatory peak is lower than the last until equilibrium is reached, a phenomenon commonly called ringing. This contrasts with critically damped or over-damped systems, which typically avoid such reversal. In both DC and pulsed circuits, this damping influences current and voltage reversal. Additionally, reversal is found in AC circuits, where the peak current is equal in each direction.

input: In a June 2008 speech, President and CEO of the New York Federal Reserve Bank Timothy Geithner—who in 2009 became Secretary of the United States Treasury—placed significant blame for the freezing of credit markets on a "run" on the entities in the "parallel" banking system, also called the shadow banking system. These entities became critical to the credit markets underpinning the financial system, but were not subject to the same regulatory controls. Further, these entities were vulnerable because of maturity mismatch, meaning that they borrowed short-term in liquid markets to purchase long-term, illiquid and risky assets. This meant that disruptions in credit markets would make them subject to rapid deleveraging, selling their long-term assets at depressed prices. He described the significance of these entities:
rewrite: In a 2008 address, Timothy Geithner—then President of the New York Federal Reserve Bank and later U.S. Treasury Secretary in 2009—attributed much of the credit market freeze to a "run" on the shadow banking sector. This parallel system, crucial to the financial system's credit markets, operated without equivalent regulatory oversight. Its entities faced particular vulnerability due to maturity mismatch: they funded themselves with short-term borrowing to invest in long-term, illiquid, and risky assets. Consequently, any credit market disruption forced rapid deleveraging, compelling sales of these assets at sharply reduced prices. Geithner underscored the profound significance of these institutions within the broader financial landscape.

input: The AVL, created by the Valencian parliament, is in charge of dictating the official rules governing the use of Valencian, and its standard is based on the Norms of Castelló (Normes de Castelló). Currently, everyone who writes in Valencian uses this standard, except the Royal Academy of Valencian Culture (Acadèmia de Cultura Valenciana, RACV), which uses for Valencian an independent standard.
rewrite: Established by the Valencian parliament, the AVL sets the official rules for Valencian usage, adhering to the Norms of Castelló. This standard is now universally followed by those writing in Valencian. The sole exception is the Royal Academy of Valencian Culture (RACV), which employs its own independent standard.

input: Many instruments originated during the Renaissance; others were variations of, or improvements upon, instruments that had existed previously. Some have survived to the present day; others have disappeared, only to be recreated in order to perform music of the period on authentic instruments. As in the modern day, instruments may be classified as brass, strings, percussion, and woodwind.
rewrite: Numerous Renaissance instruments were new inventions, while many others evolved from earlier designs. Some remain in use today, but others vanished and were later reconstructed for historically accurate performances. Instruments from this era, much like modern ones, fall into categories such as brass, strings, percussion, and woodwind.

input: Various classes of Vajrayana literature developed as a result of royal courts sponsoring both Buddhism and Saivism. The Mañjusrimulakalpa, which later came to classified under Kriyatantra, states that mantras taught in the Saiva, Garuda and Vaisnava tantras will be effective if applied by Buddhists since they were all taught originally by Manjushri. The Guhyasiddhi of Padmavajra, a work associated with the Guhyasamaja tradition, prescribes acting as a Saiva guru and initiating members into Saiva Siddhanta scriptures and mandalas. The Samvara tantra texts adopted the pitha list from the Saiva text Tantrasadbhava, introducing a copying error where a deity was mistaken for a place.
rewrite: Royal patronage of both Buddhism and Saivism led to the development of diverse Vajrayana literary classes. One text, the later Kriyatantra-classified *Mañjusrimulakalpa*, declares that mantras from Saiva, Garuda, and Vaisnava tantras remain potent for Buddhists, as Manjushri originally taught them all. In the Guhyasamaja tradition, Padmavajra’s *Guhyasiddhi* advises practitioners to act as Saiva gurus, initiating followers into Saiva Siddhanta scriptures and mandalas. Furthermore, the Samvara tantra literature borrowed its pitha list from the Saiva *Tantrasadbhava*, resulting in a copying error that misidentified a deity as a place.

input: The process was completed in 27 BC when the Roman Emperor Augustus annexed the rest of Greece and constituted it as the senatorial province of Achaea. Despite their military superiority, the Romans admired and became heavily influenced by the achievements of Greek culture, hence Horace's famous statement: Graecia capta ferum victorem cepit ("Greece, although captured, took its wild conqueror captive"). The epics of Homer inspired the Aeneid of Virgil, and authors such as Seneca the younger wrote using Greek styles. Roman heroes such as Scipio Africanus, tended to study philosophy and regarded Greek culture and science as an example to be followed. Similarly, most Roman emperors maintained an admiration for things Greek in nature. The Roman Emperor Nero visited Greece in AD 66, and performed at the Ancient Olympic Games, despite the rules against non-Greek participation. Hadrian was also particularly fond of the Greeks; before he became emperor he served as an eponymous archon of Athens.
rewrite: In 27 BC, the Roman Emperor Augustus annexed the remaining Greek territories, forming the senatorial province of Achaea, thereby completing the process of conquest. Despite their military dominance, the Romans greatly admired and were profoundly shaped by Greek cultural achievements. This influence is captured in Horace’s famous line: *Graecia capta ferum victorem cepit* (“Greece, although captured, took its wild conqueror captive”). Greek styles were adopted by Roman authors like Seneca the Younger, and Virgil’s *Aeneid* was inspired by Homer’s epics. Roman heroes, such as Scipio Africanus, studied philosophy and viewed Greek culture and science as models to emulate. Most Roman emperors shared this admiration for Greek culture. Nero, for instance, visited Greece in AD 66 and performed at the Ancient Olympic Games, flouting the rules barring non-Greek participants. Hadrian, too, was particularly fond of the Greeks, having served as the eponymous archon of Athens before becoming emperor.

input: The managing director of London Weekend Television (LWT), Greg Dyke, met with the representatives of the "big five" football clubs in England in 1990. The meeting was to pave the way for a break away from The Football League. Dyke believed that it would be more lucrative for LWT if only the larger clubs in the country were featured on national television and wanted to establish whether the clubs would be interested in a larger share of television rights money. The five clubs decided it was a good idea and decided to press ahead with it; however, the league would have no credibility without the backing of The Football Association and so David Dein of Arsenal held talks to see whether the FA were receptive to the idea. The FA did not enjoy an amicable relationship with the Football League at the time and considered it as a way to weaken the Football League's position.
rewrite: In 1990, Greg Dyke, the managing director of London Weekend Television (LWT), held a meeting with representatives from England's "big five" football clubs. His aim was to explore the possibility of a breakaway from The Football League. Dyke's belief was that featuring only the larger clubs on national television would prove more lucrative for LWT, and he sought to gauge their interest in securing a larger portion of television rights revenue. The clubs, receptive to the idea, agreed to proceed. Recognizing that any new league would lack credibility without the support of The Football Association, David Dein of Arsenal initiated talks to determine the FA's receptiveness. At the time, the FA's relationship with the Football League was strained, and it viewed the proposal as a potential means to weaken the League's standing.

input: In abstract algebra, more general structures are defined by relaxing some of the axioms defining a group. For example, if the requirement that every element has an inverse is eliminated, the resulting algebraic structure is called a monoid. The natural numbers N (including 0) under addition form a monoid, as do the nonzero integers under multiplication (Z ∖ {0}, ·), see above. There is a general method to formally add inverses to elements to any (abelian) monoid, much the same way as (Q ∖ {0}, ·) is derived from (Z ∖ {0}, ·), known as the Grothendieck group. Groupoids are similar to groups except that the composition a • b need not be defined for all a and b. They arise in the study of more complicated forms of symmetry, often in topological and analytical structures, such as the fundamental groupoid or stacks. Finally, it is possible to generalize any of these concepts by replacing the binary operation with an arbitrary n-ary one (i.e. an operation taking n arguments). With the proper generalization of the group axioms this gives rise to an n-ary group. The table gives a list of several structures generalizing groups.
rewrite: By relaxing certain group axioms, abstract algebra introduces more general structures. For instance, removing the requirement for every element to have an inverse yields a monoid. Examples include the natural numbers under addition (including zero) and the nonzero integers under multiplication. A formal method exists to add inverses to any abelian monoid, known as constructing the Grothendieck group, analogous to how the nonzero rationals arise from the nonzero integers. Another generalization is the groupoid, where the composition operation need not be defined for every pair of elements. Groupoids emerge in analyzing complex symmetries within topological and analytical contexts, such as fundamental groupoids or stacks. Furthermore, these concepts can be extended by replacing the binary operation with an n-ary operation (taking n arguments), leading to n-ary groups when appropriate axioms are adapted. The accompanying table summarizes various structures that generalize groups.

input: The most notable cricket club in Cork is Cork County Cricket Club, which was formed in 1874. Although located within the Munster jurisdiction, the club plays in the Leinster Senior League. The club plays at the Mardyke, a ground which has hosted three first-class matches in 1947, 1961 and 1973. All three involved Ireland playing Scotland. The Cork Cricket Academy operates within the city, with the stated aim of introducing the sport to schools in the city and county. Cork's other main cricket club, Harlequins Cricket Club, play close to Cork Airport.
rewrite: Cork County Cricket Club, established in 1874, is the city's most prominent cricket club. Despite being in Munster, it competes in the Leinster Senior League. Its home ground, the Mardyke, hosted three first-class matches in 1947, 1961, and 1973, all between Ireland and Scotland. Meanwhile, the Cork Cricket Academy works to introduce the sport to local schools. The other primary club, Harlequins Cricket Club, is situated near Cork Airport.

input: Throughout its prehistory and early history, the region and its vicinity in the Yangtze region was the cradle of unique local civilizations which can be dated back to at least the 15th century BC and coinciding with the later years of the Shang and Zhou dynasties in North China. Sichuan was referred to in ancient Chinese sources as Ba-Shu (巴蜀), an abbreviation of the kingdoms of Ba and Shu which existed within the Sichuan Basin. Ba included Chongqing and the land in eastern Sichuan along the Yangtze and some tributary streams, while Shu included today's Chengdu, its surrounding plain and adjacent territories in western Sichuan.
rewrite: The ancient region of Ba-Shu, encompassing present-day Sichuan and Chongqing, was home to unique civilizations dating back to at least the 15th century BC. This period in the Yangtze region coincided with the later phases of the Shang and Zhou dynasties in North China. The name Ba-Shu derives from the two kingdoms that occupied the Sichuan Basin. The kingdom of Ba covered eastern areas, including Chongqing and lands along the Yangtze and its tributaries. Meanwhile, Shu was centered on the Chengdu plain and the adjacent western territories.

input: In addressing the question of who invented the incandescent lamp, historians Robert Friedel and Paul Israel list 22 inventors of incandescent lamps prior to Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison. They conclude that Edison's version was able to outstrip the others because of a combination of three factors: an effective incandescent material, a higher vacuum than others were able to achieve (by use of the Sprengel pump) and a high resistance that made power distribution from a centralized source economically viable.
rewrite: Historians Robert Friedel and Paul Israel note that 22 inventors created incandescent lamps before Joseph Swan and Thomas Edison. They argue Edison's design surpassed all others due to three key elements: a superior incandescent material, a higher vacuum achieved with the Sprengel pump, and a high resistance enabling cost-effective centralized power distribution.

input: Literature consists of written productions, often restricted to those deemed to have artistic or intellectual value. Its Latin root literatura/litteratura (derived itself from littera, letter or handwriting) was used to refer to all written accounts, but intertwined with the roman concept of cultura: learning or cultivation. Literature often uses language differently than ordinary language (see literariness). Literature can be classified according to whether it is fiction or non-fiction and whether it is poetry or prose; it can be further distinguished according to major forms such as the novel, short story or drama; and works are often categorised according to historical periods or their adherence to certain aesthetic features or expectations (genre).
rewrite: Derived from the Latin *literatura*, itself from *littera* (letter), literature originally meant all written accounts, a concept intertwined with Roman *cultura*, or cultivation. Today, it typically refers to writings credited with artistic or intellectual value. Its language often differs from ordinary speech, a quality called literariness. Works are classified as fiction or non-fiction and as poetry or prose. Further distinctions include major forms like the novel, short story, or drama. Additionally, literature is often categorized by historical periods or by genre, which denotes adherence to specific aesthetic features and expectations.

input: The court ruled in 2014, after lengthy testimony, that at least two districts had to be redrawn because of gerrymandering. After this was appealed, in July 2015 the Florida Supreme Court ruled that lawmakers had followed an illegal and unconstitutional process overly influenced by party operatives, and ruled that at least eight districts had to be redrawn. On December 2, 2015, a 5-2 majority of the Court accepted a new map of congressional districts, some of which was drawn by challengers. Their ruling affirmed the map previously approved by Leon County Judge Terry Lewis, who had overseen the original trial. It particularly makes changes in South Florida. There are likely to be additional challenges to the map and districts.
rewrite: Following lengthy testimony, a 2014 court ruling mandated the redrawing of at least two districts due to gerrymandering. Upon appeal, the Florida Supreme Court decided in July 2015 that the process had been illegally and unconstitutionally shaped by party operatives, ordering at least eight districts to be revised. A new congressional map, partially drawn by challengers, was later accepted by a 5-2 Court majority on December 2, 2015. This ruling affirmed a map earlier approved by Leon County Judge Terry Lewis, who oversaw the initial trial, with changes particularly focused in South Florida. Further challenges to the map and districts are anticipated.

input: All signatories to the CPPCG are required to prevent and punish acts of genocide, both in peace and wartime, though some barriers make this enforcement difficult. In particular, some of the signatories—namely, Bahrain, Bangladesh, India, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, the United States, Vietnam, Yemen, and former Yugoslavia—signed with the proviso that no claim of genocide could be brought against them at the International Court of Justice without their consent. Despite official protests from other signatories (notably Cyprus and Norway) on the ethics and legal standing of these reservations, the immunity from prosecution they grant has been invoked from time to time, as when the United States refused to allow a charge of genocide brought against it by former Yugoslavia following the 1999 Kosovo War.
rewrite: The Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (CPPCG) obligates all signatories to prevent and punish genocide during peace and war. However, enforcement faces obstacles. Several nations—including Bahrain, Bangladesh, India, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, the United States, Vietnam, Yemen, and the former Yugoslavia—ratified the treaty with a specific reservation. This condition stipulates that no genocide claim can be brought against them at the International Court of Justice without their explicit consent. Countries like Cyprus and Norway have formally protested the ethics and legality of these reservations. Nevertheless, the conferred immunity has been utilized, such as when the United States rejected a genocide charge filed by the former Yugoslavia after the 1999 Kosovo War.

input: In the high villages people live in homes built according to medieval designs that withstand cold winters. The kitchen is separated from the living area (called the stube, the area of the home heated by a stove), and second-floor bedrooms benefit from rising heat. The typical Swiss chalet originated in the Bernese Oberland. Chalets often face south or downhill, and are built of solid wood, with a steeply gabled roof to allow accumulated snow to slide off easily. Stairs leading to upper levels are sometimes built on the outside, and balconies are sometimes enclosed.
rewrite: Homes in the high villages follow medieval designs to endure cold winters. Originating in the Bernese Oberland, the classic Swiss chalet is built of solid wood, often facing south or downhill. Its steeply gabled roof allows snow to slide off easily. Inside, the kitchen is separate from the heated living area, or stube, with second-floor bedrooms warmed by rising heat. Exterior stairs sometimes lead to upper levels, and balconies are occasionally enclosed.

input: Like other governmental economic activities, also privatization, such as in the sale of government-owned property, is particularly at the risk of cronyism. Privatizations in Russia, Latin America, and East Germany were accompanied by large-scale corruption during the sale of the state owned companies. Those with political connections unfairly gained large wealth, which has discredited privatization in these regions. While media have reported widely the grand corruption that accompanied the sales, studies have argued that in addition to increased operating efficiency, daily petty corruption is, or would be, larger without privatization, and that corruption is more prevalent in non-privatized sectors. Furthermore, there is evidence to suggest that extralegal and unofficial activities are more prevalent in countries that privatized less.
rewrite: Privatization, such as the sale of government property, faces a high risk of cronyism, like other state economic activities. The sales of state-owned companies in Russia, Latin America, and East Germany involved large-scale corruption, allowing those with political ties to amass unfair wealth and discrediting the process in these areas. Although media widely cover such grand corruption, studies contend that daily petty corruption is or would be greater without privatization, citing increased operational efficiency and more prevalent corruption in non-privatized sectors. Additionally, evidence indicates that extralegal and unofficial activities are more common in countries with less privatization.

input: Marvel held its own comic book convention, Marvelcon '75, in spring 1975, and promised a Marvelcon '76. At the 1975 event, Stan Lee used a Fantastic Four panel discussion to announce that Jack Kirby, the artist co-creator of most of Marvel's signature characters, was returning to Marvel after having left in 1970 to work for rival DC Comics. In October 1976, Marvel, which already licensed reprints in different countries, including the UK, created a superhero specifically for the British market. Captain Britain debuted exclusively in the UK, and later appeared in American comics.
rewrite: In spring 1975, Marvel hosted its own convention, Marvelcon '75, and pledged a follow-up for 1976. During a Fantastic Four panel there, Stan Lee announced artist Jack Kirby's return. Kirby, co-creator of most major Marvel characters, had left for DC Comics in 1970. Separately, by October 1976, Marvel—already licensing reprints internationally—developed a superhero for the British market. Captain Britain thus debuted exclusively in the UK before later appearing in American comics.

input: Caesar became consul in 59 BC. His colleague, Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus, was an extreme aristocrat. Caesar submitted the laws that he had promised Pompey to the assemblies. Bibulus attempted to obstruct the enactment of these laws, and so Caesar used violent means to ensure their passage. Caesar was then made governor of three provinces. He facilitated the election of the former patrician Publius Clodius Pulcher to the tribunate for 58 BC. Clodius set about depriving Caesar's senatorial enemies of two of their more obstinate leaders in Cato and Cicero. Clodius was a bitter opponent of Cicero because Cicero had testified against him in a sacrilege case. Clodius attempted to try Cicero for executing citizens without a trial during the Catiline conspiracy, resulting in Cicero going into self-imposed exile and his house in Rome being burnt down. Clodius also passed a bill that forced Cato to lead the invasion of Cyprus which would keep him away from Rome for some years. Clodius also passed a law to expand the previous partial grain subsidy to a fully free grain dole for citizens.
rewrite: In 59 BC, Caesar attained the consulship alongside his colleague, the staunch aristocrat Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus. To fulfill promises made to Pompey, Caesar presented laws to the public assemblies. When Bibulus moved to obstruct their passage, Caesar resorted to force to push them through. Subsequently appointed governor of three provinces, Caesar then engineered the election of the former patrician Publius Clodius Pulcher to the tribunate for 58 BC. Clodius, a bitter enemy of Cicero due to the orator's testimony against him in a sacrilege case, targeted Caesar's senatorial opponents. He prosecuted Cicero for executing citizens without trial during the Catiline conspiracy, driving Cicero into exile and seeing his Roman house destroyed. Furthermore, Clodius passed a bill compelling Cato to lead the Cyprus invasion, thus removing him from Rome for years. Additionally, he enacted a law transforming the existing partial grain subsidy into a fully free grain dole for citizens.

input: In the early 1970s (1973, to be particular) when the military junta took over power in Uruguay, art suffered in Montevideo. The art studios went into protest mode, with Rimer Cardillo, one of the country's leading artists, making the National Institute of Fine Arts, Montevideo a "hotbed of resistance". This resulted in the military junta coming down heavily on artists by closing the Fine Art Institute and carting away all the presses and other studio equipment. Consequently, the learning of fine arts was only in private studios run by people who had been let out of jail, in works of printing and on paper and also painting and sculpture. It resumed much later.
rewrite: When the military junta seized control of Uruguay in 1973, artistic life in Montevideo was severely impacted. Leading artist Rimer Cardillo transformed the National Institute of Fine Arts into a center of protest, a "hotbed of resistance." In heavy-handed response, the junta shut down the Institute, confiscating all presses and studio equipment. Thereafter, fine arts education persisted only privately, conducted by former political prisoners through printing, works on paper, painting, and sculpture. This clandestine form of learning continued until its official revival occurred much later.

input: Native American music in North America is almost entirely monophonic, but there are notable exceptions. Traditional Native American music often centers around drumming. Rattles, clappersticks, and rasps were also popular percussive instruments. Flutes were made of rivercane, cedar, and other woods. The tuning of these flutes is not precise and depends on the length of the wood used and the hand span of the intended player, but the finger holes are most often around a whole step apart and, at least in Northern California, a flute was not used if it turned out to have an interval close to a half step. The Apache fiddle is a single stringed instrument.
rewrite: Traditional Native American music in North America is predominantly monophonic, with drumming as a central element. Other common percussive instruments include rattles, clappersticks, and rasps. Flutes, crafted from materials like rivercane and cedar, feature a tuning that is not exact. Their pitch relies on the wood's length and the player's hand span, with finger holes typically spaced about a whole step apart. Notably, in Northern California, a flute would be avoided if it produced an interval nearing a half step. Among stringed instruments, the Apache fiddle, with its single string, is a notable exception.

input: A revolution in 1332 resulted in a broad-based city government with participation of the guilds, and Strasbourg declared itself a free republic. The deadly bubonic plague of 1348 was followed on 14 February 1349 by one of the first and worst pogroms in pre-modern history: over a thousand Jews were publicly burnt to death, with the remainder of the Jewish population being expelled from the city. Until the end of the 18th century, Jews were forbidden to remain in town after 10 pm. The time to leave the city was signalled by a municipal herald blowing the Grüselhorn (see below, Museums, Musée historique);. A special tax, the Pflastergeld (pavement money), was furthermore to be paid for any horse that a Jew would ride or bring into the city while allowed to.
rewrite: In 1332, a revolution established a broad-based city government involving the guilds, leading Strasbourg to declare itself a free republic. Following the deadly bubonic plague of 1348, one of the earliest and most severe pogroms in pre-modern history occurred on 14 February 1349; over a thousand Jews were publicly burned, and the rest were expelled. Thereafter, until the late 18th century, Jews were prohibited from staying in town after 10 pm, with a municipal herald blowing the Grüselhorn to signal the departure time. Additionally, a special tax called the Pflastergeld was imposed for any horse a Jew rode or brought into the city during permitted hours.

input: Valleys and plains are found along the coastline and rivers. The north of the province lies just south of the Yangtze Delta, and consists of plains around the cities of Hangzhou, Jiaxing, and Huzhou, where the Grand Canal of China enters from the northern border to end at Hangzhou. Another relatively flat area is found along the Qu River around the cities of Quzhou and Jinhua. Major rivers include the Qiangtang and Ou Rivers. Most rivers carve out valleys in the highlands, with plenty of rapids and other features associated with such topography. Well-known lakes include the West Lake of Hangzhou and the South Lake of Jiaxing.
rewrite: Along the coastline and rivers, valleys and plains characterize the landscape. The province's northern section, situated just south of the Yangtze Delta, features plains around Hangzhou, Jiaxing, and Huzhou; here, the Grand Canal of China crosses the northern border to terminate at Hangzhou. Another flat area surrounds the Qu River near Quzhou and Jinhua. Major rivers like the Qiangtang and Ou carve valleys through the highlands, creating numerous rapids and related topographic features. Notable lakes include Hangzhou's West Lake and Jiaxing's South Lake.

input: After almost a year in the area around Peenemünde, Soviet officials moved most of the captured German rocket specialists to Gorodomlya Island on Lake Seliger, about 240 kilometers (150 mi) northwest of Moscow. They were not allowed to participate in Soviet missile design, but were used as problem-solving consultants to the Soviet engineers. They helped in the following areas: the creation of a Soviet version of the A-4; work on "organizational schemes"; research in improving the A-4 main engine; development of a 100-ton engine; assistance in the "layout" of plant production rooms; and preparation of rocket assembly using German components. With their help, particularly Helmut Groettrup's group, Korolev reverse-engineered the A-4 and built his own version of the rocket, the R-1, in 1948. Later, he developed his own distinct designs, though many of these designs were influenced by the Groettrup Group's G4-R10 design from 1949. The Germans were eventually repatriated in 1951–53.
rewrite: Following nearly a year near Peenemünde, the captured German rocket specialists were relocated by Soviet officials to Gorodomlya Island on Lake Seliger, roughly 240 kilometers northwest of Moscow. Their role was not direct involvement in Soviet missile design, but rather to serve as consultants who solved problems for Soviet engineers. Their assistance proved crucial in several key areas: developing a Soviet variant of the A-4 rocket, refining organizational plans, researching improvements to the A-4 main engine, designing a 100-ton engine, aiding in the layout of production facilities, and preparing rocket assemblies from German parts. Notably, with help from Helmut Groettrup's team, Sergei Korolev reverse-engineered the A-4 to produce his own version, the R-1, by 1948. While Korolev later pursued his own distinct designs, many were influenced by the Groettrup Group's 1949 G4-R10 concept. The German specialists were finally repatriated between 1951 and 1953.

input: Various evolutionary ideas had already been proposed to explain new findings in biology. There was growing support for such ideas among dissident anatomists and the general public, but during the first half of the 19th century the English scientific establishment was closely tied to the Church of England, while science was part of natural theology. Ideas about the transmutation of species were controversial as they conflicted with the beliefs that species were unchanging parts of a designed hierarchy and that humans were unique, unrelated to other animals. The political and theological implications were intensely debated, but transmutation was not accepted by the scientific mainstream.
rewrite: During the first half of the 19th century, the English scientific establishment remained closely linked to the Church of England, with science viewed as a component of natural theology. This context made ideas about the transmutation of species highly controversial. Such proposals, which had been advanced to explain new biological findings, directly challenged the prevailing beliefs in a fixed, designed hierarchy of unchanging species and in humanity's unique, separate status from animals. Although these evolutionary concepts gained support among some dissident anatomists and the wider public, and their political and theological implications were hotly debated, transmutation was not embraced by the scientific mainstream.

input: In May 1967, the Eastern Region declared independence as a state called the Republic of Biafra, under the leadership of Lt. Colonel Emeka Ojukwu. The Nigerian Civil War began as the official Nigerian government side (predominated by soldiers from the North and West) attacked Biafra (Southeastern) on 6 July 1967 at Garkem. The 30 month war, with a long siege of Biafra and its isolation from trade and supplies, ended in January 1970. Estimates of the number of dead in the former Eastern Region are between 1 and 3 million people, from warfare, disease, and starvation, during the 30-month civil war.
rewrite: Under Lt. Colonel Emeka Ojukwu's leadership, the Eastern Region proclaimed itself the independent Republic of Biafra in May 1967. The Nigerian Civil War commenced on 6 July 1967 when federal forces, primarily from the North and West, launched an attack at Garkem against the Southeastern Biafrans. Lasting for 30 months, the conflict involved a prolonged siege that cut Biafra off from trade and supplies, concluding in January 1970. Warfare, disease, and starvation during this period resulted in an estimated 1 to 3 million deaths in the former Eastern Region.

input: Meleager and the infantry supported the candidacy of Alexander's half-brother, Philip Arrhidaeus, while Perdiccas, the leading cavalry commander, supported waiting until the birth of Alexander's unborn child by Roxana. After the infantry stormed the palace of Babylon, a compromise was arranged – Arrhidaeus (as Philip III) should become king, and should rule jointly with Roxana's child, assuming that it was a boy (as it was, becoming Alexander IV). Perdiccas himself would become regent (epimeletes) of the empire, and Meleager his lieutenant. Soon, however, Perdiccas had Meleager and the other infantry leaders murdered, and assumed full control. The generals who had supported Perdiccas were rewarded in the partition of Babylon by becoming satraps of the various parts of the empire, but Perdiccas' position was shaky, because, as Arrian writes, "everyone was suspicious of him, and he of them".
rewrite: Meleager, backed by the infantry, advocated for Philip Arrhidaeus, Alexander the Great’s half-brother, to become king. In contrast, the cavalry commander Perdiccas favored awaiting the birth of Alexander’s posthumous child by Roxana. Following a storming of the Babylonian palace by the infantry, a settlement was reached. Philip III (Arrhidaeus) would rule jointly with Roxana’s son if the child were male—which he was, becoming Alexander IV. Perdiccas was appointed regent, with Meleager as his lieutenant. This arrangement proved fleeting, as Perdiccas soon ordered the murder of Meleager and other infantry commanders, seizing full authority. His supporting generals were granted satrapies in the ensuing Partition of Babylon. Yet Perdiccas’s control remained precarious, for, as Arrian noted, a mutual suspicion pervaded: "everyone was suspicious of him, and he of them."

input: In 1873, one of the first papers in modern medicine on the subject tried to explain the pathophysiology of the disease while one in 1872, concluded that asthma can be cured by rubbing the chest with chloroform liniment. Medical treatment in 1880, included the use of intravenous doses of a drug called pilocarpin. In 1886, F.H. Bosworth theorized a connection between asthma and hay fever. Epinephrine was first referred to in the treatment of asthma in 1905. Oral corticosteroids began to be used for this condition in the 1950s while inhaled corticosteroids and selective short acting beta agonist came into wide use in the 1960s.
rewrite: Early attempts to understand and treat asthma varied widely. An 1872 paper claimed chest-rubbing with chloroform liniment could cure it, while an 1873 study sought to explain the disease's pathophysiology. By 1880, treatment involved intravenous pilocarpin. F.H. Bosworth proposed a link between asthma and hay fever in 1886. The use of epinephrine was first noted in 1905. Oral corticosteroids emerged in the 1950s, followed by the widespread adoption of inhaled corticosteroids and selective short-acting beta agonists in the 1960s.

input: In January 2008, Kaz Hirai, CEO of Sony Computer Entertainment, suggested that the console may start making a profit by early 2009, stating that, "the next fiscal year starts in April and if we can try to achieve that in the next fiscal year that would be a great thing" and that "[profitability] is not a definite commitment, but that is what I would like to try to shoot for". However, market analysts Nikko Citigroup have predicted that PlayStation 3 could be profitable by August 2008. In a July 2008 interview, Hirai stated that his objective is for PlayStation 3 to sell 150 million units by its ninth year, surpassing PlayStation 2's sales of 140 million in its nine years on the market. In January 2009 Sony announced that their gaming division was profitable in Q3 2008.
rewrite: In early 2008, Sony Computer Entertainment CEO Kaz Hirai expressed a target for the PlayStation 3 console to become profitable in the fiscal year starting April 2009, calling it a goal rather than a firm commitment. This contrasted with market analysts Nikko Citigroup, who had forecast the console could reach profitability as soon as August 2008. By July of that year, Hirai had set a further long-term objective: for the PlayStation 3 to surpass the PlayStation 2's lifetime sales of 140 million units by selling 150 million over its first nine years. Ultimately, Sony announced in January 2009 that its gaming division had already returned to profitability in the third quarter of 2008.

input: Besides emptiness, Mahayana schools often place emphasis on the notions of perfected spiritual insight (prajñāpāramitā) and Buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha). There are conflicting interpretations of the tathāgatagarbha in Mahāyāna thought. The idea may be traced to Abhidharma, and ultimately to statements of the Buddha in the Nikāyas. In Tibetan Buddhism, according to the Sakya school, tathāgatagarbha is the inseparability of the clarity and emptiness of one's mind. In Nyingma, tathāgatagarbha also generally refers to inseparability of the clarity and emptiness of one's mind. According to the Gelug school, it is the potential for sentient beings to awaken since they are empty (i.e. dependently originated). According to the Jonang school, it refers to the innate qualities of the mind that expresses themselves as omniscience etc. when adventitious obscurations are removed. The "Tathāgatagarbha Sutras" are a collection of Mahayana sutras that present a unique model of Buddha-nature. Even though this collection was generally ignored in India, East Asian Buddhism provides some significance to these texts.
rewrite: Mahayana schools frequently highlight not only emptiness but also perfected spiritual insight (prajñāpāramitā) and Buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha). The interpretation of tathāgatagarbha within Mahāyāna thought varies. This concept, traceable to Abhidharma and ultimately to the Buddha’s statements in the Nikāyas, is understood differently across traditions. In Tibetan Buddhism, the Sakya and Nyingma schools both generally define it as the inseparability of the clarity and emptiness of one's mind. The Gelug school views it as the potential for sentient beings to awaken, rooted in their empty, dependently originated nature. For the Jonang school, it denotes the mind's innate qualities, such as omniscience, which manifest when adventitious obscurations are cleared. Presenting a distinct model of Buddha-nature, the "Tathāgatagarbha Sutras" form a collection of Mahayana texts. While largely overlooked in India, these sutras hold some significance in East Asian Buddhism.

input: In 1978, Josep Lluís Núñez became the first elected president of FC Barcelona, and, since then, the members of Barcelona have elected the club president. The process of electing a president of FC Barcelona was closely tied to Spain's transition to democracy in 1974 and the end of Franco's dictatorship. The new president's main objective was to develop Barcelona into a world-class club by giving it stability both on and off the pitch. His presidency was to last for 22 years, and it deeply affected the image of Barcelona, as Núñez held to a strict policy regarding wages and discipline, letting go of such players as Maradona, Romário and Ronaldo rather than meeting their demands.
rewrite: The election of FC Barcelona's president by its members began in 1978 with Josep Lluís Núñez, a process linked to Spain's democratic transition after Franco's dictatorship. His primary goal was to build Barcelona into a world-class club with stability on and off the field. Núñez's 22-year presidency profoundly shaped the club's identity through a strict wage and discipline policy. This approach led to the departures of star players like Maradona, Romário, and Ronaldo when their demands were not met.

input: The United Kingdom's constitution, being uncodified and largely unwritten, makes no mention of a prime minister. Though it had de facto existed for centuries, its first mention in official state documents did not occur until the first decade of the twentieth century. Accordingly, it is often said "not to exist", indeed there are several instances of parliament declaring this to be the case. The prime minister sits in the cabinet solely by virtue of occupying another office, either First Lord of the Treasury (office in commission), or more rarely Chancellor of the Exchequer (the last of whom was Balfour in 1905).
rewrite: Unlike many nations, the United Kingdom lacks a single, written constitution, and its foundational documents do not formally establish the office of prime minister. The role, which had operated in practice for centuries, only received its first official mention in state papers in the early 1900s. Consequently, it has often been declared, even by Parliament itself, to "not exist." The prime minister gains a place in the cabinet only through holding another position, typically that of First Lord of the Treasury, or, less commonly, Chancellor of the Exchequer, as was last the case with Balfour in 1905.

input: The earliest known avialan fossils come from the Tiaojishan Formation of China, which has been dated to the late Jurassic period (Oxfordian stage), about 160 million years ago. The avialan species from this time period include Anchiornis huxleyi, Xiaotingia zhengi, and Aurornis xui. The well-known early avialan, Archaeopteryx, dates from slightly later Jurassic rocks (about 155 million years old) from Germany. Many of these early avialans shared unusual anatomical features that may be ancestral to modern birds, but were later lost during bird evolution. These features include enlarged claws on the second toe which may have been held clear of the ground in life, and long feathers or "hind wings" covering the hind limbs and feet, which may have been used in aerial maneuvering.
rewrite: Fossils of the earliest known avialans, dating to approximately 160 million years ago (the Oxfordian stage of the late Jurassic), are found in China's Tiaojishan Formation. This period includes species such as *Anchiornis huxleyi*, *Xiaotingia zhengi*, and *Aurornis xui*. Slightly younger, at about 155 million years old, is the famous early avialan *Archaeopteryx* from German Jurassic deposits. These ancient species possessed distinctive anatomical traits, possibly ancestral to modern birds but later abandoned in evolution. Among these were enlarged second-toe claws, likely held off the ground, and long hind-limb feathers or "hind wings" that might have assisted in aerial maneuvering.

input: Also in 2005, Spielberg directed a modern adaptation of War of the Worlds (a co-production of Paramount and DreamWorks), based on the H. G. rewrite: In 2005, Steven Spielberg directed a modern adaptation of *War of the Worlds*, based on H.G. Wells's novel, which he had long admired along with the 1953 film. This Paramount and DreamWorks co-production starred Tom Cruise and Dakota Fanning and featured visual effects by Industrial Light & Magic (ILM), a frequent collaborator. input: Alongside the capital, the most popular tourist destinations are Isfahan, Mashhad and Shiraz. In the early 2000s, the industry faced serious limitations in infrastructure, communications, industry standards and personnel training. The majority of the 300,000 tourist visas granted in 2003 were obtained by Asian Muslims, who presumably intended to visit important pilgrimage sites in Mashhad and Qom. Several organized tours from Germany, France and other European countries come to Iran annually to visit archaeological sites and monuments. In 2003, Iran ranked 68th in tourism revenues worldwide. According to UNESCO and the deputy head of research for Iran Travel and Tourism Organization (ITTO), Iran is rated 4th among the top 10 destinations in the Middle East. Domestic tourism in Iran is one of the largest in the world. Weak advertising, unstable regional conditions, a poor public image in some parts of the world, and absence of efficient planning schemes in the tourism sector have all hindered the growth of tourism.
rewrite: While Isfahan, Mashhad, and Shiraz rank among Iran’s top tourist draws alongside the capital, the industry’s growth has been constrained. In the early 2000s, it faced significant challenges in infrastructure, communications, standards, and training. Notably, domestic tourism within Iran is one of the largest globally. Yet, international figures from 2003 show Iran placed only 68th worldwide in tourism revenues, with the majority of its 300,000 tourist visas that year granted to Asian Muslims visiting pilgrimage sites like Mashhad and Qom. Although organized tours from European nations such as Germany and France regularly visit Iran’s archaeological sites, broader expansion is hampered by weak advertising, regional instability, a negative international image in some regions, and a lack of efficient tourism planning. Despite these hurdles, Iran holds the 4th position among the top ten Middle Eastern destinations, according to UNESCO and Iran Travel and Tourism Organization research.

input: During the Reformation, the term was hardly used outside of the German politics. The word evangelical (German: evangelisch), which refers to the gospel, was much more widely used for those involved in the religious movement. Nowadays, this word is still preferred among some of the historical Protestant denominations, above all the ones in the German-speaking area such as the EKD. The German word evangelisch means Protestant, and is different from the German evangelikal, which refers to churches shaped by Evangelicalism. The English word evangelical usually refers to Evangelical Protestant churches, and therefore not to Protestantism as a whole. It traces its roots back to the Puritans in England, where Evangelicalism originated, and then was brought to the United States. The word reformatorisch is used as an alternative for evangelisch in German, and is different from English reformed (German: reformiert), which refers to churches shaped by ideas of John Calvin, Huldrych Zwingli and other Reformed theologians.
rewrite: The term was rarely employed outside German politics during the Reformation. Instead, the word "evangelisch" (from the gospel) was far more common for describing participants in the religious movement. This preference persists today among some historical Protestant denominations, particularly in German-speaking regions like the EKD. It is crucial to distinguish the German "evangelisch," meaning Protestant generally, from "evangelikal," which denotes churches shaped by Evangelicalism. Similarly, in English, "evangelical" typically specifies Evangelical Protestant churches rather than all of Protestantism. This English usage has roots in the Puritan movements of England, Evangelicalism's birthplace, before spreading to the United States. Meanwhile, in German, "reformatorisch" serves as another word for "evangelisch." This differs from the English "reformed" (German: "reformiert"), which specifically describes churches influenced by John Calvin, Huldrych Zwingli, and other Reformed theologians.

input: Roofs are traditionally constructed from Alpine rocks such as pieces of schist, gneiss or slate. Such chalets are typically found in the higher parts of the valleys, as in the Maurienne valley in Savoy, where the amount of snow during the cold months is important. The inclination of the roof cannot exceed 40%, allowing the snow to stay on top, thereby functioning as insulation from the cold. In the lower areas where the forests are widespread, wooden tiles are traditionally used. Commonly made of Norway spruce, they are called "tavaillon". The Alpine regions are multicultural and linguistically diverse. Dialects are common, and vary from valley to valley and region to region. In the Slavic Alps alone 19 dialects have been identified. Some of the French dialects spoken in the French, Swiss and Italian alps of Aosta Valley derive from Arpitan, while the southern part of the western range is related to Old Provençal; the German dialects derive from Germanic tribal languages. Romansh, spoken by two percent of the population in southeast Switzerland, is an ancient Rhaeto-Romanic language derived from Latin, remnants of ancient Celtic languages and perhaps Etruscan.
rewrite: In the higher valley areas, such as Savoy's Maurienne valley, where significant snow accumulates in winter, traditional chalet roofs are constructed from local Alpine rocks like schist, gneiss, or slate. These roofs are intentionally built with an inclination not exceeding 40%, which allows snow to remain atop them, serving as a layer of insulation against the cold. Conversely, in lower, more forested areas, wooden tiles known as "tavaillon"—commonly made from Norway spruce—are the traditional roofing material. The Alps are marked by considerable multicultural and linguistic diversity, with dialects shifting from one valley and region to another. For instance, nineteen distinct dialects have been identified just within the Slavic Alps. French dialects in the French, Swiss, and Italian Aosta Valley Alps often stem from Arpitan, while those in the southern western range relate to Old Provençal. German dialects originate from ancient Germanic tribal languages. Additionally, Romansh, spoken by a small percentage in southeastern Switzerland, is an ancient Rhaeto-Romanic language with roots in Latin, along with remnants of Celtic and possibly Etruscan influences.

input: There was a linguistic predisposition to use such terms. The Romans had used them in near Gaul / far Gaul, near Spain / far Spain and others. Before them the Greeks had the habit, which appears in Linear B, the oldest known script of Europe, referring to the near province and the far province of the kingdom of Pylos. Usually these terms were given with reference to a geographic feature, such as a mountain range or a river.
rewrite: The practice of using terms like "near" and "far" has deep linguistic roots. Greeks, as seen in Europe's oldest script, Linear B, designated Pylos's near and far provinces. Romans later applied this to regions like Gaul and Spain. Typically, these distinctions were made in relation to a geographical feature, such as a river or mountain range.

input: Winter, and a deteriorating supply situation on both sides of troops and materiel, led to a halt in ground operations. Sevastopol remained invested by the allies, while the allied armies were hemmed in by the Russian army in the interior. On 14 November a storm sank thirty allied transport ships including HMS Prince which was carrying a cargo of winter clothing.:435 The storm and heavy traffic caused the road from the coast to the troops to disintegrate into a quagmire, requiring engineers to devote most of their time to its repair including quarrying stone. A tramroad was ordered. It arrived in January with a civilian engineering crew, however it was March before it was sufficiently advanced to be of any appreciable value.:439 An Electrical telegraph was also ordered, but the frozen ground delayed its installation until March, when communications from the base port of Balaklava to the British HQ was established. The Pipe-and-cable-laying plough failed because of the hard frozen soil, but even so 21 miles of cable were laid.:449
rewrite: Winter brought worsening shortages of troops and supplies to both sides, halting all ground operations. While the allies maintained their siege of Sevastopol, their own armies were in turn confined by Russian forces in the interior. A fierce storm on 14 November sank thirty allied transport vessels, among them HMS *Prince*, which had been carrying vital winter clothing. This tempest, combined with relentless military traffic, turned the crucial road from the coast into an impassable quagmire. Engineers were forced to spend most of their time repairing it, even quarrying stone for the purpose. A tramroad was commissioned, arriving with a civilian crew in January, yet it was not until March that it became truly useful. An electrical telegraph was also ordered, but frozen ground delayed its setup until spring, when a line was finally completed from Balaklava to British headquarters. Attempts to use a pipe-and-cable-laying plough failed against the hardened earth, though twenty-one miles of cable were still installed.

input: In November 1790, François-Louis-Thibault de Menonville, a member of the National Assembly of France, wrote to Burke, praising Reflections and requesting more "very refreshing mental food" that he could publish. This Burke did in April 1791 when he published A Letter to a Member of the National Assembly. Burke called for external forces to reverse the revolution and included an attack on the late French philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau, as being the subject of a personality cult that had developed in revolutionary France. Although Burke conceded that Rousseau sometimes showed "a considerable insight into human nature" he mostly was critical. Although he did not meet Rousseau on his visit to Britain in 1766–7 Burke was a friend of David Hume, with whom Rousseau had stayed. Burke said Rousseau "entertained no principle either to influence of his heart, or to guide his understanding—but vanity"—which he "was possessed to a degree little short of madness". He also cited Rousseau's Confessions as evidence that Rousseau had a life of "obscure and vulgar vices" that was not "chequered, or spotted here and there, with virtues, or even distinguished by a single good action". Burke contrasted Rousseau's theory of universal benevolence and his having sent his children to a foundling hospital: "a lover of his kind, but a hater of his kindred".
rewrite: In April 1791, Edmund Burke published *A Letter to a Member of the National Assembly*. This work was a response to a request made months earlier, in November 1790, by François-Louis-Thibault de Menonville, a member of that Assembly. Menonville had written to Burke praising his *Reflections on the Revolution in France* and asking for more of what he called "very refreshing mental food" suitable for publication. In the *Letter*, Burke issued a call for external forces to overturn the French Revolution. The text also contained a fierce critique of the late philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau, whom Burke accused of being the object of a personality cult in revolutionary France. While granting that Rousseau occasionally demonstrated "a considerable insight into human nature," Burke’s assessment was overwhelmingly negative. Though Burke had not met Rousseau during the latter's 1766–7 visit to Britain, he was a friend of David Hume, who had hosted Rousseau. Burke asserted that Rousseau "entertained no principle either to influence of his heart, or to guide his understanding—but vanity," a trait he possessed "to a degree little short of madness." Citing Rousseau's *Confessions*, Burke portrayed his life as one of "obscure and vulgar vices," unrelieved by virtue or "a single good action." He highlighted the contradiction between Rousseau's theory of universal benevolence and his decision to send his own children to a foundling hospital, condemning him as "a lover of his kind, but a hater of his kindred."

input: In some cases a wrestler may possess admirable physical traits but perceived mediocre public speaking abilities (such as Brock Lesnar), or their gimmick may be that of a "wild savage" needing a handler (such as Kamala). Such performers have historically employed a manager, who speaks on their behalf and adds to the performance. Managers have sometimes become major personalities, including Bobby Heenan, Paul Heyman, Ernie Roth, and Paul Bearer. A manager role may also be filled by a "valet", typically an appealing female who may participate in love triangle storylines, "damsel in distress" situations, and scripted fights with female wrestlers. Some of these have also gone on to become recognized stars, such as Tammy Lynn Sytch, Stacy Keibler, and Miss Elizabeth.
rewrite: Some wrestlers exhibit impressive physicality but are viewed as lacking in public speaking skills, like Brock Lesnar, or portray a "wild savage" character requiring a handler, as Kamala did. Historically, such performers have utilized a manager to speak for them and enhance their act. These managers, like Bobby Heenan, Paul Heyman, Ernie Roth, and Paul Bearer, have often risen to become major personalities themselves. Alternatively, the role may be filled by a "valet," usually an attractive woman involved in love triangles, "damsel in distress" plots, or scripted bouts with other female wrestlers. Valets such as Tammy Lynn Sytch, Stacy Keibler, and Miss Elizabeth have also achieved notable stardom.

input: The clock does not run during convert attempts in the last three minutes of a half. If the 15 minutes of a quarter expire while the ball is live, the quarter is extended until the ball becomes dead. If a quarter's time expires while the ball is dead, the quarter is extended for one more scrimmage. A quarter cannot end while a penalty is pending: after the penalty yardage is applied, the quarter is extended one scrimmage. Note that the non-penalized team has the option to decline any penalty it considers disadvantageous, so a losing team cannot indefinitely prolong a game by repeatedly committing infractions.
rewrite: During the final three minutes of each half, the game clock stops for convert attempts. Should a quarter's fifteen minutes elapse with the ball live, play continues until the ball is dead. If time expires while the ball is dead, the quarter extends for one additional scrimmage. A quarter also cannot end with a penalty pending; following the enforcement of yardage, one more scrimmage is granted. Notably, the non-penalized team may decline any penalty deemed unfavorable, preventing a losing team from endlessly prolonging the game through repeated infractions.

input: In the 1840s Nicholas I reduced 64,000 szlachta to commoner status. Despite this, 62.8% of Russia's nobles were szlachta in 1858 and still 46.1% in 1897. Serfdom was abolished in Russian Poland on February 19, 1864. It was deliberately enacted in a way that would ruin the szlachta. It was the only area where peasants paid the market price in redemption for the land (the average for the empire was 34% above the market price). All land taken from Polish peasants since 1846 was to be returned without redemption payments. The ex serfs could only sell land to other peasants, not szlachta. 90% of the ex serfs in the empire who actually gained land after 1861 were in the 8 western provinces. Along with Romania, Polish landless or domestic serfs were the only ones to be given land after serfdom was abolished. All this was to punish the szlachta's role in the uprisings of 1830 and 1863. By 1864 80% of szlachta were déclassé, 1/4 petty nobles were worse off than the average serf, 48.9% of land in Russian Poland was in peasant hands, nobles still held 46%. In Second Polish Republic the privileges of the nobility were lawfully abolished by the March Constitution in 1921 and as such not granted by any future Polish law.
rewrite: During the 1840s, Tsar Nicholas I stripped 64,000 members of the szlachta, the Polish nobility, of their status, reducing them to commoners. Nevertheless, this class remained significant, comprising 62.8% of Russia's nobles in 1858 and 46.1% as late as 1897. The abolition of serfdom in Russian Poland on February 19, 1864, was deliberately designed to undermine the szlachta. Unlike in the rest of the empire, where peasants paid an average of 34% above market price, here they paid only the market price for land redemption. All land taken from peasants since 1846 was returned without any redemption payments. Furthermore, former serfs were restricted from selling land to the szlachta, permitted to sell only to other peasants. Notably, 90% of the empire's former serfs who actually obtained land after the 1861 reforms were in the eight western provinces. Alongside Romania, Polish landless or domestic serfs were unique in receiving land post-emancipation. These measures collectively served as punishment for the szlachta's involvement in the 1830 and 1863 uprisings. By 1864, 80% of the szlachta were déclassé, with a quarter of petty nobles faring worse than the average serf. Land ownership shifted, with peasants holding 48.9% of land in Russian Poland and nobles retaining 46%. Finally, in the Second Polish Republic, the March Constitution of 1921 legally abolished all noble privileges, a status never restored by subsequent Polish law.

input: In 1976 the future Labour prime minister James Callaghan launched what became known as the 'great debate' on the education system. He went on to list the areas he felt needed closest scrutiny: the case for a core curriculum, the validity and use of informal teaching methods, the role of school inspection and the future of the examination system. Comprehensive school remains the most common type of state secondary school in England, and the only type in Wales. They account for around 90% of pupils, or 64% if one does not count schools with low-level selection. This figure varies by region.
rewrite: In 1976, James Callaghan, who would later become the Labour prime minister, initiated the 'great debate' on education. He highlighted several key areas for close examination: the potential need for a core curriculum, the effectiveness of informal teaching methods, the function of school inspections, and the future of examinations. In England, the comprehensive school is the predominant form of state secondary education and is the exclusive type in Wales. These schools serve approximately 90% of students, or about 64% when excluding those with minimal selection processes, a proportion that differs across regions.

input: Kerry's commanding officer, Lieutenant Commander George Elliott, stated to Douglas Brinkley in 2003 that he did not know whether to court-martial Kerry for beaching the boat without orders or give him a medal for saving the crew. Elliott recommended Kerry for the Silver Star, and Zumwalt flew into An Thoi to personally award medals to Kerry and the rest of the sailors involved in the mission. The Navy's account of Kerry's actions is presented in the original medal citation signed by Zumwalt. The engagement was documented in an after-action report, a press release written on March 1, 1969, and a historical summary dated March 17, 1969.
rewrite: In 2003, Lieutenant Commander George Elliott, Kerry's commanding officer, told Douglas Brinkley he was uncertain whether to court-martial Kerry for beaching the boat without orders or to award him a medal for saving the crew. Ultimately, Elliott recommended Kerry for the Silver Star. Admiral Zumwalt then flew to An Thoi to personally present medals to Kerry and the other sailors from the mission. The Navy's official record of Kerry's actions is captured in the original citation signed by Zumwalt. Documentation of the engagement includes an after-action report, a press release from March 1, 1969, and a historical summary dated March 17, 1969.

input: Carrying a Louis Vuitton backpack filled with old disks and demos to the studio and back, West crafted much of his production for his debut album in less than fifteen minutes at a time. He recorded the remainder of the album in Los Angeles while recovering from the car accident. Once he had completed the album, it was leaked months before its release date. However, West decided to use the opportunity to review the album, and The College Dropout was significantly remixed, remastered, and revised before being released. As a result, certain tracks originally destined for the album were subsequently retracted, among them "Keep the Receipt" with Ol' Dirty Bastard and "The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly" with Consequence. West meticulously refined the production, adding string arrangements, gospel choirs, improved drum programming and new verses. West's perfectionism led The College Dropout to have its release postponed three times from its initial date in August 2003.
rewrite: West produced much of his debut album in brief bursts, often completing tracks in under fifteen minutes while transporting old disks and demos in a Louis Vuitton backpack between his studio sessions. Following a car accident, he finished recording the remainder of the album in Los Angeles during his recovery. Months ahead of its planned release, the completed album was leaked. Rather than seeing this as a setback, West seized the chance to re-evaluate his work. He embarked on significant revisions, remixing, remastering, and refining *The College Dropout*. This process involved adding string arrangements, gospel choirs, enhanced drum programming, and new verses. Consequently, several originally intended tracks, including "Keep the Receipt" featuring Ol' Dirty Bastard and "The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly" with Consequence, were cut. His meticulous perfectionism resulted in the album's release being postponed three times from its initial August 2003 date.

input: Instead, he formulated the spearhead model of evolution, a version of genetic pluralism. According to this model, living organisms themselves have goals, and act according to these goals, each guided by a central control. In its most sophisticated form, this is the brain of humans, but controls also exist in much less sophisticated ways for species of lower complexity, such as the amoeba. This control organ plays a special role in evolution—it is the "spearhead of evolution". The goals bring the purpose into the world. Mutations in the genes that determine the structure of the control may then cause drastic changes in behaviour, preferences and goals, without having an impact on the organism's phenotype. Popper postulates that such purely behavioural changes are less likely to be lethal for the organism compared to drastic changes of the phenotype.
rewrite: He proposed the spearhead model of evolution, a form of genetic pluralism. This model holds that living organisms possess inherent goals and act upon them, each directed by a central control mechanism. In humans, this control is most sophisticated as the brain, but even simpler species like the amoeba possess their own versions. This controlling organ serves as the "spearhead of evolution," introducing purpose into the world. Genetic mutations affecting the control structure can trigger significant shifts in behavior, preferences, and objectives, all without altering the organism's physical form. Popper suggests that such purely behavioral alterations are less prone to being fatal for the organism than would be drastic phenotypic changes.

input: Political color schemes in the United States diverge from international norms. Since 2000, red has become associated with the right-wing Republican Party and blue with the left-wing Democratic Party. However, unlike political color schemes of other countries, the parties did not choose those colors; they were used in news coverage of 2000 election results and ensuing legal battle and caught on in popular usage. Prior to the 2000 election the media typically alternated which color represented which party each presidential election cycle. The color scheme happened to get inordinate attention that year, so the cycle was stopped lest it cause confusion the following election.
rewrite: In the United States, the political color scheme differs from global conventions. Here, red is linked to the right-leaning Republican Party and blue to the left-leaning Democratic Party, an association solidified since the 2000 election. Interestingly, the parties themselves did not select these colors. Instead, they emerged from television news graphics during the protracted coverage of that year's election results and legal disputes, eventually entering common use. Before 2000, media outlets traditionally switched the color assignments for each party every presidential cycle. However, the scheme received exceptional focus that year, halting the alternation to prevent confusion in future elections.

input: Marvel counts among its characters such well-known superheroes as Spider-Man, Iron Man, Captain America, Wolverine, Thor, Hulk, Ant-Man, such teams as the Avengers, the Guardians of the Galaxy, the Fantastic Four, the Inhumans and the X-Men, and antagonists such as Doctor Doom, The Enchantress, Green Goblin, Ultron, Doctor Octopus, Thanos, Magneto and Loki. Most of Marvel's fictional characters operate in a single reality known as the Marvel Universe, with locations that mirror real-life cities. Characters such as Spider-Man, the Fantastic Four, the Avengers, Daredevil and Doctor Strange are based in New York City, whereas the X-Men have historically been based in Salem Center, New York and Hulk's stories often have been set in the American Southwest.
rewrite: Marvel's vast array of characters includes iconic superheroes like Spider-Man, Iron Man, and Captain America, alongside teams such as the Avengers, the X-Men, and the Fantastic Four. They are opposed by notable antagonists including Doctor Doom, Magneto, Loki, and Thanos. The majority of these figures inhabit the shared Marvel Universe, which features settings resembling actual places. New York City serves as a base for Spider-Man, Daredevil, Doctor Strange, and the Fantastic Four.
