Historically, the X-Men have been located in Salem Center, New York, while the Hulk's adventures frequently unfold across the American Southwest.

input: The Macintosh (/ˈmækᵻntɒʃ/ MAK-in-tosh; branded as Mac since 1997) is a series of personal computers (PCs) designed, developed, and marketed by Apple Inc. Steve Jobs introduced the original Macintosh computer on January 24, 1984. This was the first mass-market personal computer featuring an integral graphical user interface and mouse. This first model was later renamed to "Macintosh 128k" for uniqueness amongst a populous family of subsequently updated models which are also based on Apple's same proprietary architecture. Since 1998, Apple has largely phased out the Macintosh name in favor of "Mac", though the product family has been nicknamed "Mac" or "the Mac" since the development of the first model.
rewrite: Introduced by Steve Jobs on January 24, 1984, the original Macintosh was the first mass-market PC with a built-in graphical user interface and mouse. This series of personal computers is designed, developed, and marketed by Apple Inc. That inaugural model was later renamed the "Macintosh 128k" to distinguish it within the growing family of subsequent models, all based on Apple's proprietary architecture. While branded as Mac since 1997 and nicknamed as such from the start, the Macintosh name was largely phased out by Apple after 1998 in favor of the shorter "Mac."

input: Even though, both Kashmir Shaivism and Advaita Vedanta are non-dual philosophies which give primacy to Universal Consciousness (Chit or Brahman), in Kashmir Shavisim, as opposed to Advaita, all things are a manifestation of this Consciousness. This implies that from the point of view of Kashmir Shavisim, the phenomenal world (Śakti) is real, and it exists and has its being in Consciousness (Chit). Whereas, Advaita holds that Brahman is inactive (niṣkriya) and the phenomenal world is an illusion (māyā). The objective of human life, according to Kashmir Shaivism, is to merge in Shiva or Universal Consciousness, or to realize one's already existing identity with Shiva, by means of wisdom, yoga and grace.
rewrite: While both Kashmir Shaivism and Advaita Vedanta are non-dual philosophies prioritizing Universal Consciousness (Chit or Brahman), they differ fundamentally. Kashmir Shaivism views all things as real manifestations of this Consciousness, with the phenomenal world (Śakti) having its being within Chit. In contrast, Advaita Vedanta sees Brahman as inactive and the phenomenal world as an illusion (māyā). For Kashmir Shaivism, the human aim is to merge with or realize one's inherent identity with Shiva, achieved through wisdom, yoga, and divine grace.

input: The broad field of animal communication encompasses most of the issues in ethology. Animal communication can be defined as any behavior of one animal that affects the current or future behavior of another animal. The study of animal communication, called zoo semiotics (distinguishable from anthroposemiotics, the study of human communication) has played an important part in the development of ethology, sociobiology, and the study of animal cognition. Animal communication, and indeed the understanding of the animal world in general, is a rapidly growing field, and even in the 21st century so far, a great share of prior understanding related to diverse fields such as personal symbolic name use, animal emotions, animal culture and learning, and even sexual conduct, long thought to be well understood, has been revolutionized. A special field of animal communication has been investigated in more detail such as vibrational communication.
rewrite: Encompassing most issues in ethology, the broad field of animal communication involves any behavior by one animal that influences another's current or future actions. A significant subfield, zoo semiotics—distinct from anthroposemiotics, which studies human communication—has been crucial in developing ethology, sociobiology, and animal cognition research. Understanding of the animal world, including communication, is expanding rapidly. Even in the 21st century, long-held assumptions in areas like symbolic name use, animal emotions, culture, learning, and sexual conduct have been revolutionized. More detailed investigation has also focused on specific areas, such as vibrational communication.

input: Barcelona is one of the most supported teams in the world, and has the largest social media following in the world among sports teams. Barcelona's players have won a record number of Ballon d'Or awards (11), as well as a record number of FIFA World Player of the Year awards (7). In 2010, the club made history when three players who came through its youth academy (Messi, Iniesta and Xavi) were chosen as the three best players in the world in the FIFA Ballon d'Or awards, an unprecedented feat for players from the same football school.
rewrite: With the largest social media following of any sports team globally, Barcelona stands as one of the world's most supported clubs. Its players have claimed a record eleven Ballon d'Or and seven FIFA World Player of the Year awards. An unprecedented feat occurred in 2010, when three graduates of the club's youth academy—Messi, Iniesta, and Xavi—were selected as the top three players in the world for the FIFA Ballon d'Or, a historic achievement for a single football school.

input: Craig Venter and Francis Collins of the National Institute of Health jointly made the announcement of the mapping of the human genome in 2000. Upon examining the data from the genome mapping, Venter realized that although the genetic variation within the human species is on the order of 1–3% (instead of the previously assumed 1%), the types of variations do not support notion of genetically defined races. Venter said, "Race is a social concept. It's not a scientific one. There are no bright lines (that would stand out), if we could compare all the sequenced genomes of everyone on the planet." "When we try to apply science to try to sort out these social differences, it all falls apart."
rewrite: In 2000, Craig Venter and Francis Collins of the National Institute of Health jointly announced the mapping of the human genome. Venter’s subsequent examination of the data revealed that, while human genetic variation is about 1–3% rather than the earlier estimate of 1%, the patterns of this variation do not uphold the idea of genetically distinct races. He stated, “Race is a social concept. It's not a scientific one. There are no bright lines that would stand out if we could compare all the sequenced genomes of everyone on the planet.” Venter added, “When we try to apply science to try to sort out these social differences, it all falls apart.”

input: There are several sources of the seedlessness trait, and essentially all commercial cultivators get it from one of three sources: Thompson Seedless, Russian Seedless, and Black Monukka, all being cultivars of Vitis vinifera. There are currently more than a dozen varieties of seedless grapes. Several, such as Einset Seedless, Benjamin Gunnels's Prime seedless grapes, Reliance, and Venus, have been specifically cultivated for hardiness and quality in the relatively cold climates of northeastern United States and southern Ontario.
rewrite: The seedlessness trait in commercial grapes originates primarily from three Vitis vinifera cultivars: Thompson Seedless, Russian Seedless, and Black Monukka. Today, over a dozen seedless varieties exist. Several, including Einset Seedless, Benjamin Gunnels's Prime, Reliance, and Venus, were bred for hardiness and quality in colder regions like the northeastern United States and southern Ontario.

input: Philosophical empiricists hold no knowledge to be properly inferred or deduced unless it is derived from one's sense-based experience. This view is commonly contrasted with rationalism, which states that knowledge may be derived from reason independently of the senses. For example, John Locke held that some knowledge (e.g. knowledge of God's existence) could be arrived at through intuition and reasoning alone. Similarly Robert Boyle, a prominent advocate of the experimental method, held that we have innate ideas. The main continental rationalists (Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz) were also advocates of the empirical "scientific method".
rewrite: Empiricists in philosophy assert that true knowledge must originate from sensory experience, opposing rationalism’s claim that reason alone can yield knowledge. For instance, John Locke accepted that intuition and reasoning could lead to certain truths, like the existence of God. Robert Boyle, despite championing experimentation, believed in innate ideas. Meanwhile, key continental rationalists such as Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz also supported the empirical scientific method, illustrating the nuanced interplay between these schools of thought.

input: There has, however, been interest among railroad operators in returning to DC use at higher voltages than previously used. At the same voltage, DC often has less loss than AC, and for this reason high-voltage direct current is already used on some bulk power transmission lines. DC avoids the electromagnetic radiation inherent with AC, and on a railway this also reduces interference with signalling and communications and mitigates hypothetical EMF risks. DC also avoids the power factor problems of AC. Of particular interest to railroading is that DC can supply constant power with a single ungrounded wire. Constant power with AC requires three-phase transmission with at least two ungrounded wires. Another important consideration is that mains-frequency 3-phase AC must be carefully planned to avoid unbalanced phase loads. Parts of the system are supplied from different phases on the assumption that the total loads of the 3 phases will even out. At the phase break points between regions supplied from different phases, long insulated supply breaks are required to avoid them being shorted by rolling stock using more than one pantograph at a time. A few railroads have tried 3-phase but its substantial complexity has made single-phase standard practice despite the interruption in power flow that occurs twice every cycle. An experimental 6 kV DC railway was built in the Soviet Union.
rewrite: Railroad operators have shown renewed interest in adopting direct current (DC) systems at higher voltages than in the past. Compared to alternating current (AC) at equivalent voltage, DC typically experiences lower energy loss, a principle already applied in high-voltage direct current transmission for bulk power lines. In railway contexts, DC eliminates the electromagnetic radiation associated with AC, thereby reducing interference with signaling and communications while addressing potential electromagnetic field (EMF) concerns. Additionally, DC sidesteps the power factor issues common to AC systems. For rail operations, a key advantage is that constant power can be delivered through a single ungrounded wire with DC. Achieving constant power with AC necessitates three-phase transmission, requiring at least two ungrounded wires. Three-phase AC at mains frequency also demands careful planning to prevent unbalanced phase loads, as different sections of the system rely on different phases with the expectation that overall loads will balance. At phase break points between these sections, lengthy insulated gaps are essential to avoid short circuits when trains use multiple pantographs simultaneously. Although a few railroads have experimented with three-phase AC, its considerable complexity has made single-phase AC the standard, despite the brief interruptions in power flow that occur twice each cycle. Historically, an experimental 6 kV DC railway was constructed in the Soviet Union.

input: At times a character may "turn", altering their face/heel alignment. This may be an abrupt, surprising event, or it may slowly build up over time. It almost always is accomplished with a markable change in behavior on the part of the character. Some turns become defining points in a wrestler's career, as was the case when Hulk Hogan turned heel after being a top face for over a decade. Others may have no noticeable effect on the character's status. If a character repeatedly switches between being a face and heel, this lessens the effect of such turns, and may result in apathy from the audience. Vince McMahon is a good example of having more heel and face turns than anyone in WWE history.
rewrite: A character's alignment can shift, leading them to "turn" from face to heel or vice versa. This transformation might be a sudden, shocking moment or a gradual development over time. In almost every instance, it involves a significant and observable change in the character's behavior. While some turns become defining career milestones—such as Hulk Hogan's iconic heel turn after more than ten years as a top face—others have little impact on the character's standing. Frequent switching between alignments, however, diminishes the impact of these turns and can breed audience apathy. Vince McMahon serves as a prime example, having undergone more heel and face turns than anyone else in WWE history.

input: Chengdu Hi-tech Development Zone covers an area of 82.5 km2 (31.9 sq mi), consisting of the South Park and the West Park. By relying on the city sub-center, which is under construction, the South Park is focusing on creating a modernized industrial park of science and technology with scientific and technological innovation, incubation R&D, modern service industry and Headquarters economy playing leading roles. Priority has been given to the development of software industry. Located on both sides of the "Chengdu-Dujiangyan-Jiuzhaigou" golden tourism channel, the West Park aims at building a comprehensive industrial park targeting at industrial clustering with complete supportive functions. The West Park gives priority to three major industries i.e. electronic information, biomedicine and precision machinery.
rewrite: Covering 82.5 km² (31.9 sq mi), the Chengdu Hi-tech Development Zone comprises a South Park and a West Park. The South Park leverages an emerging city sub-center to establish a modern science and technology industrial park. This area emphasizes scientific innovation, incubation R&D, modern services, and headquarters economy, with the software industry as a key priority. Situated along the "Chengdu-Dujiangyan-Jiuzhaigou" golden tourism route, the West Park focuses on forming a comprehensive, clustered industrial zone with full supporting functions. It prioritizes three core industries: electronic information, biomedicine, and precision machinery.

input: In 1960, Columbia/CBS began negotiations with its main international distributor Philips Records with the goal of CBS starting its own global record company. Philips' acquisition of Mercury Records in the US in 1961 paved the way for this. CBS only had the rights to the Columbia name in North America; therefore the international arm founded in 1961 and launched in 1962 utilized the "CBS Records" name only, with Philips Records distributing the label in Europe. CBS's Mexican record company, Discos Columbia, was renamed Discos CBS by 1963.
rewrite: In 1961, CBS sought to establish its own global record company, initiating talks with its primary international distributor, Philips Records. This move was facilitated by Philips' acquisition of Mercury Records that same year. Since CBS held rights to the "Columbia" name solely in North America, its new international division, founded in 1961 and launched in 1962, operated exclusively as "CBS Records" under Philips' European distribution. By 1963, the Mexican branch, Discos Columbia, was also rebranded as Discos CBS.

input: According to the tradition, Virgil traveled to Greece in about 19 BC to revise the Aeneid. After meeting Augustus in Athens and deciding to return home, Virgil caught a fever while visiting a town near Megara. After crossing to Italy by ship, weakened with disease, Virgil died in Brundisium harbor on September 21, 19 BC. Augustus ordered Virgil's literary executors, Lucius Varius Rufus and Plotius Tucca, to disregard Virgil's own wish that the poem be burned, instead ordering it published with as few editorial changes as possible. As a result, the text of the Aeneid that exists may contain faults which Virgil was planning to correct before publication. However, the only obvious imperfections are a few lines of verse that are metrically unfinished (i.e. not a complete line of dactylic hexameter). Some scholars have argued that Virgil deliberately left these metrically incomplete lines for dramatic effect. Other alleged imperfections are subject to scholarly debate.
rewrite: In about 19 BC, following tradition, Virgil journeyed to Greece to revise the Aeneid. He met Emperor Augustus in Athens and resolved to return to Italy. However, while visiting a town near Megara, he contracted a fever. Though he crossed by ship to Italy, his health had failed; Virgil died in Brundisium harbor on September 21 of that year. Augustus subsequently commanded Virgil’s literary executors, Lucius Varius Rufus and Plotius Tucca, to ignore the poet’s own deathbed wish that the epic be burned. Instead, they were to publish it with minimal editorial changes. Consequently, the surviving text may include faults Virgil intended to correct. The most visible imperfections are a few metrically unfinished lines—incomplete dactylic hexameters. Some scholars contend these were left deliberately for dramatic effect, while other alleged flaws remain topics of debate.

input: The team placed fifth in the Premier League automatically qualifies for the UEFA Europa League, and the sixth and seventh-placed teams can also qualify, depending on the winners of the two domestic cup competitions i.e. the FA Cup and the Capital One Cup (League Cup). Two Europa League places are reserved for the winners of each tournament; if the winner of either the FA Cup or League Cup qualifies for the Champions League, then that place will go to the next-best placed finisher in the Premier League. A further place in the UEFA Europa League is also available via the Fair Play initiative. If the Premier League has one of the three highest Fair Play rankings in Europe, the highest ranked team in the Premier League Fair Play standings which has not already qualified for Europe will automatically qualify for the UEFA Europa League first qualifying round.
rewrite: A place in the UEFA Europa League is automatically awarded to the team finishing fifth in the Premier League. Additionally, the sixth and seventh-placed teams may qualify, contingent upon the outcomes of the domestic cup competitions—the FA Cup and the Capital One Cup (League Cup). Each of these cups offers a Europa League berth to its winner. Should a cup winner already secure a Champions League spot, their Europa League place is instead allocated to the next highest-ranked Premier League side not yet qualified. Beyond these routes, a further Europa League place can be obtained through the Fair Play initiative. If the Premier League ranks among Europe's top three in Fair Play, the highest-placed team in its Fair Play standings that has not otherwise qualified for Europe earns a spot in the tournament's first qualifying round.

input: Hokkien /hɒˈkiɛn/ (traditional Chinese: 福建話; simplified Chinese: 福建话; pinyin: Fújiànhuà; Pe̍h-ōe-jī: Hok-kiàn oē) or Quanzhang (Quanzhou–Zhangzhou / Chinchew–Changchew; BP: Zuánziū–Ziāngziū) is a group of mutually intelligible Min Nan Chinese dialects spoken throughout Southeast Asia, Taiwan, and by many other overseas Chinese. Hokkien originated from a dialect in southern Fujian. It is closely related to the Teochew, though mutual comprehension is difficult, and is somewhat more distantly related to Hainanese. Besides Hokkien, there are also other Min and Hakka dialects in Fujian province, most of which are not mutually intelligible with Hokkien.
rewrite: Hokkien, also known as Quanzhang, refers to a collection of mutually intelligible Min Nan Chinese dialects. Its origins lie in southern Fujian province. While closely related to Teochew, the two are not easily understood between speakers, and it is more distantly connected to Hainanese. Spoken widely in Southeast Asia, Taiwan, and among overseas communities, Hokkien is distinct from the other Min and Hakka dialects also found in Fujian, most of which are not mutually intelligible with it.

input: Santa Monica is a beachfront city in western Los Angeles County, California, United States. The city is named after the Christian saint, Monica. Situated on Santa Monica Bay, it is bordered on three sides by the city of Los Angeles – Pacific Palisades to the north, Brentwood on the northeast, Sawtelle on the east, Mar Vista on the southeast, and Venice on the south. Santa Monica is well known for its affluent single-family neighborhoods but also has many neighborhoods consisting primarily of condominiums and apartments. Over two-thirds of Santa Monica's residents are renters. The Census Bureau population for Santa Monica in 2010 was 89,736.
rewrite: Located in western Los Angeles County, California, Santa Monica is a beachfront city named after Saint Monica. It lies on Santa Monica Bay and is surrounded on three sides by Los Angeles neighborhoods: Pacific Palisades to the north, Brentwood to the northeast, Sawtelle to the east, Mar Vista to the southeast, and Venice to the south. While famed for its affluent single-family areas, the city also has many neighborhoods of condominiums and apartments. Renters make up over two-thirds of the population, which was recorded as 89,736 in the 2010 census.

input: In 1862, paper money was issued without the backing of precious metals, due to the Civil War. Silver and gold coins continued to be issued and in 1878 the link between paper money and coins was reinstated. This disconnection from gold and silver backing also occurred during the War of 1812. The use of paper money not backed by precious metals had also occurred under the Articles of Confederation from 1777 to 1788. With no solid backing and being easily counterfeited, the continentals quickly lost their value, giving rise to the phrase "not worth a continental". This was a primary reason for the "No state shall... make any thing but gold and silver coin a tender in payment of debts" clause in article 1, section 10 of the United States Constitution.
rewrite: During the War of 1812 and again amid the Civil War in 1862, the United States issued paper currency not backed by gold or silver. This practice had an even earlier precedent under the Articles of Confederation from 1777 to 1788. The continentals from that era, lacking solid backing and being easily counterfeited, rapidly depreciated, leading to the phrase "not worth a continental." That experience was a primary reason for including a clause in Article 1, Section 10 of the Constitution, stating, "No state shall... make any thing but gold and silver coin a tender in payment of debts." Although paper money was disconnected from precious metals during these conflicts, silver and gold coins continued to be minted, and the link to coinage was restored for paper currency in 1878.

input: Somali society is traditionally ethnically endogamous. So to extend ties of alliance, marriage is often to another ethnic Somali from a different clan. Thus, for example, a recent study observed that in 89 marriages contracted by men of the Dhulbahante clan, 55 (62%) were with women of Dhulbahante sub-clans other than those of their husbands; 30 (33.7%) were with women of surrounding clans of other clan families (Isaaq, 28; Hawiye, 3); and 3 (4.3%) were with women of other clans of the Darod clan family (Majerteen 2, Ogaden 1).
rewrite: Traditionally, Somali society practices ethnic endogamy, yet marriages frequently occur between different clans to forge alliances. A recent study of Dhulbahante clan men illustrates this: in 89 marriages, 55 (62%) were with women from other Dhulbahante sub-clans. Another 30 (33.7%) involved women from surrounding clans of other clan families, such as Isaaq and Hawiye. The remaining 3 (4.3%) were with women from other Darod clans, namely Majerteen and Ogaden.

input: The monastic communities of the Judean Desert also decorated their monasteries with mosaic floors. The Monastery of Martyrius was founded in the end of the 5th century and it was re-discovered in 1982–85. The most important work of art here is the intact geometric mosaic floor of the refectory although the severely damaged church floor was similarly rich. The mosaics in the church of the nearby Monastery of Euthymius are of later date (discovered in 1930). They were laid down in the Umayyad era, after a devastating earthquake in 659. Two six pointed stars and a red chalice are the most important surviving features.
rewrite: Monasteries in the Judean Desert featured mosaic floor decorations. Among these, the Monastery of Martyrius, established in the late 5th century and rediscovered between 1982 and 1985, contains a significant intact geometric mosaic in its refectory. The church floor there was also once richly adorned, though now severely damaged. Nearby, the mosaics in the Monastery of Euthymius's church date from later, having been laid after a major earthquake in 659 during the Umayyad period and uncovered in 1930. Their most notable preserved elements include two six-pointed stars and a red chalice.

input: Many arrangements of electrical contacts are used. Large lamps may have a screw base (one or more contacts at the tip, one at the shell) or a bayonet base (one or more contacts on the base, shell used as a contact or used only as a mechanical support). Some tubular lamps have an electrical contact at either end. Miniature lamps may have a wedge base and wire contacts, and some automotive and special purpose lamps have screw terminals for connection to wires. Contacts in the lamp socket allow the electric current to pass through the base to the filament. Power ratings for incandescent light bulbs range from about 0.1 watt to about 10,000 watts.
rewrite: Electrical contacts come in many arrangements. For large lamps, bases may be screw types—with contacts at the tip and shell—or bayonet types, where contacts are on the base and the shell may serve as a contact or just for support. Tubular lamps often feature a contact at each end. Miniature versions frequently use wedge bases with wire contacts, while some automotive and special-purpose lamps employ screw terminals for wire connections. Within the socket, contacts enable current to flow through the base to the filament. Incandescent bulbs have power ratings spanning from approximately 0.1 watt up to around 10,000 watts.

input: During the revival, in 1809 linguist and historian Josef Dobrovský released a German-language grammar of Old Czech entitled Ausführliches Lehrgebäude der böhmischen Sprache (Comprehensive Doctrine of the Bohemian Language). Dobrovský had intended his book to be descriptive, and did not think Czech had a realistic chance of returning as a major language. However, Josef Jungmann and other revivalists used Dobrovský's book to advocate for a Czech linguistic revival. Changes during this time included spelling reform (notably, í in place of the former j and j in place of g), the use of t (rather than ti) to end infinitive verbs and the non-capitalization of nouns (which had been a late borrowing from German). These changes differentiated Czech from Slovak. Modern scholars disagree about whether the conservative revivalists were motivated by nationalism or considered contemporary spoken Czech unsuitable for formal, widespread use.
rewrite: In 1809, linguist and historian Josef Dobrovský published a German-language grammar of Old Czech, "Ausführliches Lehrgebäude der böhmischen Sprache" (Comprehensive Doctrine of the Bohemian Language). Although Dobrovský intended his work as descriptive and doubted Czech could regain prominence, revivalists like Josef Jungmann used it to advocate for the language's renewal. This period introduced key reforms: spelling changes (such as í replacing j and j replacing g), infinitives ending in t instead of ti, and ceasing to capitalize nouns—a practice borrowed earlier from German. These modifications helped distinguish Czech from Slovak. Modern scholars debate whether the conservative revivalists were driven by nationalism or viewed everyday Czech as inadequate for formal and broad application.

input: In 1997, the mammals were comprehensively revised by Malcolm C. McKenna and Susan K. Bell, which has resulted in the McKenna/Bell classification. Their 1997 book, Classification of Mammals above the Species Level, is the most comprehensive work to date on the systematics, relationships, and occurrences of all mammal taxa, living and extinct, down through the rank of genus, though recent molecular genetic data challenge several of the higher level groupings. The authors worked together as paleontologists at the American Museum of Natural History, New York. McKenna inherited the project from Simpson and, with Bell, constructed a completely updated hierarchical system, covering living and extinct taxa that reflects the historical genealogy of Mammalia.
rewrite: The McKenna/Bell classification of mammals originated from a comprehensive 1997 revision by Malcolm C. McKenna and Susan K. Bell, both paleontologists at the American Museum of Natural History in New York. Their collaborative work, *Classification of Mammals above the Species Level*, remains the most exhaustive reference on mammal systematics, relationships, and occurrences for all living and extinct genera. McKenna inherited this project from Simpson and, alongside Bell, developed a fully updated hierarchical system reflecting the historical genealogy of Mammalia. While foundational, some of its higher-level groupings are now contested by recent molecular genetic data.

input: The structure of the Swiss militia system stipulates that the soldiers keep their Army issued equipment, including all personal weapons, at home. Some organizations and political parties find this practice controversial but mainstream Swiss opinion is in favour of the system. Compulsory military service concerns all male Swiss citizens; women can serve voluntarily. Men usually receive military conscription orders for training at the age of 18. About two thirds of the young Swiss are found suited for service; for those found unsuited, various forms of alternative service exist. Annually, approximately 20,000 persons are trained in recruit centres for a duration from 18 to 21 weeks. The reform "Army XXI" was adopted by popular vote in 2003, it replaced the previous model "Army 95", reducing the effectives from 400,000 to about 200,000. Of those, 120,000 are active in periodic Army training and 80,000 are non-training reserves.
rewrite: Under the Swiss militia system, soldiers store their Army-issued equipment, such as personal weapons, at home. While certain organizations and political parties view this practice as controversial, it retains broad public support. Military service is compulsory for all male citizens, whereas women may volunteer. Typically, men receive conscription orders at age 18 for initial training. Roughly two-thirds of young Swiss are deemed fit for duty; the remainder have access to alternative service options. Each year, recruit centers train about 20,000 individuals over 18 to 21 weeks. The "Army XXI" reform, approved by popular vote in 2003, succeeded the earlier "Army 95" model, cutting overall troop numbers from 400,000 to around 200,000. From this total, 120,000 participate in periodic training, and 80,000 serve as non-training reserves.

input: More than 200 newspapers and 350 consumer magazines have an office in the city, and the publishing industry employs about 25,000 people. Two of the three national daily newspapers in the United States are New York papers: The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times, which has won the most Pulitzer Prizes for journalism. Major tabloid newspapers in the city include: The New York Daily News, which was founded in 1919 by Joseph Medill Patterson and The New York Post, founded in 1801 by Alexander Hamilton. The city also has a comprehensive ethnic press, with 270 newspapers and magazines published in more than 40 languages. El Diario La Prensa is New York's largest Spanish-language daily and the oldest in the nation. The New York Amsterdam News, published in Harlem, is a prominent African American newspaper. The Village Voice is the largest alternative newspaper.
rewrite: New York City is a major hub for the publishing industry, with over 200 newspapers and 350 consumer magazines maintaining offices there, employing roughly 25,000 people. The city’s influence is underscored by the fact that two of the nation’s three major daily newspapers are based there: The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times, the latter having earned more Pulitzer Prizes for journalism than any other. Its tabloid landscape is defined by The New York Daily News, founded in 1919 by Joseph Medill Patterson, and The New York Post, established in 1801 by Alexander Hamilton. A comprehensive ethnic press thrives, with 270 publications in over 40 languages. Notable among these are El Diario La Prensa, the nation's oldest and New York's largest Spanish-language daily; the prominent African American New York Amsterdam News, published in Harlem; and The Village Voice, the largest alternative newspaper.

input: The main crops grown are barley, wheat, buckwheat, rye, potatoes, and assorted fruits and vegetables. Tibet is ranked the lowest among China’s 31 provinces on the Human Development Index according to UN Development Programme data. In recent years, due to increased interest in Tibetan Buddhism, tourism has become an increasingly important sector, and is actively promoted by the authorities. Tourism brings in the most income from the sale of handicrafts. These include Tibetan hats, jewelry (silver and gold), wooden items, clothing, quilts, fabrics, Tibetan rugs and carpets. The Central People's Government exempts Tibet from all taxation and provides 90% of Tibet's government expenditures. However most of this investment goes to pay migrant workers who do not settle in Tibet and send much of their income home to other provinces.
rewrite: According to data from the UN Development Programme, Tibet ranks last among China’s 31 provinces on the Human Development Index. The region’s main agricultural crops include barley, wheat, buckwheat, rye, potatoes, and various fruits and vegetables. In recent years, tourism has grown into a major sector, spurred by rising interest in Tibetan Buddhism and actively promoted by local authorities. The sale of handicrafts—such as Tibetan hats, silver and gold jewelry, wooden items, clothing, quilts, fabrics, rugs, and carpets—generates the largest share of tourism income. While the Central People's Government exempts Tibet from taxation and funds 90% of its government expenditures, most of this investment pays migrant workers who typically remit their earnings to other provinces rather than settling in Tibet.

input: Providing 25% of Namibia's revenue, mining is the single most important contributor to the economy. Namibia is the fourth largest exporter of non-fuel minerals in Africa and the world's fourth largest producer of uranium. There has been significant investment in uranium mining and Namibia is set to become the largest exporter of uranium by 2015. Rich alluvial diamond deposits make Namibia a primary source for gem-quality diamonds. While Namibia is known predominantly for its gem diamond and uranium deposits, a number of other minerals are extracted industrially such as lead, tungsten, gold, tin, fluorspar, manganese, marble, copper and zinc. There are offshore gas deposits in the Atlantic Ocean that are planned to be extracted in the future. According to "The Diamond Investigation", a book about the global diamond market, from 1978, De Beers, the largest diamond company, bought most of the Namibian diamonds, and would continue to do so, because "whatever government eventually comes to power they will need this revenue to survive".
rewrite: Mining stands as the foremost contributor to Namibia's economy, generating a quarter of the nation's revenue. The country ranks as Africa's fourth largest exporter of non-fuel minerals and holds the position of the world's fourth largest uranium producer. Significant investment in this sector positioned Namibia to become the leading global uranium exporter by 2015. Beyond uranium, Namibia is a primary source for gem-quality diamonds due to its rich alluvial deposits. Although renowned for these diamonds and uranium, the country industrially extracts numerous other minerals including lead, tungsten, gold, tin, fluorspar, manganese, marble, copper, and zinc. Future plans also include tapping offshore gas deposits in the Atlantic Ocean. As noted in the 1978 book "The Diamond Investigation," De Beers, the largest diamond company, historically purchased most Namibian diamonds—a practice expected to persist because any governing body would require this vital revenue.

input: French members of Parliament and other French politicians also organised a protest. All political parties in Parliament—UMP, Socialists, New Centre, Communists, Democratic Movement (centre) and Greens—jointly requested a pause in the National Assembly's session, which was granted, so that MPs could step outside and unfurl a banner which read "Respect for Human Rights in China". The coach containing the torch drove past the National Assembly and the assembled protesting MPs, who shouted "Freedom for Tibet!" several times as it passed.
rewrite: French politicians, including members of Parliament, coordinated a demonstration. MPs from all parliamentary parties—UMP, Socialists, New Centre, Communists, Democratic Movement, and Greens—collectively secured a pause in the National Assembly session. They then gathered outside to display a banner stating "Respect for Human Rights in China." As the torch relay coach passed the Assembly, the protesting MPs repeatedly shouted "Freedom for Tibet!"

input: Plymouth lies between the River Plym to the east and the River Tamar to the west; both rivers flow into the natural harbour of Plymouth Sound. Since 1967, the unitary authority of Plymouth has included the, once independent, towns of Plympton and Plymstock which lie along the east of the River Plym. The River Tamar forms the county boundary between Devon and Cornwall and its estuary forms the Hamoaze on which is sited Devonport Dockyard.
rewrite: Bordered by the River Plym to the east and the River Tamar to the west, Plymouth sits where both rivers meet Plymouth Sound. The Tamar defines the Devon-Cornwall border, with its estuary forming the Hamoaze, home to Devonport Dockyard. Since 1967, Plymouth's unitary authority has incorporated the formerly separate eastern towns of Plympton and Plymstock.

input: Meanwhile, in Renaissance Italy, a new period in the history of translation had opened in Florence with the arrival, at the court of Cosimo de' Medici, of the Byzantine scholar Georgius Gemistus Pletho shortly before the fall of Constantinople to the Turks (1453). A Latin translation of Plato's works was undertaken by Marsilio Ficino. This and Erasmus' Latin edition of the New Testament led to a new attitude to translation. For the first time, readers demanded rigor of rendering, as philosophical and religious beliefs depended on the exact words of Plato, Aristotle and Jesus.
rewrite: A new chapter in translation history began in Renaissance Florence with Byzantine scholar Georgius Gemistus Pletho's arrival at Cosimo de' Medici's court, shortly before Constantinople's fall in 1453. Marsilio Ficino produced a Latin translation of Plato's works, and Erasmus created a Latin New Testament. These works fostered a novel approach to translation. For the first time, readers insisted on rigorous accuracy, as the precise words of Plato, Aristotle, and Jesus were seen as foundational to philosophical and religious truth.

input: After the English Civil War the Royal Citadel was built in 1666 on the east end of Plymouth Hoe, to defend the port from naval attacks, suppress Plymothian Parliamentary leanings and to train the armed forces. Guided tours are available in the summer months. Further west is Smeaton's Tower, which was built in 1759 as a lighthouse on rocks 14 miles (23 km) off shore, but dismantled and the top two thirds rebuilt on the Hoe in 1877. It is open to the public and has views over the Plymouth Sound and the city from the lantern room. Plymouth has 20 war memorials of which nine are on The Hoe including: Plymouth Naval Memorial, to remember those killed in World Wars I and II, and the Armada Memorial, to commemorate the defeat of the Spanish Armada.
rewrite: Constructed in 1666 following the English Civil War, the Royal Citadel occupies the eastern part of Plymouth Hoe. Its purposes were to protect the port, curb Parliamentary sympathies in the town, and provide military training. Summer months offer guided tours of the site. To the west stands Smeaton's Tower, originally a lighthouse built offshore in 1759. Its upper sections were relocated to the Hoe in 1877, and it is now open to visitors, providing panoramic views of Plymouth Sound and the city from its lantern room. The Hoe features nine of Plymouth's twenty war memorials, such as the Plymouth Naval Memorial for the World Wars and the Armada Memorial marking the defeat of the Spanish fleet.

input: Plymouth was granted the dignity of Lord Mayor by King George V in 1935. The position is elected each year by a group of six councillors. It is traditional that the position of the Lord Mayor alternates between the Conservative Party and the Labour Party annually and that the Lord Mayor chooses the Deputy Lord Mayor. Conservative councillor Dr John Mahony is the incumbent for 2015–16.
rewrite: In 1935, King George V granted Plymouth the dignity of having a Lord Mayor. Each year, a group of six councillors elects the position. Traditionally, the role alternates annually between the Conservative and Labour Parties, and the Lord Mayor selects the Deputy Lord Mayor. For the 2015–16 term, the incumbent is Conservative councillor Dr John Mahony.

input: The Consortium first published The Unicode Standard (ISBN 0-321-18578-1) in 1991 and continues to develop standards based on that original work. The latest version of the standard, Unicode 8.0, was released in June 2015 and is available from the consortium's website. The last of the major versions (versions x.0) to be published in book form was Unicode 5.0 (ISBN 0-321-48091-0), but since Unicode 6.0 the full text of the standard is no longer being published in book form. In 2012, however, it was announced that only the core specification for Unicode version 6.1 would be made available as a 692-page print-on-demand paperback. Unlike the previous major version printings of the Standard, the print-on-demand core specification does not include any code charts or standard annexes, but the entire standard, including the core specification, will still remain freely available on the Unicode website.
rewrite: First published in 1991 as The Unicode Standard (ISBN 0-321-18578-1), the original work by the Consortium continues to serve as the foundation for its ongoing development of standards. While the latest version, Unicode 8.0, was released in June 2015 and is accessible online, the last major edition printed as a book was Unicode 5.0 (ISBN 0-321-48091-0). Starting with Unicode 6.0, the full standard ceased formal book publication. However, a 2012 announcement indicated that the core specification for Unicode 6.1 would be offered as a 692-page print-on-demand paperback. This print-on-demand version, unlike prior major printed editions, excludes code charts and standard annexes. Nevertheless, the complete standard, including its core specification, remains freely available on the Unicode website.

input: The American observer Ingersoll reported at this time that "as to the accuracy of the bombing of military objectives, here I make no qualifications. The aim is surprisingly, astonishingly, amazingly inaccurate ... The physical damage to civilian London, to sum up, was more general and more extensive than I had imagined. The damage to military targets much less", and stated that he had seen numerous examples of untouched targets surrounded by buildings destroyed by errant bombs. For example, in two months of bombing, Battersea Power Station, perhaps the largest single target in London, had only received one minor hit ("a nick"). No bridge over the Thames had been hit, and the docks were still functioning despite great damage. An airfield was hit 56 times but the runways were never damaged and the field was never out of operation, despite German pilots' familiarity with it from prewar commercial flights. Ingersoll wrote that the difference between the failure of the German campaign against military targets versus its success in continental Europe was the RAF retaining control of the air.:79–80,174
rewrite: Ingersoll, an American observer, noted the stark contrast between the widespread destruction of civilian areas in London and the minimal impact on military sites. He described the bombing accuracy as "surprisingly, astonishingly, amazingly inaccurate," emphasizing that physical damage to the city was far more extensive than he had anticipated. In his assessment, military targets suffered significantly less harm. He reported seeing many instances where key objectives remained completely untouched, while surrounding buildings were leveled by stray bombs. For instance, over two months, the massive Battersea Power Station sustained only a single minor hit. No Thames bridges were struck, and the docks, though damaged, continued operations. An airfield was hit dozens of times, yet its runways were never impaired and it remained functional, despite German pilots' prior familiarity with the location from prewar flights. Ingersoll attributed the failure of the German campaign against military targets in Britain, unlike its successes in Europe, to the Royal Air Force maintaining air superiority.

input: As in much of Europe, the prosperity of Alsace came to an end in the 14th century by a series of harsh winters, bad harvests, and the Black Death. These hardships were blamed on Jews, leading to the pogroms of 1336 and 1339. In 1349, Jews of Alsace were accused of poisoning the wells with plague, leading to the massacre of thousands of Jews during the Strasbourg pogrom. Jews were subsequently forbidden to settle in the town. An additional natural disaster was the Rhine rift earthquake of 1356, one of Europe's worst which made ruins of Basel. Prosperity returned to Alsace under Habsburg administration during the Renaissance.
rewrite: Like much of Europe, Alsace saw its prosperity collapse in the 14th century due to severe winters, poor harvests, and the Black Death. Jews were scapegoated for these calamities, resulting in pogroms in 1336 and 1339. During the Strasbourg pogrom of 1349, thousands of Jews were massacred after being falsely accused of poisoning wells with plague, and they were later banned from settling in the town. Further devastation came with the 1356 Rhine rift earthquake, which devastated Basel and ranks among Europe's worst. Prosperity only returned to the region under Habsburg rule in the Renaissance period.

input: Industrialized societies generally follow a clock-based schedule for daily activities that do not change throughout the course of the year. The time of day that individuals begin and end work or school, and the coordination of mass transit, for example, usually remain constant year-round. In contrast, an agrarian society's daily routines for work and personal conduct are more likely governed by the length of daylight hours and by solar time, which change seasonally because of the Earth's axial tilt. North and south of the tropics daylight lasts longer in summer and shorter in winter, the effect becoming greater as one moves away from the tropics.
rewrite: Daily routines in industrialized societies are typically organized around fixed clock-based schedules, which remain constant throughout the year. For instance, work, school, and mass transit schedules do not vary seasonally. Conversely, agrarian societies often structure their work and personal activities according to solar time and the changing length of daylight, which shifts with the seasons due to the Earth's axial tilt. This seasonal effect is especially pronounced outside the tropics, where summer brings longer days and winter shorter ones, increasing in intensity farther from the equatorial region.

input: Much of the early paper made from wood pulp contained significant amounts of alum, a variety of aluminium sulfate salts that is significantly acidic. Alum was added to paper to assist in sizing, making it somewhat water resistant so that inks did not "run" or spread uncontrollably. Early papermakers did not realize that the alum they added liberally to cure almost every problem encountered in making their product would eventually be detrimental. The cellulose fibres that make up paper are hydrolyzed by acid, and the presence of alum would eventually degrade the fibres until the paper disintegrated in a process that has come to be known as "slow fire". Documents written on rag paper were significantly more stable. The use of non-acidic additives to make paper is becoming more prevalent, and the stability of these papers is less of an issue.
rewrite: Early papermakers liberally added alum, a form of aluminum sulfate, to wood pulp paper as a sizing agent to prevent ink from spreading. While this addressed immediate production issues, they did not foresee its long-term detrimental effects. Alum is highly acidic, and this acidity hydrolyzes the paper's cellulose fibers. Over time, this leads to a gradual degradation known as "slow fire," where the paper eventually disintegrates. In contrast, documents on rag paper proved far more stable. Recognizing this problem, the modern paper industry is increasingly adopting non-acidic additives, greatly reducing concerns over the long-term stability of contemporary papers.

input: In October 2014, it was announced that Beyoncé with her management company Parkwood Entertainment would be partnering with London-based fashion retailer Topshop, in a new 50/50 split subsidiary business named Parkwood Topshop Athletic Ltd. The new division was created for Topshop to break into the activewear market, with an athletic, street wear brand being produced. "Creating a partnership with Beyoncé, one of the most hard-working and talented people in the world, who spends many hours of her life dancing, rehearsing and training is a unique opportunity to develop this category" stated Sir Philip Green on the partnership. The company and collection is set to launch and hit stores in the fall of 2015.
rewrite: In October 2014, a partnership was revealed between Beyoncé’s Parkwood Entertainment and the London retailer Topshop. Together, they formed a 50/50 venture called Parkwood Topshop Athletic Ltd. This new subsidiary aimed to launch Topshop into the activewear market with an athletic streetwear line. Sir Philip Green commented on the collaboration, noting that partnering with Beyoncé—an intensely hard-working talent who dedicates countless hours to dance, rehearsal, and training—presented a unique chance to develop this category. The resulting company and its collection are scheduled for launch, arriving in stores by the fall of 2015.

input: In grading lumber and structural timber, knots are classified according to their form, size, soundness, and the firmness with which they are held in place. This firmness is affected by, among other factors, the length of time for which the branch was dead while the attaching stem continued to grow.
rewrite: When grading lumber and structural timber, knots are categorized by their form, size, soundness, and how firmly they are held. This firmness depends on factors like how long the branch was dead while the tree's stem kept growing.

input: The Nabatean Kingdom was an Arab state located between the Sinai Peninsula and the Arabian Peninsula. Its capital was the city of Petra, an important trading city on the incense route. The Nabateans resisted the attacks of Antigonous and were allies of the Hasmoneans in their struggle against the Seleucids, but later fought against Herod the great. The hellenization of the Nabateans accured relatively late in comparison to the surrounding regions. Nabatean material culture does not show any Greek influence until the reign of Aretas III Philhellene in the 1st century BCE. Aretas captured Damascus and built the Petra pool complex and gardens in the Hellenistic style. Though the Nabateans originally worshipped their traditional gods in symbolic form such as stone blocks or pillars, during the Hellenistic period they began to identify their gods with Greek gods and depict them in figurative forms influenced by Greek sculpture. Nabatean art shows Greek influences and paintings have been found depicting Dionysian scenes. They also slowly adopted Greek as a language of commerce along with Aramaic and Arabic.
rewrite: Situated between the Sinai and Arabian Peninsulas, the Nabatean Kingdom had its capital at Petra, a key hub on the incense trade route. While the Nabateans successfully resisted assaults by Antigonous and initially allied with the Hasmoneans against the Seleucids, they later entered into conflict with Herod the Great. Hellenization reached this Arab state later than its neighbors, with Nabatean material culture revealing no Greek influence until the first century BCE under King Aretas III Philhellene. It was he who captured Damascus and constructed the Hellenistic-style pool complex and gardens at Petra. Originally, their traditional deities were worshipped as symbolic stone blocks or pillars. During the Hellenistic period, however, they began to equate these gods with Greek counterparts, portraying them in figurative forms shaped by Greek sculpture. This Greek influence is evident in Nabatean art, which includes paintings of Dionysian scenes. Gradually, Greek also came into use alongside Aramaic and Arabic as a commercial language.

input: In the mid 1970s, various American groups (some with ties to Downtown Manhattan's punk scene, including Television and Suicide) had begun expanding on the vocabulary of punk music. Midwestern groups such as Pere Ubu and Devo drew inspiration from the region's derelict industrial environments, employing conceptual art techniques, musique concrète and unconventional verbal styles that would presage the post-punk movement by several years. A variety of subsequent groups, including New York-based Talking Heads and Boston-based Mission of Burma, combined elements of punk with art school sensibilities. In 1978, the former band began a series of collaborations with British ambient pioneer and ex-Roxy Music member Brian Eno, experimenting with Dada-influenced lyrical techniques, dance music, and African polyrhythms. San Francisco's vibrant post-punk scene was centered around such groups as Chrome, the Residents and Tuxedomoon, who incorporated multimedia experimentation, film and ideas from Antonin Artaud's Theater of Cruelty.
rewrite: During the mid-1970s, the foundations of punk music were being expanded by several American groups. Some, like Television and Suicide, had connections to Downtown Manhattan's punk scene. Meanwhile, Midwestern acts such as Pere Ubu and Devo found inspiration in decaying industrial landscapes, utilizing conceptual art, musique concrète, and unusual verbal styles—elements that foreshadowed the post-punk movement years in advance. This art school sensibility was later blended with punk by bands including New York's Talking Heads and Boston's Mission of Burma. In 1978, Talking Heads initiated collaborations with British ambient pioneer Brian Eno, formerly of Roxy Music, exploring Dada-influenced lyrics, dance rhythms, and African polyrhythms. Simultaneously, a vibrant San Francisco scene revolved around groups like Chrome, the Residents, and Tuxedomoon, who integrated multimedia, film, and concepts from Antonin Artaud's Theater of Cruelty.

input: According to Martin Heidegger we do not exist inside time, we are time. Hence, the relationship to the past is a present awareness of having been, which allows the past to exist in the present. The relationship to the future is the state of anticipating a potential possibility, task, or engagement. It is related to the human propensity for caring and being concerned, which causes "being ahead of oneself" when thinking of a pending occurrence. Therefore, this concern for a potential occurrence also allows the future to exist in the present. The present becomes an experience, which is qualitative instead of quantitative. Heidegger seems to think this is the way that a linear relationship with time, or temporal existence, is broken or transcended. We are not stuck in sequential time. We are able to remember the past and project into the future—we have a kind of random access to our representation of temporal existence; we can, in our thoughts, step out of (ecstasis) sequential time.
rewrite: Martin Heidegger proposes that we are not merely within time, but rather we are time itself. Consequently, our connection to the past is a present awareness of having been, enabling the past to live within the now. Similarly, our relationship to the future is defined by anticipating potential tasks or engagements, tied to our inherent capacity for care and concern. This very concern, which places us “ahead of ourselves” when considering what is to come, also permits the future to inhabit the present. Thus, the present transforms into a qualitative experience rather than a quantitative measure. In this manner, Heidegger suggests we break from a linear, sequential existence in time. We are not confined to its strict progression. Instead, we possess a kind of random access to our temporal existence—able to remember the past and project into the future. Through our thoughts, we can step out of sequential time, achieving a state of ecstasis.

input: The events of the summer of 1974 dominate the politics on the island, as well as Greco-Turkish relations. Around 150,000 settlers from Turkey are believed to be living in the north—many of whom were forced from Turkey by the Turkish government—in violation of the Geneva Convention and various UN resolutions. Following the invasion and the capture of its northern territory by Turkish troops, the Republic of Cyprus announced that all of its ports of entry in the north were closed, as they were effectively not under its control.[citation needed]
rewrite: The summer of 1974 remains a defining force in the island's politics and Greco-Turkish relations. After Turkish troops invaded and captured the northern territory, the Republic of Cyprus declared all northern ports of entry closed, as they were no longer under its control. In the north, an estimated 150,000 settlers from Turkey now reside. Many were reportedly relocated by the Turkish government, a move considered in violation of the Geneva Convention and multiple UN resolutions.

input: International influences help to encourage legal actions to be taken in India, such as the Geneva Declaration of the Right of Children Act was passed in 1924. This act was followed by The Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948 to which incorporated the basic human rights and needs of children for proper progression and growth in their younger years. These international acts encouraged major changes to the workforce in India which occurred in 1986 when the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act was put into place. This act prohibited hiring children younger than the age of 14, and from working in hazardous conditions.
rewrite: International influences have spurred legal measures in India, beginning with the 1924 Geneva Declaration on the Rights of the Child. Subsequently, the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights reinforced essential rights and needs for children's healthy development. These global standards prompted significant national reforms, notably the 1986 Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act. This legislation banned the employment of children under 14 and prohibited their work in dangerous environments.

input: The Government of Punjab is a provincial government in the federal structure of Pakistan, is based in Lahore, the capital of the Punjab Province. The Chief Minister of Punjab (CM) is elected by the Provincial Assembly of the Punjab to serve as the head of the provincial government in Punjab, Pakistan. The current Chief Minister is Shahbaz Sharif, who became the Chief Minister of Punjab as being restored after Governor's rule starting from 25 February 2009 to 30 March 2009. Thereafter got re-elected as a result of 11 May 2013 elections. The Provincial Assembly of the Punjab is a unicameral legislature of elected representatives of the province of Punjab, which is located in Lahore in eastern Pakistan. The Assembly was established under Article 106 of the Constitution of Pakistan as having a total of 371 seats, with 66 seats reserved for women and eight reserved for non-Muslims.
rewrite: Based in Lahore, the capital of Punjab Province, the Government of Punjab operates as a provincial administration within Pakistan's federal system. The head of this government is the Chief Minister, who is elected by the Provincial Assembly of the Punjab. Shahbaz Sharif currently holds this office; he initially assumed the role after a period of Governor's rule ended on 30 March 2009 and was later re-elected following the elections of 11 May 2013. This unicameral Provincial Assembly, also situated in Lahore in eastern Pakistan, constitutes the province's elected legislature. Its establishment and composition are defined by Article 106 of the Constitution of Pakistan, providing for a total of 371 seats. Among these, 66 seats are reserved for women and eight for non-Muslims.

input: Differences in feasts may also originate from doctrinal issues—the Feast of the Assumption is such an example. Given that there is no agreement among all Christians on the circumstances of the death, Dormition or Assumption of Mary, the feast of assumption is celebrated among some denominations and not others.  While the Catholic Church celebrates the Feast of the Assumption on August 15, some Eastern Catholics celebrate it as Dormition of the Theotokos, and may do so on August 28, if they follow the Julian calendar. The Eastern Orthodox also celebrate it as the Dormition of the Theotokos, one of their 12 Great Feasts. Protestants do not celebrate this, or any other Marian feasts.
rewrite: Doctrinal disagreements can lead to differences in feast days, as seen with the observance of Mary's Assumption. Since Christians do not universally agree on the details of Mary's death or assumption, only certain denominations mark this occasion. Catholics observe the Feast of the Assumption on August 15. Meanwhile, many Eastern Catholics and the Eastern Orthodox Church commemorate it as the Dormition of the Theotokos, a principal feast for the latter. Some Eastern communities using the Julian calendar observe it on August 28. Protestant traditions, however, typically do not celebrate this or any other feasts dedicated to Mary.

input: The Greek economy is classified as advanced and high-income. Greece was a founding member of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and the Organization of the Black Sea Economic Cooperation (BSEC). In 1979 the accession of the country in the European Communities and the single market was signed, and the process was completed in 1982. Greece was accepted into the Economic and Monetary Union of the European Union on 19 June 2000, and in January 2001 adopted the Euro as its currency, replacing the Greek drachma at an exchange rate of 340.75 drachma to the Euro. Greece is also a member of the International Monetary Fund and the World Trade Organization, and is ranked 24th on the KOF Globalization Index for 2013.
rewrite: Greece maintains an advanced, high-income economy and holds membership in several major international organizations. It was a founding member of both the OECD and the Black Sea Economic Cooperation. The country joined the European Communities in 1979, a process finalized in 1982, and later entered the Economic and Monetary Union on June 19, 2000. In January 2001, Greece adopted the Euro, replacing the drachma at a fixed rate of 340.75 drachma per Euro. Additionally, Greece is a member of the International Monetary Fund and the World Trade Organization, and it ranked 24th on the 2013 KOF Globalization Index.

input: Due to the lack of success lately on the international level, in recent years, Armenia has rebuilt 16 Soviet-era sports schools and furnished them with new equipment for a total cost of $1.9 million. The rebuilding of the regional schools was financed by the Armenian government. $9.3 million has been invested in the resort town of Tsaghkadzor to improve the winter sports infrastructure because of dismal performances at recent winter sports events. In 2005, a cycling center was opened in Yerevan with the aim of helping produce world class Armenian cyclists. The government has also promised a cash reward of $700,000 to Armenians who win a gold medal at the Olympics.
rewrite: In recent years, Armenia has undertaken several initiatives to improve its international athletic standing. This includes rebuilding and equipping 16 Soviet-era regional sports schools at a cost of $1.9 million, a project financed by the government. Furthermore, $9.3 million was invested to upgrade winter sports infrastructure in Tsaghkadzor, a response to poor results in recent competitions. A cycling center opened in Yerevan in 2005 to develop world-class cyclists. Additionally, the government has pledged a $700,000 reward for any Armenian athlete winning an Olympic gold medal.

input: All of the highways into Wenchuan, and others throughout the province, were damaged, resulting in delayed arrival of the rescue troops. In Beichuan County, 80% of the buildings collapsed according to Xinhua News. In the city of Shifang, the collapse of two chemical plants led to leakage of some 80 tons of liquid ammonia, with hundreds of people reported buried. In the city of Dujiangyan, south-east of the epicenter, a whole school collapsed with 900 students buried and fewer than 60 survived. The Juyuan Middle School, where many teenagers were buried, was excavated by civilians and cranes. Dujiangyan is home of the Dujiangyan Irrigation System, an ancient water diversion project which is still in use and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The project's famous Fish Mouth was cracked but not severely damaged otherwise.
rewrite: Highways across the province, including all routes into Wenchuan, sustained damage, delaying rescue teams. Xinhua News reported an 80% building collapse rate in Beichuan County. In Shifang, two chemical plant collapses caused roughly 80 tons of liquid ammonia to leak, and hundreds were buried. Southeast of the epicenter, in Dujiangyan, a school collapse buried 900 students, with fewer than 60 survivors. Civilians and cranes excavated the Juyuan Middle School, where many teenagers were trapped. Dujiangyan hosts the ancient, still-functional Dujiangyan Irrigation System, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The system's famous Fish Mouth feature was cracked but otherwise not severely damaged.

input: At the beginning of the 13th century, there were reasonably accurate Latin translations of the main works of almost all the intellectually crucial ancient authors, allowing a sound transfer of scientific ideas via both the universities and the monasteries. By then, the natural philosophy contained in these texts began to be extended by notable scholastics such as Robert Grosseteste, Roger Bacon, Albertus Magnus and Duns Scotus. Precursors of the modern scientific method, influenced by earlier contributions of the Islamic world, can be seen already in Grosseteste's emphasis on mathematics as a way to understand nature, and in the empirical approach admired by Bacon, particularly in his Opus Majus. Pierre Duhem's provocative thesis of the Catholic Church's Condemnation of 1277 led to the study of medieval science as a serious discipline, "but no one in the field any longer endorses his view that modern science started in 1277". However, many scholars agree with Duhem's view that the Middle Ages were a period of important scientific developments.
rewrite: By the start of the 13th century, the principal works of nearly all vital ancient thinkers were available in acceptably accurate Latin translations. This enabled a reliable transmission of scientific concepts through monastic and university channels. Within these texts, the natural philosophy started to be expanded by such notable scholastics as Robert Grosseteste, Roger Bacon, Albertus Magnus, and Duns Scotus. Early signs of the modern scientific method, bearing influences from earlier Islamic scholarship, are evident. They appear in Grosseteste’s focus on using mathematics to comprehend nature and in the empirical methods Bacon championed, especially within his *Opus Majus*. Although Pierre Duhem’s provocative thesis concerning the Catholic Church’s 1277 Condemnation helped establish medieval science as a serious field of study, his specific claim that modern science began in that year is no longer endorsed. Still, numerous scholars concur with his broader view that the Middle Ages were a time of significant scientific progress.

input: Japan conscripted many soldiers from its colonies of Korea and Formosa (Taiwan). To a small extent, some Vichy French, Indian National Army, and Burmese National Army forces were active in the area of the Pacific War. Collaborationist units from Hong Kong (reformed ex-colonial police), Philippines, Dutch East Indies (the PETA) and Dutch Guinea, British Malaya and British Borneo, Inner Mongolia and former French Indochina (after the overthrow of Vichy French regime) as well as Timorese militia also assisted Japanese war efforts.
rewrite: During the Pacific War, Japan drew numerous soldiers from its Korean and Formosan (Taiwanese) colonies. Collaborationist forces from Hong Kong, the Philippines, the Dutch East Indies (like the PETA), Dutch Guinea, British Malaya, British Borneo, Inner Mongolia, former French Indochina, and Timorese militia also aided its efforts. Additionally, some units from the Vichy French, the Indian National Army, and the Burmese National Army operated in the theater, albeit to a lesser extent.

input: By the mid-18th century, the Qing had successfully put outer regions such as Inner and Outer Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang under its control. Imperial commissioners and garrisons were sent to Mongolia and Tibet to oversee their affairs. These territories were also under supervision of a central government institution called Lifan Yuan. Qinghai was also put under direct control of the Qing court. Xinjiang, also known as Chinese Turkestan, was subdivided into the regions north and south of the Tian Shan mountains, also known today as Dzungaria and Tarim Basin respectively, but the post of Ili General was established in 1762 to exercise unified military and administrative jurisdiction over both regions. Dzungaria was fully opened to Han migration by the Qianlong Emperor from the beginning. Han migrants were at first forbidden from permanently settling in the Tarim Basin but were the ban was lifted after the invasion by Jahangir Khoja in the 1820s. Likewise, Manchuria was also governed by military generals until its division into provinces, though some areas of Xinjiang and Northeast China were lost to the Russian Empire in the mid-19th century. Manchuria was originally separated from China proper by the Inner Willow Palisade, a ditch and embankment planted with willows intended to restrict the movement of the Han Chinese, as the area was off-limits to civilian Han Chinese until the government started colonizing the area, especially since the 1860s.
rewrite: By the mid-1700s, the Qing Dynasty had extended its control over several outer regions, including Inner and Outer Mongolia, Tibet, and Xinjiang. Oversight of these territories was managed by the Lifan Yuan, a central government institution. To administer local affairs, the court dispatched imperial commissioners and stationed garrisons in Mongolia and Tibet, while Qinghai was brought under its direct rule. Xinjiang, often called Chinese Turkestan, was geographically divided by the Tian Shan mountains into Dzungaria to the north and the Tarim Basin to the south. In 1762, the position of Ili General was created to unify military and administrative control across both of these Xinjiang regions. Initially, the Qianlong Emperor permitted Han migration into Dzungaria but prohibited permanent Han settlement in the Tarim Basin. This ban was only revoked following Jahangir Khoja’s invasion in the 1820s. Manchuria, similarly, was administered by military generals until it was later organized into provinces. Historically, the Inner Willow Palisade—a barrier of ditches, embankments, and trees—separated Manchuria from China proper and restricted Han Chinese movement, as the region was off-limits to civilian Han settlement until government-sponsored colonization intensified, particularly from the 1860s onward. Despite this consolidation, some areas in Xinjiang and Northeast China were lost to the Russian Empire during the mid-19th century.

input: The first known smelting of iron began in Anatolia, around 1800 BC. Called the bloomery process, it produced very soft but ductile wrought iron. By 800 BC, iron-making technology had spread to Europe, arriving in Japan around 700 AD. Pig iron, a very hard but brittle alloy of iron and carbon, was being produced in China as early as 1200 BC, but did not arrive in Europe until the Middle Ages. Pig iron has a lower melting point than iron, and was used for making cast-iron. However, these metals found little practical use until the introduction of crucible steel around 300 BC. These steels were of poor quality, and the introduction of pattern welding, around the 1st century AD, sought to balance the extreme properties of the alloys by laminating them, to create a tougher metal. Around 700 AD, the Japanese began folding bloomery-steel and cast-iron in alternating layers to increase the strength of their swords, using clay fluxes to remove slag and impurities. This method of Japanese swordsmithing produced one of the purest steel-alloys of the early Middle Ages.
rewrite: Iron smelting first emerged in Anatolia around 1800 BC through the bloomery process, yielding soft yet ductile wrought iron. This technology reached Europe by 800 BC and Japan by approximately 700 AD. Separately, pig iron—a hard but brittle iron-carbon alloy—was being produced in China as early as 1200 BC, though it only arrived in Europe during the Middle Ages. With a lower melting point than pure iron, pig iron was suited for casting. Yet, these early metals saw limited practical application until crucible steel appeared around 300 BC. Initially of poor quality, steel improved with techniques like pattern welding in the 1st century AD, which laminated alloys to create tougher metals. By 700 AD, Japanese swordsmiths were folding bloomery steel and cast iron into alternating layers, employing clay fluxes to eliminate slag and impurities. This refined process resulted in one of the purest steel alloys of the early Middle Ages.

input: On 16 March 1934, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the Migratory Bird Hunting Stamp Act, which requires an annual stamp purchase by all hunters over the age of sixteen. The stamps are created on behalf of the program by the US Postal Service and depict wildlife artwork chosen through an annual contest. They play an important role in habitat conservation because ninety-eight percent of all funds generated by their sale go directly toward the purchase or lease of wetland habitat for protection in the National Wildlife Refuge System.[citation needed] In addition to waterfowl, it is estimated that one third of the nation's endangered species seek food and shelter in areas protected using Duck Stamp funds.[citation needed]
rewrite: Signed into law by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on March 16, 1934, the Migratory Bird Hunting Stamp Act mandates that all hunters aged sixteen and older purchase an annual stamp. The U.S. Postal Service produces these stamps, which feature winning designs from a yearly wildlife art contest. Crucially, ninety-eight percent of the revenue from sales is dedicated to acquiring or leasing wetlands for the National Wildlife Refuge System, making the program a vital conservation tool.[citation needed] These protected areas, funded by the Duck Stamp, also provide essential habitat for approximately one third of the nation's endangered species, beyond just waterfowl.[citation needed]

input: Before World War II, Oklahoma City developed major stockyards, attracting jobs and revenue formerly in Chicago and Omaha, Nebraska. With the 1928 discovery of oil within the city limits (including under the State Capitol), Oklahoma City became a major center of oil production. Post-war growth accompanied the construction of the Interstate Highway System, which made Oklahoma City a major interchange as the convergence of I-35, I-40 and I-44. It was also aided by federal development of Tinker Air Force Base.
rewrite: Prior to World War II, Oklahoma City established significant stockyards, drawing jobs and revenue away from cities like Chicago and Omaha. The 1928 discovery of oil, even beneath the State Capitol, further established it as a major oil production center. Post-war expansion was fueled by its position as a key interchange for Interstates 35, 40, and 44, alongside federal investment in Tinker Air Force Base.

input: Very small lamps may have the filament support wires extended through the base of the lamp, and can be directly soldered to a printed circuit board for connections. Some reflector-type lamps include screw terminals for connection of wires. Most lamps have metal bases that fit in a socket to support the lamp and conduct current to the filament wires. In the late 19th century, manufacturers introduced a multitude of incompatible lamp bases. General Electric introduced standard base sizes for tungsten incandescent lamps under the Mazda trademark in 1909. This standard was soon adopted across the US, and the Mazda name was used by many manufacturers under license through 1945. Today most incandescent lamps for general lighting service use an Edison screw in candelabra, intermediate, or standard or mogul sizes, or double contact bayonet base. Technical standards for lamp bases include ANSI standard C81.67 and IEC standard 60061-1 for common commercial lamp sizes, to ensure interchangeablitity between different manufacturer's products. Bayonet base lamps are frequently used in automotive lamps to resist loosening due to vibration. A bipin base is often used for halogen or reflector lamps.
