rewrite: To support the lamp and conduct electricity, most lamps feature metal bases that fit into sockets. In the late 19th century, numerous incompatible lamp bases were introduced by manufacturers. Standardization came in 1909 when General Electric established uniform base sizes for tungsten incandescent lamps under the Mazda trademark. This standard quickly gained adoption across the United States, and the Mazda name was licensed for use by many manufacturers until 1945. For connections, very small lamps might have their filament support wires extended through the base, allowing them to be soldered directly onto a printed circuit board. Some reflector-type lamps incorporate screw terminals for wire attachment. Today, general lighting incandescent lamps commonly use an Edison screw in candelabra, intermediate, standard, or mogul sizes, or a double contact bayonet base. Technical standards, such as ANSI C81.67 and IEC 60061-1 for common commercial sizes, ensure interchangeability between products from different manufacturers. Bayonet bases are often preferred in automotive lighting for their resistance to vibration-induced loosening, while a bipin base is typical for halogen or certain reflector lamps.

input: An antenna transmits and receives radio waves with a particular polarization which can be reoriented by tilting the axis of the antenna in many (but not all) cases. The physical size of an antenna is often a practical issue, particularly at lower frequencies (longer wavelengths). Highly directional antennas need to be significantly larger than the wavelength. Resonant antennas usually use a linear conductor (or element), or pair of such elements, each of which is about a quarter of the wavelength in length (an odd multiple of quarter wavelengths will also be resonant). Antennas that are required to be small compared to the wavelength sacrifice efficiency and cannot be very directional. Fortunately at higher frequencies (UHF, microwaves) trading off performance to obtain a smaller physical size is usually not required.
rewrite: Antennas send and receive radio waves with a specific polarization, which can frequently—though not always—be changed by tilting the antenna's axis. Their physical dimensions are a common practical concern, especially at lower frequencies where wavelengths are longer. For high directionality, an antenna must be considerably larger than the wavelength. Resonant types typically employ a linear conductor or element, or a pair of such elements, each roughly a quarter-wavelength long (odd multiples of quarter wavelengths also achieve resonance). When an antenna must be small relative to the wavelength, it loses efficiency and directivity. However, at higher frequencies like UHF and microwaves, compromising performance for a more compact size is generally unnecessary.

input: In flood lamps used for photographic lighting, the tradeoff is made in the other direction. Compared to general-service bulbs, for the same power, these bulbs produce far more light, and (more importantly) light at a higher color temperature, at the expense of greatly reduced life (which may be as short as two hours for a type P1 lamp). The upper temperature limit for the filament is the melting point of the metal. Tungsten is the metal with the highest melting point, 3,695 K (6,191 °F). A 50-hour-life projection bulb, for instance, is designed to operate only 50 °C (122 °F) below that melting point. Such a lamp may achieve up to 22 lumens per watt, compared with 17.5 for a 750-hour general service lamp.
rewrite: Photographic flood lamps prioritize performance over longevity, in contrast to general-service bulbs. For equivalent power, they emit significantly more light and, crucially, light at a higher color temperature. This comes at the cost of a greatly reduced lifespan; a P1 lamp, for example, may last only two hours. The filament's maximum temperature is constrained by its metal's melting point. Tungsten, with the highest melting point of 3,695 K (6,191 °F), is used. A projection bulb with a 50-hour life is engineered to run merely 50 °C (122 °F) below this limit. This design allows such a lamp to reach about 22 lumens per watt, whereas a 750-hour general service lamp provides roughly 17.5.

input: The noise-based speed is defined as the exposure that will lead to a given signal-to-noise ratio on individual pixels. Two ratios are used, the 40:1 ("excellent image quality") and the 10:1 ("acceptable image quality") ratio. These ratios have been subjectively determined based on a resolution of 70 pixels per cm (178 DPI) when viewed at 25 cm (9.8 inch) distance. The signal-to-noise ratio is defined as the standard deviation of a weighted average of the luminance and color of individual pixels. The noise-based speed is mostly determined by the properties of the sensor and somewhat affected by the noise in the electronic gain and AD converter.
rewrite: Noise-based speed refers to the exposure needed to achieve a specific signal-to-noise ratio per pixel. This ratio, defined as the standard deviation of a weighted average of pixel luminance and color, uses two benchmarks: 40:1 for "excellent image quality" and 10:1 for "acceptable image quality." These thresholds were established subjectively, assuming a resolution of 70 pixels per cm (178 DPI) viewed from 25 cm (9.8 inches). Primarily influenced by sensor characteristics, noise-based speed is also slightly impacted by noise from the electronic gain and AD converter.

input: Islamic art frequently adopts the use of geometrical floral or vegetal designs in a repetition known as arabesque. Such designs are highly nonrepresentational, as Islam forbids representational depictions as found in pre-Islamic pagan religions. Despite this, there is a presence of depictional art in some Muslim societies, notably the miniature style made famous in Persia and under the Ottoman Empire which featured paintings of people and animals, and also depictions of Quranic stories and Islamic traditional narratives. Another reason why Islamic art is usually abstract is to symbolize the transcendence, indivisible and infinite nature of God, an objective achieved by arabesque. Islamic calligraphy is an omnipresent decoration in Islamic art, and is usually expressed in the form of Quranic verses. Two of the main scripts involved are the symbolic kufic and naskh scripts, which can be found adorning the walls and domes of mosques, the sides of minbars, and so on.
rewrite: Islamic art is often characterized by abstract, nonrepresentational designs, primarily due to the Islamic prohibition against representational depictions common in pre-Islamic pagan religions. This abstraction is exemplified by the arabesque, a repetitive pattern of geometrical floral or vegetal motifs. Beyond symbolizing the faith's rejection of idolatry, this style also aims to evoke the transcendence, indivisible and infinite nature of God. Despite this prevailing abstraction, some Muslim societies have produced depictional art, such as the Persian and Ottoman miniature paintings illustrating people, animals, and scenes from Quranic stories. Another omnipresent decorative element is Islamic calligraphy, typically featuring Quranic verses. Prominent scripts like the symbolic kufic and naskh are used to adorn mosque walls, domes, minbars, and other surfaces.

input: Since 2001, Miami has been undergoing a large building boom with more than 50 skyscrapers rising over 400 feet (122 m) built or currently under construction in the city. Miami's skyline is ranked third-most impressive in the U.S., behind New York City and Chicago, and 19th in the world according to the Almanac of Architecture and Design. The city currently has the eight tallest (as well as thirteen of the fourteen tallest) skyscrapers in the state of Florida, with the tallest being the 789-foot (240 m) Four Seasons Hotel & Tower.
rewrite: Miami's skyline, ranked third in the U.S. and 19th globally, has been transformed by a major building boom since 2001. Over 50 skyscrapers exceeding 400 feet have been completed or are underway. The city holds Florida's eight tallest buildings, including the top thirteen of fourteen. Dominating them all is the Four Seasons Hotel & Tower, which rises 789 feet as the state's tallest.

input: In Darwin's time there was no agreed-upon model of heredity; in Chapter I Darwin admitted, "The laws governing inheritance are quite unknown." He accepted a version of the inheritance of acquired characteristics (which after Darwin's death came to be called Lamarckism), and Chapter V discusses what he called the effects of use and disuse; he wrote that he thought "there can be little doubt that use in our domestic animals strengthens and enlarges certain parts, and disuse diminishes them; and that such modifications are inherited", and that this also applied in nature. Darwin stated that some changes that were commonly attributed to use and disuse, such as the loss of functional wings in some island dwelling insects, might be produced by natural selection. In later editions of Origin, Darwin expanded the role attributed to the inheritance of acquired characteristics. Darwin also admitted ignorance of the source of inheritable variations, but speculated they might be produced by environmental factors. However, one thing was clear: whatever the exact nature and causes of new variations, Darwin knew from observation and experiment that breeders were able to select such variations and produce huge differences in many generations of selection. The observation that selection works in domestic animals is not destroyed by lack of understanding of the underlying hereditary mechanism.
rewrite: During Darwin’s era, no established model of heredity existed. He acknowledged this uncertainty in Chapter I, stating, "The laws governing inheritance are quite unknown." Darwin incorporated a form of the inheritance of acquired characteristics—later termed Lamarckism—and in Chapter V he examined the effects of use and disuse. He expressed his belief that in domestic animals, use strengthens and enlarges certain parts while disuse diminishes them, and that such modifications are inherited, applying this also to nature. Yet Darwin noted that some changes often linked to use and disuse, like the loss of functional wings in certain island insects, could instead arise through natural selection. In later editions of *Origin*, he gave greater emphasis to the inheritance of acquired characteristics. While admitting he did not know the origin of inheritable variations, Darwin speculated that environmental factors might produce them. Crucially, however, he recognized from observation and experiment that breeders could select variations and, over many generations, achieve dramatic differences. This demonstrated that selection’s effectiveness in domestic animals remained intact even without a full understanding of the hereditary mechanism.

input: Many ancient works, such as the Bible and the Greek tragedies,[citation needed] survive in hundreds of copies, and the relationship of each copy to the original may be unclear. Textual scholars have debated for centuries which sources are most closely derived from the original, hence which readings in those sources are correct.[citation needed] Although biblical books that are letters, like Greek plays, presumably had one original, the question of whether some biblical books, like the Gospels, ever had just one original has been discussed. Interest in applying textual criticism to the Qur'an has also developed after the discovery of the Sana'a manuscripts in 1972, which possibly date back to the 7–8th centuries.
rewrite: Numerous ancient texts, including the Bible and Greek tragedies, exist today through hundreds of copies, often obscuring their connection to a single original. For centuries, textual scholars have disputed which surviving sources are most faithful and which readings within them are accurate. While epistolary biblical books and Greek dramas likely each began with one origin, scholars have questioned whether books like the Gospels ever had a sole initial version. The discovery of the Sana'a manuscripts in 1972, potentially dating to the 7th or 8th century, has further spurred interest in applying such textual criticism to the Qur'an.

input: The Bovington signal course's director reported that Gaddafi successfully overcame problems learning English, displaying a firm command of voice procedure. Noting that Gaddafi's favourite hobbies were reading and playing football, he thought him an "amusing officer, always cheerful, hard-working, and conscientious." Gaddafi disliked England, claiming British Army officers racially insulted him and finding it difficult adjusting to the country's culture; asserting his Arab identity in London, he walked around Piccadilly wearing traditional Libyan robes. He later related that while he travelled to England believing it more advanced than Libya, he returned home "more confident and proud of our values, ideals and social character."
rewrite: According to the Bovington signal course director, Gaddafi mastered English voice procedure despite initial difficulties. Described as an amusing, cheerful, hard-working, and conscientious officer, his favorite hobbies were reading and football. However, he disliked England, struggling with the culture and alleging racial insults from British officers. In London, he asserted his Arab identity by wearing traditional Libyan robes in Piccadilly. He later stated that while he initially believed England more advanced, he returned to Libya more confident and proud of his homeland's values, ideals, and social character.

input: In addition to Somali, Arabic, which is also an Afro-Asiatic tongue, is an official national language in both Somalia and Djibouti. Many Somalis speak it due to centuries-old ties with the Arab world, the far-reaching influence of the Arabic media, and religious education. Somalia and Djibouti are also both members of the Arab League.
rewrite: Arabic is an official language in Somalia and Djibouti, both members of the Arab League. Many Somalis speak this Afro-Asiatic tongue due to historical Arab ties, widespread Arabic media, and religious education.

input: Because of a low literacy rate among the public (about 2–3% until the early 19th century and just about 15% at the end of 19th century),[citation needed] ordinary people had to hire scribes as "special request-writers" (arzuhâlcis) to be able to communicate with the government. The ethnic groups continued to speak within their families and neighborhoods (mahalles) with their own languages (e.g., Jews, Greeks, Armenians, etc.). In villages where two or more populations lived together, the inhabitants would often speak each other's language. In cosmopolitan cities, people often spoke their family languages; many of those who were not ethnic Turks spoke Turkish as a second language.
rewrite: Until the early 19th century, the general public's literacy rate was very low, around 2–3%, rising only to about 15% by the century's end. Consequently, ordinary individuals needed to employ scribes known as "special request-writers" (arzuhâlcis) for official correspondence. Within their own families and local neighborhoods (mahalles), various ethnic communities—such as Jews, Greeks, and Armenians—continued using their native languages. In villages with mixed populations, inhabitants commonly learned and spoke each other's languages. Meanwhile, in cosmopolitan urban centers, people typically used their family language at home, with many non-ethnic Turks speaking Turkish as a secondary language.

input: New Haven Harbor is home to the Port of New Haven, a deep-water seaport with three berths capable of hosting vessels and barges as well as the facilities required to handle break bulk cargo. The port has the capacity to load 200 trucks a day from the ground or via loading docks. Rail transportation access is available, with a private switch engine for yard movements and private siding for loading and unloading. Approximately 400,000 square feet (40,000 m2) of inside storage and 50 acres (200,000 m2) of outside storage are available at the site. Five shore cranes with a 250-ton capacity and 26 forklifts, each with a 26-ton capacity, are also available.
rewrite: The Port of New Haven, located within New Haven Harbor, is a deep-water seaport featuring three berths for vessels and barges, equipped to manage break bulk cargo. Its operations are supported by substantial storage, including roughly 400,000 square feet indoors and 50 acres outdoors. For cargo handling, the port offers five shore cranes with a 250-ton capacity and 26 forklifts, each capable of lifting 26 tons. Logistics are further enhanced by the capacity to load 200 trucks daily, either from the ground or via docks, and by rail access that includes a private switch engine and siding for efficient yard movements and transfers.

input: Scientists do not know the exact cause of sexual orientation, but they believe that it is caused by a complex interplay of genetic, hormonal, and environmental influences. They favor biologically-based theories, which point to genetic factors, the early uterine environment, both, or the inclusion of genetic and social factors. There is no substantive evidence which suggests parenting or early childhood experiences play a role when it comes to sexual orientation. Research over several decades has demonstrated that sexual orientation ranges along a continuum, from exclusive attraction to the opposite sex to exclusive attraction to the same sex.
rewrite: The precise origins of sexual orientation remain unknown, though science indicates a complex combination of genetic, hormonal, and environmental factors. Most research supports biologically-based explanations, involving genetics, the early uterine environment, or a blend of genetic and social influences. Decades of study show that sexual orientation exists along a spectrum, from exclusive attraction to the opposite sex to exclusive attraction to the same sex. No substantive evidence links it to parenting or early childhood experiences.

input: When military conflicts broke out between the Ottoman Empire and other states, Greeks usually took arms against the Empire, with few exceptions. Prior to the Greek revolution, there had been a number of wars which saw Greeks fight against the Ottomans, such as the Greek participation in the Battle of Lepanto in 1571, the Epirus peasants' revolts of 1600–1601, the Morean War of 1684–1699, and the Russian-instigated Orlov Revolt in 1770, which aimed at breaking up the Ottoman Empire in favor of Russian interests.[page needed] These uprisings were put down by the Ottomans with great bloodshed.
rewrite: During conflicts involving the Ottoman Empire, Greeks typically took up arms against it, with only rare exceptions. Before the Greek revolution, several wars featured Greek opposition. Examples include their role in the 1571 Battle of Lepanto, the Epirus peasant revolts (1600–1601), the Morean War (1684–1699), and the Russian-backed Orlov Revolt of 1770, which sought to dismantle the Empire for Russia's gain. The Ottomans suppressed all these uprisings with severe bloodshed.

input: Many of London's pubs are known to have been used by famous people, but in some cases, such as the association between Samuel Johnson and Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese, this is speculative, based on little more than the fact that the person is known to have lived nearby. However, Charles Dickens is known to have visited the Cheshire Cheese, the Prospect of Whitby, Ye Olde Cock Tavern and many others. Samuel Pepys is also associated with the Prospect of Whitby and the Cock Tavern.
rewrite: While numerous London pubs boast ties to famous figures, some connections, like Samuel Johnson's link to Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese, rely more on proximity than documented proof. In contrast, Charles Dickens is confirmed to have visited establishments such as the Cheshire Cheese, the Prospect of Whitby, and Ye Olde Cock Tavern. Samuel Pepys is also historically associated with the Prospect of Whitby and the Cock Tavern.

input: Myanmar (myan-MAR i/miɑːnˈmɑːr/ mee-ahn-MAR, /miˈɛnmɑːr/ mee-EN-mar or /maɪˈænmɑːr/ my-AN-mar (also with the stress on first syllable); Burmese pronunciation: [mjəmà]),[nb 1] officially the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and also known as Burma, is a sovereign state in Southeast Asia bordered by Bangladesh, India, China, Laos and Thailand. One-third of Myanmar's total perimeter of 1,930 km (1,200 miles) forms an uninterrupted coastline along the Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea. The country's 2014 census revealed a much lower population than expected, with 51 million people recorded. Myanmar is 676,578 square kilometres (261,227 sq mi) in size. Its capital city is Naypyidaw and its largest city is Yangon (Rangoon).
rewrite: Officially called the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and also known as Burma, Myanmar is a sovereign Southeast Asian nation. It shares borders with Bangladesh, India, China, Laos, and Thailand. The country spans 676,578 square kilometres (261,227 sq mi). Its capital is Naypyidaw, while its largest city is Yangon (Rangoon). A significant portion of its 1,930 km (1,200 miles) perimeter is coastline along the Bay of Bengal and the Andaman Sea. According to the 2014 census, the population was 51 million, which was lower than anticipated. The name is pronounced in various ways, such as myan-MAR or mee-ahn-MAR, with Burmese pronunciation being [mjəmà].

input: Widespread rumors of Napoleon's return from St. Helena and Napoleon as an inspiration for patriotism, individual and collective liberties, and political mobilization manifested themselves in seditious materials, displaying the tricolor and rosettes. There were also subversive activities celebrating anniversaries of Napoleon's life and reign and disrupting royal celebrations—they demonstrated the prevailing and successful goal of the varied supporters of Napoleon to constantly destabilize the Bourbon regime.
rewrite: Rumors of Napoleon's return from St. Helena spread widely, alongside his image as a symbol for patriotism, liberties, and political action. This manifested in seditious items showing tricolors and rosettes. Supporters also engaged in subversive acts, marking anniversaries of his life and disrupting royal events. These sustained efforts successfully aimed to destabilize the Bourbon regime.

input: Anthropologists have most frequently employed the term 'identity' to refer to this idea of selfhood in a loosely Eriksonian way (Erikson 1972) properties based on the uniqueness and individuality which makes a person distinct from others. Identity became of more interest to anthropologists with the emergence of modern concerns with ethnicity and social movements in the 1970s. This was reinforced by an appreciation, following the trend in sociological thought, of the manner in which the individual is affected by and contributes to the overall social context. At the same time, the Eriksonian approach to identity remained in force, with the result that identity has continued until recently to be used in a largely socio-historical way to refer to qualities of sameness in relation to a person's connection to others and to a particular group of people.
rewrite: In a loosely Eriksonian sense (Erikson 1972), anthropologists have most often used 'identity' to describe selfhood—those properties of uniqueness and individuality distinguishing one person from another. Modern interest in ethnicity and social movements during the 1970s heightened anthropology's focus on identity. This was further strengthened by an understanding, aligned with sociological trends, of how the individual both shapes and is shaped by the broader social context. Throughout this period, the Eriksonian framework persisted. Consequently, until recently, the term has largely retained a socio-historical usage, denoting qualities of sameness that arise from a person's bonds with others and membership in a specific group.

input: Epic poetry, notably the "acritic songs", flourished during Middle Ages. Two chronicles, one written by Leontios Machairas and the other by Georgios Voustronios, cover the entire Middle Ages until the end of Frankish rule (4th century–1489). Poèmes d'amour written in medieval Greek Cypriot date back from the 16th century. Some of them are actual translations of poems written by Petrarch, Bembo, Ariosto and G. Sannazzaro. Many Cypriot scholars fled Cyprus at troubled times such as Ioannis Kigalas (c. 1622–1687) who migrated from Cyprus to Italy in the 17th century, several of his works have survived in books of other scholars.
rewrite: During the Middle Ages, epic poetry, especially the "acritic songs," saw significant flourishing. The period from the 4th century until 1489, the end of Frankish rule, is documented in two chronicles by Leontios Machairas and Georgios Voustronios. From the 16th century come Poèmes d'amour, composed in medieval Greek Cypriot; some are direct translations of works by Petrarch, Bembo, Ariosto, and G. Sannazzaro. In turbulent eras, many Cypriot scholars left the island, like Ioannis Kigalas (c. 1622–1687), who moved to Italy in the 17th century. Several of his writings survive within the books of other scholars.

input: Sevastopol fell after eleven months, and formerly neutral countries began to join the allied cause. Isolated and facing a bleak prospect of invasion from the west if the war continued, Russia sued for peace in March 1856. This was welcomed by France and the UK, where the citizens began to turn against their governments as the war dragged on. The war was officially ended by the Treaty of Paris, signed on 30 March 1856. Russia lost the war, and was forbidden from hosting warships in the Black Sea. The Ottoman vassal states of Wallachia and Moldavia became largely independent. Christians were granted a degree of official equality, and the Orthodox church regained control of the Christian churches in dispute.:415
rewrite: Following an eleven-month siege, Sevastopol fell, prompting previously neutral nations to align with the allies. Facing isolation and the grim threat of a western invasion should the conflict persist, Russia sought peace in March 1856. France and Britain, where public support for the war was waning, welcomed this development. The conflict was formally concluded by the Treaty of Paris on 30 March 1856. The terms stipulated that Russia, having lost the war, could not station warships in the Black Sea. Wallachia and Moldavia, former Ottoman vassal states, gained significant autonomy. Christians achieved a measure of legal equality, and the Orthodox Church reestablished its authority over the disputed Christian churches.

input: According to the latest International Monetary Fund estimates, its per capita GDP (adjusted for purchasing power) at $30,769 is just above the average of the European Union.[citation needed] Cyprus has been sought as a base for several offshore businesses for its low tax rates. Tourism, financial services and shipping are significant parts of the economy. Economic policy of the Cyprus government has focused on meeting the criteria for admission to the European Union. The Cypriot government adopted the euro as the national currency on 1 January 2008.
rewrite: Cyprus’s economy relies significantly on tourism, financial services, and shipping. The nation has also attracted numerous offshore businesses due to its favorable tax rates. With a purchasing power-adjusted GDP per capita of $30,769, it slightly exceeds the European Union average, based on recent IMF estimates. Historically, government policy prioritized meeting EU accession requirements. This culminated in Cyprus adopting the euro as its official currency on January 1, 2008.

input: Four separate and distinct state universities are located in Houston. The University of Houston is a nationally recognized Tier One research university, and is the flagship institution of the University of Houston System. The third-largest university in Texas, the University of Houston has nearly 40,000 students on its 667-acre campus in southeast Houston. The University of Houston–Clear Lake and the University of Houston–Downtown are stand-alone universities; they are not branch campuses of the University of Houston. Located in the historic community of Third Ward is Texas Southern University, one of the largest historically black colleges and universities in the United States.
rewrite: Houston is home to four separate state universities. The University of Houston, the flagship of its system, is a nationally recognized Tier One research institution. With nearly 40,000 students on its 667-acre southeast campus, it ranks as the third-largest university in Texas. Two other stand-alone universities, not branches of the main campus, are the University of Houston–Clear Lake and the University of Houston–Downtown. Additionally, Texas Southern University, situated in the historic Third Ward, is one of the nation's largest historically black colleges and universities.

input: 1,500 V DC is used in the Netherlands, Japan, Republic Of Indonesia, Hong Kong (parts), Republic of Ireland, Australia (parts), India (around the Mumbai area alone, has been converted to 25 kV AC like the rest of India), France (also using 25 kV 50 Hz AC), New Zealand (Wellington) and the United States (Chicago area on the Metra Electric district and the South Shore Line interurban line). In Slovakia, there are two narrow-gauge lines in the High Tatras (one a cog railway). In Portugal, it is used in the Cascais Line and in Denmark on the suburban S-train system.
rewrite: A 1,500 V DC railway system operates in several global locations. These include the Netherlands, Japan, parts of Hong Kong and Australia, the Republic of Ireland, and the Republic of Indonesia. In India, it was formerly used around Mumbai but has been converted to 25 kV AC. France also primarily uses 25 kV AC, while New Zealand utilizes this standard in Wellington. In the United States, it serves Chicago's Metra Electric and South Shore Line. Additionally, Slovakia employs it on two High Tatras narrow-gauge lines, Portugal on the Cascais Line, and Denmark on its suburban S-train network.

input: The fate of Willett's 1907 proposal illustrates several political issues involved. The proposal attracted many supporters, including Balfour, Churchill, Lloyd George, MacDonald, Edward VII (who used half-hour DST at Sandringham), the managing director of Harrods, and the manager of the National Bank. However, the opposition was stronger: it included Prime Minister H. H. Asquith, Christie (the Astronomer Royal), George Darwin, Napier Shaw (director of the Meteorological Office), many agricultural organizations, and theatre owners. After many hearings the proposal was narrowly defeated in a Parliament committee vote in 1909. Willett's allies introduced similar bills every year from 1911 through 1914, to no avail. The US was even more skeptical: Andrew Peters introduced a DST bill to the US House of Representatives in May 1909, but it soon died in committee.
rewrite: Willett's 1907 proposal, though ultimately unsuccessful, highlights key political divisions. It garnered notable supporters such as Balfour, Churchill, Lloyd George, MacDonald, King Edward VII (who privately adopted half-hour DST at Sandringham), the managing director of Harrods, and the National Bank's manager. Yet opposition proved stronger, featuring Prime Minister H. H. Asquith, Astronomer Royal Christie, George Darwin, Meteorological Office director Napier Shaw, numerous farm groups, and theatre owners. After extensive hearings, Parliament's committee narrowly defeated the measure in 1909. Similar bills were introduced annually from 1911 to 1914, all failing. In the United States, skepticism was even greater; a 1909 House bill from Andrew Peters quickly died in committee.

input: The term "Moors" has been used in Europe in a broader, somewhat derogatory sense to refer to Muslims, especially those of Arab or Berber descent, whether living in North Africa or Iberia. Moors were not a distinct or self-defined people. Medieval and early modern Europeans applied the name to Muslim Arabs, Berbers, Black Africans and Europeans alike.
rewrite: Historically, Europeans broadly and often pejoratively used "Moors" for Muslims, particularly of Arab or Berber origin from North Africa or Iberia. It was not a self-defined identity. The term was applied indiscriminately to Muslim Arabs, Berbers, Black Africans, and Europeans during medieval and early modern periods.

input: Thousands of Soviet troops were sent to the Fergana Valley, southeast of the Uzbek capital Tashkent, to re-establish order after clashes in which local Uzbeks hunted down members of the Meskhetian minority in several days of rioting between June 4–11, 1989; about 100 people were killed. On June 23, 1989, Gorbachev removed Rafiq Nishonov as First Secretary of the Communist Party of the Uzbek SSR and replaced him with Karimov, who went on to lead Uzbekistan as a Soviet Republic and subsequently as an independent state.
rewrite: In June 1989, from the 4th to the 11th, violent riots erupted in the Fergana Valley southeast of Tashkent. Local Uzbeks targeted the Meskhetian minority, resulting in approximately 100 deaths. To restore order, thousands of Soviet troops were deployed to the region. Shortly thereafter, on June 23, Mikhail Gorbachev replaced Rafiq Nishonov as the Uzbek SSR's Communist Party First Secretary with Islam Karimov. Karimov would later lead Uzbekistan as a Soviet republic and then as an independent nation.

input: Broadcasters were faced with having to adapt daily to the varied recording characteristics of many sources: various makers of "home recordings" readily available to the public, European recordings, lateral-cut transcriptions, and vertical-cut transcriptions. Efforts were started in 1942 to standardize within the National Association of Broadcasters (NAB), later known as the National Association of Radio and Television Broadcasters (NARTB). The NAB, among other items, issued recording standards in 1949 for laterally and vertically cut records, principally transcriptions. A number of 78 rpm record producers as well as early LP makers also cut their records to the NAB/NARTB lateral standard.
rewrite: Broadcasters had to constantly adjust to diverse recording traits from multiple sources. These included various brands of publicly available "home recordings," European releases, and both lateral-cut and vertical-cut transcriptions. Starting in 1942, the National Association of Broadcasters (NAB)—later renamed the National Association of Radio and Television Broadcasters (NARTB)—began efforts to establish uniformity. In 1949, the NAB released standards primarily for transcription records, covering both lateral and vertical cuts. Subsequently, many producers of 78 rpm records and early LPs also adopted the NAB/NARTB lateral standard.

input: A satellite ground station with a 7.6-metre (25 ft) satellite dish installed in 1989 at The Briars is the only international connection providing satellite links through Intelsat 707 to Ascension island and the United Kingdom. Since all international telephone and internet communications are relying on this single satellite link both internet and telephone service are subject to sun outages.
rewrite: Installed in 1989 at The Briars, a 7.6-metre satellite dish provides the sole international link via Intelsat 707 to Ascension Island and the United Kingdom. All telephone and internet communications depend on this single satellite connection, making both services vulnerable to sun outages.

input: The 1950s and early 1960s are considered by many to be a golden age of Greek cinema. Directors and actors of this era were recognized as important historical figures in Greece and some gained international acclaim: Irene Papas, Melina Mercouri, Mihalis Kakogiannis, Alekos Sakellarios, Nikos Tsiforos, Iakovos Kambanelis, Katina Paxinou, Nikos Koundouros, Ellie Lambeti, and others. More than sixty films per year were made, with the majority having film noir elements. Notable films were Η κάλπικη λίρα (1955 directed by Giorgos Tzavellas), Πικρό Ψωμί (1951, directed by Grigoris Grigoriou), O Drakos (1956 directed by Nikos Koundouros), Stella (1955 directed by Cacoyannis and written by Kampanellis).
rewrite: Many regard the 1950s and early 1960s as a golden age for Greek cinema, a period producing over sixty films annually, most featuring film noir elements. This era celebrated directors and actors as major historical figures, with several achieving international fame, such as Irene Papas, Melina Mercouri, and Mihalis Kakogiannis. Other key contributors included Alekos Sakellarios, Nikos Tsiforos, Iakovos Kambanelis, Katina Paxinou, Nikos Koundouros, and Ellie Lambeti. Notable films from this time include *Η κάλπικη λίρα* (1955), *Πικρό Ψωμί* (1951), *O Drakos* (1956), and *Stella* (1955).

input: Alpine glaciers can be straight rivers of ice, long sweeping rivers, spread in a fan-like shape (Piedmont glaciers), and curtains of ice that hang from vertical slopes of the mountain peaks. The stress of the movement causes the ice to break and crack loudly, perhaps explaining why the mountains were believed to be home to dragons in the medieval period. The cracking creates unpredictable and dangerous crevasses, often invisible under new snowfall, which cause the greatest danger to mountaineers.
rewrite: Alpine glaciers take varied forms, from straight or sweeping rivers of ice to fan-shaped Piedmont glaciers and icy curtains hanging from vertical slopes. Their movement stresses the ice, causing loud cracks—a sound that may have fueled medieval beliefs in mountain dragons. This cracking also produces dangerous crevasses, often hidden under new snow, which pose the greatest risk to mountaineers.

input: Drinks especially high in simple sugars, such as soft drinks and fruit juices, are not recommended in children under 5 years of age as they may increase dehydration. A too rich solution in the gut draws water from the rest of the body, just as if the person were to drink sea water. Plain water may be used if more specific and effective ORT preparations are unavailable or are not palatable. Additionally, a mix of both plain water and drinks perhaps too rich in sugar and salt can alternatively be given to the same person, with the goal of providing a medium amount of sodium overall. A nasogastric tube can be used in young children to administer fluids if warranted.
rewrite: For children under five, beverages with high simple sugar content—like soft drinks and fruit juices—should be avoided, as they can worsen dehydration. Similar to drinking seawater, an overly concentrated solution in the intestines pulls water from bodily tissues. When oral rehydration therapy (ORT) solutions are not accessible or acceptable, plain water may serve as an alternative. Alternatively, combining plain water with drinks that might be excessively high in sugar and salt can achieve a moderate total sodium intake. If necessary, fluids can also be delivered to young children via a nasogastric tube.

input: According to the U.S. Census Bureau, in 2004, Miami had the third highest incidence of family incomes below the federal poverty line in the United States, making it the third poorest city in the USA, behind only Detroit, Michigan (ranked #1) and El Paso, Texas (ranked #2). Miami is also one of the very few cities where its local government went bankrupt, in 2001. However, since that time, Miami has experienced a revival: in 2008, Miami was ranked as "America's Cleanest City" according to Forbes for its year-round good air quality, vast green spaces, clean drinking water, clean streets and city-wide recycling programs. In a 2009 UBS study of 73 world cities, Miami was ranked as the richest city in the United States (of four U.S. cities included in the survey) and the world's fifth-richest city, in terms of purchasing power.
rewrite: In 2004, the U.S. Census Bureau reported Miami had the nation's third highest rate of family incomes below the federal poverty line, ranking it as the third poorest city, following Detroit and El Paso. The city had also faced municipal bankruptcy in 2001. Despite this, a significant revival followed. By 2008, Forbes named Miami "America's Cleanest City," citing its consistent air quality, extensive green spaces, clean water and streets, and comprehensive recycling. Furthermore, a 2009 UBS study of 73 global cities positioned Miami as the wealthiest city in the United States among those surveyed and the fifth-richest worldwide, measured by purchasing power.

input: Napoleon ended lawlessness and disorder in post-Revolutionary France. He was, however, considered a tyrant and usurper by his opponents. His critics charge that he was not significantly troubled when faced with the prospect of war and death for thousands, turned his search for undisputed rule into a series of conflicts throughout Europe and ignored treaties and conventions alike. His role in the Haitian Revolution and decision to reinstate slavery in France's oversea colonies are controversial and have an impact on his reputation.
rewrite: Napoleon brought order to post-Revolutionary France, ending its lawlessness. Critics, who viewed him as a tyrant and usurper, argue he showed little concern for the prospect of war and death for thousands. His pursuit of undisputed power sparked conflicts across Europe, disregarding treaties and conventions. Furthermore, his controversial actions during the Haitian Revolution and his reinstatement of slavery in the colonies continue to impact his reputation.

input: In Prussia, some officials considered a war against France both inevitable and necessary to arouse German nationalism in those states that would allow the unification of a great German empire. This aim was epitomized by Prussian Chancellor Otto von Bismarck's later statement: "I did not doubt that a Franco-German war must take place before the construction of a United Germany could be realised." Bismarck also knew that France should be the aggressor in the conflict to bring the southern German states to side with Prussia, hence giving Germans numerical superiority. Many Germans also viewed the French as the traditional destabilizer of Europe, and sought to weaken France to prevent further breaches of the peace.
rewrite: Prussian officials deemed a war with France inevitable and necessary, believing it would ignite German nationalism and enable unification into a great empire. This objective was later summarized by Chancellor Otto von Bismarck, who stated, "I did not doubt that a Franco-German war must take place before the construction of a United Germany could be realised." Crucially, Bismarck understood that France needed to be seen as the aggressor. This would rally the southern German states to Prussia's side, ensuring numerical superiority. Additionally, many Germans perceived France as Europe's traditional destabilizer and aimed to weaken it to prevent future disruptions of peace.

input: Feathers require maintenance and birds preen or groom them daily, spending an average of around 9% of their daily time on this. The bill is used to brush away foreign particles and to apply waxy secretions from the uropygial gland; these secretions protect the feathers' flexibility and act as an antimicrobial agent, inhibiting the growth of feather-degrading bacteria. This may be supplemented with the secretions of formic acid from ants, which birds receive through a behaviour known as anting, to remove feather parasites.
rewrite: Birds invest roughly 9% of their day in preening to maintain their feathers. Using their bills, they remove debris and spread protective waxy secretions from the uropygial gland. This wax preserves feather flexibility and combats harmful bacteria. Additionally, many birds engage in anting, applying formic acid from ants to their plumage. This supplementary behavior helps eliminate feather parasites.

input: Maintaining the household was the main duty of samurai women. This was especially crucial during early feudal Japan, when warrior husbands were often traveling abroad or engaged in clan battles. The wife, or okugatasama (meaning: one who remains in the home), was left to manage all household affairs, care for the children, and perhaps even defend the home forcibly. For this reason, many women of the samurai class were trained in wielding a polearm called a naginata or a special knife called the kaiken in an art called tantojutsu (lit. the skill of the knife), which they could use to protect their household, family, and honor if the need arose.
rewrite: In early feudal Japan, the primary responsibility of samurai women was maintaining the household. With their warrior husbands frequently away traveling or fighting in clan battles, the wife—known as the okugatasama, or "one who remains in the home"—took charge of all domestic affairs and child-rearing. She might also be required to defend the home. Consequently, many women of this class were trained in weapons like the polearm naginata or the knife kaiken, mastering arts such as tantojutsu (the skill of the knife) to protect their family, household, and honor if necessary.

input: Early house music was generally dance-based music characterized by repetitive 4/4 beats, rhythms mainly provided by drum machines, off-beat hi-hat cymbals, and synthesized basslines. While house displayed several characteristics similar to disco music, it was more electronic and minimalistic, and the repetitive rhythm of house was more important than the song itself. House music in the 2010s, while keeping several of these core elements, notably the prominent kick drum on every beat, varies widely in style and influence, ranging from the soulful and atmospheric deep house to the more minimalistic microhouse. House music has also fused with several other genres creating fusion subgenres, such as euro house, tech house, electro house and jump house.
rewrite: Originating as dance-focused music, early house was built on repetitive 4/4 beats. Its rhythms relied on drum machines, off-beat hi-hats, and synthesized basslines. Though sharing traits with disco, house was more electronic and minimalistic, prioritizing its insistent rhythm over the song. The genre has continually evolved. In the 2010s, while retaining core elements like a steady kick drum, house varied widely from soulful deep house to sparse microhouse. It has also blended with other genres, spawning fusions like tech house, electro house, and euro house.

input: The Umayyad Caliphate (Arabic: الخلافة الأموية‎, trans. Al-Khilāfat al-ʾumawiyya) was the second of the four major Islamic caliphates established after the death of Muhammad. This caliphate was centered on the Umayyad dynasty (Arabic: الأمويون‎, al-ʾUmawiyyūn, or بنو أمية, Banū ʾUmayya, "Sons of Umayya"), hailing from Mecca. The Umayyad family had first come to power under the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan (r. 644–656), but the Umayyad regime was founded by Muawiya ibn Abi Sufyan, long-time governor of Syria, after the end of the First Muslim Civil War in 661 CE/41 AH. Syria remained the Umayyads' main power base thereafter, and Damascus was their capital. The Umayyads continued the Muslim conquests, incorporating the Caucasus, Transoxiana, Sindh, the Maghreb and the Iberian Peninsula (Al-Andalus) into the Muslim world. At its greatest extent, the Umayyad Caliphate covered 15 million km2 (5.79 million square miles), making it the largest empire (in terms of area - not in terms of population) the world had yet seen, and the fifth largest ever to exist.
rewrite: Centered on the Umayyad dynasty (Arabic: الأمويون‎, al-ʾUmawiyyūn, or Banū ʾUmayya, "Sons of Umayya") from Mecca, the Umayyad Caliphate (Arabic: الخلافة الأموية‎, Al-Khilāfat al-ʾumawiyya) was the second of the four major Islamic caliphates founded after Muhammad's death. While the Umayyad family initially gained power under Caliph Uthman ibn Affan (r. 644–656), the regime itself was established by Muawiya ibn Abi Sufyan. As the long-time governor of Syria, he founded the caliphate following the First Muslim Civil War in 661 CE/41 AH. Syria, with its capital at Damascus, remained the Umayyads' primary power base. They extended the Muslim conquests, bringing regions including the Caucasus, Transoxiana, Sindh, the Maghreb, and the Iberian Peninsula (Al-Andalus) into the Muslim world. At its peak, the empire spanned 15 million km2 (5.79 million square miles). This made it the largest empire by area the world had seen up to that time, and the fifth largest in history, though not by population.

input: The scope of the term "post-punk" has been subject to controversy. While some critics, such as AllMusic's Stephen Thomas Erlewine, have employed the term "post-punk" to denote "a more adventurous and arty form of punk", others have suggested it pertains to a set of artistic sensibilities and approaches rather than any unifying style. Music journalist and post-punk scholar Simon Reynolds has advocated that post-punk be conceived as "less a genre of music than a space of possibility", suggesting that "what unites all this activity is a set of open-ended imperatives: innovation; willful oddness; the willful jettisoning of all things precedented or 'rock'n'roll'". Nicholas Lezard, problematizing the categorization of post-punk as a genre, described the movement as "so multifarious that only the broadest use of the term is possible".
rewrite: The term "post-punk" is controversially defined. Some, like critic Stephen Thomas Erlewine, use it to describe "a more adventurous and arty form of punk." Others argue it refers not to a single style, but to a collection of artistic sensibilities. Scholar Simon Reynolds proposes viewing post-punk as "less a genre of music than a space of possibility," united by "open-ended imperatives: innovation; willful oddness; the willful jettisoning of all things precedented or 'rock'n'roll'." Further complicating its categorization, Nicholas Lezard described the movement as "so multifarious that only the broadest use of the term is possible."

input: The centre of Paris contains the most visited monuments in the city, including the Notre Dame Cathedral and the Louvre as well as the Sainte-Chapelle; Les Invalides, where the tomb of Napoleon is located, and the Eiffel Tower are located on the Left Bank south-west of the centre. The banks of the Seine from the Pont de Sully to the Pont d'Iéna have been listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. Other landmarks are laid out east to west along the historic axis of Paris, which runs from the Louvre through the Tuileries Garden, the Luxor Column in the Place de la Concorde, the Arc de Triomphe, to the Grande Arche of La Défense.
rewrite: Paris boasts numerous renowned landmarks, many concentrated in its center. These include the Notre Dame Cathedral, the Louvre, and the Sainte-Chapelle. To the south-west, on the Left Bank, stand Les Invalides—home to Napoleon's tomb—and the Eiffel Tower. Since 1991, the Seine's banks, stretching from the Pont de Sully to the Pont d'Iéna, have held UNESCO World Heritage status. Further sights align along the city's historic east-west axis, running from the Louvre through the Tuileries Garden and the Place de la Concorde with its Luxor Column, then onward to the Arc de Triomphe and the Grande Arche of La Défense.

input: His family was long associated with the teaching of elocution: his grandfather, Alexander Bell, in London, his uncle in Dublin, and his father, in Edinburgh, were all elocutionists. His father published a variety of works on the subject, several of which are still well known, especially his The Standard Elocutionist (1860), which appeared in Edinburgh in 1868. The Standard Elocutionist appeared in 168 British editions and sold over a quarter of a million copies in the United States alone. In this treatise, his father explains his methods of how to instruct deaf-mutes (as they were then known) to articulate words and read other people's lip movements to decipher meaning. Bell's father taught him and his brothers not only to write Visible Speech but to identify any symbol and its accompanying sound. Bell became so proficient that he became a part of his father's public demonstrations and astounded audiences with his abilities. He could decipher Visible Speech representing virtually every language, including Latin, Scottish Gaelic, and even Sanskrit, accurately reciting written tracts without any prior knowledge of their pronunciation.
rewrite: For generations, Bell’s family was deeply connected to elocution instruction. His grandfather, Alexander Bell, practiced in London, an uncle in Dublin, and his father, Melville Bell, in Edinburgh. The latter produced numerous works on the subject, several remaining notable. Among these, *The Standard Elocutionist* (first published in Edinburgh in 1868, though dated 1860) achieved remarkable reach: it went through 168 British editions and sold more than 250,000 copies in the United States alone. Within this treatise, Bell’s father detailed his techniques for teaching deaf individuals—then termed deaf-mutes—to articulate speech and to read lips for comprehension. He instructed his sons, including Alexander Graham Bell, not only in writing Visible Speech but also in recognizing every symbol and its corresponding sound. Bell mastered the system so completely that he joined his father’s public exhibitions, astonishing observers with his skill. He could interpret Visible Speech notations for nearly any language, including Latin, Scottish Gaelic, and Sanskrit, accurately reciting written passages without any previous exposure to their pronunciation.

input: Melbourne has a temperate oceanic climate (Köppen climate classification Cfb) and is well known for its changeable weather conditions. This is mainly due to Melbourne's location situated on the boundary of the very hot inland areas and the cool southern ocean. This temperature differential is most pronounced in the spring and summer months and can cause very strong cold fronts to form. These cold fronts can be responsible for all sorts of severe weather from gales to severe thunderstorms and hail, large temperature drops, and heavy rain.
rewrite: With its temperate oceanic climate (Köppen Cfb), Melbourne is famed for highly changeable weather. This variability stems from the city's position between hot inland regions and the cool southern ocean. The resulting temperature contrast, strongest in spring and summer, often generates powerful cold fronts. These fronts can bring severe conditions, including gales, intense thunderstorms, hail, sharp temperature declines, and heavy rainfall.

input: John XXIII died of peritonitis caused by a perforated stomach at 19:49 local time on 3 June 1963 at the age of 81, ending a historic pontificate of four years and seven months. He died just as a Mass for him finished in Saint Peter's Square below, celebrated by Luigi Traglia. After he died, his brow was ritually tapped to see if he was dead, and those with him in the room said prayers. Then the room was illuminated, thus informing the people of what had happened. He was buried on 6 June in the Vatican grottos. Two wreaths, placed on the two sides of his tomb, were donated by the prisoners of the Regina Coeli prison and the Mantova jail in Verona. On 22 June 1963, one day after his friend and successor Pope Paul VI was elected, the latter prayed at his tomb.
rewrite: On 3 June 1963, at 19:49 local time, Pope John XXIII died at the age of 81. His death resulted from peritonitis due to a perforated stomach, concluding a historic pontificate lasting four years and seven months. At the moment of his passing, a Mass celebrated by Luigi Traglia in Saint Peter's Square below had just finished. Following his death, a ritual tapping of his brow confirmed his passing, and prayers were said by those present in the room. The room was then illuminated to signal the event to the people outside. His burial took place in the Vatican grottos on 6 June. Two wreaths placed beside his tomb were donated by inmates from Regina Coeli prison and Mantova jail in Verona. On 22 June, the newly elected Pope Paul VI, his friend and successor, prayed at the tomb.

input: The capital city, Washington, District of Columbia, is a federal district located on land donated by the state of Maryland. (Virginia had also donated land, but it was returned in 1849.) The United States also has overseas territories with varying levels of independence and organization: in the Caribbean the territories of Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, and in the Pacific the inhabited territories of Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands, along with a number of uninhabited island territories.
rewrite: Washington, District of Columbia, the capital, is a federal district situated on land donated by Maryland. (Virginia also contributed land, but it was returned in 1849.) Additionally, the United States maintains several overseas territories. These include Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands in the Caribbean, as well as Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands in the Pacific, plus various uninhabited island territories, all with differing degrees of self-governance.

input: New York's non-white population was 36,620 in 1890. New York City was a prime destination in the early twentieth century for African Americans during the Great Migration from the American South, and by 1916, New York City was home to the largest urban African diaspora in North America. The Harlem Renaissance of literary and cultural life flourished during the era of Prohibition. The larger economic boom generated construction of skyscrapers competing in height and creating an identifiable skyline.
rewrite: In 1890, New York’s non-white population stood at 36,620. During the early twentieth-century Great Migration, the city became a prime destination for African Americans from the South. By 1916, it housed North America’s largest urban African diaspora. The Prohibition era saw the Harlem Renaissance flourish in literary and cultural life. Concurrently, a major economic boom spurred the construction of competing skyscrapers, forming a distinctive skyline.

input: In eastern Pennsylvania the Great Appalachian Valley, or Great Valley, was accessible by reason of a broad gateway between the end of South Mountain and the Highlands, and many Germans and Moravians settled here between the Susquehanna and Delaware Rivers forming the Pennsylvania Dutch community, some of whom even now speak a unique American dialect of German known as the "Pennsylvania German language" or "Pennsylvania Dutch." These latecomers to the New World were forced to the frontier to find cheap land. With their followers of both German, English and Scots-Irish origin, they worked their way southward and soon occupied all of the Shenandoah Valley, ceded by the Iroquois, and the upper reaches of the Great Valley tributaries of the Tennessee River, ceded by the Cherokee.
rewrite: In eastern Pennsylvania, the Great Appalachian Valley—also called the Great Valley—was reached through a broad gateway between South Mountain’s end and the Highlands. Many Germans and Moravians settled here between the Susquehanna and Delaware Rivers, establishing the Pennsylvania Dutch community. Some among them still speak a distinctive American dialect of German, referred to as the "Pennsylvania German language" or "Pennsylvania Dutch." As late arrivals to the New World, these settlers were pushed to the frontier in search of affordable land. Alongside followers of German, English, and Scots-Irish descent, they moved southward. They soon filled the Shenandoah Valley, which had been ceded by the Iroquois, and the upper sections of the Great Valley’s tributaries flowing into the Tennessee River, lands ceded by the Cherokee.

input: Temperatures below 0 °C (32 °F) or above 25 °C (77 °F) are rare. Cork Airport records an average of 1,227.9 millimetres (4.029 ft) of precipitation annually, most of which is rain. The airport records an average of 7 days of hail and 11 days of snow or sleet a year; though it only records lying snow for 2 days of the year. The low altitude of the city, and moderating influences of the harbour, mean that lying snow very rarely occurs in the city itself. There are on average 204 "rainy" days a year (over 0.2 millimetres (0.0079 in) of rainfall), of which there are 73 days with "heavy rain" (over 5 millimetres (0.20 in)). Cork is also a generally foggy city, with an average of 97 days of fog a year, most common during mornings and during winter. Despite this, however, Cork is also one of Ireland's sunniest cities, with an average of 3.9 hours of sunshine every day and only having 67 days where there is no "recordable sunshine", mostly during and around winter.
rewrite: Cork experiences a temperate climate, with temperatures seldom dropping below 0 °C (32 °F) or rising above 25 °C (77 °F). Precipitation at Cork Airport averages 1,227.9 millimetres (4.029 ft) annually, predominantly as rain. The city sees an average of 204 "rainy" days each year, receiving over 0.2 millimetres (0.0079 in) of rainfall; 73 of these days have "heavy rain" exceeding 5 millimetres (0.20 in). Fog is common, occurring on roughly 97 days, primarily in the morning and during winter. Despite this frequent fog and precipitation, Cork ranks among Ireland's sunniest cities, enjoying an average of 3.9 hours of sunshine daily. Only 67 days, largely in winter, see no "recordable sunshine." Snow and sleet are infrequent, with the airport recording about 11 such days annually, but lying snow is rare, averaging just 2 days at the airport and even less in the city due to its low altitude and the harbour's moderating influence. Hail occurs on approximately 7 days a year.

input: After the scandal, actress Brigitte Nielsen came forward and stated that she too had an affair with Schwarzenegger while he was in a relationship with Shriver, saying, "Maybe I wouldn't have got into it if he said 'I'm going to marry Maria' and this is dead serious, but he didn't, and our affair carried on." When asked in 2014 "Of all the things you are famous for … which are you least proud of?", Schwarzenegger replied "I'm least proud of the mistakes I made that caused my family pain and split us up".
rewrite: Actress Brigitte Nielsen later revealed she also had an affair with Schwarzenegger during his relationship with Maria Shriver. She explained, "If he had said 'I'm going to marry Maria' and it was serious, maybe I wouldn't have gotten involved. But he didn't, so our affair continued." In a 2014 interview, when questioned about what he was least proud of among his famous deeds, Schwarzenegger responded, "It is the mistakes that hurt my family and led to our separation that I regret the most."

input: A more sophisticated MP3 encoder can produce variable bitrate audio. MPEG audio may use bitrate switching on a per-frame basis, but only layer III decoders must support it. VBR is used when the goal is to achieve a fixed level of quality. The final file size of a VBR encoding is less predictable than with constant bitrate. Average bitrate is VBR implemented as a compromise between the two: the bitrate is allowed to vary for more consistent quality, but is controlled to remain near an average value chosen by the user, for predictable file sizes. Although an MP3 decoder must support VBR to be standards compliant, historically some decoders have bugs with VBR decoding, particularly before VBR encoders became widespread.
rewrite: A more advanced MP3 encoder can generate audio with a variable bitrate (VBR). This method allows the bitrate to change per frame to maintain a consistent quality level, though only Layer III decoders are required to support such switching. While VBR aims for uniform audio quality, it results in less predictable final file sizes compared to constant bitrate encoding. To balance this, average bitrate encoding serves as a compromise: it permits variation for quality but keeps the bitrate close to a user-selected average, offering more reliable file size estimates. Despite standards requiring MP3 decoders to handle VBR, some older decoders, especially before VBR encoders were common, contained bugs affecting VBR playback.

input: During the early 20th century it became increasingly common to bury cremated remains rather than coffins in the abbey. In 1905 the actor Sir Henry Irving was cremated and his ashes buried in Westminster Abbey, thereby becoming the first person ever to be cremated prior to interment at the abbey. The majority of interments at the Abbey are of cremated remains, but some burials still take place - Frances Challen, wife of the Rev Sebastian Charles, Canon of Westminster, was buried alongside her husband in the south choir aisle in 2014. Members of the Percy Family have a family vault, The Northumberland Vault, in St Nicholas's chapel within the abbey.
rewrite: In the early 20th century, burying cremated remains instead of coffins grew more frequent at Westminster Abbey. Sir Henry Irving, the actor, was the first to be cremated before interment there, with his ashes buried in 1905. Today, most Abbey interments are of cremated remains, though traditional burials occasionally occur, such as Frances Challen's in 2014 beside her husband in the south choir aisle. Additionally, the Percy Family maintains a family vault, The Northumberland Vault, located in St Nicholas's chapel within the abbey.

input: Subsequently, it became one of Britain's most significant honours to be buried or commemorated in the abbey. The practice of burying national figures in the abbey began under Oliver Cromwell with the burial of Admiral Robert Blake in 1657. The practice spread to include generals, admirals, politicians, doctors and scientists such as Isaac Newton, buried on 4 April 1727, and Charles Darwin, buried 26 April 1882. Another was William Wilberforce who led the movement to abolish slavery in the United Kingdom and the Plantations, buried on 3 August 1833. Wilberforce was buried in the north transept, close to his friend, the former Prime Minister, William Pitt.[citation needed]
rewrite: Over time, burial or commemoration in the abbey grew into one of Britain's most distinguished honors. This tradition of interring national figures originated with Oliver Cromwell, starting with Admiral Robert Blake in 1657. It later expanded to encompass generals, admirals, politicians, doctors, and scientists. Notable examples include Isaac Newton, buried on April 4, 1727, and Charles Darwin, laid to rest on April 26, 1882. Another key figure was William Wilberforce, leader of the movement to abolish slavery in the UK and the Plantations, who was buried on August 3, 1833, in the north transept near his friend, former Prime Minister William Pitt.

input: The geographical regions in which Iranian languages were spoken were pushed back in several areas by newly neighbouring languages. Arabic spread into some parts of Western Iran (Khuzestan), and Turkic languages spread through much of Central Asia, displacing various Iranian languages such as Sogdian and Bactrian in parts of what is today Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. In Eastern Europe, mostly comprising the territory of modern-day Ukraine, southern European Russia, and parts of the Balkans, the core region of the native Scythians, Sarmatians, and Alans had been decisively been taken over as a result of absorption and assimilation (e.g. Slavicisation) by the various Proto-Slavic population of the region, by the 6th century AD. This resulted in the displacement and extinction of the once predominant Scythian languages of the region. Sogdian's close relative Yaghnobi barely survives in a small area of the Zarafshan valley east of Samarkand, and Saka as Ossetic in the Caucasus, which is the sole remnant of the once predominant Scythian languages in Eastern Europe proper and large parts of the North Caucasus. Various small Iranian languages in the Pamirs survive that are derived from Eastern Iranian.
rewrite: The spread of newly neighbouring languages gradually reduced the geographical reach of Iranian languages across several regions. In Western Iran, specifically Khuzestan, Arabic made inroads. Meanwhile, Turkic languages expanded across Central Asia, displacing Iranian tongues like Sogdian and Bactrian in areas now part of Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan. By the 6th century AD, in Eastern Europe—encompassing modern Ukraine, southern European Russia, and parts of the Balkans—the core territories of the Scythians, Sarmatians, and Alans were decisively taken over. This occurred through absorption and assimilation, such as Slavicisation, by the region's Proto-Slavic populations, leading to the displacement and extinction of the once-predominant Scythian languages. Today, only remnants persist: Yaghnobi, a close relative of Sogdian, barely endures in a small part of the Zarafshan valley east of Samarkand, while Saka survives as Ossetic in the Caucasus. Ossetic is the sole remnant of the Scythian languages that were once widespread in Eastern Europe and large sections of the North Caucasus. Additionally, various small Eastern Iranian-derived languages continue to survive in the Pamir Mountains.

input: All iPods except for the iPod Touch can function in "disk mode" as mass storage devices to store data files but this may not be the default behavior, and in the case of the iPod Touch, requires special software.[citation needed] If an iPod is formatted on a Mac OS computer, it uses the HFS+ file system format, which allows it to serve as a boot disk for a Mac computer. If it is formatted on Windows, the FAT32 format is used. With the release of the Windows-compatible iPod, the default file system used on the iPod line switched from HFS+ to FAT32, although it can be reformatted to either file system (excluding the iPod Shuffle which is strictly FAT32). Generally, if a new iPod (excluding the iPod Shuffle) is initially plugged into a computer running Windows, it will be formatted with FAT32, and if initially plugged into a Mac running Mac OS it will be formatted with HFS+.
rewrite: Most iPods, excluding the iPod Touch, can operate in "disk mode" to store data files as mass storage devices, though this is often not the default setting; for the iPod Touch, special software is required.[citation needed] The file system an iPod uses depends on where it is formatted. When formatted on a Mac OS computer, it employs the HFS+ format, enabling it to function as a boot disk for a Mac. If formatted on Windows, it uses FAT32. Following the introduction of the Windows-compatible iPod, the default file system across the lineup shifted from HFS+ to FAT32, though most models (except the strictly FAT32 iPod Shuffle) can be reformatted to either system. Typically, a new iPod (excluding the Shuffle) connected first to a Windows computer will be formatted with FAT32, while if first connected to a Mac OS system, it will use HFS+.

input: Cardigan formed up his unit and charged the length of the Valley of the Balaclava, under fire from Russian batteries in the hills. The charge of the Light Brigade caused 278 casualties of the 700-man unit. The Light Brigade was memorialized in the famous poem by Alfred Lord Tennyson, "The Charge of the Light Brigade." Although traditionally the charge of the Light Brigade was looked upon as a glorious but wasted sacrifice of good men and horses, recent historians say that the charge of the Light Brigade did succeed in at least some of its objectives. The aim of any cavalry charge is to scatter the enemy lines and frighten the enemy off the battlefield. The charge of the Light Brigade had so unnerved the Russian cavalry, which had previously been routed by the Heavy Brigade, that the Russian Cavalry was set to full-scale flight by the subsequent charge of the Light Brigade.:252
rewrite: Under fire from Russian batteries positioned in the hills, Cardigan led his unit in a charge down the length of the Valley of Balaclava. This action, the Charge of the Light Brigade, resulted in 278 casualties from the 700-man force. However, recent historical analysis suggests it achieved some of its intended goals. The primary objective of any cavalry charge is to break enemy lines and instill fear. The Russian cavalry, already shaken by an earlier engagement with the Heavy Brigade, was so unnerved by the Light Brigade's assault that it was driven into full-scale retreat.

input: Larry Christenson, a Lutheran theologian based in San Pedro, California, did much in the 1960s and 1970s to interpret the charismatic movement for Lutherans. A very large annual conference regarding that matter was held in Minneapolis. Charismatic Lutheran congregations in Minnesota became especially large and influential; especially "Hosanna!" in Lakeville, and North Heights in St. Paul. The next generation of Lutheran charismatics cluster around the Alliance of Renewal Churches. There is considerable charismatic activity among young Lutheran leaders in California centered around an annual gathering at Robinwood Church in Huntington Beach. Richard A. Jensen's Touched by the Spirit published in 1974, played a major role of the Lutheran understanding to the charismatic movement.
rewrite: During the 1960s and 1970s, Lutheran theologian Larry Christenson, from San Pedro, California, worked extensively to interpret the charismatic movement for his tradition. A major annual conference on this subject was hosted in Minneapolis. In Minnesota, charismatic Lutheran congregations like "Hosanna!" in Lakeville and North Heights in St. Paul grew notably large and influential. Richard A. Jensen's 1974 book, *Touched by the Spirit*, was pivotal for Lutheran engagement with the movement. input: The other directly attested Old Iranian dialects are the two forms of Avestan, which take their name from their use in the Avesta, the liturgical texts of indigenous Iranian religion that now goes by the name of Zoroastrianism but in the Avesta itself is simply known as vohu daena (later: behdin). The language of the Avesta is subdivided into two dialects, conventionally known as "Old (or 'Gathic') Avestan", and "Younger Avestan". These terms, which date to the 19th century, are slightly misleading since 'Younger Avestan' is not only much younger than 'Old Avestan', but also from a different geographic region. The Old Avestan dialect is very archaic, and at roughly the same stage of development as Rigvedic Sanskrit. On the other hand, Younger Avestan is at about the same linguistic stage as Old Persian, but by virtue of its use as a sacred language retained its "old" characteristics long after the Old Iranian languages had yielded to their Middle Iranian stage. Unlike Old Persian, which has Middle Persian as its known successor, Avestan has no clearly identifiable Middle Iranian stage (the effect of Middle Iranian is indistinguishable from effects due to other causes).
rewrite: Among the directly attested Old Iranian dialects are two forms of Avestan, named for their appearance in the Avesta. This collection of liturgical texts belongs to an indigenous Iranian religion, today called Zoroastrianism but referred to in the Avesta itself as vohu daena (later behdin). The language of these texts falls into two dialect groups, conventionally termed "Old (or 'Gathic') Avestan" and "Younger Avestan". While these 19th-century labels are somewhat misleading, they remain in use. 'Younger Avestan' is not only significantly more recent than 'Old Avestan' but also originates from a different geographic area. Old Avestan is a highly archaic dialect, comparable in its stage of development to Rigvedic Sanskrit. Younger Avestan, however, aligns linguistically with Old Persian. Yet, because it was preserved as a sacred language, it maintained its ancient features well after other Old Iranian languages had transitioned into their Middle Iranian phases. A key distinction from Old Persian, which clearly evolved into Middle Persian, is that Avestan lacks a clearly identifiable Middle Iranian stage; the influence of Middle Iranian is indistinguishable from other linguistic effects.

input: Since playing Pong while filming Jaws in 1974, Spielberg has been an avid video gamer. Spielberg played many of LucasArts adventure games, including the first Monkey Island games. He owns a Wii, a PlayStation 3, a PSP, and Xbox 360, and enjoys playing first-person shooters such as the Medal of Honor series and Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare. He has also criticized the use of cut scenes in games, calling them intrusive, and feels making story flow naturally into the gameplay is a challenge for future game developers.

He enjoys first-person shooters like the Medal of Honor series and Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare, and has played many LucasArts adventures, including the early Monkey Island titles.
