At the same time, influential writers such as Richard Hakluyt and John Dee (who was the first to use the term "British Empire") were beginning to press for the establishment of England's own empire. By this time, Spain had become the dominant power in the Americas and was exploring the Pacific ocean, Portugal had established trading posts and forts from the coasts of Africa and Brazil to China, and France had begun to settle the Saint Lawrence River area, later to become New France.
rewrite:
Following the Protestant Reformation, England and Catholic Spain became entrenched adversaries. It was not until the latter part of Queen Elizabeth I's reign in the 16th century that new efforts to found English colonies in the Americas emerged. During this period, influential figures including writers Richard Hakluyt and John Dee—who coined the term "British Empire"—began advocating for England to build its own imperial domain. Meanwhile, other European powers were expanding aggressively: Spain had secured dominance in the Americas and was probing the Pacific, Portugal had built a network of trading posts and forts from Africa and Brazil to China, and France was settling the Saint Lawrence River region, later known as New France.

Against this backdrop of rivalry, England pursued a strategy of maritime disruption. As early as 1562, the Crown supported privateers like John Hawkins and Francis Drake in slave-raiding assaults on Spanish and Portuguese ships off West Africa, aiming to infiltrate the Atlantic trade system. After this initial effort was repelled, and as the Anglo-Spanish Wars escalated, Elizabeth I sanctioned further privateering campaigns. These raids targeted Spanish ports in the Americas and treasure-laden ships returning across the Atlantic from the New World.

input: In a movie theater, steps in the aisles are usually marked with a row of small lights for convenience and safety, when the film has started and the other lights are off. Traditionally made up of small low wattage, low voltage lamps in a track or translucent tube, these are rapidly being replaced with LED based versions.
rewrite: For convenience and safety, aisles in movie theaters typically have steps marked by small lights, especially after the main lights dim. Traditionally using low-wattage lamps in tracks or tubes, these are now quickly being replaced with LED versions.

input: Chopin's polonaises show a marked advance on those of his Polish predecessors in the form (who included his teachers Zywny and Elsner). As with the traditional polonaise, Chopin's works are in triple time and typically display a martial rhythm in their melodies, accompaniments and cadences. Unlike most of their precursors, they also require a formidable playing technique.
rewrite: Chopin's polonaises demonstrate a clear progression beyond those of his Polish forerunners, such as teachers Zywny and Elsner. While retaining the traditional triple meter and martial rhythms in melodies and cadences, they demand a formidable technique, unlike most earlier examples in the form.

input: Erich Koch headed the East Prussian Nazi party from 1928. He led the district from 1932. This period was characterized by efforts to collectivize the local agriculture and ruthlessness in dealing with his critics inside and outside the Party. He also had long-term plans for mass-scale industrialization of the largely agricultural province. These actions made him unpopular among the local peasants. In 1932 the local paramilitary SA had already started to terrorise their political opponents. On the night of 31 July 1932 there was a bomb attack on the headquarters of the Social Democrats in Königsberg, the Otto-Braun-House. The Communist politician Gustav Sauf was killed; the executive editor of the Social Democrat "Königsberger Volkszeitung", Otto Wyrgatsch, and the German People's Party politician Max von Bahrfeldt were severely injured. Members of the Reichsbanner were attacked and the local Reichsbanner Chairman of Lötzen, Kurt Kotzan, was murdered on 6 August 1932.
rewrite: From 1928, Erich Koch led the Nazi party in East Prussia, assuming control of the district in 1932. His tenure featured a harsh drive to collectivize agriculture and brutal suppression of critics, alongside ambitious plans to industrialize the predominantly rural province, alienating the local peasantry. Political terror escalated that year, with the local SA paramilitary targeting opponents. On July 31, 1932, a bomb struck the Social Democrat headquarters, the Otto-Braun-House, in Königsberg. The attack killed Communist politician Gustav Sauf and severely injured Otto Wyrgatsch, editor of the "Königsberger Volkszeitung," and German People's Party figure Max von Bahrfeldt. Further violence followed, including assaults on Reichsbanner members and the murder of its Lötzen chairman, Kurt Kotzan, on August 6.

input:
Spanish Supreme Court is the highest court for all cases in Spain (both private and public). Only those cases related to human rights can be appealed at the Constitutional Court (which also decides about acts accordance with Spanish Constitution).
In Spain, high courts cannot create binding precedents; however, lower rank courts usually observe Supreme Court interpretations. In most private law cases, two Supreme Court judgements supporting a claim are needed to appeal at the Supreme Court.
Five sections form the Spanish Supreme court:
rewrite: The Spanish Supreme Court, composed of five sections, serves as the nation's highest judicial body for all private and public cases. While high courts in Spain do not establish binding precedents, lower courts typically follow the Supreme Court's interpretations. For most private law matters, appealing to the Supreme Court requires two prior judgments supporting the claim. Only cases involving human rights may be escalated to the Constitutional Court, which also rules on the constitutionality of legislative acts.

input: The High Middle Ages was a period of tremendous expansion of population. The estimated population of Europe grew from 35 to 80 million between 1000 and 1347, although the exact causes remain unclear: improved agricultural techniques, the decline of slaveholding, a more clement climate and the lack of invasion have all been suggested. As much as 90 per cent of the European population remained rural peasants. Many were no longer settled in isolated farms but had gathered into small communities, usually known as manors or villages. These peasants were often subject to noble overlords and owed them rents and other services, in a system known as manorialism. There remained a few free peasants throughout this period and beyond, with more of them in the regions of Southern Europe than in the north. The practice of assarting, or bringing new lands into production by offering incentives to the peasants who settled them, also contributed to the expansion of population.
rewrite: Between 1000 and 1347, Europe experienced a dramatic population surge, with numbers rising from an estimated 35 to 80 million. While the precise reasons are debated, proposed factors include more efficient farming methods, a reduction in slavery, a milder climate, and a period free from major invasions. Throughout the High Middle Ages, up to 90 percent of Europeans were rural peasants. Increasingly, these individuals lived not on isolated farms but within small communities called manors or villages. Under the system of manorialism, they were typically subject to noble lords, owing rents and various services. Nonetheless, some free peasants persisted, more commonly in Southern Europe than in the north. Further aiding population growth was the practice of assarting, which encouraged peasants to settle and cultivate new lands through specific incentives.

input: Small-scale artisanal mining of gold is another source of dangerous child labour in poor rural areas in certain parts of the world. This form of mining uses labour-intensive and low-tech methods. It is informal sector of the economy. Human Rights Watch group estimates that about 12 percent of global gold production comes from artisanal mines. In west Africa, in countries such as Mali - the third largest exporter of gold in Africa - between 20,000 and 40,000 children work in artisanal mining. Locally known as orpaillage, children as young as 6 years old work with their families. These children and families suffer chronic exposure to toxic chemicals including mercury, and do hazardous work such as digging shafts and working underground, pulling up, carrying and crushing the ore. The poor work practices harm the long term health of children, as well as release hundreds of tons of mercury every year into local rivers, ground water and lakes. Gold is important to the economy of Mali and Ghana. For Mali, it is the second largest earner of its export revenue. For many poor families with children, it is the primary and sometimes the only source of income.
rewrite: In certain impoverished rural regions globally, small-scale artisanal gold mining represents a significant source of hazardous child labour. Operating within the informal economy, this sector relies on labour-intensive, low-technology methods. According to Human Rights Watch, artisanal mines contribute an estimated 12 percent of the world's gold production. The economic importance of gold is substantial, particularly for countries like Mali—Africa’s third-largest gold exporter—where it ranks as the second biggest export revenue earner, and for neighbouring Ghana. For numerous poor families, this mining provides the primary, and often sole, source of income. Known locally as orpaillage, this work frequently involves entire families, with children as young as six participating. These children, alongside their families, engage in perilous tasks including digging shafts, working underground, and hauling, carrying, and crushing ore. They also face chronic exposure to toxic chemicals like mercury. The poor work practices not only severely harm children's long-term health but also result in the annual release of hundreds of tons of mercury into local rivers, groundwater, and lakes. In West Africa, specifically in nations such as Mali, between 20,000 and 40,000 children are engaged in this mining.

input: In past times, mending was an art. A meticulous tailor or seamstress could mend rips with thread raveled from hems and seam edges so skillfully that the tear was practically invisible. When the raw material – cloth – was worth more than labor, it made sense to expend labor in saving it. Today clothing is considered a consumable item. Mass-manufactured clothing is less expensive than the labor required to repair it. Many people buy a new piece of clothing rather than spend time mending. The thrifty still replace zippers and buttons and sew up ripped hems.
rewrite: Mending was once a skilled craft, where tears were expertly repaired using thread from hems and seams, rendering them nearly undetectable. In an era when fabric was more valuable than labor, investing time to salvage cloth was practical. Now, clothing is often seen as disposable, with mass-produced items cheaper to replace than to fix. Consequently, many opt to buy new rather than mend, though those practicing thrift still replace zippers, buttons, and stitch up torn hems.

input: In early 1757, Frederick II again took the initiative by marching into the Kingdom of Bohemia, hoping to inflict a decisive defeat on Austrian forces. After winning the bloody Battle of Prague on 6 May 1757, in which both forces suffered major casualties, the Prussians forced the Austrians back into the fortifications of Prague. The Prussian army then laid siege to the city. Following the battle at Prague, Frederick took 5,000 troops from the siege at Prague and sent them to reinforce the 19,000-man army under the Duke of Brunswick-Bevern at Kolin in Bohemia. Austrian Marshal Daun arrived too late to participate in the battle of Prague, but picked up 16,000 men who had escaped from the battle. With this army he slowly moved to relieve Prague. The Prussian army was too weak to simultaneously besiege Prague and keep Daun away, and Frederick was forced to attack prepared positions. The resulting Battle of Kolin was a sharp defeat for Frederick, his first military defeat. His losses further forced him to lift the siege and withdraw from Bohemia altogether.
rewrite: In early 1757, Frederick II seized the initiative, marching his forces into the Kingdom of Bohemia with the aim of delivering a decisive blow to the Austrians. This campaign led to the bloody Battle of Prague on 6 May, a costly engagement for both sides that ultimately forced the Austrians to retreat into the city's fortifications, where they were then besieged by the Prussians. From this siege, Frederick detached 5,000 men to bolster the 19,000-strong Prussian army under the Duke of Brunswick-Bevern stationed at Kolin. Meanwhile, Austrian Marshal Daun, having arrived too late for the Prague battle, gathered 16,000 survivors from that defeat. With this force, he advanced deliberately to relieve the besieged city. Frederick, finding his army too weak to both maintain the siege and contain Daun, felt compelled to assault the Austrian's prepared positions. The ensuing Battle of Kolin proved a sharp and definitive defeat for Frederick, marking his first military loss. These casualties compelled him to abandon the siege of Prague and withdraw his forces completely from Bohemia.

input: A new generation of clubs such as Liverpool's Cream and the Ministry of Sound were opened to provide a venue for more commercial sounds. Major record companies began to open "superclubs" promoting their own acts. These superclubs entered into sponsorship deals initially with fast food, soft drinks, and clothing companies. Flyers in clubs in Ibiza often sported many corporate logos. A new subgenre, Chicago hard house, was developed by DJs such as Bad Boy Bill, DJ Lynnwood, DJ Irene, Richard "Humpty" Vission and DJ Enrie, mixing elements of Chicago house, funky house and hard house together. Additionally, Producers such as George Centeno, Darren Ramirez, and Martin O. Cairo would develop the Los Angeles Hard House sound. Similar to gabber or hardcore techno from the Netherlands, this sound was often associated with the "rebel" culture of the time. These 3 producers are often considered "ahead of their time" since many of the sounds they engineered during the late 20th century became more prominent during the 21st century.
rewrite: A fresh wave of clubs, including Liverpool's Cream and the Ministry of Sound, emerged to host more commercial music. Alongside this, major record companies launched their own "superclubs" to promote signed acts. These venues quickly formed sponsorship agreements, first with brands from the fast food, soft drink, and clothing industries. This corporate presence was evident in places like Ibiza, where club flyers frequently displayed multiple logos. Musically, a new subgenre called Chicago hard house was crafted by DJs like Bad Boy Bill, DJ Lynnwood, DJ Irene, Richard "Humpty" Vission, and DJ Enrie, blending Chicago house, funky house, and hard house. Parallel to this, the Los Angeles Hard House sound was developed by producers such as George Centeno, Darren Ramirez, and Martin O. Cairo. Often linked to the period's "rebel" culture, this sound shared similarities with Dutch gabber or hardcore techno. These three producers are frequently viewed as pioneers ahead of their time, as many of the sonic elements they created in the late 20th century grew significantly more prominent in the 21st century.

input: In August 1836, two real estate entrepreneurs—Augustus Chapman Allen and John Kirby Allen—from New York, purchased 6,642 acres (26.88 km2) of land along Buffalo Bayou with the intent of founding a city. The Allen brothers decided to name the city after Sam Houston, the popular general at the Battle of San Jacinto, who was elected President of Texas in September 1836. The great majority of slaves in Texas came with their owners from the older slave states. Sizable numbers, however, came through the domestic slave trade. New Orleans was the center of this trade in the Deep South, but there were slave dealers in Houston. Thousands of enslaved African-Americans lived near the city before the Civil War. Many of them near the city worked on sugar and cotton plantations, while most of those in the city limits had domestic and artisan jobs. In 1860 forty-nine percent of the city's population was enslaved. A few slaves, perhaps as many as 2,000 between 1835 and 1865, came through the illegal African trade. Post-war Texas grew rapidly as migrants poured into the cotton lands of the state. They also brought or purchased enslaved African Americans, whose numbers nearly tripled in the state from 1850 to 1860, from 58,000 to 182,566.
rewrite: In August 1836, Augustus Chapman Allen and John Kirby Allen, real estate entrepreneurs from New York, acquired 6,642 acres (26.88 km²) of land along Buffalo Bayou to establish a city. They named it after Sam Houston, the revered general of the Battle of San Jacinto, who was elected President of Texas that September. While the majority of slaves in Texas arrived with their owners from older slave states, a sizable number were trafficked through the domestic slave trade. Though New Orleans served as the primary hub for this trade in the Deep South, slave dealers also operated in Houston. Thousands of enslaved African-Americans resided near the city prior to the Civil War, with many on surrounding sugar and cotton plantations, while those within the city limits largely held domestic and artisan roles. By 1860, enslaved individuals comprised forty-nine percent of Houston’s population. A small number, perhaps up to 2,000 between 1835 and 1865, were imported via the illegal African trade. After the war, Texas expanded quickly as migrants flooded into its cotton lands, often bringing or buying enslaved African Americans. This practice caused the enslaved population in the state to nearly triple from 1850 to 1860, soaring from 58,000 to 182,566.

input: Early Muslim armies stayed in encampments away from cities because Umar feared that they might get attracted to wealth and luxury. In the process, they might turn away from the worship of God and start accumulating wealth and establishing dynasties. When Uthman ibn al-Affan became very old, Marwan I, a relative of Muawiyah I, slipped into the vacuum, became his secretary, slowly assumed more control and relaxed some of these restrictions. Marwan I had previously been excluded from positions of responsibility. In 656, Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, the son of Abu Bakr, the adopted son of Ali ibn Abi Talib, and the great grandfather of Ja'far al-Sadiq, showed some Egyptians the house of Uthman ibn al-Affan. Later the Egyptians ended up killing Uthman ibn al-Affan.
rewrite: To prevent early Muslim armies from being drawn to urban wealth and luxury—a shift Umar believed could divert them from worship and lead to dynastic accumulation—they were stationed in separate encampments. Later, as Uthman ibn al-Affan aged, Marwan I, a relative of Muawiyah I who had previously been barred from authority, gradually filled the resulting void. Serving as Uthman’s secretary, he gained increasing influence and eased several of these earlier restrictions. In 656, Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr—son of Abu Bakr, adopted son of Ali ibn Abi Talib, and great-grandfather of Ja’far al-Sadiq—guided a group of Egyptians to Uthman’s residence. This encounter ultimately led to Uthman’s death at the hands of the Egyptians.

input: In the lead up to the Iraq War, Kerry said on October 9, 2002; "I will be voting to give the President of the United States the authority to use force, if necessary, to disarm Saddam Hussein because I believe that a deadly arsenal of weapons of mass destruction in his hands is a real and grave threat to our security." Bush relied on that resolution in ordering the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Kerry also gave a January 23, 2003 speech to Georgetown University saying "Without question, we need to disarm Saddam Hussein. He is a brutal, murderous dictator; leading an oppressive regime he presents a particularly grievous threat because he is so consistently prone to miscalculation. So the threat of Saddam Hussein with weapons of mass destruction is real." Kerry did, however, warn that the administration should exhaust its diplomatic avenues before launching war: "Mr. President, do not rush to war, take the time to build the coalition, because it's not winning the war that's hard, it's winning the peace that's hard."
rewrite: On October 9, 2002, John Kerry stated his intent to vote in favor of granting the President authority to use force to disarm Saddam Hussein, citing the “real and grave threat” posed by the Iraqi leader’s presumed arsenal of weapons of mass destruction. This resolution later served as a foundation for President Bush’s decision to invade Iraq in 2003. In a subsequent address at Georgetown University on January 23, 2003, Kerry reiterated his position, describing Hussein as a brutal and oppressive dictator whose propensity for miscalculation made him a particularly grievous danger. He affirmed, “the threat of Saddam Hussein with weapons of mass destruction is real.” Nevertheless, Kerry also issued a caution, urging the administration to fully exhaust diplomatic options before any military engagement. He advised, “Mr. President, do not rush to war, take the time to build the coalition,” emphasizing that winning a lasting peace would prove more difficult than winning the war itself.

input: The same considerations about barriers and detours that apply to long-distance land-bird migration apply to water birds, but in reverse: a large area of land without bodies of water that offer feeding sites may also be a barrier to a bird that feeds in coastal waters. Detours avoiding such barriers are observed: for example, brent geese Branta bernicla migrating from the Taymyr Peninsula to the Wadden Sea travel via the White Sea coast and the Baltic Sea rather than directly across the Arctic Ocean and northern Scandinavia.
rewrite: While similar principles of barriers and detours govern both land and water bird migrations, the obstacles are reversed. For water birds, an extensive stretch of land lacking aquatic feeding sites can act as a barrier. Consequently, detours are common, as seen with brent geese (Branta bernicla). These birds journey from the Taymyr Peninsula to the Wadden Sea by following the White Sea coast and Baltic Sea, avoiding a direct route over the Arctic Ocean and northern Scandinavia.

input: Domestication of sheep and goats reached Egypt from the Near East possibly as early as 6,000 BC. Graeme Barker states "The first indisputable evidence for domestic plants and animals in the Nile valley is not until the early fifth millennium bc in northern Egypt and a thousand years later further south, in both cases as part of strategies that still relied heavily on fishing, hunting, and the gathering of wild plants" and suggests that these subsistence changes were not due to farmers migrating from the Near East but was an indigenous development, with cereals either indigenous or obtained through exchange. Other scholars argue that the primary stimulus for agriculture and domesticated animals (as well as mud-brick architecture and other Neolithic cultural features) in Egypt was from the Middle East.
rewrite: The arrival of domesticated sheep and goats in Egypt from the Near East may date back to around 6,000 BC. According to Graeme Barker, definitive proof for domestic species in the Nile valley appears only by the early fifth millennium BC in the north and a millennium later in the south. He notes these practices were integrated with ongoing fishing, hunting, and gathering. Barker views this shift not as a result of migrating farmers, but as a local adaptation, with cereals being either indigenous or acquired via trade. Conversely, other scholars maintain that the main impetus for agriculture, domesticated animals, and associated Neolithic innovations in Egypt originated from the Middle East.

input: The story sees Bond pitted against the global criminal organisation Spectre, marking the group's first appearance in an Eon Productions film since 1971's Diamonds Are Forever,[N 2] and tying Craig's series of films together with an overarching storyline. Several recurring James Bond characters, including M, Q and Eve Moneypenny return, with the new additions of Léa Seydoux as Dr. Madeleine Swann, Dave Bautista as Mr. Hinx, Andrew Scott as Max Denbigh and Monica Bellucci as Lucia Sciarra.
rewrite: In this film, Bond confronts the global criminal organization Spectre, which marks the group's first return to an Eon Productions movie since 1971's "Diamonds Are Forever." It also connects Craig's series through an overarching plot. Familiar characters like M, Q, and Eve Moneypenny reappear, joined by new faces: Léa Seydoux as Dr. Madeleine Swann, Dave Bautista as Mr. Hinx, Andrew Scott as Max Denbigh, and Monica Bellucci as Lucia Sciarra.

input: Trading companies became active in Tuvalu in the mid-19th century; the trading companies engaged palagi traders who lived on the islands. John (also known as Jack) O'Brien was the first European to settle in Tuvalu, he became a trader on Funafuti in the 1850s. He married Salai, the daughter of the paramount chief of Funafuti. Louis Becke, who later found success as a writer, was a trader on Nanumanga from April 1880 until the trading-station was destroyed later that year in a cyclone. He then became a trader on Nukufetau.
rewrite: In the mid-19th century, trading companies began operating in Tuvalu, employing palagi traders to live on the islands. The first European settler was John (or Jack) O'Brien, who established himself as a trader on Funafuti during the 1850s and married Salai, the daughter of the paramount chief. Later, the writer Louis Becke worked as a trader on Nanumanga starting in April 1880. After a cyclone destroyed that station within the year, he moved his operations to Nukufetau.

input: Following their wedding, the couple leased Windlesham Moor, near Windsor Castle, until 4 July 1949, when they took up residence at Clarence House in London. At various times between 1949 and 1951, the Duke of Edinburgh was stationed in the British Crown Colony of Malta as a serving Royal Navy officer. He and Elizabeth lived intermittently, for several months at a time, in the hamlet of Gwardamanġa, at Villa Guardamangia, the rented home of Philip's uncle, Lord Mountbatten. The children remained in Britain.
rewrite: After their marriage, the couple resided at a leased property, Windlesham Moor near Windsor Castle, until July 4, 1949. They then moved to London's Clarence House. From 1949 to 1951, the Duke of Edinburgh served in the Royal Navy in Malta. During his postings, he and Elizabeth lived periodically for months at a time in Gwardamanġa at Villa Guardamangia, which was rented from his uncle, Lord Mountbatten. Their children stayed in Britain.

input: Ann Arbor is part of Michigan's 12th congressional district, represented in Congress by Representative Debbie Dingell, a Democrat. On the state level, the city is part of the 18th district in the Michigan Senate, represented by Democrat Rebekah Warren. In the Michigan House of Representatives, representation is split between the 55th district (northern Ann Arbor, part of Ann Arbor Township, and other surrounding areas, represented by Democrat Adam Zemke), the 53rd district (most of downtown and the southern half of the city, represented by Democrat Jeff Irwin) and the 52nd district (southwestern areas outside Ann Arbor proper and western Washtenaw County, represented by Democrat Gretchen Driskell).
rewrite: Represented in Congress by Democrat Debbie Dingell, Ann Arbor lies within Michigan's 12th congressional district. At the state level, the city is part of the 18th Michigan Senate district, represented by Democrat Rebekah Warren. In the Michigan House of Representatives, Ann Arbor's representation is divided among three districts: the 55th (northern Ann Arbor, part of Ann Arbor Township, and surrounding areas, represented by Democrat Adam Zemke), the 53rd (most of downtown and the southern half of the city, represented by Democrat Jeff Irwin), and the 52nd (southwestern areas outside the city proper and western Washtenaw County, represented by Democrat Gretchen Driskell).

input: On 5 July 2004, the BBC celebrated the fiftieth anniversary of its television news bulletins (although it had produced the Television Newsreel for several years before 1954). This event was marked by the release of a DVD, which showed highlights of the BBC's television coverage of significant events over the half-century, as well as changes in the format of the BBC television news; from the newsreel format of the first BBC Television News bulletins, to the 24-hour, worldwide news coverage available in 2004. A special edition of Radio Times was also produced, as well as a special section of the BBC News Online website. In 2005 the pioneering BBC television series Little Angels won a BAFTA award. Little Angels was the first reality parenting show and its most famous episode saw Welsh actress Jynine James try to cope with the tantrums of her six-year-old son.
rewrite: Marking the fiftieth anniversary of its television news bulletins on 5 July 2004, the BBC released a commemorative DVD. This collection highlighted pivotal moments from a half-century of television news coverage and traced the evolution of the format, from the early newsreel style to the 24-hour global service available in 2004. Alongside the DVD, the occasion was celebrated with a special edition of Radio Times and a dedicated section on BBC News Online. The following year, in 2005, the pioneering BBC reality parenting series Little Angels received a BAFTA award. Notably the first show of its kind, its most famous episode featured Welsh actress Jynine James managing the tantrums of her six-year-old son.

input: Though the true dimensions of species diversity remain uncertain, estimates range from 2.6–7.8 million species with a mean of 5.5 million. This probably represents less than 20% of all species on Earth[citation needed], and with only about 20,000 new species of all organisms being described each year, most species likely will remain undescribed for many years unless species descriptions increase in rate. About 850,000–1,000,000 of all described species are insects. Of the 24 orders of insects, four dominate in terms of numbers of described species, with at least 3 million species included in Coleoptera, Diptera, Hymenoptera and Lepidoptera. A recent study estimated the number of beetles at 0.9–2.1 million with a mean of 1.5 million.
rewrite: The full scope of Earth's species diversity is still unknown, with current estimates averaging around 5.5 million species, within a range of 2.6 to 7.8 million. This figure likely constitutes less than 20% of all species. Given that only approximately 20,000 new species are documented annually, most will remain undescribed unless the rate of discovery accelerates significantly. Insects make up a substantial portion of described life, numbering between 850,000 and 1,000,000 species. Dominance is held by four key orders: Coleoptera, Diptera, Hymenoptera, and Lepidoptera, which collectively contain at least 3 million species. Among these, beetles alone are recently estimated to number 1.5 million on average, within a range of 0.9 to 2.1 million.

input: Since before 2000 BC, humans have utilized pesticides to protect their crops. The first known pesticide was elemental sulfur dusting used in ancient Sumer about 4,500 years ago in ancient Mesopotamia. The Rig Veda, which is about 4,000 years old, mentions the use of poisonous plants for pest control. By the 15th century, toxic chemicals such as arsenic, mercury, and lead were being applied to crops to kill pests. In the 17th century, nicotine sulfate was extracted from tobacco leaves for use as an insecticide. The 19th century saw the introduction of two more natural pesticides, pyrethrum, which is derived from chrysanthemums, and rotenone, which is derived from the roots of tropical vegetables. Until the 1950s, arsenic-based pesticides were dominant. Paul Müller discovered that DDT was a very effective insecticide. Organochlorines such as DDT were dominant, but they were replaced in the U.S. by organophosphates and carbamates by 1975. Since then, pyrethrin compounds have become the dominant insecticide. Herbicides became common in the 1960s, led by "triazine and other nitrogen-based compounds, carboxylic acids such as 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid, and glyphosate".
rewrite: The use of pesticides dates back over four millennia, with ancient Sumerians in Mesopotamia applying elemental sulfur dust to crops around 2000 BC. Historical records, including the roughly 4,000-year-old Rig Veda, note the employment of poisonous plants for controlling pests. By the 1400s, farmers turned to toxic chemicals like arsenic, mercury, and lead. The 17th century brought the extraction of nicotine sulfate from tobacco for insecticidal purposes. Two natural pesticides emerged in the 1800s: pyrethrum from chrysanthemums and rotenone from tropical vegetable roots. Arsenic-based products remained prevalent until the 1950s, when Paul Müller's discovery of DDT's efficacy ushered in an era of dominant organochlorines. These were largely supplanted in the U.S. by organophosphates and carbamates around 1975, after which pyrethrin compounds rose to prominence. Herbicides gained widespread use in the 1960s, key examples being triazine and other nitrogen-based compounds, carboxylic acids like 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid, and glyphosate.

input: Precipitation is moderate and somewhat evenly distributed throughout the year, although the warmer months such as May and June average more, averaging 33.5 inches (850 mm) annually, but historically ranging from 20.49 in (520 mm) in 1963 to 47.70 in (1,212 mm) in 2011. Snowfall, which typically falls in measurable amounts between November 15 through April 4 (occasionally in October and very rarely in May), averages 42.5 inches (108 cm) per season, although historically ranging from 11.5 in (29 cm) in 1881−82 to 94.9 in (241 cm) in 2013−14. A thick snowpack is not often seen, with an average of only 27.5 days with 3 in (7.6 cm) or more of snow cover. Thunderstorms are frequent in the Detroit area. These usually occur during spring and summer.
rewrite: Annual precipitation averages 33.5 inches (850 mm), distributed moderately through the year with higher amounts typically in warmer months like May and June. Historical records show a range from 20.49 inches (520 mm) in 1963 to 47.70 inches (1,212 mm) in 2011. Snowfall, generally occurring from November 15 to April 4 and occasionally in October or rarely May, averages 42.5 inches (108 cm) per season. This has varied historically from 11.5 inches (29 cm) in 1881–82 to 94.9 inches (241 cm) in 2013–14. A deep snowpack is uncommon, with only about 27.5 days per season having at least 3 inches (7.6 cm) of cover. Frequent thunderstorms, common in the Detroit area, mostly happen in spring and summer.

input: Ben Goldacre has argued that regulators – such as the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) in the UK, or the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in the United States – advance the interests of the drug companies rather than the interests of the public due to revolving door exchange of employees between the regulator and the companies and friendships develop between regulator and company employees. He argues that regulators do not require that new drugs offer an improvement over what is already available, or even that they be particularly effective.
rewrite: According to Ben Goldacre, regulators like the UK's MHRA or the US FDA prioritize drug companies over the public interest. This is attributed to a revolving door of employees and personal friendships between the agencies and the firms. He further contends that these regulators fail to demand new drugs demonstrate improvement over existing options or prove especially effective.

input: New Haven has a variety of museums, many of them associated with Yale. The Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library features an original copy of the Gutenberg Bible. There is also the Connecticut Children's Museum; the Knights of Columbus museum near that organization's world headquarters; the Peabody Museum of Natural History; the Yale University Collection of Musical Instruments; the Eli Whitney Museum (across the town line in Hamden, Connecticut, on Whitney Avenue); the Yale Center for British Art, which houses the largest collection of British art outside the U.K., and the Yale University Art Gallery, the nation's oldest college art museum.[citation needed] New Haven is also home to the New Haven Museum and Historical Society on Whitney Avenue, which has a library of many primary source treasures dating from Colonial times to the present.
rewrite: Many of New Haven's diverse museums are connected to Yale University. These include the Yale University Art Gallery, the oldest college art museum in the nation, and the Yale Center for British Art, which holds the largest collection of British art outside the United Kingdom. Other notable institutions are the Peabody Museum of Natural History, the Yale University Collection of Musical Instruments, and the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, home to an original Gutenberg Bible. Beyond the university, the city offers the Connecticut Children's Museum and the Knights of Columbus museum near its global headquarters. Located on Whitney Avenue are the Eli Whitney Museum (just across the town line in Hamden) and the New Haven Museum and Historical Society, the latter preserving a library of primary sources from Colonial times to the present.

input: From around 750, during the Abbasid Caliphate, women “became renowned for their brains as well as their beauty”. In particular, many well known women of the time were trained from childhood in music, dancing and poetry. Mahbuba was one of these. Another feminine figure to be remembered for her achievements was Tawaddud, "a slave girl who was said to have been bought at great cost by Hārūn al-Rashīd because she had passed her examinations by the most eminent scholars in astronomy, medicine, law, philosophy, music, history, Arabic grammar, literature, theology and chess". Moreover, among the most prominent feminine figures was Shuhda who was known as "the Scholar" or "the Pride of Women" during the 12th century in Baghdad. Despite the recognition of women's aptitudes during the Abbasid dynasty, all these came to an end in Iraq with the sack of Baghdad in 1258.
rewrite: Beginning around 750 under the Abbasid Caliphate, women gained renown for intellect alongside beauty. Many were trained from youth in music, poetry, and dance, like the celebrated Mahbuba. Another notable figure was Tawaddud, a slave girl purchased at great price by Hārūn al-Rashīd after she passed examinations administered by eminent scholars in fields ranging from astronomy, medicine, and law to philosophy, music, and chess. The 12th century in Baghdad saw Shuhda, honored as "the Scholar" or "the Pride of Women." This recognition of feminine aptitude, however, was extinguished in Iraq following the sack of Baghdad in 1258, bringing the era to a close.

input: The classification of speech varieties as dialects or languages and their relationship to other varieties of speech can be controversial and the verdicts inconsistent. English and Serbo-Croatian illustrate the point. English and Serbo-Croatian each have two major variants (British and American English, and Serbian and Croatian, respectively), along with numerous other varieties. For political reasons, analyzing these varieties as "languages" or "dialects" yields inconsistent results: British and American English, spoken by close political and military allies, are almost universally regarded as dialects of a single language, whereas the standard languages of Serbia and Croatia, which differ from each other to a similar extent as the dialects of English, are being treated by some linguists from the region as distinct languages, largely because the two countries oscillate from being brotherly to being bitter enemies. (The Serbo-Croatian language article deals with this topic much more fully.)
rewrite: Determining whether speech varieties are distinct languages or dialects often leads to inconsistent and politically charged judgments. A comparison of English and Serbo-Croatian highlights this. Each has two major variants—British and American English, and Serbian and Croatian—plus many other forms. Despite similar linguistic differences between these pairs, they are classified differently. British and American English, used by close allies, are widely seen as dialects of one language. In contrast, Serbian and Croatian standards, whose divergence is comparable, are sometimes considered separate languages by regional linguists. This stems largely from the volatile political relationship between Serbia and Croatia, which has swung from brotherhood to enmity. (A fuller treatment is found in the Serbo-Croatian language article.)

input: Although the numbered streets begin just north of East Houston Street in the East Village, they generally do not extend west into Greenwich Village, which already had streets when the grid plan was laid out by the Commissioners' Plan of 1811. Streets that do continue farther west change direction before reaching the Hudson River. The grid covers the length of the island from 14th Street north.
rewrite: The grid system established by the 1811 Commissioners' Plan extends from 14th Street northward. However, the numbered streets starting just north of East Houston Street in the East Village typically do not continue west into Greenwich Village, as that area already had streets. Those that do extend further west shift direction before arriving at the Hudson River.

input: Gaddafi was later infuriated when Egypt and Syria planned the Yom Kippur War against Israel without consulting him, and was angered when Egypt conceded to peace talks rather than continuing the war. Gaddafi become openly hostile to Egypt's leader, calling for Sadat's overthrow, and when Sudanese President Gaafar Nimeiry took Sadat's side, Gaddafi by 1975 sponsored the Sudan People's Liberation Army to overthrow Nimeiry. Focusing his attention elsewhere in Africa, in late 1972 and early 1973, Libya invaded Chad to annex the uranium-rich Aouzou Strip. Offering financial incentives, he successfully convinced 8 African states to break off diplomatic relations with Israel in 1973. Intent on propagating Islam, in 1973 Gaddafi founded the Islamic Call Society, which had opened 132 centres across Africa within a decade. In 1973 he converted Gabonese President Omar Bongo, an action which he repeated three years later with Jean-Bédel Bokassa, president of the Central African Republic.
rewrite: Infuriated by Egypt and Syria planning the Yom Kippur War without consulting him, and further angered by Egypt’s move toward peace talks, Gaddafi grew openly hostile toward Egyptian leader Sadat, even calling for his overthrow. When Sudanese President Gaafar Nimeiry sided with Sadat, Gaddafi responded by 1975 with sponsorship of the Sudan People’s Liberation Army to topple Nimeiry. Elsewhere in Africa, he invaded Chad in late 1972 and early 1973 to seize the uranium-rich Aouzou Strip. Through financial incentives, he persuaded eight African states to sever diplomatic ties with Israel in 1973. Intent on propagating Islam, Gaddafi founded the Islamic Call Society that same year; it established 132 centres across Africa within a decade. His efforts at religious persuasion included converting Gabonese President Omar Bongo in 1973 and, three years later, Jean-Bédel Bokassa of the Central African Republic.

input: Another occasionally used criterion for discriminating dialects from languages is that of linguistic authority, a more sociolinguistic notion. According to this definition, two varieties are considered dialects of the same language if (under at least some circumstances) they would defer to the same authority regarding some questions about their language. For instance, to learn the name of a new invention, or an obscure foreign species of plant, speakers of Bavarian German and East Franconian German might each consult a German dictionary or ask a German-speaking expert in the subject. By way of contrast, although Yiddish is classified by linguists as a language in the "Middle High German" group of languages, a Yiddish speaker would not consult a German dictionary to determine the word to use in such a case.
rewrite: A more sociolinguistic concept known as linguistic authority offers another, though less common, standard for distinguishing dialects from languages. This criterion holds that two varieties are dialects of a single language if they acknowledge the same authority for linguistic guidance in certain situations. Such guidance might involve learning the term for a new invention or an unfamiliar foreign plant. For example, speakers of Bavarian German and East Franconian German would both likely refer to a German dictionary or a German-speaking specialist. In contrast, Yiddish, despite being linguistically categorized within the Middle High German language group, illustrates a different case. A Yiddish speaker would not turn to a German dictionary to find the appropriate word in a similar scenario.

input: The northern side of the borough includes the largest park in New York City—Pelham Bay Park, which includes Orchard Beach—and the fourth largest, Van Cortlandt Park, which is west of Woodlawn Cemetery and borders Yonkers. Also in the northern Bronx, Wave Hill, the former estate of George W. Perkins—known for a historic house, gardens, changing site-specific art installations and concerts—overlooks the New Jersey Palisades from a promontory on the Hudson in Riverdale. Nearer the borough's center, and along the Bronx River, is Bronx Park; its northern end houses the New York Botanical Gardens, which preserve the last patch of the original hemlock forest that once covered the entire county, and its southern end the Bronx Zoo, the largest urban zoological gardens in the United States. Just south of Van Cortlandt Park is the Jerome Park Reservoir, surrounded by 2 miles (3 km) of stone walls and bordering several small parks in the Bedford Park neighborhood; the reservoir was built in the 1890s on the site of the former Jerome Park Racetrack. Further south is Crotona Park, home to a 3.3-acre (1.3 ha) lake, 28 species of trees, and a large swimming pool. The land for these parks, and many others, was bought by New York City in 1888, while land was still open and inexpensive, in anticipation of future needs and future pressures for development.
rewrite:
Pelham Bay Park, the largest park in New York City and home to Orchard Beach, lies in the borough's northern section. Nearby is the fourth largest, Van Cortlandt Park, situated west of Woodlawn Cemetery and bordering Yonkers. Just south of Van Cortlandt Park sits the Jerome Park Reservoir, enclosed by 2 miles (3 km) of stone walls and adjacent to several small parks in Bedford Park; it was constructed in the 1890s on the grounds of the former Jerome Park Racetrack. Also in the northern Bronx, the Riverdale area features Wave Hill. This former estate of George W. Perkins, noted for its historic house, gardens, rotating art installations, and concerts, occupies a promontory on the Hudson River with views of the New Jersey Palisades.

Closer to the borough's center and following the Bronx River is Bronx Park. Its northern section contains the New York Botanical Gardens, safeguarding the last remnant of the original hemlock forest that once blanketed the entire county. The park's southern end holds the Bronx Zoo, the largest urban zoological gardens in the United States. Further south is Crotona Park, which features a 3.3-acre (1.3 ha) lake, 28 tree species, and a large swimming pool. The land for these and numerous other parks was acquired by New York City in 1888. At that time, with land still open and inexpensive, the city acted in anticipation of future needs and developmental pressures.

input: The public water supply network was completed in 1850, and in 1858 the architects Sebastián Monleón Estellés, Antonino Sancho, and Timoteo Calvo drafted a general expansion project for the city that included demolishing its ancient walls (a second version was printed in 1868). Neither proposed project received final approval, but they did serve as a guide, though not closely followed, for future growth. By 1860 the municipality had 140,416 inhabitants, and beginning in 1866 the ancient city walls were almost entirely demolished to facilitate urban expansion. Electricity was introduced to Valencia in 1882.
rewrite: Completed in 1850, the public water supply network was followed in 1858 by a general city expansion plan drafted by architects Sebastián Monleón Estellés, Antonino Sancho, and Timoteo Calvo, which proposed demolishing the ancient walls (a second version was printed in 1868). While neither plan received final approval, they loosely guided future development. Starting in 1866, the walls were almost entirely demolished to aid urban growth for a population that had reached 140,416 by 1860. Electricity arrived in Valencia in 1882.

input: Fossilized spores suggest that higher plants (embryophytes) have lived on land for at least 475 million years. Early land plants reproduced sexually with flagellated, swimming sperm, like the green algae from which they evolved. An adaptation to terrestrialization was the development of upright meiosporangia for dispersal by spores to new habitats. This feature is lacking in the descendants of their nearest algal relatives, the Charophycean green algae. A later terrestrial adaptation took place with retention of the delicate, avascular sexual stage, the gametophyte, within the tissues of the vascular sporophyte. This occurred by spore germination within sporangia rather than spore release, as in non-seed plants. A current example of how this might have happened can be seen in the precocious spore germination in Selaginella, the spike-moss. The result for the ancestors of angiosperms was enclosing them in a case, the seed. The first seed bearing plants, like the ginkgo, and conifers (such as pines and firs), did not produce flowers. The pollen grains (males) of Ginkgo and cycads produce a pair of flagellated, mobile sperm cells that "swim" down the developing pollen tube to the female and her eggs.
rewrite: Evidence from fossilized spores indicates that embryophytes, or higher plants, have inhabited terrestrial environments for no less than 475 million years. Evolving from green algae, these early land plants reproduced sexually using flagellated, swimming sperm. A key adaptation to life on land was the formation of upright meiosporangia, which allowed dispersal via spores to new areas—a trait absent in their closest algal relatives, the Charophycean green algae. Further terrestrial adaptation involved retaining the vulnerable, non-vascular gametophyte stage within the tissues of the vascular sporophyte. This was achieved through spore germination inside sporangia, instead of releasing spores as in non-seed plants. A modern parallel can be observed in the spike-moss Selaginella, where spores germinate precociously. For the ancestors of flowering plants, this process culminated in the development of the seed, a protective case. The earliest seed-bearing plants, such as ginkgo and conifers including pines and firs, did not form flowers. In ginkgo and cycads, pollen grains generate a pair of flagellated, motile sperm cells that navigate down the pollen tube to reach the female eggs.

input: In July 2012, Ancestry.com reported on historic and DNA research by its staff that discovered that Obama is likely a descendant through his mother of John Punch, considered by some historians to be the first African slave in the Virginia colony. An indentured servant, he was "bound for life" in 1640 after trying to escape. The story of him and his descendants is that of multi-racial America since it appeared he and his sons married or had unions with white women, likely indentured servants and working-class like them. Their multi-racial children were free because they were born to free English women. Over time, Obama's line of the Bunch family (as they became known) were property owners and continued to "marry white"; they became part of white society, likely by the early to mid-18th century.
rewrite: In July 2012, Ancestry.com released research combining history and genetics. Its findings indicated President Obama is probably a descendant, through his mother, of John Punch. Historians regard Punch as potentially the first African slave in colonial Virginia; originally an indentured servant, he was sentenced to servitude for life in 1640 after an attempted escape. His story, and that of his descendants, mirrors a multi-racial America. Punch and his sons are believed to have married or partnered with white women, often indentured servants or members of the working class like themselves. Since these women were free English citizens, their multi-racial children were born free. This line of the family, later known as Bunch, acquired property and continued intermarrying with white partners. By the early to mid-1700s, they had integrated into white society.

input: Most French rulers since the Middle Ages made a point of leaving their mark on a city that, contrary to many other of the world's capitals, has never been destroyed by catastrophe or war. In modernising its infrastructure through the centuries, Paris has preserved even its earliest history in its street map.[citation needed] At its origin, before the Middle Ages, the city was composed around several islands and sandbanks in a bend of the Seine; of those, two remain today: the île Saint-Louis, the île de la Cité; a third one is the 1827 artificially created île aux Cygnes. Modern Paris owes much to its late 19th century Second Empire remodelling by the Baron Haussmann: many of modern Paris' busiest streets, avenues and boulevards today are a result of that city renovation. Paris also owes its style to its aligned street-fronts, distinctive cream-grey "Paris stone" building ornamentation, aligned top-floor balconies, and tree-lined boulevards. The high residential population of its city centre makes it much different from most other western global cities.
rewrite: Throughout the centuries, Paris has modernized its infrastructure while preserving the earliest layers of its history within its street map, a city never destroyed by catastrophe or war. Most French rulers since the Middle Ages have deliberately left their mark upon it, unlike many other world capitals. The city originated from several islands and sandbanks in a Seine river bend; today, two remain—the île Saint-Louis and the île de la Cité—along with the artificial île aux Cygnes, created in 1827. Modern Paris is largely shaped by the late 19th-century Second Empire remodelling directed by Baron Haussmann, resulting in many of its busiest avenues and boulevards. Its distinctive style comes from aligned street-fronts, ornamentation in cream-grey "Paris stone," uniform top-floor balconies, and tree-lined boulevards. Furthermore, the high residential population in its city centre distinguishes Paris from most other Western global cities.

input: A local industry manufacturing fibre from New Zealand flax was successfully reestablished in 1907 and generated considerable income during the First World War. Ascension Island was made a dependency of Saint Helena in 1922, and Tristan da Cunha followed in 1938. During the Second World War, the United States built Wideawake airport on Ascension in 1942, but no military use was made of Saint Helena.
rewrite: In 1907, a local industry producing fibre from New Zealand flax was successfully revived, yielding significant income during World War I. Ascension Island became a dependency of Saint Helena in 1922, with Tristan da Cunha following in 1938. During World War II, the U.S. constructed Wideawake airport on Ascension in 1942, though Saint Helena saw no military use.

input: Scientists are still debating when people started wearing clothes. Ralf Kittler, Manfred Kayser and Mark Stoneking, anthropologists at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, have conducted a genetic analysis of human body lice that suggests clothing originated quite recently, around 170,000 years ago. Body lice is an indicator of clothes-wearing, since most humans have sparse body hair, and lice thus require human clothing to survive. Their research suggests the invention of clothing may have coincided with the northward migration of modern Homo sapiens away from the warm climate of Africa, thought to have begun between 50,000 and 100,000 years ago. However, a second group of researchers using similar genetic methods estimate that clothing originated around 540,000 years ago (Reed et al. 2004. PLoS Biology 2(11): e340). For now, the date of the origin of clothing remains unresolved.[citation needed]
rewrite: The origin of clothing remains a subject of scientific debate. Anthropologists Ralf Kittler, Manfred Kayser, and Mark Stoneking from the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology performed a genetic study on human body lice. Since these lice depend on garments for survival due to sparse human body hair, their presence indicates clothes-wearing. This analysis points to a relatively recent origin approximately 170,000 years ago. The researchers propose this innovation might have been connected to the migration of modern *Homo sapiens* out of Africa into cooler regions, an event thought to have started between 50,000 and 100,000 years ago. In contrast, another team using comparable genetic techniques, Reed et al. (2004), estimated a much earlier origin around 540,000 years ago. Consequently, the precise timeline for when people first wore clothes is still unresolved.

input: As soon as Schwarzenegger was elected governor, Willie Brown said he would start a drive to recall the governor. Schwarzenegger was equally entrenched in what he considered to be his mandate in cleaning up gridlock. Building on a catchphrase from the sketch "Hans and Franz" from Saturday Night Live (which partly parodied his bodybuilding career), Schwarzenegger called the Democratic State politicians "girlie men".
rewrite: Upon his election as governor, Schwarzenegger faced a recall threat from Willie Brown. Firm in his mandate to end political gridlock, he borrowed a phrase from a "Saturday Night Live" sketch parodying his past, labeling Democratic State politicians as "girlie men."

input: Also founded in 1935 and based in Detroit the Michigan Chronicle is one of the oldest and most respected African-American weekly newspapers in America. Covering politics, entertainment, sports and community events. The Detroit television market is the 11th largest in the United States; according to estimates that do not include audiences located in large areas of Ontario, Canada (Windsor and its surrounding area on broadcast and cable TV, as well as several other cable markets in Ontario, such as the city of Ottawa) which receive and watch Detroit television stations.

input: Besides their traditional areas of inhabitation in Greater Somalia, a Somali community mainly consisting of entrepreneurs, academics, and students also exists in Egypt. In addition, there is an historical Somali community in the general Sudan area. Primarily concentrated in the north and Khartoum, the expatriate community mainly consists of students as well as some businesspeople. More recently, Somali entrepreneurs have established themselves in Kenya, investing over $1.5 billion in the Somali enclave of Eastleigh alone. In South Africa, Somali businesspeople also provide most of the retail trade in informal settlements around the Western Cape province.
rewrite: Somali communities extend beyond their traditional Greater Somalia homeland. In Egypt, a group of entrepreneurs, academics, and students resides. Historically, Somalis have also lived in the broader Sudan region, with an expatriate community concentrated in the north and Khartoum, largely made up of students and some businesspeople. More recent entrepreneurial activity includes over $1.5 billion invested by Somalis in Kenya's Eastleigh enclave. Additionally, in South Africa's Western Cape province, Somali businesspeople dominate retail trade within informal settlements.

input: Gaddafi organized demonstrations and distributed posters criticizing the monarchy. In October 1961, he led a demonstration protesting Syria's secession from the United Arab Republic. During this they broke windows of a local hotel accused of serving alcohol. Catching the authorities' attention, they expelled his family from Sabha. Gaddafi moved to Misrata, there attending Misrata Secondary School. Maintaining his interest in Arab nationalist activism, he refused to join any of the banned political parties active in the city – including the Arab Nationalist Movement, the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party, and the Muslim Brotherhood – claiming he rejected factionalism. He read voraciously on the subjects of Nasser and the French Revolution of 1789, as well as the works of Syrian political theorist Michel Aflaq and biographies of Abraham Lincoln, Sun Yat-sen, and Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.

This activism drew official scrutiny, leading to his family's expulsion from Sabha. Relocating to Misrata, he attended Misrata Secondary School. input: Although provision is made in Title 10 of the United States Code for the Secretary of the Air Force to appoint warrant officers, the Air Force does not currently use warrant officer grades, and is the only one of the U.S. Armed Services not to do so. The Air Force inherited warrant officer ranks from the Army at its inception in 1947, but their place in the Air Force structure was never made clear.[citation needed] When the Congress authorized the creation of two new senior enlisted ranks in 1958, Air Force officials privately concluded that these two new "super grades" could fill all Air Force needs then performed at the warrant officer level, although this was not publicly acknowledged until years later.[citation needed] The Air Force stopped appointing warrant officers in 1959, the same year the first promotions were made to the new top enlisted grade, Chief Master Sergeant. Most of the existing Air Force warrant officers entered the commissioned officer ranks during the 1960s, but small numbers continued to exist in the warrant officer grades for the next 21 years.
rewrite: While the U.S. Code authorizes the Secretary of the Air Force to appoint warrant officers, the Air Force remains the sole branch of the U.S. Armed Services that does not utilize these ranks. This is despite having inherited the warrant officer system from the Army upon its establishment in 1947, a position whose specific role within the Air Force was never clearly defined. The turning point came in 1958 when Congress created two new senior enlisted ranks. Air Force leadership privately determined these new "super grades" could fulfill all functions previously handled by warrant officers, a rationale not publicly admitted until much later. Consequently, the Air Force ceased appointing warrant officers in 1959, coinciding with the first promotions to the new top enlisted rank of Chief Master Sergeant. Throughout the 1960s, most existing warrant officers transitioned to commissioned officer status, yet a small number continued to serve in warrant officer grades for another two decades.

input: As a schoolboy, Gaddafi adopted the ideologies of Arab nationalism and Arab socialism, influenced in particular by Nasserism, the thought of Egyptian revolutionary and president Gamal Abdel Nasser, whom Gaddafi adopted as his hero. During the early 1970s, Gaddafi formulated his own particular approach to Arab nationalism and socialism, known as Third International Theory, which has been described as a combination of "utopian socialism, Arab nationalism, and the Third World revolutionary theory that was in vogue at the time". He laid out the principles of this Theory in the three volumes of The Green Book, in which he sought to "explain the structure of the ideal society." His Arab nationalist views led him to believe that there needed to be unity across the Arab world, combining the Arab nation under a single nation-state. He described his approach to economics as "Islamic socialism", although biographers Blundy and Lycett noted that Gaddafi's socialism had a "curiously Marxist undertone", with political scientist Sami Hajjar arguing that Gaddafi's model of socialism offered a simplification of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels' theories. Gaddafi saw his socialist Jamahiriyah as a model for the Arab, Islamic, and non-aligned worlds to follow.
rewrite: During his school years, Gaddafi embraced Arab nationalism and Arab socialism, deeply inspired by Nasserism—the ideas of Egyptian revolutionary and president Gamal Abdel Nasser, who became his personal hero. In the early 1970s, he developed his own distinct framework, termed the Third International Theory. This ideology has been characterized as a blend of "utopian socialism, Arab nationalism, and the Third World revolutionary theory that was in vogue at the time." Gaddafi detailed its principles in the three-volume work *The Green Book*, aiming to "explain the structure of the ideal society." His Arab nationalist convictions drove him to advocate for a unified Arab world under a single nation-state. Economically, he described his system as "Islamic socialism," though biographers Blundy and Lycett observed a "curiously Marxist undertone" in his socialism. Political scientist Sami Hajjar further suggested that Gaddafi’s model simplified the theories of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. Gaddafi envisioned his socialist Jamahiriyah as a guiding example for the Arab, Islamic, and non-aligned worlds.

input: Bird eggs are usually laid in a nest. Most species create somewhat elaborate nests, which can be cups, domes, plates, beds scrapes, mounds, or burrows. Some bird nests, however, are extremely primitive; albatross nests are no more than a scrape on the ground. Most birds build nests in sheltered, hidden areas to avoid predation, but large or colonial birds—which are more capable of defence—may build more open nests. During nest construction, some species seek out plant matter from plants with parasite-reducing toxins to improve chick survival, and feathers are often used for nest insulation. Some bird species have no nests; the cliff-nesting common guillemot lays its eggs on bare rock, and male emperor penguins keep eggs between their body and feet. The absence of nests is especially prevalent in ground-nesting species where the newly hatched young are precocial.
rewrite: Bird nests vary widely in form, from simple scrapes to complex cups, domes, plates, mounds, or burrows. While many species build these structures in hidden spots to deter predators, larger or colonial birds often opt for more exposed locations, relying on their greater defensive abilities. Remarkably, some nests are extremely basic; the albatross, for instance, uses only a shallow ground scrape. During building, birds may incorporate specific plant materials for their parasite-reducing properties and often add feathers for insulation to boost chick survival. Not all birds use nests, however. The common guillemot lays eggs directly on bare cliff rock, and the male emperor penguin incubates its egg between its body and feet. This nestless strategy is common among ground-nesting birds whose chicks are precocial at hatching.

input: The game features nine dungeons—large, contained areas where Link battles enemies, collects items, and solves puzzles. Link navigates these dungeons and fights a boss at the end in order to obtain an item or otherwise advance the plot. The dungeons are connected by a large overworld, across which Link can travel on foot; on his horse, Epona; or by teleporting.
