To progress the plot or obtain an item, Link must navigate each dungeon and defeat its final boss. These dungeons are linked by a vast overworld, traversable on foot, by horse with Epona, or through teleportation.

input: Cork was originally a monastic settlement, reputedly founded by Saint Finbarr in the 6th century. Cork achieved an urban character at some point between 915 and 922 when Norseman (Viking) settlers founded a trading port. It has been proposed that, like Dublin, Cork was an important trading centre in the global Scandinavian trade network. The ecclesiastical settlement continued alongside the Viking longphort, with the two developing a type of symbiotic relationship; the Norsemen providing otherwise unobtainable trade goods for the monastery, and perhaps also military aid.
rewrite: Originally a monastic community said to have been established by Saint Finbarr in the 6th century, Cork gained its urban character later. Between 915 and 922, Norse settlers established a trading port there. This port likely made Cork a significant hub in the wider Scandinavian trade network, similar to Dublin. The original ecclesiastical settlement persisted alongside the Viking longphort, fostering a symbiotic relationship where the Norsemen supplied trade goods and possibly military support to the monastery.

input: The abbey became the coronation site of Norman kings. None were buried there until Henry III, intensely devoted to the cult of the Confessor, rebuilt the abbey in Anglo-French Gothic style as a shrine to venerate King Edward the Confessor and as a suitably regal setting for Henry's own tomb, under the highest Gothic nave in England. The Confessor's shrine subsequently played a great part in his canonisation. The work continued between 1245 and 1517 and was largely finished by the architect Henry Yevele in the reign of Richard II. Henry III also commissioned unique Cosmati pavement in front of the High Altar (the pavement has recently undergone a major cleaning and conservation programme and was re-dedicated by the Dean at a service on 21 May 2010).
rewrite: Norman kings were crowned at the abbey, though none were buried there until Henry III. Deeply devoted to the cult of the Confessor, Henry rebuilt the abbey in Anglo-French Gothic style between 1245 and 1517. This created both a shrine for venerating King Edward the Confessor and a regal setting for his own tomb beneath England’s highest Gothic nave. The shrine significantly aided the Confessor's canonisation. Architect Henry Yevele largely completed the work under Richard II. Henry III also commissioned the unique Cosmati pavement before the High Altar, which underwent a major cleaning and conservation programme before being re-dedicated by the Dean on 21 May 2010.

input: The use of traditional Chinese characters versus simplified Chinese characters varies greatly, and can depend on both the local customs and the medium. Before the official reform, character simplifications were not officially sanctioned and generally adopted vulgar variants and idiosyncratic substitutions. Orthodox variants were mandatory in printed works, while the (unofficial) simplified characters would be used in everyday writing or quick notes. Since the 1950s, and especially with the publication of the 1964 list, the People's Republic of China has officially adopted simplified Chinese characters for use in mainland China, while Hong Kong, Macau, and the Republic of China (Taiwan) were not affected by the reform. There is no absolute rule for using either system, and often it is determined by what the target audience understands, as well as the upbringing of the writer.
rewrite: The choice between traditional and simplified Chinese characters is shaped by regional practices and context. Prior to formal reform, simplifications were unofficial, often drawing from common shorthand or personal adaptations. In printed materials, orthodox forms were required, whereas everyday writing or quick notes might employ these informal variants. Mainland China officially adopted simplified characters in the 1950s, a move solidified by the 1964 list, while Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan continued using traditional forms. Today, usage is not strictly governed; it frequently depends on the intended audience's familiarity and the writer's own background.

input: In May 1778, Burke supported a parliamentary motion revising restrictions on Irish trade. His constituents, citizens of the great trading city of Bristol, however urged Burke to oppose free trade with Ireland. Burke resisted their protestations and said: "If, from this conduct, I shall forfeit their suffrages at an ensuing election, it will stand on record an example to future representatives of the Commons of England, that one man at least had dared to resist the desires of his constituents when his judgment assured him they were wrong".
rewrite: In May 1778, Burke backed a motion to ease Irish trade restrictions. His constituents in the major trading hub of Bristol pressed him to oppose this free trade measure. Defying their protests, Burke declared that should his stance cost him their votes, it would remain "on record an example to future representatives... that one man at least had dared to resist the desires of his constituents when his judgment assured him they were wrong."

input: Her mature artistic statement was visible in True Blue (1986) and Like a Prayer (1989). In True Blue, she incorporated classical music in order to engage an older audience who had been skeptical of her music. Like a Prayer introduced live recorded songs and incorporated different genres of music, including dance, funk, R&B and gospel music. Her versatility was further shown on I'm Breathless, which consists predominantly of the 1940s Broadway showtune-flavoured jazz, swing and big band tracks. Madonna continued to compose ballads and uptempo dance songs for Erotica (1992) and Bedtime Stories (1994). Both albums explored element of new jack swing, with Jim Farber from Entertainment Weekly saying that "she could actually be viewed as new jack swing's godmother." She tried to remain contemporary by incorporating samples, drum loops and hip hop into her music. With Ray of Light, Madonna brought electronic music from its underground status into massive popularity in mainstream music scene.
rewrite: Madonna’s mature artistic vision became clear with *True Blue* (1986) and *Like a Prayer* (1989). To engage a skeptical older audience, *True Blue* incorporated classical music. *Like a Prayer* blended live recordings with diverse genres like dance, funk, R&B, and gospel. Her versatility extended to *I’m Breathless*, featuring 1940s-inspired jazz, swing, and big band tracks. For *Erotica* (1992) and *Bedtime Stories* (1994), she continued crafting ballads and uptempo dance songs, exploring new jack swing—so much so that critic Jim Farber called her the genre’s "godmother." She maintained contemporary relevance by weaving in samples, drum loops, and hip hop. Later, with *Ray of Light*, Madonna propelled electronic music from underground circles into mainstream popularity.

input: Perhaps the most prominent, controversial and far-reaching theory in all of science has been the theory of evolution by natural selection put forward by the British naturalist Charles Darwin in his book On the Origin of Species in 1859. Darwin proposed that the features of all living things, including humans, were shaped by natural processes over long periods of time. The theory of evolution in its current form affects almost all areas of biology. Implications of evolution on fields outside of pure science have led to both opposition and support from different parts of society, and profoundly influenced the popular understanding of "man's place in the universe". In the early 20th century, the study of heredity became a major investigation after the rediscovery in 1900 of the laws of inheritance developed by the Moravian monk Gregor Mendel in 1866. Mendel's laws provided the beginnings of the study of genetics, which became a major field of research for both scientific and industrial research. By 1953, James D. Watson, Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins clarified the basic structure of DNA, the genetic material for expressing life in all its forms. In the late 20th century, the possibilities of genetic engineering became practical for the first time, and a massive international effort began in 1990 to map out an entire human genome (the Human Genome Project).
rewrite: In 1859, British naturalist Charles Darwin published *On the Origin of Species*, introducing the theory of evolution by natural selection. This concept, arguably science's most prominent, controversial, and far-reaching theory, proposed that all living organisms, humans included, acquired their features through natural processes over vast timescales. Its modern form now underpins virtually every area of biology. Beyond pure science, evolutionary implications have deeply shaped popular conceptions of humanity's place in the universe, simultaneously drawing support and opposition from various societal sectors. The study of heredity gained momentum in the early 20th century following the 1900 rediscovery of inheritance laws, originally formulated by Moravian monk Gregor Mendel in 1866. Mendel’s work laid the foundation for genetics, which grew into a major field of scientific and industrial research. A pivotal breakthrough came in 1953 when James D. Watson, Francis Crick, and Maurice Wilkins elucidated the basic structure of DNA, the genetic material essential to all life. By the late 20th century, genetic engineering turned practical, prompting a massive international endeavor: the Human Genome Project, launched in 1990 to map the entire human genome.

input: It has been pointed out that Khmer and Indonesian classical arts were concerned with depicting the life of the gods, but to the Southeast Asian mind the life of the gods was the life of the peoples themselves—joyous, earthy, yet divine. The Tai, coming late into Southeast Asia, brought with them some Chinese artistic traditions, but they soon shed them in favour of the Khmer and Mon traditions, and the only indications of their earlier contact with Chinese arts were in the style of their temples, especially the tapering roof, and in their lacquerware.
rewrite: Classical arts in Khmer and Indonesian cultures focused on portraying the life of the gods. To Southeast Asians, however, this divine existence mirrored their own—joyous, earthy, and sacred. The Tai arrived later in the region, bringing certain Chinese artistic practices. They quickly adopted Khmer and Mon traditions instead, leaving only subtle traces of Chinese influence. These were evident primarily in temple architecture, notably the tapering roof, and in their lacquerware.

input: Popular opinion remained firmly behind the celebration of Mary's conception. In 1439, the Council of Basel, which is not reckoned an ecumenical council, stated that belief in the immaculate conception of Mary is in accord with the Catholic faith. By the end of the 15th century the belief was widely professed and taught in many theological faculties, but such was the influence of the Dominicans, and the weight of the arguments of Thomas Aquinas (who had been canonised in 1323 and declared "Doctor Angelicus" of the Church in 1567) that the Council of Trent (1545–63)—which might have been expected to affirm the doctrine—instead declined to take a position.
rewrite: Public support for celebrating Mary's conception persisted strongly. Although the Council of Basel in 1439—not considered an ecumenical council—declared this belief aligned with Catholic faith, and it was widely held by the late 1400s, the Council of Trent (1545–63) refrained from affirming it. This was due to the considerable influence of the Dominicans and the arguments of Thomas Aquinas, who had been canonized in 1323 and named the "Doctor Angelicus" in 1567. Thus, despite expectations, the council chose not to adopt an official stance.

input: In May 2014, the Government of China banned the internal purchase of Windows 8-based products under government contracts requiring "energy-efficient" devices. The Xinhua News Agency claimed that Windows 8 was being banned in protest of Microsoft's support lifecycle policy and the end of support for Windows XP (which, as of January 2014, had a market share of 49% in China), as the government "obviously cannot ignore the risks of running OS [sic] without guaranteed technical support." However, Ni Guangnan of the Chinese Academy of Sciences had also previously warned that Windows 8 could allegedly expose users to surveillance by the United States government due to its heavy use of internet-based services.
rewrite: In May 2014, China's government prohibited the purchase of Windows 8 products for official use under energy-efficient device contracts. Officials stated they could not ignore the risks of using an operating system without assured technical support, a move linked by Xinhua News Agency to Microsoft ending support for the still-popular Windows XP. Additionally, prior warnings from the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Ni Guangnan suggested Windows 8's reliance on internet services might enable surveillance by the United States government.

input: Filming temporarily returned to England to shoot scenes at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire, which stood in for a location in Rome, before moving on to the city itself for a five-week shoot across the city, with locations including the Ponte Sisto bridge and the Roman Forum. The production faced opposition from a variety of special interest groups and city authorities, who were concerned about the potential for damage to historical sites around the city, and problems with graffiti and rubbish appearing in the film. A car chase scene set along the banks of the Tiber River and through the streets of Rome featured an Aston Martin DB10 and a Jaguar C-X75. The C-X75 was originally developed as a hybrid electric vehicle with four independent electric engines powered by two jet turbines, before the project was cancelled. The version used for filming was converted to use a conventional internal combustion engine, to minimise the potential for disruption from mechanical problems with the complex hybrid system. The C-X75s used for filming were developed by the engineering division of Formula One racing team Williams, who built the original C-X75 prototype for Jaguar.

Locations there included the Ponte Sisto bridge and the Roman Forum. This phase of filming, however, was met with resistance from several city authorities and special interest groups. input: The Scottish philosopher David Hume (1711–1776) responded to Berkeley's criticisms of Locke, as well as other differences between early modern philosophers, and moved empiricism to a new level of skepticism. Hume argued in keeping with the empiricist view that all knowledge derives from sense experience, but he accepted that this has implications not normally acceptable to philosophers. He wrote for example, "Locke divides all arguments into demonstrative and probable. On this view, we must say that it is only probable that all men must die or that the sun will rise to-morrow, because neither of these can be demonstrated. But to conform our language more to common use, we ought to divide arguments into demonstrations, proofs, and probabilities—by ‘proofs’ meaning arguments from experience that leave no room for doubt or opposition." And,
rewrite: David Hume (1711–1776), the Scottish philosopher, advanced empiricism toward a deeper skepticism by engaging with George Berkeley’s critiques of John Locke and other disputes among early modern thinkers. While upholding the empiricist principle that all knowledge originates from sensory experience, Hume acknowledged its troubling philosophical consequences. He illustrated this by examining Locke’s classification of arguments as either demonstrative or probable. Hume noted that, strictly speaking, we could only call it probable that all men must die or that the sun will rise tomorrow, since neither fact can be logically demonstrated. Yet to align with everyday language, Hume proposed a threefold division: demonstrations, proofs, and probabilities. Here, “proofs” signify arguments derived from experience that exclude any doubt or contradiction.

input: Modern Nationalism, as developed especially since the French Revolution, has made the distinction between "language" and "dialect" an issue of great political importance. A group speaking a separate "language" is often seen as having a greater claim to being a separate "people", and thus to be more deserving of its own independent state, while a group speaking a "dialect" tends to be seen not as "a people" in its own right, but as a sub-group, part of a bigger people, which must content itself with regional autonomy.[citation needed] The distinction between language and dialect is thus inevitably made at least as much on a political basis as on a linguistic one, and can lead to great political controversy, or even armed conflict.
rewrite: Since the French Revolution, modern nationalism has elevated the distinction between "language" and "dialect" to a matter of significant political weight. A community identified with a distinct "language" is frequently granted a stronger claim to being a separate "people," thereby justifying aspirations for an independent state. Conversely, a group speaking what is termed a "dialect" is often perceived not as an independent people, but as a subgroup within a larger national body, expected to settle for regional autonomy. Consequently, this critical distinction is drawn at least as much on political grounds as on linguistic ones. This politicization can, and often does, fuel substantial political controversy and even armed conflict.

input: In 2014 the Notre Dame student body consisted of 12,179 students, with 8,448 undergraduates, 2,138 graduate and professional and 1,593 professional (Law, M.Div., Business, M.Ed.) students. Around 21–24% of students are children of alumni, and although 37% of students come from the Midwestern United States, the student body represents all 50 states and 100 countries. As of March 2007[update] The Princeton Review ranked the school as the fifth highest 'dream school' for parents to send their children. As of March 2015[update] The Princeton Review ranked Notre Dame as the ninth highest. The school has been previously criticized for its lack of diversity, and The Princeton Review ranks the university highly among schools at which "Alternative Lifestyles [are] Not an Alternative." It has also been commended by some diversity oriented publications; Hispanic Magazine in 2004 ranked the university ninth on its list of the top–25 colleges for Latinos, and The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education recognized the university in 2006 for raising enrollment of African-American students. With 6,000 participants, the university's intramural sports program was named in 2004 by Sports Illustrated as the best program in the country, while in 2007 The Princeton Review named it as the top school where "Everyone Plays Intramural Sports." The annual Bookstore Basketball tournament is the largest outdoor five-on-five tournament in the world with over 700 teams participating each year, while the Notre Dame Men's Boxing Club hosts the annual Bengal Bouts tournament that raises money for the Holy Cross Missions in Bangladesh.
rewrite:
In 2014, Notre Dame’s total enrollment was 12,179 students, comprising 8,448 undergraduates along with 2,138 graduate and professional students and an additional 1,593 professional students in Law, M.Div., Business, and M.Ed. programs. Representing all 50 states and over 100 countries, the student body draws 37% of its population from the Midwestern United States, while approximately 21–24% are children of alumni. The Princeton Review has recognized the university in various rankings over the years: in March 2007 it was listed as the fifth highest ‘dream school’ for parents, and by March 2015 it had moved to ninth place. Despite past criticism concerning limited diversity, the school also receives notable acknowledgments. The Princeton Review ranks it highly among institutions where “Alternative Lifestyles [are] Not an Alternative.” Conversely, diversity-focused publications have offered praise; Hispanic Magazine placed Notre Dame ninth in 2004 among top colleges for Latinos, and The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education commended it in 2006 for increasing African-American enrollment.

Notre Dame’s extensive intramural sports program, involving 6,000 participants, was hailed by Sports Illustrated in 2004 as the nation’s best. Similarly, The Princeton Review in 2007 named it the top school where “Everyone Plays Intramural Sports.” The university hosts distinctive athletic events, including the annual Bookstore Basketball tournament—the world’s largest outdoor five-on-five tournament, with more than 700 teams competing each year. Additionally, the Notre Dame Men’s Boxing Club organizes the Bengal Bouts tournament yearly, which raises funds for the Holy Cross Missions in Bangladesh.

input: The Constitution does not explicitly indicate the pre-eminence of any particular branch of government. However, James Madison wrote in Federalist 51, regarding the ability of each branch to defend itself from actions by the others, that "it is not possible to give to each department an equal power of self-defense. In republican government, the legislative authority necessarily predominates."
rewrite: While the Constitution does not expressly state which branch of government holds primary authority, James Madison addressed the issue in Federalist 51. He noted the impossibility of granting each department equal defensive power against the others, concluding that in a republic, the legislative branch necessarily holds a predominant position.

input: To put it another way, a thing or person is often seen as having a "defining essence" or a "core identity" that is unchanging, and describes what the thing or person really is. In this way of thinking, things and people are seen as fundamentally the same through time, with any changes being qualitative and secondary to their core identity (e.g. "Mark's hair has turned gray as he has gotten older, but he is still the same person"). But in Whitehead's cosmology, the only fundamentally existent things are discrete "occasions of experience" that overlap one another in time and space, and jointly make up the enduring person or thing. On the other hand, what ordinary thinking often regards as "the essence of a thing" or "the identity/core of a person" is an abstract generalization of what is regarded as that person or thing's most important or salient features across time. Identities do not define people, people define identities. Everything changes from moment to moment, and to think of anything as having an "enduring essence" misses the fact that "all things flow", though it is often a useful way of speaking.
rewrite:
In Whitehead's cosmology, the only fundamentally existent things are discrete "occasions of experience." These occasions overlap in time and space and jointly constitute what we perceive as an enduring person or object. This stands in contrast to a more common way of thinking, where a thing or person is seen as possessing a fixed "defining essence" or "core identity." From that conventional view, any entity remains fundamentally the same through time, with changes considered merely qualitative and secondary—for instance, noting that while Mark's hair has grayed with age, he is still the same person.

What ordinary thought often calls "the essence of a thing" or "a person's core identity" is, in Whitehead's framework, an abstract generalization. It is derived from what are considered that entity's most important or salient features across time. Thus, identities do not define people; rather, people define identities. Everything is in constant flux from moment to moment. To attribute an "enduring essence" to anything overlooks the fundamental reality that "all things flow," even if such language can be a useful shorthand for everyday communication.

input: According to statistics published by the American Pet Products Manufacturers Association in the National Pet Owner Survey in 2009–2010, it is estimated there are 77.5 million people with pet dogs in the United States. The same survey shows nearly 40% of American households own at least one dog, of which 67% own just one dog, 25% two dogs and nearly 9% more than two dogs. There does not seem to be any gender preference among dogs as pets, as the statistical data reveal an equal number of female and male dog pets. Yet, although several programs are undergoing to promote pet adoption, less than a fifth of the owned dogs come from a shelter.
rewrite: Based on the 2009–2010 National Pet Owner Survey by the American Pet Products Manufacturers Association, approximately 77.5 million Americans own pet dogs. This represents nearly 40% of all U.S. households. Among these dog-owning households, about 67% have one dog, 25% have two, and nearly 9% have more than two. Statistics indicate no gender preference, with equal numbers of female and male dogs kept as pets. Despite various programs encouraging adoption, fewer than 20% of owned dogs are obtained from shelters.

input: The second main principle, sola fide (by faith alone), states that faith in Christ is sufficient alone for eternal salvation. Though argued from scripture, and hence logically consequent to sola scriptura, this is the guiding principle of the work of Luther and the later reformers. Because sola scriptura placed the Bible as the only source of teaching, sola fide epitomises the main thrust of the teaching the reformers wanted to get back to, namely the direct, close, personal connection between Christ and the believer, hence the reformers' contention that their work was Christocentric.
rewrite: Sola fide (by faith alone), the second main principle, asserts that faith in Christ alone ensures eternal salvation. While derived from scripture and thus following logically from sola scriptura, it became the guiding force for Luther and later reformers. By establishing the Bible as the sole teaching source, sola scriptura paved the way for sola fide. This principle captures the reformers' core aim: restoring a direct, personal connection between Christ and the believer, which is why they viewed their work as Christocentric.

input: A common misperception is that the Supreme Court is the only court that may determine constitutionality; the power is exercised even by the inferior courts. But only Supreme Court decisions are binding across the nation. Decisions of a Court of Appeals, for instance, are binding only in the circuit over which the court has jurisdiction.
rewrite: While many believe only the Supreme Court can rule on constitutionality, even lower courts exercise this power. However, only its rulings are nationally binding. For example, a Court of Appeals decision is binding solely within its own circuit.

input: Unicode has become the dominant scheme for internal processing and storage of text. Although a great deal of text is still stored in legacy encodings, Unicode is used almost exclusively for building new information processing systems. Early adopters tended to use UCS-2 (the fixed-width two-byte precursor to UTF-16) and later moved to UTF-16 (the variable-width current standard), as this was the least disruptive way to add support for non-BMP characters. The best known such system is Windows NT (and its descendants, Windows 2000, Windows XP, Windows Vista and Windows 7), which uses UTF-16 as the sole internal character encoding. The Java and .NET bytecode environments, Mac OS X, and KDE also use it for internal representation. Unicode is available on Windows 95 through Microsoft Layer for Unicode, as well as on its descendants, Windows 98 and Windows ME.
rewrite: While a significant amount of text remains in older formats, Unicode is now the principal system for internal text processing and storage, and is nearly always chosen for new systems. Early implementations often began with UCS-2, a fixed-width two-byte forerunner to UTF-16, later transitioning to the variable-width UTF-16 standard to more easily incorporate characters beyond the Basic Multilingual Plane. A prominent example is the Windows NT lineage, including Windows 2000, XP, Vista, and 7, which employs UTF-16 as its exclusive internal encoding. This representation is also used in Java, .NET, Mac OS X, and KDE. For earlier systems like Windows 95, 98, and ME, Unicode support was provided via the Microsoft Layer for Unicode.

input: In 1238, King James I of Aragon, with an army composed of Aragonese, Catalans, Navarrese and crusaders from the Order of Calatrava, laid siege to Valencia and on 28 September obtained a surrender. Fifty thousand Moors were forced to leave. Poets such as Ibn al-Abbar and Ibn Amira mourned this exile from their beloved Valencia. After the Christian victory and the expulsion of the Muslim population the city was divided between those who had participated in the conquest, according to the testimony in the Llibre del Repartiment (Book of Distribution). James I granted the city new charters of law, the Furs of Valencia, which later were extended to the whole kingdom of Valencia. Thenceforth the city entered a new historical stage in which a new society and a new language developed, forming the basis of the character of the Valencian people as they are known today.
rewrite: In September of 1238, following a siege, King James I of Aragon secured the surrender of Valencia. His forces included Aragonese, Catalans, Navarrese, and knights from the Order of Calatrava. The conquest resulted in the expulsion of approximately fifty thousand Moors, an exile poignantly lamented by contemporary poets like Ibn al-Abbar and Ibn Amira. Subsequently, the city's lands were apportioned among the conquerors, a process documented in the *Llibre del Repartiment* (Book of Distribution). King James I also established new legal charters, the Furs of Valencia, which would later be applied throughout the kingdom. This marked the beginning of a distinct historical era, characterized by the development of a new society and language. These foundations ultimately shaped the essential character of the Valencian people.

input: The executive branch consists of the Governor, their staff, and other elected officials. The principal head of government, the Governor is the chief executive of the Oklahoma executive branch, serving as the ex officio Commander-in-Chief of the Oklahoma National Guard when not called into Federal use and reserving the power to veto bills passed through the Legislature. The responsibilities of the Executive branch include submitting the budget, ensuring that state laws are enforced, and ensuring peace within the state is preserved.
rewrite: The Governor, as the chief executive and principal head of government, leads the Oklahoma executive branch, which also includes their staff and other elected officials. This branch is responsible for submitting the budget, enforcing state laws, and preserving peace. The Governor serves as the ex officio Commander-in-Chief of the state's National Guard when not federalized and holds the power to veto legislative bills.

input: Some of the best-known traditions, including carnal parades and masquerade balls, were first recorded in medieval Italy. The carnival of Venice was, for a long time, the most famous carnival (although Napoleon abolished it in 1797 and only in 1979 was the tradition restored). From Italy, Carnival traditions spread to Spain, Portugal and France and from France to New France in North America. From Spain and Portugal it spread with colonization to the Caribbean and Latin America. In the early 19th century in the German Rhineland and Southern Netherlands, the weakened medieval tradition also revive. Continuously in the 18th and 19th centuries CE, as part of the annual Saturnalia abuse of the carnival in Rome, rabbis of the ghetto were forced to march through the city streets wearing foolish guise, jeered upon and pelted by a variety of missiles from the crowd. A petition of the Jewish community of Rome sent in 1836 to Pope Gregory XVI to stop the annual anti-semitic Saturnalia abuse got a negation: “It is not opportune to make any innovation.”
rewrite: Many of the most iconic traditions, such as masquerade balls and carnal parades, trace their earliest documented origins to medieval Italy. The Venetian carnival stood as the preeminent celebration for centuries, though it was abolished by Napoleon in 1797 and not revived until 1979. These Italian customs subsequently spread to Spain, Portugal, and France, and from France to its North American colony of New France. Through Spanish and Portuguese colonization, Carnival further extended to the Caribbean and Latin America. A weakened medieval tradition also saw a revival in the early 19th century within the German Rhineland and Southern Netherlands. Elsewhere, during the 18th and 19th centuries, the Roman carnival's annual Saturnalia included a grievous abuse: rabbis from the ghetto were forced to march in foolish guise through city streets, subjected to jeers and a hail of thrown objects from crowds. In 1836, the Jewish community of Rome petitioned Pope Gregory XVI to halt this anti-semitic practice, only to receive the dismissive reply that it was “not opportune to make any innovation.”

input: The first issue was ammunition. Before the war it was recognised that ammunition needed to explode in the air. Both high explosive (HE) and shrapnel were used, mostly the former. Airburst fuses were either igniferious (based on a burning fuse) or mechanical (clockwork). Igniferious fuses were not well suited for anti-aircraft use. The fuse length was determined by time of flight, but the burning rate of the gunpowder was affected by altitude. The British pom-poms had only contact-fused ammunition. Zeppelins, being hydrogen filled balloons, were targets for incendiary shells and the British introduced these with airburst fuses, both shrapnel type-forward projection of incendiary 'pot' and base ejection of an incendiary stream. The British also fitted tracers to their shells for use at night. Smoke shells were also available for some AA guns, these bursts were used as targets during training.
rewrite: Ammunition presented the initial challenge, with the need for airburst capability recognized even before the conflict began. While both high explosive and shrapnel shells were employed, high explosive was more common. Fuses to achieve airbursts were either igniferous, relying on a burning gunpowder fuse, or mechanical clockwork types. The igniferous type proved poorly suited for anti-aircraft purposes because, although the fuse length was set for time of flight, the burning rate varied unpredictably with altitude. For targeting hydrogen-filled Zeppelins, the British developed incendiary shells with airburst fuses. These included designs that projected an incendiary 'pot' forward or ejected a stream of fire from the base. British forces also equipped shells with tracers for night engagements and used smoke shells, which provided visible burst markers for training exercises. Notably, British pom-pom guns were limited to contact-fused ammunition.

input: Eventually, the Licchavi ruler Gunakamadeva merged Koligram and Dakshin Koligram, founding the city of Kathmandu. The city was designed in the shape of Chandrahrasa, the sword of Manjushri. The city was surrounded by eight barracks guarded by Ajimas. One of these barracks is still in use at Bhadrakali (in front of Singha Durbar). The city served as an important transit point in the trade between India and Tibet, leading to tremendous growth in architecture. Descriptions of buildings such as Managriha, Kailaskut Bhawan, and Bhadradiwas Bhawan have been found in the surviving journals of travelers and monks who lived during this era. For example, the famous 7th-century Chinese traveller Xuanzang described Kailaskut Bhawan, the palace of the Licchavi king Amshuverma. The trade route also led to cultural exchange as well. The artistry of the Newar people—the indigenous inhabitants of the Kathmandu Valley—became highly sought after during this era, both within the Valley and throughout the greater Himalayas. Newar artists travelled extensively throughout Asia, creating religious art for their neighbors. For example, Araniko led a group of his compatriot artists through Tibet and China. Bhrikuti, the princess of Nepal who married Tibetan monarch Songtsän Gampo, was instrumental in introducing Buddhism to Tibet.
rewrite: Under the Licchavi ruler Gunakamadeva, the settlements of Koligram and Dakshin Koligram were merged to establish the city of Kathmandu. Its layout was deliberately fashioned in the form of Chandrahrasa, the sword wielded by Manjushri. For protection, the city was encircled by eight barracks, each guarded by Ajimas, with one such structure still present at Bhadrakali, facing Singha Durbar. Kathmandu’s position as a vital transit point on the trade route between India and Tibet spurred significant architectural advancement. Contemporary accounts from travelers and monks reference notable buildings like Managriha, Kailaskut Bhawan, and Bhadradiwas Bhawan. The 7th-century Chinese traveler Xuanzang, for instance, provided a description of Kailaskut Bhawan, the palace of King Amshuverma. This commerce also facilitated profound cultural exchange. The Newar people, indigenous to the Kathmandu Valley, saw their artistry become widely prized across the Valley and the broader Himalayan region. Newar artists journeyed extensively throughout Asia to produce religious art for neighboring cultures. A prominent example is Araniko, who led a cohort of fellow artists into Tibet and China. Furthermore, the Nepali princess Bhrikuti, upon marrying the Tibetan ruler Songtsän Gampo, played a key role in bringing Buddhism to Tibet.

input: In addition to concerns over subsidies, the cotton industries of some countries are criticized for employing child labor and damaging workers' health by exposure to pesticides used in production. The Environmental Justice Foundation has campaigned against the prevalent use of forced child and adult labor in cotton production in Uzbekistan, the world's third largest cotton exporter. The international production and trade situation has led to "fair trade" cotton clothing and footwear, joining a rapidly growing market for organic clothing, fair fashion or "ethical fashion". The fair trade system was initiated in 2005 with producers from Cameroon, Mali and Senegal.
rewrite: Beyond worries about subsidies, the cotton sectors in certain nations face criticism for using child labor and endangering worker health through pesticide exposure. Notably, the Environmental Justice Foundation has targeted Uzbekistan, the third-largest cotton exporter, for its widespread use of forced labor involving both children and adults. This international context has spurred the rise of "fair trade" cotton apparel and footwear, part of a fast-expanding market for organic and ethical fashion. The fair trade framework itself began in 2005 with producers in Cameroon, Mali, and Senegal.

input: The capital is Nashville, though Knoxville, Kingston, and Murfreesboro have all served as state capitals in the past. Memphis has the largest population of any city in the state. Nashville's 13-county metropolitan area has been the state's largest since c. 1990. Chattanooga and Knoxville, both in the eastern part of the state near the Great Smoky Mountains, each has approximately one-third of the population of Memphis or Nashville. The city of Clarksville is a fifth significant population center, some 45 miles (72 km) northwest of Nashville. Murfreesboro is the sixth-largest city in Tennessee, consisting of some 108,755 residents.
rewrite: While Memphis is Tennessee's most populous city, Nashville serves as the capital, a role previously held by Knoxville, Kingston, and Murfreesboro. Since around 1990, the Nashville metropolitan area, spanning 13 counties, has been the state's largest. In the east near the Great Smoky Mountains, Chattanooga and Knoxville each have roughly a third of the population of Memphis or Nashville. Other key population centers include Clarksville, located about 45 miles northwest of Nashville, and Murfreesboro, the sixth-largest city with approximately 108,755 residents.

input: The first half of the 14th century saw much important scientific work being done, largely within the framework of scholastic commentaries on Aristotle's scientific writings. William of Ockham introduced the principle of parsimony: natural philosophers should not postulate unnecessary entities, so that motion is not a distinct thing but is only the moving object and an intermediary "sensible species" is not needed to transmit an image of an object to the eye. Scholars such as Jean Buridan and Nicole Oresme started to reinterpret elements of Aristotle's mechanics. In particular, Buridan developed the theory that impetus was the cause of the motion of projectiles, which was a first step towards the modern concept of inertia. The Oxford Calculators began to mathematically analyze the kinematics of motion, making this analysis without considering the causes of motion.
rewrite: During the first half of the 14th century, significant scientific advances occurred, primarily through scholastic commentaries on Aristotle's works. A key figure, William of Ockham, proposed the principle of parsimony, arguing against unnecessary entities. He stated that motion is not separate from the moving object and that no intermediary "sensible species" is required for vision. Concurrently, thinkers like Jean Buridan and Nicole Oresme reexamined Aristotle's mechanics. Buridan's theory of impetus, explaining projectile motion, marked an early move toward the modern idea of inertia. Meanwhile, the Oxford Calculators independently focused on the mathematical analysis of motion's kinematics, deliberately setting aside its causes.

input: The modern Conservative Party was created out of the 'Pittite' Tories of the early 19th century. In the late 1820s disputes over political reform broke up this grouping. A government led by the Duke of Wellington collapsed amidst dire election results. Following this disaster Robert Peel set about assembling a new coalition of forces. Peel issued the Tamworth Manifesto in 1834 which set out the basic principles of Conservatism; – the necessity in specific cases of reform in order to survive, but an opposition to unnecessary change, that could lead to "a perpetual vortex of agitation". Meanwhile, the Whigs, along with free trade Tory followers of Robert Peel, and independent Radicals, formed the Liberal Party under Lord Palmerston in 1859, and transformed into a party of the growing urban middle-class, under the long leadership of William Ewart Gladstone.
rewrite: Emerging from the early 19th-century 'Pittite' Tories, the modern Conservative Party was forged amid disputes over political reform in the late 1820s, which broke up the original grouping. After the Duke of Wellington's government collapsed following poor election results, Robert Peel began assembling a new coalition. In 1834, Peel issued the Tamworth Manifesto, outlining core Conservative principles: a pragmatic acceptance of necessary reform for survival, coupled with opposition to needless change that might create a "perpetual vortex of agitation." Concurrently, the Liberal Party formed in 1859 under Lord Palmerston, uniting Whigs, Peel's free-trade Tory followers, and independent Radicals. It later evolved, under William Ewart Gladstone's long leadership, into a party representing the expanding urban middle-class.

input: Several versions of a semi-official, structured pantheon were developed during the political, social and religious instability of the Late Republican era. Jupiter, the most powerful of all gods and "the fount of the auspices upon which the relationship of the city with the gods rested", consistently personified the divine authority of Rome's highest offices, internal organization and external relations. During the archaic and early Republican eras, he shared his temple, some aspects of cult and several divine characteristics with Mars and Quirinus, who were later replaced by Juno and Minerva. A conceptual tendency toward triads may be indicated by the later agricultural or plebeian triad of Ceres, Liber and Libera, and by some of the complementary threefold deity-groupings of Imperial cult. Other major and minor deities could be single, coupled, or linked retrospectively through myths of divine marriage and sexual adventure. These later Roman pantheistic hierarchies are part literary and mythographic, part philosophical creations, and often Greek in origin. The Hellenization of Latin literature and culture supplied literary and artistic models for reinterpreting Roman deities in light of the Greek Olympians, and promoted a sense that the two cultures had a shared heritage.
rewrite: During the Late Republican era, marked by political, social, and religious instability, multiple versions of a semi-official, structured pantheon emerged. Jupiter consistently embodied the divine authority of Rome’s highest offices, its internal order, and foreign relations; as the most powerful god, he was "the fount of the auspices upon which the relationship of the city with the gods rested." In earlier archaic and Republican times, he shared his temple, certain cult aspects, and divine traits with Mars and Quirinus—figures later supplanted by Juno and Minerva. A leaning toward triads is suggested by the later plebeian triad of Ceres, Liber, and Libera, and by various threefold groupings in Imperial cult. Deities, both major and minor, could appear singly, in pairs, or be connected retroactively via myths of marriage and sexual adventure. These later pantheistic hierarchies are partly literary and mythographic, partly philosophical constructs, often derived from Greek sources. The Hellenization of Latin literature and culture provided models for reimagining Roman gods in terms of Greek Olympians, fostering a perception of a shared heritage between the two civilizations.

input: From the second half of the 20th century on parties which continued to rely on donations or membership subscriptions ran into mounting problems. Along with the increased scrutiny of donations there has been a long-term decline in party memberships in most western democracies which itself places more strains on funding. For example, in the United Kingdom and Australia membership of the two main parties in 2006 is less than an 1/8 of what it was in 1950, despite significant increases in population over that period.
rewrite: Since the mid-20th century, political parties depending on donations or member dues have faced growing difficulties. Most Western democracies have seen a long-term drop in party membership, increasing funding pressures amid greater scrutiny of contributions. To illustrate, membership in the two major parties of the United Kingdom and Australia by 2006 was less than one-eighth of its 1950 level, even as the overall population rose significantly.

input: A route through Beringia is seen as more likely than the Solutrean hypothesis. Kashani et al. 2012 state that "The similarities in ages and geographical distributions for C4c and the previously analyzed X2a lineage provide support to the scenario of a dual origin for Paleo-Indians. Taking into account that C4c is deeply rooted in the Asian portion of the mtDNA phylogeny and is indubitably of Asian origin, the finding that C4c and X2a are characterized by parallel genetic histories definitively dismisses the controversial hypothesis of an Atlantic glacial entry route into North America."
rewrite: The Solutrean hypothesis, proposing an Atlantic entry into North America, is considered less probable than a Beringia route. Research by Kashani et al. (2012) supports a dual origin for Paleo-Indians. Their analysis notes that mitochondrial lineages C4c and X2a share similar ages and distributions. Since C4c is unequivocally of Asian origin, the parallel genetic histories of these two lineages definitively refute an Atlantic glacial migration.

input: Fetuvalu offers the Cambridge syllabus. Motufoua offers the Fiji Junior Certificate (FJC) at year 10, Tuvaluan Certificate at Year 11 and the Pacific Senior Secondary Certificate (PSSC) at Year 12, set by the Fiji-based exam board SPBEA. Sixth form students who pass their PSSC go on to the Augmented Foundation Programme, funded by the government of Tuvalu. This program is required for tertiary education programmes outside of Tuvalu and is available at the University of the South Pacific (USP) Extension Centre in Funafuti.
rewrite: Fetuvalu follows the Cambridge syllabus. In contrast, Motufoua provides the Fiji Junior Certificate (FJC) in year 10, the Tuvaluan Certificate in year 11, and the Pacific Senior Secondary Certificate (PSSC) in year 12, which is administered by the SPBEA exam board in Fiji. Successful PSSC graduates in sixth form enter the government-funded Augmented Foundation Programme. Hosted at the USP Extension Centre in Funafuti, this program is a prerequisite for pursuing tertiary studies abroad.

input: The largest ethnic groups are Newar (29.6%), Matwali (25.1% Sunuwar, Gurung, Magars, Tamang etc.), Khas Brahmins (20.51%) and Chettris (18.5%) . Tamangs originating from surrounding hill districts can be seen in Kathmandu. More recently, other hill ethnic groups and Caste groups from Terai have come to represent a substantial proportion of the city's population. The major languages are Nepali and Nepal Bhasa, while English is understood by many, particularly in the service industry. The major religions are Hinduism and Buddhism.
rewrite: Newar (29.6%), Matwali (25.1%, including Sunuwar and Gurung), Khas Brahmins (20.51%), and Chettris (18.5%) form the largest ethnic groups. Many Tamangs, originating from nearby hill districts, reside in Kathmandu. The city now also has a substantial population of other hill ethnicities and Terai caste groups. Nepali and Nepal Bhasa are the major languages, with English widely understood in services. Hinduism and Buddhism are the predominant religions.

input: Galileo Galilei was brought before the Inquisition for heresy, but abjured his views and was sentenced to house arrest, under which he spent the rest of his life. Galileo was found "vehemently suspect of heresy", namely of having held the opinions that the Sun lies motionless at the centre of the universe, that the Earth is not at its centre and moves, and that one may hold and defend an opinion as probable after it has been declared contrary to Holy Scripture. He was required to "abjure, curse and detest" those opinions.
rewrite: Galileo Galilei was accused of heresy for holding that the Sun motionlessly rests at the universe's center while the Earth moves around it, and for defending such opinions even after they were deemed contrary to Scripture. Declared "vehemently suspect of heresy," he was brought before the Inquisition. Forced to renounce, curse, and detest his views, he abjured them. His sentence was house arrest, where he remained until the end of his life.

input: According to reciprocity, the efficiency of an antenna used as a receiving antenna is identical to the efficiency as defined above. The power that an antenna will deliver to a receiver (with a proper impedance match) is reduced by the same amount. In some receiving applications, the very inefficient antennas may have little impact on performance. At low frequencies, for example, atmospheric or man-made noise can mask antenna inefficiency. For example, CCIR Rep. 258-3 indicates man-made noise in a residential setting at 40 MHz is about 28 dB above the thermal noise floor. Consequently, an antenna with a 20 dB loss (due to inefficiency) would have little impact on system noise performance. The loss within the antenna will affect the intended signal and the noise/interference identically, leading to no reduction in signal to noise ratio (SNR).
rewrite: Due to reciprocity, an antenna’s efficiency remains the same whether it is transmitting or receiving. Consequently, when used for reception with proper impedance matching, the power delivered to a receiver is reduced proportionally to this efficiency. However, in certain receiving scenarios, even highly inefficient antennas may not significantly degrade performance. At lower frequencies, factors like atmospheric or man-made noise can overshadow antenna losses. For instance, CCIR Rep. 258-3 notes that in residential areas at 40 MHz, man-made noise is approximately 28 dB above the thermal noise floor. In such conditions, an antenna with a 20 dB loss from inefficiency would have minimal effect on overall system noise. This is because the antenna’s loss attenuates both the desired signal and the noise equally, leaving the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) unchanged.

input: In 2011, Bandai posted a countdown on a teaser site. Once the countdown was finished, it revealed a reboot of the Digimon World series titled Digimon World Re:Digitize. An enhanced version of the game released on Nintendo 3DS as Digimon World Re:Digitize Decode in 2013. Another role-playing game by the name Digimon Story: Cyber Sleuth is set for release in 2015 for PlayStation Vita. It is part of the Digimon Story sub-series, originally on Nintendo DS and has also been released with English subtitles in North America.
rewrite: In 2011, a teaser site from Bandai featured a countdown, culminating in the announcement of Digimon World Re:Digitize, a reboot of the series. An enhanced edition, Digimon World Re:Digitize Decode, followed on the Nintendo 3DS in 2013. Separately, 2015 will see the release of Digimon Story: Cyber Sleuth for PlayStation Vita. input: On 25 February 1991, the Warsaw Pact was declared disbanded at a meeting of defense and foreign ministers from remaining Pact countries meeting in Hungary. On 1 July 1991, in Prague, the Czechoslovak President Václav Havel formally ended the 1955 Warsaw Treaty Organization of Friendship, Cooperation, and Mutual Assistance and so disestablished the Warsaw Treaty after 36 years of military alliance with the USSR. In fact, the treaty was de facto disbanded in December 1989 during the violent revolution in Romania, which toppled the communist government, without military intervention form other member states. The USSR disestablished itself in December 1991.
rewrite: At a meeting in Hungary on February 25, 1991, defense and foreign ministers from the remaining member states declared the Warsaw Pact disbanded. The formal end came later that year on July 1 in Prague, when Czechoslovak President Václav Havel terminated the 1955 Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation, and Mutual Assistance, thereby dissolving the 36-year military alliance with the USSR. In practice, however, the pact had ceased to function de facto in December 1989 following the violent Romanian revolution, which overthrew the communist regime without intervention from fellow members. The USSR itself was dissolved in December 1991.

input: Public funding and private investment have also been made with promises to rehabilitate neighborhoods. In April 2008, the city announced a $300-million stimulus plan to create jobs and revitalize neighborhoods, financed by city bonds and paid for by earmarking about 15% of the wagering tax. The city's working plans for neighborhood revitalizations include 7-Mile/Livernois, Brightmoor, East English Village, Grand River/Greenfield, North End, and Osborn. Private organizations have pledged substantial funding to the efforts. Additionally, the city has cleared a 1,200-acre (490 ha) section of land for large-scale neighborhood construction, which the city is calling the Far Eastside Plan. In 2011, Mayor Bing announced a plan to categorize neighborhoods by their needs and prioritize the most needed services for those neighborhoods.
rewrite: Efforts to rehabilitate neighborhoods have drawn both public funding and private investment. A key public initiative was a $300-million stimulus plan announced in April 2008, financed by city bonds and supported by allocating roughly 15% of the wagering tax to create jobs and revitalize areas. These targeted neighborhoods include 7-Mile/Livernois, Brightmoor, East English Village, Grand River/Greenfield, North End, and Osborn. Substantial funding pledges have also come from private organizations. For large-scale construction, the city has prepared a 1,200-acre (490 ha) area under the Far Eastside Plan. Furthermore, in 2011, Mayor Bing introduced a strategy to classify neighborhoods by need to prioritize essential services.

input: In Epperson v. Arkansas, 393 U.S. 97 (1968), the Supreme Court considered an Arkansas law that made it a crime "to teach the theory or doctrine that mankind ascended or descended from a lower order of animals," or "to adopt or use in any such institution a textbook that teaches" this theory in any school or university that received public funds. The court's opinion, written by Justice Abe Fortas, ruled that the Arkansas law violated "the constitutional prohibition of state laws respecting an establishment of religion or prohibiting the free exercise thereof. The overriding fact is that Arkansas' law selects from the body of knowledge a particular segment which it proscribes for the sole reason that it is deemed to conflict with a particular religious doctrine; that is, with a particular interpretation of the Book of Genesis by a particular religious group." The court held that the Establishment Clause prohibits the state from advancing any religion, and that "[T]he state has no legitimate interest in protecting any or all religions from views distasteful to them."
rewrite: In Epperson v. Arkansas, 393 U.S. 97 (1968), the Supreme Court reviewed an Arkansas statute criminalizing the teaching of the theory "that mankind ascended or descended from a lower order of animals" in any publicly funded school. The law also forbade the use of textbooks presenting this theory. Justice Abe Fortas authored the opinion, which found the statute unconstitutional. The Court determined it breached the Establishment Clause by promoting a specific religious doctrine. The law, the opinion stated, singled out a specific scientific concept for prohibition solely because it conflicted with a particular religious interpretation—namely, a certain reading of the Book of Genesis. The ruling emphasized that the state has no legitimate authority to shield religions from ideas they find disagreeable, and it cannot advance any particular faith. Therefore, the Arkansas law was struck down as a violation of the First Amendment.

input: Although unpleasantness is an essential part of the IASP definition of pain, it is possible to induce a state described as intense pain devoid of unpleasantness in some patients, with morphine injection or psychosurgery. Such patients report that they have pain but are not bothered by it; they recognize the sensation of pain but suffer little, or not at all. Indifference to pain can also rarely be present from birth; these people have normal nerves on medical investigations, and find pain unpleasant, but do not avoid repetition of the pain stimulus.
rewrite: While the IASP defines pain as inherently unpleasant, certain medical interventions like morphine or psychosurgery can create a state of intense pain without the associated distress. Patients in this condition acknowledge the painful sensation but are not bothered by it. Additionally, a rare congenital indifference to pain exists from birth; individuals with this condition perceive pain as unpleasant, yet they do not avoid painful stimuli, despite having normal neurological function.

input: The Qur'an relates detailed narrative accounts of Maryam (Mary) in two places, Qur'an 3:35–47 and 19:16–34. These state beliefs in both the Immaculate Conception of Mary and the Virgin birth of Jesus. The account given in Sura 19 is nearly identical with that in the Gospel according to Luke, and both of these (Luke, Sura 19) begin with an account of the visitation of an angel upon Zakariya (Zecharias) and Good News of the birth of Yahya (John), followed by the account of the annunciation. It mentions how Mary was informed by an angel that she would become the mother of Jesus through the actions of God alone.
rewrite: The Qur'an presents detailed narratives of Maryam (Mary) in two sections: 3:35–47 and 19:16–34. These passages affirm the Immaculate Conception of Mary and the Virgin birth of Jesus. Sura 19's account closely parallels that in the Gospel of Luke. Both begin with an angel's visitation to Zakariya (Zecharias), announcing the birth of Yahya (John), followed by the annunciation to Mary. In this event, an angel informs Mary that she will bear Jesus solely through divine will.

input: As a relatively small and isolated oceanic island, Norfolk has few land birds but a high degree of endemicity among them. Many of the endemic species and subspecies have become extinct as a result of massive clearance of the island's native vegetation of subtropical rainforest for agriculture, hunting and persecution as agricultural pests. The birds have also suffered from the introduction of mammals such as rats, cats, pigs and goats, as well as from introduced competitors such as common blackbirds and crimson rosellas.
rewrite: Norfolk is a small, isolated oceanic island with limited land bird species, yet a notable degree of endemicity among them. Extensive clearing of the native subtropical rainforest for agriculture, along with hunting and persecution as pests, has led to the extinction of many endemic species and subspecies. Additionally, introduced mammals like rats, cats, pigs, and goats, as well as competitor birds such as common blackbirds and crimson rosellas, have further impacted these birds.

input: Physical pain is an important political topic in relation to various issues, including pain management policy, drug control, animal rights or animal welfare, torture, and pain compliance. In various contexts, the deliberate infliction of pain in the form of corporal punishment is used as retribution for an offence, or for the purpose of disciplining or reforming a wrongdoer, or to deter attitudes or behaviour deemed unacceptable. In some cultures, extreme practices such as mortification of the flesh or painful rites of passage are highly regarded.
rewrite: Physical pain holds significant political relevance across areas like pain management policy, drug control, animal welfare, torture, and pain compliance. Corporal punishment is often deliberately used as retribution, for discipline or reform, or to deter unacceptable behavior. Additionally, some cultures highly value extreme practices, including mortification of the flesh or painful rites of passage. These varied contexts illustrate how the infliction and management of pain intersect with societal and ethical frameworks.

input: This trend for the king to rely on his own men at the expense of the barons was exacerbated by the tradition of Angevin royal ira et malevolentia – "anger and ill-will" – and John's own personality. From Henry II onwards, ira et malevolentia had come to describe the right of the king to express his anger and displeasure at particular barons or clergy, building on the Norman concept of malevoncia – royal ill-will. In the Norman period, suffering the king's ill-will meant difficulties in obtaining grants, honours or petitions; Henry II had infamously expressed his fury and ill-will towards Thomas Becket; this ultimately resulted in Becket's death. John now had the additional ability to "cripple his vassals" on a significant scale using his new economic and judicial measures, which made the threat of royal anger all the more serious.
rewrite: The Angevin tradition of royal *ira et malevolentia* – "anger and ill-will" – intensified the king's growing reliance on his personal followers over the barons. This concept, rooted in the Norman idea of *malevoncia*, evolved from Henry II onward to signify the monarch's formal right to show displeasure toward specific barons or clergy. In Norman times, incurring the king's ill-will hindered one's chances of securing grants, honors, or favorable rulings. Henry II notoriously directed his fury and ill-will at Thomas Becket, leading to Becket's death. King John compounded this threat; his novel economic and judicial measures enabled him to "cripple his vassals" on an unprecedented scale, making the royal anger far more dangerous.

input: During the 1960s and 1970s, the city gained a reputation as an important center for liberal politics. Ann Arbor also became a locus for left-wing activism and served as a hub for the civil-rights movement and anti-Vietnam War movement, as well as the student movement. The first major meetings of the national left-wing campus group Students for a Democratic Society took place in Ann Arbor in 1960; in 1965, the city was home to the first U.S. teach-in against the Vietnam War. During the ensuing 15 years, many countercultural and New Left enterprises sprang up and developed large constituencies within the city. These influences washed into municipal politics during the early and mid-1970s when three members of the Human Rights Party (HRP) won city council seats on the strength of the student vote. During their time on the council, HRP representatives fought for measures including pioneering antidiscrimination ordinances, measures decriminalizing marijuana possession, and a rent-control ordinance; many of these remain in effect in modified form. Alongside these liberal and left-wing efforts, a small group of conservative institutions were born in Ann Arbor. These include Word of God (established in 1967), a charismatic inter-denominational movement; and the Thomas More Law Center (established in 1999), a religious-conservative advocacy group.
rewrite: In the 1960s and 1970s, Ann Arbor emerged as a significant hub for liberal politics. It also developed into a focal point for left-wing activism, functioning as a central node for the civil-rights movement, the anti-Vietnam War effort, and broader student activism. The city hosted the first major gatherings of the national left-wing group Students for a Democratic Society in 1960. By 1965, it was the site of the nation’s first teach-in opposing the Vietnam War. Over the next fifteen years, numerous countercultural and New Left initiatives arose, attracting substantial local followings. This political energy translated directly into municipal government in the early to mid-1970s, when three candidates from the Human Rights Party (HRP) were elected to the city council, propelled largely by student support. While serving, HRP council members championed pioneering anti-discrimination laws, measures to decriminalize marijuana possession, and rent-control policies; many of these, albeit modified, persist today. Concurrently with these liberal and left-wing movements, a small cluster of conservative institutions also took root in Ann Arbor. Among them are the charismatic inter-denominational movement Word of God, founded in 1967, and the religious-conservative advocacy organization the Thomas More Law Center, established in 1999.

input: The USA PATRIOT Act of October 2001 dramatically reduces restrictions on law enforcement agencies' ability to search telephone, e-mail communications, medical, financial, and other records; eases restrictions on foreign intelligence gathering within the United States; expands the Secretary of the Treasury's authority to regulate financial transactions, particularly those involving foreign individuals and entities; and broadens the discretion of law enforcement and immigration authorities in detaining and deporting immigrants suspected of terrorism-related acts. The act also expanded the definition of terrorism to include domestic terrorism, thus enlarging the number of activities to which the USA PATRIOT Act's expanded law enforcement powers could be applied. A new Terrorist Finance Tracking Program monitored the movements of terrorists' financial resources (discontinued after being revealed by The New York Times). Global telecommunication usage, including those with no links to terrorism, is being collected and monitored through the NSA electronic surveillance program. The Patriot Act is still in effect.
rewrite: Enacted in October 2001, the USA PATRIOT Act significantly broadened governmental powers. It lessened constraints on law enforcement, allowing enhanced searches of telephone, email, medical, and financial records. Gathering foreign intelligence inside the U.S. faced fewer restrictions. Authority for the Treasury Secretary to oversee financial transactions, especially with foreign parties, was increased. The act also granted wider latitude to law enforcement and immigration officials in detaining and deporting immigrants suspected of terrorism. By redefining terrorism to include domestic acts, it extended the reach of these new powers. A Terrorist Finance Tracking Program was created to follow monetary resources, though it ended after a New York Times disclosure. Furthermore, the NSA surveillance program collects global telecommunications data, even absent terrorism links. The Patriot Act remains active today.

input: On February 8, 1847, Doniphan continued his march with 924 men mostly from Missouri; he accompanied a train of 315 wagons of a large commercial caravan heading to the state capital. Meanwhile, the Mexican forces in the state had time to prepare a defense against the Americans. About 20 miles (32 km) north of the capital where two mountain ranges join from east to west is the only pass into the capital; known as Sacramento Pass, this point is now part of present-day Chihuahua City. The Battle of Sacramento was the most important battle fought in the state of Chihuahua because it was the sole defense for the state capital. The battle ended quickly because of some devastating defensive errors from the Mexican forces and the ingenious strategic moves by the American forces. After their loss at the Battle of Sacramento, the remaining Mexican soldiers retreated south, leaving the city to American occupation. Almost 300 Mexicans were killed in the battle, as well as almost 300 wounded. The Americans also confiscated large amounts of Mexican supplies and took 400 Mexican soldiers prisoners of war. American forces maintained an occupation of the state capital for the rest of the Mexican–American War.
rewrite: On February 8, 1847, Doniphan advanced with a force of 924 men, predominantly from Missouri. His troops escorted a substantial commercial caravan of 315 wagons bound for the state capital. Mexican forces in the region used this time to organize their defenses. The crucial point of engagement was Sacramento Pass, located roughly 20 miles (32 km) north of the capital where two mountain ranges converge; this pass, now within modern Chihuahua City, was the sole entry route. The Battle of Sacramento became the most significant conflict in Chihuahua, representing the capital's only defensive stand. Due to severe defensive mistakes by the Mexicans and clever American strategy, the battle concluded swiftly. Following this defeat, the remaining Mexican troops withdrew southward, abandoning the city to American control. The conflict resulted in nearly 300 Mexican fatalities and approximately 300 more wounded. American forces captured large quantities of supplies and took 400 soldiers as prisoners of war. They proceeded to occupy the state capital for the remainder of the Mexican–American War.

input: Lester Brown has argued that "a world facing the prospect of economically disruptive climate change can no longer justify subsidies to expand the burning of coal and oil. Shifting these subsidies to the development of climate-benign energy sources such as wind, solar, biomass, and geothermal power is the key to stabilizing the earth's climate." The International Solar Energy Society advocates "leveling the playing field" by redressing the continuing inequities in public subsidies of energy technologies and R&D, in which the fossil fuel and nuclear power receive the largest share of financial support.
rewrite: Lester Brown contends that economically disruptive climate change makes subsidies for expanding coal and oil use unjustifiable. He asserts that shifting these subsidies to climate-benign sources like wind, solar, biomass, and geothermal power is crucial for climate stabilization. Echoing this need for change, the International Solar Energy Society advocates "leveling the playing field." They call for redressing inequities in public subsidies and R&D support, which currently favor fossil fuel and nuclear power with the largest share of funding.

input: Several hundred pro-Tibet protesters gathered at the Trocadéro with banners and Tibetan flags, and remained there for a peaceful protest, never approaching the torch relay itself. Among them was Jane Birkin, who spoke to the media about the "lack of freedom of speech" in China. Also present was Thupten Gyatso, President of the French Tibetan community, who called upon pro-Tibet demonstrators to "remain calm, non-violent, peaceful".
rewrite: Holding banners and Tibetan flags, several hundred pro-Tibet demonstrators staged a peaceful gathering at the Trocadéro, keeping their distance from the torch relay. Thupten Gyatso, President of the French Tibetan community, urged protesters to "remain calm, non-violent, peaceful." Among the crowd, Jane Birkin addressed the press, criticizing what she termed a "lack of freedom of speech" in China.

input: The Dutch written grammar has simplified over the past 100 years: cases are now mainly used for the pronouns, such as ik (I), mij, me (me), mijn (my), wie (who), wiens (whose: masculine or neuter singular), wier (whose: feminine singular; masculine, feminine or neuter plural). Nouns and adjectives are not case inflected (except for the genitive of proper nouns (names): -s, -'s or -'). In the spoken language cases and case inflections had already gradually disappeared from a much earlier date on (probably the 15th century) as in many continental West Germanic dialects.
rewrite: Over the past century, Dutch written grammar has become simpler, with cases now primarily applying to pronouns like "ik" (I) and "mijn" (my). Nouns and adjectives no longer use case inflections, aside from the genitive form for proper names. In spoken Dutch, however, cases began fading much earlier, likely from the 15th century onward, mirroring the evolution seen in other continental West Germanic dialects.

input: The World Health Organization and the UN Environment Programme estimate that each year, 3 million workers in agriculture in the developing world experience severe poisoning from pesticides, about 18,000 of whom die. Owing to inadequate regulation and safety precautions, 99% of pesticide related deaths occur in developing countries that account for only 25% of pesticide usage. According to one study, as many as 25 million workers in developing countries may suffer mild pesticide poisoning yearly. There are several careers aside from agriculture that may also put individuals at risk of health effects from pesticide exposure including pet groomers, groundskeepers, and fumigators.
rewrite: Each year in the developing world, about 3 million agricultural workers suffer severe pesticide poisoning, leading to approximately 18,000 deaths, as estimated by the World Health Organization and the UN Environment Programme. Notably, 99% of all pesticide-related fatalities occur in these nations, which use just 25% of the world's pesticides, highlighting inadequate regulation and safety. One study suggests mild pesticide poisoning may affect up to 25 million workers annually in developing countries. Beyond agriculture, professions like pet grooming, groundskeeping, and fumigation also pose health risks from such exposure.

input: Peel, widely regarded as the father of modern policing, was heavily influenced by the social and legal philosophy of Jeremy Bentham, who called for a strong and centralized, but politically neutral, police force for the maintenance of social order, for the protection of people from crime and to act as a visible deterrent to urban crime and disorder. Peel decided to standardise the police force as an official paid profession, to organise it in a civilian fashion, and to make it answerable to the public.
rewrite: Influenced by Jeremy Bentham's philosophy, which advocated for a centralized, neutral police force to ensure order and deter crime, Sir Robert Peel is considered the father of modern policing. He standardized policing as a paid profession, organizing it in a civilian structure. Crucially, he made it accountable to the public for maintaining social order and protecting people from urban crime and disorder.

input: The western section of the state is part of the Appalachian Mountain range. Among the subranges of the Appalachians located in the state are the Great Smoky Mountains, Blue Ridge Mountains, Great Balsam Mountains, and Black Mountains. The Black Mountains are the highest in the eastern United States, and culminate in Mount Mitchell at 6,684 feet (2,037 m) the highest point east of the Mississippi River. Although agriculture still remains important, tourism has become a dominant industry in the mountains. Growing Christmas trees has recently become an important industry as well. Because of the higher altitude, the climate in the mountains often differs markedly from that of the rest of the state. Winter in western North Carolina typically features high snowfall and subfreezing temperatures more akin to those of a midwestern state than of a southern state.
rewrite: The state's western portion lies within the Appalachian Mountain range, which includes such subranges as the Great Smoky Mountains, the Blue Ridge Mountains, the Great Balsam Mountains, and the Black Mountains. The Black Mountains, home to the highest peak east of the Mississippi River—Mount Mitchell at 6,684 feet (2,037 m)—are the tallest in the eastern United States. Tourism now dominates the regional economy, though agriculture retains importance, and Christmas tree farming has recently emerged as a significant industry. Due to the higher elevation, the mountain climate frequently contrasts sharply with the rest of the state. Winters in western North Carolina, for instance, bring substantial snowfall and subfreezing temperatures more characteristic of the Midwest than the South.

input: Within six years of the official criminalization of heresy by the Emperor, the first Christian heretic to be executed, Priscillian, was condemned in 386 by Roman secular officials for sorcery, and put to death with four or five followers. However, his accusers were excommunicated both by Ambrose of Milan and Pope Siricius, who opposed Priscillian's heresy, but "believed capital punishment to be inappropriate at best and usually unequivocally evil". For some years after the Reformation, Protestant churches were also known to execute those they considered heretics, including Catholics.
