The last known heretic executed by sentence of the Roman Catholic Church was Spanish schoolmaster Cayetano Ripoll in 1826. The number of people executed as heretics under the authority of the various "ecclesiastical authorities"[note 1] is not known.[note 2] One of the first examples of the word as translated from the Nag Hammadi's Apocalypse of Peter was" they will cleave to the name of a dead man thinking that they will become pure. But they will become greatly defiled and they will fall into the name of error and into the hands of an evil cunning man and a manifold dogma, and they will be ruled heretically".
rewrite: Six years after heresy was formally criminalized by the Emperor, Roman secular authorities condemned Priscillian for sorcery in 386, leading to his execution alongside four or five followers, marking the first such death of a Christian heretic. Notably, his accusers faced excommunication by both Ambrose of Milan and Pope Siricius; while opposed to Priscillian's beliefs, they deemed capital punishment inappropriate or outright evil. In the years following the Reformation, Protestant churches similarly executed individuals they deemed heretical, including Catholics. The Roman Catholic Church's final known execution of a heretic was that of Spanish schoolmaster Cayetano Ripoll in 1826. The total number executed under various ecclesiastical authorities remains unknown. An early translation of the term "heretic" appears in the Nag Hammadi's Apocalypse of Peter, describing those who "will cleave to the name of a dead man thinking that they will become pure. But they will become greatly defiled and they will fall into the name of error and into the hands of an evil cunning man and a manifold dogma, and they will be ruled heretically."

input: Greece is today relatively homogeneous in linguistic terms, with a large majority of the native population using Greek as their first or only language. Among the Greek-speaking population, speakers of the distinctive Pontic dialect came to Greece from Asia Minor after the Greek genocide and constitute a sizable group. The Cappadocian dialect came to Greece due to the genocide as well, but is endangered and is barely spoken now. Indigenous Greek dialects include the archaic Greek spoken by the Sarakatsani, traditionally transhument mountain shepherds of Greek Macedonia and other parts of Northern Greece. The Tsakonian language, a distinct Greek language deriving from Doric Greek instead of Ionic Greek, is still spoken in some villages in the southeastern Peloponnese.
rewrite: Today, Greece is linguistically quite uniform, with most of its native population speaking Greek as their primary or sole language. Within this Greek-speaking majority, there are notable groups speaking distinctive dialects. For instance, speakers of the Pontic dialect arrived from Asia Minor following the Greek genocide and form a considerable community. Also stemming from that period is the Cappadocian dialect, now critically endangered and rarely used. Among indigenous dialects is the archaic form spoken by the Sarakatsani, the traditionally transhumant shepherds of Greek Macedonia and northern regions. Additionally, the Tsakonian language, a separate branch derived from Doric rather than Ionic Greek, persists in a few southeastern Peloponnese villages.

input: The Bologna process has been adopted, since 2006, by Portuguese universities and poly-technical institutes. Higher education in state-run educational establishments is provided on a competitive basis, a system of numerus clausus is enforced through a national database on student admissions. However, every higher education institution offers also a number of additional vacant places through other extraordinary admission processes for sportsmen, mature applicants (over 23 years old), international students, foreign students from the Lusosphere, degree owners from other institutions, students from other institutions (academic transfer), former students (readmission), and course change, which are subject to specific standards and regulations set by each institution or course department. Most student costs are supported with public money. However, with the increasing tuition fees a student has to pay to attend a Portuguese state-run higher education institution and the attraction of new types of students (many as part-time students or in evening classes) like employees, businessmen, parents, and pensioners, many departments make a substantial profit from every additional student enrolled in courses, with benefits for the college or university's gross tuition revenue and without loss of educational quality (teacher per student, computer per student, classroom size per student, etc.).
rewrite:
Since 2006, Portuguese universities and polytechnic institutes have implemented the Bologna process. Admission to state-run higher education is competitive, utilizing a national database to enforce a numerus clausus system. Beyond this primary route, each institution provides additional vacant places through extraordinary admission processes. These cater to specific groups such as sportsmen, international students, applicants over 23, students from Lusophone countries, degree holders, transfer students, and those seeking readmission or course changes, with standards set by individual institutions or departments.

While public funds cover most student costs, rising tuition fees have altered the financial landscape. The appeal to new student demographics—including employees, businesspeople, parents, and pensioners, often enrolling part-time or in evening classes—has enabled many departments to realize substantial profit from each additional enrollee. This boosts the gross tuition revenue of colleges and universities without compromising educational quality, as metrics like teacher-to-student ratios, computer access, and classroom sizes are maintained.

input: The loss of industrial and working-class jobs in the city has resulted in high rates of poverty and associated problems. From 2000 to 2009, the city's estimated median household income fell from $29,526 to $26,098. As of 2010[update] the mean income of Detroit is below the overall U.S. average by several thousand dollars. Of every three Detroit residents, one lives in poverty. Luke Bergmann, author of Getting Ghost: Two Young Lives and the Struggle for the Soul of an American City, said in 2010, "Detroit is now one of the poorest big cities in the country."
rewrite: High poverty rates and related issues have emerged in the city due to the decline of industrial and working-class employment. Between 2000 and 2009, the estimated median household income dropped from $29,526 to $26,098. By 2010, Detroit's mean income was thousands of dollars below the national average. One in every three residents lives in poverty. As Luke Bergmann noted in his 2010 book *Getting Ghost: Two Young Lives and the Struggle for the Soul of an American City*, Detroit had become one of the nation's poorest major cities.

input: The Bithynians were a Thracian people living in northwest Anatolia. After Alexander's conquests the region of Bithynia came under the rule of the native king Bas, who defeated Calas, a general of Alexander the Great, and maintained the independence of Bithynia. His son, Zipoetes I of Bithynia maintained this autonomy against Lysimachus and Seleucus I, and assumed the title of king (basileus) in 297 BCE. His son and successor, Nicomedes I, founded Nicomedia, which soon rose to great prosperity, and during his long reign (c. 278 – c. 255 BCE), as well as those of his successors, the kingdom of Bithynia held a considerable place among the minor monarchies of Anatolia. Nicomedes also invited the Celtic Galatians into Anatolia as mercenaries, and they later turned on his son Prusias I, who defeated them in battle. Their last king, Nicomedes IV, was unable to maintain himself against Mithridates VI of Pontus, and, after being restored to his throne by the Roman Senate, he bequeathed his kingdom by will to the Roman republic (74 BCE).
rewrite: Originally a Thracian people in northwest Anatolia, the Bithynians preserved their independence following Alexander the Great’s conquests. Their native king, Bas, achieved this by defeating Alexander’s general Calas. This autonomy was sustained by his son, Zipoetes I, who successfully resisted Lysimachus and Seleucus I, formally taking the title of king in 297 BCE. Under Zipoetes’s successor, Nicomedes I, whose reign lasted from approximately 278 to 255 BCE, the kingdom grew in prominence among Anatolia’s minor monarchies. Nicomedes founded the prosperous city of Nicomedia and, in a consequential move, invited Celtic Galatians as mercenaries. These Galatians later attacked his son, Prusias I, though Prusias managed to defeat them. The final ruler, Nicomedes IV, struggled against Mithridates VI of Pontus. After the Roman Senate reinstated him, he ultimately willed the entire kingdom to the Roman Republic in 74 BCE.

input: The Space Race was a 20th-century competition between two Cold War rivals, the Soviet Union (USSR) and the United States (US), for supremacy in spaceflight capability. It had its origins in the missile-based nuclear arms race between the two nations that occurred following World War II, enabled by captured German rocket technology and personnel. The technological superiority required for such supremacy was seen as necessary for national security, and symbolic of ideological superiority. The Space Race spawned pioneering efforts to launch artificial satellites, unmanned space probes of the Moon, Venus, and Mars, and human spaceflight in low Earth orbit and to the Moon. The competition began on August 2, 1955, when the Soviet Union responded to the US announcement four days earlier of intent to launch artificial satellites for the International Geophysical Year, by declaring they would also launch a satellite "in the near future". The Soviet Union beat the US to this, with the October 4, 1957 orbiting of Sputnik 1, and later beat the US to the first human in space, Yuri Gagarin, on April 12, 1961. The Space Race peaked with the July 20, 1969 US landing of the first humans on the Moon with Apollo 11. The USSR tried but failed manned lunar missions, and eventually cancelled them and concentrated on Earth orbital space stations. A period of détente followed with the April 1972 agreement on a co-operative Apollo–Soyuz Test Project, resulting in the July 1975 rendezvous in Earth orbit of a US astronaut crew with a Soviet cosmonaut crew.
rewrite:
A 20th-century rivalry for supremacy in spaceflight capability, known as the Space Race, unfolded between the Cold War adversaries, the Soviet Union and the United States. Its foundations lay in the post-World War II missile-based nuclear arms race, accelerated by captured German rocket technology and personnel. Achieving the necessary technological edge was viewed as crucial for national security and as a symbol of ideological superiority. This competition triggered pioneering endeavors, including the launch of artificial satellites, unmanned probes to the Moon, Venus, and Mars, and human spaceflight in low Earth orbit and to the Moon.

The rivalry formally commenced on August 2, 1955, when the Soviet Union, responding to a U.S. announcement from four days prior, declared its own intent to launch a satellite "in the near future" for the International Geophysical Year. The USSR took an early lead, successfully orbiting Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957, and later achieving the first human spaceflight with Yuri Gagarin on April 12, 1961. The Space Race reached its zenith with the U.S. Apollo 11 mission, landing the first humans on the Moon on July 20, 1969. Although the Soviet Union attempted manned lunar missions, it ultimately canceled these efforts after failures, shifting focus to Earth orbital space stations.

A subsequent period of détente was marked by the April 1972 agreement on the cooperative Apollo-Soyuz Test Project. This culminated in July 1975 with a U.S. astronaut crew and a Soviet cosmonaut crew rendezvousing in Earth orbit.

input: The last major building work took place during the reign of King George V when, in 1913, Sir Aston Webb redesigned Blore's 1850 East Front to resemble in part Giacomo Leoni's Lyme Park in Cheshire. This new, refaced principal façade (of Portland stone) was designed to be the backdrop to the Victoria Memorial, a large memorial statue of Queen Victoria, placed outside the main gates. George V, who had succeeded Edward VII in 1910, had a more serious personality than his father; greater emphasis was now placed on official entertaining and royal duties than on lavish parties. He arranged a series of command performances featuring jazz musicians such as the Original Dixieland Jazz Band (1919) – the first jazz performance for a head of state, Sidney Bechet, and Louis Armstrong (1932), which earned the palace a nomination in 2009 for a (Kind of) Blue Plaque by the Brecon Jazz Festival as one of the venues making the greatest contribution to jazz music in the United Kingdom. George V's wife Queen Mary was a connoisseur of the arts, and took a keen interest in the Royal Collection of furniture and art, both restoring and adding to it. Queen Mary also had many new fixtures and fittings installed, such as the pair of marble Empire-style chimneypieces by Benjamin Vulliamy, dating from 1810, which the Queen had installed in the ground floor Bow Room, the huge low room at the centre of the garden façade. Queen Mary was also responsible for the decoration of the Blue Drawing Room. This room, 69 feet (21 metres) long, previously known as the South Drawing Room, has a ceiling designed specially by Nash, coffered with huge gilt console brackets.
rewrite:
During the reign of King George V, the last significant architectural changes were made to the palace. In 1913, Sir Aston Webb undertook a redesign of Blore's 1850 East Front, drawing partial inspiration from Giacomo Leoni's Lyme Park in Cheshire. This new principal façade, refaced in Portland stone, was created specifically to serve as a grand backdrop for the Victoria Memorial—a large statue of Queen Victoria situated outside the main gates. Succeeding Edward VII in 1910, George V possessed a more serious disposition than his father, shifting the focus from lavish parties toward official entertaining and royal duties. His patronage of music included arranging command performances by pioneering jazz artists. These featured the Original Dixieland Jazz Band in 1919, marking the first jazz performance for a head of state, and later legends like Sidney Bechet and Louis Armstrong in 1932. This musical legacy led the palace to be nominated in 2009 for a (Kind of) Blue Plaque by the Brecon Jazz Festival, recognizing it as a venue of major importance to jazz in the United Kingdom.

George V's wife, Queen Mary, was a knowledgeable connoisseur of the arts. She took a deep interest in the Royal Collection, both restoring existing pieces and adding to its holdings of furniture and art. Her influence extended to numerous interior updates, including the installation of new fixtures and fittings. Among these were a pair of marble Empire-style chimneypieces from 1810 by Benjamin Vulliamy, which she placed in the ground floor Bow Room. This is the vast, low-ceilinged space at the center of the garden façade. Queen Mary also oversaw the redecoration of the Blue Drawing Room. Previously called the South Drawing Room, this 69-foot (21-meter) long space features a ceiling specially designed by Nash, coffered and adorned with substantial gilt console brackets.

input: In 2011, the Aragonese government passed a decree for the establishment of a new language regulator of Catalan in La Franja (the so-called Catalan-speaking areas of Aragon). The new entity, designated as Acadèmia Aragonesa del Català, shall allow a facultative education in Catalan and a standardization of the Catalan language in La Franja.
rewrite: In 2011, Aragon's government decreed a new Catalan language regulator for La Franja, its Catalan-speaking areas. Named the Acadèmia Aragonesa del Català, this entity will enable optional Catalan education and standardize the language there.

input: An influx of interstate and overseas migrants, particularly Irish, German and Chinese, saw the development of slums including a temporary "tent city" established on the southern banks of the Yarra. Chinese migrants founded the Melbourne Chinatown in 1851, which remains the longest continuous Chinese settlement in the Western World. In the aftermath of the Eureka Stockade, mass public support for the plight of the miners resulted in major political changes to the colony, including changes to working conditions across local industries including mining, agriculture and manufacturing. The nationalities involved in the Eureka revolt and Burke and Wills expedition gave an indication of immigration flows in the second half of the nineteenth century.
rewrite: The arrival of interstate and overseas migrants, such as Irish, German, and Chinese settlers, led to slum development, including a provisional "tent city" on the Yarra's southern banks. Chinese migrants established Melbourne Chinatown in 1851, the Western World's oldest continuous Chinese settlement. Following the Eureka Stockade, widespread public sympathy for the miners spurred major political reforms in the colony, improving working conditions in mining, agriculture, and manufacturing. Immigration patterns in the latter nineteenth century were reflected in the nationalities participating in both the Eureka revolt and the Burke and Wills expedition.

input: In December 1994, after being tipped off by his former FBI handler about a pending indictment under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, Bulger fled Boston and went into hiding. For 16 years, he remained at large. For 12 of those years, Bulger was prominently listed on the FBI Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list. Beginning in 1997, the New England media exposed criminal actions by federal, state, and local law enforcement officials tied to Bulger. The revelation caused great embarrassment to the FBI. In 2002, Special Agent John J Connolly was convicted of federal racketeering charges for helping Bulger avoid arrest. In 2008, Special Agent Connolly completed his term on the federal charges and was transferred to Florida where he was convicted of helping plan the murder of John B Callahan, a Bulger rival. In 2014, that conviction was overturned on a technicality. Connolly was the agent leading the investigation of Bulger.
rewrite: After being alerted by his former FBI handler in December 1994 of an imminent RICO indictment, James "Whitey" Bulger vanished from Boston, evading capture for 16 years. For 12 of those years, he was a mainstay on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list. Starting in 1997, New England media began uncovering crimes committed by law enforcement officials connected to Bulger, revelations that severely embarrassed the FBI. The agent who had led the Bulger investigation, John J. Connolly, was convicted in 2002 on federal racketeering charges for aiding Bulger’s evasion. Following his federal sentence in 2008, Connolly was transferred to Florida, where he was convicted of conspiring to murder Bulger’s rival, John B. Callahan. That 2008 murder conspiracy conviction was later overturned on a technicality in 2014.

input: Ecuador was the site of many indigenous cultures, and civilizations of different proportions. An early sedentary culture, known as the Valdivia culture, developed in the coastal region, while the Caras and the Quitus unified to form an elaborate civilization that ended at the birth of the Capital Quito. The Cañaris near Cuenca were the most advanced, and most feared by the Inca, due to their fierce resistance to the Incan expansion. Their architecture remains were later destroyed by Spaniards and the Incas.
rewrite: The coastal region saw the early sedentary Valdivia culture, while the Caras and Quitus united to form a sophisticated civilization that ended with the founding of Quito. Among Ecuador's many indigenous cultures, the Cañaris near Cuenca were the most advanced and, owing to their fierce resistance, the most feared by the Inca. Later, both Spanish and Inca forces destroyed the remains of their architecture.

input: Only the Theravada school does not include the Mahayana scriptures in its canon. As the modern Theravada school is descended from a branch of Buddhism that diverged and established itself in Sri Lanka prior to the emergence of the Mahayana texts, debate exists as to whether the Theravada were historically included in the hinayana designation; in the modern era, this label is seen as derogatory, and is generally avoided.
rewrite: The Theravada school excludes Mahayana scriptures from its canon, as it descends from a branch established in Sri Lanka before those texts emerged. Historically, debate exists over whether Theravada was included in the hinayana designation, a term now viewed as derogatory and generally avoided in the modern era.

input: In 2006, Jian Li, a Chinese undergraduate at Yale University, filed a civil rights complaint with the Office for Civil Rights against Princeton University, claiming that his race played a role in their decision to reject his application for admission and seeking the suspension of federal financial assistance to the university until it "discontinues discrimination against Asian Americans in all forms" by eliminating race and legacy preferences. Princeton Dean of Admissions Janet Rapelye responded to the claims in the November 30, 2006, issue of the Daily Princetonian by stating that "the numbers don't indicate [discrimination]." She said that Li was not admitted because "many others had far better qualifications." Li's extracurricular activities were described as "not all that outstanding". Li countered in an email, saying that his placement on the waitlist undermines Rapelye's claim. "Princeton had initially waitlisted my application," Li said. "So if it were not for a yield which was higher than expected, the admissions office very well may have admitted a candidate whose "outside activities were not all that outstanding".
rewrite: In 2006, Yale undergraduate Jian Li, who is Chinese, lodged a civil rights complaint with the Office for Civil Rights targeting Princeton University. He alleged that his race was a factor in Princeton’s decision to reject his admission application. Li sought to suspend federal financial assistance to the university until it ended all forms of discrimination against Asian Americans by abolishing race and legacy preferences in admissions. Responding to these claims in the November 30, 2006, issue of the Daily Princetonian, Princeton’s Dean of Admissions, Janet Rapelye, asserted that "the numbers don't indicate [discrimination]." She explained Li’s rejection by stating "many others had far better qualifications," and described his extracurricular activities as "not all that outstanding." Li countered this in an email, arguing that his initial placement on the waitlist weakened Rapelye’s claim. He noted, "Princeton had initially waitlisted my application," adding that had the admissions yield been lower, the office might well have admitted a candidate whose "outside activities were not all that outstanding."

input: The Monreale mosaics constitute the largest decoration of this kind in Italy, covering 0,75 hectares with at least 100 million glass and stone tesserae. This huge work was executed between 1176 and 1186 by the order of King William II of Sicily. The iconography of the mosaics in the presbytery is similar to Cefalu while the pictures in the nave are almost the same as the narrative scenes in the Cappella Palatina. The Martorana mosaic of Roger II blessed by Christ was repeated with the figure of King William II instead of his predecessor. Another panel shows the king offering the model of the cathedral to the Theotokos.
rewrite: Commissioned by King William II of Sicily, the monumental mosaics at Monreale were created between 1176 and 1186. They form Italy's largest such decoration, employing over 100 million glass and stone tesserae across 0.75 hectares. The presbytery's iconography resembles that of Cefalu, while the nave's narrative scenes closely mirror those in the Cappella Palatina. One panel adapts the Martorana mosaic, showing William II blessed by Christ instead of his predecessor, Roger II. In another, the king presents a model of the cathedral to the Theotokos.

input: Following the 2013 emergencies, the Minister of Foreign Affairs Tony de Brum was encouraged by the Obama administration in the United States to turn the crises into an opportunity to promote action against climate change. De Brum demanded new commitment and international leadership to stave off further climate disasters from battering his country and other similarly vulnerable countries. In September 2013, the Marshall Islands hosted the 44th Pacific Islands Forum summit. De Brum proposed a Majuro Declaration for Climate Leadership to galvanize concrete action on climate change.
rewrite: After the 2013 emergencies, U.S. President Obama's administration urged Marshall Islands Foreign Minister Tony de Brum to leverage the crises for climate action. De Brum called for renewed international commitment and leadership to protect his nation and other vulnerable countries from further climate disasters. To spur concrete measures, he proposed the Majuro Declaration for Climate Leadership during the 44th Pacific Islands Forum summit, which the Marshall Islands hosted in September 2013.

input: Composers of classical music have often made use of folk music (music created by musicians who are commonly not classically trained, often from a purely oral tradition). Some composers, like Dvořák and Smetana, have used folk themes to impart a nationalist flavor to their work, while others like Bartók have used specific themes lifted whole from their folk-music origins.
rewrite: Classical composers frequently incorporate folk music, which arises from oral traditions and musicians without classical training. To infuse a nationalist character, figures such as Dvořák and Smetana employed folk themes. Others, like Bartók, directly borrowed specific themes entirely from their folk origins.

input: Ronald Inden writes that by the 8th century CE symbols of Hindu gods "replaced the Buddha at the imperial centre and pinnacle of the cosmo-political system, the image or symbol of the Hindu god comes to be housed in a monumental temple and given increasingly elaborate imperial-style puja worship". Although Buddhism did not disappear from India for several centuries after the eighth, royal proclivities for the cults of Vishnu and Shiva weakened Buddhism's position within the sociopolitical context and helped make possible its decline.
rewrite: By the 8th century CE, as Ronald Inden notes, symbols of Hindu deities had displaced the Buddha at the empire's symbolic core. The Hindu god's image, housed in a monumental temple, received increasingly elaborate imperial worship. While Buddhism persisted in India for centuries afterward, royal preferences for the cults of Vishnu and Shiva eroded its sociopolitical standing. This shift in patronage was a key factor enabling Buddhism's subsequent decline.

input: In fledgling democracies funding can also be provided by foreign aid. International donors provide financing to political parties in developing countries as a means to promote democracy and good governance. Support can be purely financial or otherwise. Frequently it is provided as capacity development activities including the development of party manifestos, party constitutions and campaigning skills. Developing links between ideologically linked parties is another common feature of international support for a party. Sometimes this can be perceived as directly supporting the political aims of a political party, such as the support of the US government to the Georgian party behind the Rose Revolution. Other donors work on a more neutral basis, where multiple donors provide grants in countries accessible by all parties for various aims defined by the recipients. There have been calls by leading development think-tanks, such as the Overseas Development Institute, to increase support to political parties as part of developing the capacity to deal with the demands of interest-driven donors to improve governance.
rewrite: Foreign aid serves as another source of funding in emerging democracies. To foster democracy and sound governance, international donors often extend financing to political parties in developing nations. This support may be purely monetary or take other forms, frequently appearing as capacity-building initiatives like crafting party manifestos and constitutions or enhancing campaigning skills. Another typical aspect is forging connections between parties that share ideological ties. At times, such backing can be seen as directly advancing a party’s political goals—for instance, U.S. government support for the Georgian party instrumental in the Rose Revolution. Alternatively, many donors operate neutrally, offering grants accessible to all parties within a country for purposes set by the recipients themselves. Prominent development think-tanks, including the Overseas Development Institute, have advocated for greater assistance to political parties. This is viewed as essential for building their capacity to manage the expectations of interest-driven donors and thereby improve governance.

input: Swayambhu is a Buddhist stupa atop a hillock at the northwestern part of the city. This is among the oldest religious sites in Nepal. Although the site is considered Buddhist, it is revered by both Buddhists and Hindus. The stupa consists of a dome at the base; above the dome, there is a cubic structure with the eyes of Buddha looking in all four directions.[clarification needed] There are pentagonal Toran above each of the four sides, with statues engraved on them. Behind and above the torana there are thirteen tiers. Above all the tiers, there is a small space above which lies a gajur.
rewrite: Perched on a hill in the city's northwest, Swayambhu is an ancient Buddhist stupa and one of Nepal's oldest religious sites. Revered by both Buddhists and Hindus, its structure features a base dome. Above this rests a cube adorned with Buddha's all-seeing eyes on each of its four sides. Each side also has a pentagonal Toran bearing engraved statues. Rising behind these are thirteen tiers, topped by a small space and finally a gajur.

input: In 1887, the British Empire celebrated Victoria's Golden Jubilee. Victoria marked the fiftieth anniversary of her accession on 20 June with a banquet to which 50 kings and princes were invited. The following day, she participated in a procession and attended a thanksgiving service in Westminster Abbey. By this time, Victoria was once again extremely popular. Two days later on 23 June, she engaged two Indian Muslims as waiters, one of whom was Abdul Karim. He was soon promoted to "Munshi": teaching her Hindustani, and acting as a clerk. Her family and retainers were appalled, and accused Abdul Karim of spying for the Muslim Patriotic League, and biasing the Queen against the Hindus. Equerry Frederick Ponsonby (the son of Sir Henry) discovered that the Munshi had lied about his parentage, and reported to Lord Elgin, Viceroy of India, "the Munshi occupies very much the same position as John Brown used to do." Victoria dismissed their complaints as racial prejudice. Abdul Karim remained in her service until he returned to India with a pension on her death.
rewrite: In June of 1887, the British Empire commemorated Queen Victoria’s Golden Jubilee, honoring the fiftieth year of her reign. A banquet on June 20th welcomed fifty kings and princes, followed the next day by a grand procession and a thanksgiving service at Westminster Abbey. Victoria, by then restored to great public popularity, soon made a notable addition to her household. Just two days later, on June 23rd, she hired two Indian Muslims as attendants, including Abdul Karim. He was quickly elevated to the role of “Munshi,” tasked with teaching the Queen Hindustani and performing clerical duties. This appointment provoked dismay among her family and staff, who accused Karim of espionage for the Muslim Patriotic League and of prejudicing Victoria against Hindus. After Equerry Frederick Ponsonby found the Munshi had misrepresented his family background, he informed Lord Elgin, Viceroy of India, that Karim held a position akin to that once occupied by John Brown. The Queen, dismissing these objections as racial bias, kept Abdul Karim in her service until her death, after which he returned to India with a pension.

input: Some new immigrants arrived as refugees with no possessions and were housed in temporary camps known as ma'abarot; by 1952, over 200,000 immigrants were living in these tent cities. During this period, food, clothes and furniture had to be rationed in what became known as the Austerity Period. The need to solve the crisis led Ben-Gurion to sign a reparations agreement with West Germany that triggered mass protests by Jews angered at the idea that Israel could accept monetary compensation for the Holocaust.
rewrite: Arriving as destitute refugees, some new immigrants were placed in temporary camps called ma'abarot; these tent cities housed over 200,000 people by 1952. This era, known as the Austerity Period, required the rationing of food, clothing, and furniture. To resolve the crisis, Ben-Gurion signed a reparations agreement with West Germany. This act sparked mass protests from Jews outraged at the notion of Israel accepting monetary compensation for the Holocaust.

input: Asthma is thought to be caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors. Environmental factors include exposure to air pollution and allergens. Other potential triggers include medications such as aspirin and beta blockers. Diagnosis is usually based on the pattern of symptoms, response to therapy over time, and spirometry. Asthma is classified according to the frequency of symptoms, forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), and peak expiratory flow rate. It may also be classified as atopic or non-atopic where atopy refers to a predisposition toward developing a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction.
rewrite: Asthma arises from both genetic and environmental influences, including allergens and air pollution. Medications like aspirin and beta blockers can also act as triggers. Diagnosis typically relies on symptom patterns, response to treatment, and spirometry results. The condition is categorized by symptom frequency, forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), and peak expiratory flow rate. Additionally, it may be designated as atopic or non-atopic, with atopy indicating a tendency for type 1 hypersensitivity reactions.

input: There are 17 universities of technology in Germany with about 290,000 students enrolled. The four states of Bremen, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Saxony-Anhalt and Schleswig-Holstein are not operating a Technische Universität. Saxony and Lower Saxony have the highest counts of TUs, while in Saxony three out of four universities are universities of technology.
rewrite: Germany hosts 17 universities of technology, enrolling roughly 290,000 students. While Bremen, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Saxony-Anhalt, and Schleswig-Holstein have none, Saxony and Lower Saxony contain the most. Notably, three of Saxony's four universities are technical.

input: At the end of 2004, May and Taylor announced that they would reunite and return to touring in 2005 with Paul Rodgers (founder and former lead singer of Free and Bad Company). Brian May's website also stated that Rodgers would be "featured with" Queen as "Queen + Paul Rodgers", not replacing Mercury. The retired John Deacon would not be participating. In November 2004, Queen were among the inaugural inductees into the UK Music Hall of Fame, and the award ceremony was the first event at which Rodgers joined May and Taylor as vocalist.
rewrite: In November 2004, Queen was inducted into the UK Music Hall of Fame. At this inaugural ceremony, Paul Rodgers first performed as vocalist with Brian May and Roger Taylor. Later that year, May and Taylor announced a 2005 touring reunion, featuring Rodgers—founder and former lead singer of Free and Bad Company. They clarified this collaboration as "Queen + Paul Rodgers," with Rodgers appearing alongside the band, not as a replacement for Freddie Mercury. The retired John Deacon would not take part.

input: South West Africa became known as Namibia by the UN when the General Assembly changed the territory's name by Resolution 2372 (XXII) of 12 June 1968. In 1978 the UN Security Council passed UN Resolution 435 which planned a transition toward independence for Namibia. Attempts to persuade South Africa to agree to the plan's implementation were not successful until 1988 when the transition to independence finally started under a diplomatic agreement between South Africa, Angola and Cuba, with the USSR and the USA as observers, under which South Africa agreed to withdraw and demobilise its forces in Namibia. As a result, Cuba agreed to pull back its troops in southern Angola sent to support the MPLA in its war for control of Angola with UNITA.
rewrite: The United Nations General Assembly renamed South West Africa as Namibia through Resolution 2372 (XXII) on June 12, 1968. A decade later, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 435, outlining a plan for Namibian independence. However, implementing this plan required South Africa's agreement, which was not secured until 1988. A diplomatic accord was then reached involving South Africa, Angola, and Cuba, with the United States and the Soviet Union as observers. Under this agreement, South Africa committed to withdrawing and demobilizing its forces from Namibia. In a reciprocal move, Cuba agreed to withdraw its troops from southern Angola, where they had been supporting the MPLA in its conflict with UNITA. This finally initiated the transition to independence.

input: Von Neumann worked on lattice theory between 1937 and 1939. Von Neumann provided an abstract exploration of dimension in completed complemented modular topological lattices: "Dimension is determined, up to a positive linear transformation, by the following two properties. It is conserved by perspective mappings ("perspectivities") and ordered by inclusion. The deepest part of the proof concerns the equivalence of perspectivity with "projectivity by decomposition"—of which a corollary is the transitivity of perspectivity." Garrett Birkhoff writes: "John von Neumann's brilliant mind blazed over lattice theory like a meteor".
rewrite: Between 1937 and 1939, John von Neumann engaged in work on lattice theory. He offered an abstract investigation of dimension within completed complemented modular topological lattices, stating that dimension is ordered by inclusion and conserved by perspectivities, being determined up to a positive linear transformation by these properties. A key proof element establishes the equivalence of perspectivity with "projectivity by decomposition," leading to a corollary of perspectivity's transitivity. Garrett Birkhoff remarked that von Neumann's brilliant mind "blazed over lattice theory like a meteor."

input: From early in its development, ASCII was intended to be just one of several national variants of an international character code standard, ultimately published as ISO/IEC 646 (1972), which would share most characters in common but assign other locally useful characters to several code points reserved for "national use." However, the four years that elapsed between the publication of ASCII-1963 and ISO's first acceptance of an international recommendation during 1967 caused ASCII's choices for the national use characters to seem to be de facto standards for the world, causing confusion and incompatibility once other countries did begin to make their own assignments to these code points.
rewrite: Originally conceived as one among multiple national versions of an international standard—later formalized as ISO/IEC 646 in 1972—ASCII was designed to share a common core of characters while allowing localized symbols in designated "national use" code points. Yet the four-year gap between ASCII’s 1963 release and ISO’s initial international endorsement in 1967 led ASCII’s specific assignments for these points to become entrenched as de facto global norms. This created widespread confusion and incompatibility when other nations eventually began assigning their own characters to the same code positions.

input: A striking technical innovation of the Komnenian period was the production of very precious, miniature mosaic icons. In these icons the small tesserae (with sides of 1 mm or less) were set on wax or resin on a wooden panel. These products of extraordinary craftmanship were intended for private devotion. The Louvre Transfiguration is a very fine example from the late 12th century. The miniature mosaic of Christ in the Museo Nazionale at Florence illustrates the more gentle, humanistic conception of Christ which appeared in the 12th century.
rewrite: During the Komnenian period, a remarkable technical innovation emerged: the creation of highly precious, miniature mosaic icons. These were crafted for private devotion, displaying extraordinary skill. Artisans set minuscule tesserae—with sides measuring 1 mm or less—into wax or resin on wooden panels. A superb late-12th century example is the Louvre Transfiguration. Meanwhile, the miniature mosaic of Christ in Florence's Museo Nazionale reflects the more gentle, humanistic interpretation of Christ that developed in that era.

input: Modern Orthodoxy, as a stream of Orthodox Judaism represented by institutions such as the U.S. National Council for Young Israel, is pro-Zionist and thus places a high national, as well as religious, significance on the State of Israel, and its affiliates are, typically, Zionist in orientation. It also practices involvement with non-Orthodox Jews that extends beyond "outreach (Kiruv)" to continued institutional relations and cooperation; see further under Torah Umadda. Other "core beliefs" are a recognition of the value and importance of secular studies, a commitment to equality of education for both men and women, and a full acceptance of the importance of being able to financially support oneself and one's family.
rewrite: Represented by groups like the U.S. National Council for Young Israel, Modern Orthodoxy is a pro-Zionist stream of Orthodox Judaism. It attributes profound national and religious significance to the State of Israel, with its affiliates typically sharing this Zionist orientation. Core beliefs include valuing secular studies, supporting equal education for men and women, and emphasizing financial self-sufficiency for the family. Furthermore, it engages with non-Orthodox Jews beyond mere outreach, maintaining ongoing institutional relations and cooperation, as discussed under Torah Umadda.

input: Strasbourg is situated on the eastern border of France with Germany. This border is formed by the River Rhine, which also forms the eastern border of the modern city, facing across the river to the German town Kehl. The historic core of Strasbourg however lies on the Grande Île in the River Ill, which here flows parallel to, and roughly 4 kilometres (2.5 mi) from, the Rhine. The natural courses of the two rivers eventually join some distance downstream of Strasbourg, although several artificial waterways now connect them within the city.
rewrite: Strasbourg lies along France's eastern border with Germany, delineated by the River Rhine. The Rhine also serves as the modern city's eastern boundary, directly opposite the German town of Kehl. Historically, the city's core is located on the Grande Île in the River Ill, which runs parallel to the Rhine approximately 4 kilometres (2.5 mi) away. While the two rivers naturally converge downstream, they are also linked within Strasbourg by several artificial waterways.

input: As Universal's main product had always been low-budget film, it was one of the last major studios to have a contract with Technicolor. The studio did not make use of the three-strip Technicolor process until Arabian Nights (1942), starring Jon Hall and Maria Montez. The following year, Technicolor was also used in Universal's remake of their 1925 horror melodrama, Phantom of the Opera with Claude Rains and Nelson Eddy. With the success of their first two pictures, a regular schedule of high-budget, Technicolor films followed.
rewrite: Universal was among the last major studios to secure a Technicolor contract, largely due to its focus on low-budget films. It first employed the three-strip process for 1942's *Arabian Nights*, featuring Jon Hall and Maria Montez. The next year saw Technicolor used in the remake of the 1925 horror melodrama *Phantom of the Opera*, starring Claude Rains and Nelson Eddy. Encouraged by the success of these initial pictures, the studio then established a regular schedule of high-budget Technicolor productions.

input: Digimon started out as digital pets called "Digital Monsters", similar in style and concept to the Tamagotchi. It was planned by WiZ and released by Bandai on June 26, 1997. The toy began as the simple concept of a Tamagotchi mainly for boys. The V-Pet is similar to its predecessors, with the exceptions of being more difficult and being able to fight other Digimon v-pets. Every owner would start with a Baby Digimon, train it, evolve it, take care of it, and then have battles with other Digimon owners to see who was stronger. The Digimon pet had several evolution capabilities and abilities too, so many owners had different Digimon. In December, the second generation of Digital Monster was released, followed by a third edition in 1998.
rewrite: Originally conceived as a digital pet akin to the Tamagotchi but targeted primarily at boys, Digimon—short for "Digital Monsters"—was developed by WiZ and launched by Bandai on June 26, 1997. While resembling earlier virtual pets, the V-Pet version introduced greater difficulty and the innovative feature of battling other devices. Owners would raise a Baby Digimon through training, care, and evolution, then test its strength in competitions. With multiple possible evolutionary paths, each pet could develop unique abilities, leading to a wide variety of Digimon. A second generation debuted that December, with a third edition following in 1998.

input: The element was probably named by the alchemist Paracelsus after the German word Zinke (prong, tooth). German chemist Andreas Sigismund Marggraf is credited with discovering pure metallic zinc in 1746. Work by Luigi Galvani and Alessandro Volta uncovered the electrochemical properties of zinc by 1800. Corrosion-resistant zinc plating of iron (hot-dip galvanizing) is the major application for zinc. Other applications are in batteries, small non-structural castings, and alloys, such as brass. A variety of zinc compounds are commonly used, such as zinc carbonate and zinc gluconate (as dietary supplements), zinc chloride (in deodorants), zinc pyrithione (anti-dandruff shampoos), zinc sulfide (in luminescent paints), and zinc methyl or zinc diethyl in the organic laboratory.
rewrite: The major application for zinc is corrosion-resistant plating of iron through hot-dip galvanizing. It is also used in batteries, small non-structural castings, and alloys like brass. The element's name likely comes from the German word "Zinke" (meaning prong or tooth), as given by the alchemist Paracelsus. Pure metallic zinc was discovered in 1746 by German chemist Andreas Sigismund Marggraf. By 1800, Luigi Galvani and Alessandro Volta had revealed its electrochemical properties. Commonly used zinc compounds include dietary supplements (zinc carbonate, zinc gluconate), zinc chloride in deodorants, zinc pyrithione in anti-dandruff shampoos, zinc sulfide in luminescent paints, and zinc methyl or diethyl in organic laboratories.

input: During the 1920s and 1930s, British civil servants and politicians, looking back at the performance of the state during World War I, concluded that there was a need for greater co-ordination between the three Services that made up the armed forces of the United Kingdom—the British Army, the Royal Navy, and the Royal Air Force. The formation of a united ministry of defence was rejected by David Lloyd George's coalition government in 1921; but the Chiefs of Staff Committee was formed in 1923, for the purposes of inter-Service co-ordination. As rearmament became a concern during the 1930s, Stanley Baldwin created the position of Minister for Coordination of Defence. Lord Chatfield held the post until the fall of Neville Chamberlain's government in 1940; his success was limited by his lack of control over the existing Service departments and his limited political influence.
rewrite: Reflecting on the state’s role in World War I, British officials in the 1920s and 1930s identified a pressing need for improved coordination among the three armed services: the British Army, Royal Navy, and Royal Air Force. Although David Lloyd George’s coalition government rejected a unified defence ministry in 1921, the Chiefs of Staff Committee was established in 1923 to facilitate inter-Service cooperation. By the 1930s, as rearmament grew urgent, Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin introduced the role of Minister for Coordination of Defence. Lord Chatfield occupied this position until 1940, when Neville Chamberlain’s government fell. However, his effectiveness was constrained by minimal authority over the separate Service departments and his limited political influence.

input: Under contract from the U.S. Military, Matrox produced a combination computer/LaserDisc player for instructional purposes. The computer was a 286, the LaserDisc player only capable of reading the analog audio tracks. Together they weighed 43 lb (20 kg) and sturdy handles were provided in case two people were required to lift the unit. The computer controlled the player via a 25-pin serial port at the back of the player and a ribbon cable connected to a proprietary port on the motherboard. Many of these were sold as surplus by the military during the 1990s, often without the controller software. Nevertheless, it is possible to control the unit by removing the ribbon cable and connecting a serial cable directly from the computer's serial port to the port on the LaserDisc player.
rewrite: Commissioned by the U.S. Military, Matrox developed an instructional device that combined a computer with a LaserDisc player. The system featured a 286 computer and a LaserDisc player, the latter limited to reading analog audio tracks. Weighing 43 lb (20 kg), the unit included sturdy handles for lifting, potentially by two people. Control was achieved through a 25-pin serial port on the player and a ribbon cable linked to a proprietary motherboard port. In the 1990s, the military sold many units as surplus, frequently lacking the original controller software. However, control remains possible by detaching the ribbon cable and connecting a standard serial cable directly from the computer to the player's port.

input: In the United Kingdom, a bill is presented for royal assent after it has passed all the required stages in both the House of Commons and the House of Lords. Under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949, the House of Commons may, under certain circumstances, direct that a bill be presented for assent despite lack of passage by the House of Lords. Officially, assent is granted by the sovereign or by Lords Commissioners authorised to act by letters patent. It may be granted in parliament or outside parliament; in the latter case, each house must be separately notified before the bill takes effect.
rewrite: Once a bill has completed all necessary stages in both the House of Commons and the House of Lords, it is presented for royal assent in the United Kingdom. The sovereign or authorised Lords Commissioners acting via letters patent grant this assent officially. It may be given within or outside of parliament; if outside, each house must be separately notified before the bill becomes effective. Furthermore, under the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949, the House of Commons can, in specific circumstances, direct that a bill be presented for assent even without passage by the Lords.

input: In the late eighteenth- and early nineteenth-century Germany, three pioneer physical educators – Johann Friedrich GutsMuths (1759–1839) and Friedrich Ludwig Jahn (1778–1852) – created exercises for boys and young men on apparatus they had designed that ultimately led to what is considered modern gymnastics. Don Francisco Amorós y Ondeano, was born on February 19, 1770 in Valence and died on August 8, 1848 in Paris. He was a Spanish colonel, and the first person to introduce educative gymnastic in France. Jahn promoted the use of parallel bars, rings and high bar in international competition.
rewrite: During the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries in Germany, Johann Friedrich GutsMuths (1759–1839) and Friedrich Ludwig Jahn (1778–1852) pioneered physical education by designing apparatus and exercises for boys and young men, forming the foundation of modern gymnastics. Jahn specifically advocated for parallel bars, rings, and the high bar in international competitions. Meanwhile, Spanish colonel Don Francisco Amorós y Ondeano (born February 19, 1770, in Valence; died August 8, 1848, in Paris) first introduced educative gymnastics to France.

input: As the President, Tito had access to extensive (state-owned) property associated with the office, and maintained a lavish lifestyle. In Belgrade he resided in the official residence, the Beli dvor, and maintained a separate private home. The Brijuni islands were the site of the State Summer Residence from 1949 on. The pavilion was designed by Jože Plečnik, and included a zoo. Close to 100 foreign heads of state were to visit Tito at the island residence, along with film stars such as Elizabeth Taylor, Richard Burton, Sophia Loren, Carlo Ponti, and Gina Lollobrigida.
rewrite: As President, Tito enjoyed a lavish lifestyle supported by extensive state-owned property. His official residence in Belgrade was the Beli dvor, and he also kept a private home. From 1949, the State Summer Residence was located on the Brijuni islands. Designed by architect Jože Plečnik, its pavilion complex included a zoo. This island retreat hosted nearly 100 visiting foreign heads of state, as well as film stars like Elizabeth Taylor, Richard Burton, Sophia Loren, Carlo Ponti, and Gina Lollobrigrigida.

input: The tradition holds that Virgil was born in the village of Andes, near Mantua in Cisalpine Gaul. Analysis of his name has led to beliefs that he descended from earlier Roman colonists. Modern speculation ultimately is not supported by narrative evidence either from his own writings or his later biographers. Macrobius says that Virgil's father was of a humble background; however, scholars generally believe that Virgil was from an equestrian landowning family which could afford to give him an education. He attended schools in Cremona, Mediolanum, Rome and Naples. After considering briefly a career in rhetoric and law, the young Virgil turned his talents to poetry.
rewrite: Tradition states Virgil was born in Andes village near Mantua, within Cisalpine Gaul. His name suggests descent from early Roman colonists, though modern speculation lacks support from his own works or later biographers. Scholars generally hold that he came from an educated, landowning equestrian family, despite Macrobius noting his father's humble origins. Virgil studied in Cremona, Mediolanum, Rome, and Naples. Initially considering rhetoric and law, he ultimately devoted his talents to poetry.

input: Longstanding political tensions from the 27 year rule of William Tubman resulted in a military coup in 1980 that overthrew the leadership soon after his death, marking the beginning of political instability. Five years of military rule by the People's Redemption Council and five years of civilian rule by the National Democratic Party of Liberia were followed by the First and Second Liberian Civil Wars. These resulted in the deaths and displacement of more than half a million people and devastated Liberia's economy. A peace agreement in 2003 led to democratic elections in 2005. Recovery proceeds but about 85% of the population live below the international poverty line.
rewrite: Political instability began in 1980 with a military coup, which followed the 27-year rule of William Tubman and overthrew the leadership soon after his death. Subsequently, five years of rule by the military People's Redemption Council and five years under the civilian National Democratic Party of Liberia preceded the First and Second Liberian Civil Wars. These conflicts killed and displaced over half a million people, devastating the nation's economy. A 2003 peace agreement enabled democratic elections by 2005. Recovery continues, yet approximately 85% of Liberians live below the international poverty line.

input: The production for sulfidic zinc ores produces large amounts of sulfur dioxide and cadmium vapor. Smelter slag and other residues of process also contain significant amounts of heavy metals. About 1.1 million tonnes of metallic zinc and 130 thousand tonnes of lead were mined and smelted in the Belgian towns of La Calamine and Plombières between 1806 and 1882. The dumps of the past mining operations leach significant amounts of zinc and cadmium, and, as a result, the sediments of the Geul River contain significant amounts of heavy metals. About two thousand years ago emissions of zinc from mining and smelting totaled 10 thousand tonnes a year. After increasing 10-fold from 1850, zinc emissions peaked at 3.4 million tonnes per year in the 1980s and declined to 2.7 million tonnes in the 1990s, although a 2005 study of the Arctic troposphere found that the concentrations there did not reflect the decline. Anthropogenic and natural emissions occur at a ratio of 20 to 1.
rewrite: The processing of sulfidic zinc ores releases substantial sulfur dioxide and cadmium vapor, while smelter slag and other residues retain heavy metals. Between 1806 and 1882, mining and smelting in the Belgian towns of La Calamine and Plombières yielded approximately 1.1 million tonnes of zinc and 130 thousand tonnes of lead. Legacy mining dumps leach significant zinc and cadmium, contaminating Geul River sediments with heavy metals. Historically, around two thousand years ago, annual zinc emissions from mining and smelting reached 10 thousand tonnes. Following a ten-fold rise from 1850, emissions peaked at 3.4 million tonnes annually in the 1980s before falling to 2.7 million tonnes in the 1990s. However, a 2005 Arctic troposphere study noted concentrations there did not match this decline. Anthropogenic emissions outweigh natural sources by a ratio of twenty to one.

input: The first written account of a game played was on October 15, 1862, on the Montreal Cricket Grounds. It was between the First Battalion Grenadier Guards and the Second Battalion Scots Fusilier Guards resulting in a win by the Grenadier Guards 3 goals, 2 rouges to nothing.[citation needed] In 1864, at Trinity College, Toronto, F. Barlow Cumberland, Frederick A. Bethune, and Christopher Gwynn, one of the founders of Milton, Massachusetts, devised rules based on rugby football. The game gradually gained a following, with the Hamilton Football Club formed on November 3, 1869, (the oldest football club in Canada). Montreal formed a team April 8, 1872, Toronto was formed on October 4, 1873, and the Ottawa FBC on September 20, 1876.
rewrite: On October 15, 1862, the first recorded game was played at the Montreal Cricket Grounds. The First Battalion Grenadier Guards defeated the Second Battalion Scots Fusilier Guards with a score of 3 goals and 2 rouges to nothing. Later, in 1864, F. Barlow Cumberland, Frederick A. Bethune, and Christopher Gwynn—a founder of Milton, Massachusetts—established rugby-based rules at Trinity College in Toronto. As the sport's popularity grew, the Hamilton Football Club, Canada's oldest, was founded on November 3, 1869. Subsequent teams emerged in Montreal on April 8, 1872, Toronto on October 4, 1873, and Ottawa with the Ottawa FBC on September 20, 1876.

input: In 1982, Regis McKenna was brought in to shape the marketing and launch of the Macintosh. Later the Regis McKenna team grew to include Jane Anderson, Katie Cadigan and Andy Cunningham, who eventually led the Apple account for the agency. Cunningham and Anderson were the primary authors of the Macintosh launch plan. The launch of the Macintosh pioneered many different tactics that are used today in launching technology products, including the "multiple exclusive," event marketing (credited to John Sculley, who brought the concept over from Pepsi), creating a mystique around a product and giving an inside look into a product's creation.
rewrite: Regis McKenna oversaw the Macintosh's marketing and launch in 1982. His team later expanded to include Andy Cunningham, who would lead the Apple account, along with Jane Anderson and Katie Cadigan. Cunningham and Anderson authored the primary launch plan. This pioneering introduction established many tactics now standard in technology launches. These include the "multiple exclusive," event marketing—a concept credited to John Sculley, who brought it from Pepsi—as well as building product mystique and offering an inside view into its creation.

input: As of 2012, renewable energy plays a major role in the energy mix of many countries globally. Renewables are becoming increasingly economic in both developing and developed countries. Prices for renewable energy technologies, primarily wind power and solar power, continued to drop, making renewables competitive with conventional energy sources. Without a level playing field, however, high market penetration of renewables is still dependent on a robust promotional policies. Fossil fuel subsidies, which are far higher than those for renewable energy, remain in place and quickly need to be phased out.
rewrite: By 2012, renewable energy had become a significant part of the global energy supply for many nations. The costs for technologies like wind and solar power kept falling, enhancing their competitiveness with traditional sources. This growing economic viability is evident across both developed and developing countries. Nevertheless, achieving high market penetration for renewables still relies on strong supportive policies, as a level playing field is absent. Persistent and substantial fossil fuel subsidies, which dwarf those for clean energy, must be rapidly eliminated.

input: The region, as part of Lorraine, was part of the Holy Roman Empire, and then was gradually annexed by France in the 17th century, and formalized as one of the provinces of France. The Calvinist manufacturing republic of Mulhouse, known as Stadtrepublik Mülhausen, became a part of Alsace after a vote by its citizens on 4 January 1798. Alsace is frequently mentioned with and as part of Lorraine and the former duchy of Lorraine, since it was a vital part of the duchy, and later because German possession as the imperial province (Alsace-Lorraine, 1871–1918) was contested in the 19th and 20th centuries; France and Germany exchanged control of parts of Lorraine (including Alsace) four times in 75 years.
rewrite: Originally part of the Holy Roman Empire within Lorraine, the area was progressively annexed by France during the 17th century, becoming a formal French province. Following a citizen vote on January 4, 1798, the Calvinist manufacturing republic of Mulhouse, or Stadtrepublik Mülhausen, joined Alsace. Alsace is often referenced alongside Lorraine, not only because it was a crucial component of the former Duchy of Lorraine, but also due to the contested German possession of the imperial province Alsace-Lorraine from 1871 to 1918. This dispute led France and Germany to exchange control over these territories, including Alsace, four times within a span of 75 years during the 19th and 20th centuries.

input: Armenians have had a presence in the Armenian Highland for over four thousand years, since the time when Hayk, the legendary patriarch and founder of the first Armenian nation, led them to victory over Bel of Babylon. Today, with a population of 3.5 million, they not only constitute an overwhelming majority in Armenia, but also in the disputed region of Nagorno-Karabakh. Armenians in the diaspora informally refer to them as Hayastantsis (Հայաստանցի), meaning those that are from Armenia (that is, those born and raised in Armenia). They, as well as the Armenians of Iran and Russia speak the Eastern dialect of the Armenian language. The country itself is secular as a result of Soviet domination, but most of its citizens identify themselves as Apostolic Armenian Christian.
rewrite: For over four millennia, Armenians have inhabited the Armenian Highland, tracing their origins to the legendary patriarch Hayk, who led them to triumph over Bel of Babylon. While forming an overwhelming majority in Armenia’s 3.5 million population and in Nagorno-Karabakh, those born and raised in Armenia are informally called Hayastantsis by the diaspora. Eastern Armenian is spoken by these Hayastantsis, as well as by Armenians in Iran and Russia. Although the nation is secular due to its Soviet history, most citizens identify as Apostolic Armenian Christians.

input: According to a National Geographic article, the novel is so revered in Monroeville that people quote lines from it like Scripture; yet Harper Lee herself refused to attend any performances, because "she abhors anything that trades on the book's fame". To underscore this sentiment, Lee demanded that a book of recipes named Calpurnia's Cookbook not be published and sold out of the Monroe County Heritage Museum. David Lister in The Independent states that Lee's refusal to speak to reporters made them desire to interview her all the more, and her silence "makes Bob Dylan look like a media tart". Despite her discouragement, a rising number of tourists made to Monroeville a destination, hoping to see Lee's inspiration for the book, or Lee herself. Local residents call them "Mockingbird groupies", and although Lee was not reclusive, she refused publicity and interviews with an emphatic "Hell, no!"
rewrite: In Monroeville, the novel is held in such high esteem that, as a National Geographic article notes, people quote its lines like Scripture. Harper Lee, however, adamantly avoided the spotlight her fame created. She refused to attend any performances, reportedly because she despised anything capitalizing on the book's renown. This sentiment was further illustrated when Lee blocked the publication and sale of "Calpurnia's Cookbook" from the Monroe County Heritage Museum. According to David Lister in The Independent, her steadfast silence only intensified the media's desire for an interview, making "Bob Dylan look like a media tart" by comparison. Despite her discouragement, a growing stream of tourists, dubbed "Mockingbird groupies" by locals, flocked to Monroeville seeking the book's inspiration or a glimpse of Lee. Though not a recluse, she met such publicity with an emphatic "Hell, no!"

input: The Hanoverian king George II of Great Britain was passionately devoted to his family’s continental holdings, but his commitments in Germany were counterbalanced by the demands of the British colonies overseas. If war against France for colonial expansion was to be resumed, then Hanover had to be secured against Franco-Prussian attack. France was very much interested in colonial expansion and was willing to exploit the vulnerability of Hanover in war against Great Britain, but it had no desire to divert forces to central Europe for Prussia's interest.
rewrite: King George II of Great Britain was deeply committed to his German territory of Hanover. However, this continental focus was balanced by the pressing needs of the British colonies abroad. To resume war with France for colonial gains, securing Hanover from Franco-Prussian assault was essential. France, equally eager for colonial expansion, was prepared to target Hanover's weakness against Britain. Yet, it had no wish to deploy its forces into central Europe merely for Prussia's benefit.

input: Meanwhile, with the advent and popularity of Internet-based distribution of files in lossily-compressed audio formats such as MP3, sales of CDs began to decline in the 2000s. For example, between 2000 - 2008, despite overall growth in music sales and one anomalous year of increase, major-label CD sales declined overall by 20%, although independent and DIY music sales may be tracking better according to figures released 30 March 2009, and CDs still continue to sell greatly. As of 2012, CDs and DVDs made up only 34 percent of music sales in the United States. In Japan, however, over 80 percent of music was bought on CDs and other physical formats as of 2015.
rewrite: The rise of Internet-based file sharing and lossy audio formats like MP3 drove a decline in CD sales during the 2000s. For instance, major-label CD sales fell by 20% between 2000 and 2008, despite overall growth in music sales and one year of increase. Figures from March 30, 2009, suggested independent and DIY sales fared better, and CDs still sold in significant volume. By 2012, CDs and DVDs accounted for just 34% of U.S. music sales. In contrast, as of 2015, over 80% of music in Japan was purchased on CDs and other physical formats.

input: Following the Norman Conquest in 1066, Southampton became the major port of transit between the then capital of England, Winchester, and Normandy. Southampton Castle was built in the 12th century and by the 13th century Southampton had become a leading port, particularly involved in the import of French wine in exchange for English cloth and wool.
rewrite: After the Norman Conquest of 1066, Southampton emerged as the primary transit port linking Winchester, then England's capital, to Normandy. The 12th-century construction of Southampton Castle preceded its rise to a leading 13th-century port, heavily engaged in trading English cloth and wool for French wine.

input: Air defence in naval tactics, especially within a carrier group, is often built around a system of concentric layers with the aircraft carrier at the centre. The outer layer will usually be provided by the carrier's aircraft, specifically its AEW&C aircraft combined with the CAP. If an attacker is able to penetrate this layer, then the next layers would come from the surface-to-air missiles carried by the carrier's escorts; the area-defence missiles, such as the RIM-67 Standard, with a range of up to 100 nmi, and the point-defence missiles, like the RIM-162 ESSM, with a range of up to 30 nmi. Finally, virtually every modern warship will be fitted with small-calibre guns, including a CIWS, which is usually a radar-controlled Gatling gun of between 20mm and 30mm calibre capable of firing several thousand rounds per minute.
rewrite: In naval tactics, particularly for a carrier group, air defence is typically structured as concentric layers centered on the aircraft carrier. The outermost layer relies on the carrier's aircraft, specifically AEW&C planes combined with the Combat Air Patrol (CAP). Should an intruder breach this, the next layers involve surface-to-air missiles from escort ships. These include long-range area-defence missiles like the RIM-67 Standard, with ranges reaching 100 nautical miles, and shorter-range point-defence missiles such as the RIM-162 ESSM, effective up to 30 nautical miles. As a final defensive measure, nearly all modern warships are equipped with small-calibre guns. This includes a Close-In Weapon System (CIWS), typically a radar-guided Gatling gun of 20mm to 30mm calibre that can fire thousands of rounds per minute.

input: Throughout history there have been a series of lingua francas in the area to allow for better communication. The dialects spoken in Hangzhou, Shaoxing, and Ningbo have taken on this role historically. Since the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949, Mandarin, which is not mutually intelligible with any of the local dialects, has been promoted as the standard language of communication throughout China. As a result, most of the population now can, to some degree, speak and comprehend Mandarin and can code-switch when necessary. A majority of the population educated since 1978 can speak Mandarin. Urban residents tend to be more fluent in Mandarin than rural people. Nevertheless, a Zhejiang accent is detectable in almost everyone from the area communicating in Mandarin, and the home dialect remains an important part of the everyday lives and cultural identities of most Zhejiang residents.
rewrite: Historically, the dialects of Hangzhou, Shaoxing, and Ningbo have each served as a lingua franca within the region to facilitate communication. Following the establishment of the People's Republic of China in 1949, the national promotion of Mandarin—a language not mutually intelligible with local dialects—established it as the standard across China. Consequently, a majority of the population now possesses at least a basic ability to speak and understand Mandarin, with most educated since 1978 being speakers. Urban residents generally achieve greater fluency than those in rural areas. Code-switching is common when needed. Despite this widespread adoption, a distinctive Zhejiang accent is nearly always present when locals speak Mandarin. Furthermore, the native dialect continues to play a crucial role in daily life and in preserving the cultural identity for most residents of Zhejiang.

input: The major opponent of Freemasonry was the Roman Catholic Church, so that in countries with a large Catholic element, such as France, Italy, Spain, and Mexico, much of the ferocity of the political battles involve the confrontation between what Davies calls the reactionary Church and enlightened Freemasonry. Even in France, Masons did not act as a group. American historians, while noting that Benjamin Franklin and George Washington were indeed active Masons, have downplayed the importance of Freemasonry in causing the American Revolution because the Masonic order was non-political and included both Patriots and their enemy the Loyalists.
rewrite: Freemasonry's primary adversary was the Roman Catholic Church. Consequently, in nations with significant Catholic populations—like France, Italy, Spain, and Mexico—political strife was often intensely shaped by this clash, described as between the reactionary Church and enlightened Freemasonry. Notably, even in France, Masons did not operate collectively. In the American context, historians acknowledge the Masonic activity of figures like Benjamin Franklin and George Washington but minimize its revolutionary impact, as the non-political order included both Patriots and Loyalists.

input: A German ethnicity emerged in the course of the Middle Ages, ultimately as a result of the formation of the kingdom of Germany within East Francia and later the Holy Roman Empire, beginning in the 9th century. The process was gradual and lacked any clear definition, and the use of exonyms designating "the Germans" develops only during the High Middle Ages. The title of rex teutonicum "King of the Germans" is first used in the late 11th century, by the chancery of Pope Gregory VII, to describe the future Holy Roman Emperor of the German Nation Henry IV. Natively, the term ein diutscher ("a German") is used for the people of Germany from the 12th century.
rewrite: The emergence of a German ethnicity was a gradual medieval process, stemming from the kingdom of Germany's formation within East Francia and the later Holy Roman Empire from the 9th century onward. This development lacked clear definition. Exonyms for "the Germans" only arose during the High Middle Ages. Pope Gregory VII's chancery first employed the title *rex teutonicum*, "King of the Germans," for the future Emperor Henry IV in the late 11th century. Natively, the term *ein diutscher* ("a German") for the people of Germany came into use from the 12th century.

input: The rise of port cities saw the clustering of populations caused by the development of steamships and railroads. Urbanization increased from 1700 to 1922, with towns and cities growing. Improvements in health and sanitation made them more attractive to live and work in. Port cities like Salonica, in Greece, saw its population rise from 55,000 in 1800 to 160,000 in 1912 and İzmir which had a population of 150,000 in 1800 grew to 300,000 by 1914. Some regions conversely had population falls – Belgrade saw its population drop from 25,000 to 8,000 mainly due to political strife.
rewrite: Between 1700 and 1922, urbanization advanced as towns and cities expanded. This growth was partly driven by advancements in health and sanitation, which made urban areas more desirable. The development of steamships and railroads further concentrated populations, particularly in port cities. For example, Salonica, Greece, grew from 55,000 people in 1800 to 160,000 by 1912, while İzmir increased from 150,000 to 300,000 between 1800 and 1914. Conversely, some areas declined; Belgrade’s population fell from 25,000 to 8,000, largely due to political strife.

input: The state is well known for its handicrafts. The carpets, leather works, shawls, metalware, woodwork and paintings are worth appreciating. Pashmina shawls are a product that is highly in demand in Himachal and all over the country. Himachali caps are famous art work of the people. Extreme cold winters of Himachal necessitated wool weaving. Nearly every household in Himachal owns a pit-loom. Wool is considered as pure and is used as a ritual cloth. The well-known woven object is the shawl, ranging from fine pashmina to the coarse desar. Kullu is famous for its shawls with striking patterns and vibrant colours. Kangra and Dharamshala are famous for Kangra miniature paintings.
rewrite: Renowned for its handicrafts, this state produces highly valued items such as carpets, leather goods, metalware, woodwork, and paintings. Among these, Pashmina shawls are in great demand both locally and nationally. The famous Himachali caps represent another skilled art form. Due to the region's harsh winters, wool weaving became essential, and nearly every household possesses a pit-loom. Wool is regarded as pure and serves as a ritual cloth. Shawls are the most prominent woven product, varying from fine pashmina to coarse desar. Kullu is celebrated for its vibrant, patterned shawls, while Kangra and Dharamshala are noted for Kangra miniature paintings.

input: On 16 June 2006, it was announced that Everton had entered into talks with Knowsley Council and Tesco over the possibility of building a new 55,000 seat stadium, expandable to over 60,000, in Kirkby. The club took the unusual move of giving its supporters a say in the club's future by holding a ballot on the proposal, finding a split of 59% to 41% in favour.
