In verbs, 1st person present indicative desinence is -e (∅ in verbs of the 2nd and 3rd conjugation), or -o.
E.g. parle, tem, sent (Valencian); parlo, temo, sento (Northwestern). In verbs, 1st person present indicative desinence is -o, -i or ∅ in all conjugations.
E.g. parlo (Central), parl (Balearic), parli (Northern), ('I speak').
rewrite: For the first person present indicative, verbs take the ending -e (or -∅ in the 2nd/3rd conjugations), as in Valencian "parle." Elsewhere, endings include -o, -i, or -∅, such as Central "parlo," Balearic "parl," or Northern "parli."

input: One of the most prominent movies filmed in Alaska is MGM's Eskimo/Mala The Magnificent, starring Alaska Native Ray Mala. In 1932 an expedition set out from MGM's studios in Hollywood to Alaska to film what was then billed as "The Biggest Picture Ever Made." Upon arriving in Alaska, they set up "Camp Hollywood" in Northwest Alaska, where they lived during the duration of the filming. Louis B. Mayer spared no expense in spite of the remote location, going so far as to hire the chef from the Hotel Roosevelt in Hollywood to prepare meals.
rewrite: MGM’s “Eskimo/Mala The Magnificent,” starring Alaska Native Ray Mala, stands among the most notable films shot in Alaska. In 1932, an expedition departed Hollywood for Alaska to create what was promoted as “The Biggest Picture Ever Made.” Establishing “Camp Hollywood” in Northwest Alaska, the crew lived there throughout production. Despite the remote setting, studio head Louis B. Mayer spared no expense—even hiring the chef from Hollywood’s Hotel Roosevelt to prepare meals.

input: In an essay on Sephardi Jewry, Daniel Elazar at the Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs summarized the demographic history of Ashkenazi Jews in the last thousand years, noting that at the end of the 11th century, 97% of world Jewry was Sephardic and 3% Ashkenazi; by the end of XVI century, the: 'Treaty on the redemption of captives', by Gracian of the God's Mother, Mercy Priest, who was imprisoned by Turks, cites a Tunisian Hebrew, made captive when arriving to Gaeta, who aided others with money, named: 'Simon Escanasi', in the mid-17th century, "Sephardim still outnumbered Ashkenazim three to two", but by the end of the 18th century, "Ashkenazim outnumbered Sephardim three to two, the result of improved living conditions in Christian Europe versus the Ottoman Muslim world." By 1931, Ashkenazi Jews accounted for nearly 92% of world Jewry. These factors are sheer demography showing the migration patterns of Jews from Southern and Western Europe to Central and Eastern Europe.
rewrite: In an essay addressing Sephardi Jewry, Daniel Elazar of the Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs outlines the shifting demographics between Ashkenazi and Sephardi Jews over centuries. At the close of the 11th century, Sephardim comprised 97% of world Jewry, with Ashkenazim at just 3%. A mid-17th century reference, found in Gracian of the God's Mother's 'Treaty on the redemption of captives', mentions a captive Tunisian Hebrew named 'Simon Escanasi' aiding others in Gaeta, reflecting the era's conditions. By that period, Sephardim still maintained a majority, outnumbering Ashkenazim three to two. However, a reversal occurred by the late 18th century, with Ashkenazim coming to outnumber Sephardim by the same ratio. Elazar attributes this shift to improved living conditions in Christian Europe compared to the Ottoman Muslim world. By 1931, Ashkenazi Jews represented nearly 92% of all Jews globally. These demographic trends illustrate the broader migration of Jewish populations from Southern and Western Europe toward Central and Eastern Europe.

input: The cellular phone carrier group Open Mobile Terminal Platform (OMTP) in 2007 endorsed micro-USB as the standard connector for data and power on mobile devices In addition, on 22 October 2009 the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) has also announced that it had embraced micro-USB as the Universal Charging Solution its "energy-efficient one-charger-fits-all new mobile phone solution," and added: "Based on the Micro-USB interface, UCS chargers also include a 4-star or higher efficiency rating—​​up to three times more energy-efficient than an unrated charger."
rewrite: In 2007, the Open Mobile Terminal Platform (OMTP) group established micro-USB as the standard connector for mobile device data and power. Later, on October 22, 2009, the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) also adopted micro-USB for its Universal Charging Solution, describing it as an energy-efficient, universal charger for new phones. The ITU further noted that these UCS chargers, using the Micro-USB interface, achieve a high-efficiency rating—making them up to three times more energy-efficient than unrated chargers.

input: Just as artist and inventor Leonardo da Vinci – partaking of the zeitgeist though not himself a humanist – advocated study of human anatomy, nature, and weather to enrich Renaissance works of art, so Spanish-born humanist Juan Luis Vives (c. 1493–1540) advocated observation, craft, and practical techniques to improve the formal teaching of Aristotelian philosophy at the universities, helping to free them from the grip of Medieval Scholasticism. Thus, the stage was set for the adoption of an approach to natural philosophy, based on empirical observations and experimentation of the physical universe, making possible the advent of the age of scientific inquiry that followed the Renaissance.
rewrite: While not a humanist himself, Leonardo da Vinci embraced his era’s spirit by urging the study of anatomy, nature, and weather to enhance Renaissance art. Similarly, the Spanish humanist Juan Luis Vives (c. 1493–1540) promoted observation, craft, and practical methods to reform the university teaching of Aristotelian philosophy, loosening the hold of Medieval Scholasticism. This helped establish a new foundation for natural philosophy, one rooted in empirical observation and experimentation of the physical world. These developments paved the way for the age of scientific inquiry that emerged after the Renaissance.

input: The Cubist contribution to the 1912 Salon d'Automne created scandal regarding the use of government owned buildings, such as the Grand Palais, to exhibit such artwork. The indignation of the politician Jean Pierre Philippe Lampué made the front page of Le Journal, 5 October 1912. The controversy spread to the Municipal Council of Paris, leading to a debate in the Chambre des Députés about the use of public funds to provide the venue for such art. The Cubists were defended by the Socialist deputy, Marcel Sembat.
rewrite: The 1912 Salon d'Automne's Cubist display sparked scandal over using state-owned venues like the Grand Palais. This indignation, highlighted by politician Jean Pierre Philippe Lampué on the front page of *Le Journal* (October 5, 1912), reached the Paris Municipal Council. It prompted a parliamentary debate in the Chambre des Députés concerning public funding for such exhibitions. In defense of the Cubists stood Socialist deputy Marcel Sembat.

input: According to Eurostat, the EU statistical agency, in 2012 the Commune of Paris was the most densely populated city in the European Union, with 21,616 people per square kilometre within the city limits (the NUTS-3 statistical area), ahead of Inner London West, which had 10,374 people per square kilometre. According to the same census, three departments bordering Paris, Hauts-de-Seine, Seine-Saint-Denis and Val-de-Marne, had population densities of over ten thousand people per square kilometre, ranking among the ten most densely populated areas of the EU.
rewrite: In 2012, the Commune of Paris was the EU's most densely populated city, reports Eurostat. Its city limits held 21,616 people per square kilometre, surpassing Inner London West's 10,374. The same census noted that three bordering Paris departments—Hauts-de-Seine, Seine-Saint-Denis, and Val-de-Marne—each exceeded ten thousand people per square kilometre. Consequently, these areas ranked among the ten most densely populated in the European Union.

input: Baptists, like other Christians, are defined by doctrine—some of it common to all orthodox and evangelical groups and a portion of it distinctive to Baptists. Through the years, different Baptist groups have issued confessions of faith—without considering them to be creeds—to express their particular doctrinal distinctions in comparison to other Christians as well as in comparison to other Baptists. Most Baptists are evangelical in doctrine, but Baptist beliefs can vary due to the congregational governance system that gives autonomy to individual local Baptist churches. Historically, Baptists have played a key role in encouraging religious freedom and separation of church and state.
rewrite: Baptists share core Christian doctrines with other orthodox and evangelical groups, while also holding certain beliefs unique to themselves. Their distinct doctrinal positions, both in contrast to other Christians and to fellow Baptists, have often been outlined in confessions of faith—documents they do not treat as binding creeds. A congregational governance system, granting autonomy to each local church, leads to variations in Baptist beliefs, though most remain evangelical in doctrine. Historically, the tradition has been crucial in advocating for religious freedom and the separation of church and state.

input: 20th century developments in plant biochemistry have been driven by modern techniques of organic chemical analysis, such as spectroscopy, chromatography and electrophoresis. With the rise of the related molecular-scale biological approaches of molecular biology, genomics, proteomics and metabolomics, the relationship between the plant genome and most aspects of the biochemistry, physiology, morphology and behaviour of plants can be subjected to detailed experimental analysis. The concept originally stated by Gottlieb Haberlandt in 1902 that all plant cells are totipotent and can be grown in vitro ultimately enabled the use of genetic engineering experimentally to knock out a gene or genes responsible for a specific trait, or to add genes such as GFP that report when a gene of interest is being expressed. These technologies enable the biotechnological use of whole plants or plant cell cultures grown in bioreactors to synthesise pesticides, antibiotics or other pharmaceuticals, as well as the practical application of genetically modified crops designed for traits such as improved yield.
rewrite: Modern techniques like spectroscopy, chromatography, and electrophoresis have propelled plant biochemistry forward in the 20th century. Detailed experimental analysis of the connections between the plant genome and its biochemistry, physiology, morphology, and behavior is now possible, especially with the advent of molecular-scale approaches including molecular biology, genomics, proteomics, and metabolomics. A foundational concept, first proposed by Gottlieb Haberlandt in 1902, is that all plant cells are totipotent and can be cultivated in vitro. This principle ultimately enabled genetic engineering, allowing scientists to delete genes responsible for specific traits or to insert reporter genes like GFP to monitor expression. Consequently, whole plants or plant cell cultures in bioreactors can be used biotechnologically to produce pesticides, antibiotics, and other pharmaceuticals. These technologies also underpin the development of genetically modified crops engineered for traits such as enhanced yield.

input: The Industrial Revolution in the Midlands and Northern England spelled the end for most of Somerset's cottage industries. Farming continued to flourish, however, and the Bath and West of England Society for the Encouragement of Agriculture, Arts, Manufactures and Commerce was founded in 1777 to improve farming methods. Despite this, 20 years later John Billingsley conducted a survey of the county's agriculture in 1795 and found that agricultural methods could still be improved. Coal mining was an important industry in north Somerset during the 18th and 19th centuries, and by 1800 it was prominent in Radstock. The Somerset Coalfield reached its peak production by the 1920s, but all the pits have now been closed, the last in 1973. Most of the surface buildings have been removed, and apart from a winding wheel outside Radstock Museum, little evidence of their former existence remains. Further west, the Brendon Hills were mined for iron ore in the late 19th century; this was taken by the West Somerset Mineral Railway to Watchet Harbour for shipment to the furnaces at Ebbw Vale.
rewrite: The cottage industries that once thrived in Somerset largely met their demise due to the Industrial Revolution’s rise in the Midlands and Northern England. Farming, by contrast, remained prosperous. To advance agricultural methods, the Bath and West of England Society for the Encouragement of Agriculture, Arts, Manufactures and Commerce was established in 1777. Yet when John Billingsley surveyed the county’s agriculture in 1795, he concluded that significant improvements were still possible. Meanwhile, coal mining grew into a vital industry in north Somerset during the 18th and 19th centuries, becoming especially prominent around Radstock by 1800. Although the Somerset Coalfield peaked in the 1920s, every pit eventually closed, the last one in 1973. Today, most surface structures are gone, leaving little trace beyond a winding wheel outside Radstock Museum. In the west, the Brendon Hills yielded iron ore in the late 19th century, transported via the West Somerset Mineral Railway to Watchet Harbour for shipment to Ebbw Vale’s furnaces.

input: The Macintosh's minimal memory became apparent, even compared with other personal computers in 1984, and could not be expanded easily. It also lacked a hard disk drive or the means to easily attach one. Many small companies sprang up to address the memory issue. Suggestions revolved around either upgrading the memory to 512 KB or removing the computer's 16 memory chips and replacing them with larger-capacity chips, a tedious and difficult operation. In October 1984, Apple introduced the Macintosh 512K, with quadruple the memory of the original, at a price of US$3,195. It also offered an upgrade for 128k Macs that involved replacing the logic board.
rewrite: Even in 1984, the Macintosh's limited memory was notable compared to other personal computers, and it could not be readily expanded. It also had no hard disk drive or a simple way to add one. To solve the memory problem, numerous small companies emerged. Their proposals typically involved either boosting the memory to 512 KB or undertaking the arduous task of swapping out the 16 original memory chips for higher-capacity ones. In response, Apple released the Macintosh 512K in October 1984, featuring four times the original memory for $3,195. They also provided an upgrade for 128k models that required replacing the logic board.

input: Nevertheless, whether and to what degree any of these types of intermediaries have secondary liability is the subject of ongoing litigation. The decentralised structure of peer-to-peer networks, in particular, does not sit easily with existing laws on online intermediaries' liability. The BitTorrent protocol established an entirely decentralised network architecture in order to distribute large files effectively. Recent developments in peer-to-peer technology towards more complex network configurations are said to have been driven by a desire to avoid liability as intermediaries under existing laws.
rewrite: The BitTorrent protocol created a fully decentralized network architecture to efficiently distribute large files. Ongoing litigation continues to debate whether, and to what extent, such intermediaries bear secondary liability. The decentralized nature of peer-to-peer networks, in particular, fits poorly with current laws on online intermediary liability. It is argued that recent advances toward more complex peer-to-peer configurations are motivated by a wish to avoid this legal liability.

input: In January 1989, Madonna signed an endorsement deal with soft-drink manufacturer, Pepsi. In one of her Pepsi commercials, she debuted her song "Like a Prayer". The corresponding music video featured many Catholic symbols such as stigmata and cross burning, and a dream of making love to a saint, leading the Vatican to condemn the video. Religious groups sought to ban the commercial and boycott Pepsi products. Pepsi revoked the commercial and canceled her sponsorship contract. The song was included on Madonna's fourth studio album, Like a Prayer, which was co-written and co-produced by Patrick Leonard and Stephen Bray. Madonna received positive feedback for the album, with Rolling Stone writing that it was "as close to art as pop music gets". Like a Prayer peaked at number one on the Billboard 200 and sold 15 million copies worldwide, with 4 million copies sold in the U.S. alone. Six singles were released from the album, including "Like a Prayer", which reached number one, and "Express Yourself" and "Cherish", both peaking at number two. By the end of the 1980s, Madonna was named as the "Artist of the Decade" by MTV, Billboard and Musician magazine.
rewrite: In January 1989, Madonna entered into an endorsement agreement with Pepsi. A commercial for the soft-drink giant served as the debut platform for her song "Like a Prayer." However, the song's official video, filled with Catholic imagery like stigmata and burning crosses along with a dream sequence involving a saint, provoked condemnation from the Vatican. This led religious groups to call for a ban on the commercial and a boycott of Pepsi products, prompting the company to pull the advertisement and terminate Madonna's sponsorship deal. The track was featured on her fourth studio album, *Like a Prayer*, a collaborative effort with co-writers and co-producers Patrick Leonard and Stephen Bray. The album earned critical acclaim, described by Rolling Stone as being "as close to art as pop music gets." It reached number one on the Billboard 200, achieving worldwide sales of 15 million copies, including 4 million in the United States. From the album, six singles were released; "Like a Prayer" hit number one, while "Express Yourself" and "Cherish" both peaked at number two. As the decade closed, Madonna was honored as the "Artist of the Decade" by MTV, Billboard, and Musician magazine.

input: Bioscience is the overall major in which undergraduate students who are interested in general well-being take in college. Immunology is a branch of bioscience for undergraduate programs but the major gets specified as students move on for graduate program in immunology. The aim of immunology is to study the health of humans and animals through effective yet consistent research, (AAAAI, 2013). The most important thing about being immunologists is the research because it is the biggest portion of their jobs.
rewrite: Bioscience serves as a broad undergraduate major for students focused on general well-being. Within it, immunology is a specialized branch that becomes more defined in graduate programs. According to the AAAAI (2013), immunology aims to study human and animal health through effective, consistent research. For immunologists, research constitutes the most significant part of their work, forming the core of their professional responsibilities.

input: The Western family includes Parthian (Arsacid Pahlavi) and Middle Persian, while Bactrian, Sogdian, Khwarezmian, Saka, and Old Ossetic (Scytho-Sarmatian) fall under the Eastern category. The two languages of the Western group were linguistically very close to each other, but quite distinct from their eastern counterparts. On the other hand, the Eastern group was an areal entity whose languages retained some similarity to Avestan. They were inscribed in various Aramaic-derived alphabets which had ultimately evolved from the Achaemenid Imperial Aramaic script, though Bactrian was written using an adapted Greek script.
rewrite: The Eastern Iranian languages comprise Bactrian, Sogdian, Khwarezmian, Saka, and Old Ossetic (Scytho-Sarmatian). These formed an areal group, maintaining certain similarities to Avestan. They were typically written in alphabets derived from Aramaic, which themselves evolved from the Achaemenid Imperial Aramaic script; an exception is Bactrian, which used a modified Greek alphabet. In contrast, the Western group includes Parthian and Middle Persian. These two languages were linguistically very close to each other but distinctly different from the Eastern languages.

input: The climate of New Delhi is a monsoon-influenced humid subtropical climate (Köppen Cwa) with high variation between summer and winter in terms of both temperature and rainfall. The temperature varies from 46 °C (115 °F) in summers to around 0 °C (32 °F) in winters. The area's version of a humid subtropical climate is noticeably different from many other cities with this climate classification in that it features long and very hot summers, relatively dry and mild winters, a monsoonal period, and dust storms. Summers are long, extending from early April to October, with the monsoon season occurring in the middle of the summer. Winter starts in November and peaks in January. The annual mean temperature is around 25 °C (77 °F); monthly daily mean temperatures range from approximately 14 to 34 °C (57 to 93 °F). New Delhi's highest temperature ever recorded is 49.1 °C (120.4 °F) while the lowest temperature ever recorded is −3.2 °C (26.2 °F). Those for Delhi metropolis stand at 49.9 °C (121.8 °F) and −3.2 °C (26.2 °F) respectively. The average annual rainfall is 784 millimetres (30.9 in), most of which is during the monsoons in July and August.
rewrite: New Delhi experiences a humid subtropical climate under the Köppen Cwa classification, marked by extreme seasonal contrasts in temperature and precipitation. Temperatures swing dramatically from summer highs around 46 °C (115 °F) down to winter lows near 0 °C (32 °F). While sharing a broad climate classification with other cities, New Delhi’s pattern is distinct: it endures prolonged, intensely hot summers, relatively dry and mild winters, a pronounced monsoon phase, and dust storms. The summer season is extensive, lasting from early April through October, with the monsoon period embedded within it. Winter commences in November and reaches its coldest point in January. The city's annual mean temperature is approximately 25 °C (77 °F), with monthly averages ranging from about 14 °C (57 °F) to 34 °C (93 °F). Recorded extremes show a highest temperature of 49.1 °C (120.4 °F) and a lowest of −3.2 °C (26.2 °F); the broader Delhi metropolis has seen 49.9 °C (121.8 °F) and the same −3.2 °C low. Rainfall averages 784 millimetres (30.9 in) yearly, the majority falling during the monsoon months of July and August.

input: The majority of insects hatch from eggs. The fertilization and development takes place inside the egg, enclosed by a shell (chorion) that consists of maternal tissue. In contrast to eggs of other arthropods, most insect eggs are drought resistant. This is because inside the chorion two additional membranes develop from embryonic tissue, the amnion and the serosa. This serosa secretes a cuticle rich in chitin that protects the embryo against desiccation. In Schizophora however the serosa does not develop, but these flies lay their eggs in damp places, such as rotting matter. Some species of insects, like the cockroach Blaptica dubia, as well as juvenile aphids and tsetse flies, are ovoviviparous. The eggs of ovoviviparous animals develop entirely inside the female, and then hatch immediately upon being laid. Some other species, such as those in the genus of cockroaches known as Diploptera, are viviparous, and thus gestate inside the mother and are born alive.:129, 131, 134–135 Some insects, like parasitic wasps, show polyembryony, where a single fertilized egg divides into many and in some cases thousands of separate embryos.:136–137 Insects may be univoltine, bivoltine or multivoltine, i.e. they may have one, two or many broods (generations) in a year.
rewrite: Most insects begin life by hatching from eggs. Within a protective shell called the chorion, which is formed from maternal tissue, fertilization and embryonic development occur. Unlike many other arthropod eggs, those of most insects are resistant to drying out. This key adaptation arises from two membranes—the amnion and the serosa—that form from embryonic tissue inside the chorion. The serosa specifically produces a chitin-rich cuticle that shields the embryo from desiccation. An exception is found in Schizophora flies, which lack a serosa but instead deposit their eggs in moist environments like decaying material. Reproduction varies significantly among insects. Some, including the cockroach *Blaptica dubia*, along with juvenile aphids and tsetse flies, are ovoviviparous; their eggs develop fully inside the female and hatch immediately upon laying. Others, such as cockroaches in the genus *Diploptera*, are viviparous, gestating within the mother and being born alive. Additionally, insects like certain parasitic wasps exhibit polyembryony, where one fertilized egg divides into numerous, sometimes thousands, of separate embryos. Reproductive cycles also differ, with insects being classified as univoltine, bivoltine, or multivoltine based on whether they have one, two, or many generations in a single year.

input: Seattle is located between the saltwater Puget Sound (an arm of the Pacific Ocean) to the west and Lake Washington to the east. The city's chief harbor, Elliott Bay, is part of Puget Sound, which makes the city an oceanic port. To the west, beyond Puget Sound, are the Kitsap Peninsula and Olympic Mountains on the Olympic Peninsula; to the east, beyond Lake Washington and the eastside suburbs, are Lake Sammamish and the Cascade Range. Lake Washington's waters flow to Puget Sound through the Lake Washington Ship Canal (consisting of two man-made canals, Lake Union, and the Hiram M. Chittenden Locks at Salmon Bay, ending in Shilshole Bay on Puget Sound).
rewrite: Flanked by Puget Sound to the west and Lake Washington to the east, Seattle is an oceanic port whose chief harbor, Elliott Bay, lies within the Sound. Westward beyond the Sound stand the Kitsap Peninsula and Olympic Mountains. Eastward, past the lake and its suburbs, are Lake Sammamish and the Cascade Range. The waters of Lake Washington reach Puget Sound via the Lake Washington Ship Canal. This system includes two artificial canals, Lake Union, and the Hiram M. Chittenden Locks at Salmon Bay, ultimately discharging into Shilshole Bay.

input: Among the parish churches are Saints John (Baptist and Evangelist), rebuilt in 1368, whose dome, decorated by Palonino, contains some of the best frescoes in Spain; El Templo (the Temple), the ancient church of the Knights Templar, which passed into the hands of the Order of Montesa and was rebuilt in the reigns of Ferdinand VI and Charles III; the former convent of the Dominicans, at one time the headquarters of the Capital General, the cloister of which has a beautiful Gothic wing and the chapter room, large columns imitating palm trees; the Colegio del Corpus Christi, which is devoted to the Blessed Sacrament, and in which perpetual adoration is carried on; the Jesuit college, which was destroyed in 1868 by the revolutionary Committee of the Popular Front, but later rebuilt; and the Colegio de San Juan (also of the Society), the former college of the nobles, now a provincial institute for secondary instruction.
rewrite: The parish churches include Saints John (Baptist and Evangelist), reconstructed in 1368. Its dome, adorned by Palonino, holds some of Spain's finest frescoes. Also notable is El Templo, the ancient church of the Knights Templar that later transferred to the Order of Montesa and was rebuilt under Ferdinand VI and Charles III. There is the former Dominican convent, once the headquarters of the Capital General, featuring a beautiful Gothic wing in its cloister and a chapter room with large columns shaped like palm trees. Dedicated to the Blessed Sacrament, the Colegio del Corpus Christi maintains perpetual adoration. The Jesuit college, destroyed in 1868 by the revolutionary Committee of the Popular Front, was later reconstructed. Finally, the Colegio de San Juan, also of the Society, was originally the nobles' college and now serves as a provincial secondary institute.

input: Detroit's protracted decline has resulted in severe urban decay and thousands of empty buildings around the city. Some parts of Detroit are so sparsely populated that the city has difficulty providing municipal services. The city has considered various solutions, such as demolishing abandoned homes and buildings; removing street lighting from large portions of the city; and encouraging the small population in certain areas to move to more populated locations. While some have estimated 20,000 stray dogs roam the city, studies have shown the true number to be around 1,000-3,000. Roughly half of the owners of Detroit's 305,000 properties failed to pay their 2011 tax bills, resulting in about $246 million in taxes and fees going uncollected, nearly half of which was due to Detroit; the rest of the money would have been earmarked for Wayne County, Detroit Public Schools, and the library system.
rewrite: Detroit’s extended period of decline has led to widespread urban decay, leaving thousands of structures vacant. Municipal services are challenging to maintain in some severely depopulated areas. Proposed measures have included demolishing abandoned properties, eliminating street lighting across large districts, and incentivizing residents of sparsely populated zones to relocate. Regarding the stray dog population, earlier estimates of 20,000 have been corrected by studies indicating a more accurate range of 1,000 to 3,000. Tax delinquency further compounds the city’s troubles; in 2011, nearly half of Detroit’s 305,000 property owners did not pay taxes, leaving approximately $246 million uncollected. Of that total, close to half was owed to the city itself, with the remainder destined for Wayne County, Detroit Public Schools, and the library system.

input: Cyberspace Support is foundational, continuous, or responsive operations ensuring information integrity and availability in, through, and from Air Force-controlled infrastructure and its interconnected analog and digital portion of the battle space. Inherent in this mission is the ability to establish, extend, secure, protect, and defend in order to sustain assigned networks and missions. This includes protection measures against supply chain components plus critical C2 networks/communications links and nuclear C2 networks. The cyberspace support mission incorporates CNE and CND techniques. It incorporates all elements of Air Force Network Operations, information transport, enterprise management, and information assurance, and is dependent on ISR and all-source intelligence.
rewrite: Cyberspace Support involves foundational, continuous, or responsive operations that guarantee information integrity and availability across Air Force-controlled infrastructure and its connected analog and digital battle space areas. This mission inherently requires the capacity to establish, extend, secure, protect, and defend in order to maintain assigned networks and missions. Protection extends to supply chain components, critical command and control networks, communications links, and nuclear command and control networks. Incorporating computer network exploitation and defense techniques, it encompasses all facets of Air Force Network Operations, information transport, enterprise management, and information assurance, while relying on intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and all-source intelligence.

input: In Canada, "college" generally refers to a two-year, non-degree-granting institution, while "university" connotes a four-year, degree-granting institution. Universities may be sub-classified (as in the Macleans rankings) into large research universities with many PhD granting programs and medical schools (for example, McGill University); "comprehensive" universities that have some PhDs but aren't geared toward research (such as Waterloo); and smaller, primarily undergraduate universities (such as St. Francis Xavier).
rewrite: In Canada, "college" typically means a two-year institution that does not grant degrees, whereas "university" indicates a four-year, degree-granting school. Universities themselves are often categorized: large research institutions with medical schools and many PhD programs (e.g., McGill); "comprehensive" universities with some PhDs but less research focus (like Waterloo); and smaller, primarily undergraduate universities (such as St. Francis Xavier).

input: Baroque instruments included some instruments from the earlier periods (e.g., the hurdy-gurdy and recorder) and a number of new instruments (e.g, the cello, contrabass and fortepiano). Some instruments from previous eras fell into disuse, such as the shawm and the wooden cornet. The key Baroque instruments for strings included the violin, viol, viola, viola d'amore, cello, contrabass, lute, theorbo (which often played the basso continuo parts), mandolin, cittern, Baroque guitar, harp and hurdy-gurdy. Woodwinds included the Baroque flute, Baroque oboe, rackett, recorder and the bassoon. Brass instruments included the cornett, natural horn, Baroque trumpet, serpent and the trombone. Keyboard instruments included the clavichord, tangent piano, the fortepiano (an early version of the piano), the harpsichord and the pipe organ. Percussion instruments included the timpani, snare drum, tambourine and the castanets.
rewrite: Baroque music employed a diverse array of instruments, blending older models with new inventions. While some earlier instruments like the shawm and wooden cornet fell from favor, others such as the recorder and hurdy-gurdy remained in use. Significant innovations included the cello, contrabass, and fortepiano. The string section was particularly rich, featuring the violin, viol, viola, lute, theorbo (frequent in basso continuo), mandolin, cittern, Baroque guitar, harp, and the viola d'amore. Woodwinds encompassed the Baroque flute, oboe, recorder, bassoon, and rackett. Brass instruments included the cornett, natural horn, Baroque trumpet, serpent, and trombone. Keyboard options ranged from the clavichord and harpsichord to the pipe organ, tangent piano, and early fortepiano. Percussion instruments like timpani, snare drum, tambourine, and castanets were also utilized.

So, for example, the sentence "Snow is white" is true if and only if snow is white. Although many philosophers have interpreted, and continue to interpret, Tarski's theory as a deflationary theory, Popper refers to it as a theory in which "is true" is replaced with "corresponds to the facts". He bases this interpretation on the fact that examples such as the one described above refer to two things: assertions and the facts to which they refer. He identifies Tarski's formulation of the truth conditions of sentences as the introduction of a "metalinguistic predicate" and distinguishes the following cases:
rewrite: This theory holds that both sentences and the conditions for their truth belong to a metalanguage. For instance, the statement "Snow is white" is true precisely when snow is, in fact, white. While numerous philosophers have viewed—and still view—Tarski’s theory as deflationary, Popper instead describes it as replacing "is true" with "corresponds to the facts." He grounds this reading in examples like the one above, which involve two elements: assertions and the facts they reference. Popper further identifies Tarski’s formulation of truth conditions as introducing a "metalinguistic predicate," and he distinguishes between the following cases.

input: In Britain, Willett's 1907 proposal used the term daylight saving, but by 1911 the term summer time replaced daylight saving time in draft legislation. Continental Europe uses similar phrases, such as Sommerzeit in Germany, zomertijd in Dutch-speaking regions, kesäaika in Finland, horario de verano or hora de verano in Spain and heure d'été in France, whereas in Italy the term is ora legale, that is, legal time (legally enforced time) as opposed to "ora solare", solar time, in winter.
rewrite: Willett's 1907 British proposal introduced "daylight saving," yet by 1911 draft legislation adopted "summer time." Across continental Europe, similar terms prevail: Germany's *Sommerzeit*, Dutch *zomertijd*, Finland's *kesäaika*, and in Spain *horario/hora de verano*. France uses *heure d'été*, while Italy employs *ora legale* (legal or enforced time), contrasting with winter's solar time, *ora solare*.

input: Long a major population center and site of worldwide automobile manufacturing, Detroit has suffered a long economic decline produced by numerous factors. Like many industrial American cities, Detroit reached its population peak in the 1950 census. The peak population was 1.8 million people. Following suburbanization, industrial restructuring, and loss of jobs (as described above), by the 2010 census, the city had less than 40 percent of that number, with just over 700,000 residents. The city has declined in population in each census since 1950.
rewrite: Once a populous hub of global auto manufacturing, Detroit has faced prolonged economic decline due to multiple causes. Its population peaked at 1.8 million in the 1950 census, typical of many U.S. industrial cities. However, suburbanization, industrial restructuring, and job losses reduced the figure to just over 700,000 by 2010—less than 40% of the peak. Since 1950, each census has recorded a further drop in residents.

input: Theories given for the success of Southerners on Idol have been: more versatility with musical genres, as the Southern U.S. is home to several music genre scenes; not having as many opportunities to break into the pop music business; text-voting due to the South having the highest percentage of cell-phone only households; and the strong heritage of music and singing, which is notable in the Bible Belt, where it is in church that many people get their start in public singing. Others also suggest that the Southern character of these contestants appeal to the South, as well as local pride. According to season five winner Taylor Hicks, who is from the state of Alabama, "People in the South have a lot of pride ... So, they're adamant about supporting the contestants who do well from their state or region."
rewrite: Explanations for the consistent success of Southern contestants on American Idol point to several factors. One is the region's deep musical heritage, particularly within the Bible Belt, where many first experience public singing in church. This background may contribute to greater versatility across musical genres, supported by the South's vibrant scenes for various styles of music. Additionally, some theorize that having fewer conventional avenues into the pop industry motivates these performers. The South's high rate of cell-phone-only households is also cited as boosting text-voting numbers. The appeal of the Southern character and strong regional pride further galvanizes support. As Alabama native and season five winner Taylor Hicks noted, "People in the South have a lot of pride ... So, they're adamant about supporting the contestants who do well from their state or region."

input: Clothing protects against many things that might injure the uncovered human body. Clothes protect people from the elements, including rain, snow, wind, and other weather, as well as from the sun. However, clothing that is too sheer, thin, small, tight, etc., offers less protection. Clothes also reduce risk during activities such as work or sport. Some clothing protects from specific environmental hazards, such as insects, noxious chemicals, weather, weapons, and contact with abrasive substances. Conversely, clothing may protect the environment from the clothing wearer, as with doctors wearing medical scrubs.
rewrite: Clothing serves as a vital shield, guarding the body from potential injuries and various elements like rain, snow, wind, and sun exposure. It also lowers risks in work or sports activities. Certain garments provide specialized protection against specific hazards, including insects, chemicals, weapons, or abrasive materials. However, overly sheer, thin, or tight items offer diminished safety. Conversely, attire such as medical scrubs can protect the environment from the wearer.

input: The most important state-owned companies headquartered in Montevideo are: AFE (railways), ANCAP (Energy), Administracion Nacional de Puertos (Ports), ANTEL (telecommunications), BHU (savings and loan), BROU (bank), BSE (insurance), OSE (water & sewage), UTE (electricity). These companies operate under public law, using a legal entity defined in the Uruguayan Constitution called Ente Autonomo ("autonomous entity"). The government also owns part of other companies operating under private law, such as those owned wholly or partially by the CND (National Development Corporation).
rewrite: Montevideo hosts key state-owned firms like AFE (railways), ANCAP (energy), Administracion Nacional de Puertos (ports), ANTEL (telecommunications), BHU (savings and loan), BROU (bank), BSE (insurance), OSE (water & sewage), and UTE (electricity). These operate as Entes Autonomos, autonomous entities under public law per Uruguay's Constitution. Additionally, the government holds stakes in companies under private law, including those fully or partly owned by the National Development Corporation (CND).

input: The value of the Bell patent was acknowledged throughout the world, and patent applications were made in most major countries, but when Bell had delayed the German patent application, the electrical firm of Siemens & Halske (S&H) managed to set up a rival manufacturer of Bell telephones under their own patent. The Siemens company produced near-identical copies of the Bell telephone without having to pay royalties. The establishment of the International Bell Telephone Company in Brussels, Belgium in 1880, as well as a series of agreements in other countries eventually consolidated a global telephone operation. The strain put on Bell by his constant appearances in court, necessitated by the legal battles, eventually resulted in his resignation from the company.[N 19]
rewrite: The global significance of the Bell patent led to applications in most major nations. However, a delay in filing within Germany allowed the firm Siemens & Halske (S&H) to establish a rival manufacturer under their own patent. Producing near-identical copies of the Bell telephone, S&H avoided royalty payments. A worldwide telephone operation was later consolidated through the founding of the International Bell Telephone Company in Brussels (1880) and subsequent international agreements. The relentless legal battles, demanding Bell's frequent court appearances, placed immense strain on him. This ultimately necessitated his resignation from the company.

input: The change is evident in the reports of influential British travellers to the Balkans. In 1894, Sir Henry Norman, 1st Baronet, a journalist, travelled to the Far East, afterwards writing a book called The Peoples and Politics of the Far East, which came out in 1895. By "Far East" he meant Siberia, China, Japan, Korea, Siam and Malaya. As the book was a big success, he was off to the Balkan states with his wife in 1896 to develop detail for a sequel, The People and Politics of the Near East, which Scribners planned to publish in 1897. Mrs. Norman, a writer herself, wrote glowing letters of the home and person of Mme. Zakki, "the wife of a Turkish cabinet minister," who, she said, was a cultivated woman living in a country home full of books. As for the natives of the Balkans, they were "a semi-civilized people."
rewrite: Influential British travelers to the Balkans clearly documented a shift in perspective. Sir Henry Norman, 1st Baronet, a journalist, journeyed to the Far East in 1894. His subsequent book, *The Peoples and Politics of the Far East* (1895), covering Siberia, China, Japan, Korea, Siam, and Malaya, was a major success. This prompted a trip with his wife to the Balkan states in 1896 to gather material for a planned sequel, *The People and Politics of the Near East*, scheduled for 1897 by Scribners. Mrs. Norman, also a writer, sent enthusiastic letters describing Mme. Zakki, "the wife of a Turkish cabinet minister," as a cultivated woman in a book-filled country home. In contrast, she referred to the Balkan natives as "a semi-civilized people."

input: Kim Philby, a Soviet double agent, was a correspondent for the newspaper in Spain during the Spanish Civil War of the late 1930s. Philby was admired for his courage in obtaining high-quality reporting from the front lines of the bloody conflict. He later joined MI6 during World War II, was promoted into senior positions after the war ended, then eventually defected to the Soviet Union in 1963.
rewrite: During the Spanish Civil War in the late 1930s, Kim Philby served as a newspaper correspondent in Spain while secretly acting as a Soviet double agent. He earned admiration for his courageous, high-quality frontline reporting from the bloody conflict. After later joining MI6 in World War II and rising to senior postwar positions, he ultimately defected to the Soviet Union in 1963.

input: In 1978, Sewall Wright suggested that human populations that have long inhabited separated parts of the world should, in general, be considered different subspecies by the usual criterion that most individuals of such populations can be allocated correctly by inspection. Wright argued that it does not require a trained anthropologist to classify an array of Englishmen, West Africans, and Chinese with 100% accuracy by features, skin color, and type of hair despite so much variability within each of these groups that every individual can easily be distinguished from every other. However, it is customary to use the term race rather than subspecies for the major subdivisions of the human species as well as for minor ones.
rewrite: In 1978, Sewall Wright proposed that distinct human populations, having long resided in separate regions, would generally qualify as different subspecies under the standard criterion: most individuals from these groups can be accurately identified by observation. He noted that even without anthropological training, one could correctly classify Englishmen, West Africans, and Chinese with complete accuracy based on features like skin color and hair type, despite significant individual variation within each group. Nevertheless, for both major and minor subdivisions of humanity, the term "race" is conventionally used instead of "subspecies."

input: Philadelphia Gas Works (PGW), overseen by the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission, is the nation's largest municipally owned natural gas utility. It serves over 500,000 homes and businesses in the Philadelphia area. Founded in 1836, the company came under city ownership in 1987 and has been providing the majority of gas distributed within city limits. In 2014, the Philadelphia City Council refused to conduct hearings on a $1.86 billion sale of PGW, part of a two-year effort that was proposed by the mayor. The refusal led to the prospective buyer terminating its offer.
rewrite: Overseeing Philadelphia Gas Works (PGW) is the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission. As the largest municipally owned natural gas utility in the nation, PGW serves more than 500,000 homes and businesses locally. Founded in 1836, it came under city ownership in 1987 and now distributes most of the gas within Philadelphia. A proposed $1.86 billion sale, part of a two-year effort by the mayor, was halted in 2014 when the City Council refused to hold hearings. This refusal caused the prospective buyer to withdraw its offer.

input: Hokkien originated from Quanzhou. After the Opium War in 1842, Xiamen (Amoy) became one of the major treaty ports to be opened for trade with the outside world. From mid-19th century onwards, Xiamen slowly developed to become the political and economical center of the Hokkien-speaking region in China. This caused Amoy dialect to gradually replace the position of dialect variants from Quanzhou and Zhangzhou. From mid-19th century until the end of World War II, western diplomats usually learned Amoy Hokkien as the preferred dialect if they were to communicate with the Hokkien-speaking populace in China or South-East Asia. In the 1940s and 1950s, Taiwan also held Amoy Hokkien as its standard and tended to incline itself towards Amoy dialect.
rewrite: Originating in Quanzhou, Hokkien saw a shift in its linguistic center following the 1842 Opium War, when Xiamen (Amoy) was opened as a treaty port. From the mid-19th century, Xiamen evolved into the political and economic hub of the Hokkien-speaking region in China. Consequently, the Amoy dialect gradually supplanted the earlier variants from Quanzhou and Zhangzhou. From that period until the end of World War II, Western diplomats aiming to communicate with Hokkien speakers in China or Southeast Asia typically learned Amoy Hokkien as the standard. This preference extended to Taiwan in the 1940s and 1950s, which also adopted Amoy Hokkien as its benchmark, leaning toward this dialect.

input: Nonverbal communication describes the process of conveying meaning in the form of non-word messages. Examples of nonverbal communication include haptic communication, chronemic communication, gestures, body language, facial expression, eye contact, and how one dresses. Nonverbal communication also relates to intent of a message. Examples of intent are voluntary, intentional movements like shaking a hand or winking, as well as involuntary, such as sweating. Speech also contains nonverbal elements known as paralanguage, e.g. rhythm, intonation, tempo, and stress. There may even be a pheromone component. Research has shown that up to 55% of human communication may occur through non-verbal facial expressions, and a further 38% through paralanguage. It affects communication most at the subconscious level and establishes trust. Likewise, written texts include nonverbal elements such as handwriting style, spatial arrangement of words and the use of emoticons to convey emotion.
rewrite: Nonverbal communication conveys meaning through messages that do not rely on words. This encompasses gestures, body language, facial expressions, eye contact, dress, haptic (touch) and chronemic (time) signals. Intent plays a role, ranging from voluntary acts like a handshake to involuntary ones like sweating. Speech contains nonverbal paralanguage—rhythm, intonation, tempo, and stress—and pheromones may also be a component. Research indicates up to 55% of human communication can occur via facial expressions, with an additional 38% through paralanguage. Operating largely at the subconscious level, it is crucial for establishing trust. Even written texts involve nonverbal elements, such as handwriting style, spatial arrangement, and emoticons, which convey emotional nuance.

input: According to an October 1998 report by the United States Bureau of Land Management, approximately 65% of Alaska is owned and managed by the U.S. federal government as public lands, including a multitude of national forests, national parks, and national wildlife refuges. Of these, the Bureau of Land Management manages 87 million acres (35 million hectares), or 23.8% of the state. The Arctic National Wildlife Refuge is managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service. It is the world's largest wildlife refuge, comprising 16 million acres (6.5 million hectares).
rewrite: A 1998 report from the U.S. Bureau of Land Management states that about 65% of Alaska is federally owned public land, encompassing many national forests, parks, and wildlife refuges. The Bureau itself oversees 87 million acres, or 23.8% of the state. Within this system is the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge. Managed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, it spans 16 million acres, making it the largest wildlife refuge in the world.

input: In September 2003, retired four-star general Wesley Clark announced his intention to run in the presidential primary election for the Democratic Party nomination. His campaign focused on themes of leadership and patriotism; early campaign ads relied heavily on biography. His late start left him with relatively few detailed policy proposals. This weakness was apparent in his first few debates, although he soon presented a range of position papers, including a major tax-relief plan. Nevertheless, the Democrats did not flock to support his campaign.
rewrite: Retired four-star general Wesley Clark declared his candidacy for the Democratic presidential nomination in September 2003. Emphasizing leadership and patriotism, his early ads leaned on biographical themes. A late entry meant he initially offered few detailed policies, a shortcoming evident in his early debates. He later issued various position papers, featuring a significant tax-relief plan. Despite this, the candidate failed to attract substantial support from Democratic voters.

input: YouTube is a global video-sharing website headquartered in San Bruno, California, United States. The service was created by three former PayPal employees in February 2005. In November 2006, it was bought by Google for US$1.65 billion. YouTube now operates as one of Google's subsidiaries. The site allows users to upload, view, rate, share, and comment on videos, and it makes use of WebM, H.264/MPEG-4 AVC, and Adobe Flash Video technology to display a wide variety of user-generated and corporate media video. Available content includes video clips, TV clips, music videos, movie trailers, and other content such as video blogging, short original videos, and educational videos.
rewrite: Headquartered in San Bruno, California, YouTube is a worldwide video-sharing platform. Founded in February 2005 by three former PayPal employees, it was acquired by Google for $1.65 billion in November 2006 and now operates as a Google subsidiary. Users can upload, view, rate, share, and comment on videos. The platform utilizes WebM, H.264/MPEG-4 AVC, and Adobe Flash Video technology to display a broad array of content. This includes user-generated and corporate media, such as video clips, TV clips, music videos, movie trailers, video blogs, short original videos, and educational videos.

input: The Mantoux tuberculin skin test is often used to screen people at high risk for TB. Those who have been previously immunized may have a false-positive test result. The test may be falsely negative in those with sarcoidosis, Hodgkin's lymphoma, malnutrition, and most notably, active tuberculosis. Interferon gamma release assays (IGRAs), on a blood sample, are recommended in those who are positive to the Mantoux test. These are not affected by immunization or most environmental mycobacteria, so they generate fewer false-positive results. However, they are affected by M. szulgai, M. marinum, and M. kansasii. IGRAs may increase sensitivity when used in addition to the skin test, but may be less sensitive than the skin test when used alone.
rewrite: The Mantoux tuberculin skin test is a common screening tool for individuals at high risk of tuberculosis. However, it can yield a false-positive result in people who have been previously immunized. Conversely, false-negative results may occur in cases of sarcoidosis, Hodgkin's lymphoma, malnutrition, and notably, active TB. For those with a positive Mantoux test, interferon gamma release assays (IGRAs) on a blood sample are advised. Unlike the skin test, IGRAs are not influenced by prior immunization or most environmental mycobacteria, leading to fewer false positives, though they can be affected by M. szulgai, M. marinum, and M. kansasii. When combined with the skin test, IGRAs may enhance sensitivity, but used alone, they can be less sensitive.

input: The characteristic forms that were to define Gothic architecture grew out of Romanesque architecture and developed at several different geographic locations, as the result of different influences and structural requirements. While barrel vaults and groin vaults are typical of Romanesque architecture, ribbed vaults were used in the naves of two Romanesque churches in Caen, Abbey of Saint-Étienne and Abbaye aux Dames in 1120. Another early example is the nave and apse area of the Cathedral of Cefalù in 1131. The ribbed vault over the north transept at Durham Cathedral in England, built from 1128 to 1133, is probably earlier still and was the first time pointed arches were used in a high vault.
rewrite: Gothic architecture emerged from Romanesque forms, shaped by varied geographic influences and structural needs. While Romanesque design favored barrel and groin vaults, early ribbed vaults appeared in the naves of two Caen churches—the Abbey of Saint-Étienne and Abbaye aux Dames—around 1120. Another early instance is found in the nave and apse of Cefalù Cathedral in 1131. Yet an even earlier example is the ribbed vault over the north transept at Durham Cathedral, constructed between 1128 and 1133, which also marked the first use of pointed arches in a high vault.

input: While Southeast Asia is rich in flora and fauna, Southeast Asia is facing severe deforestation which causes habitat loss for various endangered species such as orangutan and the Sumatran tiger. Predictions have been made that more than 40% of the animal and plant species in Southeast Asia could be wiped out in the 21st century. At the same time, haze has been a regular occurrence. The two worst regional hazes were in 1997 and 2006 in which multiple countries were covered with thick haze, mostly caused by "slash and burn" activities in Sumatra and Borneo. In reaction, several countries in Southeast Asia signed the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution to combat haze pollution.
rewrite: Southeast Asia's rich biodiversity is under severe threat from widespread deforestation, leading to habitat loss for endangered species like the orangutan and Sumatran tiger. Predictions indicate over 40% of the region's plant and animal species could be lost this century. Compounding this, haze has become a regular crisis, with the worst episodes in 1997 and 2006 blanketing multiple countries. This pollution primarily stems from "slash and burn" agriculture in Sumatra and Borneo. In response, several Southeast Asian nations have adopted the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution to address the issue.

input: The city generally has a climate with warm days followed by cool nights and mornings. Unpredictable weather is expected, given that temperatures can drop to 1 °C (34 °F) or less during the winter. During a 2013 cold front, the winter temperatures of Kathmandu dropped to −4 °C (25 °F), and the lowest temperature was recorded on January 10, 2013, at −9.2 °C (15.4 °F). Rainfall is mostly monsoon-based (about 65% of the total concentrated during the monsoon months of June to August), and decreases substantially (100 to 200 cm (39 to 79 in)) from eastern Nepal to western Nepal. Rainfall has been recorded at about 1,400 millimetres (55.1 in) for the Kathmandu valley, and averages 1,407 millimetres (55.4 in) for the city of Kathmandu. On average humidity is 75%. The chart below is based on data from the Nepal Bureau of Standards & Meteorology, "Weather Meteorology" for 2005. The chart provides minimum and maximum temperatures during each month. The annual amount of precipitation was 1,124 millimetres (44.3 in) for 2005, as per monthly data included in the table above. The decade of 2000-2010 saw highly variable and unprecedented precipitation anomalies in Kathmandu. This was mostly due to the annual variation of the southwest monsoon.[citation needed] For example, 2003 was the wettest year ever in Kathmandu, totalling over 2,900 mm (114 in) of precipitation due to an exceptionally strong monsoon season. In contrast, 2001 recorded only 356 mm (14 in) of precipitation due to an extraordinarily weak monsoon season.
rewrite:
Kathmandu’s climate typically features warm days followed by cool nights and mornings. Winter can bring unpredictable conditions, with temperatures sometimes falling to 1 °C (34 °F) or lower. Notably, during a 2013 cold front, the city’s winter temperatures plunged to −4 °C (25 °F), and the all-time low of −9.2 °C (15.4 °F) was recorded on January 10, 2013. Rainfall in the region is predominantly monsoon-driven, with approximately 65% of the annual total concentrated between June and August. Precipitation decreases significantly from eastern to western Nepal, ranging from 100 to 200 cm (39 to 79 in). For the Kathmandu valley, rainfall measurements average around 1,400 millimetres (55.1 in), while the city itself sees a mean of 1,407 millimetres (55.4 in). Average humidity stands at 75%.

The chart below, derived from 2005 data by the Nepal Bureau of Standards & Meteorology in “Weather Meteorology,” displays monthly minimum and maximum temperatures. That year, the total annual precipitation was 1,124 millimetres (44.3 in), as detailed in the accompanying table. The decade from 2000 to 2010 witnessed highly variable and unprecedented precipitation anomalies in Kathmandu, primarily due to annual fluctuations in the southwest monsoon. For instance, 2003 became the wettest year on record, with over 2,900 mm (114 in) of rainfall following an exceptionally strong monsoon. In stark contrast, 2001 registered just 356 mm (14 in) of precipitation due to an unusually weak monsoon season.

input: In 1657, Oliver Cromwell granted the English East India Company a charter to govern Saint Helena and the following year the company decided to fortify the island and colonise it with planters. The first governor, Captain John Dutton, arrived in 1659, making Saint Helena one of Britain's oldest colonies outside North America and the Caribbean. A fort and houses were built. After the Restoration of the English monarchy in 1660, the East India Company received a royal charter giving it the sole right to fortify and colonise the island. The fort was renamed James Fort and the town Jamestown, in honour of the Duke of York, later James II of England.
rewrite: In 1657, Oliver Cromwell issued a charter authorizing the English East India Company to govern Saint Helena. The company began fortifying and colonizing the island with planters the next year. Captain John Dutton, arriving as the first governor in 1659, established Saint Helena as one of Britain's earliest colonies beyond North America and the Caribbean, overseeing the construction of a fort and houses. Following the monarchy's Restoration in 1660, a royal charter reaffirmed the Company's exclusive right to fortify and colonize the island. The fort and town were then renamed James Fort and Jamestown to honor the Duke of York, the future James II.

input: Although theoretically a collegial body operating through consensus building, Gaddafi dominated the RCC, although some of the others attempted to constrain what they saw as his excesses. Gaddafi remained the government's public face, with the identities of the other RCC members only being publicly revealed on 10 January 1970. All young men from (typically rural) working and middle-class backgrounds, none had university degrees; in this way they were distinct from the wealthy, highly educated conservatives who previously governed the country.
rewrite: Gaddafi dominated the RCC, despite its theoretical reliance on consensus, even as some members tried to curb his perceived excesses. He served as the public face of the government, while his colleagues' identities remained secret until 10 January 1970. All were young men from working or middle-class rural backgrounds without university degrees, setting them apart from the wealthy, educated conservatives who had ruled before.

input: Scarab beetles held religious and cultural symbolism in Old Egypt, Greece and some shamanistic Old World cultures. The ancient Chinese regarded cicadas as symbols of rebirth or immortality. In Mesopotamian literature, the epic poem of Gilgamesh has allusions to Odonata which signify the impossibility of immortality. Amongst the Aborigines of Australia of the Arrernte language groups, honey ants and witchety grubs served as personal clan totems. In the case of the 'San' bush-men of the Kalahari, it is the praying mantis which holds much cultural significance including creation and zen-like patience in waiting.:9
rewrite: In ancient China, cicadas symbolized rebirth or immortality. Meanwhile, scarab beetles carried religious and cultural meaning in Old Egypt, Greece, and certain shamanistic Old World cultures. The Gilgamesh epic from Mesopotamia references Odonata, alluding to the unattainability of eternal life. For Australia's Arrernte Aboriginal people, honey ants and witchety grubs acted as personal clan totems. Among the Kalahari's 'San' bush-men, the praying mantis holds great cultural significance, associated with creation and a zen-like patience.

input: In the 7th century, the Frankish merchant Samo, who supported the Slavs fighting their Avar rulers, became the ruler of the first known Slav state in Central Europe, which, however, most probably did not outlive its founder and ruler. This provided the foundation for subsequent Slavic states to arise on the former territory of this realm with Carantania being the oldest of them. Very old also are the Principality of Nitra and the Moravian principality (see under Great Moravia). In this period, there existed central Slavic groups and states such as the Balaton Principality, but the subsequent expansion of the Magyars, as well as the Germanisation of Austria, separated the northern and southern Slavs. The First Bulgarian Empire was founded in 681, the Slavic language Old Bulgarian became the main and official of the empire in 864. Bulgaria was instrumental in the spread of Slavic literacy and Christianity to the rest of the Slavic world.
rewrite: During the 7th century, Frankish merchant Samo rose to lead the first recorded Slav state in Central Europe after aiding Slavs against their Avar rulers. This polity likely dissolved upon his death, yet it established a foundation for later Slavic states within its former territory. Among these, Carantania is considered the oldest. Similarly ancient are the Principality of Nitra and the Moravian principality, associated with Great Moravia. This era saw central Slavic entities like the Balaton Principality, but the later Magyar expansion and the Germanisation of Austria effectively divided northern and southern Slavs. Meanwhile, the First Bulgarian Empire, established in 681, adopted the Slavic Old Bulgarian language as its primary official language in 864. Bulgaria subsequently played a crucial role in disseminating Slavic literacy and Christianity throughout the Slavic world.

input: The Masonic Lodge is the basic organisational unit of Freemasonry. The Lodge meets regularly to conduct the usual formal business of any small organisation (pay bills, organise social and charitable events, elect new members, etc.). In addition to business, the meeting may perform a ceremony to confer a Masonic degree or receive a lecture, which is usually on some aspect of Masonic history or ritual. At the conclusion of the meeting, the Lodge might adjourn for a formal dinner, or festive board, sometimes involving toasting and song.
rewrite: As the fundamental unit of Freemasonry, the Masonic Lodge holds regular meetings. These sessions handle standard organizational affairs, such as financial matters, event planning, and member elections. Beyond administrative duties, meetings often include ceremonies to confer Masonic degrees or educational lectures on historical or ritualistic topics. Following the formal proceedings, the Lodge may adjourn to a festive board—a formal dinner that can feature toasting and singing.

input: Several universities located outside Boston have a major presence in the city. Harvard University, the nation's oldest institute of higher education, is centered across the Charles River in Cambridge but has the majority of its land holdings and a substantial amount of its educational activities in Boston. Its business, medical, dental, and public health schools are located in Boston's Allston and Longwood neighborhoods. Harvard has plans for additional expansion into Allston. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), which originated in Boston and was long known as "Boston Tech", moved across the river to Cambridge in 1916. Tufts University, whose main campus is north of the city in Somerville and Medford, locates its medical and dental school in Boston's Chinatown at Tufts Medical Center, a 451-bed academic medical institution that is home to both a full-service hospital for adults and the Floating Hospital for Children.
rewrite: While Harvard University, the nation's oldest institution of higher learning, is centered in Cambridge across the Charles River, it maintains a significant portion of its operations within Boston itself. The city hosts Harvard's business, medical, dental, and public health schools, situated in the Allston and Longwood areas, where the university also plans further expansion. Similarly, Tufts University's primary campus is north of Boston in Somerville and Medford, yet its medical and dental school reside at Tufts Medical Center in Boston's Chinatown. This 451-bed academic center comprises a full-service adult hospital and the Floating Hospital for Children. Another notable presence is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), which originated in Boston as "Boston Tech" before relocating to Cambridge in 1916. Thus, several universities based outside the city exert a major influence within Boston.

input: In 1965, Pope Paul VI decreed in his motu proprio Ad Purpuratorum Patrum that patriarchs of the Eastern Catholic Churches who were named cardinals (i.e., patriarch cardinals) would also be part of the episcopal order, ranking after the six cardinal bishops of the suburbicarian sees (who had been relieved of direct responsibilities for those sees by Pope John XXIII three years earlier). Patriarch cardinals do not receive title of a suburbicarian see, and as such they cannot elect the dean or become dean. There are currently three Eastern Patriarchs who are cardinal bishops:
rewrite: In 1965, Pope Paul VI established through his motu proprio *Ad Purpuratorum Patrum* that Eastern Catholic patriarchs elevated to cardinals would join the episcopal order. These patriarch cardinals rank below the six cardinal bishops of the suburbicarian sees, whose direct duties for those sees had been removed by Pope John XXIII in 1962. Unlike other cardinal bishops, patriarch cardinals are not assigned a suburbicarian see and thus cannot elect or serve as dean of the College of Cardinals. Presently, three Eastern Patriarchs hold this rank as cardinal bishops.

input: Mechanically scanned, 30-line television broadcasts by John Logie Baird began in 1929, using the BBC transmitter in London, and by 1930 a regular schedule of programmes was transmitted from the BBC antenna in Brookmans Park. Television production was switched from Baird's company to what is now known as BBC One on 2 August 1932, and continued until September 1935. Regularly scheduled electronically scanned television began from Alexandra Palace in London on 2 November 1936, to just a few hundred viewers in the immediate area. The first programme broadcast – and thus the first ever, on a dedicated TV channel – was "Opening of the BBC Television Service" at 15:00. The first major outside broadcast was the coronation of King George VI and Queen Elizabeth in May 1937. The service was reaching an estimated 25,000–40,000 homes before the outbreak of World War II which caused the service to be suspended in September 1939. The VHF broadcasts would have provided an ideal radio beacon for German bombers homing in on London, and the engineers and technicians of the service would be needed for the war effort, in particular the radar programme.
rewrite: John Logie Baird's mechanically scanned, 30-line television broadcasts commenced in 1929 via a BBC transmitter in London. By 1930, a regular programming schedule was being transmitted from the BBC antenna at Brookmans Park. Control of television production shifted from Baird's company to what is now BBC One on August 2, 1932, continuing until September 1935. The era of regularly scheduled, electronically scanned television opened on November 2, 1936, from London's Alexandra Palace, reaching merely a few hundred local viewers. The inaugural broadcast on this dedicated channel was the "Opening of the BBC Television Service" at 15:00. A major milestone followed with the outside broadcast of the coronation of King George VI and Queen Elizabeth in May 1937. Before the outbreak of World War II, the service was estimated to reach 25,000–40,000 homes. Suspension came in September 1939, primarily because the VHF signals could have served as a radio beacon for German bombers targeting London. Furthermore, the service's engineers and technicians were vital for the war effort, especially for radar development.

input: Alternative proposals for the etymology of *Slověninъ propounded by some scholars have much less support. Lozinski argues that the word *slava once had the meaning of worshipper, in this context meaning "practicer of a common Slavic religion," and from that evolved into an ethnonym. S.B. Bernstein speculates that it derives from a reconstructed Proto-Indo-European *(s)lawos, cognate to Ancient Greek λαός laós "population, people," which itself has no commonly accepted etymology. Meanwhile, others have pointed out that the suffix -enin indicates a man from a certain place, which in this case should be a place called Slova or Slava, possibly a river name. The Old East Slavic Slavuta for the Dnieper River was argued by Henrich Bartek (1907–1986) to be derived from slova and also the origin of Slovene.
rewrite: Some scholars have advanced alternative proposals for the etymology of *Slověninъ, though these have far less support. One suggestion posits that the suffix -enin denotes a man from a specific place, hypothetically named Slova or Slava, which might refer to a river. In this vein, Henrich Bartek argued the Old East Slavic name Slavuta for the Dnieper came from *slova* and also gave rise to Slovene. Separately, Lozinski contends the term *slava* once meant "worshipper," specifically a practicer of common Slavic religion, later evolving into an ethnonym. S.B. Bernstein, meanwhile, speculates a derivation from a reconstructed Proto-Indo-European *(s)lawos, related to Ancient Greek λαός (laós), meaning "population, people," a word itself of unclear origin.

input: The dominance of American Idol in the ratings had made it the most profitable show in U.S. TV for many years. The show was estimated to generate $900 million for the year 2004 through sales of TV ads, albums, merchandise and concert tickets. By season seven, the show was estimated to earn around $900 million from its ad revenue alone, not including ancillary sponsorship deals and other income. One estimate puts the total TV revenue for the first eight seasons of American at $6.4 billion. Sponsors that bought fully integrated packages can expect a variety of promotions of their products on the show, such as product placement, adverts and product promotion integrated into the show, and various promotional opportunities. Other off-air promotional partners pay for the rights to feature "Idol" branding on their packaging, products and marketing programs. American Idol also partnered with Disney in its theme park attraction The American Idol Experience.
rewrite: For many years, American Idol dominated television ratings, making it the most profitable U.S. TV show. Its revenue streams were vast, including TV advertising, album sales, merchandise, and concert tickets. In 2004 alone, total earnings were estimated at $900 million from these sources. By the show's seventh season, advertising revenue alone reached approximately $900 million, a figure that excluded ancillary sponsorship deals and other income. Over its first eight seasons, total television revenue is estimated to have reached $6.4 billion. Sponsors purchasing fully integrated packages received product placements, integrated advertisements, and various promotional opportunities within the show. Additional partners paid for the rights to use "Idol" branding on their packaging and in marketing programs. The franchise also extended to a theme park attraction, The American Idol Experience, through a partnership with Disney.

input: During the 18th and 19th centuries, federal law traditionally focused on areas where there was an express grant of power to the federal government in the federal Constitution, like the military, money, foreign relations (especially international treaties), tariffs, intellectual property (specifically patents and copyrights), and mail. Since the start of the 20th century, broad interpretations of the Commerce and Spending Clauses of the Constitution have enabled federal law to expand into areas like aviation, telecommunications, railroads, pharmaceuticals, antitrust, and trademarks. In some areas, like aviation and railroads, the federal government has developed a comprehensive scheme that preempts virtually all state law, while in others, like family law, a relatively small number of federal statutes (generally covering interstate and international situations) interacts with a much larger body of state law. In areas like antitrust, trademark, and employment law, there are powerful laws at both the federal and state levels that coexist with each other. In a handful of areas like insurance, Congress has enacted laws expressly refusing to regulate them as long as the states have laws regulating them (see, e.g., the McCarran-Ferguson Act).
rewrite: From the 18th through the 19th century, the scope of federal law was largely confined to subjects for which the Constitution provided an express grant of authority. These included matters such as the military, currency, foreign relations—particularly international treaties—tariffs, intellectual property in the form of patents and copyrights, and the postal service. A significant shift began in the 20th century, when expansive readings of the Constitution's Commerce and Spending Clauses permitted federal authority to extend into new domains. These came to encompass aviation, telecommunications, railroads, pharmaceuticals, antitrust, and trademarks. The resulting federal role varies considerably by field. In sectors like aviation and railroads, federal regulation is so comprehensive that it almost entirely displaces state law. Conversely, in areas like family law, a limited set of federal statutes, typically addressing interstate or international circumstances, operates alongside a far more extensive body of state law. Powerful federal and state laws coexist in realms such as antitrust, trademark, and employment law.
