In a few sectors, notably insurance, Congress has passed legislation, such as the McCarran-Ferguson Act, that explicitly declines to impose federal regulation provided that state laws are in place.

input: After 1870, the new railroads across the Plains brought hunters who killed off almost all the bison for their hides. The railroads offered attractive packages of land and transportation to European farmers, who rushed to settle the land. They (and Americans as well) also took advantage of the homestead laws to obtain free farms. Land speculators and local boosters identified many potential towns, and those reached by the railroad had a chance, while the others became ghost towns. In Kansas, for example, nearly 5000 towns were mapped out, but by 1970 only 617 were actually operating. In the mid-20th century, closeness to an interstate exchange determined whether a town would flourish or struggle for business.
rewrite: Following the arrival of trans-Plains railroads after 1870, hunters decimated the bison herds for their hides. These railroads also promoted settlement by offering European farmers appealing deals on both land and travel. Settlers, including Americans, utilized homestead laws to acquire farms at no cost. As towns were plotted by speculators and boosters, connection to the rail line became critical for survival, leaving unconnected settlements to become ghost towns. Kansas alone saw nearly 5000 towns mapped, yet only 617 persisted by 1970. Later, in the mid-20th century, a town's proximity to an interstate exchange became the key factor for its commercial prosperity or decline.

input: Boundaries can be inclusive or exclusive depending on how they are perceived by other people. An exclusive boundary arises, for example, when a person adopts a marker that imposes restrictions on the behaviour of others. An inclusive boundary is created, by contrast, by the use of a marker with which other people are ready and able to associate. At the same time, however, an inclusive boundary will also impose restrictions on the people it has included by limiting their inclusion within other boundaries. An example of this is the use of a particular language by a newcomer in a room full of people speaking various languages. Some people may understand the language used by this person while others may not. Those who do not understand it might take the newcomer's use of this particular language merely as a neutral sign of identity. But they might also perceive it as imposing an exclusive boundary that is meant to mark them off from her. On the other hand, those who do understand the newcomer's language could take it as an inclusive boundary, through which the newcomer associates herself with them to the exclusion of the other people present. Equally, however, it is possible that people who do understand the newcomer but who also speak another language may not want to speak the newcomer's language and so see her marker as an imposition and a negative boundary. It is possible that the newcomer is either aware or unaware of this, depending on whether she herself knows other languages or is conscious of the plurilingual quality of the people there and is respectful of it or not.
rewrite: The perception of boundaries by others determines whether they function inclusively or exclusively. For instance, an exclusive boundary emerges when someone adopts a marker that restricts others' behavior. Conversely, an inclusive boundary is formed through a marker that others are willing and able to embrace. Yet, even an inclusive boundary imposes restrictions on those within it, by confining their inclusion within other social spheres. Consider a newcomer entering a room where multiple languages are spoken and choosing to use one specific language. Some present may understand it, while others may not. Those who do not might interpret the language merely as a neutral identity marker, or they could perceive it as an exclusive boundary deliberately separating them from the speaker. Meanwhile, those who understand the language might view it as an inclusive boundary, uniting them with the newcomer while excluding others. However, even individuals who comprehend the language might resist speaking it—perhaps preferring another tongue—and thus see the newcomer’s marker as an unwelcome imposition, a negative boundary. The newcomer’s awareness of these dynamics varies; she may be conscious or unaware of the plurilingual environment, depending on her own linguistic knowledge and her sensitivity or respect toward the diversity present. Ultimately, boundaries are defined not just by their intent but by the interpretations and reactions they provoke in others.

input: Architects such as Mies van der Rohe, Philip Johnson and Marcel Breuer worked to create beauty based on the inherent qualities of building materials and modern construction techniques, trading traditional historic forms for simplified geometric forms, celebrating the new means and methods made possible by the Industrial Revolution, including steel-frame construction, which gave birth to high-rise superstructures. By mid-century, Modernism had morphed into the International Style, an aesthetic epitomized in many ways by the Twin Towers of New York's World Trade Center designed by Minoru Yamasaki.
rewrite: Modernists like Mies van der Rohe, Philip Johnson, and Marcel Breuer embraced the Industrial Revolution’s innovations, such as steel-frame construction that enabled skyscrapers. They pursued beauty through the inherent qualities of materials and modern techniques, rejecting traditional historic forms in favor of simplified geometry. This celebration of new methods evolved by mid-century into the International Style. That aesthetic was epitomized in many ways by Minoru Yamasaki’s design for the Twin Towers of New York’s World Trade Center.

input: Damaged spots on a LaserDisc can be played through or skipped over, while a DVD will often become unplayable past the damage. Some newer DVD players feature a repair+skip algorithm, which alleviates this problem by continuing to play the disc, filling in unreadable areas of the picture with blank space or a frozen frame of the last readable image and sound. The success of this feature depends upon the amount of damage. LaserDisc players, when working in full analog, recover from such errors faster than DVD players. Direct comparison here is almost impossible due to the sheer size differences between the two media. A 1 in (3 cm) scratch on a DVD will probably cause more problems than a 1 in (3 cm) scratch on a LaserDisc, but a fingerprint taking up 1% of the area of a DVD would almost certainly cause fewer problems than a similar mark covering 1% of the surface of a LaserDisc.[citation needed]
rewrite: While a DVD often becomes unplayable past a damaged area, LaserDiscs can typically have such spots played through or skipped. To mitigate this issue, certain newer DVD players employ a repair+skip algorithm. This function allows the disc to continue playing by filling unreadable sections of the picture with either blank space or a frozen frame from the last readable image and sound, though its success is contingent on the extent of the damage. Operating in full analog, LaserDisc players generally recover from these errors more swiftly than their DVD counterparts. A direct comparison is challenging due to the significant size difference between the two media formats. For instance, a 1-inch (3 cm) scratch would likely cause more disruption on a DVD than on a LaserDisc. Conversely, a fingerprint covering 1% of a DVD's surface would almost certainly create fewer problems than a similar mark occupying 1% of a LaserDisc's area.

input: In China, urbanization increased as the population grew and as the division of labor grew more complex. Large urban centers, such as Nanjing and Beijing, also contributed to the growth of private industry. In particular, small-scale industries grew up, often specializing in paper, silk, cotton, and porcelain goods. For the most part, however, relatively small urban centers with markets proliferated around the country. Town markets mainly traded food, with some necessary manufactures such as pins or oil. Despite the xenophobia and intellectual introspection characteristic of the increasingly popular new school of neo-Confucianism, China under the early Ming dynasty was not isolated. Foreign trade and other contacts with the outside world, particularly Japan, increased considerably. Chinese merchants explored all of the Indian Ocean, reaching East Africa with the treasure voyages of Zheng He.
rewrite: As China's population expanded and labor became more specialized, urbanization advanced. Across the nation, numerous relatively small urban centers with markets proliferated. These town markets primarily dealt in food and basic manufactured goods like pins and oil. Larger cities, including Nanjing and Beijing, further stimulated private industry. This often involved small-scale operations specializing in paper, silk, cotton, and porcelain. The early Ming dynasty, despite the inward-looking tendencies of rising neo-Confucianism, was not isolated. Contacts with the outside world grew significantly, especially with Japan. Chinese merchants extensively explored the Indian Ocean, and Zheng He's treasure voyages even reached East Africa, reflecting a considerable increase in foreign trade.

input: In 1846, the United States went to war against Mexico and sent a naval and land expedition to conquer Alta California. At first they had an easy time of it capturing the major ports including San Diego, but the Californios in southern Alta California struck back. Following the successful revolt in Los Angeles, the American garrison at San Diego was driven out without firing a shot in early October 1846. Mexican partisans held San Diego for three weeks until October 24, 1846, when the Americans recaptured it. For the next several months the Americans were blockaded inside the pueblo. Skirmishes occurred daily and snipers shot into the town every night. The Californios drove cattle away from the pueblo hoping to starve the Americans and their Californio supporters out. On December 1 the Americans garrison learned that the dragoons of General Stephen W. Kearney were at Warner's Ranch. Commodore Robert F. Stockton sent a mounted force of fifty under Captain Archibald Gillespie to march north to meet him. Their joint command of 150 men, returning to San Diego, encountered about 93 Californios under Andrés Pico. In the ensuing Battle of San Pasqual, fought in the San Pasqual Valley which is now part of the city of San Diego, the Americans suffered their worst losses in the campaign. Subsequently a column led by Lieutenant Gray arrived from San Diego, rescuing Kearny's battered and blockaded command.
rewrite:
The American campaign to seize Alta California during the 1846 war with Mexico initially met little resistance, with major ports like San Diego falling quickly. This changed when Californios in the south revolted. After successfully retaking Los Angeles, they forced the American garrison out of San Diego in early October without a shot being fired. Mexican partisans controlled the town for three weeks until an American recapture on October 24. For months afterward, the Americans found themselves blockaded within the San Diego pueblo, enduring nightly sniper fire and daily skirmishes. The Californios sought to starve them out by driving away nearby cattle, targeting both the Americans and their local Californio allies.

Learning in December that General Stephen W. Kearny's dragoons were at Warner's Ranch, Commodore Robert F. Stockton dispatched a fifty-man mounted force under Captain Archibald Gillespie to meet them. Their combined group of 150 men, while returning to San Diego, was met by roughly 93 Californios commanded by Andrés Pico. The clash that followed, the Battle of San Pasqual, occurred in the San Pasqual Valley—now within San Diego city limits. It resulted in the worst American losses of the entire California campaign. Ultimately, a relief column from San Diego led by Lieutenant Gray arrived to rescue Kearny's besieged and battered force.

input: The tram system that now criss-crosses the historic city centre complements walking and biking in it. The centre has been transformed into a pedestrian priority zone that enables and invites walking and biking by making these active modes of transport comfortable, safe and enjoyable. These attributes are accomplished by applying the principle of "filtered permeability" to the existing irregular network of streets. It means that the network adaptations favour active transportation and, selectively, "filter out" the car by reducing the number of streets that run through the centre. While certain streets are discontinuous for cars, they connect to a network of pedestrian and bike paths which permeate the entire centre. In addition, these paths go through public squares and open spaces increasing the enjoyment of the trip. This logic of filtering a mode of transport is fully expressed in a comprehensive model for laying out neighbourhoods and districts – the Fused Grid.
rewrite: Now threading through the historic city centre, the tram system works alongside walking and biking. A pedestrian priority zone has been created there, designed to make these active forms of transport comfortable, safe, and pleasant. This is achieved by applying "filtered permeability" to the area's irregular street network. Adaptations favour walking and cycling while selectively "filtering out" cars by limiting the number of through streets. Although some streets are now discontinuous for vehicles, they link into a comprehensive network of pedestrian and bike paths that reach every part of the centre. These paths also weave through public squares and open spaces, enhancing the enjoyment of the journey. This principle of filtering transportation modes is fully embodied in a comprehensive neighbourhood planning model known as the Fused Grid.

input: Alison Jing Xu, assistant professor of management at the University of Toronto Scarborough and Aparna Labroo of Northwestern University conducted a series of studies analyzing the correlation between lighting and human emotion. The researchers asked participants to rate a number of things such as: the spiciness of chicken-wing sauce, the aggressiveness of a fictional character, how attractive someone was, their feelings about specific words, and the taste of two juices–all under different lighting conditions. In their study, they found that both positive and negative human emotions are felt more intensely in bright light. Professor Xu stated, "we found that on sunny days depression-prone people actually become more depressed." They also found that dim light makes people make more rational decisions and settle negotiations easier. In the dark, emotions are slightly suppressed. However, emotions are intensified in the bright light.
rewrite: Researchers from the University of Toronto Scarborough and Northwestern University explored how lighting influences emotional intensity. In a series of studies led by Alison Jing Xu and Aparna Labroo, participants evaluated various items—including the spiciness of a sauce, a character's aggressiveness, personal attractiveness, and juice flavors—under different lighting conditions. The findings revealed that bright light amplifies both positive and negative feelings. "We found that on sunny days depression-prone people actually become more depressed," noted Professor Xu. Conversely, dim illumination fosters more rational decision-making and eases negotiations, as darker settings slightly suppress emotions. Ultimately, while emotions are moderated in the dark, they become heightened under bright light.

input: Summers in the state are generally hot and humid, with most of the state averaging a high of around 90 °F (32 °C) during the summer months. Winters tend to be mild to cool, increasing in coolness at higher elevations. Generally, for areas outside the highest mountains, the average overnight lows are near freezing for most of the state. The highest recorded temperature is 113 °F (45 °C) at Perryville on August 9, 1930 while the lowest recorded temperature is −32 °F (−36 °C) at Mountain City on December 30, 1917.
rewrite: Summers across the state are typically hot and humid, with average highs near 90°F (32°C). Winters are generally mild to cool, becoming colder at higher elevations. For most areas outside the highest mountains, average overnight lows hover around freezing. The record high of 113°F (45°C) occurred in Perryville on August 9, 1930. Conversely, the record low of -32°F (-36°C) was set in Mountain City on December 30, 1917.

input: Both languages are still largely mutually intelligible, although this relation can in some fields (such as lexicon, spelling and grammar) be asymmetric, as it is easier for Dutch speakers to understand written Afrikaans than it is for Afrikaans speakers to understand written Dutch. Afrikaans is grammatically far less complex than Dutch, and vocabulary items are generally altered in a clearly patterned manner, e.g. vogel becomes voël ("bird") and regen becomes reën ("rain"). In South Africa, the number of students following Dutch at university, is difficult to estimate, since the academic study of Afrikaans inevitably includes the study of Dutch. Elsewhere in the world, the number of people learning Dutch is relatively small.
rewrite: While still largely mutually intelligible, the relationship between Dutch and Afrikaans can be asymmetrical in areas like lexicon, spelling, and grammar. Dutch speakers typically find written Afrikaans easier to understand than Afrikaans speakers do written Dutch. This is partly because Afrikaans grammar is far less complex, and its vocabulary often alters Dutch words in predictable patterns, such as *vogel* becoming *voël* ("bird"). Estimating Dutch students in South Africa is difficult, as studying Afrikaans at university inevitably involves Dutch. Globally, the number of people learning Dutch remains relatively small.

input: Church and state are officially separated since 1916 in Uruguay. The religion with most followers in Montevideo is Roman Catholicism and has been so since the foundation of the city. The Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Montevideo was created as the Apostolic Vicariate of Montevideo in 1830. The vicariate was promoted to the Diocese of Montevideo on 13 July 1878. Pope Leo XIII elevated it to the rank of a metropolitan archdiocese on 14 April 1897. The new archdiocese became the Metropolitan of the suffragan sees of Canelones, Florida, Maldonado–Punta del Este, Melo, Mercedes, Minas, Salto, San José de Mayo, Tacuarembó.
rewrite: Since 1916, Uruguay has maintained an official separation of church and state. Roman Catholicism has been the predominant faith in Montevideo since the city's founding. The establishment of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Montevideo traces back to 1830, when it began as the Apostolic Vicariate of Montevideo. This vicariate was elevated to the Diocese of Montevideo on July 13, 1878. Later, Pope Leo XIII raised it to a metropolitan archdiocese on April 14, 1897. As a metropolitan see, it oversees the suffragan dioceses of Canelones, Florida, Maldonado–Punta del Este, Melo, Mercedes, Minas, Salto, San José de Mayo, and Tacuarembó.

input: Tito's estrangement from the USSR enabled Yugoslavia to obtain US aid via the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA), the same US aid institution which administered the Marshall Plan. Still, he did not agree to align with the West, which was a common consequence of accepting American aid at the time. After Stalin's death in 1953, relations with the USSR were relaxed and he began to receive aid as well from the COMECON. In this way, Tito played East-West antagonism to his advantage. Instead of choosing sides, he was instrumental in kick-starting the Non-Aligned Movement, which would function as a 'third way' for countries interested in staying outside of the East-West divide.
rewrite: Tito's break with the USSR allowed Yugoslavia to secure American assistance through the Economic Cooperation Administration (ECA), the body overseeing the Marshall Plan. However, accepting this aid did not lead him to side with the West, a typical outcome during that era. Following Stalin's death in 1953, tensions with the Soviet Union eased, and Yugoslavia started receiving support from COMECON as well. By skillfully leveraging East-West rivalries, Tito avoided aligning with either bloc. He played a key role in founding the Non-Aligned Movement, thereby establishing a 'third way' for nations wishing to remain independent of the superpower divide.

input: In 1926, Universal opened a production unit in Germany, Deutsche Universal-Film AG, under the direction of Joe Pasternak. This unit produced three to four films per year until 1936, migrating to Hungary and then Austria in the face of Hitler's increasing domination of central Europe. With the advent of sound, these productions were made in the German language or, occasionally, Hungarian or Polish. In the U.S., Universal Pictures did not distribute any of this subsidiary's films, but at least some of them were exhibited through other, independent, foreign-language film distributors based in New York, without benefit of English subtitles. Nazi persecution and a change in ownership for the parent Universal Pictures organization resulted in the dissolution of this subsidiary.
rewrite: Universal established Deutsche Universal-Film AG in Germany in 1926, placing it under Joe Pasternak's direction. Until 1936, this subsidiary generated three to four films annually. As Hitler's control over central Europe intensified, operations shifted to Hungary and later Austria. Following the introduction of sound, productions were primarily in German, though sometimes in Hungarian or Polish. While Universal Pictures in the U.S. did not directly distribute these films, at least a portion were screened by independent, New York-based foreign-language distributors, lacking English subtitles. The subsidiary was ultimately dissolved due to Nazi persecution and a change in ownership at the parent Universal company.

input: As the economy and the middle class expanded, there was an increasing number of amateur musicians. One manifestation of this involved women, who became more involved with music on a social level. Women were already engaged in professional roles as singers, and increased their presence in the amateur performers' scene, especially with keyboard music. Music publishers begin to print music that amateurs could understand and play. The majority of the works that were published were for keyboard, voice and keyboard, and chamber ensemble. After these initial genres were popularized, from the mid-century on, amateur groups sang choral music, which then became a new trend for publishers to capitalize on. The increasing study of the fine arts, as well as access to amateur-friendly published works, led to more people becoming interested in reading and discussing music. Music magazines, reviews, and critical works which suited amateurs as well as connoisseurs began to surface.
rewrite: The growth of the economy and the middle class produced a rising number of amateur musicians. This was notably reflected in the expanding social involvement of women with music. While women had long held professional roles as singers, they now participated more widely as amateur performers, particularly in keyboard music. To serve this growing audience, publishers began issuing works designed to be accessible and playable by non-professionals. Most publications were for keyboard, for voice and keyboard, or for chamber ensembles. Following the popularity of these forms, a new trend emerged from mid-century as amateur groups took up choral music, which publishers quickly adopted. Greater engagement with the fine arts, combined with the availability of these amateur-friendly publications, spurred broader interest in reading about and discussing music. Consequently, music magazines, reviews, and critical works appealing to both amateurs and connoisseurs began to appear.

input: In 1211, the Jewish community in the country was strengthened by the arrival of a group headed by over 300 rabbis from France and England, among them Rabbi Samson ben Abraham of Sens. Nachmanides, the 13th-century Spanish rabbi and recognised leader of Jewry greatly praised the land of Israel and viewed its settlement as a positive commandment incumbent on all Jews. He wrote "If the gentiles wish to make peace, we shall make peace and leave them on clear terms; but as for the land, we shall not leave it in their hands, nor in the hands of any nation, not in any generation."
rewrite: In 1211, a group of over 300 rabbis from France and England, led by Rabbi Samson ben Abraham of Sens, arrived and strengthened the local Jewish community. The 13th-century Spanish rabbi Nachmanides, a recognized leader of Jewry, greatly praised the land of Israel. He viewed settling it as a positive commandment for all Jews, writing, "If the gentiles wish to make peace, we shall make peace and leave them on clear terms; but as for the land, we shall not leave it in their hands, nor in the hands of any nation, not in any generation."

input: After DNA replication is complete, the cell must physically separate the two copies of the genome and divide into two distinct membrane-bound cells.:18.2 In prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) this usually occurs via a relatively simple process called binary fission, in which each circular genome attaches to the cell membrane and is separated into the daughter cells as the membrane invaginates to split the cytoplasm into two membrane-bound portions. Binary fission is extremely fast compared to the rates of cell division in eukaryotes. Eukaryotic cell division is a more complex process known as the cell cycle; DNA replication occurs during a phase of this cycle known as S phase, whereas the process of segregating chromosomes and splitting the cytoplasm occurs during M phase.:18.1
rewrite: Once DNA replication finishes, the cell faces the task of dividing its duplicated genome and itself into two separate, membrane-enclosed units. In prokaryotes such as bacteria and archaea, this is typically achieved through binary fission, a relatively straightforward mechanism. Here, each circular genome attaches to the cell membrane, and as the membrane pinches inward to partition the cytoplasm, the genomes are pulled into the two resulting daughter cells. This process is remarkably swift compared to eukaryotic division. Eukaryotes undergo a more elaborate sequence called the cell cycle. Within this cycle, DNA is copied during the S phase, while the actual separation of chromosomes and division of the cytoplasm take place in the M phase.

input: North Carolina became one of the English Thirteen Colonies and with the territory of South Carolina was originally known as the Province of Carolina. The northern and southern parts of the original province separated in 1729. Originally settled by small farmers, sometimes having a few slaves, who were oriented toward subsistence agriculture, the colony lacked cities or towns. Pirates menaced the coastal settlements, but by 1718 the pirates had been captured and killed. Growth was strong in the middle of the 18th century, as the economy attracted Scots-Irish, Quaker, English and German immigrants. The colonists generally supported the American Revolution, as the number of Loyalists was smaller than in some other colonies.
rewrite: Originally known as the Province of Carolina, this territory encompassed what would become North and South Carolina. Settled largely by small, subsistence-oriented farmers who owned few slaves, the early colony developed without major towns. While pirate raids once threatened the coast, this menace was eliminated by 1718. The northern and southern sections formally separated in 1729. During the mid-18th century, robust growth drew immigrants such as the Scots-Irish, Quakers, English, and Germans. When the American Revolution began, the colony largely supported it, having a smaller Loyalist population compared to others. North Carolina had been established as one of the English Thirteen Colonies.

input: Japan used the name Greater East Asia War (大東亜戦争, Dai Tō-A Sensō?), as chosen by a cabinet decision on 10 December 1941, to refer to both the war with the Western Allies and the ongoing war in China. This name was released to the public on 12 December, with an explanation that it involved Asian nations achieving their independence from the Western powers through armed forces of the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere. Japanese officials integrated what they called the Japan–China Incident (日支事変, Nisshi Jihen?) into the Greater East Asia War.
rewrite: On 10 December 1941, a Japanese cabinet decision selected the name Greater East Asia War (大東亜戦争, Dai Tō-A Sensō?). This term was publicly released two days later, on 12 December, to encompass the conflict with the Western Allies. Officials explained it signified Asian nations, via the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere's forces, gaining independence from Western powers. They also incorporated the ongoing Japan–China Incident (日支事変, Nisshi Jihen?) into this broader war designation.

input: The term "bacteria" was traditionally applied to all microscopic, single-cell prokaryotes. However, molecular systematics showed prokaryotic life to consist of two separate domains, originally called Eubacteria and Archaebacteria, but now called Bacteria and Archaea that evolved independently from an ancient common ancestor. The archaea and eukaryotes are more closely related to each other than either is to the bacteria. These two domains, along with Eukarya, are the basis of the three-domain system, which is currently the most widely used classification system in microbiolology. However, due to the relatively recent introduction of molecular systematics and a rapid increase in the number of genome sequences that are available, bacterial classification remains a changing and expanding field. For example, a few biologists argue that the Archaea and Eukaryotes evolved from Gram-positive bacteria.
rewrite: Originally, all microscopic, single-cell prokaryotes were referred to as "bacteria." Modern molecular systematics, however, revealed that prokaryotic life comprises two distinct domains. These were initially named Eubacteria and Archaebacteria but are now known as Bacteria and Archaea, both having evolved independently from an ancient common ancestor. Interestingly, archaea share a closer evolutionary relationship with eukaryotes than with bacteria. Together with Eukarya, these domains form the three-domain system, the predominant classification framework in microbiology today. Yet bacterial classification is a dynamic and growing discipline, fueled by the recent advent of molecular systematics and a swiftly expanding library of genome sequences. Some biologists, for instance, contend that Archaea and Eukaryotes originated from Gram-positive bacteria.

input: Under Walter Dill Scott's presidency from 1920 to 1939, Northwestern began construction of an integrated campus in Chicago designed by James Gamble Rogers to house the professional schools; established the Kellogg School of Management; and built several prominent buildings on the Evanston campus, Dyche Stadium (now named Ryan Field) and Deering Library among others. In 1933, a proposal to merge Northwestern with the University of Chicago was considered but rejected. Northwestern was also one of the first six universities in the country to establish a Naval Reserve Officers Training Corps (NROTC) in the 1920s. Northwestern played host to the first-ever NCAA Men's Division I Basketball Championship game in 1939 in the original Patten Gymnasium, which was later demolished and relocated farther north along with the Dearborn Observatory to make room for the Technological Institute.
rewrite: During Walter Dill Scott's tenure as president from 1920 to 1939, Northwestern University undertook significant expansion. This included launching the Kellogg School of Management and erecting notable Evanston buildings like Dyche Stadium (now Ryan Field) and Deering Library. Furthermore, the university began constructing an integrated Chicago campus for its professional schools, designed by James Gamble Rogers. The 1920s also saw Northwestern become an early adopter of the Naval Reserve Officers Training Corps (NROTC), being among the first six U.S. universities to do so. In 1939, the original Patten Gymnasium hosted the inaugural NCAA Men's Division I Basketball Championship game. This gymnasium, along with the Dearborn Observatory, was later demolished and moved northward to accommodate the new Technological Institute. A 1933 proposal to merge with the University of Chicago was ultimately rejected.

input: Island genetics provides one proposed explanation for the sudden, fully developed appearance of flowering plants. Island genetics is believed to be a common source of speciation in general, especially when it comes to radical adaptations that seem to have required inferior transitional forms. Flowering plants may have evolved in an isolated setting like an island or island chain, where the plants bearing them were able to develop a highly specialized relationship with some specific animal (a wasp, for example). Such a relationship, with a hypothetical wasp carrying pollen from one plant to another much the way fig wasps do today, could result in the development of a high degree of specialization in both the plant(s) and their partners. Note that the wasp example is not incidental; bees, which, it is postulated, evolved specifically due to mutualistic plant relationships, are descended from wasps.
rewrite: The sudden, fully developed appearance of flowering plants may be explained by island genetics. This concept is considered a common driver of speciation, particularly for radical adaptations that appear to lack inferior transitional forms. Evolution might have occurred in an isolated environment, such as an island or archipelago. There, plants could have formed a highly specialized relationship with a specific animal, like a wasp. Imagine a hypothetical wasp pollinating plants similarly to modern fig wasps; such mutualism could drive a high degree of specialization in both partners. Notably, the wasp example is key: bees, thought to have evolved through such mutualistic relationships, are actually descended from wasps.

input: Over time, the relative power of these five nations fluctuated, which by the dawn of the 20th century had served to create an entirely different balance of power. Some, such as the United Kingdom and Prussia (as the founder of the newly formed German state), experienced continued economic growth and political power. Others, such as Russia and Austria-Hungary, stagnated. At the same time, other states were emerging and expanding in power, largely through the process of industrialization. These countries seeking to attain great power status were: Italy after the Risorgimento, Japan after the Meiji Restoration, and the United States after its civil war. By the dawn of the 20th century, the balance of world power had changed substantially since the Congress of Vienna. The Eight-Nation Alliance was a belligerent alliance of eight nations against the Boxer Rebellion in China. It formed in 1900 and consisted of the five Congress powers plus Italy, Japan, and the United States, representing the great powers at the beginning of 20th century.
rewrite: By the dawn of the 20th century, the global balance of power had shifted dramatically from the era of the Congress of Vienna. The relative strength of the five original Congress powers had fluctuated considerably. While the United Kingdom and Prussia—the core of the new German state—saw sustained growth in their economic and political might, empires like Russia and Austria-Hungary entered a period of stagnation. Simultaneously, the force of industrialization propelled other states to prominence. Following its Risorgimento, Italy sought great power status, as did Japan after the Meiji Restoration and the United States after its civil war. This new constellation of power was clearly demonstrated in 1900 by the formation of the Eight-Nation Alliance, a belligerent coalition against the Boxer Rebellion in China. It comprised the five original powers alongside the three emerging nations of Italy, Japan, and the United States, collectively defining the great powers at the century's start.

input: Grapes are a type of fruit that grow in clusters of 15 to 300, and can be crimson, black, dark blue, yellow, green, orange, and pink. "White" grapes are actually green in color, and are evolutionarily derived from the purple grape. Mutations in two regulatory genes of white grapes turn off production of anthocyanins, which are responsible for the color of purple grapes. Anthocyanins and other pigment chemicals of the larger family of polyphenols in purple grapes are responsible for the varying shades of purple in red wines. Grapes are typically an ellipsoid shape resembling a prolate spheroid.
rewrite: Growing in clusters ranging from 15 to 300, grapes come in many colors, including crimson, black, dark blue, yellow, green, orange, and pink. So-called "white" grapes are actually green, having evolved from purple varieties. In these white grapes, mutations in two regulatory genes halt anthocyanin production—the pigments that give purple grapes their color. These anthocyanins, part of the polyphenol family, also create the varying purple shades in red wines. Typically, the fruit itself is ellipsoid, similar to a prolate spheroid in shape.

input: Egypt has a wide range of beaches situated on the Mediterranean and the Red Sea that extend to over 3,000 km. The Red Sea has serene waters, coloured coral reefs, rare fish and beautiful mountains. The Akba Gulf beaches also provide facilities for practising sea sports. Safaga tops the Red Sea zone with its beautiful location on the Suez Gulf. Last but not least, Sharm el-Sheikh (or City of Peace), Hurghada, Luxor (known as world's greatest open-air museum/ or City of the ⅓ of world monuments), Dahab, Ras Sidr, Marsa Alam, Safaga and the northern coast of the Mediterranean are major tourist's destinations of the recreational tourism.
rewrite: Egypt's coastline spans more than 3,000 km along both the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. The Red Sea is renowned for its calm waters, vibrant coral reefs, rare fish species, and scenic mountains. Key destinations for recreational tourism include Sharm el-Sheikh, Hurghada, Luxor—often called the world's greatest open-air museum—Dahab, Ras Sidr, Marsa Alam, and the Mediterranean's northern coast. Within the Red Sea zone, Safaga stands out for its location on the Gulf of Suez and its facilities for water sports, such as those found at Akba Gulf beaches.

input: Lewis Latimer, employed at the time by Edison, developed an improved method of heat-treating carbon filaments which reduced breakage and allowed them to be molded into novel shapes, such as the characteristic "M" shape of Maxim filaments. On 17 January 1882, Latimer received a patent for the "Process of Manufacturing Carbons", an improved method for the production of light bulb filaments, which was purchased by the United States Electric Light Company. Latimer patented other improvements such as a better way of attaching filaments to their wire supports.
rewrite: Employed by Edison, Lewis Latimer created an enhanced process for heat-treating carbon filaments on January 17, 1882, patenting his "Process of Manufacturing Carbons." This method minimized breakage and enabled molding into new forms, like the distinctive "M" shape of Maxim filaments. The United States Electric Light Company bought this patent for producing light bulb filaments. Latimer also secured patents for further refinements, including an improved technique for attaching filaments to their wire supports.

input: On April 22, 1971, Kerry appeared before a U.S. Senate committee hearing on proposals relating to ending the war. The day after this testimony, Kerry participated in a demonstration with thousands of other veterans in which he and other Vietnam War veterans threw their medals and service ribbons over a fence erected at the front steps of the United States Capitol building to dramatize their opposition to the war. Jack Smith, a Marine, read a statement explaining why the veterans were returning their military awards to the government. For more than two hours, almost 1000 angry veterans tossed their medals, ribbons, hats, jackets, and military papers over the fence. Each veteran gave his or her name, hometown, branch of service and a statement. Kerry threw some of his own decorations and awards as well as some given to him by other veterans to throw. As Kerry threw his decorations over the fence, his statement was: "I'm not doing this for any violent reasons, but for peace and justice, and to try and make this country wake up once and for all."
rewrite: On April 22, 1971, John Kerry testified before a U.S. Senate committee hearing on proposals to end the Vietnam War. The following day, he joined thousands of fellow veterans in a dramatic demonstration of opposition. To symbolize their protest, these veterans threw their medals, service ribbons, and other military items over a fence erected on the steps of the United Capitol building. Jack Smith, a Marine, read a statement explaining the act of returning these awards to the government. For over two hours, nearly 1000 angry veterans participated, each offering their name, hometown, branch of service, and a personal statement as they discarded their symbols of service. Kerry threw not only some of his own decorations but also those given to him by others to cast away. While tossing his awards, he declared, “I’m not doing this for any violent reasons, but for peace and justice, and to try and make this country wake up once and for all.”

input: Vinson Massif, the highest peak in Antarctica at 4,892 m (16,050 ft), is located in the Ellsworth Mountains. Antarctica contains many other mountains, on both the main continent and the surrounding islands. Mount Erebus on Ross Island is the world's southernmost active volcano. Another well-known volcano is found on Deception Island, which is famous for a giant eruption in 1970. Minor eruptions are frequent and lava flow has been observed in recent years. Other dormant volcanoes may potentially be active. In 2004, a potentially active underwater volcano was found in the Antarctic Peninsula by American and Canadian researchers.
rewrite: Rising to 4,892 m (16,050 ft) in the Ellsworth Mountains, Vinson Massif is Antarctica's highest peak. The continent and its islands feature many other mountains. Among its notable volcanoes is Mount Erebus on Ross Island, the southernmost active volcano on Earth. Another is on Deception Island, site of a major 1970 eruption, where minor eruptions are frequent and recent lava flows have been seen. While other volcanoes remain dormant, they could become active. In 2004, American and Canadian researchers discovered a potentially active underwater volcano near the Antarctic Peninsula.

input: All birds lay amniotic eggs with hard shells made mostly of calcium carbonate. Hole and burrow nesting species tend to lay white or pale eggs, while open nesters lay camouflaged eggs. There are many exceptions to this pattern, however; the ground-nesting nightjars have pale eggs, and camouflage is instead provided by their plumage. Species that are victims of brood parasites have varying egg colours to improve the chances of spotting a parasite's egg, which forces female parasites to match their eggs to those of their hosts.
rewrite: Birds universally produce amniotic eggs featuring hard, calcium carbonate-rich shells. While hole or burrow nesters typically lay white or pale eggs, those nesting in the open lay camouflaged ones. Exceptions exist, such as ground-nesting nightjars, whose pale eggs are concealed by their plumage. In species targeted by brood parasites, eggs exhibit diverse colors to help detect intruder eggs. This diversity, in turn, compels female parasites to closely match their own eggs to those of their specific hosts.

input: While successful predation results in a gain of energy, hunting invariably involves energetic costs as well. When hunger is not an issue, in general most predators will not seek to attack prey since the costs outweigh the benefits. For instance, a large predatory fish like a shark that is well fed in an aquarium will typically ignore the smaller fish swimming around it (while the prey fish take advantage of the fact that the apex predator is apparently uninterested). Surplus killing represents a deviation from this type of behaviour. The treatment of consumption in terms of cost-benefit analysis is known as optimal foraging theory, and has been quite successful in the study of animal behavior. In general, costs and benefits are considered in energy gain per unit time, though other factors are also important, such as essential nutrients that have no caloric value but are necessary for survival and health.
rewrite: Although hunting provides energy through successful kills, it also demands considerable energetic effort. Typically, when not driven by hunger, predators avoid attacking prey because the costs involved surpass the gains. This principle is illustrated by a well-fed shark in an aquarium, which will usually disregard smaller fish nearby—an opening those prey fish exploit. Surplus killing, however, departs from such expected conduct. The framework analyzing consumption through a cost-benefit lens is called optimal foraging theory, a highly effective approach in animal behavior studies. Generally, calculations weigh energy gained per unit of time, yet other elements also play critical roles. These include essential nutrients that, despite lacking caloric content, remain vital for an organism’s survival and overall health.

input: Initial reactions to the novel were varied. The New Yorker declared it "skilled, unpretentious, and totally ingenious", and The Atlantic Monthly's reviewer rated it as "pleasant, undemanding reading", but found the narrative voice—"a six-year-old girl with the prose style of a well-educated adult"—to be implausible. Time magazine's 1960 review of the book states that it "teaches the reader an astonishing number of useful truths about little girls and about Southern life" and calls Scout Finch "the most appealing child since Carson McCullers' Frankie got left behind at the wedding". The Chicago Sunday Tribune noted the even-handed approach to the narration of the novel's events, writing: "This is in no way a sociological novel. It underlines no cause ... To Kill a Mockingbird is a novel of strong contemporary national significance."
rewrite: Reactions to the novel were mixed upon its release. *Time* magazine’s 1960 review asserted that it “teaches the reader an astonishing number of useful truths about little girls and about Southern life,” praising Scout Finch as “the most appealing child since Carson McCullers' Frankie got left behind at the wedding.” While *The New Yorker* called it “skilled, unpretentious, and totally ingenious,” *The Atlantic Monthly* offered a more measured view, describing it as “pleasant, undemanding reading” yet criticizing the adult-like narrative voice of the six-year-old girl as implausible. Meanwhile, *The Chicago Sunday Tribune* highlighted the book’s balanced perspective, noting: “This is in no way a sociological novel. It underlines no cause...” and concluding it was “a novel of strong contemporary national significance.”

input: In its Basic Laws, Israel defines itself as a Jewish and democratic state. Israel is a representative democracy with a parliamentary system, proportional representation and universal suffrage. The prime minister serves as head of government and the Knesset serves as the legislature. Israel is a developed country and an OECD member, with the 35th-largest economy in the world by nominal gross domestic product as of 2015[update]. The country benefits from a highly skilled workforce and is among the most educated countries in the world with the one of the highest percentage of its citizens holding a tertiary education degree. The country has the highest standard of living in the Middle East and the fourth highest in Asia, and has one of the highest life expectancies in the world.
rewrite: Israel is a developed nation and member of the OECD, with the world's 35th-largest nominal GDP as of 2015. It defines itself as both a Jewish and democratic state in its Basic Laws. The government is a representative democracy featuring a parliamentary system, proportional representation, and universal suffrage. Leadership includes a prime minister as head of government and the Knesset as the legislative body. Israel possesses a highly skilled and educated workforce, with one of the highest global rates of citizens holding a tertiary degree. This contributes to the highest standard of living in the Middle East and the fourth highest in Asia, alongside one of the world's highest life expectancies.

input: Horizontal gene transfer is invoked to explain how there is often extreme similarity between small portions of the genomes of two organisms that are otherwise very distantly related. Horizontal gene transfer seems to be common among many microbes. Also, eukaryotic cells seem to have experienced a transfer of some genetic material from their chloroplast and mitochondrial genomes to their nuclear chromosomes.
rewrite: Horizontal gene transfer is frequently observed among many microbes. It explains the extreme similarity in small genome portions between otherwise distantly related organisms. Additionally, eukaryotic cells appear to have undergone transfer of some genetic material from their chloroplast and mitochondrial genomes into their nuclear chromosomes.

input: For example, in order to meet the expectations for good color rendering in retail applications, research suggests using the well-established CRI along with another metric called gamut area index (GAI). GAI represents the relative separation of object colors illuminated by a light source; the greater the GAI, the greater the apparent saturation or vividness of the object colors. As a result, light sources which balance both CRI and GAI are generally preferred over ones that have only high CRI or only high GAI.
rewrite: To achieve optimal color rendering in retail settings, research recommends combining the traditional Color Rendering Index (CRI) with the Gamut Area Index (GAI). GAI measures how much a light source separates object colors, where a higher value enhances their apparent saturation and vividness. Consequently, lighting that balances both CRI and GAI is favored over sources excelling in only one metric.

input: Alexander faced pressure from his brother, Duke Constantine, to make peace with Napoleon. Given the victory he had just achieved, the French emperor offered the Russians relatively lenient terms–demanding that Russia join the Continental System, withdraw its forces from Wallachia and Moldavia, and hand over the Ionian Islands to France. By contrast, Napoleon dictated very harsh peace terms for Prussia, despite the ceaseless exhortations of Queen Louise. Wiping out half of Prussian territories from the map, Napoleon created a new kingdom of 1,100 square miles called Westphalia. He then appointed his young brother Jérôme as the new monarch of this kingdom. Prussia's humiliating treatment at Tilsit caused a deep and bitter antagonism which festered as the Napoleonic era progressed. Moreover, Alexander's pretensions at friendship with Napoleon led the latter to seriously misjudge the true intentions of his Russian counterpart, who would violate numerous provisions of the treaty in the next few years. Despite these problems, the Treaties of Tilsit at last gave Napoleon a respite from war and allowed him to return to France, which he had not seen in over 300 days.
rewrite: Under pressure from his brother Duke Constantine to seek peace with Napoleon, Alexander found the French emperor offering relatively lenient terms following his recent victory. These terms required Russia to join the Continental System, withdraw from Wallachia and Moldavia, and cede the Ionian Islands to France. In stark contrast, despite Queen Louise’s persistent appeals, Napoleon imposed severe conditions on Prussia. He erased half of its territories, carving out a new 1,100-square-mile kingdom named Westphalia, and installed his younger brother Jérôme as its monarch. This humiliation at Tilsit bred a deep and lasting bitterness in Prussia that grew throughout the Napoleonic era. Meanwhile, Alexander’s overtures of friendship led Napoleon to misjudge the tsar’s true intentions, resulting in Russia violating multiple treaty provisions in subsequent years. Nevertheless, the Treaties of Tilsit finally provided Napoleon a respite from war, enabling his return to France after an absence of over 300 days.

input: Its written transmission, along with the veneration bestowed on certain classical works, has led to the expectation that performers will play a work in a way that realizes in detail the original intentions of the composer. During the 19th century the details that composers put in their scores generally increased. Yet the opposite trend—admiration of performers for new "interpretations" of the composer's work—can be seen, and it is not unknown for a composer to praise a performer for achieving a better realization of the original intent than the composer was able to imagine. Thus, classical performers often achieve high reputations for their musicianship, even if they do not compose themselves. Generally however, it is the composers who are remembered more than the performers.
rewrite: The expectation that performers will realize a composer's original intentions in detail stems from the written transmission of music and the veneration of classical works. Throughout the 19th century, composers generally included more detailed instructions in their scores. Paradoxically, a trend admiring performers for new "interpretations" also emerged. Composers have even been known to praise a performer for achieving a better realization of their intent than they themselves imagined. Consequently, performers often gain high reputations for musicianship without being composers. Yet, it is typically the composers, rather than the performers, who are more remembered by history.

input: In the following months, NATO took a wide range of measures to respond to the threat of terrorism. On 22 November 2002, the member states of the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council (EAPC) decided on a Partnership Action Plan against Terrorism, which explicitly states, "EAPC States are committed to the protection and promotion of fundamental freedoms and human rights, as well as the rule of law, in combating terrorism." NATO started naval operations in the Mediterranean Sea designed to prevent the movement of terrorists or weapons of mass destruction as well as to enhance the security of shipping in general called Operation Active Endeavour.
rewrite: In response to the threat of terrorism, NATO implemented numerous measures over the subsequent months. A naval initiative, Operation Active Endeavour, commenced in the Mediterranean Sea to block terrorist movement and the transit of weapons of mass destruction, while also improving overall maritime security. Earlier, on 22 November 2002, the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council (EAPC) member states had adopted a Partnership Action Plan against Terrorism. This plan clearly affirms the commitment to uphold fundamental freedoms, human rights, and the rule of law in all counter-terrorism efforts.

input: Tourism is also an important industry in Miami. Along with finance and business, the beaches, conventions, festivals and events draw over 38 million visitors annually into the city, from across the country and around the world, spending $17.1 billion. The Art Deco District in South Beach, is reputed as one of the most glamorous in the world for its nightclubs, beaches, historical buildings, and shopping. Annual events such as the Sony Ericsson Open, Art Basel, Winter Music Conference, South Beach Wine & Food Festival, and Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Miami attract millions to the metropolis every year.
rewrite: Miami’s economy thrives not only on finance and business but also on a robust tourism sector. Each year, the city draws more than 38 million domestic and international visitors, who spend approximately $17.1 billion. They are attracted by its famous beaches, conventions, and vibrant festivals. South Beach’s Art Deco District is globally renowned for its nightlife, historic architecture, and shopping. Major annual events like Art Basel, the Sony Ericsson Open, the South Beach Wine & Food Festival, and Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Miami consistently draw millions to the metropolis.

input: Some NPOs which are particularly well known, often for the charitable or social nature of their activities performed during a long period of time, include Amnesty International, Oxfam, Rotary International, Kiwanis International, Carnegie Corporation of New York, Nourishing USA, DEMIRA Deutsche Minenräumer (German Mine Clearers), FIDH International Federation for Human Rights, Goodwill Industries, United Way, ACORN (now defunct), Habitat for Humanity, Teach For America, the Red Cross and Red Crescent organizations, UNESCO, IEEE, INCOSE, World Wide Fund for Nature, Heifer International, Translators Without Borders and SOS Children's Villages.
rewrite: Amnesty International, Oxfam, and the Red Cross are among many prominent non-profits. These organizations, such as Rotary International, UNESCO, and the World Wide Fund for Nature, are widely recognized for their long-standing charitable or social work. Other notable examples include Habitat for Humanity, United Way, IEEE, and SOS Children's Villages, alongside groups like Translators Without Borders, Heifer International, and the now-defunct ACORN. DEMIRA Deutsche Minenräumer, FIDH, Goodwill Industries, Teach For America, Carnegie Corporation of New York, Nourishing USA, Kiwanis International, and INCOSE also belong to this well-known group.

input: The United Nations designates Tuvalu as a least developed country (LDC) because of its limited potential for economic development, absence of exploitable resources and its small size and vulnerability to external economic and environmental shocks. Tuvalu participates in the Enhanced Integrated Framework for Trade-Related Technical Assistance to Least Developed Countries (EIF), which was established in October 1997 under the auspices of the World Trade Organisation. In 2013 Tuvalu deferred its graduation from least developed country (LDC) status to a developing country to 2015. Prime Minister Enele Sopoaga said that this deferral was necessary to maintain access by Tuvalu to the funds provided by the United Nations's National Adaptation Programme of Action (NAPA), as "Once Tuvalu graduates to a developed country, it will not be considered for funding assistance for climate change adaptation programmes like NAPA, which only goes to LDCs". Tuvalu had met targets so that Tuvalu was to graduate from LDC status. Prime minister, Enele Sopoaga wants the United Nations to reconsider its criteria for graduation from LDC status as not enough weight is given to the environmental plight of small island states like Tuvalu in the application of the Environmental Vulnerability Index (EVI).
rewrite: Due to its constrained economic prospects, lack of natural resources, small scale, and susceptibility to external economic and environmental disruptions, Tuvalu is classified by the United Nations as a least developed country (LDC). The nation is part of the Enhanced Integrated Framework for Trade-Related Technical Assistance to Least Developed Countries (EIF), an initiative launched under World Trade Organisation guidance in October 1997. Although Tuvalu had achieved the benchmarks to leave the LDC category, it postponed this graduation from 2013 to 2015. Prime Minister Enele Sopoaga explained this decision was essential to preserve Tuvalu's eligibility for United Nations climate adaptation funds, specifically the National Adaptation Programme of Action (NAPA), which is reserved for LDCs. Sopoaga has urged the United Nations to re-evaluate the standards for LDC graduation. He argues that the Environmental Vulnerability Index (EVI), used in this process, fails to adequately account for the severe environmental challenges facing small island states such as Tuvalu.

input: The same divine agencies who caused disease or harm also had the power to avert it, and so might be placated in advance. Divine consideration might be sought to avoid the inconvenient delays of a journey, or encounters with banditry, piracy and shipwreck, with due gratitude to be rendered on safe arrival or return. In times of great crisis, the Senate could decree collective public rites, in which Rome's citizens, including women and children, moved in procession from one temple to the next, supplicating the gods.
rewrite: The same divine forces capable of inflicting illness or misfortune also held the power to prevent it, making them worthy of preemptive appeasement. One might seek divine favor to bypass travel delays, bandits, piracy, or shipwreck, pledging thanks upon safe arrival. During major crises, the Senate could order public rites where Roman citizens—men, women, and children—processed between temples, collectively supplicating the gods.

input: Yerevan Vernissage (arts and crafts market), close to Republic Square, bustles with hundreds of vendors selling a variety of crafts on weekends and Wednesdays (though the selection is much reduced mid-week). The market offers woodcarving, antiques, fine lace, and the hand-knotted wool carpets and kilims that are a Caucasus specialty. Obsidian, which is found locally, is crafted into assortment of jewellery and ornamental objects. Armenian gold smithery enjoys a long tradition, populating one corner of the market with a selection of gold items. Soviet relics and souvenirs of recent Russian manufacture – nesting dolls, watches, enamel boxes and so on – are also available at the Vernisage.
rewrite: Near Republic Square, the Yerevan Vernissage arts and crafts market comes alive on weekends and Wednesdays, hosting hundreds of vendors. While the mid-week selection is smaller, the array of goods remains diverse. Visitors find Caucasus specialties like hand-knotted wool carpets and kilims, alongside woodcarvings, antiques, and fine lace. Locally sourced obsidian is shaped into jewellery and ornaments. Reflecting a long tradition, Armenian gold smithery fills one corner with its items. The market also offers Soviet relics and recent Russian souvenirs, including nesting dolls, watches, and enamel boxes.

input: Botany was greatly stimulated by the appearance of the first "modern" text book, Matthias Schleiden's Grundzüge der Wissenschaftlichen Botanik, published in English in 1849 as Principles of Scientific Botany. Schleiden was a microscopist and an early plant anatomist who co-founded the cell theory with Theodor Schwann and Rudolf Virchow and was among the first to grasp the significance of the cell nucleus that had been described by Robert Brown in 1831. In 1855, Adolf Fick formulated Fick's laws that enabled the calculation of the rates of molecular diffusion in biological systems.
rewrite: The publication of Matthias Schleiden's *Principles of Scientific Botany* in 1849, a key modern textbook, greatly stimulated botany. Schleiden, a microscopist and early plant anatomist, co-founded cell theory with Theodor Schwann and Rudolf Virchow. He was also among the first to recognize the importance of the cell nucleus, described by Robert Brown in 1831. Later, in 1855, Adolf Fick formulated Fick's laws, allowing the calculation of molecular diffusion rates in biological systems.

input: The Dean of the College of Cardinals, or Cardinal-dean, is the primus inter pares of the College of Cardinals, elected by the cardinal bishops holding suburbicarian sees from among their own number, an election, however, that must be approved by the Pope. Formerly the position of dean belonged by right to the longest-serving of the cardinal bishops.
rewrite: The Dean of the College of Cardinals, known as the Cardinal-dean, is elected by the cardinal bishops from their own ranks and approved by the Pope. This role is the first among equals. Historically, the longest-serving cardinal bishop held the position by right.

input: One of the most important victories of the magnates was the late 16th century right to create ordynacja's (similar to majorats), which ensured that a family which gained wealth and power could more easily preserve this. Ordynacje's of families of Radziwiłł, Zamoyski, Potocki or Lubomirski often rivalled the estates of the king and were important power bases for the magnates.
rewrite: A key triumph for the magnates came in the late 16th century: the right to establish ordynacja's (akin to majorats). This allowed wealthy, powerful families to better secure their status. The vast ordynacje's of clans like the Radziwiłł, Zamoyski, Potocki, or Lubomirski frequently rivaled royal estates, serving as crucial power bases.

input: Adolescence is frequently characterized by a transformation of an adolescent's understanding of the world, the rational direction towards a life course, and the active seeking of new ideas rather than the unquestioning acceptance of adult authority. An adolescent begins to develop a unique belief system through his or her interaction with social, familial, and cultural environments. While organized religion is not necessarily a part of every adolescent's life experience, youth are still held responsible for forming a set of beliefs about themselves, the world around them, and whatever higher powers they may or may not believe in. This process is often accompanied or aided by cultural traditions that intend to provide a meaningful transition to adulthood through a ceremony, ritual, confirmation, or rite of passage.
rewrite: During adolescence, young people often shift from passively accepting adult authority to actively exploring new ideas. This period involves reshaping one’s worldview and deliberately choosing a path in life. Through interactions with family, society, and culture, each adolescent forms a personal belief system. Although not every youth engages with organized religion, all are tasked with developing convictions about themselves, their surroundings, and any higher powers they might acknowledge. Cultural traditions frequently support this journey by offering ceremonies, rituals, confirmations, or rites of passage. These practices aim to mark a meaningful transition into adulthood.

input: Special procedures apply to legislation passed by Tynwald, the legislature of the Isle of Man. Before the lordship of the Island was purchased by the British Crown in 1765 (the Revestment), the assent of the Lord of Mann to a bill was signified by letter to the governor. After 1765, royal assent was at first signified by letter from the Secretary of State to the governor; but, during the British Regency, the practice began of granting royal assent by Order in Council, which continues to this day, though limited to exceptional cases since 1981.
rewrite: Legislation passed by Tynwald, the Isle of Man's legislature, follows special procedures. Prior to 1765, when the British Crown purchased the lordship (the Revestment), the Lord of Mann signified assent to a bill via letter to the governor. After that, royal assent was initially given by letter from the Secretary of State. However, during the British Regency, the practice shifted to granting assent by Order in Council. This method continues now, though it has been restricted to exceptional cases since 1981.

input: The franchise was first created in 1997 as a series of virtual pets, akin to—and influenced in style by—the contemporary Tamagotchi or nano Giga Pet toys. The creatures were first designed to look cute and iconic even on the devices' small screens; later developments had them created with a harder-edged style influenced by American comics. The franchise gained momentum with its first anime incarnation, Digimon Adventure, and an early video game, Digimon World, both released in 1999. Several seasons of the anime and films based on them have aired, and the video game series has expanded into genres such as role-playing, racing, fighting, and MMORPGs. Other media forms have also been released.
rewrite: First launched in 1997, the franchise began as a series of virtual pets, stylistically similar to popular toys like Tamagotchi and nano Giga Pets. Initially, the creatures were designed to appear cute and recognizable on small screens, though later iterations adopted a sharper, American comic-inspired aesthetic. Momentum grew significantly in 1999 with the debut of the anime *Digimon Adventure* and the video game *Digimon World*. Since then, numerous anime seasons and films have followed, while the game series has branched into various genres, including role-playing, racing, fighting, and MMORPGs. Additional media formats have also been produced.

input: Around 1300, centuries of prosperity and growth in Europe came to a halt. A series of famines and plagues, including the Great Famine of 1315–1317 and the Black Death, reduced the population to around half of what it was before the calamities. Along with depopulation came social unrest and endemic warfare. France and England experienced serious peasant uprisings, such as the Jacquerie and the Peasants' Revolt, as well as over a century of intermittent conflict in the Hundred Years' War. To add to the many problems of the period, the unity of the Catholic Church was shattered by the Western Schism. Collectively these events are sometimes called the Crisis of the Late Middle Ages.
rewrite: Beginning around 1300, Europe's long era of expansion and prosperity ended abruptly. Devastating famines, notably the Great Famine of 1315–1317, and the Black Death decimated the population, cutting it by nearly half. This catastrophic depopulation triggered widespread social turmoil and persistent warfare. For over a century, France and England were embroiled in the intermittent battles of the Hundred Years' War, alongside major peasant revolts like the Jacquerie and the Peasants' Revolt. Further compounding these crises, the Catholic Church's unity fractured during the Western Schism. This confluence of disasters is often termed the Crisis of the Late Middle Ages.

input: La Cueva De Las Ventanas (The Cave of Windows), a series of cliff dwellings along an important trade route, and Las Jarillas Cave scrambled along the canyons of the Sierra Madre in Northwestern Chihuahua date between AD 1205 and 1260 and belong to the Paquimé culture. Cuarenta Casas is thought to have been a branch settlement from Paquime to protect the trade route from attack. Archaeologists believe the civilization began to decline during the 13th century and by the 15th century the inhabitants of Paquime sought refuge in the Sierra Madre Occidental while others are thought to have emigrated north and joined the Ancestral Pueblo peoples. According to anthropologist current natives tribes (Yaqui, Mayo, Opata, and Tarahumara) are descendants of the Casas Grandes culture.
rewrite: Dating from approximately AD 1205 to 1260, the cliff dwellings of La Cueva De Las Ventanas and Las Jarillas Cave in northwestern Chihuahua’s Sierra Madre were part of the Paquimé culture. Cuarenta Casas is considered a protective outpost for their trade routes. By the 13th century, this civilization entered decline. Within two centuries, inhabitants sought refuge in the Sierra Madre Occidental or migrated north to join Ancestral Pueblo communities. Anthropologists link present-day indigenous groups like the Yaqui, Mayo, Opata, and Tarahumara to this Casas Grandes heritage.

input: Three other efforts to improve regulation of international pesticide trade are the United Nations London Guidelines for the Exchange of Information on Chemicals in International Trade and the United Nations Codex Alimentarius Commission.[citation needed] The former seeks to implement procedures for ensuring that prior informed consent exists between countries buying and selling pesticides, while the latter seeks to create uniform standards for maximum levels of pesticide residues among participating countries. Both initiatives operate on a voluntary basis.
rewrite: Three initiatives aim to better regulate international pesticide trade, including the United Nations London Guidelines and the Codex Alimentarius Commission. The Guidelines promote prior informed consent between trading nations, and the Commission works to harmonize maximum pesticide residue limits. Both of these United Nations efforts function voluntarily.

input: Christianity (59%), particularly Catholicism (33%), was the most prevalently practiced religion in New York as of 2014, followed by Judaism, with approximately 1.1 million Jews in New York City, over half living in Brooklyn. Islam ranks third in New York City, with official estimates ranging between 600,000 and 1,000,000 observers and including 10% of the city's public schoolchildren, followed by Hinduism, Buddhism, and a variety of other religions, as well as atheism. In 2014, 24% self-identified with no organized religious affiliation.
rewrite: As of 2014, Christianity, at 59% of the population, was the most common religion in New York, with Catholicism making up 33%. Judaism followed, represented by about 1.1 million people in New York City, more than half residing in Brooklyn. The third most observed faith was Islam, with an estimated 600,000 to 1,000,000 adherents, accounting for 10% of public school students. Other groups included Hinduism, Buddhism, various religions, and atheism, while 24% reported no organized religious affiliation.

input: Other awards and recognition for Popper included the City of Vienna Prize for the Humanities (1965), Karl Renner Prize (1978), Austrian Decoration for Science and Art (1980), Dr. Leopold Lucas Prize (1981), Ring of Honour of the City of Vienna (1983) and the Premio Internazionale of the Italian Federico Nietzsche Society (1988). In 1992, he was awarded the Kyoto Prize in Arts and Philosophy for "symbolising the open spirit of the 20th century" and for his "enormous influence on the formation of the modern intellectual climate".
rewrite: Popper received numerous other awards and recognitions. Among these were the City of Vienna Prize for the Humanities (1965), the Karl Renner Prize (1978), and the Austrian Decoration for Science and Art (1980). Later honors included the Dr. Leopold Lucas Prize (1981), the Ring of Honour of the City of Vienna (1983), and the Premio Internazionale from the Italian Federico Nietzsche Society (1988). In 1992, he was granted the Kyoto Prize in Arts and Philosophy for symbolizing the open spirit of the 20th century and his vast influence on the modern intellectual climate.

input: The traditional parish system persisted until the Reconstruction Era, when counties were imposed.[citation needed] Nevertheless, traditional parishes still exist in various capacities, mainly as public service districts. When the city of Charleston was formed, it was defined by the limits of the Parish of St. Philip and St. Michael, now also includes parts of St. James' Parish, St. George's Parish, St. Andrew's Parish, and St. John's Parish, although the last two are mostly still incorporated rural parishes.
rewrite: During the Reconstruction Era, counties replaced the longstanding parish system, though parishes endure today primarily as public service districts. Charleston’s original boundaries matched those of the Parish of St. Philip and St. Michael. The city has since expanded to include sections of St. James’, St. George’s, St. Andrew’s, and St. John’s Parishes, with the latter two remaining largely rural and incorporated.

input: The last glacial period of the current ice age ended about 10,000 years ago. Ice melt caused world sea levels to rise about 35 metres (115 ft) in the early part of the Holocene. In addition, many areas above about 40 degrees north latitude had been depressed by the weight of the Pleistocene glaciers and rose as much as 180 metres (591 ft) over the late Pleistocene and Holocene, and are still rising today. The sea level rise and temporary land depression allowed temporary marine incursions into areas that are now far from the sea. Holocene marine fossils are known from Vermont, Quebec, Ontario and Michigan. Other than higher latitude temporary marine incursions associated with glacial depression, Holocene fossils are found primarily in lakebed, floodplain and cave deposits. Holocene marine deposits along low-latitude coastlines are rare because the rise in sea levels during the period exceeds any likely upthrusting of non-glacial origin. Post-glacial rebound in Scandinavia resulted in the emergence of coastal areas around the Baltic Sea, including much of Finland. The region continues to rise, still causing weak earthquakes across Northern Europe. The equivalent event in North America was the rebound of Hudson Bay, as it shrank from its larger, immediate post-glacial Tyrrell Sea phase, to near its present boundaries.
rewrite: Approximately 10,000 years ago marked the conclusion of the last glacial period within the ongoing ice age. This melting ice triggered a significant rise in global sea levels, increasing them by about 35 metres (115 ft) early in the Holocene epoch. Simultaneously, vast regions situated above roughly 40 degrees north latitude, which had been weighed down by Pleistocene ice sheets, experienced uplift of up to 180 metres (591 ft) from the late Pleistocene through the Holocene, a process that continues in the present day. The combination of rising seas and this temporary land depression enabled the sea to encroach inland into areas now distant from coastlines. Evidence of this exists in the form of Holocene marine fossils discovered in places like Vermont, Quebec, Ontario, and Michigan. Generally, Holocene fossils are mainly located in lakebed, floodplain, and cave sediments, aside from these higher-latitude marine incursions linked to glacial depression. Low-latitude coastlines seldom preserve Holocene marine deposits, as the era's substantial sea level rise outpaced any probable tectonic uplift not caused by glaciers. In Scandinavia, post-glacial rebound lifted coastal zones around the Baltic Sea, forming much of Finland's landmass; this ongoing uplift still generates minor earthquakes in Northern Europe. A comparable phenomenon in North America was the rebound of the Hudson Bay region, which gradually receded from its larger post-glacial form, known as the Tyrrell Sea, to approximately its current size.

input: The Federal Council constitutes the federal government, directs the federal administration and serves as collective Head of State. It is a collegial body of seven members, elected for a four-year mandate by the Federal Assembly which also exercises oversight over the Council.
