The President of the Confederation is elected by the Assembly from among the seven members, traditionally in rotation and for a one-year term; the President chairs the government and assumes representative functions. However, the president is a primus inter pares with no additional powers, and remains the head of a department within the administration.
rewrite: Composed of seven members, the Federal Council acts as both the federal government and the collective Head of State, while also directing the federal administration. The Federal Assembly elects this collegial body for four-year terms and maintains oversight of its work. From among the seven, the Assembly elects the President of the Confederation, typically following a rotational system for a one-year term. The President chairs the government and performs representative duties but remains a first among equals with no extra powers, continuing to lead a departmental portfolio.

input: Washington University has a large number of student-run musical groups on campus, including 12 official a cappella groups. The Pikers, an all-male group, is the oldest such group on campus. The Greenleafs, an all-female group is the oldest (and only) female group on campus. The Mosaic Whispers, founded in 1991, is the oldest co-ed group on campus. They have produced 9 albums and have appeared on a number of compilation albums, including Ben Folds' Ben Folds Presents: University A Cappella! The Amateurs, who also appeared on this album, is another co-ed a cappella group on campus, founded in 1991. They have recorded seven albums and toured extensively. After Dark is a co-ed a cappella group founded in 2001. It has released three albums and has won several Contemporary A Capella Recording (CARA) awards. In 2008 the group performed on MSNBC during coverage of the vice presidential debate with specially written songs about Joe Biden and Sarah Palin. The Ghost Lights, founded in 2010, is the campus's newest and only Broadway, Movies, and Television soundtrack group. They have performed multiple philanthropic concerts in the greater St. Louis area and were honored in November 2010 with the opportunity to perform for Nobel Laureate Douglass North at his birthday celebration.
rewrite: Washington University hosts a diverse array of student-managed musical ensembles. Among these are twelve official a cappella groups. The oldest all-male group is The Pikers, while The Greenleafs holds the distinction of being the oldest and only all-female group. In the co-ed category, The Mosaic Whispers, established in 1991, is the longest-running. This group has released nine albums and was featured on the compilation *Ben Folds Presents: University A Cappella!*, which also included another co-ed group founded the same year, The Amateurs. The Amateurs have recorded seven albums and undertaken wide-ranging tours. Founded later, in 2001, the co-ed group After Dark has produced three albums and earned multiple Contemporary A Capella Recording (CARA) awards. This group gained national exposure in 2008 by performing original songs about Joe Biden and Sarah Palin on MSNBC during vice presidential debate coverage. The most recent addition is The Ghost Lights, formed in 2010 as the sole group dedicated to Broadway, movie, and television soundtracks. They have staged several charity concerts in the St. Louis region and had the honor of performing for Nobel Laureate Douglass North at his birthday celebration in November 2010.

input: Not all introduced species are invasive, nor all invasive species deliberately introduced. In cases such as the zebra mussel, invasion of US waterways was unintentional. In other cases, such as mongooses in Hawaii, the introduction is deliberate but ineffective (nocturnal rats were not vulnerable to the diurnal mongoose). In other cases, such as oil palms in Indonesia and Malaysia, the introduction produces substantial economic benefits, but the benefits are accompanied by costly unintended consequences.
rewrite: Introduced species are not always invasive, nor are invasive species always brought in intentionally. For instance, zebra mussels invaded US waterways accidentally. Deliberate introductions can be ineffective, like mongooses in Hawaii failing to control nocturnal rats. Conversely, species like oil palms in Indonesia and Malaysia yield major economic gains, yet these come with significant unintended costs.

input: The shift in the Cubs' fortunes was characterized June 23 on the "NBC Saturday Game of the Week" contest against the St. Louis Cardinals. it has since been dubbed simply "The Sandberg Game." With the nation watching and Wrigley Field packed, Sandberg emerged as a superstar with not one, but two game-tying home runs against Cardinals closer Bruce Sutter. With his shots in the 9th and 10th innings Wrigley Field erupted and Sandberg set the stage for a comeback win that cemented the Cubs as the team to beat in the East. No one would catch them, except the Padres in the playoffs.
rewrite: On June 23, during the nationally televised "NBC Saturday Game of the Week" against the St. Louis Cardinals, the Cubs' changing fortunes were dramatically illustrated. This contest, now known simply as "The Sandberg Game," saw Ryne Sandberg become a superstar before a packed Wrigley Field. He hit two game-tying home runs off Cardinals closer Bruce Sutter in the 9th and 10th innings, causing the stadium to erupt. These shots set up a comeback victory that established the Cubs as the team to beat in the East, a status only later challenged by the Padres in the playoffs.

input: There is no single definition of an "aircraft carrier", and modern navies use several variants of the type. These variants are sometimes categorized as sub-types of aircraft carriers, and sometimes as distinct types of naval aviation-capable ships. Aircraft carriers may be classified according to the type of aircraft they carry and their operational assignments. Admiral Sir Mark Stanhope, former head of the Royal Navy, has said that "To put it simply, countries that aspire to strategic international influence have aircraft carriers".
rewrite: No universal definition exists for an "aircraft carrier," with modern navies employing multiple variants. These are sometimes considered sub-types and other times as separate classes of aviation-capable ships. Classification can depend on the embarked aircraft and their operational roles. As former Royal Navy head Admiral Sir Mark Stanhope noted, nations seeking strategic global influence possess aircraft carriers.

input: Between 1872 and 1905, a series of protests took place in response to the sale of concessions to foreigners by Nasser od Din and Mozaffar od Din shahs of Qajar, and led to the Iranian Constitutional Revolution. The first Iranian Constitution and the first national parliament of Iran were founded in 1906, through the ongoing revolution. The Constitution included the official recognition of Iran's three religious minorities, namely Christians, Zoroastrians, and Jews, which has remained a basis in the legislation of Iran since then.
rewrite: From 1872 to 1905, protests arose against the Qajar shahs Nasser od Din and Mozaffar od Din for selling concessions to foreigners, sparking the Iranian Constitutional Revolution. This ongoing movement established Iran's first national parliament and Constitution in 1906. That document formally recognized the nation's three religious minorities—Christians, Zoroastrians, and Jews—a provision that has since remained foundational in Iranian law.

input: Saint FM provided a local radio service for the island which was also available on internet radio and relayed in Ascension Island. The station was not government funded. It was launched in January 2005 and closed on 21 December 2012. It broadcast news, features and music in collaboration with its sister newspaper, the St Helena Independent (which continues).
rewrite: Saint FM, a non-government funded station, launched in January 2005 and served the island locally, online, and via relay in Ascension Island. Broadcasting news, features, and music alongside its sister newspaper, the St Helena Independent, it operated until closing on December 21, 2012. The newspaper continues.

input: The Red Rose of Lancaster is the county flower found on the county's heraldic badge and flag. The rose was a symbol of the House of Lancaster, immortalised in the verse "In the battle for England's head/York was white, Lancaster red" (referring to the 15th-century Wars of the Roses). The traditional Lancashire flag, a red rose on a white field, was not officially registered. When an attempt was made to register it with the Flag Institute it was found that it was officially registered by Montrose in Scotland, several hundred years earlier with the Lyon Office. Lancashire's official flag is registered as a red rose on a gold field.
rewrite: Found on Lancashire’s heraldic badge and flag, the Red Rose of Lancaster serves as the county flower. It historically symbolized the House of Lancaster, a connection captured in the lines: “In the battle for England's head/York was white, Lancaster red,” referencing the Wars of the Roses. The traditional design—a red rose on a white field—was never officially registered for Lancashire. An attempt to register it revealed the Flag Institute already listed it for Montrose in Scotland, registered centuries prior with the Lyon Office. Consequently, Lancashire’s official flag features a red rose on a gold field.

input: The activities that constitute illegal corruption differ depending on the country or jurisdiction. For instance, some political funding practices that are legal in one place may be illegal in another. In some cases, government officials have broad or ill-defined powers, which make it difficult to distinguish between legal and illegal actions. Worldwide, bribery alone is estimated to involve over 1 trillion US dollars annually. A state of unrestrained political corruption is known as a kleptocracy, literally meaning "rule by thieves".
rewrite: Definitions of illegal corruption vary by country or jurisdiction. Practices like political funding permitted in one place may be forbidden elsewhere. Broad or vague official powers can further blur the line between legal and illegal acts. Globally, bribery alone accounts for an estimated 1 trillion US dollars each year. When such corruption becomes unrestrained, the state may be termed a kleptocracy, or "rule by thieves."

input: On February 14, 2009, The Walt Disney Company debuted "The American Idol Experience" at its Disney's Hollywood Studios theme park at the Walt Disney World Resort in Florida. In this live production, co-produced by 19 Entertainment, park guests chose from a list of songs and auditioned privately for Disney cast members. Those selected then performed on a stage in a 1000-seat theater replicating the Idol set. Three judges, whose mannerisms and style mimicked those of the real Idol judges, critiqued the performances. Audience members then voted for their favorite performer. There were several preliminary-round shows during the day that culminated in a "finals" show in the evening where one of the winners of the previous rounds that day was selected as the overall winner. The winner of the finals show received a "Dream Ticket" that granted them front-of-the-line privileges at any future American Idol audition. The attraction closed on August 30, 2014.
rewrite: Debuting on February 14, 2009, at Disney's Hollywood Studios in Florida, "The American Idol Experience" was a live attraction co-produced by 19 Entertainment. Park guests could audition privately for Disney cast members, selecting from a provided song list. Successful participants then performed on a replica Idol stage within a 1,000-seat theater. Their performances were critiqued by three judges who mimicked the style of the television show's panel, after which the audience voted for a favorite. Multiple preliminary shows were held throughout the day, each culminating in an evening finals show. This final round featured winners from the earlier sessions, with one being named the overall winner. That victor received a "Dream Ticket," ensuring front-of-the-line access at any future American Idol audition. The attraction concluded its run on August 30, 2014.

input: Leading up to the American Civil War, Baptists became embroiled in the controversy over slavery in the United States. Whereas in the First Great Awakening, Methodist and Baptist preachers had opposed slavery and urged manumission, over the decades they made more of an accommodation with the institution. They worked with slaveholders in the South to urge a paternalistic institution. Both denominations made direct appeals to slaves and free blacks for conversion. The Baptists particularly allowed them active roles in congregations. By the mid-19th century, northern Baptists tended to oppose slavery. As tensions increased, in 1844 the Home Mission Society refused to appoint a slaveholder as a missionary who had been proposed by Georgia. It noted that missionaries could not take servants with them, and also that the Board did not want to appear to condone slavery.
rewrite: In the decades before the American Civil War, Baptists in the United States were deeply involved in the national conflict over slavery. This represented a shift from the First Great Awakening, when Baptist and Methodist preachers had advocated for manumission and opposed the institution. Over time, however, they reached a greater accommodation with it, cooperating with southern slaveholders to promote a paternalistic system. Both denominations actively sought to convert slaves and free Black people, with Baptists notably offering them active roles within congregations. By the mid-1800s, northern Baptists generally held antislavery views. Rising tensions culminated in 1844 when the Home Mission Society declined to appoint a slaveholder nominated by Georgia as a missionary. The Society stated that missionaries could not bring servants and that the Board wished to avoid any appearance of condoning slavery.

input: With the occupation by Napoleon, Portugal began a slow but inexorable decline that lasted until the 20th century. This decline was hastened by the independence in 1822 of the country's largest colonial possession, Brazil. In 1807, as Napoleon's army closed in on Lisbon, the Prince Regent João VI of Portugal transferred his court to Brazil and established Rio de Janeiro as the capital of the Portuguese Empire. In 1815, Brazil was declared a Kingdom and the Kingdom of Portugal was united with it, forming a pluricontinental State, the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves.
rewrite: Following Napoleon's invasion, Portugal entered a prolonged period of decline, which extended into the twentieth century. This process accelerated when Brazil, its most significant colony, gained independence in 1822. Earlier, as Napoleonic forces approached Lisbon in 1807, Prince Regent João VI relocated the royal court to Brazil, making Rio de Janeiro the empire's capital. Subsequently, in 1815, Brazil was elevated to a kingdom, uniting with Portugal to create the pluricontinental United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves.

input: The titles of state supreme court vary, which can cause confusion between jurisdictions because one state may use a name for its highest court that another uses for a lower court. In New York, Maryland, and the District of Columbia the highest court is called the Court of Appeals, a name used by many states for their intermediate appellate courts. Further, trial courts of general jurisdiction in New York are called the Supreme Court, and the intermediate appellate court is called the Supreme Court, Appellate Division. In West Virginia, the highest court of the state is the Supreme Court of Appeals. In Maine and Massachusetts the highest court is styled the "Supreme Judicial Court"; the last is the oldest appellate court of continuous operation in the Western Hemisphere.
rewrite: The names of state supreme courts differ across jurisdictions, often leading to confusion, as a title used for the highest court in one state may designate a lower court in another. For instance, New York, Maryland, and the District of Columbia label their highest court the Court of Appeals, a term many states apply to intermediate appellate courts. In New York, trial courts of general jurisdiction are named the Supreme Court, while its intermediate appellate body is the Supreme Court, Appellate Division. West Virginia’s highest court is the Supreme Court of Appeals. Meanwhile, Maine and Massachusetts use "Supreme Judicial Court" for their top courts, with Massachusetts holding the distinction of being the Western Hemisphere’s oldest continuously operating appellate court.

input: A fundamental problem with software testing is that testing under all combinations of inputs and preconditions (initial state) is not feasible, even with a simple product.:17-18 This means that the number of defects in a software product can be very large and defects that occur infrequently are difficult to find in testing. More significantly, non-functional dimensions of quality (how it is supposed to be versus what it is supposed to do)—usability, scalability, performance, compatibility, reliability—can be highly subjective; something that constitutes sufficient value to one person may be intolerable to another.
rewrite: Testing all possible input combinations and initial states is infeasible, even for simple software, making it a fundamental challenge. Consequently, many defects can remain, with rare ones being particularly hard to detect. Beyond functionality, non-functional aspects like usability, scalability, performance, compatibility, and reliability introduce further subjectivity. Perceptions of quality vary greatly; what one person finds acceptable, another may deem entirely insufficient.

input: Austrian-born Adolf Hitler had a lifelong romantic fascination with the Alps and by the 1930s established a home in the Obersalzberg region outside of Berchtesgaden. His first visit to the area was in 1923 and he maintained a strong tie there until the end of his life. At the end of World War II the US Army occupied Obersalzberg, to prevent Hitler from retreating with the Wehrmacht into the mountains.
rewrite: Adolf Hitler, who was Austrian by birth, felt a lasting romantic attachment to the Alps. He first visited the Obersalzberg area near Berchtesgaden in 1923 and by the 1930s had established a home there, maintaining a strong connection until his death. To block any potential retreat by Hitler and the Wehrmacht into the mountains, the US Army occupied Obersalzberg at the close of World War II.

input: Stone and brick became the city's building materials of choice after the construction of wood-frame houses was limited in the aftermath of the Great Fire of 1835. A distinctive feature of many of the city's buildings is the wooden roof-mounted water towers. In the 1800s, the city required their installation on buildings higher than six stories to prevent the need for excessively high water pressures at lower elevations, which could break municipal water pipes. Garden apartments became popular during the 1920s in outlying areas, such as Jackson Heights.
rewrite: Following the Great Fire of 1835, limits on wood-frame construction made stone and brick the city's preferred building materials. A common sight on many buildings became the wooden roof-mounted water tower. Mandated in the 1800s for structures over six stories, these towers prevented excessive water pressure at lower levels that could rupture city pipes. Later, during the 1920s, garden apartments grew popular in outlying areas like Jackson Heights.

input: The United States Mint produces Proof Sets specifically for collectors and speculators. Silver Proofs tend to be the standard designs but with the dime, quarter, and half dollar containing 90% silver. Starting in 1983 and ending in 1997, the Mint also produced proof sets containing the year's commemorative coins alongside the regular coins. Another type of proof set is the Presidential Dollar Proof Set where four special $1 coins are minted each year featuring a president. Because of budget constraints and increasing stockpiles of these relatively unpopular coins, the production of new Presidential dollar coins for circulation was suspended on December 13, 2011, by U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy F. Geithner. Future minting of such coins will be made solely for collectors.
rewrite: Proof Sets from the United States Mint are designed for collectors and speculators. Silver Proofs typically feature standard designs, though the dime, quarter, and half dollar are struck in 90% silver. Between 1983 and 1997, the Mint also issued sets that included the year's commemorative coins alongside the regular issues. Another variety is the Presidential Dollar Proof Set, containing four special dollar coins honoring presidents, released annually. Due to budget limits and growing inventories of these less-circulated coins, U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy F. Geithner halted new Presidential dollar coin production for general circulation on December 13, 2011. Any future minting will be exclusively for collectors.

input: Sicily fell under the control of the Holy Roman Empire in 1194. Palermo was the preferred city of the Emperor Frederick II. Muslims of Palermo emigrated or were expelled during Holy Roman rule. After an interval of Angevin rule (1266–1282), Sicily came under control of the Aragon and Barcelona dynasties. By 1330, Palermo's population had declined to 51,000. From 1479 until 1713 Palermo was ruled by the Kingdom of Spain, and again between 1717 and 1718. Palermo was also under Savoy control between 1713 and 1717 and 1718–1720 as a result of the Treaty of Utrecht. It was also ruled by Austria between 1720 and 1734.
rewrite: In 1194, Sicily came under Holy Roman Empire control, with Palermo favored by Emperor Frederick II. During this period, the city's Muslims either emigrated or were expelled. Following a brief phase of Angevin rule from 1266 to 1282, the Aragon and Barcelona dynasties took power. By 1330, Palermo's population had fallen to 51,000. From 1479 to 1713, the Kingdom of Spain governed, with a brief return from 1717 to 1718. Intermittently, due to the Treaty of Utrecht, Savoy controlled the city from 1713 to 1717 and again from 1718 to 1720. Austrian rule then lasted from 1720 until 1734.

input: During the 1890s, the Armenian Revolutionary Federation, commonly known as Dashnaktsutyun, became active within the Ottoman Empire with the aim of unifying the various small groups in the empire that were advocating for reform and defending Armenian villages from massacres that were widespread in some of the Armenian-populated areas of the empire. Dashnaktsutyun members also formed fedayi groups that defended Armenian civilians through armed resistance. The Dashnaks also worked for the wider goal of creating a "free, independent and unified" Armenia, although they sometimes set aside this goal in favor of a more realistic approach, such as advocating autonomy.
rewrite: Active within the Ottoman Empire during the 1890s, the Armenian Revolutionary Federation (Dashnaktsutyun) sought to unify small reform-advocating groups and defend Armenian villages from widespread massacres in certain regions. Its members organized armed fedayi units to protect civilians through resistance. While working toward the broader objective of a "free, independent and unified" Armenia, the Dashnaks occasionally adopted a more pragmatic stance, setting aside this ideal in favor of advocating for autonomy.

input: There are many non-incandescent light sources, such as the fluorescent lamp, high-intensity discharge lamps and LED lamps, which have higher luminous efficiency, and some have been designed to be retrofitted in fixtures for incandescent lights. These devices produce light by luminescence. These lamps produce discrete spectral lines and do not have the broad "tail" of invisible infrared emissions. By careful selection of which electron energy level transitions are used, and fluorescent coatings which modify the spectral distribution, the spectrum emitted can be tuned to mimic the appearance of incandescent sources, or other different color temperatures of white light. Due to the discrete spectral lines rather than a continuous spectrum, the light is not ideal for applications such as photography and cinematography.
rewrite: Non-incandescent light sources, including fluorescent lamps, high-intensity discharge lamps, and LEDs, operate through luminescence and offer higher luminous efficiency. Many are designed as direct replacements for traditional incandescent fixtures. Unlike incandescent bulbs, these lamps emit discrete spectral lines without a broad spectrum of invisible infrared radiation. Their output can be carefully adjusted by selecting specific electron energy level transitions and applying fluorescent coatings, allowing the spectrum to mimic the warm glow of incandescent light or achieve various white color temperatures. However, because the light is produced from distinct spectral lines rather than a continuous spectrum, it is often less suitable for applications like photography and cinematography.

input: In the audition rounds, 121 contestants were selected from around 10,000 who attended the auditions. These were cut to 30 for the semifinal, with ten going on to the finals. One semifinalist, Delano Cagnolatti, was disqualified for lying to evade the show's age limit. One of the early favorites, Tamyra Gray, was eliminated at the top four, the first of several such shock eliminations that were to be repeated in later seasons. Christina Christian was hospitalized before the top six result show due to chest pains and palpitations, and she was eliminated while she was in the hospital. Jim Verraros was the first openly gay contestant on the show; his sexual orientation was revealed in his online journal, however it was removed during the competition after a request from the show producers over concerns that it might be unfairly influencing votes.
rewrite: From approximately 10,000 audition attendees, 121 contestants were initially chosen. This group was later reduced to 30 semifinalists, and finally to 10 finalists. Among the semifinalists, Delano Cagnolatti faced disqualification for dishonesty regarding the program's age requirement. The competition saw notable early departures, including early favorite Tamyra Gray, whose elimination in the top four marked the first of several surprising outcomes that would recur in future seasons. Before the top six results show, Christina Christian was hospitalized with chest pains and palpitations, leading to her elimination from her hospital bed. Additionally, Jim Verraros participated as the first openly gay contestant; his online journal revealed his sexual orientation, though the show's producers requested its removal during the competition, fearing it could unduly sway voting.

input: The English Province was a component of the international order from which it obtained its laws, direction, and instructions. It was also, however, a group of Englishmen. Its direct supervisors were from England, and the members of the English Province dwelt and labored in English cities, towns, villages, and roadways. English and European ingredients constantly came in contact. The international side of the province's existence influenced the national, and the national responded to, adapted, and sometimes constrained the international.
rewrite: As part of an international order, the English Province received its laws, guidance, and instructions from abroad. Yet it remained a community of Englishmen, living and working in England's urban and rural settings under direct supervisors from England. Constant contact occurred between English and European elements. While the province's international dimension shaped its national character, this national aspect in turn responded to, adapted, and at times limited those international influences.

input: Plymouth has about 150 churches and its Roman Catholic cathedral (1858) is in Stonehouse. The city's oldest church is St Andrew's (Anglican) located at the top of Royal Parade—it is the largest parish church in Devon and has been a site of gathering since AD 800. The city also includes five Baptist churches, over twenty Methodist chapels, and thirteen Roman Catholic churches. In 1831 the first Brethren assembly in England, a movement of conservative non-denominational Evangelical Christians, was established in the city, so that Brethren are often called Plymouth Brethren, although the movement did not begin locally.
rewrite: Plymouth is home to approximately 150 churches. Its Roman Catholic cathedral, dating from 1858, is situated in Stonehouse. The largest parish church in Devon is the city's oldest, the Anglican St Andrew's, positioned atop Royal Parade—a gathering site since 800 AD. Among the city's many places of worship are five Baptist churches, over twenty Methodist chapels, and thirteen Roman Catholic churches. Notably, the first Brethren assembly in England, a conservative non-denominational Evangelical movement, was established here in 1831. This is why its followers are often called Plymouth Brethren, despite the movement not originating locally.

input: The appearance of more systematic, abstract thinking is another notable aspect of cognitive development during adolescence. For example, adolescents find it easier than children to comprehend the sorts of higher-order abstract logic inherent in puns, proverbs, metaphors, and analogies. Their increased facility permits them to appreciate the ways in which language can be used to convey multiple messages, such as satire, metaphor, and sarcasm. (Children younger than age nine often cannot comprehend sarcasm at all.) This also permits the application of advanced reasoning and logical processes to social and ideological matters such as interpersonal relationships, politics, philosophy, religion, morality, friendship, faith, democracy, fairness, and honesty.
rewrite: A key feature of adolescent cognitive development is the emergence of more systematic and abstract thought. This allows teenagers to grasp higher-order logic in puns, proverbs, metaphors, and analogies more readily than younger children. With this ability, they can better understand nuanced uses of language, including satire, metaphor, and sarcasm—the latter often being entirely lost on children under nine. Furthermore, this advanced reasoning can be applied to social and ideological concepts, such as relationships, politics, philosophy, morality, and fairness.

input: The earliest recorded history of the region dates back to about 500 BCE when much, if not all, of modern Tajikistan was part of the Achaemenid Empire. Some authors have also suggested that in the 7th and 6th century BCE parts of modern Tajikistan, including territories in the Zeravshan valley, formed part of Kambojas before it became part of the Achaemenid Empire. After the region's conquest by Alexander the Great it became part of the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, a successor state of Alexander's empire. Northern Tajikistan (the cities of Khujand and Panjakent) was part of Sogdia, a collection of city-states which was overrun by Scythians and Yuezhi nomadic tribes around 150 BCE. The Silk Road passed through the region and following the expedition of Chinese explorer Zhang Qian during the reign of Wudi (141–87 BCE) commercial relations between Han China and Sogdiana flourished. Sogdians played a major role in facilitating trade and also worked in other capacities, as farmers, carpetweavers, glassmakers, and woodcarvers.
rewrite: Modern Tajikistan's history can be traced to approximately 500 BCE, when it was largely incorporated into the Achaemenid Empire. Even earlier, during the 7th and 6th centuries BCE, some scholars propose that areas including the Zeravshan valley belonged to the Kambojas prior to Achaemenid rule. Following conquests by Alexander the Great, the region later formed a segment of the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom. Northern areas, such as Khujand and Panjakent, were once part of Sogdia, a coalition of city-states overrun by Scythian and Yuezhi nomads around 150 BCE. The Silk Road traversed this territory, and after Chinese explorer Zhang Qian's journeys under Emperor Wudi (141–87 BCE), trade between Han China and Sogdiana expanded significantly. The Sogdians were crucial to this commerce, also serving as farmers, carpetweavers, glassmakers, and woodcarvers.

input: In the north Eristov pushed southwest, fought two battles, forced the Turks back to Batum, retired behind the Cholok River and suspended action for the rest of the year (June). In the far south Wrangel pushed west, fought a battle and occupied Bayazit. In the center the main forces stood at Kars and Gyumri. Both slowly approached along the Kars-Gyumri road and faced each other, neither side choosing to fight (June–July). On 4 August Russian scouts saw a movement which they thought was the start of a withdrawal, the Russians advanced and the Turks attacked first. They were defeated, losing 8000 men to the Russian 3000. 10000 irregulars deserted to their villages. Both sides withdrew to their former positions. About this time the Persians made a semi-secret agreement to remain neutral in exchange for the cancellation of the indemnity from the previous war.
rewrite: Advancing southwest from the north, Eristov engaged in two battles, driving Turkish forces back toward Batum before withdrawing behind the Cholok River and halting operations for the year in June. Meanwhile, far to the south, Wrangel moved west, fought a battle, and captured Bayazit. The central fronts saw main forces positioned at Kars and Gyumri, gradually converging along the connecting road through June and July in a prolonged standoff where neither initiated combat. On August 4th, Russian scouts observed movements mistaken for a retreat; as the Russians advanced, the Turks struck first but were decisively defeated, suffering 8,000 casualties against 3,000 Russian losses. Approximately 10,000 irregular troops deserted to their villages. Following the battle, both armies returned to their original positions. Around this period, Persia reached a semi-secret neutrality agreement in return for the cancellation of a prior war indemnity.

input: The disadvantage of the ski-jump is the penalty it exacts on aircraft size, payload, and fuel load (and thus range); heavily laden aircraft can not launch using a ski-jump because their high loaded weight requires either a longer takeoff roll than is possible on a carrier deck, or assistance from a catapult or JATO rocket. For example, the Russian Su-33 is only able to launch from the carrier Admiral Kuznetsov with a minimal armament and fuel load. Another disadvantage is on mixed flight deck operations where helicopters are also present such as a US Landing Helicopter Dock or Landing Helicopter Assault amphibious assault ship a ski jump is not included as this would eliminate one or more helicopter landing areas, this flat deck limits the loading of Harriers but is somewhat mitigated by the longer rolling start provided by a long flight deck compared to many STOVL carriers.
rewrite: A ski-jump imposes significant limitations on aircraft capabilities, particularly concerning size, payload, and fuel capacity, which directly reduces operational range. Aircraft carrying heavy loads cannot use a ski-jump for launch, as their weight demands a longer takeoff roll than available on a carrier deck, necessitating alternative aids like a catapult or JATO rockets. This is illustrated by the Russian Su-33, which can only take off from the Admiral Kuznetsov with minimal armament and fuel. Additionally, ski-jumps are unsuitable for mixed-deck operations involving helicopters, such as on U.S. amphibious assault ships. Including a ramp would remove crucial helicopter landing spots. While the resulting flat deck restricts Harrier loading, this drawback is partially offset by the extended rolling start afforded by a longer flight deck compared to many other STOVL carriers.

input: The University of Swaziland, Southern African Nazarene University, Swaziland Christian University are the institutions that offer university education in the country. A campus of Limkokwing University of Creative Technology can be found at Sidvwashini, a suburb of the capital Mbabane. There are some teaching and nursing assistant colleges around the country. Ngwane Teacher's College and William Pitcher College are the country's teaching colleges. The Good Shepherd Hospital in Siteki is home to the College for Nursing Assistants.
rewrite: University education in the country is provided by the University of Swaziland, Southern African Nazarene University, and Swaziland Christian University. Additionally, a campus of Limkokwing University of Creative Technology is located in Sidvwashini, a suburb of the capital Mbabane. Among the teaching colleges are Ngwane Teacher's College and William Pitcher College. For nursing assistants, the College for Nursing Assistants is based at the Good Shepherd Hospital in Siteki, alongside other similar colleges nationwide.

input: Sho-1 called for V. Adm. Jisaburo Ozawa's force to use an apparently vulnerable carrier force to lure the U.S. 3rd Fleet away from Leyte and remove air cover from the Allied landing forces, which would then be attacked from the west by three Japanese forces: V. Adm. Takeo Kurita's force would enter Leyte Gulf and attack the landing forces; R. Adm. Shoji Nishimura's force and V. Adm. Kiyohide Shima's force would act as mobile strike forces. The plan was likely to result in the destruction of one or more of the Japanese forces, but Toyoda justified it by saying that there would be no sense in saving the fleet and losing the Philippines.
rewrite: The Sho-1 plan involved using Vice Admiral Jisaburo Ozawa’s carrier group as a decoy. Its apparent vulnerability was intended to draw the U.S. 3rd Fleet away from Leyte, stripping air cover from the Allied landings. From the west, three Japanese forces would then attack. Vice Admiral Takeo Kurita’s unit was to enter Leyte Gulf and strike the landing forces directly, while Rear Admiral Shoji Nishimura’s and Vice Admiral Kiyohide Shima’s forces would operate as mobile strike units. Although the plan risked the destruction of one or more Japanese forces, Admiral Toyoda defended it, arguing that saving the fleet while losing the Philippines would be pointless.

input: A computer's memory can be viewed as a list of cells into which numbers can be placed or read. Each cell has a numbered "address" and can store a single number. The computer can be instructed to "put the number 123 into the cell numbered 1357" or to "add the number that is in cell 1357 to the number that is in cell 2468 and put the answer into cell 1595." The information stored in memory may represent practically anything. Letters, numbers, even computer instructions can be placed into memory with equal ease. Since the CPU does not differentiate between different types of information, it is the software's responsibility to give significance to what the memory sees as nothing but a series of numbers.
rewrite: A computer's memory consists of cells, each with a unique numeric address capable of storing a single number. Information of any kind—letters, numbers, or even program instructions—can be stored there with equal ease. The computer executes commands such as placing the number 123 into address 1357, or adding the contents of cell 1357 to those of cell 2468 and storing the result in cell 1595. Practically anything can be represented by the data held in memory. Because the CPU makes no distinction between types of information, software must interpret what the memory treats merely as a sequence of numbers.

input: In September 2006, German officials seized MP3 players from SanDisk's booth at the IFA show in Berlin after an Italian patents firm won an injunction on behalf of Sisvel against SanDisk in a dispute over licensing rights. The injunction was later reversed by a Berlin judge, but that reversal was in turn blocked the same day by another judge from the same court, "bringing the Patent Wild West to Germany" in the words of one commentator.
rewrite: During the IFA show in Berlin in September 2006, German officials confiscated SanDisk's MP3 players. This followed an injunction secured by an Italian patents firm for Sisvel in a licensing dispute. Although a Berlin judge later reversed this order, another judge from the same court blocked the reversal that very day. A commentator remarked that this sequence of events was "bringing the Patent Wild West to Germany."

input: From 1898, it was commonly accepted that the name was of Celtic origin and meant place belonging to a man called *Londinos; this explanation has since been rejected. Richard Coates put forward an explanation in 1998 that it is derived from the pre-Celtic Old European *(p)lowonida, meaning 'river too wide to ford', and suggested that this was a name given to the part of the River Thames which flows through London; from this, the settlement gained the Celtic form of its name, *Lowonidonjon; this requires quite a serious amendment however. The ultimate difficulty lies in reconciling the Latin form Londinium with the modern Welsh Llundain, which should demand a form *(h)lōndinion (as opposed to *londīnion), from earlier *loundiniom. The possibility cannot be ruled out that the Welsh name was borrowed back in from English at a later date, and thus cannot be used as a basis from which to reconstruct the original name.
rewrite: Since 1898, the prevailing view held that the name had Celtic roots, signifying a place belonging to *Londinos, though this theory was later dismissed. In 1998, Richard Coates proposed an alternative origin from a pre-Celtic Old European term, *(p)lowonida, meaning 'a river too wide to ford'. He posited this described the Thames section flowing through London, leading to the Celtic form *Lowonidonjon for the settlement, albeit requiring significant revision. A central challenge is aligning the Latin Londinium with the modern Welsh Llundain, which implies an earlier form like *(h)lōndinion rather than *londīnion. It remains possible that the Welsh term was borrowed from English later, thus undermining its use for reconstructing the original name.

input: The title of "world's oldest airport" is disputed, but College Park Airport in Maryland, US, established in 1909 by Wilbur Wright, is generally agreed to be the world's oldest continually operating airfield, although it serves only general aviation traffic. Bisbee-Douglas International Airport in Arizona was declared "the first international airport of the Americas" by US president Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1943. Pearson Field Airport in Vancouver, Washington had a dirigible land in 1905 and planes in 1911 and is still in use. Bremen Airport opened in 1913 and remains in use, although it served as an American military field between 1945 and 1949. Amsterdam Airport Schiphol opened on September 16, 1916 as a military airfield, but only accepted civil aircraft from December 17, 1920, allowing Sydney Airport in Sydney, Australia—which started operations in January 1920—to claim to be one of the world's oldest continually operating commercial airports. Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport in Minneapolis-Saint Paul, Minnesota, opened in 1920 and has been in continuous commercial service since. It serves about 35,000,000 passengers each year and continues to expand, recently opening a new 11,000 foot (3,355 meter) runway. Of the airports constructed during this early period in aviation, it is one of the largest and busiest that is still currently operating. Rome Ciampino Airport, opened 1916, is also a contender, as well as the Don Mueang International Airport near Bangkok,Thailand, which opened in 1914. Increased aircraft traffic during World War I led to the construction of landing fields. Aircraft had to approach these from certain directions and this led to the development of aids for directing the approach and landing slope.
rewrite:
While the designation of the world's oldest airport is contested, College Park Airport in Maryland holds wide recognition as the oldest continually operating airfield. Founded by Wilbur Wright in 1909, it remains active today, though it exclusively serves general aviation. Other early airfields also maintain their operations. Pearson Field Airport in Vancouver, Washington, witnessed a dirigible landing in 1905 and airplanes by 1911. Bremen Airport opened in 1913, functioning continuously aside from a period as an American military field from 1945 to 1949. Similarly, Amsterdam Airport Schiphol launched as a military base in September 1916, transitioning to civil use in December 1920.

This latter date allows Sydney Airport, which began operations in January 1920, to claim status as one of the world's oldest continually operating commercial airports. Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport also opened in 1920 and has provided uninterrupted commercial service since. Now one of the largest and busiest surviving airports from aviation's early period, it handles approximately 35 million annual passengers and continues expanding, having recently inaugurated a new 11,000-foot runway. Other notable contenders from this era include Rome Ciampino Airport (1916) and Don Mueang International Airport near Bangkok (1914).

The surge in aircraft traffic during World War I necessitated the construction of dedicated landing fields. The requirement for aircraft to approach from specific directions spurred the development of early aids to guide both the approach path and the landing slope. In a related historical designation, Bisbee-Douglas International Airport in Arizona was proclaimed "the first international airport of the Americas" by President Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1943.

input: Around 66 BC, a movement to use constitutional, or at least peaceful, means to address the plight of various classes began. After several failures, the movement's leaders decided to use any means that were necessary to accomplish their goals. The movement coalesced under an aristocrat named Lucius Sergius Catilina. The movement was based in the town of Faesulae, which was a natural hotbed of agrarian agitation. The rural malcontents were to advance on Rome, and be aided by an uprising within the city. After assassinating the consuls and most of the senators, Catiline would be free to enact his reforms. The conspiracy was set in motion in 63 BC. The consul for the year, Marcus Tullius Cicero, intercepted messages that Catiline had sent in an attempt to recruit more members. As a result, the top conspirators in Rome (including at least one former consul) were executed by authorisation (of dubious constitutionality) of the senate, and the planned uprising was disrupted. Cicero then sent an army, which cut Catiline's forces to pieces.
rewrite: Beginning in 66 BC, an effort emerged to resolve the struggles of different social classes through constitutional or peaceful methods. Following repeated disappointments, its leaders resolved to pursue their aims by any means necessary. This movement found its focus under the aristocrat Lucius Sergius Catilina, centered in the town of Faesulae—a natural breeding ground for agrarian discontent. The conspiracy, launched in 63 BC, involved a plan for rural malcontents to march on Rome while allies staged an uprising inside the city. With the consuls and most senators assassinated, Catiline could then implement his reforms. However, the consul Marcus Tullius Cicero intercepted Catiline’s messages recruiting new supporters. Consequently, the leading conspirators in Rome, among them a former consul, were executed under the Senate’s authorization—a move of questionable legality—disrupting the planned revolt. Cicero then dispatched an army that decisively destroyed Catiline’s forces.

input: On September 9, 2007, West suggested that his race had something to do with his being overlooked for opening the 2007 MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs) in favor of Britney Spears; he claimed, "Maybe my skin’s not right." West was performing at the event; that night, he lost all five awards that he was nominated for, including Best Male Artist and Video of the Year. After the show, he was visibly upset that he had lost at the VMAs two years in a row, stating that he would not come back to MTV ever again. He also appeared on several radio stations saying that when he made the song "Stronger" that it was his dream to open the VMAs with it. He has also stated that Spears has not had a hit in a long period of time and that MTV exploited her for ratings.
rewrite: On September 9, 2007, while performing at the MTV Video Music Awards, Kanye West lost all five of his nominations, such as Best Male Artist and Video of the Year. Following this second consecutive year of losses at the VMAs, he was visibly upset and declared he would never return to MTV. West had earlier suggested his race played a role in MTV choosing Britney Spears to open the show instead of him, remarking, "Maybe my skin’s not right." In subsequent radio appearances, he expressed that performing his song "Stronger" to open the VMAs had been a dream. He also contended that Spears had not had a hit in a long time and that MTV was exploiting her for ratings.
