Regulars often favor a pub as their "local" for various reasons: its nearness to home or work, a preferred beer, a place to smoke or avoid smoke, social attractions like a darts team or pool table, or simply because friends gather there.

input: On 7 June 1981, the Israeli air force destroyed Iraq's sole nuclear reactor, in order to impede Iraq's nuclear weapons program. The reactor was under construction just outside Baghdad. Following a series of PLO attacks in 1982, Israel invaded Lebanon that year to destroy the bases from which the PLO launched attacks and missiles into northern Israel. In the first six days of fighting, the Israelis destroyed the military forces of the PLO in Lebanon and decisively defeated the Syrians. An Israeli government inquiry – the Kahan Commission – would later hold Begin, Sharon and several Israeli generals as indirectly responsible for the Sabra and Shatila massacre. In 1985, Israel responded to a Palestinian terrorist attack in Cyprus by bombing the PLO headquarters in Tunis. Israel withdrew from most of Lebanon in 1986, but maintained a borderland buffer zone in southern Lebanon until 2000, from where Israeli forces engaged in conflict with Hezbollah.
rewrite: On June 7, 1981, the Israeli air force carried out an attack on Iraq's sole nuclear reactor, then under construction near Baghdad, aiming to halt the country's nuclear weapons program. In 1982, following a series of PLO attacks, Israel invaded Lebanon to eliminate bases used for launching assaults into northern Israel. Within the first six days, Israeli forces dismantled the PLO's military presence in Lebanon and achieved a decisive victory over Syrian troops. Later, the Israeli Kahan Commission would assign indirect responsibility for the Sabra and Shatila massacre to Prime Minister Begin, Defense Minister Sharon, and several generals. Responding to a Palestinian terrorist attack in Cyprus, Israel bombed the PLO headquarters in Tunis in 1985. Although Israel withdrew from most of Lebanon in 1986, it maintained a buffer zone in the south until 2000, during which its forces frequently clashed with Hezbollah.

input: Mīmāṃsā gave rise to the study of philology and the philosophy of language. While their deep analysis of language and linguistics influenced other schools, their views were not shared by others. Mīmāṃsākas considered the purpose and power of language was to clearly prescribe the proper, correct and right. In contrast, Vedantins extended the scope and value of language as a tool to also describe, develop and derive. Mīmāṃsākas considered orderly, law-driven, procedural life as central purpose and noblest necessity of dharma and society, and divine (theistic) sustenance means to that end. The Mimamsa school was influential and foundational to the Vedanta school, with the difference that Mīmāṃsā school developed and emphasized karmakāṇḍa (that part of the śruti which relates to ceremonial acts and sacrificial rites, the early parts of the Vedas), while the Vedanta school developed and emphasized jñānakāṇḍa (that portion of the Vedas which relates to knowledge of monism, the latter parts of the Vedas).
rewrite: The Mīmāṃsā school was foundational and influential to Vedanta, yet the two diverged in key areas. Mīmāṃsā emphasized karmakāṇḍa—the sections of the Vedas dealing with ceremonial acts and sacrificial rites. Vedanta, in contrast, focused on jñānakāṇḍa, the portions concerning monistic knowledge. In their philosophy of language, Mīmāṃsākas held that language’s primary purpose was to prescribe what is proper and correct. Vedantins, however, extended language’s value to also describe, develop, and derive meaning. Furthermore, Mīmāṃsā viewed an orderly, law-driven life as the central purpose of dharma and society, seeing theistic devotion as a means to that end. While Mīmāṃsā’s deep linguistic analysis influenced other schools and gave rise to philology, its specific views were not universally shared.

input: Nothing in the principle of any of the motors described above requires that the iron (steel) portions of the rotor actually rotate. If the soft magnetic material of the rotor is made in the form of a cylinder, then (except for the effect of hysteresis) torque is exerted only on the windings of the electromagnets. Taking advantage of this fact is the coreless or ironless DC motor, a specialized form of a PM DC motor. Optimized for rapid acceleration, these motors have a rotor that is constructed without any iron core. The rotor can take the form of a winding-filled cylinder, or a self-supporting structure comprising only the magnet wire and the bonding material. The rotor can fit inside the stator magnets; a magnetically soft stationary cylinder inside the rotor provides a return path for the stator magnetic flux. A second arrangement has the rotor winding basket surrounding the stator magnets. In that design, the rotor fits inside a magnetically soft cylinder that can serve as the housing for the motor, and likewise provides a return path for the flux.
rewrite: None of the motors previously discussed depend on the rotation of their iron or steel rotor components in principle. By forming the rotor's soft magnetic material into a cylinder, torque—aside from hysteresis effects—acts solely upon the electromagnet windings. This principle is utilized in the coreless or ironless DC motor, a specialized type of PM DC motor designed for quick acceleration. Its rotor lacks an iron core entirely. Instead, it may be a cylinder packed with windings or a self-supporting structure made only of magnet wire and bonding agent. One configuration places the rotor inside the stator magnets, with a stationary, magnetically soft cylinder within the rotor guiding the stator's magnetic flux back. Alternatively, the rotor winding basket can encircle the stator magnets. In this layout, the rotor sits inside a magnetically soft cylinder that acts as both the motor housing and a return path for the flux.

input: Unlike in multicellular organisms, increases in cell size (cell growth) and reproduction by cell division are tightly linked in unicellular organisms. Bacteria grow to a fixed size and then reproduce through binary fission, a form of asexual reproduction. Under optimal conditions, bacteria can grow and divide extremely rapidly, and bacterial populations can double as quickly as every 9.8 minutes. In cell division, two identical clone daughter cells are produced. Some bacteria, while still reproducing asexually, form more complex reproductive structures that help disperse the newly formed daughter cells. Examples include fruiting body formation by Myxobacteria and aerial hyphae formation by Streptomyces, or budding. Budding involves a cell forming a protrusion that breaks away and produces a daughter cell.
rewrite: In unicellular organisms, cell growth and reproduction through division are closely connected, unlike in multicellular life forms. Bacteria, for instance, reach a specific size and then undergo binary fission, a type of asexual reproduction. This process yields two genetically identical daughter cells. Given ideal conditions, bacterial populations can double in as little as 9.8 minutes due to rapid growth and division. Although reproduction remains asexual, some bacteria develop more complex structures to aid in dispersing offspring. Examples are the fruiting bodies of Myxobacteria, the aerial hyphae of Streptomyces, and budding. Budding occurs when a cell forms an outgrowth that detaches to become a new daughter cell.

input: The elimination of wolves from Yellowstone National Park had profound impacts on the trophic pyramid. Without predation, herbivores began to over-graze many woody browse species, affecting the area's plant populations. In addition, wolves often kept animals from grazing in riparian areas, which protected beavers from having their food sources encroached upon. The removal of wolves had a direct effect on beaver populations, as their habitat became territory for grazing. Furthermore, predation keeps hydrological features such as creeks and streams in normal working order. Increased browsing on willows and conifers along Blacktail Creek due to a lack of predation caused channel incision because they helped slow the water down and hold the soil in place.
rewrite: The removal of wolves from Yellowstone National Park disrupted the ecosystem significantly. Herbivores, freed from predation, overgrazed woody plants, depleting key vegetation. This grazing pressure extended into riparian zones, which wolves had previously helped protect. Consequently, beaver populations suffered as their habitat and food sources, like willows, were consumed. The loss of vegetation along waterways, such as Blacktail Creek, also led to hydrological changes. Plants like willows and conifers normally stabilize soil and slow water flow; their decline caused channel incision, altering the natural function of streams and creeks. Thus, wolf predation proved essential for maintaining ecological balance.

input: Symbiosis (from Greek σύν "together" and βίωσις "living") is close and often long-term interaction between two different biological species. In 1877 Albert Bernhard Frank used the word symbiosis (which previously had been used to depict people living together in community) to describe the mutualistic relationship in lichens. In 1879, the German mycologist Heinrich Anton de Bary defined it as "the living together of unlike organisms."
rewrite: Symbiosis describes the close, frequently long-term interaction of two distinct biological species. The term originates from Greek words meaning "together" and "living." Albert Bernhard Frank first applied it in 1877 to the mutualistic relationship in lichens, broadening its prior use for human communities. Later, in 1879, mycologist Heinrich Anton de Bary defined it as "the living together of unlike organisms."

input: Of the territories of Poland annexed by the Soviet Union between 1939 and 1940, the region around Białystok and a minor part of Galicia east of the San river around Przemyśl were returned to the Polish state at the end of World War II. Of all other territories annexed by the USSR in 1939–40, the ones detached from Finland (Karelia, Petsamo), Estonia (Ingrian area and Petseri County) and Latvia (Abrene) remained part of the Russian Federation, the successor state of the Soviet Union, after 1991. Northern Bukovina, Southern Bessarabia and Hertza remain part of Ukraine.
rewrite: At the conclusion of World War II, only the Białystok region and a small portion of Galicia east of the San River near Przemyśl were restored to Poland from the territories annexed by the Soviet Union between 1939 and 1940. All other areas seized during that period remained under Soviet control. Following the 1991 dissolution of the USSR, the territories taken from Finland, Estonia, and Latvia were retained by the Russian Federation. Meanwhile, Northern Bukovina, Southern Bessarabia, and Hertza became part of Ukraine.

input: The city is home to 261,546 (mid-2014 est.) people, making it the 30th most populous built-up area in the United Kingdom. It is governed locally by Plymouth City Council and is represented nationally by three MPs. Plymouth's economy remains strongly influenced by shipbuilding and seafaring including ferry links to Brittany (Roscoff and St Malo) and Spain (Santander), but has tended toward a service-based economy since the 1990s. It has the largest operational naval base in Western Europe – HMNB Devonport and is home to Plymouth University.
rewrite: With a population of 261,546 (mid-2014 estimate), Plymouth ranks as the UK's 30th most populous built-up area. Locally governed by Plymouth City Council and represented nationally by three MPs, its economy has historically been shaped by shipbuilding and seafaring. This includes ferry connections to Roscoff and St Malo in Brittany, and Santander in Spain. Since the 1990s, it has increasingly shifted toward services. The city hosts the largest operational naval base in Western Europe, HMNB Devonport, and is home to Plymouth University.

input: The northern section of the Divide, where the mountains give way rapidly to prairie, is part of the Rocky Mountain Front. The front is most pronounced in the Lewis Range, located primarily in Glacier National Park. Due to the configuration of mountain ranges in Glacier National Park, the Northern Divide (which begins in Alaska's Seward Peninsula) crosses this region and turns east in Montana at Triple Divide Peak. It causes the Waterton River, Belly, and Saint Mary rivers to flow north into Alberta, Canada. There they join the Saskatchewan River, which ultimately empties into Hudson Bay.
rewrite: At the Rocky Mountain Front's northern section, mountains quickly transition to prairie. This front is especially distinct in Glacier National Park's Lewis Range. Here, due to the park's mountain configuration, the Northern Divide—originating in Alaska's Seward Peninsula—turns eastward at Montana's Triple Divide Peak. This shift directs the Waterton, Belly, and Saint Mary rivers north into Alberta, Canada. These waters join the Saskatchewan River, which eventually flows into Hudson Bay.

input: In The Open Society and Its Enemies and The Poverty of Historicism, Popper developed a critique of historicism and a defence of the "Open Society". Popper considered historicism to be the theory that history develops inexorably and necessarily according to knowable general laws towards a determinate end. He argued that this view is the principal theoretical presupposition underpinning most forms of authoritarianism and totalitarianism. He argued that historicism is founded upon mistaken assumptions regarding the nature of scientific law and prediction. Since the growth of human knowledge is a causal factor in the evolution of human history, and since "no society can predict, scientifically, its own future states of knowledge", it follows, he argued, that there can be no predictive science of human history. For Popper, metaphysical and historical indeterminism go hand in hand.
rewrite: Popper's critique of historicism and his defense of the "Open Society" are central to works like *The Open Society and Its Enemies* and *The Poverty of Historicism*. He defined historicism as the theory that history moves inexorably according to knowable laws toward a fixed end. This view, he contended, is a key presupposition behind authoritarian and totalitarian systems, resting on flawed assumptions about scientific law and prediction. Popper maintained that human knowledge growth is a causal factor in history's evolution. Because a society cannot scientifically predict its own future knowledge, he concluded there can be no predictive science of human history. For him, metaphysical and historical indeterminism are fundamentally linked.

input: IBM's employee management practices can be traced back to its roots. In 1914, CEO Thomas J. Watson boosted company spirit by creating employee sports teams, hosting family outings, and furnishing a company band. IBM sports teams still continue in the present day; the IBM Big Blue continue to exist as semi-professional company rugby and American football teams. In 1924 the Quarter Century Club, which recognizes employees with 25 years of service, was organized and the first issue of Business Machines, IBM's internal publication, was published. In 1925, the first meeting of the Hundred Percent Club, composed of IBM salesmen who meet their quotas, convened in Atlantic City, New Jersey.
rewrite: IBM's approach to employee management originates in its early history. In 1914, CEO Thomas J. Watson fostered morale through sports teams, family outings, and a company band. This legacy persists today with the semi-professional IBM Big Blue rugby and football teams. The company further institutionalized recognition in 1924 by founding the Quarter Century Club for 25-year veterans and launching the internal *Business Machines* publication. The following year, 1925, saw the inaugural gathering in Atlantic City of the Hundred Percent Club, honoring salespeople who achieved their quotas.

input: Appointments to the Order of the British Empire were at first made on the nomination of the self-governing Dominions of the Empire, the Viceroy of India, and the colonial governors, as well as on nominations from within the United Kingdom. As the Empire evolved into the Commonwealth, nominations continued to come from the Commonwealth realms, in which the monarch remained head of state. These overseas nominations have been discontinued in realms that have established their own Orders—such as the Order of Australia, the Order of Canada, and the New Zealand Order of Merit—but members of the Order are still appointed in the British Overseas Territories.
rewrite: Initially, appointments to the Order of the British Empire were based on nominations from the United Kingdom, the self-governing Dominions, the Viceroy of India, and colonial governors. As the Empire transitioned to the Commonwealth, Commonwealth realms where the monarch is head of state continued submitting nominations. However, overseas nominations have ceased in realms that created their own national honors, like the Order of Australia, the Order of Canada, and the New Zealand Order of Merit. Appointments still occur in the British Overseas Territories.

input: After several failed attempts, in 1930 the first aeroplane reached Bermuda. A Stinson Detroiter seaplane flying from New York, it had to land twice in the ocean: once because of darkness and again to refuel. Navigation and weather forecasting improved in 1933 when the Royal Air Force (then responsible for providing equipment and personnel for the Royal Navy's Fleet Air Arm) established a station at the Royal Naval Dockyard to repair (and supply replacement) float planes for the fleet. In 1936 Luft Hansa began to experiment with seaplane flights from Berlin via the Azores with continuation to New York City.
rewrite: In 1930, after multiple failed efforts, the first aircraft arrived in Bermuda. This Stinson Detroiter seaplane, departing from New York, was forced to land on the ocean twice—first due to darkness and then to refuel. By 1933, navigation and weather forecasting advanced when the Royal Air Force set up a station at the Royal Naval Dockyard to maintain and supply float planes for the fleet, a duty tied to supporting the Royal Navy's Fleet Air Arm. Later, in 1936, Luft Hansa commenced trials of seaplane routes from Berlin to New York City, with a stop in the Azores.

input: There are four hundred securities listed on the stock exchange, of which almost three hundred are offshore funds and alternative investment structures attracted by Bermuda's regulatory environment. The Exchange specialises in listing and trading of capital market instruments such as equities, debt issues, funds (including hedge fund structures) and depository receipt programmes. The BSX is a full member of the World Federation of Exchanges and is located in an OECD member nation. It also has Approved Stock Exchange status under Australia's Foreign Investment Fund (FIF) taxation rules and Designated Investment Exchange status by the UK's Financial Services Authority.
rewrite: With nearly three hundred offshore funds and alternative investment structures drawn by Bermuda's regulations, the stock exchange lists four hundred securities in total. It focuses on the listing and trading of capital market instruments, including equities, debt issues, funds—such as hedge fund structures—and depository receipt programmes. Located in an OECD member nation, the BSX is a full member of the World Federation of Exchanges. Additionally, it holds Approved Stock Exchange status under Australia's Foreign Investment Fund tax rules and Designated Investment Exchange status from the UK's Financial Services Authority.

input: During the Protestant Reformation, the Church of England (Anglicans) separated from the Roman Catholic Church. There were some Christians who were not content with the achievements of the mainstream Protestant Reformation. There also were Christians who were disappointed that the Church of England had not made corrections of what some considered to be errors and abuses. Of those most critical of the Church's direction, some chose to stay and try to make constructive changes from within the Anglican Church. They became known as "Puritans" and are described by Gourley as cousins of the English Separatists. Others decided they must leave the Church because of their dissatisfaction and became known as the Separatists.
rewrite: While the Church of England broke from Roman Catholicism during the Protestant Reformation, some Christians remained dissatisfied. They felt mainstream reforms were insufficient and that the Anglican Church had failed to correct perceived errors and abuses. The most critical among them split into two paths. One group, later called Puritans, chose to remain within the Anglican Church to advocate for change from within. Another group, known as Separatists, concluded they must leave the church entirely due to their profound discontent. Historian Gourley describes the Puritans as cousins to these English Separatists.

input: Important Justinian era mosaics decorated the Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai in Egypt. Generally wall mosaics have not survived in the region because of the destruction of buildings but the St. Catherine's Monastery is exceptional. On the upper wall Moses is shown in two panels on a landscape background. In the apse we can see the Transfiguration of Jesus on a golden background. The apse is surrounded with bands containing medallions of apostles and prophets, and two contemporary figure, "Abbot Longinos" and "John the Deacon". The mosaic was probably created in 565/6.
rewrite: The Saint Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai in Egypt features important mosaics from the Justinian era, dating to around 565/6. While regional wall mosaics rarely survive building destruction, this site is an exception. Its upper wall depicts Moses in two panels against a landscape. The apse presents the Transfiguration of Jesus on a golden background, surrounded by bands containing medallions of apostles and prophets, along with two contemporary figures: Abbot Longinos and John the Deacon.

input: The rivalry between Nintendo and Sega resulted in what has been described as one of the most notable console wars in video game history, in which Sega positioned the Genesis as the "cool" console, with more mature titles aimed at older gamers, and edgy advertisements that occasionally attacked the competition. Nintendo however, scored an early public relations advantage by securing the first console conversion of Capcom's arcade classic Street Fighter II for SNES, which took over a year to make the transition to Genesis. Despite the Genesis's head start, much larger library of games, and lower price point, the Genesis only represented an estimated 60% of the American 16-bit console market in June 1992, and neither console could maintain a definitive lead for several years. Donkey Kong Country is said to have helped establish the SNES's market prominence in the latter years of the 16-bit generation, and for a time, maintain against the PlayStation and Saturn. According to Nintendo, the company had sold more than 20 million SNES units in the U.S. According to a 2014 Wedbush Securities report based on NPD sales data, the SNES ultimately outsold the Genesis in the U.S. market.
rewrite: One of the most notable console wars in video game history emerged from the rivalry between Nintendo and Sega. Sega marketed its Genesis as the "cool" console, featuring more mature titles for older gamers and edgy advertisements that sometimes directly targeted the competition. Despite the Genesis having a head start, a much larger game library, and a lower price, it held only an estimated 60% of the American 16-bit market by June 1992. For several years, neither console could secure a definitive lead. Nintendo gained an early public relations advantage by securing the first console conversion of Capcom's arcade hit *Street Fighter II* for the SNES, a process that took over a year to complete for the Genesis. In the latter years of the 16-bit generation, *Donkey Kong Country* is credited with helping to establish the SNES's market prominence, even allowing it to compete for a time against the subsequent PlayStation and Saturn. According to Nintendo, the company sold over 20 million SNES units in the United States. Ultimately, a 2014 Wedbush Securities report using NPD sales data confirmed that the SNES outsold the Genesis in the U.S. market.

input: Economic sanctions against Iran, such as the embargo against Iranian crude oil, have affected the economy. Sanctions have led to a steep fall in the value of the rial, and as of April 2013 one US dollar is worth 36,000 rial, compared with 16,000 in early 2012. Following a successful implementation of the 2015 nuclear and sanctions relief deal, the resulting benefits might not be distributed evenly across the Iranian economy as political elites such as the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have garnered more resources and economic interests.
rewrite: The value of Iran's rial has fallen sharply due to economic sanctions, including an embargo on its crude oil. By April 2013, one US dollar was worth 36,000 rial, a significant drop from 16,000 in early 2012. Even after the successful 2015 nuclear deal brought sanctions relief, the economic benefits were unevenly distributed. Political elites, particularly the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, captured a disproportionate share of resources and economic interests.

input: Norfolk Island was originally a colony acquired by settlement but was never within the British Settlements Act. It was accepted as a territory of Australia, separate from any state, by the Norfolk Island Act 1913 (Cth), passed under the territories power (Constitution section 122) and made effective in 1914. In 1976 the High Court of Australia held unanimously that Norfolk Island is a part of the Commonwealth. Again, in 2007 the High Court of Australia affirmed the validity of legislation that made Australian citizenship a necessary qualification for voting for, and standing for election to, the Legislative Assembly of Norfolk Island.
rewrite: Originally acquired as a settlement colony, Norfolk Island was never governed under the British Settlements Act. The Norfolk Island Act 1913, enacted under the territories power of the Constitution, formally accepted it as a non-state Australian territory, effective in 1914. The High Court of Australia unanimously confirmed in 1976 that the island is part of the Commonwealth. Later, in 2007, the High Court upheld legislation requiring Australian citizenship to vote or stand for election to the Norfolk Island Legislative Assembly.

input: In some cases and in some places the edicts were strictly enforced: some Christians resisted and were imprisoned or martyred. Others complied. Some local communities were not only pre-dominantly Christian, but powerful and influential; and some provincial authorities were lenient, notably the Caesar in Gaul, Constantius Chlorus, the father of Constantine I. Diocletian's successor Galerius maintained anti-Christian policy until his deathbed revocation in 311, when he asked Christians to pray for him. "This meant an ofﬁcial recognition of their importance in the religious world of the Roman empire, although one of the tetrarchs, Maximinus Daia, still oppressed Christians in his part of the empire up to 313."
rewrite: In certain regions, the edicts were rigorously applied, leading to imprisonment or martyrdom for Christians who resisted, while others chose compliance. Some local communities were not only predominantly Christian but also wielded significant power and influence. Provincial authorities varied in their approach, with figures like Constantius Chlorus in Gaul showing leniency. Following Diocletian, Galerius upheld anti-Christian measures until his deathbed revocation in 311, requesting prayers from Christians. This act marked an official acknowledgment of their growing importance within the empire's religious landscape, despite continued oppression by Maximinus Daia in his territories until 313.

input: These areas contain some spectacular scenery as well, as evidenced by such national parks as Yosemite and Mount Rainier. West of the Cascades and Sierra Nevada is a series of valleys, such as the Central Valley in California and the Willamette Valley in Oregon. Along the coast is a series of low mountain ranges known as the Pacific Coast Ranges. Much of the Pacific Northwest coast is inhabited by some of the densest vegetation outside of the Tropics, and also the tallest trees in the world (the Redwoods).
rewrite: National parks like Yosemite and Mount Rainier showcase the region's spectacular scenery. A series of valleys, including California's Central Valley and Oregon's Willamette Valley, lie west of the Cascades and Sierra Nevada. Bordering the coast are the low Pacific Coast Ranges. This Pacific Northwest coastline supports some of the world's tallest trees, the Redwoods, and is covered by exceptionally dense vegetation, rivaling that of the Tropics.

input: In the field of music, Germany claims some of the most renowned classical composers of the world including Bach, Mozart and Beethoven, who marked the transition between the Classical and Romantic eras in Western classical music. Other composers of the Austro-German tradition who achieved international fame include Brahms, Wagner, Haydn, Schubert, Händel, Schumann, Liszt, Mendelssohn Bartholdy, Johann Strauss II, Bruckner, Mahler, Telemann, Richard Strauss, Schoenberg, Orff, and most recently, Henze, Lachenmann, and Stockhausen.
rewrite: Germany is home to many of the world's most celebrated classical composers, such as Bach, Mozart, and Beethoven, who bridged the Classical and Romantic eras. The influential Austro-German tradition also includes internationally famous figures like Brahms, Wagner, Haydn, and Schubert, as well as Händel, Schumann, Liszt, and Mendelssohn Bartholdy. Others like Johann Strauss II, Bruckner, Mahler, Telemann, Richard Strauss, Schoenberg, Orff, and more recent contributors including Henze, Lachenmann, and Stockhausen further illustrate this rich legacy.

input: iPods have been criticized for alleged short life-span and fragile hard drives. A 2005 survey conducted on the MacInTouch website found that the iPod line had an average failure rate of 13.7% (although they note that comments from respondents indicate that "the true iPod failure rate may be lower than it appears"). It concluded that some models were more durable than others. In particular, failure rates for iPods employing hard drives was usually above 20% while those with flash memory had a failure rate below 10%. In late 2005, many users complained that the surface of the first generation iPod Nano can become scratched easily, rendering the screen unusable. A class action lawsuit was also filed. Apple initially considered the issue a minor defect, but later began shipping these iPods with protective sleeves.[citation needed]
rewrite: Criticism of iPods has often focused on their supposedly short life-span and fragile hard drives. According to a 2005 MacInTouch survey, the iPod line showed an average failure rate of 13.7%, though it was noted that respondent comments suggested "the true iPod failure rate may be lower than it appears." The survey also found durability varied by model, with hard drive-based iPods experiencing failure rates typically above 20%, compared to below 10% for flash memory models. Later that year, numerous users reported that the first generation iPod Nano scratched easily, often making the screen unreadable and leading to a class action lawsuit. Apple initially dismissed this as a minor defect but later started including protective sleeves with these devices.[citation needed]

input: Numerous recordings of Chopin's works are available. On the occasion of the composer's bicentenary, the critics of The New York Times recommended performances by the following contemporary pianists (among many others): Martha Argerich, Vladimir Ashkenazy, Emanuel Ax, Evgeny Kissin, Murray Perahia, Maurizio Pollini and Krystian Zimerman. The Warsaw Chopin Society organizes the Grand prix du disque de F. Chopin for notable Chopin recordings, held every five years.
rewrite: Many recordings of Chopin's works exist. To mark his bicentenary, The New York Times critics highlighted performances by contemporary pianists like Martha Argerich, Vladimir Ashkenazy, Emanuel Ax, Evgeny Kissin, Murray Perahia, Maurizio Pollini, and Krystian Zimerman. Notably, every five years, the Warsaw Chopin Society awards the Grand prix du disque de F. Chopin for exceptional recordings.

input: In 1978, Jim Shooter became Marvel's editor-in-chief. Although a controversial personality, Shooter cured many of the procedural ills at Marvel, including repeatedly missed deadlines. During Shooter's nine-year tenure as editor-in-chief, Chris Claremont and John Byrne's run on the Uncanny X-Men and Frank Miller's run on Daredevil became critical and commercial successes. Shooter brought Marvel into the rapidly evolving direct market, institutionalized creator royalties, starting with the Epic Comics imprint for creator-owned material in 1982; introduced company-wide crossover story arcs with Contest of Champions and Secret Wars; and in 1986 launched the ultimately unsuccessful New Universe line to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Marvel Comics imprint. Star Comics, a children-oriented line differing from the regular Marvel titles, was briefly successful during this period.
rewrite: Jim Shooter assumed the role of Marvel's editor-in-chief in 1978. A divisive figure, he nonetheless resolved many operational issues, such as chronic deadline failures. His nine-year leadership saw major critical and commercial hits, including Chris Claremont and John Byrne's *Uncanny X-Men* and Frank Miller's *Daredevil*. Shooter guided Marvel into the growing direct market and established creator royalties, launching the Epic Comics imprint for creator-owned work in 1982. He pioneered company-wide crossovers like *Contest of Champions* and *Secret Wars*. In 1986, he introduced the ultimately unsuccessful New Universe line for Marvel's 25th anniversary. Additionally, the children-focused Star Comics line enjoyed brief success during this era.

input: While the cardinalate has long been expanded beyond the Roman pastoral clergy and Roman Curia, every cardinal priest has a titular church in Rome, though they may be bishops or archbishops elsewhere, just as cardinal bishops are given one of the suburbicarian dioceses around Rome. Pope Paul VI abolished all administrative rights cardinals had with regard to their titular churches, though the cardinal's name and coat of arms are still posted in the church, and they are expected to celebrate mass and preach there if convenient when they are in Rome.
rewrite: Although cardinals now come from beyond Rome's clergy and Curia, each cardinal priest is assigned a titular church in Rome, similar to how cardinal bishops receive a suburbicarian diocese nearby. Even if they serve as bishops elsewhere, their connection to these Roman churches remains. Since Pope Paul VI ended cardinals' administrative rights over these titles, their names and coats of arms are displayed there instead. They are also expected to celebrate mass and preach at these churches when visiting Rome, if possible.

input: Retail versions of Windows 8 are only able to install these apps through Windows Store—a namesake distribution platform which offers both apps, and listings for desktop programs certified for comparability with Windows 8. A method to sideload apps from outside Windows Store is available to devices running Windows 8 Enterprise and joined to a domain; Windows 8 Pro and Windows RT devices that are not part of a domain can also sideload apps, but only after special product keys are obtained through volume licensing.
rewrite: Windows 8 retail versions restrict app installation to the Windows Store. This platform distributes apps and also lists certified desktop programs compatible with the system. However, sideloading apps from external sources is permitted for domain-joined Windows 8 Enterprise devices. Non-domain Windows 8 Pro and Windows RT devices can also sideload, but this requires obtaining special product keys via volume licensing first.

input: Raleigh is home to numerous cultural, educational, and historic sites. The Duke Energy Center for the Performing Arts in Downtown Raleigh features three theater venues and serves as the home for the North Carolina Symphony and the Carolina Ballet. Walnut Creek Amphitheatre is a large music amphitheater located in Southeast Raleigh. Museums in Raleigh include the North Carolina Museum of Art in West Raleigh, as well as the North Carolina Museum of History and North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences located next to each other near the State Capitol in Downtown Raleigh. Several major universities and colleges call Raleigh home, including North Carolina State University, the largest public university in the state, and Shaw University, the first historically black university in the American South and site of the foundation of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, an important civil rights organization of the 1960s. One U.S. president, Andrew Johnson, was born in Raleigh.
rewrite: Raleigh boasts a wealth of cultural, educational, and historic landmarks. Among its performing arts venues is the Duke Energy Center for the Performing Arts in Downtown Raleigh, housing three theaters and hosting the North Carolina Symphony and Carolina Ballet. For larger concerts, the Walnut Creek Amphitheatre is situated in Southeast Raleigh. The city's museums include the North Carolina Museum of Art in West Raleigh, while the North Carolina Museum of History and the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences stand side-by-side near the Downtown State Capitol. Raleigh is also an academic hub, home to institutions like North Carolina State University, the state's largest public university, and Shaw University. Shaw holds distinction as the American South's first historically black university and was the founding site of the 1960s civil rights group, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. Notably, U.S. President Andrew Johnson was born in the city.

input: Federal law and treaties, so long as they are in accordance with the Constitution, preempt conflicting state and territorial laws in the 50 U.S. states and in the territories. However, the scope of federal preemption is limited because the scope of federal power is not universal. In the dual-sovereign system of American federalism (actually tripartite because of the presence of Indian reservations), states are the plenary sovereigns, each with their own constitution, while the federal sovereign possesses only the limited supreme authority enumerated in the Constitution. Indeed, states may grant their citizens broader rights than the federal Constitution as long as they do not infringe on any federal constitutional rights. Thus, most U.S. law (especially the actual "living law" of contract, tort, property, criminal, and family law experienced by the majority of citizens on a day-to-day basis) consists primarily of state law, which can and does vary greatly from one state to the next.
rewrite: Within the American federal system, which functions as a dual-sovereign structure—or tripartite when considering Indian reservations—states operate as plenary sovereigns, each governed by its own constitution. The federal government, in contrast, holds only the specific supreme powers granted by the U.S. Constitution. Consequently, federal law and treaties, provided they align with the Constitution, override any conflicting state or territorial laws across all 50 states and territories. Yet, federal preemption is inherently limited, as federal authority is not all-encompassing. States retain the power to provide their citizens with broader rights than the federal Constitution, so long as these do not violate any federal constitutional protections. As a result, the bulk of everyday U.S. law—including the "living law" of contracts, torts, property, crime, and family matters encountered regularly by most citizens—is primarily state law, which varies significantly from one state to another.

input: In four months, Aonuma's team managed to present realistic horseback riding,[l] which Nintendo later revealed to the public with a trailer at Electronic Entertainment Expo 2004. The game was scheduled to be released the next year, and was no longer a follow-up to The Wind Waker; a true sequel to it was released for the Nintendo DS in 2007, in the form of Phantom Hourglass. Miyamoto explained in interviews that the graphical style was chosen to satisfy demand, and that it better fit the theme of an older incarnation of Link. The game runs on a modified The Wind Waker engine.
rewrite: At the 2004 Electronic Entertainment Expo, Nintendo unveiled a trailer showcasing realistic horseback riding, a feature Aonuma's team had developed in just four months. Originally slated for release the following year, this game was no longer a direct follow-up to *The Wind Waker*; that true sequel, *Phantom Hourglass*, arrived on the Nintendo DS in 2007. Miyamoto noted in interviews that the chosen graphical style responded to fan demand and better suited the theme of an older Link. Technically, the game operates on a modified version of *The Wind Waker* engine.

input: Freedom of the press is ostensibly officially guaranteed by the government, but independent press outlets remain restricted, as does a substantial amount of web content. According to the Institute for War & Peace Reporting, access is blocked to local and foreign websites including avesta.tj, Tjknews.com, ferghana.ru, centrasia.ru and journalists are often obstructed from reporting on controversial events. In practice, no public criticism of the regime is tolerated and all direct protest is severely suppressed and does not receive coverage in the local media.
rewrite: While the government officially guarantees press freedom, independent outlets face restrictions, and substantial web content is blocked. Access is denied to various local and foreign sites, such as avesta.tj and ferghana.ru, as noted by the Institute for War & Peace Reporting. Journalists are frequently hindered from covering controversial topics. In practice, no public criticism of the regime is allowed, all direct protest is harshly suppressed, and such events receive no coverage in local media.

input: The most commonly used forms of medium distance transport in Hyderabad include government owned services such as light railways and buses, as well as privately operated taxis and auto rickshaws. Bus services operate from the Mahatma Gandhi Bus Station in the city centre and carry over 130 million passengers daily across the entire network.:76 Hyderabad's light rail transportation system, the Multi-Modal Transport System (MMTS), is a three line suburban rail service used by over 160,000 passengers daily. Complementing these government services are minibus routes operated by Setwin (Society for Employment Promotion & Training in Twin Cities). Intercity rail services also operate from Hyderabad; the main, and largest, station is Secunderabad Railway Station, which serves as Indian Railways' South Central Railway zone headquarters and a hub for both buses and MMTS light rail services connecting Secunderabad and Hyderabad. Other major railway stations in Hyderabad are Hyderabad Deccan Station, Kachiguda Railway Station, Begumpet Railway Station, Malkajgiri Railway Station and Lingampally Railway Station. The Hyderabad Metro, a new rapid transit system, is to be added to the existing public transport infrastructure and is scheduled to operate three lines by 2015.
rewrite: In Hyderabad, medium-distance travel relies on a mix of public and private options. Government-run buses, departing from the central Mahatma Gandhi Bus Station, serve over 130 million passengers daily across their network. The suburban light rail, known as the Multi-Modal Transport System (MMTS), operates three lines and carries more than 160,000 commuters each day. These services are supplemented by Setwin minibuses and privately operated taxis and auto rickshaws. For intercity rail travel, the primary hub is Secunderabad Railway Station, which functions as the headquarters for Indian Railways' South Central zone and connects to both bus and MMTS routes. Other key stations include Hyderabad Deccan, Kachiguda, Begumpet, Malkajgiri, and Lingampally. Additionally, the new Hyderabad Metro rapid transit system is planned to launch three lines by 2015, expanding the city's public transport infrastructure.

input: Philadelphia is home to many national historical sites that relate to the founding of the United States. Independence National Historical Park is the center of these historical landmarks being one of the country's 22 UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Independence Hall, where the Declaration of Independence was signed, and the Liberty Bell are the city's most famous attractions. Other historic sites include homes for Edgar Allan Poe, Betsy Ross, and Thaddeus Kosciuszko, early government buildings like the First and Second Banks of the United States, Fort Mifflin, and the Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') Church. Philadelphia alone has 67 National Historic Landmarks, the third most of any city in the country.
rewrite: As a city rich with landmarks tied to America's founding, Philadelphia boasts many national historical sites. Its most famous attractions are Independence Hall—where the Declaration of Independence was signed—and the Liberty Bell. These are part of Independence National Historical Park, one of only 22 UNESCO World Heritage Sites in the United States. The city also contains numerous other historic places, including the homes of Edgar Allan Poe, Betsy Ross, and Thaddeus Kosciuszko, along with early government buildings, Fort Mifflin, and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') Church. With 67 National Historic Landmarks, Philadelphia holds the third-highest total of any U.S. city.

input: New York is a prominent location for the American entertainment industry, with many films, television series, books, and other media being set there. As of 2012, New York City was the second largest center for filmmaking and television production in the United States, producing about 200 feature films annually, employing 130,000 individuals, and generating an estimated $7.1 billion in direct expenditures, and by volume, New York is the world leader in independent film production; one-third of all American independent films are produced in New York City. The Association of Independent Commercial Producers is also based in New York. In the first five months of 2014 alone, location filming for television pilots in New York City exceeded the record production levels for all of 2013, with New York surpassing Los Angeles as the top North American city for the same distinction during the 2013/2014 cycle.
rewrite: New York stands as a major hub for American entertainment, serving as the setting for countless films, television series, books, and other media. By volume, it is the global leader in independent film production, with one-third of all American independent films made in New York City. As of 2012, the city ranked as the nation's second largest center for film and television production, creating roughly 200 feature films each year. This industry directly employed 130,000 people and generated an estimated $7.1 billion in expenditures. Furthermore, the Association of Independent Commercial Producers is headquartered there. Demonstrating its growth, location filming for television pilots in the first five months of 2014 alone surpassed the entire 2013 record. During the 2013/2014 cycle, New York outpaced Los Angeles as the top North American city for this activity.

input: Control of labour and inter-group conflict is characteristic of corporate-level or 'tribal' groups, headed by a charismatic individual; whether a 'big man' or a proto-chief, functioning as a lineage-group head. Whether a non-hierarchical system of organization existed is debatable, and there is no evidence that explicitly suggests that Neolithic societies functioned under any dominating class or individual, as was the case in the chiefdoms of the European Early Bronze Age. Theories to explain the apparent implied egalitarianism of Neolithic (and Paleolithic) societies have arisen, notably the Marxist concept of primitive communism.
rewrite: Corporate-level or 'tribal' groups, typically led by a charismatic lineage head like a 'big man' or proto-chief, are marked by their control of labour and inter-group conflict. However, whether a non-hierarchical structure existed remains debatable. No evidence explicitly indicates Neolithic societies had a dominating class or individual, unlike later European Bronze Age chiefdoms. This implied egalitarianism has spurred theories, most notably the Marxist idea of primitive communism, to explain Neolithic and Paleolithic social organization.

input: Following the success of season one, the second season was moved up to air in January 2003. The number of episodes increased, as did the show's budget and the charge for commercial spots. Dunkleman left the show, leaving Seacrest as the lone host. Kristin Adams was a correspondent for this season.
rewrite: Due to the first season's success, season two premiered earlier in January 2003. With a larger budget and more episodes, commercial rates also rose. Kristin Adams served as a correspondent, while Dunkleman's departure left Seacrest as the sole host.

input: The Times Literary Supplement (TLS) first appeared in 1902 as a supplement to The Times, becoming a separately paid-for weekly literature and society magazine in 1914. The Times and the TLS have continued to be co-owned, and as of 2012 the TLS is also published by News International and cooperates closely with The Times, with its online version hosted on The Times website, and its editorial offices based in Times House, Pennington Street, London.
rewrite: Launched in 1902 as a supplement to The Times, the Times Literary Supplement (TLS) became an independent paid weekly in 1914, focusing on literature and society. It remains under the same ownership as The Times. Since 2012, News International has published the TLS, which maintains close ties to The Times. Its online edition is hosted on The Times website, and its editorial offices are located in Times House on Pennington Street in London.

input: Congo is located in the central-western part of sub-Saharan Africa, along the Equator, lying between latitudes 4°N and 5°S, and longitudes 11° and 19°E. To the south and east of it is the Democratic Republic of Congo. It is also bounded by Gabon to the west, Cameroon and the Central African Republic to the north, and Cabinda (Angola) to the southwest. It has a short coast on the Atlantic Ocean.
rewrite: Situated along the Equator in central-western sub-Saharan Africa, Congo lies between latitudes 4°N and 5°S and longitudes 11° and 19°E. It shares borders with Gabon to the west, Cameroon and the Central African Republic to the north, and Cabinda (Angola) to the southwest. To its south and east is the Democratic Republic of Congo. The country also features a brief Atlantic coastline.

input: In 1219 Pope Honorius III invited Saint Dominic and his companions to take up residence at the ancient Roman basilica of Santa Sabina, which they did by early 1220. Before that time the friars had only a temporary residence in Rome at the convent of San Sisto Vecchio which Honorius III had given to Dominic circa 1218 intending it to become a convent for a reformation of nuns at Rome under Dominic's guidance. In May 1220 at Bologna the order's first General Chapter mandated that each new priory of the order maintain its own studium conventuale thus laying the foundation of the Dominican tradition of sponsoring widespread institutions of learning. The official foundation of the Dominican convent at Santa Sabina with its studium conventuale occurred with the legal transfer of property from Honorius III to the Order of Preachers on June 5, 1222. This studium was transformed into the order's first studium provinciale by Saint Thomas Aquinas in 1265. Part of the curriculum of this studium was relocated in 1288 at the studium of Santa Maria sopra Minerva which in the 16th century world be transformed into the College of Saint Thomas (Latin: Collegium Divi Thomæ). In the 20th century the college would be relocated to the convent of Saints Dominic and Sixtus and would be transformed into the Pontifical University of Saint Thomas Aquinas, Angelicum.
rewrite:
In early 1220, Saint Dominic and his companions moved into the ancient Roman basilica of Santa Sabina, following an invitation from Pope Honorius III in 1219. Previously, the friars had been housed temporarily at the convent of San Sisto Vecchio. The Pope had given this convent to Dominic around 1218, intending it to serve as a house for a reformed community of nuns in Rome under his direction. A pivotal development for Dominican education occurred in May 1220 at the order's first General Chapter in Bologna. It mandated that every new priory maintain its own *studium conventuale*, establishing a tradition of widespread learning institutions.

The Dominican convent at Santa Sabina, along with its *studium*, was officially founded on June 5, 1222, through the legal transfer of the property from Honorius III to the Order of Preachers. In 1265, Saint Thomas Aquinas elevated this school into the order's first *studium provinciale*. Part of its curriculum was transferred in 1288 to the *studium* of Santa Maria sopra Minerva. This institution was transformed in the 16th century into the College of Saint Thomas. Later, in the 20th century, the college was relocated to the convent of Saints Dominic and Sixtus, where it became the Pontifical University of Saint Thomas Aquinas, known as the Angelicum.

input: Because of Oklahoma's position between zones of differing prevailing temperature and winds, weather patterns within the state can vary widely over relatively short distances and can change drastically in a short time. As an example, on November 11, 1911, the temperature at Oklahoma City reached 83 °F (28 °C) in the afternoon (the record high for that date), then an Arctic cold front of unprecedented intensity slammed across the state, causing the temperature to crash 66 degrees, down to 17 °F (−8 °C) at midnight (the record low for that date); thus, both the record high and record low for November 11 were set on the same date. This type of phenomenon is also responsible for many of the tornadoes in the area, such as the 1912 Oklahoma tornado outbreak, when a warm front traveled along a stalled cold front, resulting in an average of about one tornado per hour over the course of a day.
rewrite: Oklahoma’s location between regions with contrasting prevailing temperatures and winds leads to highly variable weather across short distances, often shifting abruptly. A striking example occurred on November 11, 1911, in Oklahoma City: the afternoon temperature hit a record high of 83°F (28°C), only to plummet 66 degrees to a record low of 17°F (−8°C) by midnight as an intensely powerful Arctic front swept through. Thus, both the daily high and low records for that date were established in a single day. This volatile atmospheric interaction also drives frequent tornadoes in the region. For instance, during the 1912 Oklahoma tornado outbreak, a warm front advanced along a stationary cold front, generating roughly one tornado per hour over a full day.

input: On September 21, 1529, Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón commanded the Spanish ship Florida, on his second attempt to recross the Pacific from the Maluku Islands. He stood off a group of islands from which local inhabitants hurled stones at his ship. These islands, which he named "Los Pintados", may have been Ujelang. On October 1, he found another group of islands where he went ashore for eight days, exchanged gifts with the local inhabitants and took on water. These islands, which he named "Los Jardines", may have been Enewetak or Bikini Atoll.
rewrite: On September 21, 1529, during his second Pacific crossing attempt from the Maluku Islands, Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón commanded the Spanish ship Florida. He encountered islands—possibly Ujelang—where inhabitants threw stones; he called them "Los Pintados." Later, on October 1, he reached another group, perhaps Enewetak or Bikini Atoll, naming them "Los Jardines." There he landed for eight days, exchanging gifts with locals and taking on water.

input: Modern navies that operate such aircraft carriers treat them as the capital ship of the fleet, a role previously held by the battleship. This change took place during World War II in response to air power becoming a significant factor in warfare, driven by the superior range, flexibility and effectiveness of carrier-launched aircraft. Following the war, carrier operations continued to increase in size and importance. Supercarriers, displacing 75,000 tonnes or greater, have become the pinnacle of carrier development. Some are powered by nuclear reactors and form the core of a fleet designed to operate far from home. Amphibious assault ships, such as USS Tarawa and HMS Ocean, serve the purpose of carrying and landing Marines, and operate a large contingent of helicopters for that purpose. Also known as "commando carriers" or "helicopter carriers", many have the capability to operate VSTOL aircraft.
rewrite: In modern navies, the aircraft carrier has replaced the battleship as the fleet's capital ship. This shift occurred during World War II, when the superior range, flexibility, and effectiveness of carrier-launched aircraft established air power as a decisive factor in warfare. After the war, the scale and significance of carrier operations only grew. The pinnacle of this development is the supercarrier, vessels displacing at least 75,000 tonnes. Often nuclear-powered, these ships form the core of fleets capable of operating far from their home nations. For the specific purpose of transporting and landing Marines, navies employ amphibious assault ships like the USS Tarawa and HMS Ocean. These vessels, also called "commando carriers" or "helicopter carriers," operate large numbers of helicopters and many can also deploy VSTOL aircraft.

input: The earliest known human activity on the island dates to around the 10th millennium BC. Archaeological remains from this period include the well-preserved Neolithic village of Khirokitia, and Cyprus is home to some of the oldest water wells in the world. Cyprus was settled by Mycenaean Greeks in two waves in the 2nd millennium BC. As a strategic location in the Middle East, it was subsequently occupied by several major powers, including the empires of the Assyrians, Egyptians and Persians, from whom the island was seized in 333 BC by Alexander the Great. Subsequent rule by Ptolemaic Egypt, the Classical and Eastern Roman Empire, Arab caliphates for a short period, the French Lusignan dynasty and the Venetians, was followed by over three centuries of Ottoman rule between 1571 and 1878 (de jure until 1914).
rewrite: Human activity on Cyprus began as early as the 10th millennium BC, evidenced by archaeological remains like the Neolithic village of Khirokitia and some of the world's oldest water wells. Mycenaean Greeks settled the island in two distinct waves during the 2nd millennium BC. Due to its strategic Middle Eastern position, Cyprus later fell under the control of successive major powers: the Assyrians, Egyptians, and Persians. Alexander the Great seized the island from the Persians in 333 BC. Subsequent rulers included Ptolemaic Egypt, the Classical and Eastern Roman Empire, Arab caliphates briefly, the French Lusignan dynasty, and the Venetians. This was followed by over three centuries of Ottoman rule from 1571 to 1878, de jure lasting until 1914.

input: Several Americans, especially Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Jefferson, played a major role in bringing Enlightenment ideas to the New World and in influencing British and French thinkers. Franklin was influential for his political activism and for his advances in physics. The cultural exchange during the Age of Enlightenment ran in both directions across the Atlantic. Thinkers such as Paine, Locke, and Rousseau all take Native American cultural practices as examples of natural freedom. The Americans closely followed English and Scottish political ideas, as well as some French thinkers such as Montesquieu. As deists, they were influenced by ideas of John Toland (1670–1722) and Matthew Tindal (1656–1733). During the Enlightenment there was a great emphasis upon liberty, democracy, republicanism and religious tolerance. Attempts to reconcile science and religion resulted in a widespread rejection of prophecy, miracle and revealed religion in preference for Deism – especially by Thomas Paine in The Age of Reason and by Thomas Jefferson in his short Jefferson Bible – from which all supernatural aspects were removed.
rewrite: The cultural exchange of the Age of Enlightenment flowed in both directions across the Atlantic. While Americans closely followed English, Scottish, and French political ideas from thinkers like Locke and Montesquieu, they also influenced European thought. Figures such as Paine, Locke, and Rousseau pointed to Native American cultural practices as models of natural freedom. Several Americans, notably Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Jefferson, were pivotal in transmitting these ideas to the New World. Franklin exerted influence through his political activism and advances in physics. As deists, they drew upon the ideas of John Toland and Matthew Tindal, reflecting the era's great emphasis on liberty, democracy, republicanism, and religious tolerance. This period saw attempts to reconcile science and religion, leading to a widespread preference for Deism over revealed religion. This rejection of prophecy and miracle is evident in Thomas Paine's *The Age of Reason* and Thomas Jefferson's Bible, from which he removed all supernatural elements.

input: In 2013, China led the world in renewable energy production, with a total capacity of 378 GW, mainly from hydroelectric and wind power. As of 2014, China leads the world in the production and use of wind power, solar photovoltaic power and smart grid technologies, generating almost as much water, wind and solar energy as all of France and Germany's power plants combined. China's renewable energy sector is growing faster than its fossil fuels and nuclear power capacity. Since 2005, production of solar cells in China has expanded 100-fold. As Chinese renewable manufacturing has grown, the costs of renewable energy technologies have dropped. Innovation has helped, but the main driver of reduced costs has been market expansion.
rewrite: By 2014, China had become the global leader in wind power, solar photovoltaic power, and smart grid technologies. Its output from water, wind, and solar sources nearly matched the combined total of all power plants in France and Germany. Already in 2013, the country led in renewable energy production with a 378 GW capacity, primarily from hydroelectric and wind power. This renewable sector is expanding more rapidly than its fossil fuel and nuclear counterparts. Since 2005, for instance, China's solar cell production has increased one hundred times. This massive growth in manufacturing has driven down the costs of renewable technologies, where market expansion has been the primary force behind lower prices, aided by innovation.

input: Rapid decompression can be much more dangerous than vacuum exposure itself. Even if the victim does not hold his or her breath, venting through the windpipe may be too slow to prevent the fatal rupture of the delicate alveoli of the lungs. Eardrums and sinuses may be ruptured by rapid decompression, soft tissues may bruise and seep blood, and the stress of shock will accelerate oxygen consumption leading to hypoxia. Injuries caused by rapid decompression are called barotrauma. A pressure drop of 13 kPa (100 Torr), which produces no symptoms if it is gradual, may be fatal if it occurs suddenly.
rewrite: The dangers of rapid decompression often exceed those of vacuum exposure alone. Injuries from such an event, known as barotrauma, can include ruptured eardrums and sinuses, bruised and bleeding soft tissues, and fatal damage to the lungs' delicate alveoli. This lung rupture can occur even if the victim does not hold their breath, as venting through the windpipe may be too slow. The accompanying shock also accelerates oxygen use, causing hypoxia. Notably, a sudden pressure drop of 13 kPa (100 Torr), which is harmless if gradual, can prove fatal.

input: After World War I, when Britain and France divided up the Middle East's countries, apart from Turkey, between them, pursuant to the Sykes-Picot agreement—in violation of solemn wartime promises of postwar Arab autonomy—there came an immediate reaction: the Muslim Brotherhood emerged in Egypt, the House of Saud took over the Hijaz, and regimes led by army officers came to power in Iran and Turkey. "[B]oth illiberal currents of the modern Middle East," writes de Bellaigne, "Islamism and militarism, received a major impetus from Western empire-builders." As often happens in countries undergoing social crisis, the aspirations of the Muslim world's translators and modernizers, such as Muhammad Abduh, largely had to yield to retrograde currents.
rewrite: Following the post-World War I division of the Middle East by Britain and France under the Sykes-Picot agreement—a breach of pledges for Arab autonomy—a swift reaction unfolded. This included the rise of the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt, the Saudi conquest of the Hijaz, and the ascent of military-led regimes in Iran and Turkey. Historian de Bellaigne observes that Western empire-builders significantly fueled both modern Islamism and militarism, the region's dominant illiberal currents. Consequently, during this social crisis, the progressive aims of translators and modernizers like Muhammad Abduh were largely overwhelmed by more retrograde forces.

input: In 2002, Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" was voted "the UK's favourite hit of all time" in a poll conducted by the Guinness World Records British Hit Singles Book. In 2004 the song was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame. Many scholars consider the "Bohemian Rhapsody" music video ground-breaking, and credit it with popularising the medium. Rock historian Paul Fowles states the song is "widely credited as the first global hit single for which an accompanying video was central to the marketing strategy". It has been hailed as launching the MTV age. Acclaimed for their stadium rock, in 2005 an industry poll ranked Queen's performance at Live Aid in 1985 as the best live act in history. In 2007, they were also voted the greatest British band in history by BBC Radio 2 listeners.
rewrite: Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" has earned numerous accolades over the years. In a 2002 Guinness World Records British Hit Singles Book poll, it was named the UK's favourite hit of all time. Two years later, the song entered the Grammy Hall of Fame. Scholars often highlight its groundbreaking music video, crediting it with popularizing the medium and even launching the MTV age. Rock historian Paul Fowles notes it is widely considered the first global hit single where a video was central to marketing. Beyond the song, Queen's legacy as a live act is celebrated; their 1985 Live Aid performance was ranked the best live act in history in a 2005 industry poll. Furthermore, BBC Radio 2 listeners voted them the greatest British band in history in 2007.

input: By the early years of the 21st century, western clothing styles had, to some extent, become international styles. This process began hundreds of years earlier, during the periods of European colonialism. The process of cultural dissemination has perpetuated over the centuries as Western media corporations have penetrated markets throughout the world, spreading Western culture and styles. Fast fashion clothing has also become a global phenomenon. These garments are less expensive, mass-produced Western clothing. Donated used clothing from Western countries are also delivered to people in poor countries by charity organizations.
rewrite: International styles have largely adopted Western clothing trends in the 21st century, a process originating centuries prior with European colonialism. Cultural dissemination continued over time as Western media corporations expanded globally, spreading their culture and fashions. The rise of fast fashion, consisting of inexpensive, mass-produced Western garments, has further solidified this global phenomenon. Additionally, charity organizations deliver donated used clothing from Western nations to people in poorer countries.

input: As the century wore on, the factions slowly began to adopt more coherent political tendencies as the interests of their power bases began to diverge. The Whig party's initial base of support from the great aristocratic families, widened to include the emerging industrial interests and wealthy merchants. As well as championing constitutional monarchy with strict limits on the monarch's power, the Whigs adamantly opposed a Catholic king as a threat to liberty, and believed in extending toleration to nonconformist Protestants, or dissenters. A major influence on the Whigs were the liberal political ideas of John Locke, and the concepts of universal rights employed by Locke and Algernon Sidney.
rewrite: Over time, the factions developed clearer political alignments as their core supporters' interests grew apart. The Whigs, originally backed by major aristocratic families, expanded their base to incorporate new industrialists and rich merchants. They were staunch supporters of a constitutional monarchy with strong restrictions on royal authority and were fiercely opposed to a Catholic monarch, viewing it as a danger to freedom. The party also advocated for toleration of dissenting Protestants. Their ideology was significantly shaped by the liberal theories of John Locke and the universal rights principles advanced by both Locke and Algernon Sidney.

input: Although the new licensing laws prevented new beer houses from being created, those already in existence were allowed to continue and many did not close until nearly the end of the 19th century. A very small number remained into the 21st century. The vast majority of the beer houses applied for the new licences and became full pubs. These usually small establishments can still be identified in many towns, seemingly oddly located in the middle of otherwise terraced housing part way up a street, unlike purpose-built pubs that are usually found on corners or road junctions. Many of today's respected real ale micro-brewers in the UK started as home based Beer House brewers under the 1830 Act.
rewrite: While new beer houses could no longer be established under revised licensing laws, existing ones were permitted to operate, with many surviving until nearly 1900. A handful even endured into the 21st century. Most beer houses sought new licenses and transitioned into full public houses. Today, these typically small establishments remain identifiable in numerous towns. They often appear oddly situated midway along a street amidst terraced housing, contrasting with purpose-built pubs commonly located on corners or junctions. Furthermore, many of the UK’s current respected real ale micro-brewers originated as home-based brewers operating under the 1830 Beer House Act.

input: On January 8, 2006, while Schwarzenegger was riding his Harley Davidson motorcycle in Los Angeles, with his son Patrick in the sidecar, another driver backed into the street he was riding on, causing him and his son to collide with the car at a low speed. While his son and the other driver were unharmed, the governor sustained a minor injury to his lip, requiring 15 stitches. "No citations were issued", said Officer Jason Lee, a Los Angeles Police Department spokesman. Schwarzenegger did not obtain his motorcycle license until July 3, 2006.
rewrite: On January 8, 2006, Arnold Schwarzenegger was riding his Harley Davidson motorcycle in Los Angeles with his son Patrick in the sidecar. Another motorist, backing into the street, caused a low-speed collision. Schwarzenegger sustained a minor lip injury requiring 15 stitches, though his son and the other driver were unharmed. According to LAPD spokesman Officer Jason Lee, no citations were issued. Notably, Schwarzenegger did not obtain his motorcycle license until several months later, on July 3, 2006.

input: Seattle in this period attracted widespread attention as home to these many companies, but also by hosting the 1990 Goodwill Games and the APEC leaders conference in 1993, as well as through the worldwide popularity of grunge, a sound that had developed in Seattle's independent music scene. Another bid for worldwide attention—hosting the World Trade Organization Ministerial Conference of 1999—garnered visibility, but not in the way its sponsors desired, as related protest activity and police reactions to those protests overshadowed the conference itself. The city was further shaken by the Mardi Gras Riots in 2001, and then literally shaken the following day by the Nisqually earthquake.
rewrite: During the 1990s, Seattle drew global focus not only as the headquarters of numerous prominent companies but also by staging major events like the 1990 Goodwill Games and the 1993 APEC conference. The city's grunge music scene, born from its independent venues, also achieved worldwide popularity. An attempt to boost its profile further—hosting the 1999 WTO Ministerial Conference—backfired when protests and the police response eclipsed the event itself. Further turmoil followed with the 2001 Mardi Gras Riots, and the very next day, the Nisqually earthquake physically shook the city.

input: On November 18, 1990, the Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church enthroned Mstyslav as Patriarch of Kiev and all Ukraine during ceremonies at Saint Sophia's Cathedral. Also on November 18, Canada announced that its consul-general to Kiev would be Ukrainian-Canadian Nestor Gayowsky. On November 19, the United States announced that its consul to Kiev would be Ukrainian-American John Stepanchuk. On November 19, the chairmen of the Ukrainian and Russian parliaments, respectively, Kravchuk and Yeltsin, signed a 10-year bilateral pact. In early December 1990 the Party of Democratic Rebirth of Ukraine was founded; on December 15, the Democratic Party of Ukraine was founded.
rewrite: On November 18, 1990, two significant events unfolded. At Saint Sophia's Cathedral, Mstyslav was enthroned as Patriarch of Kiev and all Ukraine for the Ukrainian Autocephalous Orthodox Church. That same day, Canada named Ukrainian-Canadian Nestor Gayowsky as its consul-general to Kiev. The following day, November 19, saw the United States appoint Ukrainian-American John Stepanchuk as its consul to Kiev. Also on the 19th, Ukrainian and Russian parliamentary chairmen Kravchuk and Yeltsin signed a 10-year bilateral pact. In early December, the Party of Democratic Rebirth of Ukraine was founded, followed by the establishment of the Democratic Party of Ukraine on December 15.

input: The library is based at two public sites: the Reading Room at the RIBA's headquarters, 66 Portland Place, London; and the RIBA Architecture Study Rooms in the Henry Cole Wing of the V&A. The Reading Room, designed by the building's architect George Grey Wornum and his wife Miriam, retains its original 1934 Art Deco interior with open bookshelves, original furniture and double-height central space. The study rooms, opened in 2004, were designed by Wright & Wright. The library is funded entirely by the RIBA but it is open to the public without charge. It operates a free education programme aimed at students, education groups and families, and an information service for RIBA members and the public through the RIBA Information Centre.
rewrite: Located across two public sites, the library is fully funded by the RIBA and offers free access to all. One site is the Reading Room at 66 Portland Place, London, the RIBA's headquarters. Designed by architect George Grey Wornum and his wife Miriam, this space preserves its 1934 Art Deco interior, complete with original furniture, open bookshelves, and a double-height central area. The other is the RIBA Architecture Study Rooms, housed in the V&A's Henry Cole Wing and designed by Wright & Wright, which opened in 2004. The library runs a complimentary education programme for students, educational groups, and families. Additionally, the RIBA Information Centre provides an information service to both members and the general public.

input: Historical records show evidence of Jewish communities north of the Alps and Pyrenees as early as the 8th and 9th century. By the 11th century Jewish settlers, moving from southern European and Middle Eastern centers, appear to have begun to settle in the north, especially along the Rhine, often in response to new economic opportunities and at the invitation of local Christian rulers. Thus Baldwin V, Count of Flanders, invited Jacob ben Yekutiel and his fellow Jews to settle in his lands; and soon after the Norman Conquest of England, William the Conqueror likewise extended a welcome to continental Jews to take up residence there. Bishop Rüdiger Huzmann called on the Jews of Mainz to relocate to Speyer. In all of these decisions, the idea that Jews had the know-how and capacity to jump-start the economy, improve revenues, and enlarge trade seems to have played a prominent role. Typically Jews relocated close to the markets and churches in town centres, where, though they came under the authority of both royal and ecclesiastical powers, they were accorded administrative autonomy.
rewrite: Evidence of Jewish communities north of the Alps and Pyrenees dates to the 8th and 9th centuries, according to historical records. A more substantial northward settlement, particularly along the Rhine, began in the 11th century. This movement was often driven by new economic prospects and direct invitations from Christian rulers. For instance, Baldwin V, Count of Flanders, encouraged Jacob ben Yekutiel and other Jews to settle in his territory. Following the Norman Conquest, William the Conqueror similarly invited continental Jews to England. Bishop Rüdiger Huzmann also called for Jews from Mainz to relocate to Speyer. A key motivation in these decisions appears to have been the belief that Jews possessed the expertise to stimulate the economy, boost revenues, and expand trade. Typically settling near central markets and churches, these communities were granted administrative autonomy, even while remaining under the authority of royal and ecclesiastical powers.

input: The exact nature of relations between Tibet and the Ming dynasty of China (1368–1644) is unclear.
