Other debates center on the principle of the law of the land in America being defined not just by the Constitution's Supremacy Clause, but also by legal precedence, making an accurate reading of the Constitution subject to the mores and values of a given era, and rendering the concept of historical revisionism irrelevant when discussing the Constitution.
rewrite: Critics of the modern church-state separation point to the official religious establishments that existed in several states during the Constitution's ratification. They argue this historical context suggests that applying the Establishment Clause to state governments contradicts original constitutional intent. However, the issue is complicated by the Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868, which later served as the basis for incorporating the First Amendment against the states. These debates often stem from competing interpretive theories, like originalism versus progressive doctrines such as the Living Constitution. Further discussions highlight that American law is defined not only by the Constitution's Supremacy Clause but also by legal precedent. This means an accurate constitutional reading is influenced by the prevailing mores and values of its time, which can render historical revisionism irrelevant in such debates.

input: The official language of the Republic is Modern Standard Arabic. Arabic was adopted by the Egyptians after the Arab invasion of Egypt. The spoken languages are: Egyptian Arabic (68%), Sa'idi Arabic (29%), Eastern Egyptian Bedawi Arabic (1.6%), Sudanese Arabic (0.6%), Domari (0.3%), Nobiin (0.3%), Beja (0.1%), Siwi and others. Additionally, Greek, Armenian and Italian are the main languages of immigrants. In Alexandria in the 19th century there was a large community of Italian Egyptians and Italian was the "lingua franca" of the city.
rewrite: Modern Standard Arabic serves as the Republic's official language, a status following the Arab conquest of Egypt. The primary spoken varieties are Egyptian Arabic (68%) and Sa'idi Arabic (29%), with others including Eastern Egyptian Bedawi (1.6%), Sudanese Arabic (0.6%), Domari, Nobiin, Beja, and Siwi. Immigrant communities chiefly use Greek, Armenian, and Italian. Notably, 19th-century Alexandria hosted a large Italian Egyptian community, making Italian the city's lingua franca.

input: Catalan is split in two major dialectal blocks: Eastern Catalan, and Western Catalan. The main difference lies in the treatment of unstressed a and e; which have merged to /ə/ in Eastern dialects, but which remain distinct as /a/ and /e/ in Western dialects. There are a few other differences in pronunciation, verbal morphology, and vocabulary.
rewrite: Eastern and Western Catalan form the language's two main dialectal blocks. Their key distinction is in unstressed vowels: Eastern dialects merge 'a' and 'e' into /ə/, while Western ones keep them separate as /a/ and /e/. Additional variations occur in pronunciation, verb forms, and vocabulary.

input: On basic Church teachings, the pope was unwavering. On the tenth anniversary of Humanae vitae, he reconfirmed this teaching. In his style and methodology, he was a disciple of Pius XII, whom he deeply revered. He suffered for the attacks on Pius XII for his alleged silences during the Holocaust. Pope Paul VI was less outstanding than his predecessors: he was not credited with an encyclopedic memory, nor a gift for languages, nor the brilliant writing style of Pius XII, nor did he have the charisma and outpouring love, sense of humor and human warmth of John XXIII. He took on himself the unfinished reform work of these two popes, bringing them diligently with great humility and common sense and without much fanfare to conclusion. In doing so, Paul VI saw himself following in the footsteps of the Apostle Paul, torn to several directions as Saint Paul, who said, "I am attracted to two sides at once, because the Cross always divides."
rewrite: In matters of core Church doctrine, the pope remained steadfast, reaffirming the teaching of *Humanae vitae* on its tenth anniversary. He deeply revered Pius XII, whose style and methodology he adopted as a disciple, and he suffered from attacks leveled against his predecessor over alleged silences during the Holocaust. Pope Paul VI did not possess the encyclopedic memory, linguistic gift, or brilliant writing of Pius XII, nor did he have the charisma, outpouring love, humor, and human warmth of John XXIII. Nevertheless, he took upon himself the unfinished reform work of both popes, bringing it diligently and humbly to conclusion with common sense and little fanfare. In this labor, Paul VI saw himself following the Apostle Paul, feeling torn in multiple directions, much like the saint who said, “I am attracted to two sides at once, because the Cross always divides.”

input: The earliest known document in Galician-Portuguese dates from 1228. The Foro do bo burgo do Castro Caldelas was granted by Alfonso IX of León to the town of Burgo, in Castro Caldelas, after the model of the constitutions of the town of Allariz. A distinct Galician Literature emerged during the Middle Ages: In the 13th century important contributions were made to the romance canon in Galician-Portuguese, the most notable those by the troubadour Martín Codax, the priest Airas Nunes, King Denis of Portugal and King Alfonso X of Castile, Alfonso O Sabio ("Alfonso the Wise"), the same monarch who began the process of establishing the hegemony of Castilian. During this period, Galician-Portuguese was considered the language of love poetry in the Iberian Romance linguistic culture. The names and memories of Codax and other popular cultural figures are well preserved in modern Galicia and, despite the long period of Castilian linguistic domination, these names are again household words.
rewrite: Dating to 1228, the earliest known Galician-Portuguese document is the Foro do bo burgo do Castro Caldelas. This charter was granted by Alfonso IX of León to the town of Burgo, following the constitutional model of Allariz. The Middle Ages saw the rise of a distinct Galician Literature. Within the Iberian Romance linguistic culture, Galician-Portuguese was then regarded as the premier language for love poetry. The 13th century brought major contributions to the romance canon from figures like the troubadour Martín Codax, the priest Airas Nunes, King Denis of Portugal, and King Alfonso X of Castile, known as Alfonso the Wise. Ironically, this same Alfonso X initiated the process that established Castilian's later dominance. Today, the names and legacies of Codax and other such figures remain well preserved in modern Galicia, having once again become household words after a long period of Castilian linguistic rule.

input: The city is home to New Haven Promise, a scholarship funded by Yale University for students who meet the requirements. Students must be enrolled in a public high school (charters included) for four years, be a resident of the city during that time, carry a 3.0 cumulative grade-point average, have a 90-percent attendance rate and perform 40 hours of service to the city. The initiative was launched in 2010 and there are currently more than 500 Scholars enrolled in qualifying Connecticut colleges and universities. There are more than 60 cities in the country that have a Promise-type program for their students.
rewrite: New Haven Promise, a scholarship funded by Yale University, supports eligible city students. Launched in 2010, the program requires four years in a public or charter city high school, city residency, a 3.0 GPA, 90% attendance, and 40 hours of community service. Currently, over 500 Scholars are enrolled at qualifying Connecticut colleges. This initiative is part of a broader national trend, with more than 60 U.S. cities offering similar Promise-type programs for their students.

input: Red was the color of the banner of the Byzantine emperors. In Western Europe, Emperor Charlemagne painted his palace red as a very visible symbol of his authority, and wore red shoes at his coronation. Kings, princes and, beginning in 1295, Roman Catholic cardinals began to wear red costumes. When Abbe Suger rebuilt Saint Denis Basilica outside Paris in the early 12th century, he added stained glass windows colored blue cobalt glass and red glass tinted with copper. Together they flooded the basilica with a mystical light. Soon stained glass windows were being added to cathedrals all across France, England and Germany. In Medieval painting red was used to attract attention to the most important figures; both Christ and the Virgin Mary were commonly painted wearing red mantles.
rewrite: The banner of Byzantine emperors was red, a color that became a powerful emblem of authority in medieval Europe. Emperor Charlemagne prominently displayed red at his coronation with red shoes and by painting his palace in the hue. From kings and princes to, after 1295, Roman Catholic cardinals, red garments signaled high status. In art, red drew focus to central sacred figures, such as Christ and the Virgin Mary, who were often depicted in red mantles. Meanwhile, in architecture, Abbe Suger installed stained glass of blue cobalt and copper-tinted red in Saint Denis Basilica during the 12th century, creating a mystical light. This innovation spurred the adoption of such windows in cathedrals across France, England, and Germany.

input: Democratic Party candidates were consistently elected to local office, increasing the city's ties to the South and its dominant party. In 1861, Mayor Fernando Wood called on the aldermen to declare independence from Albany and the United States after the South seceded, but his proposal was not acted on. Anger at new military conscription laws during the American Civil War (1861–1865), which spared wealthier men who could afford to pay a $300 (equivalent to $5,766 in 2016) commutation fee to hire a substitute, led to the Draft Riots of 1863, whose most visible participants were ethnic Irish working class. The situation deteriorated into attacks on New York's elite, followed by attacks on black New Yorkers and their property after fierce competition for a decade between Irish immigrants and blacks for work. Rioters burned the Colored Orphan Asylum to the ground, but more than 200 children escaped harm due to efforts of the New York City Police Department, which was mainly made up of Irish immigrants. According to historian James M. McPherson (2001), at least 120 people were killed. In all, eleven black men were lynched over five days, and the riots forced hundreds of blacks to flee the city for Williamsburg, Brooklyn, as well as New Jersey; the black population in Manhattan fell below 10,000 by 1865, which it had last been in 1820. The white working class had established dominance. Violence by longshoremen against black men was especially fierce in the docks area. It was one of the worst incidents of civil unrest in American history.
rewrite:
Throughout the American Civil War (1861–1865), the city's political alignment with the South was reinforced by the consistent election of Democratic Party candidates to local office. This connection was underscored in 1861 when Mayor Fernando Wood, following the South's secession, urged the aldermen to declare independence from both Albany and the United States, though no action was taken on his proposal. Widespread anger later erupted over new military conscription laws that allowed wealthier men to avoid service by paying a $300 commutation fee—equivalent to $5,766 in 2016—to hire a substitute. This resentment ignited the Draft Riots of 1863, whose most visible participants were ethnic Irish working-class individuals.

The unrest rapidly deteriorated into attacks on New York's elite before shifting to target black New Yorkers and their property, fueled by a decade of fierce job competition between Irish immigrants and black residents. Rioters burned the Colored Orphan Asylum to the ground, though more than 200 children escaped harm thanks to the intervention of the New York City Police Department, a force largely composed of Irish immigrants. Historian James M. McPherson (2001) notes that at least 120 people were killed in the violence. Over five days, eleven black men were lynched, and hundreds of black residents were forced to flee to places like Williamsburg, Brooklyn, and New Jersey. As a result, Manhattan's black population fell below 10,000 by 1865, a level not seen since 1820. The riots, which included especially fierce violence by longshoremen against black men in the docks area, marked one of the worst incidents of civil unrest in American history and cemented the dominance of the white working class.

input: 90th Street is split into two segments. The first segment, West 90th Street begins at Riverside Drive and ends at Central Park West or West Drive, when it is open, in Central Park on the Upper West Side. The second segment of East 90th Street begins at East Drive, at Engineers Gate of Central Park. When East Drive is closed, East 90th Street begins at Fifth Avenue on the Upper East Side and curves to the right at the FDR Drive becoming East End Avenue. Our Lady of Good Counsel Church, is located on East 90th Street between Third Avenue and Second Avenue, across the street from Ruppert Towers (1601 and 1619 Third Avenue) and Ruppert Park. Asphalt Green, which is located on East 90th Street between York Avenue and East End Avenue.
rewrite: West 90th Street forms the initial segment, running from Riverside Drive to Central Park West (or West Drive when accessible) on the Upper West Side. The second portion, East 90th Street, starts at Engineers Gate on East Drive within Central Park. If East Drive is closed, it instead begins at Fifth Avenue on the Upper East Side, curving right at the FDR Drive to become East End Avenue. Notable locations along East 90th Street include Our Lady of Good Counsel Church, situated between Third and Second Avenues opposite Ruppert Towers and Ruppert Park. Further east, between York Avenue and East End Avenue, lies Asphalt Green.

input: Tuvalu participates in the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), which is a coalition of small island and low-lying coastal countries that have concerns about their vulnerability to the adverse effects of global climate change. Under the Majuro Declaration, which was signed on 5 September 2013, Tuvalu has commitment to implement power generation of 100% renewable energy (between 2013 and 2020), which is proposed to be implemented using Solar PV (95% of demand) and biodiesel (5% of demand). The feasibility of wind power generation will be considered. Tuvalu participates in the operations of the Pacific Islands Applied Geoscience Commission (SOPAC) and the Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme (SPREP).
rewrite: As a member of the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), Tuvalu joins other vulnerable island and coastal nations in addressing climate change threats. The country is also active in the Pacific Islands Applied Geoscience Commission (SOPAC) and the Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme (SPREP). Under the 2013 Majuro Declaration, Tuvalu committed to achieving 100% renewable power generation from 2013 to 2020. This plan primarily involves using Solar PV for 95% of demand and biodiesel for the remaining 5%, while also considering the feasibility of wind power.

input: In higher organisms (like people), these two modes of perception combine into what Whitehead terms "symbolic reference", which links appearance with causation in a process that is so automatic that both people and animals have difficulty refraining from it. By way of illustration, Whitehead uses the example of a person's encounter with a chair. An ordinary person looks up, sees a colored shape, and immediately infers that it is a chair. However, an artist, Whitehead supposes, "might not have jumped to the notion of a chair", but instead "might have stopped at the mere contemplation of a beautiful color and a beautiful shape." This is not the normal human reaction; most people place objects in categories by habit and instinct, without even thinking about it. Moreover, animals do the same thing. Using the same example, Whitehead points out that a dog "would have acted immediately on the hypothesis of a chair and would have jumped onto it by way of using it as such." In this way symbolic reference is a fusion of pure sense perceptions on the one hand and causal relations on the other, and that it is in fact the causal relationships that dominate the more basic mentality (as the dog illustrates), while it is the sense perceptions which indicate a higher grade mentality (as the artist illustrates).
rewrite: Whitehead describes "symbolic reference" as the automatic fusion, in higher organisms like humans and animals, of two modes of perception: appearance and causation. This process is so instinctive that refraining from it is difficult. He illustrates this with an encounter with a chair. An ordinary person, upon seeing a colored shape, immediately categorizes it as a chair. This reaction is typical; most people habitually and instinctively place objects into categories without conscious thought. Animals exhibit the same behavior. A dog, Whitehead notes, would immediately act on the hypothesis of a chair, jumping onto it to use it. In contrast, an artist "might not have jumped to the notion of a chair," but instead paused to contemplate "a beautiful color and a beautiful shape." This demonstrates that symbolic reference combines pure sense perceptions with causal relations. The causal relationships dominate more basic mentality, as seen with the dog, driving immediate practical action. The sense perceptions, however, indicate a higher grade of mentality, as exemplified by the artist's contemplative pause, where appearance is appreciated for itself rather than merely signaling utility.

input: Above the forestry, there is often a band of short pine trees (Pinus mugo), which is in turn superseded by Alpenrosen, dwarf shrubs, typically Rhododendron ferrugineum (on acid soils) or Rhododendron hirsutum (on alkaline soils). Although the Alpenrose prefers acidic soil, the plants are found throughout the region. Above the tree line is the area defined as "alpine" where in the alpine meadow plants are found that have adapted well to harsh conditions of cold temperatures, aridity, and high altitudes. The alpine area fluctuates greatly because of regional fluctuations in tree lines.
rewrite: Above the tree line lies the alpine zone, characterized by meadows where plants have adapted to cold, aridity, and high altitude. This alpine area varies significantly due to regional differences in the tree line's elevation. Below it, a band of short pine trees (Pinus mugo) often grows above the forestry. These pines are succeeded by Alpenrosen, dwarf shrubs such as Rhododendron ferrugineum on acid soils or Rhododendron hirsutum on alkaline soils. Although preferring acidic soil, Alpenrosen are found throughout the region.

input: Carpet-weaving is historically a major traditional profession for the majority of Armenian women, including many Armenian families. Prominent Karabakh carpet weavers there were men too. The oldest extant Armenian carpet from the region, referred to as Artsakh (see also Karabakh carpet) during the medieval era, is from the village of Banants (near Gandzak) and dates to the early 13th century. The first time that the Armenian word for carpet, gorg, was used in historical sources was in a 1242–1243 Armenian inscription on the wall of the Kaptavan Church in Artsakh.
rewrite: Historically, carpet-weaving has been a primary traditional occupation for most Armenian women and their families. Notably, in Karabakh, many skilled weavers were also men. The oldest surviving Armenian carpet from the medieval region of Artsakh (Karabakh) originates from Banants village near Gandzak and belongs to the early 13th century. Additionally, the Armenian term for carpet, "gorg," first appears in historical records within a 1242–1243 inscription on the Kaptavan Church in Artsakh.

input: "Azure, three ships with three masts, rigged and under full sail, the sails, pennants and ensigns Argent, each charged with a cross Gules; on a chief of the second a pale quarterly Azure and Gules, on the 1st and 4th a fleur-de-lis or, on the 2nd and 3rd a leopard or, between two roses Gules seeded Or barbed Vert." The shield had as a crest: "A sphere without a frame, bounded with the Zodiac in bend Or, between two pennants flottant Argent, each charged with a cross Gules, over the sphere the words DEUS INDICAT" (Latin: God Indicates). The supporters were two sea lions (lions with fishes' tails) and the motto was DEO DUCENTE NIL NOCET (Latin: Where God Leads, Nothing Hurts).
rewrite: On a blue field, three three-masted ships sail with full silver sails, pennants, and ensigns, each marked with a red cross. Above this, a silver horizontal band features a vertical stripe divided into blue and red quarters. The blue quarters display a gold fleur-de-lis, while the red quarters hold a gold leopard, all set between two red roses with gold seeds and green barbs. The crest above the shield is a frameless gold sphere encircled by a zodiac band, flanked by two floating silver pennants each bearing a red cross; the sphere is inscribed "DEUS INDICAT" (God Indicates). Supported by two sea lions, the emblem bears the motto DEO DUCENTE NIL NOCET (Where God Leads, Nothing Hurts).

input: Immunology is a branch of biomedical science that covers the study of immune systems in all organisms. It charts, measures, and contextualizes the: physiological functioning of the immune system in states of both health and diseases; malfunctions of the immune system in immunological disorders (such as autoimmune diseases, hypersensitivities, immune deficiency, and transplant rejection); the physical, chemical and physiological characteristics of the components of the immune system in vitro, in situ, and in vivo. Immunology has applications in numerous disciplines of medicine, particularly in the fields of organ transplantation, oncology, virology, bacteriology, parasitology, psychiatry, and dermatology.
rewrite: Immunology, a field of biomedical science, examines immune systems across all organisms. It investigates the immune system's physiological function in health and disease, along with its malfunctions in disorders like autoimmune diseases and immune deficiencies. The discipline also analyzes the physical, chemical, and physiological properties of immune components in various settings. Its principles are applied across many medical areas, including oncology, virology, organ transplantation, and dermatology.

input: In 1911 arsphenamine, the first synthetic anti-infective drug, was developed by Paul Ehrlich and chemist Alfred Bertheim of the Institute of Experimental Therapy in Berlin. The drug was given the commercial name Salvarsan. Ehrlich, noting both the general toxicity of arsenic and the selective absorption of certain dyes by bacteria, hypothesized that an arsenic-containing dye with similar selective absorption properties could be used to treat bacterial infections. Arsphenamine was prepared as part of a campaign to synthesize a series of such compounds, and found to exhibit partially selective toxicity. Arsphenamine proved to be the first effective treatment for syphilis, a disease which prior to that time was incurable and led inexorably to severe skin ulceration, neurological damage, and death.[citation needed]
rewrite: In 1911, Paul Ehrlich and chemist Alfred Bertheim, working at Berlin's Institute of Experimental Therapy, developed arsphenamine. This became the first synthetic anti-infective drug, marketed under the name Salvarsan. Ehrlich's hypothesis drove the research: observing both arsenic's toxicity and how certain dyes were selectively absorbed by bacteria, he proposed that an arsenic-based dye with similar properties could combat infections. The drug was created during a systematic effort to synthesize such compounds and demonstrated partially selective toxicity. It provided the first effective cure for syphilis, a previously untreatable disease that inevitably caused severe ulceration, neurological harm, and death.

input: This constitution was created when the U.S. Congress directed local government to organize a constitutional convention to write the Puerto Rico Constitution in 1951. The acceptance of that constitution by Puerto Rico's electorate, the U.S. Congress, and the U.S. president occurred in 1952. In addition, the rights, privileges and immunities attendant to United States citizens are "respected in Puerto Rico to the same extent as though Puerto Rico were a state of the union" through the express extension of the Privileges and Immunities Clause of the U.S. Constitution by the U.S. Congress in 1948.
rewrite: In 1951, the U.S. Congress directed local authorities to convene a constitutional convention, leading to the creation of Puerto Rico's Constitution. This document was subsequently accepted in 1952 by the island's electorate, the U.S. Congress, and the President. Furthermore, through an express extension by Congress in 1948, the Privileges and Immunities Clause ensures that the rights and immunities of U.S. citizens are respected in Puerto Rico as fully as if it were a state.

input: Today, this term also refers to the doctrines and practices of the Reformed churches of which Calvin was an early leader. Less commonly, it can refer to the individual teaching of Calvin himself. The particulars of Calvinist theology may be stated in a number of ways. Perhaps the best known summary is contained in the five points of Calvinism, though these points identify the Calvinist view on soteriology rather than summarizing the system as a whole. Broadly speaking, Calvinism stresses the sovereignty or rule of God in all things — in salvation but also in all of life. This concept is seen clearly in the doctrines of predestination and total depravity.
rewrite: While often associated with the five points summarizing its soteriology, Calvinism more broadly stresses the sovereignty of God in all aspects of life and salvation. This theological system, whose doctrines and practices define the Reformed churches early led by Calvin, is also less commonly used to describe his personal teachings. Its key concepts, including predestination and total depravity, clearly illustrate this overarching principle. The particulars of Calvinist theology can be articulated in various ways, with the five points being a well-known but incomplete summary of the entire system.

input: The Pagode de Vincennes Buddhist temple, near Lake Daumesnil in the Bois de Vincennes, is the former Cameroon pavilion from the 1931 Paris Colonial Exposition. It hosts several different schools of Buddhism, and does not have a single leader. It shelters the biggest Buddha statue in Europe, more than nine metres high. There are two other small temples located in the Asian community in the 13th arrondissement. A Hindu temple, dedicated to Ganesh, on Rue Pajol in the 18th arrondissement, opened in 1985.
rewrite: Originally the Cameroon pavilion at the 1931 Paris Colonial Exposition, the Pagode de Vincennes Buddhist temple stands near Lake Daumesnil in the Bois de Vincennes. It houses the largest Buddha statue in Europe, standing over nine meters tall. The temple accommodates multiple Buddhist schools without a single leader. Elsewhere in Paris, two smaller temples are in the 13th arrondissement's Asian community, and a Hindu temple dedicated to Ganesh opened on Rue Pajol in the 18th arrondissement in 1985.

input: There have been cases of a variety of speech being deliberately reclassified to serve political purposes. One example is Moldovan. In 1996, the Moldovan parliament, citing fears of "Romanian expansionism", rejected a proposal from President Mircea Snegur to change the name of the language to Romanian, and in 2003 a Moldovan–Romanian dictionary was published, purporting to show that the two countries speak different languages. Linguists of the Romanian Academy reacted by declaring that all the Moldovan words were also Romanian words; while in Moldova, the head of the Academy of Sciences of Moldova, Ion Bărbuţă, described the dictionary as a politically motivated "absurdity".
rewrite: Instances exist where speech varieties are intentionally reclassified for political aims, such as with Moldovan. In 1996, Moldova's parliament, fearing "Romanian expansionism," declined President Mircea Snegur's initiative to rename the language Romanian. Later, a 2003 Moldovan-Romanian dictionary aimed to demonstrate separate languages. Romanian Academy linguists countered that all Moldovan terms were Romanian, while Moldova's Academy of Sciences head, Ion Bărbuţă, dismissed the dictionary as a politically driven "absurdity."

input: The Neapolitan style has an almond-shaped body resembling a bowl, constructed from curved strips of wood. It usually has a bent sound table, canted in two planes with the design to take the tension of the 8 metal strings arranged in four courses. A hardwood fingerboard sits on top of or is flush with the sound table. Very old instruments may use wooden tuning pegs, while newer instruments tend to use geared metal tuners. The bridge is a movable length of hardwood. A pickguard is glued below the sound hole under the strings. European roundbacks commonly use a 13-inch scale instead of the 13.876 common on archtop Mandolins.
rewrite: Featuring an almond-shaped, bowl-like body built from curved wooden strips, the Neapolitan mandolin typically has a bent sound table. This table is angled in two planes to withstand the tension of its eight metal strings, which are arranged in four pairs. A hardwood fingerboard rests atop or level with the sound table. While older instruments often have wooden tuning pegs, modern versions usually employ geared metal tuners. The bridge is a movable piece of hardwood, and a pickguard is glued below the sound hole. Unlike many archtop mandolins with a 13.876-inch scale, European roundbacks commonly use a 13-inch scale.

input: Midtown Raleigh is a residential and commercial area just North of the I-440 Beltline and is part of North Raleigh. It is roughly framed by Glenwood/Creedmoor Road to the West, Wake Forest Road to the East, and Millbrook Road to the North. It includes shopping centers such as North Hills and Crabtree Valley Mall. It also includes North Hills Park and part of the Raleigh Greenway System. The term was coined by the Greater Raleigh Chamber of Commerce, developer John Kane and planning director Mitchell Silver. The News & Observer newspaper started using the term for marketing purposes only. The Midtown Raleigh Alliance was founded on July 25, 2011 as a way for community leaders to promote the area.
rewrite: Located just north of the I-440 Beltline within North Raleigh, Midtown Raleigh is a mixed residential and commercial district. Its approximate boundaries are Glenwood/Creedmoor Road to the west, Wake Forest Road to the east, and Millbrook Road to the north. The area features major shopping centers like North Hills and Crabtree Valley Mall, alongside North Hills Park and a section of the Raleigh Greenway System. The name itself was created by the Greater Raleigh Chamber of Commerce, developer John Kane, and planning director Mitchell Silver. While *The News & Observer* adopted the term for marketing, the community-driven Midtown Raleigh Alliance was formally established on July 25, 2011, to promote the area.

input: During the fighting, the Communards killed c. 500 people, including the Archbishop of Paris, and burned down many government buildings, including the Tuileries Palace and the Hotel de Ville. Communards captured with weapons were routinely shot by the army and Government troops killed from 7,000–30,000 Communards in the fighting and in massacres of men, women, and children during and after the Commune. More recent histories, based on studies of the number buried in Paris cemeteries and in mass graves after the fall of the Commune, put the number killed at between 6,000 and 10,000. Twenty-six courts were established to try more than 40,000 people who had been arrested, which took until 1875 and imposed 95 death sentences, of which 23 were inflicted. Forced labour for life was imposed on 251 people, 1,160 people were transported to "a fortified place" and 3,417 people were transported. About 20,000 Communards were held in prison hulks until released in 1872 and a great many Communards fled abroad to England, Switzerland, Belgium or the United States. The survivors were amnestied by a bill introduced by Gambetta in 1880 and allowed to return.
rewrite: In the course of the conflict, the Communards were responsible for approximately 500 deaths, among them the Archbishop of Paris, and the destruction of numerous government structures such as the Tuileries Palace and the Hotel de Ville. The governmental response was severe: any Communard captured bearing arms was typically executed by the army. During and after the Commune, these troops killed between 7,000 and 30,000 men, women, and children, both in combat and in outright massacres. However, more recent historical assessments, examining burial records from Paris cemeteries and mass graves, estimate the total fatalities to be between 6,000 and 10,000. Following the suppression, over 40,000 arrested individuals faced trial in twenty-six courts, a judicial process lasting until 1875. This resulted in 95 death sentences, with 23 carried out, while 251 received life at hard labor. Additionally, 1,160 individuals were transported to fortified locations, and 3,417 were sent into exile. Roughly 20,000 were detained in prison hulks until their 1872 release, and many others fled abroad to nations like England, Switzerland, Belgium, or the United States. The surviving exiles were ultimately granted amnesty through a bill introduced by Gambetta in 1880, permitting their return.

input: In the Roman Catholic Church, obstinate and willful manifest heresy is considered to spiritually cut one off from the Church, even before excommunication is incurred. The Codex Justinianus (1:5:12) defines "everyone who is not devoted to the Catholic Church and to our Orthodox holy Faith" a heretic. The Church had always dealt harshly with strands of Christianity that it considered heretical, but before the 11th century these tended to centre around individual preachers or small localised sects, like Arianism, Pelagianism, Donatism, Marcionism and Montanism. The diffusion of the almost Manichaean sect of Paulicians westwards gave birth to the famous 11th and 12th century heresies of Western Europe. The first one was that of Bogomils in modern day Bosnia, a sort of sanctuary between Eastern and Western Christianity. By the 11th century, more organised groups such as the Patarini, the Dulcinians, the Waldensians and the Cathars were beginning to appear in the towns and cities of northern Italy, southern France and Flanders.
rewrite: Within the Roman Catholic Church, manifest heresy that is both obstinate and willful is seen as spiritually severing one from the Church, even prior to any formal excommunication. Historically, the Church treated Christian strands deemed heretical with severity. Before the 11th century, however, such movements typically revolved around individual preachers or localized sects, examples being Arianism, Pelagianism, Donatism, Marcionism, and Montanism. The Codex Justinianus (1:5:12) categorizes as a heretic "everyone who is not devoted to the Catholic Church and to our Orthodox holy Faith." A shift occurred as the nearly Manichaean Paulician sect spread westward, leading to the rise of major 11th and 12th century heresies in Western Europe. The first of these was the Bogomils in modern Bosnia, a sanctuary between Eastern and Western Christianity. By the 11th century, more organized groups like the Patarini, Dulcinians, Waldensians, and Cathars began emerging in urban centers of northern Italy, southern France, and Flanders.

input: Relying exclusively on unedited machine translation, however, ignores the fact that communication in human language is context-embedded and that it takes a person to comprehend the context of the original text with a reasonable degree of probability. It is certainly true that even purely human-generated translations are prone to error; therefore, to ensure that a machine-generated translation will be useful to a human being and that publishable-quality translation is achieved, such translations must be reviewed and edited by a human.
rewrite: However, human communication is deeply rooted in context, requiring personal understanding to grasp the original meaning accurately. Sole dependence on raw machine translation overlooks this reality. While even human translations can contain errors, machine outputs demand human review and editing. This process is essential to make them truly useful and to reach a quality suitable for publication.

input: During the same court battle, Viacom won a court ruling requiring YouTube to hand over 12 terabytes of data detailing the viewing habits of every user who has watched videos on the site. The decision was criticized by the Electronic Frontier Foundation, which called the court ruling "a setback to privacy rights". In June 2010, Viacom's lawsuit against Google was rejected in a summary judgment, with U.S. federal Judge Louis L. Stanton stating that Google was protected by provisions of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. Viacom announced its intention to appeal the ruling.
rewrite: Amid the legal dispute, Viacom secured a ruling compelling YouTube to provide 12 terabytes of data on every user's viewing history, a move the Electronic Frontier Foundation decried as "a setback to privacy rights." However, in June 2010, a U.S. federal judge, Louis L. Stanton, dismissed Viacom's lawsuit against Google via summary judgment, citing protections under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act. Viacom promptly declared it would appeal this decision.

input: The largest and bloodiest American battle came at Okinawa, as the U.S. sought airbases for 3,000 B-29 bombers and 240 squadrons of B-17 bombers for the intense bombardment of Japan's home islands in preparation for a full-scale invasion in late 1945. The Japanese, with 115,000 troops augmented by thousands of civilians on the heavily populated island, did not resist on the beaches—their strategy was to maximize the number of soldier and Marine casualties, and naval losses from Kamikaze attacks. After an intense bombardment the Americans landed on 1 April 1945 and declared victory on 21 June. The supporting naval forces were the targets for 4,000 sorties, many by Kamikaze suicide planes. U.S. losses totaled 38 ships of all types sunk and 368 damaged with 4,900 sailors killed. The Americans suffered 75,000 casualties on the ground; 94% of the Japanese soldiers died along with many civilians.
rewrite: In the final stages of World War II, the U.S. sought airbases on Okinawa for 3,000 B-29s and 240 squadrons of B-17s to bombard Japan ahead of a planned 1945 invasion. This led to the largest and bloodiest American battle of the Pacific. The Japanese, with 115,000 troops and thousands of civilians on the populous island, avoided beach defenses. Their strategy aimed instead to inflict massive casualties on American soldiers and Marines, while Kamikaze attacks targeted naval forces. Following a heavy bombardment, American forces landed on 1 April 1945. The supporting fleet endured approximately 4,000 sorties, many from suicide planes. U.S. naval losses included 38 ships sunk and 368 damaged, with 4,900 sailors killed. Ground forces suffered 75,000 casualties. Victory was declared on 21 June, after 94% of Japanese soldiers and many civilians perished.

input: Plymouth is home to the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom (MBA) which conducts research in all areas of the marine sciences. The Plymouth Marine Laboratory is an offshoot of the MBA. Together with the National Marine Aquarium, the Sir Alister Hardy Foundation for Ocean Sciences, Plymouth University's Marine Institute and the Diving Diseases Research Centre, these marine-related organisations form the Plymouth Marine Sciences Partnership. The Plymouth Marine Laboratory, which focuses on global issues of climate change and sustainability. It monitors the effects of ocean acidity on corals and shellfish and reports the results to the UK government. It also cultivates algae that could be used to make biofuels or in the treatment of waste water by using technology such as photo-bioreactors. It works alongside the Boots Group to investigate the use of algae in skin care protects, taking advantage of the chemicals they contain that adapt to protect themselves from the sun.
rewrite: The Plymouth Marine Sciences Partnership brings together several key marine-related organizations, including the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom (MBA), based in Plymouth. The MBA conducts research across all marine science disciplines. An offshoot of the MBA, the Plymouth Marine Laboratory, focuses on global climate change and sustainability. This laboratory monitors impacts like ocean acidity on corals and shellfish, reporting findings to the UK government. It also cultivates algae using technologies such as photo-bioreactors, exploring applications in biofuel production and wastewater treatment. Additionally, in partnership with the Boots Group, the laboratory investigates using algae in skincare products, leveraging the sun-protective chemicals algae naturally produce. Other members of the partnership are the National Marine Aquarium, the Sir Alister Hardy Foundation for Ocean Sciences, Plymouth University's Marine Institute, and the Diving Diseases Research Centre.

input: Hellenistic poets now sought patronage from kings, and wrote works in their honor. The scholars at the libraries in Alexandria and Pergamon focused on the collection, cataloging, and literary criticism of classical Athenian works and ancient Greek myths. The poet-critic Callimachus, a staunch elitist, wrote hymns equating Ptolemy II to Zeus and Apollo. He promoted short poetic forms such as the epigram, epyllion and the iambic and attacked epic as base and common ("big book, big evil" was his doctrine). He also wrote a massive catalog of the holdings of the library of Alexandria, the famous Pinakes. Callimachus was extremely influential in his time and also for the development of Augustan poetry. Another poet, Apollonius of Rhodes, attempted to revive the epic for the Hellenistic world with his Argonautica. He had been a student of Callimachus and later became chief librarian (prostates) of the library of Alexandria, Apollonius and Callimachus spent much of their careers feuding with each other. Pastoral poetry also thrived during the Hellenistic era, Theocritus was a major poet who popularized the genre.
rewrite: During the Hellenistic era, poets turned to royal patronage, composing works to honor their kings. At the great libraries of Alexandria and Pergamon, scholars dedicated themselves to gathering, cataloging, and critically analyzing classical Athenian texts and ancient myths. A defining figure was the poet-critic Callimachus, an influential elitist who authored hymns likening Ptolemy II to gods like Zeus and Apollo. He championed concise forms—the epigram, epyllion, and iambic—while dismissing epic poetry as vulgar, famously declaring, "big book, big evil." His legacy includes the extensive Pinakes, a catalog of the Alexandria Library's holdings, which shaped not only his contemporaries but also later Augustan poetry. Meanwhile, his former student Apollonius of Rhodes sought to revive the epic tradition through his Argonautica, eventually serving as the library's chief librarian. The two poets engaged in a prolonged professional feud. This period also saw the flourishing of pastoral poetry, largely due to the popularizing efforts of the major poet Theocritus.

input: Chopin was educated in the tradition of Beethoven, Haydn, Mozart and Clementi; he used Clementi's piano method with his own students. He was also influenced by Hummel's development of virtuoso, yet Mozartian, piano technique. He cited Bach and Mozart as the two most important composers in shaping his musical outlook. Chopin's early works are in the style of the "brilliant" keyboard pieces of his era as exemplified by the works of Ignaz Moscheles, Friedrich Kalkbrenner, and others. Less direct in the earlier period are the influences of Polish folk music and of Italian opera. Much of what became his typical style of ornamentation (for example, his fioriture) is taken from singing. His melodic lines were increasingly reminiscent of the modes and features of the music of his native country, such as drones.
rewrite: Chopin's musical education was rooted in the classical traditions of Beethoven, Haydn, Mozart, and Clementi, the latter’s piano method being one he employed with his own pupils. He regarded Bach and Mozart as paramount in forming his artistic perspective, while also absorbing Hummel’s virtuosic and Mozartian approach to piano technique. His initial compositions reflected the contemporary "brilliant" style for the keyboard, as seen in the works of figures like Ignaz Moscheles and Friedrich Kalkbrenner. The inspirations from Polish folk music and Italian opera were subtler in these earlier pieces. A hallmark of his mature style, including ornamental fioriture, was adapted from vocal music. Furthermore, his melodies grew to echo distinct elements of his homeland’s music, such as the use of drones.

input: Work is undertaken from an early age by vast numbers of children in the world and may have a natural place in growing up. Work can contribute to the well-being of children in a variety of ways; children often choose to work to improve their lives, both in the short- and long-term. At the material level, children’s work often contributes to producing food or earning income that benefits themselves and their families; and such income is especially important when the families are poor. Work can provide an escape from debilitating poverty, sometimes by allowing a young person to move away from an impoverished environment. Young people often enjoy their work, especially paid work, or when work involves the company of peers. Even when work is intensive and enforced, children often find ways to combine their work with play.
rewrite: Across the globe, a vast number of children engage in work from an early age, which can hold a natural place in the process of growing up. This labor often contributes to children's well-being in multiple ways, as many choose to work to better their lives immediately and in the future. Materially, it frequently aids in producing food or generating income for themselves and their families, a crucial support in situations of poverty. For some, work offers a route to escape debilitating circumstances by enabling them to leave an impoverished environment. Young people commonly derive enjoyment from their work, particularly when it is paid or performed alongside peers. Even under conditions of intensity or compulsion, children regularly find opportunities to blend their work with play.

input: The 18th century saw a huge growth in the number of drinking establishments, primarily due to the introduction of gin. Gin was brought to England by the Dutch after the Glorious Revolution of 1688 and became very popular after the government created a market for "cuckoo grain" or "cuckoo malt" that was unfit to be used in brewing and distilling by allowing unlicensed gin and beer production, while imposing a heavy duty on all imported spirits. As thousands of gin-shops sprang up all over England, brewers fought back by increasing the number of alehouses. By 1740 the production of gin had increased to six times that of beer and because of its cheapness it became popular with the poor, leading to the so-called Gin Craze. Over half of the 15,000 drinking establishments in London were gin shops.
rewrite: A surge in drinking establishments marked the 18th century, driven chiefly by the rise of gin. Introduced to England by the Dutch following the 1688 Glorious Revolution, gin's popularity exploded after government policies created a market for substandard "cuckoo grain." By permitting unlicensed gin and beer production and heavily taxing imported spirits, authorities made this cheap spirit widely accessible. In response, brewers proliferated alehouses to compete. By 1740, gin output was six times greater than beer, and its low cost fueled a "Gin Craze" among the poor. Across England, thousands of gin-shops appeared, with over half of London's 15,000 drinking establishments dedicated to selling gin.

input: The east coast Appalachian system, originally forest covered, is relatively low and narrow and is bordered on the southeast and south by an important coastal plain. The Cordilleran system on the western side of the continent is lofty, broad and complicated having two branches, the Rocky Mountain System and the Pacific Mountain System. In between these mountain systems lie the Intermontaine Plateaus. Both the Columbia River and Colorado River rise far inland near the easternmost members of the Cordilleran system, and flow through plateaus and intermontaine basins to the ocean. Heavy forests cover the northwest coast, but elsewhere trees are found only on the higher ranges below the Alpine region. The intermontane valleys, plateaus and basins range from treeless to desert with the most arid region being in the southwest.
rewrite: Originally cloaked in forest, the relatively low and narrow Appalachian system stretches along the east coast, edged to the southeast and south by a significant coastal plain. On the continent's western side stands the lofty, broad, and complex Cordilleran system, divided into the Rocky Mountain and Pacific Mountain branches. Between these major systems are the Intermontane Plateaus. Rising far inland near the eastern edge of the Cordilleras, both the Columbia and Colorado Rivers traverse these plateaus and intermontane basins to reach the ocean. While heavy forests blanket the northwest coast, trees elsewhere are confined to higher elevations below the Alpine zone. The intermontane valleys, plateaus, and basins vary from treeless to desert, with the most arid conditions found in the southwest.

input: Philip V, who came to power when Doson died in 221 BC, was the last Macedonian ruler with both the talent and the opportunity to unite Greece and preserve its independence against the "cloud rising in the west": the ever-increasing power of Rome. He was known as "the darling of Hellas". Under his auspices the Peace of Naupactus (217 BC) brought the latest war between Macedon and the Greek leagues (the social war 220-217) to an end, and at this time he controlled all of Greece except Athens, Rhodes and Pergamum.
rewrite: Ascending to power in 221 BC after Doson's death, Philip V was hailed as "the darling of Hellas." He was the final Macedonian king possessing the skill and chance to unify Greece, defending it from Rome, the "cloud rising in the west." His influence extended over all Greece save Athens, Rhodes, and Pergamum. The Peace of Naupactus (217 BC), achieved under his leadership, concluded the recent Social War between Macedon and the Greek leagues.

input: Many were surprised by these changes to the CBC schedule, which were apparently intended to attract a younger audience to the network; some suggested they might alienate the core CBC viewership. Another note of criticism was made when the network decided to move The National in some time zones to simulcast the American version of The One over the summer. This later became a moot point, as The One was taken off the air after two weeks after extremely low American and Canadian ratings, and the newscast resumed its regular schedule.
rewrite: The CBC's schedule changes, aimed at attracting younger viewers, drew surprise and criticism for potentially alienating its core audience. A particular point of contention was the temporary move of The National in some time zones to simulcast the American show The One during the summer. This decision became irrelevant, however, when The One was cancelled after just two weeks due to extremely low ratings in both countries, allowing the newscast to return to its regular schedule.

input: Natural theology was not a unified doctrine, and while some such as Louis Agassiz were strongly opposed to the ideas in the book, others sought a reconciliation in which evolution was seen as purposeful. In the Church of England, some liberal clergymen interpreted natural selection as an instrument of God's design, with the cleric Charles Kingsley seeing it as "just as noble a conception of Deity". In the second edition of January 1860, Darwin quoted Kingsley as "a celebrated cleric", and added the phrase "by the Creator" to the closing sentence, which from then on read "life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed by the Creator into a few forms or into one". While some commentators have taken this as a concession to religion that Darwin later regretted, Darwin's view at the time was of God creating life through the laws of nature, and even in the first edition there are several references to "creation".
rewrite: Natural theology did not represent a unified position. While figures like Louis Agassiz strongly opposed the book’s ideas, others sought a purposeful interpretation of evolution to reconcile it with faith. Within the Church of England, certain liberal clergymen viewed natural selection as a mechanism of divine design. The cleric Charles Kingsley, for instance, regarded it as "just as noble a conception of Deity." Darwin incorporated this perspective into the second edition in January 1860, quoting Kingsley as "a celebrated cleric" and inserting the phrase "by the Creator" into the closing sentence. Thereafter, it referred to life "having been originally breathed by the Creator into a few forms or into one." Although some see this as a religious concession Darwin later regretted, his contemporary view held that God created life through natural laws. References to "creation" were, in fact, present even in the first edition.

input: The concept of a group arose from the study of polynomial equations, starting with Évariste Galois in the 1830s. After contributions from other fields such as number theory and geometry, the group notion was generalized and firmly established around 1870. Modern group theory—an active mathematical discipline—studies groups in their own right.a[›] To explore groups, mathematicians have devised various notions to break groups into smaller, better-understandable pieces, such as subgroups, quotient groups and simple groups. In addition to their abstract properties, group theorists also study the different ways in which a group can be expressed concretely (its group representations), both from a theoretical and a computational point of view. A theory has been developed for finite groups, which culminated with the classification of finite simple groups announced in 1983.aa[›] Since the mid-1980s, geometric group theory, which studies finitely generated groups as geometric objects, has become a particularly active area in group theory.
rewrite: Originating in the 1830s with Évariste Galois and the study of polynomial equations, the concept of a group was later generalized and solidified around 1870 through contributions from fields like number theory and geometry. Today, group theory is a vibrant mathematical discipline that investigates groups as abstract entities in their own right. Mathematicians employ notions like subgroups, quotient groups, and simple groups to decompose groups into more comprehensible components. Beyond abstract properties, research includes the concrete expressions of groups, known as group representations, examined from both theoretical and computational perspectives. The theory for finite groups achieved a major milestone with the classification of finite simple groups, announced in 1983. Additionally, since the mid-1980s, geometric group theory—treating finitely generated groups as geometric objects—has emerged as a particularly dynamic area of study.

input: Many visitors to BYU, and Utah Valley as a whole, report being surprised by the culturally conservative environment. Brigham Young University's Honor Code, which all BYU students agree to follow as a condition of studying at BYU, prohibits the consumption of alcoholic beverages, tobacco, etc. As mentioned earlier, The Princeton Review has rated BYU the "#1 stone cold sober school" in the nation for several years running, an honor which the late LDS Church president Gordon B. Hinckley had commented on with pride. BYU's 2014 "#1 stone cold" sober rating marked the 17th year in a row that the school had earned that rating. BYU has used this and other honors awarded to the school to advertise itself to prospective students, showing that BYU is proud of the rating. According to the Uniform Crime Reports, incidents of crime in Provo are lower than the national average. Murder is rare, and robberies are about 1/10 the national average. Business Insider rated BYU as the #1 safest college campus in the nation.
rewrite: Visitors to Brigham Young University and Utah Valley often express surprise at the culturally conservative atmosphere. A key aspect of this is the BYU Honor Code, which all students agree to follow, prohibiting alcohol, tobacco, and similar substances. This commitment has led The Princeton Review to repeatedly rank BYU as the nation’s "#1 stone cold sober school." Notably, the university held this rating for 17 consecutive years, including in 2014. The late LDS Church president Gordon B. Hinckley once spoke with pride about this distinction, and BYU itself uses such honors in advertising to showcase its values to prospective students. Complementing this environment, Provo’s crime rates are below the national average, according to Uniform Crime Reports. Murder is rare, and robberies occur at roughly one-tenth the national rate. This safety record contributed to Business Insider naming BYU the "#1 safest college campus" in the country.

input: Grazing organisms may also kill their prey species, but this is seldom the case. While some herbivores like zooplankton live on unicellular phytoplankton and therefore, by the individualized nature of the organism, kill their prey, many only eat a small part of the plant. Grazing livestock may pull some grass out at the roots, but most is simply grazed upon, allowing the plant to regrow once again. Kelp is frequently grazed in subtidal kelp forests, but regrows at the base of the blade continuously to cope with browsing pressure. Animals may also be 'grazed' upon; female mosquitos land on hosts briefly to gain sufficient proteins for the development of their offspring. Starfish may be grazed on, being capable of regenerating lost arms.
rewrite: While grazing organisms can sometimes kill their prey, this outcome is uncommon. Many herbivores consume only portions of plants, allowing for regrowth, as seen when livestock graze grass without uprooting it entirely. Similarly, in subtidal forests, kelp withstands browsing by continuously regrowing from the base of its blades. Even among animals, grazing occurs without fatal consequences: female mosquitoes briefly land on hosts to obtain necessary proteins, and starfish can regenerate limbs that are grazed upon. In contrast, certain herbivores like zooplankton do kill their unicellular phytoplankton prey due to the individualized nature of those organisms.

input: On April 26, 1496 King John I Albert granted the Privilege of Piotrków (Polish: "Przywilej piotrkowski", "konstytucja piotrkowska" or "statuty piotrkowskie"), increasing the nobility's feudal power over serfs. It bound the peasant to the land, as only one son (not the eldest) was permitted to leave the village; townsfolk (Polish: "mieszczaństwo") were prohibited from owning land; and positions in the Church hierarchy could be given only to nobles.
rewrite: Granted by King John I Albert on April 26, 1496, the Privilege of Piotrków greatly expanded the nobility's feudal authority over serfs. This decree bound peasants to the land, allowing only one non-elderly son to depart a village. It also barred townsfolk from land ownership and reserved high Church positions exclusively for nobles.

input: Christoph Waltz was cast in the role of Franz Oberhauser, though he refused to comment on the nature of the part. It was later revealed with the film's release that he is Ernst Stavro Blofeld. Dave Bautista was cast as Mr. Hinx after producers sought an actor with a background in contact sports. After casting Bérénice Lim Marlohe, a relative newcomer, as Sévérine in Skyfall, Mendes consciously sought out a more experienced actor for the role of Madeleine Swann, ultimately casting Léa Seydoux in the role. Monica Bellucci joined the cast as Lucia Sciarra, becoming, at the age of fifty, the oldest actress to be cast as a Bond girl. In a separate interview with Danish website Euroman, Jesper Christensen revealed he would be reprising his role as Mr. White from Casino Royale and Quantum of Solace. Christensen's character was reportedly killed off in a scene intended to be used as an epilogue to Quantum of Solace, before it was removed from the final cut of the film, enabling his return in Spectre.
rewrite: Christoph Waltz was brought on as Franz Oberhauser, though he declined to discuss the character’s specifics. Only upon the film’s release was it confirmed he portrayed Ernst Stavro Blofeld. For the part of Mr. Hinx, producers wanted someone with a contact sports history, leading to Dave Bautista’s casting. Following the selection of relative newcomer Bérénice Lim Marlohe as Sévérine in *Skyfall*, director Sam Mendes deliberately pursued a more seasoned performer for Madeleine Swann, which resulted in Léa Seydoux securing the role. Monica Bellucci, joining as Lucia Sciarra, became the oldest actress cast as a Bond girl at age fifty. input: Although John was the Count of Poitou and therefore the rightful feudal lord over the Lusignans, they could legitimately appeal John's actions in France to his own feudal lord, Philip. Hugh did exactly this in 1201 and Philip summoned John to attend court in Paris in 1202, citing the Le Goulet treaty to strengthen his case. John was unwilling to weaken his authority in western France in this way. He argued that he need not attend Philip's court because of his special status as the Duke of Normandy, who was exempt by feudal tradition from being called to the French court. Philip argued that he was summoning John not as the Duke of Normandy, but as the Count of Poitou, which carried no such special status. When John still refused to come, Philip declared John in breach of his feudal responsibilities, reassigned all of John's lands that fell under the French crown to Arthur – with the exception of Normandy, which he took back for himself – and began a fresh war against John.
rewrite: As the Count of Poitou, John held feudal authority over the Lusignans, yet they retained the right to appeal his actions in France to his own overlord, King Philip. Hugh of Lusignan exercised this right in 1201. Citing the Treaty of Le Goulet to bolster his position, Philip summoned John to the Paris court in 1202. John, however, was determined to avoid any erosion of his power in western France. He refused the summons, claiming exemption based on his status as Duke of Normandy, a title traditionally free from such calls to the French court. Philip countered that he was summoning John specifically in his capacity as Count of Poitou, a role which granted no such privilege. John’s continued refusal led Philip to declare him in breach of his feudal duties. Consequently, Philip reassigned all John’s French lands—except Normandy, which he reclaimed directly—to Arthur, and initiated a new war against John.

input: The Jordan River runs along the Jordan Rift Valley, from Mount Hermon through the Hulah Valley and the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea, the lowest point on the surface of the Earth. Further south is the Arabah, ending with the Gulf of Eilat, part of the Red Sea. Unique to Israel and the Sinai Peninsula are makhteshim, or erosion cirques. The largest makhtesh in the world is Ramon Crater in the Negev, which measures 40 by 8 kilometers (25 by 5 mi). A report on the environmental status of the Mediterranean basin states that Israel has the largest number of plant species per square meter of all the countries in the basin.
rewrite: Flowing through the Jordan Rift Valley, the Jordan River travels from Mount Hermon, past the Hulah Valley and the Sea of Galilee, to the Dead Sea—Earth's lowest surface point. South of this lies the Arabah, which concludes at the Red Sea's Gulf of Eilat. The region of Israel and the Sinai Peninsula features unique erosion cirques called makhteshim. At 40 by 8 kilometers (25 by 5 mi), the Negev's Ramon Crater is the world's largest such formation. According to a Mediterranean basin environmental report, Israel possesses the highest density of plant species per square meter in the region.

input: Manhattan Island is linked to New York City's outer boroughs and New Jersey by several tunnels as well. The Lincoln Tunnel, which carries 120,000 vehicles a day under the Hudson River between New Jersey and Midtown Manhattan, is the busiest vehicular tunnel in the world. The tunnel was built instead of a bridge to allow unfettered passage of large passenger and cargo ships that sailed through New York Harbor and up the Hudson River to Manhattan's piers. The Holland Tunnel, connecting Lower Manhattan to Jersey City, New Jersey, was the world's first mechanically ventilated vehicular tunnel when it opened in 1927. The Queens-Midtown Tunnel, built to relieve congestion on the bridges connecting Manhattan with Queens and Brooklyn, was the largest non-federal project in its time when it was completed in 1940. President Franklin D. Roosevelt was the first person to drive through it. The Hugh L. Carey Tunnel runs underneath Battery Park and connects the Financial District at the southern tip of Manhattan to Red Hook in Brooklyn.
rewrite: Several tunnels connect Manhattan Island to New York City’s outer boroughs and New Jersey. The Holland Tunnel, linking Lower Manhattan to Jersey City, was the world’s first mechanically ventilated vehicular tunnel upon its 1927 opening. To allow large ships uninterrupted access to New York Harbor and Hudson River piers, the Lincoln Tunnel was constructed under the Hudson River rather than a bridge; it now handles 120,000 vehicles daily between New Jersey and Midtown, making it the globe’s busiest vehicular tunnel. Completed in 1940 to ease bridge traffic to Queens and Brooklyn, the Queens-Midtown Tunnel was the largest non-federal project of its era, with President Franklin D. Roosevelt as its first driver. Another key passage, the Hugh L. Carey Tunnel, runs beneath Battery Park, joining Manhattan’s Financial District to Red Hook in Brooklyn.

input: However, civil war flared again when the Second Triumvirate of Octavian, Lepidus and Mark Antony failed. The ambitious Octavian built a power base of patronage and then launched a campaign against Mark Antony. At the naval Battle of Actium off the coast of Greece, Octavian decisively defeated Antony and Cleopatra. Octavian was granted a series of special powers including sole "imperium" within the city of Rome, permanent consular powers and credit for every Roman military victory, since all future generals were assumed to be acting under his command. In 27 BC Octavian was granted the use of the names "Augustus" and "Princeps", indicating his primary status above all other Romans, and he adopted the title "Imperator Caesar" making him the first Roman Emperor.
rewrite: The failure of the Second Triumvirate, comprising Octavian, Lepidus, and Mark Antony, reignited civil war. Octavian, ambitious, first consolidated a power base through patronage before turning his forces against Mark Antony. Their conflict culminated in the naval Battle of Actium off Greece, where Octavian delivered a decisive defeat to Antony and Cleopatra. Subsequently, he was granted extraordinary powers: sole imperium in Rome, permanent consular authority, and credit for all military victories, as generals were now his subordinates. In 27 BC, he accepted the names "Augustus" and "Princeps," signifying his supreme status, and adopted the title "Imperator Caesar," becoming Rome's first emperor.

input: On June 14, 1987, about 5,000 people gathered again at Freedom Monument in Riga, and laid flowers to commemorate the anniversary of Stalin's mass deportation of Latvians in 1941. This was the first large demonstration in the Baltic republics to commemorate the anniversary of an event contrary to official Soviet history. The authorities did not crack down on demonstrators, which encouraged more and larger demonstrations throughout the Baltic States. The next major anniversary after the August 23 Molotov Pact demonstration was on November 18, the date of Latvia’s independence in 1918. On November 18, 1987, hundreds of police and civilian militiamen cordoned off the central square to prevent any demonstration at Freedom Monument, but thousands lined the streets of Riga in silent protest regardless.
rewrite: On June 14, 1987, approximately 5,000 individuals assembled once more at Riga’s Freedom Monument, laying flowers to mark the anniversary of the 1941 mass deportations of Latvians under Stalin. As the first major gathering in the Baltic republics to observe a date contradicting official Soviet history, its peaceful handling by authorities spurred increasingly larger demonstrations across the region. Following a significant demonstration on August 23 for the Molotov Pact anniversary, the next key date was November 18, Latvia’s Independence Day from 1918. That day in 1987, despite hundreds of police and militiamen cordoning off the central square to block access to the monument, thousands still lined Riga’s streets in a silent protest.

input: In 1989, Gaddafi was overjoyed by the foundation of the Arab Maghreb Union, uniting Libya in an economic pact with Mauritania, Morocco, Tunisia and Algeria, viewing it as beginnings of a new Pan-Arab union. Meanwhile, Libya stepped up its support for anti-western militants such as the Provisional IRA, and in 1988, Pan Am Flight 103 was blown up over Lockerbie in Scotland, killing 243 passengers and 16 crew members, plus 11 people on the ground. British police investigations identified two Libyans – Abdelbaset al-Megrahi and Lamin Khalifah Fhimah – as the chief suspects, and in November 1991 issued a declaration demanding that Libya hand them over. When Gaddafi refused, citing the Montreal Convention, the United Nations (UN) imposed Resolution 748 in March 1992, initiating economic sanctions against Libya which had deep repercussions for the country's economy. The country suffered an estimated $900 million financial loss as a result. Further problems arose with the west when in January 1989, two Libyan warplanes were shot down by the U.S. off the Libyan coast. Many African states opposed the UN sanctions, with Mandela criticising them on a visit to Gaddafi in October 1997, when he praised Libya for its work in fighting apartheid and awarded Gaddafi the Order of Good Hope. They would only be suspended in 1998 when Libya agreed to allow the extradition of the suspects to the Scottish Court in the Netherlands, in a process overseen by Mandela.
rewrite: The late 1980s saw Libya's international relations marked by both regional ambition and deepening conflict with the West. In 1989, Muammar Gaddafi celebrated the creation of the Arab Maghreb Union, an economic pact linking Libya with Mauritania, Morocco, Tunisia, and Algeria, which he envisioned as the foundation for a broader Pan-Arab union. Concurrently, however, Libya intensified its backing of anti-Western militant groups, including the Provisional IRA. Tensions escalated following the 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, which resulted in 270 deaths. By November 1991, British police had identified two Libyans, Abdelbaset al-Megrahi and Lamin Khalifah Fhimah, as the primary suspects and demanded their extradition. Gaddafi's refusal, citing the Montreal Convention, led the United Nations to impose economic sanctions via Resolution 748 in March 1992. These sanctions crippled Libya's economy, causing an estimated $900 million in losses. Earlier, in January 1989, a separate incident had further strained relations when U.S. forces shot down two Libyan warplanes off the coast. While many African nations opposed the UN sanctions, with Nelson Mandela personally criticizing them during an October 1997 visit to Gaddafi and awarding him the Order of Good Hope for Libya's anti-apartheid efforts, the sanctions were only suspended in 1998. This occurred after Libya agreed to extradite the Lockerbie suspects for trial before a Scottish court in the Netherlands, a process overseen by Mandela.

input: Each code point has a single General Category property. The major categories are: Letter, Mark, Number, Punctuation, Symbol, Separator and Other. Within these categories, there are subdivisions. The General Category is not useful for every use, since legacy encodings have used multiple characteristics per single code point. E.g., U+000A <control-000A> Line feed (LF) in ASCII is both a control and a formatting separator; in Unicode the General Category is "Other, Control". However, this classification is not always sufficient, as legacy encodings sometimes assign multiple traits to a single point. For instance, U+000A (Line feed) in ASCII serves as both a control and formatting separator, while Unicode labels it "Other, Control."
