input: French political scientist Maurice Duverger drew a distinction between cadre parties and mass parties. Cadre parties were political elites that were concerned with contesting elections and restricted the influence of outsiders, who were only required to assist in election campaigns. Mass parties tried to recruit new members who were a source of party income and were often expected to spread party ideology as well as assist in elections.Socialist parties are examples of mass parties, while the British Conservative Party and the German Christian Democratic Union are examples of hybrid parties. In the United States, where both major parties were cadre parties, the introduction of primaries and other reforms has transformed them so that power is held by activists who compete over influence and nomination of candidates.
rewrite: Maurice Duverger, a French political scientist, distinguished between cadre parties and mass parties. Cadre parties, composed of political elites, focused on election contests and limited outsider influence, using them mainly for campaign assistance. In contrast, mass parties actively recruited members, who provided income, helped spread ideology, and aided during elections. Socialist parties exemplify mass parties, whereas hybrids like the British Conservative Party and German Christian Democratic Union blend elements. In the United States, both major parties were historically cadre parties, but primaries and reforms shifted power to activists, who now compete for influence and candidate nominations.

input: The NTFS file system used by recent versions of Windows stores the file with a UTC time stamp, but displays it corrected to local—or seasonal—time. However, the FAT filesystem commonly used on removable devices stores only the local time. Consequently, when a file is copied from the hard disk onto separate media, its time will be set to the current local time. If the time adjustment is changed, the timestamps of the original file and the copy will be different. The same effect can be observed when compressing and uncompressing files with some file archivers. It is the NTFS file that changes seen time. This effect should be kept in mind when trying to determine if a file is a duplicate of another, although there are other methods of comparing files for equality (such as using a checksum algorithm).
rewrite: In recent Windows versions, the NTFS file system records files with a UTC timestamp but shows them adjusted to local or seasonal time. By contrast, the FAT filesystem, often found on removable devices, stores only the local time. As a result, copying a file from a hard disk to external media resets its timestamp to the current local time. If the system’s time adjustment is later modified, the original file and its copy will display different timestamps. A similar discrepancy can occur when compressing and extracting files using certain archiving tools—specifically, it is the NTFS file whose displayed time shifts. This effect is important to consider when checking whether files are duplicates, even though other comparison methods—like checksum algorithms—can also verify file equality.

input: The tourism industry began in the early 19th century when foreigners visited the Alps, traveled to the bases of the mountains to enjoy the scenery, and stayed at the spa-resorts. Large hotels were built during the Belle Époque; cog-railways, built early in the 20th century, brought tourists to ever higher elevations, with the Jungfraubahn terminating at the Jungfraujoch, well above the eternal snow-line, after going through a tunnel in Eiger. During this period winter sports were slowly introduced: in 1882 the first figure skating championship was held in St. Moritz, and downhill skiing became a popular sport with English visitors early in the 20th century, as the first ski-lift was installed in 1908 above Grindelwald.
rewrite: Tourism in the Alps originated in the early 19th century, as foreigners traveled to the mountains to admire the scenery and stay at spa-resorts. The Belle Époque saw the construction of large hotels. Subsequently, early 20th-century cog-railways, like the Jungfraubahn, carried visitors to higher altitudes; this line tunnels through the Eiger to terminate at the Jungfraujoch, far above the permanent snow. Winter sports gradually emerged during this era. The first figure skating championship was held in St. Moritz in 1882. Downhill skiing grew popular with English tourists early in the 20th century, especially after the first ski-lift was installed above Grindelwald in 1908.

input: The last king of the Roman Kingdom, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, was overthrown in 509 BC by a group of noblemen led by Lucius Junius Brutus. Tarquin made a number of attempts to retake the throne, including the Tarquinian conspiracy, the war with Veii and Tarquinii and finally the war between Rome and Clusium, all of which failed to achieve Tarquin's objectives. The most important constitutional change during the transition from kingdom to republic concerned the chief magistrate. Before the revolution, a king would be elected by the senators for a life term. Now, two consuls were elected by the citizens for an annual term. Each consul would check his colleague, and their limited term in office would open them up to prosecution if they abused the powers of their office. Consular political powers, when exercised conjointly with a consular colleague, were no different from those of the old king.
rewrite: In 509 BC, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, the final king of the Roman Kingdom, was deposed by noblemen under the leadership of Lucius Junius Brutus. Despite multiple efforts to regain power—such as the Tarquinian conspiracy, conflicts with Veii and Tarquinii, and the war between Rome and Clusium—Tarquin ultimately failed in all his objectives. The shift from monarchy to republic brought a crucial constitutional reform regarding the chief executive. Previously, senators elected a king for life. Under the new system, citizens annually elected two consuls. These consuls held political authority equivalent to the former king when acting together, but their power was checked by mutual oversight and a one-year term. This limited tenure also made them subject to prosecution for any abuse of office.

input: Antibiotics are screened for any negative effects on humans or other mammals before approval for clinical use, and are usually considered safe and most are well tolerated. However, some antibiotics have been associated with a range of adverse side effects. Side-effects range from mild to very serious depending on the antibiotics used, the microbial organisms targeted, and the individual patient. Side effects may reflect the pharmacological or toxicological properties of the antibiotic or may involve hypersensitivity reactions or anaphylaxis. Safety profiles of newer drugs are often not as well established as for those that have a long history of use. Adverse effects range from fever and nausea to major allergic reactions, including photodermatitis and anaphylaxis. Common side-effects include diarrhea, resulting from disruption of the species composition in the intestinal flora, resulting, for example, in overgrowth of pathogenic bacteria, such as Clostridium difficile. Antibacterials can also affect the vaginal flora, and may lead to overgrowth of yeast species of the genus Candida in the vulvo-vaginal area. Additional side-effects can result from interaction with other drugs, such as elevated risk of tendon damage from administration of a quinolone antibiotic with a systemic corticosteroid. Some scientists have hypothesized that the indiscriminate use of antibiotics alter the host microbiota and this has been associated with chronic disease.
rewrite: Before being approved for clinical use, antibiotics undergo screening to ensure they have no harmful effects on humans or other mammals, leading to their general classification as safe and typically well-tolerated. Despite this, a variety of adverse side effects have been linked to certain antibiotics. These effects can vary from mild to severe, influenced by the specific antibiotic, the targeted microbes, and the patient’s individual characteristics. They may arise from the drug’s pharmacological or toxicological properties or manifest as hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis. While older antibiotics have well-documented safety records, newer drugs often lack such extensive historical data. Adverse reactions encompass a broad spectrum, from fever and nausea to serious allergic responses like photodermatitis. A frequent side effect is diarrhea, often caused by disruption of intestinal flora that allows pathogenic bacteria such as Clostridium difficile to proliferate. Antibacterials can similarly disturb vaginal flora, potentially leading to overgrowth of Candida yeast. Drug interactions introduce further risks; for example, combining a quinolone antibiotic with a systemic corticosteroid may increase the likelihood of tendon damage. Additionally, some researchers suggest that indiscriminate antibiotic use alters the host microbiota, which has been associated with the development of chronic diseases.

input: Beginning in August, the competition proceeds as a knockout tournament throughout, consisting of twelve rounds, a semi-final and then a final, in May. A system of byes ensures clubs above Level 9 and 10 enter the competition at later stages. There is no seeding, the fixtures in each round being determined by a random draw. Prior to the semi-finals, fixtures ending in a tie are replayed once only. The first six rounds are qualifiers, with the draws organised on a regional basis. The next six rounds are the "proper" rounds where all clubs are in one draw.
rewrite: Starting in August, the competition follows a knockout format across twelve rounds, a semi-final, and a May final. Clubs above Levels 9 and 10 join later due to a bye system. There is no seeding; each round's matches are set by random draw. Ties before the semi-finals are replayed just once. The initial six rounds are regional qualifiers. The subsequent six rounds constitute the "proper" stage, featuring a single draw for all clubs.

input: Gaddafi's earliest education was of a religious nature, imparted by a local Islamic teacher. Subsequently moving to nearby Sirte to attend elementary school, he progressed through six grades in four years. Education in Libya was not free, but his father thought it would greatly benefit his son despite the financial strain. During the week Gaddafi slept in a mosque, and at weekends walked 20 miles to visit his parents. Bullied for being a Bedouin, he was proud of his identity and encouraged pride in other Bedouin children. From Sirte, he and his family moved to the market town of Sabha in Fezzan, south-central Libya, where his father worked as a caretaker for a tribal leader while Muammar attended secondary school, something neither parent had done. Gaddafi was popular at school; some friends made there received significant jobs in his later administration, most notably his best friend Abdul Salam Jalloud.
rewrite: Gaddafi’s initial education was religious, delivered by a local Islamic teacher. He then attended elementary school in nearby Sirte, completing six grades in just four years. Although education in Libya was not free, his father believed it was worth the financial sacrifice. During the week, Gaddafi slept in a mosque, walking 20 miles on weekends to see his parents. He faced bullying for his Bedouin heritage but took pride in it, inspiring similar pride in other Bedouin children. Later, his family relocated to Sabha, a market town in south-central Libya’s Fezzan region. There, his father worked as a caretaker for a tribal leader while Muammar attended secondary school—an opportunity neither of his parents had. Gaddafi was well-liked at school, and several friends from that time, most notably his closest friend Abdul Salam Jalloud, later held important roles in his administration.

input: At the end of the Rigvedic period, the Aryan society began to expand from the northwestern region of the Indian subcontinent, into the western Ganges plain. It became increasingly agricultural and was socially organised around the hierarchy of the four varnas, or social classes. This social structure was characterized both by syncretising with the native cultures of northern India, but also eventually by the excluding of indigenous peoples by labelling their occupations impure. During this period, many of the previous small tribal units and chiefdoms began to coalesce into monarchical, state-level polities.
rewrite: Toward the close of the Rigvedic period, Aryan society extended from the subcontinent's northwest into the western Ganges plain. Social organization solidified around the four-varna hierarchy. This structure involved syncretism with native northern Indian cultures, yet also progressed to excluding indigenous groups by deeming their occupations impure. Previously common small tribes and chiefdoms increasingly consolidated into monarchical states. During this expansion, society grew more agricultural in nature.

input: After being rendered obsolete by the redesign, the 1895 replica was presented in 1910 to the FA's long-serving president Lord Kinnaird. Kinnaird died in 1923, and his family kept it in their possession, out of view, until putting it up for auction in 2005. It was duly sold at Christie's auction house on 19 May 2005 for £420,000 (£478,400 including auction fees and taxes). The sale price set a new world record for a piece of football memorabilia, surpassing the £254,000 paid for the Jules Rimet World Cup Trophy in 1997. The successful bidder was David Gold, the then joint chairman of Birmingham City; claiming the FA and government were doing nothing proactive to ensure the trophy remained in the country, Gold stated his purchase was motivated by wanting to save it for the nation. Accordingly, Gold presented the trophy to the National Football Museum in Preston on 20 April 2006, where it went on immediate public display. It later moved with the museum to its new location in Manchester. In November 2012, it was ceremonially presented to Royal Engineers, after they beat Wanderers 7–1 in a charity replay of the first FA Cup final.
rewrite: Following its redesign, which rendered the original obsolete, the 1895 replica was given in 1910 to Lord Kinnaird, the Football Association's long-serving president. Upon his death in 1923, the trophy remained with his family, kept from public view, until its 2005 auction. On 19 May 2005, it sold at Christie's for £420,000 (£478,400 with fees and taxes), setting a world record for football memorabilia by surpassing the 1997 sale of the Jules Rimet Trophy for £254,000. The buyer was David Gold, then joint chairman of Birmingham City. He asserted that his purchase was driven by a desire to save the trophy for the nation, criticizing the FA and government for not acting proactively to keep it in the country. True to his word, Gold presented it to the National Football Museum in Preston on 20 April 2006, where it was immediately displayed. The trophy later relocated with the museum to Manchester. In a ceremonial gesture in November 2012, it was presented to the Royal Engineers after they defeated Wanderers 7–1 in a charity replay of the first FA Cup final.

input: In 1971, Akira Endo, a Japanese biochemist working for the pharmaceutical company Sankyo, identified mevastatin (ML-236B), a molecule produced by the fungus Penicillium citrinum, as an inhibitor of HMG-CoA reductase, a critical enzyme used by the body to produce cholesterol. Animal trials showed very good inhibitory effect as in clinical trials, however a long term study in dogs found toxic effects at higher doses and as a result mevastatin was believed to be too toxic for human use. Mevastatin was never marketed, because of its adverse effects of tumors, muscle deterioration, and sometimes death in laboratory dogs.
rewrite: In 1971, Japanese biochemist Akira Endo, employed by Sankyo, discovered mevastatin (ML-236B). This molecule, derived from the fungus *Penicillium citrinum*, inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, a key enzyme in the body's cholesterol production. While initial animal and clinical trials demonstrated strong inhibitory effects, a long-term canine study revealed toxic outcomes at higher doses, including tumors, muscle deterioration, and sometimes death. Consequently, mevastatin was deemed too toxic for human use and was never marketed.

input: In his Science of Logic (1812–1814) Hegel argues that finite qualities are not fully "real" because they depend on other finite qualities to determine them. Qualitative infinity, on the other hand, would be more self-determining and hence more fully real. Similarly finite natural things are less "real"—because they are less self-determining—than spiritual things like morally responsible people, ethical communities and God. So any doctrine, such as materialism, that asserts that finite qualities or natural objects are fully real is mistaken.
rewrite: Hegel contends in his Science of Logic (1812–1814) that finite qualities lack full reality, as they rely on other finite qualities for definition. In contrast, qualitative infinity is more self-determining and thus more real. By this reasoning, finite natural things are less real than spiritual entities like moral individuals, ethical communities, and God, due to being less self-determining. Therefore, materialism, which claims full reality for finite qualities or natural objects, is incorrect.

input: Technology magazine T3 gave the Super Slim model a positive review, stating the console is almost "nostalgic" in the design similarities to the original "fat" model, "While we don’t know whether it will play PS3 games or Blu-ray discs any differently yet, the look and feel of the new PS3 Slim is an obvious homage to the original PS3, minus the considerable excess weight. Immediately we would be concerned about the durability of the top loading tray that feels like it could be yanked straight out off the console, but ultimately it all feels like Sony's nostalgic way of signing off the current generation console in anticipation for the PS4."
rewrite: T3 magazine reviewed the Super Slim model favorably, noting its almost nostalgic resemblance to the original "fat" PS3 in design. The review stated that while performance with PS3 games or Blu-rays remains unclear, the new Slim's look and feel clearly pay homage to its predecessor, just without the bulk. It expressed initial concern over the top-loading tray's durability, as it seems easily detachable. Ultimately, however, the magazine interpreted the design as Sony's nostalgic farewell to the current generation console ahead of the PS4's arrival.

input: The British, for their part, lacked both a unified command and a clear strategy for winning. With the use of the Royal Navy, the British were able to capture coastal cities, but control of the countryside eluded them. A British sortie from Canada in 1777 ended with the disastrous surrender of a British army at Saratoga. With the coming in 1777 of General von Steuben, the training and discipline along Prussian lines began, and the Continental Army began to evolve into a modern force. France and Spain then entered the war against Great Britain as Allies of the US, ending its naval advantage and escalating the conflict into a world war. The Netherlands later joined France, and the British were outnumbered on land and sea in a world war, as they had no major allies apart from Indian tribes.
rewrite: British forces struggled with fragmented leadership and an unclear path to victory. While the Royal Navy secured coastal cities, they failed to dominate the countryside. A 1777 campaign launched from Canada culminated in the catastrophic British surrender at Saratoga. That same year, the arrival of General von Steuben initiated rigorous Prussian-style training, transforming the Continental Army into a more professional force. The conflict expanded globally when France and Spain allied with the United States, stripping Britain of its naval supremacy. The Netherlands subsequently joined the coalition, leaving Britain without major allies beyond certain Indian tribes and decisively outnumbered on both land and sea in a world war.

input: The word genocide was later included as a descriptive term to the process of indictment, but not yet as a formal legal term According to Lemming, genocide was defined as "a coordinated strategy to destroy a group of people, a process that could be accomplished through total annihilation as well as strategies that eliminate key elements of the group's basic existence, including language, culture, and economic infrastructure.” He created a concept of mobilizing much of the international relations and community, to working together and preventing the occurrence of such events happening within history and the international society. Australian anthropologist Peg LeVine coined the term "ritualcide" to describe the destruction of a group's cultural identity without necessarily destroying its members.
rewrite: Initially included descriptively in indictments rather than as a formal legal term, genocide was defined by Lemming as a coordinated strategy to destroy a group. This could involve total annihilation or the elimination of foundational elements like language, culture, and economic infrastructure. He envisioned mobilizing international relations and the global community to collaboratively prevent such events in history and society. Later, Australian anthropologist Peg LeVine introduced the term "ritualcide" to describe the targeted destruction of a group's cultural identity, even without physically destroying its members.

input: Production capacity in Britain and the United States was improved by the invention of the cotton gin by the American Eli Whitney in 1793. Before the development of cotton gins, the cotton fibers had to be pulled from the seeds tediously by hand. By the late 1700s a number of crude ginning machines had been developed. However, to produce a bale of cotton required over 600 hours of human labor, making large-scale production uneconomical in the United States, even with the use of humans as slave labor. The gin that Whitney manufactured (the Holmes design) reduced the hours down to just a dozen or so per bale. Although Whitney patented his own design for a cotton gin, he manufactured a prior design from Henry Odgen Holmes, for which Holmes filed a patent in 1796. Improving technology and increasing control of world markets allowed British traders to develop a commercial chain in which raw cotton fibers were (at first) purchased from colonial plantations, processed into cotton cloth in the mills of Lancashire, and then exported on British ships to captive colonial markets in West Africa, India, and China (via Shanghai and Hong Kong).
rewrite: The American Eli Whitney's invention of the cotton gin in 1793 enhanced production capacity in both Britain and the United States. Prior to this development, extracting cotton fibers from seeds was a tedious manual process. Even with several crude ginning machines created by the late 1700s, producing a single bale demanded over 600 hours of human labor. This rendered large-scale production in the United States uneconomical, despite the use of enslaved labor. Whitney's gin, which was actually based on the Holmes design, drastically cut this time to roughly a dozen hours per bale. Although Whitney held a patent for his own gin model, he commercially produced an earlier design by Henry Odgen Holmes, who patented it in 1796. Meanwhile, advancing technology and growing dominance in world markets enabled British traders to establish a commercial system. This chain involved purchasing raw cotton from colonial plantations, having it processed into cloth in Lancashire mills, and then exporting the finished goods via British ships to controlled colonial markets, such as those in West Africa, India, and China—specifically through Shanghai and Hong Kong.

input: The inclusiveness of Weinreich's definition (above) directs attention to the totality of one's identity at a given phase in time, and assists in elucidating component aspects of one's total identity, such as one's gender identity, ethnic identity, occupational identity and so on. The definition readily applies to the young child, to the adolescent, to the young adult, and to the older adult in various phases of the life cycle. Depending on whether one is a young child or an adult at the height of one's powers, how one construes oneself as one was in the past will refer to very different salient experiential markers. Likewise, how one construes oneself as one aspires to be in the future will differ considerably according to one's age and accumulated experiences. (Weinreich & Saunderson, (eds) 2003, pp 26–34).
rewrite: Weinreich's inclusive definition emphasizes the complete identity of an individual at any specific moment, helping to clarify various components like gender, ethnicity, and occupation. This framework is relevant across all stages of life, from early childhood through adolescence, adulthood, and older age. A person's interpretation of their past self relies on distinct, significant experiences, which vary greatly whether one is a young child or a mature adult at their peak. Similarly, aspirations for one's future self are shaped considerably by age and the accumulation of life experiences. (Weinreich & Saunderson, (eds) 2003, pp 26–34).

input: The Crimean War marked the ascendancy of France to the position of pre-eminent power on the Continent,:411 the continued decline of the Ottoman Empire, and the beginning of a decline for Tsarist Russia. As Fuller notes, "Russia had been beaten on the Crimean peninsula, and the military feared that it would inevitably be beaten again unless steps were taken to surmount its military weakness." The Crimean War marks the demise of the Concert of Europe, the balance of power that had dominated Europe since the Congress of Vienna in 1815, and which had included France, Russia, Austria and the United Kingdom.
rewrite: France emerged as the Continent's pre-eminent power following the Crimean War, which also signaled the ongoing decline of the Ottoman Empire and the start of a downturn for Tsarist Russia. This conflict ended the Concert of Europe—the balance of power established in 1815 by the Congress of Vienna and upheld by France, Russia, Austria, and the United Kingdom. As Fuller observes, Russia's defeat on the Crimean peninsula created a military fear that future losses were inevitable without reforms to overcome its weaknesses.

input: On the field at the beginning of a play are two teams of 12 (unlike 11 in American football). The team in possession of the ball is the offence and the team defending is referred to as the defence. Play begins with a backwards pass through the legs (the snap) by a member of the offensive team, to another member of the offensive team. This is usually the quarterback or punter, but a "direct snap" to a running back is also not uncommon. If the quarterback or punter receives the ball, he may then do any of the following:
rewrite: A football play starts with two teams of 12 players each on the field, differing from the 11 in American football. The offensive team possesses the ball, while the opposing side is the defense. To initiate action, an offensive player delivers a backward pass through the legs, known as the snap, to a teammate. Typically, this teammate is the quarterback or punter, though a direct snap to a running back also occurs frequently. Upon receiving the snap, the quarterback or punter then has several options for proceeding with the play.

input: New York City's commuter rail network is the largest in North America. The rail network, connecting New York City to its suburbs, consists of the Long Island Rail Road, Metro-North Railroad, and New Jersey Transit. The combined systems converge at Grand Central Terminal and Pennsylvania Station and contain more than 250 stations and 20 rail lines. In Queens, the elevated AirTrain people mover system connects JFK International Airport to the New York City Subway and the Long Island Rail Road; a separate AirTrain system is planned alongside the Grand Central Parkway to connect LaGuardia Airport to these transit systems. For intercity rail, New York City is served by Amtrak, whose busiest station by a significant margin is Pennsylvania Station on the West Side of Manhattan, from which Amtrak provides connections to Boston, Philadelphia, and Washington, D.C. along the Northeast Corridor, as well as long-distance train service to other North American cities.
rewrite: North America’s largest commuter rail network serves New York City and its surrounding suburbs. This extensive system includes the Long Island Rail Road, Metro-North Railroad, and New Jersey Transit. Together, they operate over 20 rail lines and more than 250 stations, converging at two major hubs: Grand Central Terminal and Pennsylvania Station. For airport access, Queens features the elevated AirTrain people mover, linking JFK International Airport to both the Subway and the Long Island Rail Road. A separate AirTrain is also planned along the Grand Central Parkway to connect LaGuardia Airport to these networks. Regarding intercity travel, Amtrak provides service from New York City, primarily through its busiest station, Pennsylvania Station in Manhattan. From there, trains run along the Northeast Corridor to cities like Boston, Philadelphia, and Washington, D.C., in addition to offering long-distance routes to various destinations across North America.

input: LaserDiscs potentially had a much longer lifespan than videocassettes. Because the discs were read optically instead of magnetically, no physical contact needs to be made between the player and the disc, except for the player's clamp that holds the disc at its center as it is spun and read. As a result, playback would not wear the information-bearing part of the discs, and properly manufactured LDs would theoretically last beyond one's lifetime. By contrast, a VHS tape held all of its picture and sound information on the tape in a magnetic coating which is in contact with the spinning heads on the head drum, causing progressive wear with each use (though later in VHS's lifespan, engineering improvements allowed tapes to be made and played back without contact). Also, the tape was thin and delicate, and it was easy for a player mechanism, especially on a low quality or malfunctioning model, to mishandle the tape and damage it by creasing it, frilling (stretching) its edges, or even breaking it.
rewrite: Unlike videocassettes, LaserDiscs offered a significantly longer potential lifespan. This durability stemmed from their optical playback method; a laser read the data without physically touching the disc's information-bearing surface. The only contact was a central clamp to hold and spin the disc. Consequently, playback caused no wear to the encoded content, meaning a well-made LaserDisc could theoretically endure for a lifetime. VHS tapes, however, stored picture and sound magnetically on a delicate tape. This tape made direct contact with spinning heads inside the player, leading to progressive degradation with each viewing, despite later engineering that reduced contact. Furthermore, the thin tape was prone to damage from mishandling by players, particularly lower-quality ones, resulting in creases, stretched edges, or breaks.

input: In the longer run, however, with the NES near its end of its life many third-party publishers such as Electronic Arts supported upstart competing consoles with less strict licensing terms such as the Sega Genesis and then the PlayStation, which eroded and then took over Nintendo's dominance in the home console market, respectively. Consoles from Nintendo's rivals in the post-SNES era had always enjoyed much stronger third-party support than Nintendo, which relied more heavily on first-party games.
rewrite: As the NES neared the end of its lifespan, third-party publishers like Electronic Arts began supporting rival consoles with less restrictive terms, such as the Sega Genesis and later the PlayStation. These competing systems gradually eroded and then overtook Nintendo's market dominance. Following the SNES era, Nintendo's rivals consistently enjoyed stronger third-party support, while Nintendo itself relied more heavily on its own first-party game titles.

input: Adolescents can conceptualize multiple "possible selves" that they could become and long-term possibilities and consequences of their choices. Exploring these possibilities may result in abrupt changes in self-presentation as the adolescent chooses or rejects qualities and behaviors, trying to guide the actual self toward the ideal self (who the adolescent wishes to be) and away from the feared self (who the adolescent does not want to be). For many, these distinctions are uncomfortable, but they also appear to motivate achievement through behavior consistent with the ideal and distinct from the feared possible selves.
rewrite: Adolescents often envision various "possible selves" they might become, considering long-term outcomes of their choices. This exploration can lead to sudden shifts in self-presentation as they adopt or discard traits, steering their actual self toward an ideal version and away from a feared one. While these distinctions may cause discomfort, they also seem to drive achievement by encouraging behaviors aligned with the ideal self and opposed to the feared possible selves.

input: In the private sector, corruption increases the cost of business through the price of illicit payments themselves, the management cost of negotiating with officials and the risk of breached agreements or detection. Although some claim corruption reduces costs by cutting bureaucracy, the availability of bribes can also induce officials to contrive new rules and delays. Openly removing costly and lengthy regulations are better than covertly allowing them to be bypassed by using bribes. Where corruption inflates the cost of business, it also distorts the playing field, shielding firms with connections from competition and thereby sustaining inefficient firms.
rewrite: Corruption in business raises expenses not only through illicit payments, but also via negotiation costs and risks from broken deals or exposure. While some argue it lowers costs by sidestepping bureaucracy, the very possibility of bribes can encourage officials to create additional rules and delays. It is more effective to openly eliminate burdensome regulations than to secretly circumvent them through bribery. Furthermore, corruption distorts competition by protecting connected companies, which allows inefficient firms to survive and skews the market.

input: After Germany invaded the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941, the Wehrmacht crossed the Estonian southern border on 7 July. The Red Army retreated behind the Pärnu River – Emajõgi line on 12 July. At the end of July the Germans resumed their advance in Estonia working in tandem with the Estonian Forest Brothers. Both German troops and Estonian partisans took Narva on 17 August and the Estonian capital Tallinn on 28 August. After the Soviets were driven out from Estonia, German troops disarmed all the partisan groups.
rewrite: On 22 June 1941, Germany invaded the Soviet Union. By 7 July, the Wehrmacht had crossed into southern Estonia, prompting the Red Army to retreat behind the Pärnu-Emajõgi line by 12 July. Advancing again in late July, German forces cooperated with the Estonian Forest Brothers. Together, they captured Narva on 17 August and the capital Tallinn on 28 August. Once the Soviets were expelled from Estonia, the German troops proceeded to disarm all the partisan groups.

input: In 1957, she made a state visit to the United States, where she addressed the United Nations General Assembly on behalf of the Commonwealth. On the same tour, she opened the 23rd Canadian Parliament, becoming the first monarch of Canada to open a parliamentary session. Two years later, solely in her capacity as Queen of Canada, she revisited the United States and toured Canada. In 1961, she toured Cyprus, India, Pakistan, Nepal, and Iran. On a visit to Ghana the same year, she dismissed fears for her safety, even though her host, President Kwame Nkrumah, who had replaced her as head of state, was a target for assassins. Harold Macmillan wrote, "The Queen has been absolutely determined all through ... She is impatient of the attitude towards her to treat her as ... a film star ... She has indeed 'the heart and stomach of a man' ... She loves her duty and means to be a Queen." Before her tour through parts of Quebec in 1964, the press reported that extremists within the Quebec separatist movement were plotting Elizabeth's assassination. No attempt was made, but a riot did break out while she was in Montreal; the Queen's "calmness and courage in the face of the violence" was noted.
rewrite: During a 1957 state visit to the United States, she addressed the United Nations General Assembly representing the Commonwealth. That same tour included opening the 23rd Canadian Parliament, marking her as the first monarch of Canada to perform such a duty. She returned to the United States and toured Canada in 1959, this time acting solely in her capacity as Queen of Canada. Her travels continued in 1961 with tours of Cyprus, India, Pakistan, Nepal, and Iran. Also that year, she visited Ghana, dismissing concerns for her safety despite the fact that her host, President Kwame Nkrumah—who had replaced her as head of state—was a target for assassins. Reflecting on her resolve, Harold Macmillan wrote, "The Queen has been absolutely determined all through ... She is impatient of the attitude towards her to treat her as ... a film star ... She has indeed 'the heart and stomach of a man' ... She loves her duty and means to be a Queen." Prior to her 1964 tour through parts of Quebec, press reports indicated that extremists within the separatist movement were plotting her assassination. While no attempt occurred, a riot erupted during her time in Montreal, where her "calmness and courage in the face of the violence" was widely noted.

input: Unlike all other British Government records, the records from the East India Company (and its successor the India Office) are not in The National Archives at Kew, London, but are held by the British Library in London as part of the Asia, Pacific and Africa Collections. The catalogue is searchable online in the Access to Archives catalogues. Many of the East India Company records are freely available online under an agreement that the Families in British India Society has with the British Library. Published catalogues exist of East India Company ships' journals and logs, 1600–1834; and of some of the Company's daughter institutions, including the East India Company College, Haileybury, and Addiscombe Military Seminary.
rewrite: The British Library in London houses the records of the East India Company and the India Office within its Asia, Pacific and Africa Collections, unlike all other British Government documents held at The National Archives in Kew. These records are listed in the online Access to Archives catalogues. Through an agreement with the British Library, the Families in British India Society has made many of these documents freely available online. Additionally, published catalogues exist for the Company's ships' journals and logs from 1600–1834, as well as for related institutions like the East India Company College in Haileybury and the Addiscombe Military Seminary.

input: Virgil is traditionally ranked as one of Rome's greatest poets. His Aeneid has been considered the national epic of ancient Rome from the time of its composition to the present day. Modeled after Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, the Aeneid follows the Trojan refugee Aeneas as he struggles to fulfill his destiny and arrive on the shores of Italy—in Roman mythology the founding act of Rome. Virgil's work has had wide and deep influence on Western literature, most notably Dante's Divine Comedy, in which Virgil appears as Dante's guide through hell and purgatory.
rewrite: Traditionally regarded as one of Rome's finest poets, Virgil composed the Aeneid, which has served as the national epic of ancient Rome since its creation. Modeled on Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, it traces the journey of the Trojan refugee Aeneas struggling to fulfill his destiny by reaching Italy—the mythical founding of Rome. Virgil's influence on Western literature is profound, most directly seen in Dante's Divine Comedy, where Virgil guides Dante through hell and purgatory.

input: During the Permian all the Earth's major land masses, except portions of East Asia, were collected into a single supercontinent known as Pangaea. Pangaea straddled the equator and extended toward the poles, with a corresponding effect on ocean currents in the single great ocean (Panthalassa, the universal sea), and the Paleo-Tethys Ocean, a large ocean that was between Asia and Gondwana. The Cimmeria continent rifted away from Gondwana and drifted north to Laurasia, causing the Paleo-Tethys to shrink. A new ocean was growing on its southern end, the Tethys Ocean, an ocean that would dominate much of the Mesozoic Era. Large continental landmasses create climates with extreme variations of heat and cold ("continental climate") and monsoon conditions with highly seasonal rainfall patterns. Deserts seem to have been widespread on Pangaea.
rewrite: In the Permian period, nearly all major landmasses merged into the supercontinent Pangaea, which stretched from the equator toward the poles. Only parts of East Asia remained separate. This vast continent influenced global climate, producing extreme temperature shifts and highly seasonal monsoon rainfall, while deserts became widespread across Pangaea. Ocean currents were shaped by the arrangement of land and sea, including the single great ocean Panthalassa and the Paleo-Tethys Ocean between Asia and Gondwana. As the continent Cimmeria broke from Gondwana and moved north toward Laurasia, the Paleo-Tethys began to shrink. Meanwhile, the growing Tethys Ocean emerged to its south, destined to define much of the subsequent Mesozoic Era.

input: Though Houston is the largest city in the United States without formal zoning regulations, it has developed similarly to other Sun Belt cities because the city's land use regulations and legal covenants have played a similar role. Regulations include mandatory lot size for single-family houses and requirements that parking be available to tenants and customers. Such restrictions have had mixed results. Though some have blamed the city's low density, urban sprawl, and lack of pedestrian-friendliness on these policies, the city's land use has also been credited with having significant affordable housing, sparing Houston the worst effects of the 2008 real estate crisis. The city issued 42,697 building permits in 2008 and was ranked first in the list of healthiest housing markets for 2009.
rewrite: Houston stands as the largest U.S. city without formal zoning, yet its development mirrors that of other Sun Belt cities. This similarity arises because local land use rules and legal covenants have functioned like zoning. Mandatory lot sizes for single-family homes and parking requirements for tenants and customers are key examples. These policies yield mixed outcomes. Critics link them to low density, sprawl, and poor walkability. However, they are also credited with fostering relatively affordable housing, which helped shield Houston from the severe impacts of the 2008 real estate crash. Demonstrating resilience, the city led the nation by issuing 42,697 building permits in 2008 and topped the 2009 rankings for healthiest housing markets.

input: Swaziland is a developing country with a small economy. Its GDP per capita of $9,714 means it is classified as a country with a lower-middle income. As a member of the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) and Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA), its main local trading partner is South Africa. Swaziland's currency, the lilangeni, is pegged to the South African rand. Swaziland's major overseas trading partners are the United States and the European Union. The majority of the country's employment is provided by its agricultural and manufacturing sectors. Swaziland is a member of the Southern African Development Community (SADC), the African Union, the Commonwealth of Nations and the United Nations.
rewrite: With a GDP per capita of $9,714, Swaziland is classified as a lower-middle income developing nation possessing a small economy. Its primary local trading partner is South Africa, a relationship reinforced through membership in the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) and the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA). The country’s currency, the lilangeni, is pegged to the South African rand. Overseas, its major trading partners are the United States and the European Union. Employment within Swaziland is largely generated by the agricultural and manufacturing sectors. The country also holds membership in the Southern African Development Community (SADC), the African Union, the Commonwealth of Nations, and the United Nations.

input: In Miranda the court created safeguards against self-incriminating statements made after an arrest. The court held that "The prosecution may not use statements, whether exculpatory or inculpatory, stemming from questioning initiated by law enforcement officers after a person has been taken into custody or otherwise deprived of his freedom of action in any significant way, unless it demonstrates the use of procedural safeguards effective to secure the Fifth Amendment's privilege against self-incrimination"
rewrite: In Miranda, the court established protections to prevent self-incrimination following an arrest. It ruled that statements obtained from questioning after a person is taken into custody cannot be used by prosecutors, unless specific procedural safeguards are applied. These measures must effectively secure the Fifth Amendment's privilege against self-incrimination, covering both exculpatory and inculpatory statements initiated by law enforcement.

input: Although the Drive moved to Massachusetts for the 1994 season, the AFL had a number of other teams which it considered "dynasties", including the Tampa Bay Storm (the only team that has existed in some form for all twenty-eight contested seasons), their arch-rival the Orlando Predators, the now-defunct San Jose SaberCats of the present decade, and their rivals the Arizona Rattlers.
rewrite: While the Drive relocated to Massachusetts in 1994, the AFL recognized several other dynasties. These included the Tampa Bay Storm—the sole team present in all 28 contested seasons—and their arch-rival Orlando Predators, along with the now-defunct San Jose SaberCats of this decade and their rivals, the Arizona Rattlers.

input: Dell previously had its headquarters in the Arboretum complex in northern Austin, Texas. In 1989 Dell occupied 127,000 square feet (11,800 m2) in the Arboretum complex. In 1990, Dell had 1,200 employees in its headquarters. In 1993, Dell submitted a document to Round Rock officials, titled "Dell Computer Corporate Headquarters, Round Rock, Texas, May 1993 Schematic Design." Despite the filing, during that year the company said that it was not going to move its headquarters. In 1994, Dell announced that it was moving most of its employees out of the Arboretum, but that it was going to continue to occupy the top floor of the Arboretum and that the company's official headquarters address would continue to be the Arboretum. The top floor continued to hold Dell's board room, demonstration center, and visitor meeting room. Less than one month prior to August 29, 1994, Dell moved 1,100 customer support and telephone sales employees to Round Rock. Dell's lease in the Arboretum had been scheduled to expire in 1994.
rewrite: Originally based in the Arboretum complex in northern Austin, Texas, Dell occupied 127,000 square feet there by 1989 and employed 1,200 headquarters staff by 1990. In 1993, the company submitted schematic designs for a corporate headquarters in Round Rock, yet insisted it had no plans to relocate. The following year, Dell announced a partial move, shifting most employees out while retaining the top floor of the Arboretum as its official headquarters address. This space continued to house the board room, demonstration center, and visitor meeting room. Shortly before August 29, 1994, the company transferred 1,100 customer support and telephone sales employees to Round Rock. This relocation coincided with the scheduled 1994 expiration of Dell’s lease in the Arboretum.

input: The New York metropolitan area is home to a self-identifying gay and bisexual community estimated at 568,903 individuals, the largest in the United States and one of the world's largest. Same-sex marriages in New York were legalized on June 24, 2011 and were authorized to take place beginning 30 days thereafter.
rewrite: With an estimated 568,903 self-identifying gay and bisexual residents, the New York metropolitan area hosts the largest such community in the United States and one of the world's biggest. Same-sex marriages were legalized there on June 24, 2011, with ceremonies authorized to start 30 days later.

input: English is the official language in the state of Montana, as it is in many U.S. states. English is also the language of the majority. According to the 2000 U.S. Census, 94.8 percent of the population aged 5 and older speak English at home. Spanish is the language most commonly spoken at home other than English. There were about 13,040 Spanish-language speakers in the state (1.4 percent of the population) in 2011. There were also 15,438 (1.7 percent of the state population) speakers of Indo-European languages other than English or Spanish, 10,154 (1.1 percent) speakers of a Native American language, and 4,052 (0.4 percent) speakers of an Asian or Pacific Islander language. Other languages spoken in Montana (as of 2013) include Assiniboine (about 150 speakers in the Montana and Canada), Blackfoot (about 100 speakers), Cheyenne (about 1,700 speakers), Plains Cree (about 100 speakers), Crow (about 3,000 speakers), Dakota (about 18,800 speakers in Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, and South Dakota), German Hutterite (about 5,600 speakers), Gros Ventre (about 10 speakers), Kalispel-Pend d'Oreille (about 64 speakers), Kutenai (about 6 speakers), and Lakota (about 6,000 speakers in Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, South Dakota). The United States Department of Education estimated in 2009 that 5,274 students in Montana spoke a language at home other than English. These included a Native American language (64 percent), German (4 percent), Spanish (3 percent), Russian (1 percent), and Chinese (less than 0.5 percent).
rewrite:
In Montana, English serves as the official and predominant language, a status it holds across most U.S. states. Data from the 2000 U.S. Census indicates that 94.8% of residents aged five and older speak English at home. Beyond English, Spanish is the most common home language, with approximately 13,040 speakers representing 1.4% of the population as of 2011. Other language groups present in the state at that time included speakers of other Indo-European languages (15,438 individuals, or 1.7%), Native American languages (10,154 individuals, or 1.1%), and Asian or Pacific Islander languages (4,052 individuals, or 0.4%).

Several Native American languages are spoken within Montana, with speaker estimates from around 2013 including Crow (3,000), Cheyenne (1,700), and Assiniboine (approximately 150 in Montana and Canada). Others are Blackfoot (100), Plains Cree (100), Gros Ventre (10), Kalispel-Pend d'Oreille (64), and Kutenai (6). Regional languages spanning multiple states include Dakota (about 18,800 speakers across several states including Montana) and Lakota (approximately 6,000 speakers in a similar multi-state region). German Hutterite is also spoken by about 5,600 people.

Reflecting this linguistic diversity, a 2009 estimate by the U.S. Department of Education found 5,274 Montana students speaking a non-English language at home. Among these students, 64% spoke a Native American language, while other reported languages included German (4%), Spanish (3%), Russian (1%), and Chinese (under 0.5%).

input: A series of low-lying annexes (largely hidden) flank both ends. Also in the square are the glass-faced Planalto Palace housing the presidential offices, and the Palace of the Supreme Court. Farther east, on a triangle of land jutting into the lake, is the Palace of the Dawn (Palácio da Alvorada; the presidential residence). Between the federal and civic buildings on the Monumental Axis is the city's cathedral, considered by many to be Niemeyer's finest achievement (see photographs of the interior). The parabolically shaped structure is characterized by its 16 gracefully curving supports, which join in a circle 115 feet (35 meters) above the floor of the nave; stretched between the supports are translucent walls of tinted glass. The nave is entered via a subterranean passage rather than conventional doorways. Other notable buildings are Buriti Palace, Itamaraty Palace, the National Theater, and several foreign embassies that creatively embody features of their national architecture. The Brazilian landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx designed landmark modernist gardens for some of the principal buildings.
rewrite: Flanking both ends of the square are a series of largely hidden, low-lying annexes. The square also contains the glass-faced Planalto Palace, which houses the presidential offices, and the Palace of the Supreme Court. The city's cathedral, situated between the federal and civic buildings along the Monumental Axis, is regarded by many as Oscar Niemeyer's finest achievement. Its parabolic shape features 16 gracefully curving supports that join in a circle 115 feet (35 meters) above the nave floor, with translucent walls of tinted glass stretched between them. Entry to the nave is through a subterranean passage instead of conventional doorways. Farther east, on a triangle of land extending into the lake, stands the Palace of the Dawn (Palácio da Alvorada), the presidential residence. Other significant structures include Buriti Palace, Itamaraty Palace, the National Theater, and several foreign embassies that creatively incorporate their national architectural styles. For some of these principal buildings, the Brazilian landscape architect Roberto Burle Marx designed landmark modernist gardens.

input: The European Central Bank had stepped up the buying of member nations debt. In response to the crisis of 2010, some proposals have surfaced for a collective European bond issue that would allow the central bank to purchase a European version of US Treasury bills. To make European sovereign debt assets more similar to a US Treasury, a collective guarantee of the member states' solvency would be necessary.[b] But the German government has resisted this proposal, and other analyses indicate that "the sickness of the euro" is due to the linkage between sovereign debt and failing national banking systems. If the European central bank were to deal directly with failing banking systems sovereign debt would not look as leveraged relative to national income in the financially weaker member states.
rewrite: In response to the 2010 crisis, proposals emerged for a collective European bond issue, creating a European equivalent of U.S. Treasury bills that the European Central Bank could purchase. To make such sovereign debt assets more comparable to U.S. Treasuries, a joint guarantee of member states' solvency would be required. However, the German government has opposed this idea. Meanwhile, the European Central Bank increased its purchases of member nations' debt. Other analyses suggest the root of "the sickness of the euro" lies in the connection between sovereign debt and failing national banking systems. Addressing these banking systems directly through the central bank could reduce the apparent leverage of sovereign debt relative to national income in financially weaker states.

input: These American settlers established a permanent foothold in the area and ignored Spanish officials. The British settlers who had remained also resented Spanish rule, leading to a rebellion in 1810 and the establishment for ninety days of the so-called Free and Independent Republic of West Florida on September 23. After meetings beginning in June, rebels overcame the Spanish garrison at Baton Rouge (now in Louisiana), and unfurled the flag of the new republic: a single white star on a blue field. This flag would later become known as the "Bonnie Blue Flag".
rewrite: American settlers secured a lasting presence in the region, disregarding Spanish authorities. Resentment toward Spanish rule also grew among the remaining British settlers, sparking a rebellion in 1810. Following meetings that started in June, rebels defeated the Spanish garrison at Baton Rouge. On September 23, they proclaimed the short-lived Free and Independent Republic of West Florida, which lasted ninety days. input: The Zhengde Emperor (r. 1505–1521), who enjoyed the company of lamas at court despite protests from the censorate, had heard tales of a "living Buddha" which he desired to host at the Ming capital; this was none other than the Rinpung-supported Mikyö Dorje, 8th Karmapa Lama then occupying Lhasa. Zhengde's top advisors made every attempt to dissuade him from inviting this lama to court, arguing that Tibetan Buddhism was wildly heterodox and unorthodox. Despite protests by the Grand Secretary Liang Chu, in 1515 the Zhengde Emperor sent his eunuch official Liu Yun of the Palace Chancellery on a mission to invite this Karmapa to Beijing. Liu commanded a fleet of hundreds of ships requisitioned along the Yangtze, consuming 2,835 g (100 oz) of silver a day in food expenses while stationed for a year in Chengdu of Sichuan. After procurring necessary gifts for the mission, he departed with a cavalry force of about 1,000 troops. When the request was delivered, the Karmapa lama refused to leave Tibet despite the Ming force brought to coerce him. The Karmapa launched a surprise ambush on Liu Yun's camp, seizing all the goods and valuables while killing or wounding half of Liu Yun's entire escort. After this fiasco, Liu fled for his life, but only returned to Chengdu several years later to find that the Zhengde Emperor had died.
rewrite:
Despite protests from his censorate, the Zhengde Emperor (r. 1505–1521) frequently welcomed lamas to his court. Intrigued by stories of a "living Buddha," he became determined to host this figure—Mikyö Dorje, the 8th Karmapa Lama, then in Lhasa and supported by the Rinpung—in the Ming capital. His senior advisors strenuously objected, condemning Tibetan Buddhism as profoundly heterodox and unorthodox. Nevertheless, in 1515, overriding the protests of Grand Secretary Liang Chu, the emperor dispatched the eunuch official Liu Yun of the Palace Chancellery to extend the invitation.

Liu Yun’s mission was lavish and costly. Stationed for a year in Chengdu, Sichuan, he commanded a fleet of hundreds of ships requisitioned along the Yangtze, with daily food expenses consuming 2,835 grams of silver. After gathering necessary gifts, he departed with a cavalry escort of roughly one thousand troops. However, upon receiving the imperial request, the Karmapa refused to leave Tibet, undeterred by the Ming force intended to coerce him. Instead, he launched a surprise ambush on Liu Yun’s camp, seizing all goods and valuables and killing or wounding half the escort.

In the aftermath of this fiasco, Liu Yun fled for his life. He did not return to Chengdu until several years later, only to discover that the Zhengde Emperor had died.

input: Oklahoma City Community College in south Oklahoma City is the second-largest community college in the state. Rose State College is located east of Oklahoma City in suburban Midwest City. Oklahoma State University–Oklahoma City is located in the "Furniture District" on the Westside. Northeast of the city is Langston University, the state's historically black college (HBCU). Langston also has an urban campus in the eastside section of the city. Southern Nazarene University, which was founded by the Church of the Nazarene, is a university located in suburban Bethany, which is surrounded by the Oklahoma City city limits.
rewrite: Oklahoma City hosts several higher education institutions across its metropolitan area. The second-largest community college in the state, Oklahoma City Community College, is situated in the south. To the east, in suburban Midwest City, lies Rose State College. input: The critic Joseph Bédier (1864–1938) launched a particularly withering attack on stemmatics in 1928. He surveyed editions of medieval French texts that were produced with the stemmatic method, and found that textual critics tended overwhelmingly to produce trees divided into just two branches. He concluded that this outcome was unlikely to have occurred by chance, and that therefore, the method was tending to produce bipartite stemmas regardless of the actual history of the witnesses. He suspected that editors tended to favor trees with two branches, as this would maximize the opportunities for editorial judgment (as there would be no third branch to "break the tie" whenever the witnesses disagreed). He also noted that, for many works, more than one reasonable stemma could be postulated, suggesting that the method was not as rigorous or as scientific as its proponents had claimed.
rewrite: In 1928, critic Joseph Bédier (1864–1938) delivered a severe critique of stemmatics. Examining editions of medieval French texts created using this method, he observed an overwhelming tendency for scholars to produce stemmatic trees divided into only two branches. Bédier concluded this pattern was too consistent to be accidental, arguing the method inherently favored bipartite stemmas, irrespective of the manuscripts' true historical relationships. He suspected editors preferred two-branch trees because they maximized opportunities for editorial judgment; with no third branch, any disagreement between witnesses would require a decisive editorial "tie-breaker." Furthermore, Bédier noted that for numerous works, multiple plausible stemmas could be constructed, indicating the technique was less rigorous and scientific than its advocates asserted.

input: Some scholars[note 44] use other schemes. Buddhists themselves have a variety of other schemes. Hinayana (literally "lesser vehicle") is used by Mahayana followers to name the family of early philosophical schools and traditions from which contemporary Theravada emerged, but as this term is rooted in the Mahayana viewpoint and can be considered derogatory, a variety of other terms are increasingly used instead, including Śrāvakayāna, Nikaya Buddhism, early Buddhist schools, sectarian Buddhism, conservative Buddhism, mainstream Buddhism and non-Mahayana Buddhism.
rewrite: Some scholars employ different classification systems, as do Buddhists themselves. The term "Hinayana" (meaning "lesser vehicle") is applied by Mahayana adherents to early philosophical schools that preceded modern Theravada. However, because this label originates from a Mahayana perspective and can be seen as pejorative, numerous alternative terms are now preferred. These include Śrāvakayāna, Nikaya Buddhism, early Buddhist schools, sectarian Buddhism, conservative Buddhism, mainstream Buddhism, and non-Mahayana Buddhism.

input: Following al-Farabi's lead, Avicenna initiated a full-fledged inquiry into the question of being, in which he distinguished between essence (Mahiat) and existence (Wujud). He argued that the fact of existence can not be inferred from or accounted for by the essence of existing things, and that form and matter by themselves cannot interact and originate the movement of the universe or the progressive actualization of existing things. Existence must, therefore, be due to an agent-cause that necessitates, imparts, gives, or adds existence to an essence. To do so, the cause must be an existing thing and coexist with its effect.
rewrite: Inspired by al-Farabi, Avicenna launched a comprehensive investigation into being. He made a key distinction between essence (Mahiat) and existence (Wujud). From his perspective, existence cannot be deduced from an essence, nor can form and matter alone generate cosmic motion or the gradual realization of entities. Consequently, existence must be bestowed by an agent-cause that grants it to an essence. This necessitates that the cause itself exists and is simultaneous with its effect.

input: The wider New York City metropolitan area, with over 20 million people, about 50% greater than the second-place Los Angeles metropolitan area in the United States, is also ethnically diverse. The New York region continues to be by far the leading metropolitan gateway for legal immigrants admitted into the United States, substantially exceeding the combined totals of Los Angeles and Miami, the next most popular gateway regions. It is home to the largest Jewish as well as Israeli communities outside Israel, with the Jewish population in the region numbering over 1.5 million in 2012 and including many diverse Jewish sects from around the Middle East and Eastern Europe. The metropolitan area is also home to 20% of the nation's Indian Americans and at least 20 Little India enclaves, as well as 15% of all Korean Americans and four Koreatowns; the largest Asian Indian population in the Western Hemisphere; the largest Russian American, Italian American, and African American populations; the largest Dominican American, Puerto Rican American, and South American and second-largest overall Hispanic population in the United States, numbering 4.8 million; and includes at least 6 established Chinatowns within New York City alone, with the urban agglomeration comprising a population of 779,269 overseas Chinese as of 2013 Census estimates, the largest outside of Asia.
rewrite: With over 20 million residents, the New York City metropolitan area is the most populous in the United States, exceeding the second-place Los Angeles area by about 50%. This vast region stands as the nation’s premier gateway for legal immigrants, admitting far more than Los Angeles and Miami combined. Its ethnic diversity is extraordinary. Hosting the largest Jewish and Israeli communities outside Israel, the area was home to over 1.5 million Jewish people in 2012, representing many sects from the Middle East and Eastern Europe. It contains the Western Hemisphere's largest Asian Indian population, 20% of all Indian Americans, and at least 20 Little India enclaves. The area is also home to 15% of Korean Americans and four Koreatowns. It boasts the largest populations of Russian Americans, Italian Americans, and African Americans nationally. Furthermore, it has the largest Dominican American, Puerto Rican American, and South American communities, contributing to the second-largest overall Hispanic population in the U.S. at 4.8 million. Within New York City alone are at least six established Chinatowns; the broader urban agglomeration had 779,269 overseas Chinese residents as of 2013, the largest such community outside Asia.

input: His organisational skills led him to a career in the Roman Curia, the papal civil service. In 1931, Pacelli appointed him to teach history at the Papal Academy for Diplomats In 1937, after his mentor Giuseppe Pizzardo was named a cardinal and was succeeded by Domenico Tardini, Montini was named Substitute for Ordinary Affairs under Cardinal Pacelli, the Secretary of State under Pope Pius XI. From Pius XI, whom he viewed with awe, he adopted the view, that learning is a life long process, and that history was the magister vitae teacher of life His immediate supervisor in the Vatican was Domenico Tardini, with whom he got along well. The election of Pacelli to the papacy in 1939, anticipated by everybody and openly promoted by Pope Pius XI in his last years, was a good omen for Montini, whose position was confirmed in the position under the new Cardinal Secretary of State Luigi Maglione. rewrite: After beginning a career in the Roman Curia due to his strong organisational abilities, he was appointed by Pacelli in 1931 to teach history at the Papal Academy for Diplomats. Under Pope Pius XI, Montini later became Substitute for Ordinary Affairs in 1937, serving under Cardinal Pacelli as Secretary of State. input: During the war, the Paris National Guard, particularly in the working-class neighbourhoods of Paris, had become highly politicised and units elected officers; many refused to wear uniforms or obey commands from the national government. National guard units tried to seize power in Paris on 31 October 1870 and 22 January 1871. On 18 March 1871, when the regular army tried to remove cannons from an artillery park on Montmartre, National Guard units resisted and killed two army generals. The national government and regular army forces retreated to Versailles and a revolutionary government was proclaimed in Paris. A Commune was elected, which was dominated by socialists, anarchists and revolutionaries. The red flag replaced the French tricolour and a civil war began between the Commune and the regular army, which attacked and recaptured Paris from 21–28 May in La Semaine Sanglante (Bloody week).
rewrite: Amidst the war, the Paris National Guard grew intensely politicized, especially within the city's working-class districts. Its units elected their own officers, with many members rejecting government-issued uniforms and defying commands from the national authorities. This defiance escalated into attempted seizures of power in Paris on 31 October 1870 and 22 January 1871. The pivotal clash occurred on 18 March 1871, when National Guardsmen resisted the regular army's attempt to confiscate cannons from Montmartre, resulting in the killing of two generals. Following this, the national government and army retreated to Versailles. A revolutionary government was then proclaimed in Paris, leading to the election of a Commune dominated by socialists, anarchists, and revolutionaries. They replaced the French tricolour with the red flag, sparking a civil war. The regular army attacked and recaptured Paris from 21–28 May during the brutal period known as La Semaine Sanglante, or the Bloody Week.

input: New Zealand polytechnics are established under the Education Act 1989 as amended, and are considered state-owned tertiary institutions along with universities, colleges of education, and wānanga; there is today often much crossover in courses and qualifications offered between all these types of Tertiary Education Institutions. Some have officially taken the title 'institute of technology' which is a term recognized in government strategies equal to that of the term 'polytechnic'. One has opted for the name 'Universal College of Learning' (UCOL), and another 'Unitec New Zealand'. These are legal names but not recognized terms like 'polytechnic' or 'institute of technology'. Many if not all now grant at least bachelor-level degrees.
rewrite: Established under the Education Act 1989, New Zealand's polytechnics are state-owned tertiary institutions, a category they share with universities, colleges of education, and wānanga. Significant crossover now exists in the courses and qualifications offered by these institutions. While officially recognized government terms include both 'polytechnic' and 'institute of technology', some schools use distinct legal names like 'Universal College of Learning' (UCOL) or 'Unitec New Zealand'. Today, many, if not all, of these institutions grant qualifications up to at least the bachelor's degree level.

input: Details of the overall United States intelligence budget are classified. Under the Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949, the Director of Central Intelligence is the only federal government employee who can spend "un-vouchered" government money. The government has disclosed a total figure for all non-military intelligence spending since 2007; the fiscal 2013 figure is $52.6 billion. According to the 2013 mass surveillance disclosures, the CIA's fiscal 2013 budget is $14.7 billion, 28% of the total and almost 50% more than the budget of the National Security Agency. CIA's HUMINT budget is $2.3 billion, the SIGINT budget is $1.7 billion, and spending for security and logistics of CIA missions is $2.5 billion. "Covert action programs", including a variety of activities such as the CIA's drone fleet and anti-Iranian nuclear program activities, accounts for $2.6 billion.
rewrite: The total United States intelligence budget remains classified. Since 2007, the government has disclosed only an overall figure for non-military intelligence spending, which was $52.6 billion for fiscal 2013. Leaks in 2013 revealed the Central Intelligence Agency's portion of that total was $14.7 billion, representing 28% and exceeding the National Security Agency's budget by nearly 50%. The CIA's spending includes $2.3 billion for HUMINT (human intelligence) and $1.7 billion for SIGINT (signals intelligence). Mission security and logistics require $2.5 billion. A further $2.6 billion funds "covert action programs," encompassing activities like drone operations and efforts against Iran's nuclear program. Unique authority, granted by the 1949 Central Intelligence Agency Act, allows only the Director of Central Intelligence to spend "un-vouchered" government funds.

input: University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust is one of the city's largest employers. It provides local hospital services to 500,000 people in the Southampton area and specialist regional services to more than 3 million people across the South of England. The Trust owns and manages Southampton General Hospital, the Princess Anne Hospital and a palliative care service at Countess Mountbatten House, part of the Moorgreen Hospital site in the village of West End, just outside the city.
rewrite: As one of Southampton's largest employers, University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust serves 500,000 local residents and offers specialized care to over 3 million across the South of England. It operates Southampton General Hospital, the Princess Anne Hospital, and a palliative care service at Countess Mountbatten House. This facility is located at the Moorgreen Hospital site in West End, a village just outside the city.

input: With the exception of seasons one and two, the contestants in the semifinals onwards perform in front of a studio audience. They perform with a full band in the finals. From season four to season nine, the American Idol band was led by Rickey Minor; from season ten onwards, Ray Chew. Assistance may also be given by vocal coaches and song arrangers, such as Michael Orland and Debra Byrd to contestants behind the scene. Starting with season seven, contestants may perform with a musical instrument from the Hollywood rounds onwards. In the first nine seasons, performances were usually aired live on Tuesday nights, followed by the results shows on Wednesdays in the United States and Canada, but moved to Wednesdays and Thursdays in season ten.
