input: The Early Jurassic spans from 200 million years to 175 million years ago. The climate was much more humid than the Triassic, and as a result, the world was very tropical. In the oceans, Plesiosaurs, Ichthyosaurs and Ammonites fill waters as the dominant races of the seas. On land, dinosaurs and other reptiles stake their claim as the dominant race of the land, with species such as Dilophosaurus at the top. The first true crocodiles evolved, pushing out the large amphibians to near extinction. All-in-all, reptiles rise to rule the world. Meanwhile, the first true mammals evolve, but remained relatively small sized.
rewrite: Spanning from 200 to 175 million years ago, the Early Jurassic featured a climate far more humid than the preceding Triassic, creating a largely tropical world. In the oceans, Plesiosaurs, Ichthyosaurs, and Ammonites dominated the waters. On land, dinosaurs like Dilophosaurus and other reptiles established themselves as the primary terrestrial species. This era saw the rise of reptiles ruling the world, as the first true crocodiles evolved, displacing large amphibians nearly to extinction. Concurrently, the first true mammals emerged, though they remained relatively small in size.

input: This led Popper to conclude that what were regarded[by whom?] as the remarkable strengths of psychoanalytical theories were actually their weaknesses. Psychoanalytical theories were crafted in a way that made them able to refute any criticism and to give an explanation for every possible form of human behaviour. The nature of such theories made it impossible for any criticism or experiment - even in principle - to show them to be false. This realisation had an important consequence when Popper later tackled the problem of demarcation in the philosophy of science, as it led him to posit that the strength of a scientific theory lies in its both being susceptible to falsification, and not actually being falsified by criticism made of it. He considered that if a theory cannot, in principle, be falsified by criticism, it is not a scientific theory.
rewrite: Popper observed that the apparent strengths of psychoanalytic theories were, in fact, their fundamental weaknesses. These theories were constructed to be impervious to criticism, capable of explaining every conceivable human behavior. Consequently, no criticism or experiment could ever demonstrate them to be false, even in principle. This insight proved crucial when Popper later addressed the problem of demarcation in the philosophy of science. It led him to argue that a true scientific theory derives its strength from being open to falsification, while simultaneously surviving attempts to disprove it. He concluded that any theory which cannot, in principle, be falsified by criticism does not qualify as scientific.

input: The best-known medieval Chinese name for Tibet is Tubo (Chinese: 吐蕃 also written as 土蕃 or 土番; pinyin: Tǔbō or Tǔfān). This name first appears in Chinese characters as 土番 in the 7th century (Li Tai) and as 吐蕃 in the 10th-century (Old Book of Tang describing 608–609 emissaries from Tibetan King Namri Songtsen to Emperor Yang of Sui). In the Middle Chinese spoken during that period, as reconstructed by William H. Baxter, 土番 was pronounced thux-phjon and 吐蕃 was pronounced thux-pjon (with the x representing tone).
rewrite: The most familiar medieval Chinese term for Tibet is Tubo (Chinese: 吐蕃, also 土蕃 or 土番; pinyin: Tǔbō or Tǔfān). It initially appeared as 土番 in 7th-century records, and later as 吐蕃 in a 10th-century text describing 608–609 emissaries. Based on William H. Baxter's reconstructions of Middle Chinese pronunciation, 土番 was spoken as *thux-phjon* and 吐蕃 as *thux-pjon*, with the *x* denoting tone.

input: Starting in the mid-1990s, Valencia, formerly an industrial centre, saw rapid development that expanded its cultural and touristic possibilities, and transformed it into a newly vibrant city. Many local landmarks were restored, including the ancient Towers of the medieval city (Serrano Towers and Quart Towers), and the San Miguel de los Reyes monastery, which now holds a conservation library. Whole sections of the old city, for example the Carmen Quarter, have been extensively renovated. The Paseo Marítimo, a 4 km (2 mi) long palm tree-lined promenade was constructed along the beaches of the north side of the port (Playa Las Arenas, Playa Cabañal and Playa de la Malvarrosa).
rewrite: From the mid-1990s, Valencia transformed from an industrial centre into a vibrant city through rapid development. This growth greatly expanded its cultural and touristic appeal. Extensive renovations revived entire sections of the old city, such as the Carmen Quarter. Key landmarks were also restored, including the medieval Serrano and Quart Towers, and the San Miguel de los Reyes monastery—the latter now housing a conservation library. Furthermore, a 4 km (2 mi) palm-lined promenade, the Paseo Marítimo, was built along the northern port beaches of Playa Las Arenas, Playa Cabañal, and Playa de la Malvarrosa.

input: Modern historiography on the period has reached a consensus between the two extremes of innovation and crisis. It is now (generally) acknowledged that conditions were vastly different north and south of the Alps, and "Late Middle Ages" is often avoided entirely within Italian historiography. The term "Renaissance" is still considered useful for describing certain intellectual, cultural, or artistic developments, but not as the defining feature of an entire European historical epoch. The period from the early 14th century up until – and sometimes including – the 16th century, is rather seen as characterised by other trends: demographic and economic decline followed by recovery, the end of western religious unity and the subsequent emergence of the nation state, and the expansion of European influence onto the rest of the world.
rewrite: Contemporary historical scholarship has moved beyond the polarized views of innovation versus crisis regarding this era. While the label "Renaissance" retains some utility for specific intellectual or artistic shifts, it is no longer seen as the overarching characteristic of a European age. Research emphasizes starkly different conditions between regions north and south of the Alps, leading Italian historians to often reject the term "Late Middle Ages" altogether. The centuries from the early 1300s into the 1500s are now primarily defined by broader patterns: phases of demographic and economic downturn and revival, the dissolution of Western Christendom and the rise of nation states, and the global expansion of European power.

input: The value of the U.S. dollar declined significantly during wartime, especially during the American Civil War, World War I, and World War II. The Federal Reserve, which was established in 1913, was designed to furnish an "elastic" currency subject to "substantial changes of quantity over short periods", which differed significantly from previous forms of high-powered money such as gold, national bank notes, and silver coins. Over the very long run, the prior gold standard kept prices stable—for instance, the price level and the value of the U.S. dollar in 1914 was not very different from the price level in the 1880s. The Federal Reserve initially succeeded in maintaining the value of the U.S. dollar and price stability, reversing the inflation caused by the First World War and stabilizing the value of the dollar during the 1920s, before presiding over a 30% deflation in U.S. prices in the 1930s.
rewrite: During the American Civil War, World War I, and World War II, the U.S. dollar experienced significant declines in value. Prior to the 20th century, the gold standard had maintained long-term price stability; for example, the price level in 1914 was similar to that of the 1880s. Established in 1913, the Federal Reserve was created to provide a flexible currency capable of "substantial changes of quantity over short periods," a departure from earlier high-powered money like gold, silver coins, and national bank notes. Initially, the Federal Reserve succeeded in stabilizing the dollar's value, reversing World War I inflation and maintaining stability through the 1920s. However, it later presided over a 30% deflation in U.S. prices during the 1930s.

input: On 2 March 1882, Roderick Maclean, a disgruntled poet apparently offended by Victoria's refusal to accept one of his poems, shot at the Queen as her carriage left Windsor railway station. Two schoolboys from Eton College struck him with their umbrellas, until he was hustled away by a policeman. Victoria was outraged when he was found not guilty by reason of insanity, but was so pleased by the many expressions of loyalty after the attack that she said it was "worth being shot at—to see how much one is loved".
rewrite: On 2 March 1882, a disgruntled poet named Roderick Maclean fired at Queen Victoria's carriage as it departed Windsor railway station. He was apparently aggrieved by her refusal to accept one of his poems. Two Eton College schoolboys struck the assailant with their umbrellas until a policeman took him away. Although outraged by his subsequent acquittal on grounds of insanity, the Queen was deeply moved by the outpouring of loyalty following the attack. She remarked that it was "worth being shot at—to see how much one is loved."

input: In 1816 Byron, Percy Bysshe Shelley and his wife Mary Shelley visited Geneva and all three were inspired by the scenery in their writings. During these visits Shelley wrote the poem "Mont Blanc", Byron wrote "The Prisoner of Chillon" and the dramatic poem Manfred, and Mary Shelley, who found the scenery overwhelming, conceived the idea for the novel Frankenstein in her villa on the shores of Lake Geneva in the midst of a thunderstorm. When Coleridge travelled to Chamonix, he declaimed, in defiance of Shelley, who had signed himself "Atheos" in the guestbook of the Hotel de Londres near Montenvers, "Who would be, who could be an atheist in this valley of wonders". By the mid-19th century scientists began to arrive en masse to study the geology and ecology of the region.
rewrite: During a stay in Geneva in 1816, the scenery profoundly inspired Lord Byron, Percy Bysshe Shelley, and Mary Shelley. In a villa by Lake Geneva, amid a thunderstorm, Mary Shelley found the landscape so overwhelming it sparked her idea for Frankenstein. Percy Shelley composed "Mont Blanc," while Byron produced "The Prisoner of Chillon" and Manfred. Later, when Samuel Taylor Coleridge traveled to Chamonix, he countered Percy Shelley's earlier "Atheos" inscription in a hotel guestbook by declaring, "Who would be, who could be an atheist in this valley of wonders." By the mid-19th century, the focus shifted as scientists arrived in large numbers to examine the region's geology and ecology.

input: Although the Palaeologi emperors recaptured Constantinople from the Western Europeans in 1261, they were never able to regain control of much of the former imperial lands. They usually controlled only a small section of the Balkan Peninsula near Constantinople, the city itself, and some coastal lands on the Black Sea and around the Aegean Sea. The former Byzantine lands in the Balkans were divided between the new Kingdom of Serbia, the Second Bulgarian Empire and the city-state of Venice. The power of the Byzantine emperors was threatened by a new Turkish tribe, the Ottomans, who established themselves in Anatolia in the 13th century and steadily expanded throughout the 14th century. The Ottomans expanded into Europe, reducing Bulgaria to a vassal state by 1366 and taking over Serbia after its defeat at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. Western Europeans rallied to the plight of the Christians in the Balkans and declared a new crusade in 1396; a great army was sent to the Balkans, where it was defeated at the Battle of Nicopolis. Constantinople was finally captured by the Ottomans in 1453.
rewrite: Despite reclaiming Constantinople from Western Europeans in 1261, the Palaeologi emperors failed to restore the Byzantine Empire to its former territorial extent. Their effective dominion was largely confined to Constantinople itself, a limited portion of the nearby Balkan Peninsula, and certain coastal regions bordering the Black and Aegean Seas. The remainder of the Balkan territories formerly under Byzantine rule had been partitioned among emerging powers: the Kingdom of Serbia, the Second Bulgarian Empire, and the Venetian city-state. A more profound threat arose from the Ottomans, a Turkish tribe that settled in Anatolia during the 13th century. Their relentless expansion throughout the 1300s saw them cross into Europe, reducing Bulgaria to vassalage by 1366 and conquering Serbia following the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. In response to the Christian plight in the Balkans, Western Europeans launched a crusade in 1396, dispatching a major army that was decisively defeated at the Battle of Nicopolis. The Ottoman advance culminated in the final capture of Constantinople in 1453.

input: Canada's Armed forces operate out of 27 Canadian Forces bases (CFB) across the country, including NDHQ. This number has been gradually reduced since the 1970s with bases either being closed or merged. Both officers and non-commissioned members receive their basic training at the Canadian Forces Leadership and Recruit School in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu. Officers will generally either directly enter the Canadian Armed Forces with a degree from a civilian university, or receive their commission upon graduation from the Royal Military College of Canada. Specific element and trade training is conducted at a variety of institutions throughout Canada, and to a lesser extent, the world.
rewrite: The Canadian Armed Forces are based at 27 Canadian Forces Bases (CFBs) nationwide, including the National Defence Headquarters. Since the 1970s, this number has steadily declined through closures and mergers. Basic training for all recruits, both officers and non-commissioned members, is provided at the Canadian Forces Leadership and Recruit School in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu. Officers typically enter with a civilian university degree or earn their commission upon graduating from the Royal Military College of Canada. Specialized training for specific elements and trades occurs at various institutions, primarily across Canada and, to a smaller degree, internationally.

input: The Taragaon Museum presents the modern history of the Kathmandu Valley. It seeks to document 50 years of research and cultural heritage conservation of the Kathmandu Valley, documenting what artists photographers architects anthropologists from abroad had contributed in the second half of the 20th century. The actual structure of the Museum showcases restoration and rehabilitation efforts to preserve the built heritage of Kathmandu. It was designed by Carl Pruscha (master-planner of the Kathmandy Valley ) in 1970 and constructed in 1971. Restoration works began in 2010 to rehabilitate the Taragaon hostel into the Taragaon Museum. The design uses local brick along with modern architectural design elements, as well as the use of circle, triangles and squares. The Museum is within a short walk from the Boudhnath stupa, which itself can be seen from the Museum tower.
rewrite: Dedicated to the modern history of the Kathmandu Valley, the Taragaon Museum documents fifty years of research and cultural heritage conservation. It specifically highlights contributions from foreign artists, photographers, architects, and anthropologists during the latter half of the twentieth century. The building itself, originally the Taragaon Hostel, is a showcase of restoration. Designed in 1970 by Carl Pruscha, the Kathmandu Valley's master-planner, and constructed in 1971, it was rehabilitated into the Museum beginning in 2010. Its design innovatively combines local brick with modern elements, featuring geometric shapes like circles, triangles, and squares. Located a short walk from the Boudhnath Stupa, the museum offers a view of the stupa from its tower.

input: If any boy produces an outstanding piece of work, it may be "Sent Up For Good", storing the effort in the College Archives for posterity. This award has been around since the 18th century. As Sending Up For Good is fairly infrequent, the process is rather mysterious to many of Eton's boys. First, the master wishing to Send Up For Good must gain the permission of the relevant Head of Department. Upon receiving his or her approval, the piece of work will be marked with Sent Up For Good and the student will receive a card to be signed by House Master, tutor and division master.
rewrite: An outstanding piece of work by a boy may be "Sent Up For Good," a practice dating to the 18th century, with the effort preserved in the College Archives. Because this award is fairly infrequent, its process remains rather mysterious to many at Eton. It begins when a master must secure permission from the relevant Head of Department. Following approval, the work is marked accordingly, and the student receives a card to be signed by the House Master, tutor, and division master.

input: Shorter, black-and-white daily strips began to appear early in the 20th century, and became established in newspapers after the success in 1907 of Bud Fisher's Mutt and Jeff. Humour strips predominated at first, and in the 1920s and 1930s strips with continuing stories in genres such as adventure and drama also became popular. Thin periodicals called comic books appeared in the 1930s, at first reprinting newspaper comic strips; by the end of the decade, original content began to dominate. The success in 1938 of Action Comics and its lead hero Superman marked the beginning of the Golden Age of Comic Books, in which the superhero genre was prominent.
rewrite: Early in the 20th century, shorter black-and-white daily comic strips emerged, solidifying in newspapers following the 1907 success of Bud Fisher's *Mutt and Jeff*. Initially, humour strips were dominant. However, the 1920s and 1930s saw the rise of popular continuing stories in adventure and drama genres. The 1930s also introduced thin periodicals known as comic books, which first reprinted newspaper strips before original content dominated by the decade's end. The 1938 launch of *Action Comics* and its hero Superman was pivotal, heralding the superhero-focused Golden Age of Comic Books.

input: Umar is honored for his attempt to resolve the fiscal problems attendant upon conversion to Islam. During the Umayyad period, the majority of people living within the caliphate were not Muslim, but Christian, Jewish, Zoroastrian, or members of other small groups. These religious communities were not forced to convert to Islam, but were subject to a tax (jizyah) which was not imposed upon Muslims. This situation may actually have made widespread conversion to Islam undesirable from the point of view of state revenue, and there are reports that provincial governors actively discouraged such conversions. It is not clear how Umar attempted to resolve this situation, but the sources portray him as having insisted on like treatment of Arab and non-Arab (mawali) Muslims, and on the removal of obstacles to the conversion of non-Arabs to Islam.
rewrite: Umar is recognized for his efforts to address the fiscal challenges linked to conversion to Islam. In the Umayyad era, most inhabitants of the caliphate were not Muslim but belonged to Christian, Jewish, Zoroastrian, or other minority faiths. These communities were not compelled to convert; instead, they paid a special tax (jizyah), from which Muslims were exempt. Consequently, widespread conversion could threaten state revenue, leading some provincial governors to reportedly discourage it. Although the specifics of Umar's approach remain unclear, historical accounts emphasize his stance: he advocated for equal treatment of Arab and non-Arab (mawali) Muslims and sought to eliminate barriers to conversion for non-Arabs.

input: In the following decades there was a constant battle between the company lobby and the Parliament. The company sought a permanent establishment, while the Parliament would not willingly allow it greater autonomy and so relinquish the opportunity to exploit the company's profits. In 1712, another act renewed the status of the company, though the debts were repaid. By 1720, 15% of British imports were from India, almost all passing through the company, which reasserted the influence of the company lobby. The licence was prolonged until 1766 by yet another act in 1730.
rewrite: Over the following decades, the company lobby and Parliament were locked in constant struggle. Parliament resisted granting the company greater autonomy, unwilling to relinquish control over its profits, while the company sought a permanent establishment. An act in 1712 renewed the company's status even after its debts were settled. By 1720, 15% of British imports came from India, nearly all channeled through the company, reinforcing its lobby's influence. Subsequently, the licence was extended until 1766 by a further act in 1730.

input: In 1899, the university opened a national design contest for the new campus. The renowned Philadelphia firm Cope & Stewardson won unanimously with its plan for a row of Collegiate Gothic quadrangles inspired by Oxford and Cambridge Universities. The cornerstone of the first building, Busch Hall, was laid on October 20, 1900. The construction of Brookings Hall, Ridgley, and Cupples began shortly thereafter. The school delayed occupying these buildings until 1905 to accommodate the 1904 World's Fair and Olympics. The delay allowed the university to construct ten buildings instead of the seven originally planned. This original cluster of buildings set a precedent for the development of the Danforth Campus; Cope & Stewardson’s original plan and its choice of building materials have, with few exceptions, guided the construction and expansion of the Danforth Campus to the present day.
rewrite: In 1899, the university launched a national contest to design its new campus. Philadelphia’s celebrated firm Cope & Stewardson submitted the unanimous winning entry: a plan featuring a series of Collegiate Gothic quadrangles, modeled after Oxford and Cambridge. Construction commenced with the cornerstone of Busch Hall on October 20, 1900, followed soon by Brookings Hall, Ridgley, and Cupples. However, to accommodate the 1904 World’s Fair and Olympics, the school postponed occupying the buildings until 1905. This delay proved beneficial, enabling the construction of ten buildings rather than the initially planned seven. This original cluster established a lasting precedent for the Danforth Campus. To this day, with few exceptions, the campus’s construction and expansion have followed Cope & Stewardson’s initial vision and material choices.

input: Each team consists of a maximum of eleven players (excluding substitutes), one of whom must be the goalkeeper. Competition rules may state a minimum number of players required to constitute a team, which is usually seven. Goalkeepers are the only players allowed to play the ball with their hands or arms, provided they do so within the penalty area in front of their own goal. Though there are a variety of positions in which the outfield (non-goalkeeper) players are strategically placed by a coach, these positions are not defined or required by the Laws.
rewrite: A team may include up to eleven players, not counting substitutes, with one designated as goalkeeper. Typically, competition rules set a minimum team size, often seven players. Only the goalkeeper is permitted to use hands or arms to play the ball, and only within their own penalty area. While coaches often assign outfield players to various strategic positions, such roles are not officially mandated by the Laws of the Game.

input: The clergy was divided into two types: the secular clergy, who lived out in the world, and the regular clergy, who lived under a religious rule and were usually monks. Throughout the period monks remained a very small proportion of the population, usually less than one per cent. Most of the regular clergy were drawn from the nobility, the same social class that served as the recruiting ground for the upper levels of the secular clergy. The local parish priests were often drawn from the peasant class. Townsmen were in a somewhat unusual position, as they did not fit into the traditional three-fold division of society into nobles, clergy, and peasants. During the 12th and 13th centuries, the ranks of the townsmen expanded greatly as existing towns grew and new population centres were founded. But throughout the Middle Ages the population of the towns probably never exceeded 10 per cent of the total population.
rewrite: The clergy consisted of two groups: the secular clergy, living in the wider world, and the regular clergy, who followed a religious rule, typically as monks. Monks always represented a tiny fraction of the populace, generally below one percent. Both the regular clergy and the upper echelons of the secular clergy were primarily recruited from the nobility. In contrast, local parish priests often came from the peasantry. Townsmen occupied an anomalous social position, falling outside the conventional triad of nobles, clergy, and peasants. The 12th and 13th centuries saw a significant expansion in their numbers due to urban growth and the founding of new settlements. Despite this, the urban population likely remained under ten percent of the total throughout the medieval period.

input: It is in this time that the notation of music on a staff and other elements of musical notation began to take shape. This invention made possible the separation of the composition of a piece of music from its transmission; without written music, transmission was oral, and subject to change every time it was transmitted. With a musical score, a work of music could be performed without the composer's presence. The invention of the movable-type printing press in the 15th century had far-reaching consequences on the preservation and transmission of music.
rewrite: During this period, musical notation on a staff and other notational elements started to develop. This innovation allowed the composition of music to be separated from its transmission; previously, without written records, transmission was oral and altered with each retelling. A musical score enabled a work to be performed without the composer present. Furthermore, the 15th-century invention of the movable-type printing press profoundly impacted the preservation and dissemination of music.

input: Formal schooling did not start in Hungary until the age of ten. Instead, governesses taught von Neumann, his brothers and his cousins. Max believed that knowledge of languages other than Hungarian was essential, so the children were tutored in English, French, German and Italian. By the age of 8, von Neumann was familiar with differential and integral calculus, but he was particularly interested in history, reading his way through Wilhelm Oncken's Allgemeine Geschichte in Einzeldarstellungen. A copy was contained in a private library Max purchased. One of the rooms in the apartment was converted into a library and reading room, with bookshelves from ceiling to floor.
rewrite: In Hungary, formal schooling began only at age ten. Before that, von Neumann and his brothers and cousins were taught by governesses. Their father, Max, considered knowledge of foreign languages essential, so the children received tutoring in English, French, German, and Italian. By eight, von Neumann was already acquainted with differential and integral calculus. His particular passion, however, was history; he read through Wilhelm Oncken's *Allgemeine Geschichte in Einzeldarstellungen*, a volume from a private library Max had purchased. To house this collection, one apartment room was converted into a library with ceiling-high bookshelves.

input: Despite competition from other materials, copper remains the preferred electrical conductor in nearly all categories of electrical wiring with the major exception being overhead electric power transmission where aluminium is often preferred. Copper wire is used in power generation, power transmission, power distribution, telecommunications, electronics circuitry, and countless types of electrical equipment. Electrical wiring is the most important market for the copper industry. This includes building wire, communications cable, power distribution cable, appliance wire, automotive wire and cable, and magnet wire. Roughly half of all copper mined is used to manufacture electrical wire and cable conductors. Many electrical devices rely on copper wiring because of its multitude of inherent beneficial properties, such as its high electrical conductivity, tensile strength, ductility, creep (deformation) resistance, corrosion resistance, low thermal expansion, high thermal conductivity, solderability, and ease of installation.
rewrite: Copper continues to be the dominant electrical conductor across most applications, even amid competition from alternative materials. The primary exception is overhead power transmission, where aluminum is frequently chosen instead. Its uses span power generation, transmission, and distribution, as well as telecommunications, electronics, and numerous electrical devices. Approximately half of all mined copper is dedicated to producing electrical wire and cable, underscoring its critical role for the industry. This market encompasses building wire, communications and power distribution cables, appliance and automotive wiring, and magnet wire. Copper’s enduring preference stems from a host of advantageous properties: high electrical and thermal conductivity, tensile strength, ductility, resistance to creep and corrosion, low thermal expansion, solderability, and straightforward installation.

input: Canada allows nonprofits to be incorporated or unincorporated. Nonprofits may incorporate either federally, under Part II of the Canada Business Corporations Act or under provincial legislation. Many of the governing Acts for Canadian nonprofits date to the early 1900s, meaning that nonprofit legislation has not kept pace with legislation that governs for-profit corporations; particularly with regards to corporate governance. Federal, and in some provinces (such as Ontario), incorporation is by way of Letters Patent, and any change to the Letters Patent (even a simple name change) requires formal approval by the appropriate government, as do by-law changes. Other provinces (such as Alberta) permit incorporation as of right, by the filing of Articles of Incorporation or Articles of Association.
rewrite: In Canada, nonprofits may operate as either incorporated or unincorporated entities. Incorporation can occur federally under Part II of the Canada Business Corporations Act or under various provincial statutes. Much of the governing legislation for these organizations originates from the early 1900s, resulting in nonprofit laws that have not evolved at the same rate as those for for-profit corporations, especially concerning corporate governance. At the federal level and in provinces like Ontario, incorporation is achieved through Letters Patent. Any alteration to these documents, including a simple name change or by-law amendments, must receive formal government approval. Conversely, provinces such as Alberta allow incorporation as a right via the filing of Articles of Incorporation or Association.

input: In addition to the above, Greece is also to start oil and gas exploration in other locations in the Ionian Sea, as well as the Libyan Sea, within the Greek exclusive economic zone, south of Crete. The Ministry of the Environment, Energy and Climate Change announced that there was interest from various countries (including Norway and the United States) in exploration, and the first results regarding the amount of oil and gas in these locations were expected in the summer of 2012. In November 2012, a report published by Deutsche Bank estimated the value of natural gas reserves south of Crete at €427 billion.
rewrite: Greece plans to expand oil and gas exploration to new sites within its exclusive economic zone, specifically in the Ionian and Libyan Seas south of Crete. According to the Ministry of the Environment, Energy and Climate Change, several countries, including Norway and the United States, have shown interest. Initial findings on the reserves were anticipated in summer 2012. Later that year, in November, a Deutsche Bank report valued the natural gas deposits south of Crete at approximately €427 billion.

input: In Canada, there are Affiliate Schools, Colleges, Institutes of Technology/Polytechnic Institutes, and Universities that offer instruction in a variety of programs that can lead to: engineering and applied science degrees, apprenticeship and trade programs, certificates, and diplomas. Affiliate Schools are polytechnic divisions belonging to a national university and offer select technical and engineering programs. Colleges, Institutes of Technology/Polytechnic Institutes, and Universities tend to be independent institutions.
rewrite: Canada's educational institutions include Affiliate Schools, Colleges, Institutes of Technology/Polytechnic Institutes, and Universities. These provide diverse programs leading to engineering degrees, apprenticeships, trade certifications, and diplomas. Affiliate Schools are polytechnic divisions of a national university, offering specific technical and engineering programs. In contrast, Colleges, Institutes of Technology/Polytechnic Institutes, and Universities are generally independent institutions.

input: The Richmond metro area is served by many local television and radio stations. As of 2010[update], the Richmond-Petersburg designated market area (DMA) is the 58th largest in the U.S. with 553,950 homes according to Nielsen Market Research. The major network television affiliates are WTVR-TV 6 (CBS), WRIC-TV 8 (ABC), WWBT 12 (NBC), WRLH-TV 35 (Fox), and WUPV 65 (CW). Public Broadcasting Service stations include WCVE-TV 23 and WCVW 57. There are also a wide variety of radio stations in the Richmond area, catering to many different interests, including news, talk radio, and sports, as well as an eclectic mix of musical interests.
rewrite: The Richmond-Petersburg designated market area (DMA) ranked as the 58th largest in the nation as of 2010, encompassing 553,950 households according to Nielsen Market Research. This metro area is served by numerous local television and radio stations. Key network television affiliates are WTVR-TV 6 (CBS), WRIC-TV 8 (ABC), WWBT 12 (NBC), WRLH-TV 35 (Fox), and WUPV 65 (CW), while WCVE-TV 23 and WCVW 57 provide Public Broadcasting Service. input: Another Alaskan transportation method is the dogsled. In modern times (that is, any time after the mid-late 1920s), dog mushing is more of a sport than a true means of transportation. Various races are held around the state, but the best known is the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race, a 1,150-mile (1,850 km) trail from Anchorage to Nome (although the distance varies from year to year, the official distance is set at 1,049 miles or 1,688 km). The race commemorates the famous 1925 serum run to Nome in which mushers and dogs like Togo and Balto took much-needed medicine to the diphtheria-stricken community of Nome when all other means of transportation had failed. Mushers from all over the world come to Anchorage each March to compete for cash, prizes, and prestige. The "Serum Run" is another sled dog race that more accurately follows the route of the famous 1925 relay, leaving from the community of Nenana (southwest of Fairbanks) to Nome.
rewrite: While dog mushing persists in Alaska, it has largely transitioned from a practical transportation method to a popular sport, particularly since the late 1920s. The most renowned event is the Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race, covering approximately 1,150 miles from Anchorage to Nome, with its official distance set at 1,049 miles. This race honors the historic 1925 serum run to Nome, where mushers and their dogs, including famed canines like Balto and Togo, successfully delivered lifesaving diphtheria medicine after other transport failed. Each March, mushers globally gather in Anchorage to compete for prestige, prizes, and cash. Another significant race, the "Serum Run," more closely retraces the exact 1925 relay route from Nenana, located southwest of Fairbanks, to Nome. Various other sled dog races are also held throughout the state.

input: Digimon was first conceived as a virtual pet toy in the vein of Tamagotchis and, as such, took influence from Tamagotchis' cute and round designs. The small areas of the screens (16 by 16 pixels) meant that character designers had to create monsters whose forms would be easily recognizable. As such, many of the early Digimon—including Tyrannomon, the first one ever created—were based on dinosaurs. Many further designs were created by Kenji Watanabe, who was brought in to help with the "X-Antibody" creatures and art for the Digimon collectible card game. Watanabe was one influenced by American comics, which were beginning to gain popularity in Japan, and as such began to make his characters look stronger and "cool." The character creation process, however, has for most of the franchise's history been collaborative and reliant on conversation and brainstorming.
rewrite: Originally inspired by virtual pets like Tamagotchi, Digimon adopted similarly cute, rounded designs. Due to the limited screen resolution of 16 by 16 pixels, the initial monsters needed easily recognizable forms, leading many early creations such as Tyrannomon to be dinosaur-based. Later, Kenji Watanabe contributed significantly, designing creatures for the "X-Antibody" series and the collectible card game. Influenced by the growing popularity of American comics in Japan, Watanabe aimed for a stronger, "cooler" aesthetic. Throughout most of the franchise's history, though, the character creation process has remained a collaborative effort, built on conversation and brainstorming.

input: China's network security and information technology leadership team was established February 27, 2014. The leadership team is tasked with national security and long-term development and co-ordination of major issues related to network security and information technology. Economic, political, cultural, social and military fields as related to network security and information technology strategy, planning and major macroeconomic policy are being researched. The promotion of national network security and information technology law are constantly under study for enhanced national security capabilities.
rewrite: Established on February 27, 2014, China's network security and information technology leadership team coordinates major issues in this domain for national security and long-term development. It researches strategic planning and major macroeconomic policies tied to economic, political, cultural, social, and military fields. The team also continually studies the promotion of relevant laws to enhance national security capabilities.

input: In 1996, Marvel had some of its titles participate in "Heroes Reborn", a crossover that allowed Marvel to relaunch some of its flagship characters such as the Avengers and the Fantastic Four, and outsource them to the studios of two of the former Marvel artists turned Image Comics founders, Jim Lee and Rob Liefeld. The relaunched titles, which saw the characters transported to a parallel universe with a history distinct from the mainstream Marvel Universe, were a solid success amidst a generally struggling industry, but Marvel discontinued the experiment after a one-year run and returned the characters to the Marvel Universe proper. In 1998, the company launched the imprint Marvel Knights, taking place within Marvel continuity; helmed by soon-to-become editor-in-chief Joe Quesada, it featured tough, gritty stories showcasing such characters as the Inhumans, Black Panther and Daredevil.
rewrite: In 1996, Marvel initiated the "Heroes Reborn" crossover, outsourcing titles like the Avengers and Fantastic Four to studios led by former Marvel artists Jim Lee and Rob Liefeld. This relaunch placed the characters in a parallel universe with a unique history, separate from the mainstream Marvel Universe. Despite a generally struggling industry, these titles proved a solid success. However, Marvel ended the experiment after one year, reintegrating the characters back into their original universe. Later, in 1998, the company introduced the Marvel Knights imprint. Operating within Marvel continuity and guided by future editor-in-chief Joe Quesada, it presented gritty stories focused on characters such as Daredevil, Black Panther, and the Inhumans.

input: In Han government, the emperor was the supreme judge and lawgiver, the commander-in-chief of the armed forces and sole designator of official nominees appointed to the top posts in central and local administrations; those who earned a 600-dan salary-rank or higher. Theoretically, there were no limits to his power. However, state organs with competing interests and institutions such as the court conference (tingyi 廷議)—where ministers were convened to reach majority consensus on an issue—pressured the emperor to accept the advice of his ministers on policy decisions. If the emperor rejected a court conference decision, he risked alienating his high ministers. Nevertheless, emperors sometimes did reject the majority opinion reached at court conferences.
rewrite: Within the Han government, the emperor held ultimate authority as the supreme judge, lawgiver, and commander-in-chief. He exclusively appointed officials to the highest central and local posts, specifically those with a salary-rank of 600 *dan* or above. Theoretically, his power knew no bounds. In practice, however, state organs with competing interests and established institutions like the court conference (*tingyi*) constrained his autonomy. At these conferences, ministers were convened to form a majority consensus on policy issues, pressuring the emperor to accept their advice. Rejecting such a decision risked alienating his top ministers, yet emperors occasionally did override the majority opinion.

input: Bush focused his campaign on national security, presenting himself as a decisive leader and contrasted Kerry as a "flip-flopper." This strategy was designed to convey to American voters the idea that Bush could be trusted to be tough on terrorism while Kerry would be "uncertain in the face of danger." Bush (just as his father did with Dukakis in the 1988 election) also sought to portray Kerry as a "Massachusetts liberal" who was out of touch with mainstream Americans. One of Kerry's slogans was "Stronger at home, respected in the world." This advanced the suggestion that Kerry would pay more attention to domestic concerns; it also encapsulated Kerry's contention that Bush had alienated American allies by his foreign policy.
rewrite: In his campaign, Bush emphasized national security, casting himself as a decisive leader while labeling Kerry a "flip-flopper." This aimed to convince voters that Bush was reliably tough on terrorism, whereas Kerry would be "uncertain in the face of danger." Mirroring his father's 1988 strategy against Dukakis, Bush also depicted Kerry as an out-of-touch "Massachusetts liberal." Kerry’s slogan, "Stronger at home, respected in the world," suggested a greater focus on domestic issues. It also conveyed his argument that Bush's foreign policy had alienated America's allies.

input: Unlike many religions, Buddhism has no single central text that is universally referred to by all traditions. However, some scholars have referred to the Vinaya Pitaka and the first four Nikayas of the Sutta Pitaka as the common core of all Buddhist traditions.[page needed] This could be considered misleading, as Mahāyāna considers these merely a preliminary, and not a core, teaching. The Tibetan Buddhists have not even translated most of the āgamas (though theoretically they recognize them) and they play no part in the religious life of either clergy or laity in China and Japan. Other scholars say there is no universally accepted common core. The size and complexity of the Buddhist canons have been seen by some (including Buddhist social reformer Babasaheb Ambedkar) as presenting barriers to the wider understanding of Buddhist philosophy.
rewrite: Buddhism lacks a single central text universally embraced across all traditions, unlike many other religions. While some scholars point to the Vinaya Pitaka and the first four Nikayas of the Sutta Pitaka as a shared foundation, this view is contested. Mahāyāna traditions, for instance, regard these texts as preliminary rather than core. Furthermore, in regions like China and Japan, the āgamas—though theoretically acknowledged—are largely untranslated in Tibetan Buddhism and hold no practical role in religious practice for clergy or laity. Consequently, many scholars argue no common core is universally accepted. The sheer size and complexity of the Buddhist canons are also viewed, notably by figures like reformer Babasaheb Ambedkar, as obstacles to broader comprehension of Buddhist philosophy.

input: Another format, rhythmic AC, in addition to playing all the popular hot and soft AC music, past and present, places a heavy emphasis on disco as well as 1980s and 1990s dance hits, such as those by Amber, C&C Music Factory and Black Box, and includes dance remixes of pop songs, such as the Soul Solution mix of Toni Braxton's "Unbreak My Heart".

input: All of the executions which have taken place since the 1936 hanging of Bethea in Owensboro have been conducted within a wall or enclosure. For example, Fred Adams was legally hanged in Kennett, Missouri, on April 2, 1937, within a 10-foot (3 m) wooden stockade. Roscoe "Red" Jackson was hanged within a stockade in Galena, Missouri, on May 26, 1937. Two Kentucky hangings were conducted after Galena in which numerous persons were present within a wooden stockade, that of John "Peter" Montjoy in Covington, Kentucky on December 17, 1937, and that of Harold Van Venison in Covington on June 3, 1938. An estimated 400 witnesses were present for the hanging of Lee Simpson in Ryegate, Montana, on December 30, 1939. The execution of Timothy McVeigh on June 11, 2001 was witnessed by some 300 people, some by closed-circuit television.
rewrite: Since the 1936 hanging of Bethea in Owensboro, all executions have occurred within a walled or enclosed space. A 10-foot wooden stockade was used for the legal hanging of Fred Adams in Kennett, Missouri, on April 2, 1937. Similarly, Roscoe "Red" Jackson was executed inside a stockade in Galena, Missouri, on May 26, 1937. Subsequent Kentucky hangings also employed wooden stockades that contained numerous witnesses. These included John "Peter" Montjoy in Covington on December 17, 1937, and Harold Van Venison in the same city on June 3, 1938. Later, an estimated 400 people witnessed the hanging of Lee Simpson in Ryegate, Montana, on December 30, 1939. More recently, the execution of Timothy McVeigh on June 11, 2001, was observed by some 300 individuals, with certain witnesses viewing via closed-circuit television.
