input: Of the remaining land area, the state of Alaska owns 101 million acres (41 million hectares), its entitlement under the Alaska Statehood Act. A portion of that acreage is occasionally ceded to organized boroughs, under the statutory provisions pertaining to newly formed boroughs. Smaller portions are set aside for rural subdivisions and other homesteading-related opportunities. These are not very popular due to the often remote and roadless locations. The University of Alaska, as a land grant university, also owns substantial acreage which it manages independently.
rewrite: Alaska holds 101 million acres (41 million hectares) under the Alaska Statehood Act. From this, some land is transferred to organized boroughs as they form, while smaller parcels are allocated for rural subdivisions and homesteading. These latter offerings attract limited interest because they are frequently remote and inaccessible by road. Additionally, the University of Alaska, as a land grant institution, independently manages its own substantial land holdings.

input: By 1640, the town's theocratic government and nine-square grid plan were in place, and the town was renamed Newhaven from Quinnipiac. However, the area north of New Haven remained Quinnipiac until 1678, when it was renamed Hamden. The settlement became the headquarters of the New Haven Colony. At the time, the New Haven Colony was separate from the Connecticut Colony, which had been established to the north centering on Hartford. One of the principal differences between the two colonies was that the New Haven colony was an intolerant theocracy that did not permit other churches to be established, while the Connecticut colony permitted the establishment of other churches.
rewrite: By 1640, Quinnipiac had been renamed Newhaven, establishing its theocratic government and distinctive nine-square grid layout. The area north of the settlement retained the Quinnipiac name until 1678, when it became Hamden. New Haven served as the headquarters of the New Haven Colony, a separate entity from the Connecticut Colony centered on Hartford. A key distinction was religious tolerance: the New Haven Colony was an intolerant theocracy forbidding other churches, whereas the Connecticut Colony permitted their establishment.

input: The institutions and practices of canon law paralleled the legal development of much of Europe, and consequently both modern civil law and common law (legal system) bear the influences of canon law. Edson Luiz Sampel, a Brazilian expert in canon law, says that canon law is contained in the genesis of various institutes of civil law, such as the law in continental Europe and Latin American countries. Sampel explains that canon law has significant influence in contemporary society.
rewrite: The development of canon law closely mirrored Europe's broader legal evolution, leaving its mark on both modern civil and common law systems. According to Brazilian expert Edson Luiz Sampel, canon law forms the foundation for many civil law institutes, particularly in continental Europe and Latin America. He further emphasizes that its influence remains substantial in contemporary society.

input: Broadly speaking, Enlightenment science greatly valued empiricism and rational thought, and was embedded with the Enlightenment ideal of advancement and progress. The study of science, under the heading of natural philosophy, was divided into physics and a conglomerate grouping of chemistry and natural history, which included anatomy, biology, geology, mineralogy, and zoology. As with most Enlightenment views, the benefits of science were not seen universally; Rousseau criticized the sciences for distancing man from nature and not operating to make people happier. Science during the Enlightenment was dominated by scientific societies and academies, which had largely replaced universities as centres of scientific research and development. Societies and academies were also the backbone of the maturation of the scientific profession. Another important development was the popularization of science among an increasingly literate population. Philosophes introduced the public to many scientific theories, most notably through the Encyclopédie and the popularization of Newtonianism by Voltaire and Émilie du Châtelet. Some historians have marked the 18th century as a drab period in the history of science; however, the century saw significant advancements in the practice of medicine, mathematics, and physics; the development of biological taxonomy; a new understanding of magnetism and electricity; and the maturation of chemistry as a discipline, which established the foundations of modern chemistry.
rewrite:
The Enlightenment era framed science within the ideal of progress, emphasizing empiricism and rational thought. Scientific inquiry, known as natural philosophy, was categorized primarily into physics and a combined field of chemistry and natural history—the latter encompassing anatomy, biology, geology, mineralogy, and zoology. Dominating this period were scientific societies and academies, which supplanted universities as the principal centers for research and development, forming the core of the growing scientific profession. Concurrently, science was popularized among a more literate public. Philosophes like Voltaire and Émilie du Châtelet spread Newtonianism widely, while works such as the *Encyclopédie* introduced various theories to a broad audience.

However, Enlightenment views on science were not universally positive; figures like Rousseau criticized it for alienating humanity from nature and failing to enhance happiness. Despite some historians characterizing the 18th century as unremarkable for science, it in fact witnessed substantial progress. Key advances occurred in medicine, mathematics, and physics. The period also saw the development of biological taxonomy, groundbreaking insights into magnetism and electricity, and the maturation of chemistry into a discipline that laid the groundwork for its modern form.

input: Hospitals in Liberia include the John F. Kennedy Medical Center in Monrovia and several others. Life expectancy in Liberia is estimated to be 57.4 years in 2012. With a fertility rate of 5.9 births per woman, the maternal mortality rate stood at 990 per 100,000 births in 2010. A number of highly communicable diseases are widespread, including tuberculosis, diarrheal diseases and malaria. In 2007, the HIV infection rates stood at 2% of the population aged 15–49  whereas the incidence of tuberculosis was 420 per 100,000 people in 2008. Approximately 58.2% – 66% of women are estimated to have undergone female genital mutilation.
rewrite: Liberia's life expectancy was estimated at 57.4 years in 2012. The country faces significant public health challenges, including widespread communicable diseases such as tuberculosis, diarrheal diseases, and malaria. In 2007, HIV infection rates were 2% among people aged 15–49, while tuberculosis incidence reached 420 per 100,000 people in 2008. With a fertility rate of 5.9 births per woman, the 2010 maternal mortality rate was high at 990 per 100,000 births. An estimated 58.2% to 66% of women have undergone female genital mutilation. Healthcare facilities include the John F. Kennedy Medical Center in Monrovia and several other hospitals.

input: On July 8, 2007 The Washington Post published excerpts from UCLA Professor Amy Zegart's book Spying Blind: The CIA, the FBI, and the Origins of 9/11. The Post reported from Zegart's book that government documents show the CIA and FBI missed 23 potential chances to disrupt the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. The primary reasons for the failures included: agency cultures resistant to change and new ideas; inappropriate incentives for promotion; and a lack of cooperation between the FBI, CIA and the rest of the United States Intelligence Community. The book blamed the FBI's decentralized structure, which prevented effective communication and cooperation among different FBI offices. The book suggested that the FBI has not evolved into an effective counter-terrorism or counter-intelligence agency, due in large part to deeply ingrained agency cultural resistance to change. For example, FBI personnel practices continue to treat all staff other than special agents as support staff, classifying intelligence analysts alongside the FBI's auto mechanics and janitors.
rewrite: According to Professor Amy Zegart’s book *Spying Blind: The CIA, the FBI, and the Origins of 9/11*, government documents reveal that intelligence agencies missed 23 potential opportunities to disrupt the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks. The Washington Post published excerpts from this work on July 8, 2007. Zegart identifies several core failures: a deep-seated cultural resistance to change and new ideas within the agencies, promotion incentives that were misaligned with security priorities, and a critical lack of cooperation between the FBI, CIA, and the broader U.S. Intelligence Community. The book particularly criticizes the FBI’s decentralized structure for hampering communication and coordination among its own offices. This structure, combined with an ingrained cultural aversion to evolution, has prevented the FBI from becoming an effective counter-terrorism or counter-intelligence agency. A telling example is the FBI’s personnel system, which continues to classify intelligence analysts as mere support staff, grouping them with auto mechanics and janitors.

input: Zhu Yousong, however, fared a lot worse than his ancestor Zhu Yuanzhang three centuries earlier. Beset by factional conflicts, his regime could not offer effective resistance to Qing forces, when the Qing army, led by the Manchu prince Dodo approached Jiangnan the next spring. Days after Yangzhou fell to the Manchus in late May 1645, the Hongguang Emperor fled Nanjing, and the imperial Ming Palace was looted by local residents. On June 6, Dodo's troops approached Nanjing, and the commander of the city's garrison, Zhao the Earl of Xincheng, promptly surrendered the city to them. The Manchus soon ordered all male residents of the city to shave their heads in the Manchu queue way. They requisitioned a large section of the city for the bannermen's cantonment, and destroyed the former imperial Ming Palace, but otherwise the city was spared the mass murders and destruction that befell Yangzhou.
rewrite: Three centuries after his ancestor Zhu Yuanzhang, Zhu Yousong met a far grimmer fate. His regime, weakened by internal strife, proved incapable of mounting an effective defense against the Qing. When Manchu forces under Prince Dodo advanced toward Jiangnan in the spring of 1645, collapse followed swiftly. Shortly after the fall of Yangzhou to the Manchus in late May, the Hongguang Emperor fled Nanjing, and the imperial Ming Palace was plundered by locals. By June 6, Dodo’s army reached Nanjing, where the garrison commander, Zhao the Earl of Xincheng, surrendered the city without resistance. The Manchus mandated that all male residents adopt the Manchu queue hairstyle. They allocated a large urban sector for bannermen and razed the former Ming Palace, yet avoided the widespread slaughter and devastation inflicted upon Yangzhou.

input: The Princess Margaret Hospital on Funafuti is the only hospital in Tuvalu. The Tuvaluan medical staff at PMH in 2011 comprised the Director of Health & Surgeon, the Chief Medical Officer Public Health, an anaesthetist, a paediatric medical officer and an obstetrics and gynaecology medical officer. Allied health staff include two radiographers, two pharmacists, three laboratory technicians, two dieticians and 13 nurses with specialised training in fields including surgical nursing, anaesthesia nursing/ICU, paediatric nursing and midwifery. PMH also employs a dentist. The Department of Health also employs nine or ten nurses on the outer islands to provide general nursing and midwifery services.
rewrite: Funafuti’s Princess Margaret Hospital (PMH) is Tuvalu’s sole hospital. In 2011, its Tuvaluan medical team included the Director of Health & Surgeon, the Chief Medical Officer Public Health, and officers for anaesthesia, paediatrics, and obstetrics and gynaecology. Supporting allied health staff consisted of two radiographers, two pharmacists, three laboratory technicians, two dieticians, and 13 specially trained nurses in areas like surgery, anaesthesia/ICU, paediatrics, and midwifery. A dentist is also employed at PMH. Additionally, the Department of Health stations nine or ten nurses on the outer islands to deliver general nursing and midwifery care.

input: By the late 2000s, Dell's "configure to order" approach of manufacturing—delivering individual PCs configured to customer specifications from its US facilities was no longer as efficient or competitive with high-volume Asian contract manufacturers as PCs became powerful low-cost commodities. Dell closed plants that produced desktop computers for the North American market, including the Mort Topfer Manufacturing Center in Austin, Texas (original location) and Lebanon, Tennessee (opened in 1999) in 2008 and early 2009, respectively. The desktop production plant in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, received US$280 million in incentives from the state and opened in 2005, but ceased operations in November 2010. Dell's contract with the state required them to repay the incentives for failing to meet the conditions, and they sold the North Carolina plant to Herbalife. Most of the work that used to take place in Dell's U.S. plants was transferred to contract manufacturers in Asia and Mexico, or some of Dell's own factories overseas. The Miami, Florida, facility of its Alienware subsidiary remains in operation, while Dell continues to produce its servers (its most profitable products) in Austin, Texas. On January 8, 2009, Dell announced the closure of its manufacturing plant in Limerick, Ireland, with the loss of 1,900 jobs and the transfer of production to its plant in Łodź in Poland.
rewrite: By the late 2000s, as PCs transformed into powerful, low-cost commodities, Dell’s “configure to order” model—building individual computers to customer specifications at U.S. facilities—grew less efficient and competitive against high-volume Asian contract manufacturers. This led to a series of plant closures. In 2008 and early 2009, Dell shuttered facilities producing desktops for North America, namely the Mort Topfer Manufacturing Center in Austin, Texas (its original site) and a location in Lebanon, Tennessee, opened in 1999. Another desktop plant in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, which had opened in 2005 with $280 million in state incentives, ceased operations in November 2010. For failing to meet its conditions, Dell was required to repay those incentives and later sold the plant to Herbalife. Production from these U.S. sites was largely shifted to contract manufacturers in Asia and Mexico, or to some of Dell’s own overseas factories. Nonetheless, Dell continues server production—its most profitable line—in Austin, Texas, and its Alienware subsidiary’s facility in Miami, Florida, remains operational. Further reflecting this global shift, on January 8, 2009, Dell announced the closure of its Limerick, Ireland, manufacturing plant, eliminating 1,900 jobs and moving that production to its facility in Łódź, Poland.

input: President Franklin D. Roosevelt promoted a "good neighbor" policy that sought better relations with Mexico. In 1935 a federal judge ruled that three Mexican immigrants were ineligible for citizenship because they were not white, as required by federal law. Mexico protested, and Roosevelt decided to circumvent the decision and make sure the federal government treated Hispanics as white. The State Department, the Census Bureau, the Labor Department, and other government agencies therefore made sure to uniformly classify people of Mexican descent as white. This policy encouraged the League of United Latin American Citizens in its quest to minimize discrimination by asserting their whiteness.
rewrite: In 1935, a federal judge declared three Mexican immigrants ineligible for citizenship, citing their non-white status under existing law. This ruling drew protest from Mexico. In response, President Franklin D. Roosevelt, who advocated a "good neighbor" policy for improved relations with that country, moved to circumvent the decision. He ensured the federal government would treat Hispanics as white. Agencies like the State Department, Census Bureau, and Labor Department subsequently adopted a uniform classification of people of Mexican descent as white. This stance empowered the League of United Latin American Citizens in its fight against discrimination by asserting their whiteness.

input: During the Cold War, the Asian power of Japan and the European powers of the United Kingdom, France, and West Germany rebuilt their economies. France and the United Kingdom maintained technologically advanced armed forces with power projection capabilities and maintain large defence budgets to this day. Yet, as the Cold War continued, authorities began to question if France and the United Kingdom could retain their long-held statuses as great powers. China, with the world's largest population, has slowly risen to great power status, with large growth in economic and military power in the post-war period. After 1949, the Republic of China began to lose its recognition as the sole legitimate government of China by the other great powers, in favour of the People's Republic of China. Subsequently, in 1971, it lost its permanent seat at the UN Security Council to the People's Republic of China.
rewrite: In the post-war era, Japan in Asia and the United Kingdom, France, and West Germany in Europe rebuilt their economies. Despite maintaining advanced armed forces with power projection capabilities and substantial defense budgets—a practice continuing today—France and the United Kingdom faced growing doubts during the Cold War about their ability to retain traditional great power status. Meanwhile, China, possessing the world's largest population, gradually ascended as a great power through significant economic and military growth. Following 1949, the Republic of China saw its recognition as the sole legitimate government of China diminish among other major powers in favor of the People's Republic of China. This shift culminated in 1971 when the People's Republic of China assumed the permanent UN Security Council seat previously held by the Republic of China.

input: Hayek was concerned about the general view in Britain's academia that fascism was a capitalist reaction to socialism and The Road to Serfdom arose from those concerns. It was written between 1940 and 1943. The title was inspired by the French classical liberal thinker Alexis de Tocqueville's writings on the "road to servitude." It was first published in Britain by Routledge in March 1944 and was quite popular, leading Hayek to call it "that unobtainable book," also due in part to wartime paper rationing. When it was published in the United States by the University of Chicago in September of that year, it achieved greater popularity than in Britain. At the arrangement of editor Max Eastman, the American magazine Reader's Digest also published an abridged version in April 1945, enabling The Road to Serfdom to reach a far wider audience than academics. The book is widely popular among those advocating individualism and classical liberalism.
rewrite: The Road to Serfdom was written by Hayek between 1940 and 1943. His work emerged from a concern with the prevailing academic opinion in Britain, which viewed fascism as a capitalist response to socialism. The book’s title drew inspiration from the writings of French classical liberal thinker Alexis de Tocqueville on the “road to servitude.” First published in Britain by Routledge in March 1944, it proved quite popular. Wartime paper rationing contributed to shortages, leading Hayek to call it “that unobtainable book.” Its American publication by the University of Chicago in September that year saw it achieve even greater popularity than in Britain. An abridged version appeared in the American magazine Reader’s Digest in April 1945, arranged by editor Max Eastman, which allowed the book to reach a far wider audience beyond academics. It remains widely popular with advocates of individualism and classical liberalism.

input: Physically, clothing serves many purposes: it can serve as protection from the elements, and can enhance safety during hazardous activities such as hiking and cooking. It protects the wearer from rough surfaces, rash-causing plants, insect bites, splinters, thorns and prickles by providing a barrier between the skin and the environment. Clothes can insulate against cold or hot conditions. Further, they can provide a hygienic barrier, keeping infectious and toxic materials away from the body. Clothing also provides protection from harmful UV radiation.
rewrite: Clothing offers physical protection in numerous ways. It acts as a barrier against environmental hazards like rough surfaces, irritating plants, and insect bites. Garments insulate the body from both cold and heat, while also providing a hygienic shield from infectious or toxic substances. Furthermore, they enhance safety during activities like hiking and cooking and offer protection from the sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.

input: Whereas most Christians believe the gibbet on which Jesus was executed was the traditional two-beamed cross, the Jehovah's Witnesses hold the view that a single upright stake was used. The Greek and Latin words used in the earliest Christian writings are ambiguous. The Koine Greek terms used in the New Testament are stauros (σταυρός) and xylon (ξύλον). The latter means wood (a live tree, timber or an object constructed of wood); in earlier forms of Greek, the former term meant an upright stake or pole, but in Koine Greek it was used also to mean a cross. The Latin word crux was also applied to objects other than a cross.
rewrite: Most Christians accept that Jesus died on a conventional two-beamed cross, but Jehovah’s Witnesses maintain he was executed on a simple upright stake. The earliest Christian texts employ ambiguous terms. In the New Testament, the Koine Greek word *stauros* could denote either an upright stake or a cross, while *xylon* broadly means “wood”—a living tree, timber, or a wooden object. Similarly, the Latin *crux* was used for various structures, not exclusively a cross. This linguistic flexibility leaves the precise form open to interpretation.

input: Required attendance at school is 10 years for males and 11 years for females (2001). The adult literacy rate is 99.0% (2002). In 2010, there were 1,918 students who were taught by 109 teachers (98 certified and 11 uncertified). The teacher-pupil ratio for primary schools in Tuvalu is around 1:18 for all schools with the exception of Nauti School, which has a teacher-student ratio of 1:27. Nauti School on Funafuti is the largest primary in Tuvalu with more than 900 students (45 percent of the total primary school enrolment). The pupil-teacher ratio for Tuvalu is low compared to the Pacific region (ratio of 1:29).
rewrite: Compulsory education spans 10 years for males and 11 for females (2001). The adult literacy rate reached 99.0% by 2002. In primary schools across Tuvalu, the teacher-pupil ratio is approximately 1:18, though Nauti School on Funafuti has a higher ratio of 1:27. This school is the nation's largest primary, enrolling over 900 students, or 45 percent of total primary pupils. Overall, Tuvalu's pupil-teacher ratio is favorable compared to the Pacific regional average of 1:29. In 2010, there were 1,918 students instructed by 109 teachers, of whom 98 were certified and 11 were not.

input: The physical relief of the island is dominated by two mountain ranges, the Troodos Mountains and the smaller Kyrenia Range, and the central plain they encompass, the Mesaoria. The Mesaoria plain is drained by the Pedieos River, the longest on the island. The Troodos Mountains cover most of the southern and western portions of the island and account for roughly half its area. The highest point on Cyprus is Mount Olympus at 1,952 m (6,404 ft), located in the centre of the Troodos range. The narrow Kyrenia Range, extending along the northern coastline, occupies substantially less area, and elevations are lower, reaching a maximum of 1,024 m (3,360 ft). The island lies within the Anatolian Plate.
rewrite: Cyprus is characterized by two main mountain ranges and the central Mesaoria plain between them. The Troodos Mountains, covering much of the south and west, comprise about half the island's area. At their center lies Mount Olympus, the highest peak at 1,952 meters. The smaller, narrower Kyrenia Range stretches along the northern coast, with lower elevations reaching up to 1,024 meters. The Mesaoria plain, situated between these ranges, is drained by the island's longest river, the Pedieos. Geologically, Cyprus is part of the Anatolian Plate.

input: Many pesticides can be grouped into chemical families. Prominent insecticide families include organochlorines, organophosphates, and carbamates. Organochlorine hydrocarbons (e.g., DDT) could be separated into dichlorodiphenylethanes, cyclodiene compounds, and other related compounds. They operate by disrupting the sodium/potassium balance of the nerve fiber, forcing the nerve to transmit continuously. Their toxicities vary greatly, but they have been phased out because of their persistence and potential to bioaccumulate.:239–240 Organophosphate and carbamates largely replaced organochlorines. Both operate through inhibiting the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, allowing acetylcholine to transfer nerve impulses indefinitely and causing a variety of symptoms such as weakness or paralysis. Organophosphates are quite toxic to vertebrates, and have in some cases been replaced by less toxic carbamates.:136–137 Thiocarbamate and dithiocarbamates are subclasses of carbamates. Prominent families of herbicides include phenoxy and benzoic acid herbicides (e.g. 2,4-D), triazines (e.g., atrazine), ureas (e.g., diuron), and Chloroacetanilides (e.g., alachlor). Phenoxy compounds tend to selectively kill broad-leaf weeds rather than grasses. The phenoxy and benzoic acid herbicides function similar to plant growth hormones, and grow cells without normal cell division, crushing the plant's nutrient transport system.:300 Triazines interfere with photosynthesis.:335 Many commonly used pesticides are not included in these families, including glyphosate.
rewrite:
Pesticides are frequently categorized into distinct chemical families. Among insecticides, prominent groups are organochlorines, organophosphates, and carbamates. Organochlorine hydrocarbons, such as DDT, comprise dichlorodiphenylethanes, cyclodiene compounds, and similar substances. They function by disrupting the nerve fiber's sodium/potassium balance, causing continuous nerve transmission. Although their toxicities vary, these persistent, bioaccumulating compounds have been largely phased out. Their replacements, organophosphates and carbamates, primarily act by inhibiting the enzyme acetylcholinesterase. This inhibition allows acetylcholine to perpetuate nerve impulses indefinitely, leading to symptoms like weakness or paralysis. While organophosphates are often highly toxic to vertebrates, the generally less toxic carbamates have sometimes superseded them. Notably, thiocarbamates and dithiocarbamates are important subclasses of carbamates.

In herbicides, major families include phenoxy and benzoic acid herbicides (e.g., 2,4-D), triazines (e.g., atrazine), ureas (e.g., diuron), and Chloroacetanilides (e.g., alachlor). Phenoxy compounds often selectively target broad-leaf weeds over grasses. Mimicking plant growth hormones, phenoxy and benzoic acid herbicides induce abnormal cell growth without division, ultimately crushing the plant's nutrient transport system. Triazines, by contrast, operate by interfering with photosynthesis. It is important to note that many widely used pesticides, such as glyphosate, fall outside these established families.

input: The state united behind the Plan of Ayutla and ratified the new constitution in 1855. The state was able to survive through the Reform War with minimal damage due to the large number of liberal political figures. The 1858 conservative movement did not succeed in the state even after the successful military campaign of the conservative Zuloaga with 1,000 men occupied the cities of Chihuahua and Parral. In August 1859, Zuloaga and his forces were defeated by the liberal Orozco and his forces; Orozco soon after deposed the state governor, but had to flee to Durango two months later. In the late 1860s the conservative General Cajen briefly entered the state after his campaign through the state of Jalisco and helped establish conservative politicians and ran out the liberal leaders Jesús González Ortega and José María Patoni. Cajen took possession of the state capital and established himself as governor; he brooked no delay in uniting a large force to combat the liberal forces which he defeated in La Batalla del Gallo. Cajen attained several advantages over the liberals within the state, but soon lost his standing due to a strong resurgence of the liberal forces within the state. The successful liberal leaders José María Patoni of Durango and J.E. Muñoz of Chihuahua quickly strengthened their standing by limiting the political rights of the clergy implementing the presidential decree. The state elected General Luis Terrazas, a liberal leader, as governor; he would continue to fight small battles within the state to suppress conservative uprisings during 1861.
rewrite:
Following the adoption of the Plan of Ayutla, the state ratified the new constitution in 1855. Its survival through the Reform War with minimal damage was aided by its strong contingent of liberal political figures. Even the 1858 conservative movement failed to gain a lasting foothold, despite a successful military campaign by conservative commander Zuloaga, who occupied Chihuahua and Parral with a thousand men. By August 1859, Zuloaga’s forces were defeated by the liberal leader Orozco, who subsequently deposed the state governor. Orozco’s control was brief, however, forcing him to flee to Durango just two months later.

In the late 1860s, conservative General Cajen entered the state after campaigning in Jalisco, expelling liberal leaders Jesús González Ortega and José María Patoni and installing conservative politicians. Seizing the state capital, Cajen declared himself governor and swiftly assembled a large force. He defeated liberal troops at La Batalla del Gallo, securing several advantages. Yet his standing quickly eroded due to a powerful resurgence of liberal forces within the state.

Liberal leaders José María Patoni of Durango and J.E. Muñoz of Chihuahua swiftly consolidated power by enforcing a presidential decree that curtailed the political rights of the clergy. The state then elected liberal General Luis Terrazas as governor. Throughout 1861, Terrazas continued to engage in smaller battles to suppress conservative uprisings across the state.

input: Another example of the persecution of heretics under Protestant rule was the execution of the Boston martyrs in 1659, 1660, and 1661. These executions resulted from the actions of the Anglican Puritans, who at that time wielded political as well as ecclesiastic control in the Massachusetts Bay Colony. At the time, the colony leaders were apparently hoping to achieve their vision of a "purer absolute theocracy" within their colony .[citation needed] As such, they perceived the teachings and practices of the rival Quaker sect as heretical, even to the point where laws were passed and executions were performed with the aim of ridding their colony of such perceived "heresies".[citation needed] It should be noticed that the Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox communions generally regard the Puritans themselves as having been heterodox or heretical.
rewrite: Under Anglican Puritan control in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, the Boston martyrs were executed in 1659, 1660, and 1661, illustrating another case of heretic persecution under Protestant rule. Colony leaders, seeking to establish a "purer absolute theocracy," viewed the rival Quaker sect as heretical. Consequently, they enacted laws and carried out executions to purge these perceived "heresies" from their settlement. Notably, the Puritans themselves are generally considered heterodox or heretical by both Eastern Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox communions. This episode stemmed from the Puritans' combined political and ecclesiastic authority at the time.

input: The approaching era of jet travel, and a series of midair collisions (most notable was the 1956 Grand Canyon mid-air collision), prompted passage of the Federal Aviation Act of 1958. This legislation gave the CAA's functions to a new independent body, the Federal Aviation Agency. The act transferred air safety regulation from the CAB to the new FAA, and also gave the FAA sole responsibility for a common civil-military system of air navigation and air traffic control. The FAA's first administrator, Elwood R. Quesada, was a former Air Force general and adviser to President Eisenhower.
rewrite: The Federal Aviation Act of 1958 was spurred by the dawn of the jet age and several midair collisions, most notably the 1956 Grand Canyon disaster. It established the new, independent Federal Aviation Agency (FAA). The law shifted air safety regulation from the Civil Aeronautics Board (CAB) to the FAA and granted it exclusive control over a unified civil-military system for air navigation and traffic control. Its first leader was Elwood R. Quesada, a former Air Force general and adviser to President Eisenhower.

input: Boston's early European settlers had first called the area Trimountaine (after its "three mountains"—only traces of which remain today) but later renamed it Boston after Boston, Lincolnshire, England, the origin of several prominent colonists. The renaming, on September 7, 1630 (Old Style),[b] was by Puritan colonists from England, who had moved over from Charlestown earlier that year in quest of fresh water. Their settlement was initially limited to the Shawmut Peninsula, at that time surrounded by the Massachusetts Bay and Charles River and connected to the mainland by a narrow isthmus. The peninsula is known to have been inhabited as early as 5000 BC.
rewrite: Originally inhabited as early as 5000 BC, the Shawmut Peninsula was later settled by Puritan colonists. These colonists, seeking fresh water, had moved from Charlestown earlier in 1630. On September 7 of that year, they renamed the area Boston, after Boston in Lincolnshire, England, which was the hometown of several leading colonists. This replaced the earlier name Trimountaine, a reference to the area's "three mountains," of which little evidence remains today. Their initial settlement was confined to this peninsula, then surrounded by the Massachusetts Bay and Charles River and linked to the mainland only by a narrow isthmus.

input: When the Xbox 360 was released, Microsoft's online gaming service Xbox Live was shut down for 24 hours and underwent a major upgrade, adding a basic non-subscription service called Xbox Live Silver (later renamed Xbox Live Free) to its already established premium subscription-based service (which was renamed Gold). Xbox Live Free is included with all SKUs of the console. It allows users to create a user profile, join on message boards, and access Microsoft's Xbox Live Arcade and Marketplace and talk to other members. A Live Free account does not generally support multiplayer gaming; however, some games that have rather limited online functions already, (such as Viva Piñata) or games that feature their own subscription service (e.g. EA Sports games) can be played with a Free account. Xbox Live also supports voice the latter a feature possible with the Xbox Live Vision.
rewrite: Upon the launch of the Xbox 360, Microsoft’s Xbox Live service was temporarily taken offline for a day to implement a significant update. This overhaul introduced a new, non-subscription tier called Xbox Live Silver—later rebranded as Xbox Live Free—alongside the existing premium option, which was renamed Gold. Included with every console model, the Free tier enables users to set up a profile, participate in message boards, communicate with others, and visit the Xbox Live Arcade and Marketplace. While multiplayer gaming typically requires a Gold subscription, certain titles with minimal online features, like Viva Piñata, or games operating their own subscription services, such as some EA Sports offerings, are accessible with a Free account. Additionally, Xbox Live supports voice communication, a capability enhanced by the Xbox Live Vision accessory.

input: The Eastern Roman Empire – today conventionally named the Byzantine Empire, a name not in use during its own time – became increasingly influenced by Greek culture after the 7th century, when Emperor Heraclius (AD 575 - 641) decided to make Greek the empire's official language. Certainly from then on, but likely earlier, the Roman and Greek cultures were virtually fused into a single Greco-Roman world. Although the Latin West recognized the Eastern Empire's claim to the Roman legacy for several centuries, after Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne, king of the Franks, as the "Roman Emperor" on 25 December 800, an act which eventually led to the formation of the Holy Roman Empire, the Latin West started to favour the Franks and began to refer to the Eastern Roman Empire largely as the Empire of the Greeks (Imperium Graecorum).
rewrite: Following the 7th century, the Eastern Roman Empire—retrospectively called the Byzantine Empire—underwent a profound cultural shift. Emperor Heraclius (AD 575-641) established Greek as the official language, cementing a fusion of Roman and Greek traditions into a singular Greco-Roman civilization. For centuries, the Latin West had acknowledged the Eastern Empire as the legitimate heir to Rome. This recognition changed, however, after Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne as “Roman Emperor” on Christmas Day, 800. That pivotal act, which paved the way for the Holy Roman Empire, shifted Western allegiance toward the Franks. Consequently, the Latin West increasingly referred to the Eastern realm not as Roman, but as the Empire of the Greeks (Imperium Graecorum).

input: Allied submarines did not adopt a defensive posture and wait for the enemy to attack. Within hours after the Pearl Harbor attack, in retribution against Japan, Roosevelt promulgated a new doctrine: unrestricted submarine warfare against Japan. This meant sinking any warship, commercial vessel, or passenger ship in Axis-controlled waters, without warning and without help to survivors.[nb 13] At the outbreak of the war in the Pacific the Dutch Admiral in charge of the naval defense of the East Indies, Conrad Helfrich, gave instructions to wage war aggressively. His small force of submarines sank more Japanese ships in the first weeks of the war than the entire British and US navies together, an exploit which earned him the nickname "Ship-a-day Helfrich". The Dutch force were in fact the first to sink an enemy warship; On 24 December 1941, HNLMS K XVI torpedoed and sank the Japanese destroyer Sagiri.
rewrite: In retribution for the Pearl Harbor attack, President Roosevelt swiftly enacted a new doctrine of unrestricted submarine warfare against Japan. This policy mandated the sinking of any Axis vessel—warship, commercial, or passenger—in enemy waters, without warning or aid to survivors. Consequently, Allied submarines moved immediately to the offensive rather than adopting a defensive stance. In the Pacific, Dutch Admiral Conrad Helfrich, commanding the East Indies' naval defense, ordered aggressive action. His modest submarine fleet achieved remarkable early success, sinking more Japanese ships in the initial weeks than the combined British and US navies, earning him the nickname "Ship-a-day Helfrich." Notably, the Dutch were first to sink an enemy warship when HNLMS K XVI torpedoed and sank the Japanese destroyer Sagiri on 24 December 1941.

input: In 1368, a Han Chinese revolt known as the Red Turban Rebellion toppled the Mongol Yuan dynasty in China. Zhu Yuanzhang then established the Ming dynasty, ruling as the Hongwu Emperor (r. 1368–1398). It is not clear how much the early Ming court understood the civil war going on in Tibet between rival religious sects, but the first emperor was anxious to avoid the same trouble that Tibet had caused for the Tang dynasty. Instead of recognizing the Phagmodru ruler, the Hongwu Emperor sided with the Karmapa of the nearer Kham region and southeastern Tibet, sending envoys out in the winter of 1372–1373 to ask the Yuan officeholders to renew their titles for the new Ming court.
rewrite: The Red Turban Rebellion, a Han Chinese revolt, ended Mongol Yuan rule in China in 1368. Its leader, Zhu Yuanzhang, founded the Ming dynasty, becoming the Hongwu Emperor (r. 1368–1398). While the early Ming court's awareness of Tibet's internal sectarian conflict is uncertain, Hongwu was determined to prevent the region from becoming a problem as it had for the Tang dynasty. Rather than acknowledging the Phagmodru ruler, he supported the Karmapa in the closer Kham and southeastern Tibet. During the winter of 1372–1373, the emperor dispatched envoys to request that former Yuan officials renew their titles under Ming authority.

input: Maria Deraismes was initiated into Freemasonry in 1882, then resigned to allow her lodge to rejoin their Grand Lodge. Having failed to achieve acceptance from any masonic governing body, she and Georges Martin started a mixed masonic lodge that actually worked masonic ritual. Annie Besant spread the phenomenon to the English speaking world. Disagreements over ritual led to the formation of exclusively female bodies of Freemasons in England, which spread to other countries. Meanwhile, the French had re-invented Adoption as an all-female lodge in 1901, only to cast it aside again in 1935. The lodges, however, continued to meet, which gave rise, in 1959, to a body of women practising continental Freemasonry.
rewrite: In 1882, Maria Deraismes was initiated into Freemasonry, though she later resigned so her lodge could rejoin their Grand Lodge. After finding no acceptance from existing masonic authorities, she and Georges Martin founded a mixed lodge that actively practiced masonic ritual. Annie Besant subsequently helped spread this model to the English-speaking world. Disputes over ritual in England led to the creation of exclusively female masonic bodies, which then expanded internationally. Separately, the French revived "Adoption" as an all-female lodge in 1901, abandoning it again by 1935. Yet these lodges persisted, ultimately leading, in 1959, to an organization of women practicing continental Freemasonry.

input: John Forbes Kerry was born on December 11, 1943 in Aurora, Colorado, at Fitzsimons Army Hospital. He was the second oldest of four children born to Richard John Kerry, a Foreign Service officer and lawyer, and Rosemary Isabel Forbes, a nurse and social activist. His father was raised Catholic (John's paternal grandparents were Austro-Hungarian Jewish immigrants who converted to Catholicism) and his mother was Episcopalian. He was raised with an elder sister named Margaret (born 1941), a younger sister named Diana (born 1947) and a younger brother named Cameron (born 1950). The children were raised in their father's faith; John Kerry served as an altar boy.
rewrite: Born at Fitzsimons Army Hospital in Aurora, Colorado on December 11, 1943, John Forbes Kerry was the second of four children. His parents were Richard John Kerry, a Foreign Service officer and lawyer, and Rosemary Isabel Forbes, a nurse and social activist. His father, raised Catholic after his own Austro-Hungarian Jewish parents converted, and his Episcopalian mother raised the children in their father's faith. Kerry, who served as an altar boy, grew up with his elder sister Margaret (born 1941), younger sister Diana (born 1947), and younger brother Cameron (born 1950).

input: The US Air Force Fitness Test (AFFT) is designed to test the abdominal circumference, muscular strength/endurance and cardiovascular respiratory fitness of airmen in the USAF. As part of the Fit to Fight program, the USAF adopted a more stringent physical fitness assessment; the new fitness program was put into effect on 1 June 2010. The annual ergo-cycle test which the USAF had used for several years had been replaced in 2004. In the AFFT, Airmen are given a score based on performance consisting of four components: waist circumference, the sit-up, the push-up, and a 1.5-mile (2.4 km) run. Airmen can potentially earn a score of 100, with the run counting as 60%, waist circumference as 20%, and both strength test counting as 10% each. A passing score is 75 points. Effective 1 July 2010, the AFFT is administered by the base Fitness Assessment Cell (FAC), and is required twice a year. Personnel may test once a year if he or she earns a score above a 90%. Additionally, only meeting the minimum standards on each one of these tests will not get you a passing score of 75%, and failing any one component will result in a failure for the entire test.
rewrite: Implemented on June 1, 2010, the U.S. Air Force Fitness Test (AFFT) serves as a more rigorous physical assessment under the Fit to Fight program. This evaluation measures an airman's abdominal circumference, muscular strength and endurance, and cardiovascular respiratory fitness. It replaced an annual ergo-cycle test that had been in use until 2004. Administered by the base Fitness Assessment Cell (FAC) starting July 1, 2010, the test is required twice yearly. Personnel scoring above 90% qualify to test just once per year. The AFFT score is derived from four components: waist measurement, sit-ups, push-ups, and a 1.5-mile (2.4 km) run. Of the potential 100 points, the run comprises 60%, waist circumference 20%, and each strength test 10%. A minimum of 75 points is needed to pass. Crucially, merely meeting the minimum standard on every component does not guarantee a passing score, and failing any single element results in an overall test failure.

input: As the 10th century progressed, the Khazars were no longer able to command tribute from the Volga Bulgars, and their relationship with the Byzantines deteriorated, as Byzantium increasingly allied with the Pechenegs against them. The Pechenegs were thus secure to raid the lands of the Khazars from their base between the Volga and Don rivers, allowing them to expand to the west. Rus' relations with the Pechenegs were complex, as the groups alternately formed alliances with and against one another. The Pechenegs were nomads roaming the steppe raising livestock which they traded with the Rus' for agricultural goods and other products. The lucrative Rus' trade with the Byzantine Empire had to pass through Pecheneg-controlled territory, so the need for generally peaceful relations was essential. Nevertheless, while the Primary Chronicle reports the Pechenegs entering Rus' territory in 915 and then making peace, they were waging war with one another again in 920. Pechenegs are reported assisting the Rus' in later campaigns against the Byzantines, yet allied with the Byzantines against the Rus' at other times.
rewrite: By the 10th century, the Khazars saw their influence wane, losing the ability to demand tribute from the Volga Bulgars. Concurrently, their standing with Byzantium deteriorated as the empire increasingly aligned with the Pechenegs. This alliance secured the Pechenegs, enabling raids on Khazar lands from their territory between the Volga and Don rivers and facilitating westward expansion. The Pechenegs were steppe nomads whose economy relied on livestock, which they traded with the Rus' for agricultural and other goods. Rus' relations with them were inherently complex, marked by shifting alliances and conflicts. Peaceful interaction was crucial, however, because the lucrative Rus' trade route to the Byzantine Empire passed through Pecheneg-controlled lands. Despite this need, conflict persisted: the Primary Chronicle notes Pechenegs entering Rus' territory in 915 before making peace, only to be at war again by 920. In later campaigns, Pechenegs sometimes aided the Rus against Byzantium and at other times allied with the Byzantines against the Rus.

input: The original city council line-up of 14 members (nine district-based and five at-large positions) was based on a U.S. Justice Department mandate which took effect in 1979. At-large council members represent the entire city. Under the city charter, once the population in the city limits exceeded 2.1 million residents, two additional districts were to be added. The city of Houston's official 2010 census count was 600 shy of the required number; however, as the city was expected to grow beyond 2.1 million shortly thereafter, the two additional districts were added for, and the positions filled during, the August 2011 elections.
rewrite: In 1979, a U.S. Justice Department mandate established Houston's city council with 14 members: nine from districts and five at-large, representing the entire city. The city charter specified that two more districts would be added once the population exceeded 2.1 million. Although the official 2010 census fell 600 residents short, the city was projected to surpass that threshold imminently. Consequently, the two new districts were created and their positions were filled in the August 2011 elections.

input: Externally, Orthodox Jews can be identified by their manner of dress and family lifestyle. Orthodox women dress modestly by keeping most of their skin covered. Additionally, married women cover their hair, most commonly in the form of a scarf, also in the form of hats, bandanas, berets, snoods or, sometimes, wigs. Orthodox men wear a skullcap known as a kipa and often fringes called "tzitzit". Haredi men often grow beards and always wear black hats and suits, indoors and outdoors. However, Modern Orthodox Jews are commonly indistinguishable in their dress from those around them.
rewrite: Orthodox Jews are often recognizable externally through their attire and family customs. Women adhere to modest dress, covering most of their skin, and married women typically cover their hair with scarves, hats, or other head coverings. Men frequently wear a kipa (skullcap) and tzitzit (fringes). Haredi men usually have beards and consistently wear black hats and suits. In contrast, Modern Orthodox individuals generally dress similarly to the broader society, making them less distinguishable.

input: Gain is a parameter which measures the degree of directivity of the antenna's radiation pattern. A high-gain antenna will radiate most of its power in a particular direction, while a low-gain antenna will radiate over a wider angle. The antenna gain, or power gain of an antenna is defined as the ratio of the intensity (power per unit surface area)  radiated by the antenna in the direction of its maximum output, at an arbitrary distance, divided by the intensity  radiated at the same distance by a hypothetical isotropic antenna which radiates equal power in all directions. This dimensionless ratio is usually expressed logarithmically in decibels, these units are called "decibels-isotropic" (dBi)
rewrite: Antenna gain quantifies the directivity of an antenna's radiation pattern. While a low-gain antenna radiates power over a broad angle, a high-gain antenna concentrates most of its power in a specific direction. Technically, this gain is defined as a dimensionless ratio. It compares the power intensity radiated at the antenna's maximum output direction to the intensity from a hypothetical isotropic radiator at the same distance, which emits equally in all directions. This ratio is typically expressed logarithmically in decibels, a unit referred to as "decibels-isotropic" (dBi).

input: Light is the signal by which plants synchronize their internal clocks to their environment and is sensed by a wide variety of photoreceptors. Red and blue light are absorbed through several phytochromes and cryptochromes. One phytochrome, phyA, is the main phytochrome in seedlings grown in the dark but rapidly degrades in light to produce Cry1. Phytochromes B–E are more stable with phyB, the main phytochrome in seedlings grown in the light. The cryptochrome (cry) gene is also a light-sensitive component of the circadian clock and is thought to be involved both as a photoreceptor and as part of the clock's endogenous pacemaker mechanism. Cryptochromes 1–2 (involved in blue–UVA) help to maintain the period length in the clock through a whole range of light conditions.
rewrite: Plants rely on light as a signal to align their internal circadian clocks with the environment, using diverse photoreceptors for detection. Among these, red and blue light are absorbed by multiple phytochromes and cryptochromes. In dark-grown seedlings, phyA serves as the primary phytochrome, yet it quickly breaks down in light to generate Cry1. Conversely, phytochromes B through E are more stable, with phyB being the dominant form in light-grown seedlings. The cryptochrome (cry) gene functions as both a light-sensitive clock component and a photoreceptor, believed to participate in the endogenous pacemaker. Cryptochromes 1 and 2, responsive to blue–UVA light, aid in preserving the clock’s period length across various light conditions.

input: Genetic studies of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) of Amerindians and some Siberian and Central Asian peoples also revealed that the gene pool of the Turkic-speaking peoples of Siberia such as Altaians, Khakas, Shors and Soyots, living between the Altai and Lake Baikal along the Sayan mountains, are genetically closest to Amerindians.[citation needed] This view is shared by other researchers who argue that "the ancestors of the American Indians were the first to separate from the great Asian population in the Middle Paleolithic. 2012 research found evidence for a recent common ancestry between Native Americans and indigenous Altaians based on mitochondrial DNA and Y-Chromosome analysis. The paternal lineages of Altaians mostly belong to the subclades of haplogroup P-M45 (xR1a 38-93%; xQ1a 4-32%).
rewrite: Research based on mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) indicates that the genetic makeup of Siberian Turkic-speaking groups like Altaians, Khakas, Shors, and Soyots—located between the Altai Mountains and Lake Baikal along the Sayan range—is most closely related to Amerindians. Supporting this, other scholars contend that the ancestors of Native Americans were the earliest group to diverge from the larger Asian population during the Middle Paleolithic. Further evidence from 2012, drawn from both mitochondrial DNA and Y-Chromosome studies, points to a relatively recent shared ancestry between Native Americans and indigenous Altaians. The paternal lines among Altaians are predominantly composed of subclades belonging to haplogroup P-M45 (excluding R1a at 38-93% and Q1a at 4-32%).

input: TechRadar deemed the Xbox 360 as the most influential game system through its emphasis of digital media distribution, Xbox Live online gaming service, and game achievement feature. During the console's lifetime, the Xbox brand has grown from gaming-only to encompassing all multimedia, turning it into a hub for "living-room computing environment". input: Boston's colleges and universities have a significant effect on the regional economy. Boston attracts more than 350,000 college students from around the world, who contribute more than $4.8 billion annually to the city's economy. The area's schools are major employers and attract industries to the city and surrounding region. The city is home to a number of technology companies and is a hub for biotechnology, with the Milken Institute rating Boston as the top life sciences cluster in the country. Boston receives the highest absolute amount of annual funding from the National Institutes of Health of all cities in the United States.

Furthermore, the city receives more annual funding from the National Institutes of Health than any other U.S. city, underscoring its central economic role.

input: Another extreme case of impedance matching occurs when using a small loop antenna (usually, but not always, for receiving) at a relatively low frequency where it appears almost as a pure inductor. Resonating such an inductor with a capacitor at the frequency of operation not only cancels the reactance but greatly magnifies the very small radiation resistance of such a loop.[citation needed] This is implemented in most AM broadcast receivers, with a small ferrite loop antenna resonated by a capacitor which is varied along with the receiver tuning in order to maintain resonance over the AM broadcast band
rewrite: A small loop antenna, often used for reception, can act almost like a pure inductor at relatively low frequencies. To achieve impedance matching in this extreme case, the inductor is resonated with a capacitor at the operating frequency. This resonance not only cancels the reactance but also greatly amplifies the loop's very small radiation resistance. This principle is commonly implemented in most AM broadcast receivers. A small ferrite loop antenna is resonated by a variable capacitor, which is adjusted along with the receiver tuning to maintain resonance across the entire AM broadcast band.

input: Despite the internal stability (known as the paz porfiriana), modernization, and economic growth in Mexico during the Porfiriato from 1876 to 1910, many across the state became deeply dissatisfied with the political system. When Díaz first ran for office, he committed to a strict “No Re-election” policy in which he disqualified himself to serve consecutive terms. Eventually backtracking on many of his initial political positions Díaz became a de facto dictator. Díaz became increasingly unpopular due to brutal suppression of political dissidents by using the Rurales and manipulating the elections to solidify his political machine. The working class was frustrated with the Díaz regime due to the corruption of the political system that had increased the inequality between the rich and poor. The peasants felt disenfranchised by the policies that promoted the unfair distribution of land where 95% of the land was owned by the top 5%.
rewrite: From 1876 to 1910, the Porfiriato era in Mexico was marked by internal stability, modernization, and economic growth, yet this period also bred widespread discontent with the political system. Initially, Porfirio Díaz pledged a strict “No Re-election” policy, vowing not to serve consecutive terms. However, he later reversed many early positions, becoming a de facto dictator. His regime grew increasingly unpopular through the brutal suppression of dissidents by the Rurales and the manipulation of elections to strengthen his political machine. The working class resented the systemic corruption, which exacerbated inequality between the rich and poor. Peasants, in particular, felt disenfranchised by policies leading to an unfair distribution of land, with 95% of it owned by just 5% of the population.

input: Eton has a long list of distinguished former pupils. David Cameron is the 19th British prime minister to have attended the school, and has recommended that Eton set up a school in the state sector to help drive up standards. Eton now co-sponsors a state sixth-form college in Newham, a deprived area of East London, called the London Academy of Excellence, opened in 2012, which is free of charge and aims to get all its students into higher education. In September 2014, Eton opened, and became the sole educational sponsor for, a new purpose-built co-educational state boarding and day school for around 500 pupils, Holyport College, in Maidenhead in Berkshire, with construction costing around £15 million, in which a fifth of places for day pupils will be set aside for children from poor homes, 21 boarding places will go to youngsters on the verge of being taken into care, and a further 28 boarders will be funded or part-funded through bursaries.
rewrite: Eton boasts an extensive roster of notable alumni, including David Cameron, the nineteenth British prime minister educated there. Cameron has advocated for Eton to establish a state-sector school to help raise educational standards. In response, Eton now co-sponsors the London Academy of Excellence, a free state sixth-form college opened in 2012 in Newham, a deprived part of East London, with the goal of sending all its students to university. Furthermore, in September 2014, Eton opened Holyport College in Maidenhead, Berkshire, becoming its sole educational sponsor. This purpose-built, co-educational state boarding and day school, constructed at a cost of approximately £15 million, serves around 500 pupils. It reserves a fifth of day places for children from poor households, allocates 21 boarding places for youngsters nearly entering care, and funds or part-funds an additional 28 boarders through bursaries.

input: When learning how to write hanja, students are taught to memorize the native Korean pronunciation for the hanja's meaning and the Sino-Korean pronunciations (the pronunciation based on the Chinese pronunciation of the characters) for each hanja respectively so that students know what the syllable and meaning is for a particular hanja. For example, the name for the hanja 水 is 물 수 (mul-su) in which 물 (mul) is the native Korean pronunciation for "water", while 수 (su) is the Sino-Korean pronunciation of the character. The naming of hanja is similar to if "water" were named "water-aqua", "horse-equus", or "gold-aurum" based on a hybridization of both the English and the Latin names. Other examples include 사람 인 (saram-in) for 人 "person/people", 큰 대 (keun-dae) for 大 "big/large//great", 작을 소 (jakeul-so) for 小 "small/little", 아래 하 (arae-ha) for 下 "underneath/below/low", 아비 부 (abi-bu) for 父 "father", and 나라이름 한 (naraimreum-han) for 韓 "Han/Korea".
rewrite: Students learning to write hanja memorize two distinct pronunciations for each character: a native Korean term for its meaning and a Sino-Korean reading derived from Chinese. This dual approach ensures they understand both the syllable and the meaning associated with a given hanja. For instance, the character 水 is learned as 물 수 (mul-su), where "mul" is the native word for "water" and "su" is its Sino-Korean sound. This naming convention resembles hybrid forms like "water-aqua" or "horse-equus," blending English and Latin. Further examples illustrate the pattern: 人 is 사람 인 (saram-in) for "person," 大 is 큰 대 (keun-dae) for "big," 小 is 작을 소 (jakeul-so) for "small," 下 is 아래 하 (arae-ha) for "underneath," 父 is 아비 부 (abi-bu) for "father," and 韓 is 나라이름 한 (naraireum-han) for "Han" or "Korea."

input: Norwegian researchers at the University of Tromsø have shown that some Arctic animals (ptarmigan, reindeer) show circadian rhythms only in the parts of the year that have daily sunrises and sunsets. In one study of reindeer, animals at 70 degrees North showed circadian rhythms in the autumn, winter and spring, but not in the summer. Reindeer on Svalbard at 78 degrees North showed such rhythms only in autumn and spring. The researchers suspect that other Arctic animals as well may not show circadian rhythms in the constant light of summer and the constant dark of winter.
rewrite: Research from the University of Tromsø reveals that certain Arctic species, like ptarmigan and reindeer, exhibit circadian rhythms solely during seasons with distinct daily sunrises and sunsets. For instance, reindeer at 70 degrees North displayed these rhythms in autumn, winter, and spring, but not in summer. Those at 78 degrees North on Svalbard showed them only in autumn and spring. Scientists believe other Arctic animals may similarly lack such rhythms during the perpetual light of summer and constant dark of winter.

input: The Catholic Church has what is claimed to be the oldest continuously functioning internal legal system in Western Europe, much later than Roman law but predating the evolution of modern European civil law traditions. What began with rules ("canons") adopted by the Apostles at the Council of Jerusalem in the first century has developed into a highly complex legal system encapsulating not just norms of the New Testament, but some elements of the Hebrew (Old Testament), Roman, Visigothic, Saxon, and Celtic legal traditions.
rewrite: With roots in rules ("canons") established by the Apostles at the first-century Council of Jerusalem, the Catholic Church's legal system is considered the oldest continuously functioning internal framework in Western Europe. It evolved into a highly complex structure, incorporating norms from the New Testament along with elements of Hebrew, Roman, Visigothic, Saxon, and Celtic legal traditions. While much later than Roman law, it predates modern European civil law systems.

input: Nonetheless, within a few years of his death, Gregory of Nazianzus called him the "Pillar of the Church". His writings were well regarded by all Church fathers who followed, in both the West and the East, who noted their rich devotion to the Word-become-man, great pastoral concern, and profound interest in monasticism. Athanasius is counted as one of the four great Eastern Doctors of the Church in the Roman Catholic Church. In the Eastern Orthodox Church, he is labeled the "Father of Orthodoxy". Some Protestants label him "Father of the Canon". Athanasius is venerated as a Christian saint, whose feast day is 2 May in Western Christianity, 15 May in the Coptic Orthodox Church, and 18 January in the other Eastern Orthodox Churches. He is venerated by the Oriental and Eastern Orthodox Churches, the Roman Catholic Church, the Lutherans, and the Anglican Communion.

He is venerated as a saint across many Christian traditions, with feast days observed on May 2 in Western Christianity, May 15 in the Coptic Orthodox Church, and January 18 in other Eastern Orthodox Churches. His profound writings, celebrated by subsequent Church fathers in both East and West, are noted for their deep devotion to the incarnation, pastoral care, and monastic thought. Within the Roman Catholic Church, Athanasius is recognized as one of the four great Eastern Doctors. The Eastern Orthodox Church honors him as the "Father of Orthodoxy," while some Protestants call him "Father of the Canon." His veneration extends to the Oriental and Eastern Orthodox Churches, the Roman Catholic Church, Lutheran communities, and the Anglican Communion.
