Additionally, from the 15th century onward, Moroccan Jews were forcibly confined to walled quarters known as mellahs, a practice that intensified in the early 19th century.

input: The construction of cathedrals and castles advanced building technology, leading to the development of large stone buildings. Ancillary structures included new town halls, houses, bridges, and tithe barns. Shipbuilding improved with the use of the rib and plank method rather than the old Roman system of mortise and tenon. Other improvements to ships included the use of lateen sails and the stern-post rudder, both of which increased the speed at which ships could be sailed.
rewrite: Building technology progressed through cathedral and castle construction, enabling large stone structures. Alongside these, new town halls, houses, bridges, and tithe barns were built. In shipbuilding, the rib and plank method replaced the Roman mortise and tenon system. Further maritime advances included the lateen sail and stern-post rudder, which significantly increased sailing speeds.

input: Prior to Confederation in 1867, residents of the colonies in what is now Canada served as regular members of French and British forces and in local militia groups. The latter aided in the defence of their respective territories against attacks by other European powers, Aboriginal peoples, and later American forces during the American Revolutionary War and War of 1812, as well as in the Fenian raids, Red River Rebellion, and North-West Rebellion. Consequently, the lineages of some Canadian army units stretch back to the early 19th century, when militia units were formed to assist in the defence of British North America against invasion by the United States.
rewrite: Before 1867, when Canada was not yet a confederation, people living in the colonies served in French and British regular forces and in local militias. These militia groups helped defend their territories from various threats, including other European powers, Aboriginal peoples, and later American forces during the American Revolutionary War and the War of 1812. They also participated in the Fenian raids, the Red River Rebellion, and the North-West Rebellion. As a result, certain Canadian army units can trace their origins to the early 19th century, a time when militia units were established to protect British North America from potential U.S. invasion.

input: As well as being head of government, a prime minister may have other roles or titles—the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, for example, is also First Lord of the Treasury and Minister for the Civil Service. Prime ministers may take other ministerial posts—for example, during the Second World War, Winston Churchill was also Minister of Defence (although there was then no Ministry of Defence), and in the current cabinet of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu also serves as Minister of Communications, Foreign Affairs, Regional Cooperation, Economy and Interior
rewrite: Beyond serving as head of government, a prime minister often holds additional roles. For instance, the United Kingdom's Prime Minister is simultaneously First Lord of the Treasury and Minister for the Civil Service. It is also common for prime ministers to assume other ministerial positions. Historical and contemporary examples include Winston Churchill, who was Minister of Defence during World War II, and Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu, who currently leads the ministries of Communications, Foreign Affairs, Regional Cooperation, Economy, and Interior.

input: Laing's definition of identity closely follows Erikson's, in emphasising the past, present and future components of the experienced self. He also develops the concept of the "metaperspective of self", i.e. the self's perception of the other's view of self, which has been found to be extremely important in clinical contexts such as anorexia nervosa. (Saunderson and O'Kane, 2005). Harré also conceptualises components of self/identity – the "person" (the unique being I am to myself and others) along with aspects of self (including a totality of attributes including beliefs about one's characteristics including life history), and the personal characteristics displayed to others.
rewrite: Laing's view of identity aligns with Erikson's by stressing the experienced self across past, present, and future. Additionally, he introduces the "metaperspective of self"—how one perceives another's view of oneself—a notion shown to be crucial in clinical settings like anorexia nervosa (Saunderson and O'Kane, 2005). Similarly, Harré outlines elements of self/identity, distinguishing the "person" as the unique individual known to oneself and others, from the various aspects of self. These encompass a full range of attributes, such as personal beliefs and life history, alongside the traits one exhibits to others.

input: A German trading company, the Jaluit Gesellschaft, administered the islands from 1887 until 1905. They conscripted the islanders as laborers and mistreated them. After the German–Spanish Treaty of 1899, in which Germany acquired the Carolines, Palau, and the Marianas from Spain, Germany placed all of its Micronesian islands, including the Marshalls, under the governor of German New Guinea.
rewrite: From 1887 to 1905, the Jaluit Gesellschaft, a German trading firm, governed the islands. It forced the islanders into labor and subjected them to abuse. Following the 1899 German–Spanish Treaty, Germany gained the Carolines, Palau, and the Marianas. Subsequently, it placed all its Micronesian territories, including the Marshalls, under the administration of German New Guinea's governor.

input: The British Isles lie at the juncture of several regions with past episodes of tectonic mountain building. These orogenic belts form a complex geology that records a huge and varied span of Earth's history. Of particular note was the Caledonian Orogeny during the Ordovician Period, c. 488–444 Ma and early Silurian period, when the craton Baltica collided with the terrane Avalonia to form the mountains and hills in northern Britain and Ireland. Baltica formed roughly the northwestern half of Ireland and Scotland. Further collisions caused the Variscan orogeny in the Devonian and Carboniferous periods, forming the hills of Munster, southwest England, and southern Wales. Over the last 500 million years the land that forms the islands has drifted northwest from around 30°S, crossing the equator around 370 million years ago to reach its present northern latitude.
rewrite: Positioned at the intersection of multiple historic tectonic zones, the British Isles exhibit a complex geology that chronicles vast stretches of Earth's history. This landscape results from past mountain-building episodes, or orogenies. Notably, the Caledonian Orogeny occurred from roughly 488 to 444 million years ago, when the continental mass of Baltica—forming much of what is now northwestern Ireland and Scotland—collided with the terrane Avalonia. This event created the mountains and hills of northern Britain and Ireland. Later, during the Devonian and Carboniferous periods, further collisions triggered the Variscan orogeny, shaping the hills of Munster, southwest England, and southern Wales. Over the past 500 million years, the land comprising the islands has drifted northwest from about 30°S, crossing the equator approximately 370 million years ago to arrive at its current latitude.

input: Damage to a German steel facility occurred during a DST transition in 1993, when a computer timing system linked to a radio time synchronization signal allowed molten steel to cool for one hour less than the required duration, resulting in spattering of molten steel when it was poured. Medical devices may generate adverse events that could harm patients, without being obvious to clinicians responsible for care. These problems are compounded when the DST rules themselves change; software developers must test and perhaps modify many programs, and users must install updates and restart applications. Consumers must update devices such as programmable thermostats with the correct DST rules, or manually adjust the devices' clocks. A common strategy to resolve these problems in computer systems is to express time using the Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) rather than the local time zone. For example, Unix-based computer systems use the UTC-based Unix time internally.
rewrite: In 1993, a German steel plant suffered damage due to a Daylight Saving Time (DST) shift. A computer system synchronized by a radio time signal caused molten steel to cool for one hour less than needed, leading to dangerous spattering upon pouring. Such timing issues extend beyond industry; medical devices can produce subtle adverse events, potentially harming patients without clinicians' awareness. Challenges intensify when DST rules change, requiring software developers to test and modify numerous programs, while users must install updates and restart applications. Consumers also face the task of updating devices like programmable thermostats with new rules or adjusting clocks manually. A widespread solution in computing is to use Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) instead of local time zones. Internally, many Unix-based systems, for instance, rely on UTC-based Unix time to avoid these complications.

input: On May 1, 1960, a U.S. one-man U-2 spy plane was reportedly shot down at high altitude over Soviet Union airspace. The flight was made to gain photo intelligence before the scheduled opening of an East–West summit conference, which had been scheduled in Paris, 15 days later. Captain Francis Gary Powers had bailed out of his aircraft and was captured after parachuting down onto Russian soil. Four days after Powers disappeared, the Eisenhower Administration had NASA issue a very detailed press release noting that an aircraft had "gone missing" north of Turkey. It speculated that the pilot might have fallen unconscious while the autopilot was still engaged, and falsely claimed that "the pilot reported over the emergency frequency that he was experiencing oxygen difficulties."
rewrite: On May 1, 1960, a U.S. U-2 spy plane, piloted by a single individual, was shot down at high altitude while flying over the Soviet Union. The mission aimed to gather photographic intelligence ahead of an East-West summit set to begin in Paris fifteen days later. After bailing out, Captain Francis Gary Powers parachuted onto Russian territory and was captured. Four days following his disappearance, the Eisenhower Administration directed NASA to release a detailed statement. It claimed an aircraft had "gone missing" north of Turkey, falsely suggesting the pilot reported oxygen issues on an emergency frequency and might have been unconscious with the autopilot engaged.

input: However, the collapsing Ottoman economy could not sustain the fleet's strength for too long. Sultan Abdülhamid II distrusted the admirals who sided with the reformist Midhat Pasha, and claimed that the large and expensive fleet was of no use against the Russians during the Russo-Turkish War. He locked most of the fleet inside the Golden Horn, where the ships decayed for the next 30 years. Following the Young Turk Revolution in 1908, the Committee of Union and Progress sought to develop a strong Ottoman naval force. The Ottoman Navy Foundation was established in 1910 to buy new ships through public donations.
rewrite: Despite the Ottoman fleet's potential, its power was short-lived due to the empire's failing economy. Sultan Abdülhamid II, distrustful of admirals aligned with reformer Midhat Pasha, argued the costly navy was ineffective against Russia in the Russo-Turkish War. Consequently, he confined most ships to the Golden Horn, leaving them to deteriorate over three decades. After the 1908 Young Turk Revolution, the new Committee of Union and Progress aimed to rebuild naval strength. This led to the 1910 creation of the Ottoman Navy Foundation, which funded new ship purchases via public contributions.

input: The term heresy is also used as an ideological pigeonhole for contemporary writers because, by definition, heresy depends on contrasts with an established orthodoxy. For example, the tongue-in-cheek contemporary usage of heresy, such as to categorize a "Wall Street heresy" a "Democratic heresy" or a "Republican heresy," are metaphors that invariably retain a subtext that links orthodoxies in geology or biology or any other field to religion. These expanded metaphoric senses allude to both the difference between the person's views and the mainstream and the boldness of such a person in propounding these views.
rewrite: Contemporary writers are often placed into the ideological pigeonhole of heresy, a term that inherently relies on contrast with an established orthodoxy. Its modern, tongue-in-cheek applications—like labeling a "Wall Street heresy" or a "political heresy"—act as metaphors. These retain a subtext connecting secular orthodoxies in fields like geology or biology to religious ones. Such expanded usage alludes both to the divergence of an individual's views from the mainstream and to the boldness required to propound them.

input: Noether's theorem (1918) states that any differentiable symmetry of the action of a physical system has a corresponding conservation law. Noether's theorem has become a fundamental tool of modern theoretical physics and the calculus of variations. A generalisation of the seminal formulations on constants of motion in Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics (1788 and 1833, respectively), it does not apply to systems that cannot be modeled with a Lagrangian; for example, dissipative systems with continuous symmetries need not have a corresponding conservation law.
rewrite: Formulated in 1918, Noether's theorem establishes that a differentiable symmetry in a system's action implies a corresponding conservation law. As a generalization of earlier principles on constants of motion in Lagrangian (1788) and Hamiltonian (1833) mechanics, it is now a cornerstone of modern theoretical physics and the calculus of variations. However, the theorem does not extend to systems lacking a Lagrangian model; dissipative systems with continuous symmetries, for instance, may not obey such a law.

input: The Qing emperors were generally adept at poetry and often skilled in painting, and offered their patronage to Confucian culture. The Kangxi and Qianlong Emperors, for instance, embraced Chinese traditions both to control them and to proclaim their own legitimacy. The Kangxi Emperor sponsored the Peiwen Yunfu, a rhyme dictionary published in 1711, and the Kangxi Dictionary published in 1716, which remains to this day an authoritative reference. The Qianlong Emperor sponsored the largest collection of writings in Chinese history, the Siku Quanshu, completed in 1782. Court painters made new versions of the Song masterpiece, Zhang Zeduan's Along the River During the Qingming Festival whose depiction of a prosperous and happy realm demonstrated the beneficence of the emperor. The emperors undertook tours of the south and commissioned monumental scrolls to depict the grandeur of the occasion. Imperial patronage also encouraged the industrial production of ceramics and Chinese export porcelain.
rewrite: Generally proficient in poetry and often skilled in painting, the Qing emperors extended their patronage to Confucian culture. Emperors Kangxi and Qianlong, for example, embraced Chinese traditions both to exert control and to affirm their legitimacy. Kangxi sponsored the compilation of the *Peiwen Yunfu*, a rhyme dictionary published in 1711, and the authoritative *Kangxi Dictionary*, issued in 1716. Qianlong oversaw the creation of the largest collection of writings in Chinese history, the *Siku Quanshu*, completed in 1782. To demonstrate imperial beneficence, court painters produced new versions of the Song dynasty masterpiece, Zhang Zeduan's *Along the River During the Qingming Festival*, which depicted a prosperous realm. The emperors also embarked on southern tours, commissioning monumental scrolls to capture these grand occasions. Furthermore, imperial patronage stimulated the industrial production of ceramics, including Chinese export porcelain.

input: Deleuze's and Latour's opinions, however, are minority ones, as Whitehead has not been recognized as particularly influential within the most dominant philosophical schools. It is impossible to say exactly why Whitehead's influence has not been more widespread, but it may be partly due to his metaphysical ideas seeming somewhat counter-intuitive (such as his assertion that matter is an abstraction), or his inclusion of theistic elements in his philosophy, or the perception of metaphysics itself as passé, or simply the sheer difficulty and density of his prose.
rewrite: Despite being championed by thinkers like Deleuze and Latour, Alfred North Whitehead remains a marginal figure within mainstream philosophical traditions. The precise reasons for his limited influence are unclear, but several factors likely contribute. These include his counter-intuitive metaphysical claims—for instance, that matter is an abstraction—the inclusion of theistic elements in his work, a broader cultural dismissal of metaphysics, and the formidable difficulty of his dense prose.

input: Toxocara canis (dog roundworm) eggs in dog feces can cause toxocariasis. In the United States, about 10,000 cases of Toxocara infection are reported in humans each year, and almost 14% of the U.S. population is infected. In Great Britain, 24% of soil samples taken from public parks contained T. canis eggs. Untreated toxocariasis can cause retinal damage and decreased vision. Dog feces can also contain hookworms that cause cutaneous larva migrans in humans.
rewrite: Toxocariasis, an infection caused by Toxocara canis eggs found in dog feces, leads to roughly 10,000 human cases annually in the United States, where nearly 14% of the population is infected. In Great Britain, 24% of public park soil samples contain these eggs. Untreated, the disease can damage the retina and reduce vision. Additionally, dog feces may carry hookworms, which trigger cutaneous larva migrans in people.

input: Both the archipelagos of the Azores and Madeira have a subtropical climate, although variations between islands exist, making weather predictions very difficult (owing to rough topography). The Madeira and Azorean archipelagos have a narrower temperature range, with annual average temperatures exceeding 20 °C (68 °F) along the coast (according to the Portuguese Meteorological Institute). Some islands in Azores do have drier months in the summer. Consequently, the island of the Azores have been identified as having a Mediterranean climate (both Csa and Csb types), while some islands (such as Flores or Corvo) are classified as Maritime Temperate (Cfb) and Humid subtropical (Cfa), respectively, according to Köppen-Geiger classification.
rewrite: The Azores and Madeira archipelagos both experience a subtropical climate, though local conditions vary across islands due to rugged terrain, complicating weather forecasts. According to the Portuguese Meteorological Institute, coastal areas in both regions maintain annual averages above 20 °C (68 °F), with a relatively narrow temperature range. Summers bring drier months to parts of the Azores. Under the Köppen-Geiger system, the Azores are largely classified as Mediterranean (Csa and Csb), while islands like Flores and Corvo fall under Maritime Temperate (Cfb) and Humid subtropical (Cfa) climates, respectively.

input: Time has long been a major subject of study in religion, philosophy, and science, but defining it in a manner applicable to all fields without circularity has consistently eluded scholars. Nevertheless, diverse fields such as business, industry, sports, the sciences, and the performing arts all incorporate some notion of time into their respective measuring systems. Some simple definitions of time include "time is what clocks measure", which is a problematically vague and self-referential definition that utilizes the device used to measure the subject as the definition of the subject, and "time is what keeps everything from happening at once", which is without substantive meaning in the absence of the definition of simultaneity in the context of the limitations of human sensation, observation of events, and the perception of such events.
rewrite: Time has persistently resisted a clear, non-circular definition that works across all disciplines, despite its longstanding importance in religion, philosophy, and science. Various fields—from business and industry to sports, the sciences, and the performing arts—nevertheless embed a concept of time within their own measurement frameworks. Proposed simple definitions remain problematic. One states, "time is what clocks measure," a vague and self-referential formulation that defines the subject by its measuring instrument. Another suggests, "time is what keeps everything from happening at once," a statement devoid of substantive meaning without first defining simultaneity, especially given the constraints of human sensation, event observation, and perception.

input: In 1045, the Byzantine Empire conquered Bagratid Armenia. Soon, the other Armenian states fell under Byzantine control as well. The Byzantine rule was short lived, as in 1071 Seljuk Turks defeated the Byzantines and conquered Armenia at the Battle of Manzikert, establishing the Seljuk Empire. To escape death or servitude at the hands of those who had assassinated his relative, Gagik II, King of Ani, an Armenian named Roupen, went with some of his countrymen into the gorges of the Taurus Mountains and then into Tarsus of Cilicia. The Byzantine governor of the palace gave them shelter where the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia was eventually established on 6 January 1198 under King Leo I, a descendant of Prince Roupen.
rewrite: In 1045, the Byzantine Empire took control of Bagratid Armenia, soon extending its rule over other Armenian states. This dominance proved brief, however, as the Seljuk Turks defeated the Byzantines at the 1071 Battle of Manzikert, conquering Armenia and founding the Seljuk Empire. Fleeing potential death or servitude following the assassination of his relative, King Gagik II of Ani, an Armenian named Roupen led a group into the gorges of the Taurus Mountains. They found refuge in Tarsus of Cilicia under the protection of the local Byzantine governor. Ultimately, this led to the establishment of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia on 6 January 1198 under King Leo I, a descendant of Prince Roupen.

input: Imperial College Union, the students' union at Imperial College, is run by five full-time sabbatical officers elected from the student body for a tenure of one year, and a number of permanent members of staff. The Union is given a large subvention by the university, much of which is spent on maintaining around 300 clubs, projects and societies. Examples of notable student groups and projects are Project Nepal which sends Imperial College students to work on educational development programmes in rural Nepal and the El Salvador Project, a construction based project in Central America. The Union also hosts sports-related clubs such as Imperial College Boat Club and Imperial College Gliding Club.
rewrite: At Imperial College, the students' union, known as Imperial College Union, receives substantial funding from the university. This financial support largely maintains approximately 300 clubs, projects, and societies. Among the notable groups are Project Nepal, which sends students to support educational development in rural Nepal, and the construction-focused El Salvador Project in Central America. Sports clubs, including the Imperial College Boat Club and Gliding Club, are also part of the Union. It is managed by five full-time sabbatical officers, elected annually from the student body, alongside a team of permanent staff members.

input: The Victorian era in particular became notorious for the conditions under which children were employed. Children as young as four were employed in production factories and mines working long hours in dangerous, often fatal, working conditions. In coal mines, children would crawl through tunnels too narrow and low for adults. Children also worked as errand boys, crossing sweepers, shoe blacks, or selling matches, flowers and other cheap goods. Some children undertook work as apprentices to respectable trades, such as building or as domestic servants (there were over 120,000 domestic servants in London in the mid-18th century). Working hours were long: builders worked 64 hours a week in summer and 52 in winter, while domestic servants worked 80 hour weeks.
rewrite: During the Victorian era, the employment of children became especially infamous for its harsh realities. In production factories and mines, youngsters as young as four faced long hours in perilous, frequently deadly, conditions. Coal mines utilized children to crawl through tunnels too narrow and low for adults. Other common roles included errand boys, crossing sweepers, shoe blacks, and sellers of matches, flowers, and similar cheap goods. Some entered apprenticeships in trades like building or became domestic servants—London alone had over 120,000 in the mid-18th century. Regardless of the job, hours were grueling: builders labored 64 hours weekly in summer and 52 in winter, while domestic servants toiled for 80 hours each week.

input: Three counties of the Washington District (now part of Tennessee) broke off from North Carolina in 1784 and formed the State of Franklin. Efforts to obtain admission to the Union failed, and the counties (now numbering eight) had re-joined North Carolina by 1789. North Carolina ceded the area to the federal government in 1790, after which it was organized into the Southwest Territory. In an effort to encourage settlers to move west into the new territory, in 1787 the mother state of North Carolina ordered a road to be cut to take settlers into the Cumberland Settlements—from the south end of Clinch Mountain (in East Tennessee) to French Lick (Nashville). The Trace was called the "North Carolina Road" or "Avery's Trace", and sometimes "The Wilderness Road" (although it should not be confused with Daniel Boone's "Wilderness Road" through the Cumberland Gap).
rewrite: In 1784, three counties from the Washington District—present-day Tennessee—seceded from North Carolina to establish the State of Franklin. Despite efforts to join the Union, this initiative failed, and by 1789 the region, then comprising eight counties, returned to North Carolina. The area was later ceded to the federal government in 1790 and organized as the Southwest Territory. To promote westward settlement, North Carolina had earlier ordered, in 1787, the construction of a road from Clinch Mountain in East Tennessee to French Lick (Nashville), guiding settlers into the Cumberland Settlements. This route was known as the "North Carolina Road," "Avery's Trace," and occasionally "The Wilderness Road"—though distinct from Daniel Boone's better-known Wilderness Road through the Cumberland Gap.

input: Vinyl's lower surface noise level than shellac was not forgotten, nor was its durability. In the late 1930s, radio commercials and pre-recorded radio programs being sent to disc jockeys started being stamped in vinyl, so they would not break in the mail. In the mid-1940s, special DJ copies of records started being made of vinyl also, for the same reason. These were all 78 rpm. During and after World War II, when shellac supplies were extremely limited, some 78 rpm records were pressed in vinyl instead of shellac, particularly the six-minute 12-inch (30 cm) 78 rpm records produced by V-Disc for distribution to United States troops in World War II. In the 1940s, radio transcriptions, which were usually on 16-inch records, but sometimes 12-inch, were always made of vinyl, but cut at 33 1⁄3 rpm. Shorter transcriptions were often cut at 78 rpm.
rewrite: While vinyl's durability and lower surface noise compared to shellac were noted advantages, its practical adoption unfolded over several years. Beginning in the late 1930s, radio commercials and pre-recorded programs for disc jockeys were pressed onto unbreakable vinyl for mailing. By the mid-1940s, special DJ copies of records followed suit. These were all 78 rpm discs. The World War II shellac shortage further accelerated vinyl's use, notably for V-Disc's 12-inch 78 rpm records sent to U.S. troops. Simultaneously, radio transcriptions, typically on 16-inch discs but sometimes 12-inch, were consistently made of vinyl and cut at 33 1⁄3 rpm, though shorter ones were often cut at 78 rpm.

input: The synagogue in Eshtemoa (As-Samu) was built around the 4th century. The mosaic floor is decorated with only floral and geometric patterns. The synagogue in Khirbet Susiya (excavated in 1971–72, founded in the end of the 4th century) has three mosaic panels, the eastern one depicting a Torah shrine, two menorahs, a lulav and an etrog with columns, deer and rams. The central panel is geometric while the western one is seriously damaged but it has been suggested that it depicted Daniel in the lion’s den. The Roman synagogue in Ein Gedi was remodeled in the Byzantine era and a more elaborate mosaic floor was laid down above the older white panels. The usual geometric design was enriched with birds in the center. It includes the names of the signs of the zodiac and important figures from the Jewish past but not their images suggesting that it served a rather conservative community.
rewrite: Constructed around the 4th century, the synagogue at Eshtemoa (As-Samu) features a mosaic floor adorned solely with floral and geometric designs. In contrast, the synagogue at Khirbet Susiya, founded in the late 4th century and excavated in 1971–72, contains three mosaic panels. Its eastern panel portrays a Torah shrine, two menorahs, a lulav and an etrog alongside columns, deer, and rams. While the central panel is geometric, the western one is heavily damaged, though scholars propose it once depicted Daniel in the lion’s den. Meanwhile, the Roman synagogue in Ein Gedi was renovated during the Byzantine period, with a more intricate mosaic floor installed over older white panels. Beyond the typical geometric patterns, this mosaic centers on birds. It also lists the zodiac signs and names of significant Jewish historical figures, deliberately omitting their images—a feature indicating a conservative community.

input: The Fujiwara rulers failed to maintain adequate police forces, which left robbers free to prey on travelers. This is implicitly illustrated in novels by the terror that night travel inspired in the main characters. The shōen system enabled the accumulation of wealth by an aristocratic elite; the economic surplus can be linked to the cultural developments of the Heian period and the "pursuit of arts". The major Buddhist temples in Heian-kyō and Nara also made use of the shōen. The establishment of branches rurally and integration of some Shinto shrines within these temple networks reflects a greater "organizational dynamism".
rewrite: Due to the Fujiwara rulers' inability to sustain sufficient police forces, robbers operated freely, terrorizing travelers. This danger is implicitly depicted in period novels through the profound fear of night travel experienced by characters. Meanwhile, the shōen system facilitated wealth accumulation among the aristocracy, an economic surplus connected to the Heian era's cultural flourishing and its "pursuit of arts." This system was also utilized by major Buddhist temples in Heian-kyō and Nara. Their expansion into rural branches and incorporation of Shinto shrines into their networks demonstrated a significant "organizational dynamism."

input: Modern-day Nigeria has been the site of numerous kingdoms and tribal states over the millennia. The modern state originated from British colonial rule beginning in the 19th century, and the merging of the Southern Nigeria Protectorate and Northern Nigeria Protectorate in 1914. The British set up administrative and legal structures whilst practising indirect rule through traditional chiefdoms. Nigeria became a formally independent federation in 1960, and plunged into a civil war from 1967 to 1970. It has since alternated between democratically-elected civilian governments and military dictatorships, until it achieved a stable democracy in 1999, with its 2011 presidential elections being viewed as the first to be conducted reasonably freely and fairly.
rewrite: Over millennia, numerous kingdoms and tribal states have existed in the area of modern-day Nigeria. The contemporary state took shape from British colonial rule in the 19th century, culminating in the 1914 merger of the Southern and Northern Nigeria Protectorates. Through traditional chiefdoms, the British practised indirect rule, establishing administrative and legal structures. After becoming a formally independent federation in 1960, Nigeria endured a civil war from 1967 to 1970. The nation then alternated between civilian governments and military dictatorships until achieving stable democracy in 1999. Its 2011 presidential elections are widely considered the first to be reasonably free and fair.

input: Hyderabadi cuisine comprises a broad repertoire of rice, wheat and meat dishes and the skilled use of various spices. Hyderabadi biryani and Hyderabadi haleem, with their blend of Mughlai and Arab cuisines, have become iconic dishes of India. Hyderabadi cuisine is highly influenced by Mughlai and to some extent by French, Arabic, Turkish, Iranian and native Telugu and Marathwada cuisines. Other popular native dishes include nihari, chakna, baghara baingan and the desserts qubani ka meetha, double ka meetha and kaddu ki kheer (a sweet porridge made with sweet gourd).
rewrite: Featuring a diverse array of rice, wheat, and meat dishes prepared with expert spicing, Hyderabadi cuisine draws strong influence from Mughlai traditions, along with French, Arabic, Turkish, Iranian, and native Telugu and Marathwada culinary styles. Its iconic offerings, such as Hyderabadi biryani and haleem, blend Mughlai and Arab elements. Other beloved native dishes are nihari, chakna, and baghara baingan, alongside desserts like qubani ka meetha, double ka meetha, and kaddu ki kheer, a sweet gourd porridge.

input: The coastline of Norfolk Island consists, to varying degrees, of cliff faces. A downward slope exists towards Slaughter Bay and Emily Bay, the site of the original colonial settlement of Kingston. There are no safe harbour facilities on Norfolk Island, with loading jetties existing at Kingston and Cascade Bay. All goods not domestically produced are brought in by ship, usually to Cascade Bay. Emily Bay, protected from the Pacific Ocean by a small coral reef, is the only safe area for recreational swimming, although surfing waves can be found at Anson and Ball Bays.
rewrite: Norfolk Island's coastline is largely composed of cliffs, sloping down toward Slaughter Bay and Emily Bay, where the historic Kingston settlement was established. The island lacks a safe harbor, utilizing loading jetties at Kingston and Cascade Bay instead. All imported goods arrive by ship, typically at Cascade Bay. While Anson and Ball Bays offer surfing waves, Emily Bay is the sole safe spot for swimming, sheltered by a small coral reef from the open Pacific.

input: This view is supported by a study of the region where these notions originated. Buddhism arose in Greater Magadha, which stretched from Sravasti, the capital of Kosala in the north-west, to Rajagrha in the south east. This land, to the east of aryavarta, the land of the Aryas, was recognized as non-Vedic. Other Vedic texts reveal a dislike of the people of Magadha, in all probability because the Magadhas at this time were not Brahmanised.[page needed] It was not until the 2nd or 3rd centuries BCE that the eastward spread of Brahmanism into Greater Magadha became significant. Ideas that developed in Greater Magadha prior to this were not subject to Vedic influence. These include rebirth and karmic retribution that appear in a number of movements in Greater Magadha, including Buddhism. These movements inherited notions of rebirth and karmic retribution from an earlier culture[page needed]
rewrite: Buddhism emerged in Greater Magadha, a region stretching from Sravasti in the northwest to Rajagrha in the southeast. This area lay east of aryavarta, the Vedic heartland, and was considered non-Vedic. A study of this region supports the view that ideas developing here were free from Vedic influence initially. Vedic texts themselves express a dislike for the people of Magadha, likely because they were not yet Brahmanised. Significant Brahmanical expansion into Greater Magadha only occurred around the 2nd or 3rd centuries BCE. Prior to this, movements like Buddhism developed concepts such as rebirth and karmic retribution. These notions, appearing in several regional movements, were inherited from an earlier culture rather than from Vedic tradition.

input: People are usually well informed about their health status, the positive and negative effects of their behaviour on their health and their use of health care services. Yet their perceptions of their health can differ from what administrative and examination-based data show about levels of illness within populations. Thus, survey results based on self-reporting at the household level complement other data on health status and the use of services. Only one third of adults rated their health as good or very good in Portugal (Kasmel et al., 2004). This is the lowest of the Eur-A countries reporting and reflects the relatively adverse situation of the country in terms of mortality and selected morbidity.
rewrite: Survey findings from household self-reporting offer a valuable complement to administrative and clinical health data. While individuals are typically aware of their own health, their personal assessments can contrast with broader population-level metrics. For instance, in Portugal, only one third of adults described their health as good or very good (Kasmel et al., 2004). This represents the lowest rating among reporting Eur-A countries, indicating a comparatively unfavorable national situation regarding mortality and specific morbidity rates. These subjective perceptions, alongside objective data on behaviors and service use, together provide a fuller picture of population health.

input: The next year Madonna and Maverick sued Warner Music Group and its former parent company Time Warner, claiming that mismanagement of resources and poor bookkeeping had cost the company millions of dollars. In return, Warner filed a countersuit alleging that Maverick had lost tens of millions of dollars on its own. The dispute was resolved when the Maverick shares, owned by Madonna and Ronnie Dashev, were purchased by Warner. Madonna and Dashev's company became a wholly owned subsidiary of Warner Music, but Madonna was still signed to Warner under a separate recording contract.
rewrite: The following year, Madonna and Maverick initiated a lawsuit against Warner Music Group and its former parent, Time Warner. They alleged that millions were lost due to resource mismanagement and faulty bookkeeping. Warner responded with a countersuit, claiming Maverick itself had lost tens of millions. Resolution came when Warner purchased the Maverick shares held by Madonna and Ronnie Dashev. This made their company a fully owned Warner Music subsidiary, though Madonna remained separately signed to Warner for her recording contract.

input: One of the more prominent contestants this year was Chris Medina, whose story of caring for his brain-damaged fiancée received widespread coverage. Medina was cut in the Top 40 round. Casey Abrams, who suffers from ulcerative colitis, was hospitalized twice and missed the Top 13 result show. The judges used their one save on Abrams on the Top 11, and as a result this was the first season that 11 finalists went on tour instead of 10. In the following week, Naima Adedapo and Thia Megia were both eliminated the following week.
rewrite: Chris Medina, a prominent contestant this year, gained attention for caring for his brain-damaged fiancée, yet was eliminated in the Top 40. Casey Abrams, dealing with ulcerative colitis, was hospitalized twice and missed the Top 13 results. The judges used their one save on Abrams during the Top 11, leading to a first: eleven finalists, rather than ten, proceeded on tour. Subsequently, both Naima Adedapo and Thia Megia were eliminated the following week.

input: Until the 1990s further replays would be played until one team was victorious. Some ties took as many as six matches to settle; in their 1975 campaign, Fulham played a total of 12 games over six rounds, which remains the most games played by a team to reach a final. Replays were traditionally played three or four days after the original game, but from 1991–92 they were staged at least 10 days later on police advice. This led to penalty shoot-outs being introduced, the first of which came on 26 November 1991 when Rotherham United eliminated Scunthorpe United.
rewrite: Before the 1990s, drawn matches required replays until a winner emerged, sometimes demanding up to six games. Fulham's 1975 run set a record, needing 12 matches over six rounds to reach the final. Traditionally held within days, replays were delayed by at least ten days from the 1991–92 season on police advice. This change prompted the adoption of penalty shoot-outs, first used to decide a tie when Rotherham United beat Scunthorpe United on November 26, 1991.

input: "By May 1539, Conquistador Hernando de Soto skirted the coast of Florida, searching for a deep harbor to land. He described seeing a thick wall of red mangroves spread mile after mile, some reaching as high as 70 feet (21 m), with intertwined and elevated roots making landing difficult. Very soon, 'many smokes' appeared 'along the whole coast', billowing against the sky, when the Native ancestors of the Seminole spotted the newcomers and spread the alarm by signal fires". The Spanish introduced Christianity, cattle, horses, sheep, the Spanish language, and more to Florida.[full citation needed] Both the Spanish and French established settlements in Florida, with varying degrees of success. In 1559, Don Tristán de Luna y Arellano established a colony at present-day Pensacola, one of the first European settlements in the continental United States, but it was abandoned by 1561.
rewrite: In May 1539, the Spanish conquistador Hernando de Soto sailed along the Florida coast, seeking a suitable deep harbor for landing. He observed an extensive barrier of red mangroves, their intertwined and elevated roots complicating any approach; some trees stood as tall as 70 feet (21 m). Before long, signal fires—described as 'many smokes'—appeared across the shoreline. These were set by the Native ancestors of the Seminole, who had spotted the newcomers and raised the alarm. The Spanish later brought Christianity, livestock like cattle and horses, sheep, and their language to Florida.[full citation needed] European settlements were attempted by both Spain and France, with mixed results. Among the earliest in the continental United States was a colony founded in 1559 by Don Tristán de Luna y Arellano at present-day Pensacola, though it was abandoned by 1561.

input: The Navy was modernized in the 1880s, and by the 1890s had adopted the naval power strategy of Captain Alfred Thayer Mahan—as indeed did every major navy. The old sailing ships were replaced by modern steel battleships, bringing them in line with the navies of Britain and Germany. In 1907, most of the Navy's battleships, with several support vessels, dubbed the Great White Fleet, were featured in a 14-month circumnavigation of the world. Ordered by President Theodore Roosevelt, it was a mission designed to demonstrate the Navy's capability to extend to the global theater.
rewrite: During the 1880s, the Navy underwent modernization, replacing old sailing ships with modern steel battleships comparable to those of Britain and Germany. By the 1890s, it, like every major navy, had embraced Captain Alfred Thayer Mahan’s naval power strategy. In 1907, President Theodore Roosevelt ordered most of its battleships, along with support vessels known as the Great White Fleet, on a 14-month world circumnavigation. This mission aimed to demonstrate the Navy's ability to project power globally.

input: Jobs expanded so rapidly that 400,000 people were attracted to the city from 1941 to 1943, including 50,000 blacks in the second wave of the Great Migration, and 350,000 whites, many of them from the South. Some European immigrants and their descendants feared black competition for jobs and housing. The federal government prohibited discrimination in defense work but when in June 1943, Packard promoted three blacks to work next to whites on its assembly lines, 25,000 whites walked off the job. The Detroit race riot of 1943 took place three weeks after the Packard plant protest. Over the course of three days, 34 people were killed, of whom 25 were African American, and approximately 600 were injured, 75% black people.
rewrite: Between 1941 and 1943, rapid job growth drew 400,000 new residents to the city. This influx included 350,000 whites, many from the South, and 50,000 African Americans as part of the Great Migration's second wave. Tensions arose as some European immigrants and their descendants worried about competition for employment and housing. Although the federal government had banned discrimination in defense industries, when the Packard plant promoted three black workers to integrated assembly lines in June 1943, 25,000 white workers staged a walkout. Just three weeks later, the Detroit race riot erupted. Lasting three days, the violence resulted in 34 deaths, 25 of whom were African American, and roughly 600 injuries, with black citizens comprising 75% of the wounded.

input: Convinced that he needed a wasta, or an influential intermediary to promote his application above the others, Nasser managed to secure a meeting with Under-Secretary of War Ibrahim Khairy Pasha, the person responsible for the academy's selection board, and requested his help. Khairy Pasha agreed and sponsored Nasser's second application, which was accepted in late 1937. Nasser focused on his military career from then on, and had little contact with his family. At the academy, he met Abdel Hakim Amer and Anwar Sadat, both of whom became important aides during his presidency. After graduating from the academy in July 1938, he was commissioned a second lieutenant in the infantry, and posted to Mankabad. It was here that Nasser and his closest comrades, including Sadat and Amer, first discussed their dissatisfaction at widespread corruption in the country and their desire to topple the monarchy. Sadat would later write that because of his "energy, clear-thinking, and balanced judgement", Nasser emerged as the group's natural leader.
rewrite: Needing a wasta—an influential intermediary—to advance his application, Nasser arranged a meeting with Under-Secretary of War Ibrahim Khairy Pasha, who oversaw the academy's selection board. Khairy Pasha agreed to sponsor him, leading to Nasser's acceptance in late 1937. From that point, he devoted himself to his military career, with little contact to his family. While at the academy, he formed key friendships with Abdel Hakim Amer and Anwar Sadat, future important aides during his presidency. Commissioned as a second lieutenant in the infantry after graduating in July 1938, he was stationed at Mankabad. There, with closest comrades like Sadat and Amer, he first discussed the widespread corruption and their shared goal to overthrow the monarchy. Sadat later noted that Nasser's energy, clear-thinking, and balanced judgement made him the group's natural leader.

input: Once inside the Rotunda for the Charters of Freedom, there are no lines to see the individual documents and visitors are allowed to walk from document to document as they wish. For over 30 years the National Archives have forbidden flash photography but the advent of cameras with automatic flashes have made the rules increasingly difficult to enforce. As a result, all filming, photographing, and videotaping by the public in the exhibition areas has been prohibited since February 25, 2010.
rewrite: Inside the Rotunda for the Charters of Freedom, visitors can freely move between documents without waiting in lines. While flash photography has been banned by the National Archives for more than three decades, automatic camera flashes have made enforcement challenging. Consequently, since February 25, 2010, all public photography, videotaping, and filming within the exhibition areas has been prohibited.

input: The FAA has been cited as an example of regulatory capture, "in which the airline industry openly dictates to its regulators its governing rules, arranging for not only beneficial regulation, but placing key people to head these regulators." Retired NASA Office of Inspector General Senior Special Agent Joseph Gutheinz, who used to be a Special Agent with the Office of Inspector General for the Department of Transportation and with FAA Security, is one of the most outspoken critics of FAA. Rather than commend the agency for proposing a $10.2 million fine against Southwest Airlines for its failure to conduct mandatory inspections in 2008, he was quoted as saying the following in an Associated Press story: "Penalties against airlines that violate FAA directives should be stiffer. At $25,000 per violation, Gutheinz said, airlines can justify rolling the dice and taking the chance on getting caught. He also said the FAA is often too quick to bend to pressure from airlines and pilots." Other experts have been critical of the constraints and expectations under which the FAA is expected to operate. The dual role of encouraging aerospace travel and regulating aerospace travel are contradictory. For example, to levy a heavy penalty upon an airline for violating an FAA regulation which would impact their ability to continue operating would not be considered encouraging aerospace travel.
rewrite: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is frequently presented as a case of regulatory capture. Critics argue the airline industry effectively dictates its own governing rules to its regulators, securing favorable policies and even placing key individuals in leadership roles. Among the most vocal detractors is Joseph Gutheinz, a retired NASA Office of Inspector General Senior Special Agent with prior experience as a Special Agent for the Department of Transportation’s Office of Inspector General and FAA Security. When the FAA proposed a $10.2 million fine against Southwest Airlines in 2008 for skipping mandatory inspections, Gutheinz did not offer praise. In an Associated Press report, he contended that penalties for violating FAA directives remain insufficient. At a rate of $25,000 per violation, he argued, airlines may calculate the risk and choose to chance detection. Gutheinz further stated the agency is too prone to yield to pressure from airlines and pilots. This criticism extends to the FAA’s fundamental operating mandate. Experts note the contradictory dual mission of both promoting and regulating aerospace travel. For instance, imposing a severe penalty that could threaten an airline’s operational viability would conflict with the goal of encouraging the industry. This inherent conflict underscores the constraints shaping the FAA’s actions.

input: Plymouth has the first known reference to Jews in the South West from Sir Francis Drake's voyages in 1577 to 1580, as his log mentioned "Moses the Jew" – a man from Plymouth. The Plymouth Synagogue is a Listed Grade II* building, built in 1762 and is the oldest Ashkenazi Synagogue in the English speaking world. There are also places of worship for Islam, Bahá'í, Buddhism, Unitarianism, Chinese beliefs and Humanism.
rewrite: The earliest known reference to Jews in the South West dates from Sir Francis Drake's 1577–1580 voyages, noting "Moses the Jew" from Plymouth in his log. Built in 1762, the Plymouth Synagogue is a Grade II* listed building and the oldest Ashkenazi synagogue in the English-speaking world. The city also hosts places of worship for Islam, Bahá'í, Buddhism, Unitarianism, Chinese beliefs, and Humanism.

input: In several countries, like Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Turkey, institutes of technology and polytechnics are institutions of higher education, and have been accredited to award academic degrees and doctorates. Famous examples are the Istanbul Technical University, ETH Zurich, İYTE, Delft University of Technology and RWTH Aachen, all considered universities.[citation needed]
rewrite: Institutions of higher education such as institutes of technology and polytechnics exist in countries including Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Turkey. Accredited to grant academic degrees and doctorates, notable examples are Istanbul Technical University, ETH Zurich, İYTE, Delft University of Technology, and RWTH Aachen, all regarded as universities.

input: The Licchavi era was followed by the Malla era. Rulers from Tirhut, upon being attacked by Muslims, fled north to the Kathmandu valley. They intermarried with Nepali royalty, and this led to the Malla era. The early years of the Malla era were turbulent, with raids and attacks from Khas and Turk Muslims. There was also a devastating earthquake which claimed the lives of a third of Kathmandu's population, including the king Abhaya Malla. These disasters led to the destruction of most of the architecture of the Licchavi era (such as Mangriha and Kailashkut Bhawan), and the loss of literature collected in various monasteries within the city. Despite the initial hardships, Kathmandu rose to prominence again and, during most of the Malla era, dominated the trade between India and Tibet. Nepali currency became the standard currency in trans-Himalayan trade.
rewrite: Following the Licchavi era, the Malla period began after rulers from Tirhut, fleeing Muslim attacks, migrated north to the Kathmandu valley and intermarried with local royalty. This new era commenced under turbulent conditions, marked by raids from Khas and Turk Muslim forces. A devastating earthquake further crippled the valley, killing a third of Kathmandu's population, including King Abhaya Malla. These calamities destroyed much Licchavi architecture, like Mangriha and Kailashkut Bhawan, and caused the loss of monastic literature. Despite these initial hardships, Kathmandu eventually regained prominence. For most of the Malla era, it dominated trade between India and Tibet, with Nepali currency becoming the standard for trans-Himalayan commerce.

input: In February 2010 Shell and Cosan formed a 50:50 joint-venture, Raízen, comprising all of Cosan's Brazilian ethanol, energy generation, fuel distribution and sugar activities, and all of Shell's Brazilian retail fuel and aviation distribution businesses. In March 2010, Shell announced the sale of some of its assets, including its liquid petroleum gas (LPG) business, to meet the cost of a planned $28bn capital spending programme. Shell invited buyers to submit indicative bids, due by 22 March, with a plan to raise $2–3bn from the sale. In June 2010, Royal Dutch Shell agreed to acquire all the business of East Resources for a cash consideration of $4.7 billion. The transaction included East Resources' tight gas fields.
rewrite: In March 2010, Shell announced asset sales, including its LPG business, to fund a $28bn capital spending plan. Buyers were invited to submit indicative bids by March 22, aiming to raise $2–3bn. Earlier, in February 2010, Shell and Cosan had established Raízen, a 50:50 joint venture. This entity included all of Cosan's Brazilian operations in ethanol, energy generation, fuel distribution, and sugar, alongside all of Shell's Brazilian retail fuel and aviation distribution businesses. Subsequently, in June 2010, Royal Dutch Shell agreed to purchase East Resources entirely for $4.7 billion in cash, a transaction that incorporated East Resources' tight gas fields.

input: Near the end of the NES's lifespan, upon the release of the AV Famicom and the top-loading NES 2, the design of the game controllers was modified slightly. Though the original button layout was retained, the redesigned device abandoned the brick shell in favor of a dog bone shape. In addition, the AV Famicom joined its international counterpart and dropped the hardwired controllers in favor of detachable controller ports. However, the controllers included with the Famicom AV had cables which were 90 cm (3 feet) long, as opposed to the standard 180 cm(6 feet) of NES controllers.
rewrite: Late in the NES era, with the launch of the AV Famicom and NES 2, the game controllers underwent a modest redesign. The original button layout remained, but the brick-like shell was replaced by a dog bone shape. Furthermore, the AV Famicom adopted detachable controller ports, aligning with its international version. Despite this update, the cables on its controllers measured only 90 cm (3 feet), half the length of the standard 180 cm (6 feet) cables used for NES controllers.

input: Centered on Post Oak Boulevard and Westheimer Road, the Uptown District boomed during the 1970s and early 1980s when a collection of mid-rise office buildings, hotels, and retail developments appeared along Interstate 610 west. Uptown became one of the most prominent instances of an edge city. The tallest building in Uptown is the 64-floor, 901-foot (275 m)-tall, Philip Johnson and John Burgee designed landmark Williams Tower (known as the Transco Tower until 1999). At the time of construction, it was believed to be the world's tallest skyscraper outside of a central business district. The new 20-story Skanska building and BBVA Compass Plaza are the newest office buildings built in Uptown after 30 years. The Uptown District is also home to buildings designed by noted architects I. M. Pei, César Pelli, and Philip Johnson. In the late 1990s and early 2000s decade, there was a mini-boom of mid-rise and high-rise residential tower construction, with several over 30 stories tall. Since 2000 more than 30 high-rise buildings have gone up in Houston; all told, 72 high-rises tower over the city, which adds up to about 8,300 units. In 2002, Uptown had more than 23 million square feet (2,100,000 m²) of office space with 16 million square feet (1,500,000 m²) of Class A office space.
rewrite:
The Uptown District, centered on Post Oak Boulevard and Westheimer Road, experienced its initial boom in the 1970s and early 1980s. This period saw a collection of mid-rise offices, hotels, and retail developments emerge along Interstate 610 west, establishing Uptown as one of the most prominent examples of an edge city. Its architectural landscape features works by noted architects like I. M. Pei, César Pelli, and Philip Johnson. The tallest of these is the Philip Johnson and John Burgee-designed Williams Tower, a 64-floor, 901-foot (275 m) landmark known as the Transco Tower until 1999. Upon completion, it was considered the world's tallest skyscraper outside a central business district.

Following a 30-year gap, new office construction resumed with additions like the 20-story Skanska building and BBVA Compass Plaza. The late 1990s and early 2000s witnessed a mini-boom of residential towers, including several over 30 stories. Since the year 2000, Houston has added more than 30 high-rise buildings, contributing to a total of 72 such structures with approximately 8,300 units. By 2002, the Uptown District contained over 23 million square feet (2,100,000 m²) of office space, of which 16 million square feet (1,500,000 m²) was Class A.

input: The Communist Party of China, founded in 1920, adopted the red flag and hammer and sickle emblem of the Soviet Union, which became the national symbols when the Party took power in China in 1949. Under Party leader Mao Zedong, the Party anthem became "The East Is Red", and Mao Zedong himself was sometimes referred to as a "red sun". During the Cultural Revolution in China, Party ideology was enforced by the Red Guards, and the sayings of Mao Zedong were published as a small red book in hundreds of millions of copies. Today the Communist Party of China claims to be the largest political party in the world, with eighty million members.
rewrite: Founded in 1920, the Communist Party of China initially adopted the Soviet Union's red flag and hammer and sickle emblem. These symbols were later established as national emblems when the Party assumed power in 1949. Under the leadership of Mao Zedong, "The East Is Red" served as the Party anthem, and Mao was occasionally likened to a "red sun." The subsequent Cultural Revolution saw Party ideology enforced by the Red Guards, while Mao's quotations were disseminated globally in hundreds of millions of copies of the small red book. Currently, with eighty million members, the Communist Party of China identifies itself as the world's largest political party.

input: Manifold vacuum can be used to drive accessories on automobiles. The best-known application is the vacuum servo, used to provide power assistance for the brakes. Obsolete applications include vacuum-driven windscreen wipers and Autovac fuel pumps. Some aircraft instruments (Attitude Indicator (AI) and the Heading Indicator (HI)) are typically vacuum-powered, as protection against loss of all (electrically powered) instruments, since early aircraft often did not have electrical systems, and since there are two readily available sources of vacuum on a moving aircraft—the engine and an external venturi. Vacuum induction melting uses electromagnetic induction within a vacuum.
rewrite: Vacuum from an engine manifold can power various automotive accessories. Most notably, it operates the vacuum servo for brake assistance. Past uses included windscreen wipers and Autovac fuel pumps. In aircraft, instruments like the Attitude and Heading Indicators often rely on vacuum as a safeguard against electrical failure. This practice dates from early planes lacking electrical systems, utilizing available vacuum from engines or external venturis. Separately, vacuum induction melting employs electromagnetic induction in a vacuum environment.

input: Sanskrit, as defined by Pāṇini, evolved out of the earlier Vedic form. The present form of Vedic Sanskrit can be traced back to as early as the second millennium BCE (for Rig-vedic). Scholars often distinguish Vedic Sanskrit and Classical or "Pāṇinian" Sanskrit as separate dialects. Though they are quite similar, they differ in a number of essential points of phonology, vocabulary, grammar and syntax. Vedic Sanskrit is the language of the Vedas, a large collection of hymns, incantations (Samhitas) and theological and religio-philosophical discussions in the Brahmanas and Upanishads. Modern linguists consider the metrical hymns of the Rigveda Samhita to be the earliest, composed by many authors over several centuries of oral tradition. The end of the Vedic period is marked by the composition of the Upanishads, which form the concluding part of the traditional Vedic corpus; however, the early Sutras are Vedic, too, both in language and content.
rewrite: Sanskrit, in its Classical or "Pāṇinian" form described by Pāṇini, developed from an earlier Vedic stage. While scholars typically treat Vedic Sanskrit and Classical Sanskrit as distinct dialects due to differences in phonology, vocabulary, grammar, and syntax, they remain fundamentally similar. Vedic Sanskrit is the language of the Vedas, which include a vast collection of hymns, incantations (Samhitas), and theological discussions found in the Brahmanas and Upanishads. Linguists regard the metrical hymns of the Rigveda Samhita as the earliest of these texts, composed by numerous authors over centuries of oral tradition dating back to at least the second millennium BCE. The Vedic period concluded with the composition of the Upanishads, which complete the traditional Vedic corpus; the early Sutras are also considered Vedic in both language and content.

input: Another 44 million acres (18 million hectares) are owned by 12 regional, and scores of local, Native corporations created under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA) of 1971. Regional Native corporation Doyon, Limited often promotes itself as the largest private landowner in Alaska in advertisements and other communications. Provisions of ANCSA allowing the corporations' land holdings to be sold on the open market starting in 1991 were repealed before they could take effect. Effectively, the corporations hold title (including subsurface title in many cases, a privilege denied to individual Alaskans) but cannot sell the land. Individual Native allotments can be and are sold on the open market, however.
rewrite: Under the 1971 Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA), 12 regional and numerous local Native corporations hold title to another 44 million acres (18 million hectares). Doyon, Limited, a regional corporation, frequently advertises itself as Alaska's largest private landowner. While these corporations possess title—often including subsurface rights, a privilege not granted to individual Alaskans—they cannot sell the land. Provisions that would have allowed such sales starting in 1991 were repealed beforehand. In contrast, individual Native allotments can be and are sold on the open market.

input: Following the defeat in World War I, influence of German-speaking elites over Central and Eastern Europe was greatly limited. At the treaty of Versailles Germany was substantially reduced in size. Austria-Hungary was split up. Rump-Austria, which to a certain extent corresponded to the German-speaking areas of Austria-Hungary (a complete split into language groups was impossible due to multi-lingual areas and language-exclaves) adopted the name "German-Austria" (German: Deutschösterreich). The name German-Austria was forbidden by the victorious powers of World War I. Volga Germans living in the Soviet Union were interned in gulags or forcibly relocated during the Second World War.
rewrite: After World War I, the power of German-speaking elites across Central and Eastern Europe sharply declined. The Treaty of Versailles significantly reduced Germany's territory, while Austria-Hungary was dissolved. Its remnant, largely aligning with the German-speaking regions though a clean linguistic division proved impossible, initially took the name "German-Austria." This designation was later prohibited by the victorious Allied powers. Additionally, during World War II, the Soviet Union interned or forcibly relocated ethnic Germans from the Volga region.

input: Ibn Sīnā wrote extensively on early Islamic philosophy, especially the subjects logic, ethics, and metaphysics, including treatises named Logic and Metaphysics. Most of his works were written in Arabic – then the language of science in the Middle East – and some in Persian. Of linguistic significance even to this day are a few books that he wrote in nearly pure Persian language (particularly the Danishnamah-yi 'Ala', Philosophy for Ala' ad-Dawla'). Ibn Sīnā's commentaries on Aristotle often criticized the philosopher,[citation needed] encouraging a lively debate in the spirit of ijtihad.
rewrite: Ibn Sīnā authored numerous works on early Islamic philosophy, focusing on logic, ethics, and metaphysics, with titles such as *Logic* and *Metaphysics*. While most were composed in Arabic—the scientific lingua franca of the Middle East—some were written in Persian. A few books, like the *Danishnamah-yi 'Ala'*, are linguistically notable for their use of nearly pure Persian. His commentaries on Aristotle frequently offered criticism, fostering a vigorous spirit of ijtihad through debate.

input: From the German point of view, March 1941 saw an improvement. The Luftwaffe flew 4,000 sorties that month, including 12 major and three heavy attacks. The electronic war intensified but the Luftwaffe flew major inland missions only on moonlit nights. Ports were easier to find and made better targets. To confuse the British, radio silence was observed until the bombs fell. X- and Y-Gerät beams were placed over false targets and switched only at the last minute. Rapid frequency changes were introduced for X-Gerät, whose wider band of frequencies and greater tactical flexibility ensured it remained effective at a time when British selective jamming was degrading the effectiveness of Y-Gerät.
rewrite: From the German perspective, conditions improved in March 1941. That month, the Luftwaffe conducted 4,000 sorties, featuring 12 major and three heavy attacks. While the electronic conflict escalated, major inland raids were restricted to moonlit nights. Ports, being easier to locate, became preferred targets. To deceive the British, radio silence was maintained until bomb release. X- and Y-Gerät beams were directed over false locations, shifting only at the final moment. For X-Gerät, rapid frequency changes were adopted; its broader frequency band and superior tactical flexibility allowed it to stay effective as British selective jamming reduced the utility of Y-Gerät.

input: President Benito Juárez was re-elected in the general election of 1867 in which he received strong liberal support, especially in Chihuahua. Luis Terrazas was confirmed by the people of Chihuahua to be governor of the state. But soon after the election, President Juárez had another crisis on his hands; the Juárez administration was suspected to be involved in the assassination of the military chief José María Patoni executed by General Canto in August 1868. General Canto turned himself over to Donato Guerra. Canto was sentenced to death, but later his sentence changed to 10 years imprisonment. The sense of injustice gave rise to a new rebellion in 1869 that threatened the federal government. In response, the Juárez administration took drastic measures by temporarily suspending constitutional rights, but the governor of Chihuahua did not support this action. Hostilities continued to increase especially after the election of 1871 which was perceived to be fraudulent. A new popular leader arose among the rebels, Porfirio Díaz. The federal government was successful in quelling rebellions in Durango an Chihuahua. On July 18, 1872, President Juárez died from a heart attack; soon after, many of his supporters ceased the fighting. Peace returned to Chihuahua and the new government was led by Governor Antonio Ochoa (formerly a co-owner of the Batopilas silver mines) in 1873 after Luis Terrazas finished his term in 1872.
rewrite:
Following his re-election in 1867, President Benito Juárez enjoyed robust liberal backing, particularly in Chihuahua, where Luis Terrazas was confirmed as governor. This political stability was soon disrupted, however, by a crisis emerging in August 1868. The Juárez administration faced allegations of involvement in the assassination of military chief José María Patoni, carried out by General Canto. After surrendering to Donato Guerra, Canto initially received a death sentence, later commuted to ten years' imprisonment. This outcome fostered a widespread sense of injustice, sparking a new rebellion in 1869 that directly challenged federal authority.

To confront the threat, the Juárez administration enacted drastic measures, including the temporary suspension of constitutional rights—a move opposed by Governor Terrazas of Chihuahua. Tensions escalated further following the contentious 1871 election, widely viewed as fraudulent, which galvanized the rebels under a new popular leader, Porfirio Díaz. Although federal forces succeeded in suppressing uprisings in Durango and Chihuahua, the conflict persisted until President Juárez’s death from a heart attack on July 18, 1872. His passing prompted many supporters to lay down their arms.

Peace was subsequently restored to Chihuahua. After Luis Terrazas concluded his term in 1872, the new state government was led by Governor Antonio Ochoa in 1873, a former co-owner of the Batopilas silver mines.

input: After the war, Nasser returned to his role as an instructor at the Royal Military Academy. He sent emissaries to forge an alliance with the Muslim Brotherhood in October 1948, but soon concluded that the religious agenda of the Brotherhood was not compatible with his nationalism. From then on, Nasser prevented the Brotherhood's influence over his cadres' activities without severing ties with the organization. Nasser was sent as a member of the Egyptian delegation to Rhodes in February 1949 to negotiate a formal armistice with Israel, and reportedly considered the terms to be humiliating, particularly because the Israelis were able to easily occupy the Eilat region while negotiating with the Arabs in March.
rewrite: Following the war, Nasser resumed his position as an instructor at the Royal Military Academy. In October 1948, he dispatched emissaries to form an alliance with the Muslim Brotherhood, yet he quickly determined that their religious agenda conflicted with his nationalist views. Consequently, he acted to block the Brotherhood's influence over his cadres without cutting off relations entirely. By February 1949, Nasser was part of the Egyptian delegation sent to Rhodes to negotiate a formal armistice with Israel. He reportedly found the terms humiliating, especially due to Israel's easy occupation of the Eilat region during the talks with Arab representatives in March.

input: Monopole antennas consist of a single radiating element such as a metal rod, often mounted over a conducting surface, a ground plane. One side of the feedline from the receiver or transmitter is connected to the rod, and the other side to the ground plane, which may be the Earth. The most common form is the quarter-wave monopole which is one-quarter of a wavelength long and has a gain of 5.12 dBi when mounted over a ground plane. Monopoles have an omnidirectional radiation pattern, so they are used for broad coverage of an area, and have vertical polarization. The ground waves used for broadcasting at low frequencies must be vertically polarized, so large vertical monopole antennas are used for broadcasting in the MF, LF, and VLF bands. Small monopoles are used as nondirectional antennas on portable radios in the HF, VHF, and UHF bands.
rewrite: A monopole antenna features a single radiating element, typically a metal rod, positioned above a conducting ground plane. The feedline connects the rod on one side and the ground plane—which can be the Earth itself—on the other. Its most widespread version is the quarter-wave monopole, measuring one-quarter of a wavelength in length and achieving a gain of 5.12 dBi over a ground plane. These antennas exhibit an omnidirectional radiation pattern with vertical polarization, making them ideal for broad area coverage. This vertical polarization is essential for the ground waves utilized in low-frequency broadcasting. Consequently, large vertical monopoles are employed in the MF, LF, and VLF broadcast bands. Smaller versions serve as nondirectional antennas on portable radios operating within the HF, VHF, and UHF bands.

input: The official English name of the system is BeiDou Navigation Satellite System. It is named after the Big Dipper constellation, which is known in Chinese as Běidǒu. The name literally means "Northern Dipper", the name given by ancient Chinese astronomers to the seven brightest stars of the Ursa Major constellation. Historically, this set of stars was used in navigation to locate the North Star Polaris. As such, the name BeiDou also serves as a metaphor for the purpose of the satellite navigation system.
rewrite: Officially called the BeiDou Navigation Satellite System, it derives its name from the Big Dipper, known in Chinese as Běidǒu or "Northern Dipper." Ancient Chinese astronomers gave this title to the seven brightest stars of Ursa Major. Historically, these stars guided navigators to Polaris, the North Star. Thus, the name BeiDou metaphorically reflects the system's own purpose: to provide direction.

input: Luís Cabral, brother of Amílcar and co-founder of PAIGC, was appointed the first President of Guinea-Bissau. Following independence, the PAIGC killed thousands of local Guinean soldiers who had fought along with the Portuguese Army against guerrillas. Some escaped to settle in Portugal or other African nations. One of the massacres occurred in the town of Bissorã. In 1980 the PAIGC acknowledged in its newspaper Nó Pintcha (dated 29 November 1980) that many Gueinean soldiers had been executed and buried in unmarked collective graves in the woods of Cumerá, Portogole, and Mansabá.
rewrite: Luís Cabral, who co-founded PAIGC with his brother Amílcar, became Guinea-Bissau’s first President. After independence, the PAIGC killed thousands of local Guinean soldiers who had sided with the Portuguese Army against the guerrillas; some survivors fled to Portugal or other African nations. A massacre occurred in Bissorã. Later, in 1980, the PAIGC admitted in its newspaper Nó Pintcha (29 November) that many such soldiers had been executed and buried in unmarked mass graves in the woods of Cumerá, Portogole, and Mansabá.

input: In the Battle of Cowan's Ford, Cornwallis met resistance along the banks of the Catawba River at Cowan's Ford on February 1, 1781, in an attempt to engage General Morgan's forces during a tactical withdrawal. Morgan had moved to the northern part of the state to combine with General Greene's newly recruited forces. Generals Greene and Cornwallis finally met at the Battle of Guilford Courthouse in present-day Greensboro on March 15, 1781. Although the British troops held the field at the end of the battle, their casualties at the hands of the numerically superior Continental Army were crippling. Following this "Pyrrhic victory", Cornwallis chose to move to the Virginia coastline to get reinforcements, and to allow the Royal Navy to protect his battered army. This decision would result in Cornwallis' eventual defeat at Yorktown, Virginia, later in 1781. The Patriots' victory there guaranteed American independence.
rewrite: On February 1, 1781, Cornwallis encountered resistance at Cowan’s Ford along the Catawba River, aiming to intercept General Morgan’s forces during a tactical withdrawal. Morgan had withdrawn northward to join General Greene’s newly recruited army. The two opposing commanders, Greene and Cornwallis, finally faced one another at the Battle of Guilford Courthouse on March 15, 1781, near present-day Greensboro. While British forces held the field after the battle, they suffered crippling casualties against the larger Continental Army. In the wake of this Pyrrhic victory, Cornwallis decided to move his battered army to the Virginia coastline. His objectives were to secure reinforcements and Royal Navy protection. This strategic choice, however, led to his eventual defeat at Yorktown, Virginia, later that same year. The Patriot victory at Yorktown ultimately guaranteed American independence.
