input: Having been capital of a vast pre-Hispanic empire, and also the capital of richest viceroyalty within the Spanish Empire (ruling over a vast territory in the Americas and Spanish West Indies), and, finally, the capital of the United Mexican States, Mexico City has a rich history of artistic expression. Since the mesoamerican pre-Classical period the inhabitants of the settlements around Lake Texcoco produced many works of art and complex craftsmanship, some of which are today displayed at the world-renowned National Museum of Anthropology and the Templo Mayor museum. While many pieces of pottery and stone-engraving have survived, the great majority of the Amerindian iconography was destroyed during the Conquest of Mexico.
rewrite: Mexico City boasts a rich history of artistic expression, having served as the capital of a vast pre-Hispanic empire, the wealthiest viceroyalty in the Spanish Empire, and finally the modern Mexican state. Since the Mesoamerican pre-Classical period, inhabitants around Lake Texcoco produced complex artworks and craftsmanship. Many surviving pieces of pottery and stone-engravings are displayed at the National Museum of Anthropology and the Templo Mayor museum. However, the great majority of Amerindian iconography was lost during the Conquest of Mexico.

input: In 1853, Victoria gave birth to her eighth child, Leopold, with the aid of the new anaesthetic, chloroform. Victoria was so impressed by the relief it gave from the pain of childbirth that she used it again in 1857 at the birth of her ninth and final child, Beatrice, despite opposition from members of the clergy, who considered it against biblical teaching, and members of the medical profession, who thought it dangerous. Victoria may have suffered from post-natal depression after many of her pregnancies. Letters from Albert to Victoria intermittently complain of her loss of self-control. For example, about a month after Leopold's birth Albert complained in a letter to Victoria about her "continuance of hysterics" over a "miserable trifle".
rewrite: In 1853, Queen Victoria received chloroform during the birth of her eighth child, Leopold, a new anaesthetic that greatly relieved her pain. So profound was her appreciation that she used it again in 1857 for the birth of her ninth and final child, Beatrice. This occurred despite objections from clergy, who deemed it biblically unsound, and from some medical professionals, who considered it risky. Victoria may have experienced post-natal depression following several pregnancies. Correspondence from Prince Albert intermittently references her loss of composure; for instance, roughly a month after Leopold's birth, he wrote to complain of her "continuance of hysterics" over a minor issue.

input: In 1978, Hayek came into conflict with the Liberal Party leader, David Steel, who claimed that liberty was possible only with "social justice and an equitable distribution of wealth and power, which in turn require a degree of active government intervention" and that the Conservative Party were more concerned with the connection between liberty and private enterprise than between liberty and democracy. Hayek claimed that a limited democracy might be better than other forms of limited government at protecting liberty but that an unlimited democracy was worse than other forms of unlimited government because "its government loses the power even to do what it thinks right if any group on which its majority depends thinks otherwise".
rewrite: In 1978, Hayek disputed Liberal Party leader David Steel’s assertion that liberty depended on social justice and a fair distribution of wealth and power, which he argued necessitated active government intervention. Steel also contended that the Conservatives prioritized the link between liberty and private enterprise over that between liberty and democracy. Hayek countered that while a limited democracy could safeguard liberty better than other constrained governments, an unlimited democracy was more dangerous than other absolute regimes. He warned that in such a system, the government becomes powerless to act rightly if any group essential to its majority disagrees.

input: Since the early history of the United States, Amerindians, African–Americans, and European Americans have been classified as belonging to different races. Efforts to track mixing between groups led to a proliferation of categories, such as mulatto and octoroon. The criteria for membership in these races diverged in the late 19th century. During Reconstruction, increasing numbers of Americans began to consider anyone with "one drop" of known "Black blood" to be Black, regardless of appearance.3 By the early 20th century, this notion was made statutory in many states.4 Amerindians continue to be defined by a certain percentage of "Indian blood" (called blood quantum). To be White one had to have perceived "pure" White ancestry. The one-drop rule or hypodescent rule refers to the convention of defining a person as racially black if he or she has any known African ancestry. This rule meant that those that were mixed race but with some discernible African ancestry were defined as black. The one-drop rule is specific to not only those with African ancestry but to the United States, making it a particularly African-American experience.
rewrite: From the nation's earliest days, classifications divided people into distinct races such as Amerindian, African-American, and European American. This drive to categorize lineage spurred a multiplication of labels like mulatto and octoroon. However, the standards for belonging to these racial groups shifted significantly by the late 19th century. The period of Reconstruction saw a growing acceptance of the "one-drop" rule, where any known "Black blood" meant an individual was considered Black, irrespective of their physical appearance. This notion became codified into law across numerous states in the early 20th century. In contrast, Amerindian identity often relied on a specified "blood quantum," or percentage of "Indian blood." Meanwhile, being classified as White required perceived "pure" White ancestry. Known formally as the rule of hypodescent, the one-drop convention defined a person as Black if they possessed any known African ancestry, thereby assigning mixed-race individuals with discernible African roots to a Black identity. This rule is uniquely tied to both African ancestry and the United States, rendering it a distinctly African-American historical experience.

input: After the expulsion of the German population ethnic Russians, Belarusians, and Ukrainians were settled in the northern part. In the Soviet part of the region, a policy of eliminating all remnants of German history was pursued. All German place names were replaced by new Russian names. The exclave was a military zone, which was closed to foreigners; Soviet citizens could only enter with special permission. In 1967 the remnants of Königsberg Castle were demolished on the orders of Leonid Brezhnev to make way for a new "House of the Soviets".
rewrite: Following the removal of the German population, ethnic Russians, Belarusians, and Ukrainians were resettled in the north. Within the Soviet portion, authorities enacted a policy to erase all traces of German heritage, replacing every German place name with new Russian ones. The exclave, a restricted military zone, barred foreigners and required special permission for Soviet citizens to enter. In 1967, by order of Leonid Brezhnev, the remains of Königsberg Castle were destroyed to clear ground for the new "House of the Soviets."

input: The College of Arts and Letters was established as the university's first college in 1842 with the first degrees given in 1849. The university's first academic curriculum was modeled after the Jesuit Ratio Studiorum from Saint Louis University. Today the college, housed in O'Shaughnessy Hall, includes 20 departments in the areas of fine arts, humanities, and social sciences, and awards Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degrees in 33 majors, making it the largest of the university's colleges. There are around 2,500 undergraduates and 750 graduates enrolled in the college.
rewrite: Founded in 1842 as the university's inaugural college, the College of Arts and Letters first conferred degrees in 1849. Its original curriculum followed the Jesuit Ratio Studiorum from Saint Louis University. Now located in O'Shaughnessy Hall, it encompasses 20 departments across fine arts, humanities, and social sciences. As the largest college at the university, it offers Bachelor of Arts degrees in 33 majors to approximately 2,500 undergraduates and 750 graduate students.

input: Ann Arbor has a council-manager form of government. The City Council has 11 voting members: the mayor and 10 city council members. The mayor and city council members serve two-year terms: the mayor is elected every even-numbered year, while half of the city council members are up for election annually (five in even-numbered and five in odd-numbered years). Two council members are elected from each of the city's five wards. The mayor is elected citywide. The mayor is the presiding officer of the City Council and has the power to appoint all Council committee members as well as board and commission members, with the approval of the City Council. The current mayor of Ann Arbor is Christopher Taylor, a Democrat who was elected as mayor in 2014. Day-to-day city operations are managed by a city administrator chosen by the city council.
rewrite: Ann Arbor operates under a council-manager system. Its City Council consists of 11 voting members: the mayor and 10 council members, all serving two-year terms. The mayor is elected citywide in even-numbered years. Council members are elected from each of the city's five wards, with two representatives per ward. Elections for these seats are staggered, with five members chosen in even-numbered years and five in odd-numbered years. As presiding officer, the mayor appoints all Council committee members and board and commission members, subject to Council approval. Day-to-day municipal operations are overseen by a city administrator selected by the council. The current mayor is Christopher Taylor, a Democrat first elected to the position in 2014.

input: During the Hundred Years' War, the army of the Duke of Burgundy and a force of about two hundred English soldiers occupied Paris from May 1420 until 1436. They repelled an attempt by Joan of Arc to liberate the city in 1429. A century later, during the French Wars of Religion, Paris was a stronghold of the Catholic League. On 24 August 1572, Paris was the site of the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre, when thousands of French Protestants were killed. The last of these wars, the eighth one, ended in 1594, after Henri IV had converted to Catholicism and was finally able to enter Paris as he supposedly declared Paris vaut bien une messe ("Paris is well worth a Mass"). The city had been neglected for decades; by the time of his assassination in 1610, Henry IV had rebuilt the Pont Neuf, the first Paris bridge with sidewalks and not lined with buildings, linked with a new wing the Louvre to the Tuileries Palace, and created the first Paris residential square, the Place Royale, now Place des Vosges.
rewrite: From May 1420 until 1436, Paris was held by the Duke of Burgundy’s army alongside roughly two hundred English soldiers during the Hundred Years' War. In 1429, they successfully turned back an assault led by Joan of Arc aiming to free the city. Centuries later, during the French Wars of Religion, Paris served as a bastion for the Catholic League. The city witnessed the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre on 24 August 1572, where thousands of French Protestants lost their lives. The eighth and final war concluded in 1594 after Henri IV converted to Catholicism, famously remarking that "Paris is well worth a Mass," which allowed his entry. Having suffered decades of neglect, Paris underwent renewal under Henry IV before his assassination in 1610. His projects included constructing the Pont Neuf, the first bridge with sidewalks and free of buildings, connecting the Louvre to the Tuileries Palace with a new wing, and establishing the inaugural residential square, the Place Royale, known today as the Place des Vosges.

input: The name Montana comes from the Spanish word Montaña, meaning "mountain", or more broadly, "mountainous country". Montaña del Norte was the name given by early Spanish explorers to the entire mountainous region of the west. The name Montana was added to a bill by the United States House Committee on Territories, which was chaired at the time by Rep. James Ashley of Ohio, for the territory that would become Idaho Territory. The name was successfully changed by Representatives Henry Wilson (Massachusetts) and Benjamin F. Harding (Oregon), who complained that Montana had "no meaning". When Ashley presented a bill to establish a temporary government in 1864 for a new territory to be carved out of Idaho, he again chose Montana Territory. This time Rep. Samuel Cox, also of Ohio, objected to the name. Cox complained that the name was a misnomer given that most of the territory was not mountainous and that a Native American name would be more appropriate than a Spanish one. Other names such as Shoshone were suggested, but it was eventually decided that the Committee on Territories could name it whatever they wanted, so the original name of Montana was adopted.
rewrite: Derived from the Spanish word *Montaña*, meaning "mountain" or "mountainous country," the name Montana traces back to early Spanish explorers who called the western mountainous region *Montaña del Norte*. When establishing a territory that would become Idaho, the U.S. House Committee on Territories, chaired by Ohio Rep. James Ashley, inserted "Montana" into a bill. However, Representatives Henry Wilson of Massachusetts and Benjamin F. Harding of Oregon succeeded in changing it, arguing the word had "no meaning." In 1864, Ashley proposed another bill to form a new territory from Idaho, once more selecting Montana. Ohio Rep. Samuel Cox now objected, calling it a misnomer since much of the land was not mountainous and suggesting a Native American name like Shoshone would be preferable. Despite these disputes, it was ultimately decided the Committee on Territories held the naming authority, leading to the adoption of the original name, Montana.

input: The Old Swiss Confederacy had acquired a reputation of invincibility during these earlier wars, but expansion of the federation suffered a setback in 1515 with the Swiss defeat in the Battle of Marignano. This ended the so-called "heroic" epoch of Swiss history. The success of Zwingli's Reformation in some cantons led to inter-cantonal religious conflicts in 1529 and 1531 (Wars of Kappel). It was not until more than one hundred years after these internal wars that, in 1648, under the Peace of Westphalia, European countries recognized Switzerland's independence from the Holy Roman Empire and its neutrality.
rewrite: During the earlier wars, the Old Swiss Confederacy gained a reputation for invincibility. However, the federation's expansion faced a setback following the Swiss defeat at the Battle of Marignano in 1515, which concluded the "heroic" epoch of Swiss history. Inter-cantonal religious conflicts arose in 1529 and 1531, known as the Wars of Kappel, spurred by Zwingli's Reformation. Only over a century later, in 1648, did the Peace of Westphalia lead European countries to recognize Switzerland's independence from the Holy Roman Empire and its neutrality.

input: The period between the foundation of the Han dynasty and Wang Mang's reign is known as the Western Han dynasty (simplified Chinese: 西汉; traditional Chinese: 西漢; pinyin: Xī Hàn) or Former Han dynasty (simplified Chinese: 前汉; traditional Chinese: 前漢; pinyin: Qiánhàn) (206 BC – 9 AD). During this period the capital was at Chang'an (modern Xi'an). From the reign of Guangwu the capital was moved eastward to Luoyang. The era from his reign until the fall of Han is known as the Eastern Han dynasty (simplified Chinese: 东汉; traditional Chinese: 東漢; pinyin: Dōng Hàn) or the Later Han dynasty (simplified Chinese: 后汉; traditional Chinese: 後漢; pinyin: Hòu Hàn) (25–220 AD).
rewrite: Stretching from 206 BC to 9 AD, the era from the Han dynasty's founding until Wang Mang's reign is called the Western or Former Han dynasty (西汉/西漢, Xī Hàn; 前汉/前漢, Qiánhàn). Its capital was situated at Chang'an, present-day Xi'an. Following the reign of Guangwu, the capital shifted eastward to Luoyang. The subsequent period from his rule until the dynasty's collapse, from 25 to 220 AD, is referred to as the Eastern or Later Han dynasty (东汉/東漢, Dōng Hàn; 后汉/後漢, Hòu Hàn).

input: The sociology of culture grew from the intersection between sociology (as shaped by early theorists like Marx, Durkheim, and Weber) with the growing discipline of anthropology, where in researchers pioneered ethnographic strategies for describing and analyzing a variety of cultures around the world. Part of the legacy of the early development of the field lingers in the methods (much of cultural sociological research is qualitative), in the theories (a variety of critical approaches to sociology are central to current research communities), and in the substantive focus of the field. For instance, relationships between popular culture, political control, and social class were early and lasting concerns in the field.
rewrite: Emerging from the intersection of sociology—informed by foundational figures like Marx, Durkheim, and Weber—and the developing field of anthropology, the sociology of culture incorporated ethnographic methods for analyzing diverse societies. This early formation left a lasting imprint on the discipline. Its methods remain largely qualitative, while its theories often employ critical approaches central to contemporary research. The field's substantive focus also retains enduring concerns, such as the relationships between popular culture, political control, and social class.

input: In October 2004, Sarah Forsyth claimed that she had been dismissed unfairly by Eton College and had been bullied by senior staff. She also claimed she was instructed to do some of Prince Harry's coursework to enable him to pass AS Art. As evidence, Forsyth provided secretly recorded conversations with both Prince Harry and her Head of Department, Ian Burke. An employment tribunal in July 2005 found that she had been unfairly dismissed and criticised Burke for bullying her and for repeatedly changing his story. It also criticised the school for failing to produce its capability procedures and criticised the Head Master for not reviewing the case independently.
rewrite: In October 2004, Sarah Forsyth alleged unfair dismissal by Eton College and bullying by senior staff. She further asserted she was directed to complete portions of Prince Harry’s AS Art coursework to ensure his passing. Supporting her claims, Forsyth submitted secretly taped discussions with both the Prince and her Head of Department, Ian Burke. A July 2005 employment tribunal ruled her dismissal was unfair. It censured Burke for bullying and for repeatedly altering his account. The tribunal also faulted the school for not providing its capability procedures and criticised the Head Master for lacking an independent case review.

input: Because of its limited land area, Bermuda has had difficulty with over-population. In the first two centuries of settlement, it relied on steady human emigration to keep the population manageable.[citation needed] Before the American Revolution more than ten thousand Bermudians (over half of the total population through the years) gradually emigrated, primarily to the Southern United States. As Great Britain displaced Spain as the dominant European imperial power, it opened up more land for colonial development. A steady trickle of outward migration continued. With seafaring the only real industry in the early decades, by the end of the 18th century, at least a third of the island's manpower was at sea at any one time.
rewrite: Bermuda’s limited land area has long created challenges with overpopulation. For the first two centuries of settlement, steady outward migration was necessary to manage population levels. Before the American Revolution, over ten thousand Bermudians—more than half the cumulative population—gradually emigrated, mainly to the Southern United States. As Great Britain replaced Spain as the dominant imperial power, more colonial land became available, sustaining a continuous trickle of migrants. In the early decades, seafaring was the sole major industry; by the late 18th century, at least a third of the island’s manpower was engaged in maritime work at any given time.

input: Although an alloy is technically an impure metal, when referring to alloys, the term "impurities" usually denotes those elements which are not desired. These impurities are often found in the base metals or the solutes, but they may also be introduced during the alloying process. For instance, sulfur is a common impurity in steel. Sulfur combines readily with iron to form iron sulfide, which is very brittle, creating weak spots in the steel. Lithium, sodium and calcium are common impurities in aluminium alloys, which can have adverse effects on the structural integrity of castings. Conversely, otherwise pure-metals that simply contain unwanted impurities are often called "impure metals" and are not usually referred to as alloys. Oxygen, present in the air, readily combines with most metals to form metal oxides; especially at higher temperatures encountered during alloying. Great care is often taken during the alloying process to remove excess impurities, using fluxes, chemical additives, or other methods of extractive metallurgy.
rewrite: While technically a type of impure metal, an alloy is distinct in that the term "impurities" within it typically refers only to undesired elements. These can originate from the base metals or solutes, or be introduced during manufacturing. For example, sulfur in steel readily forms brittle iron sulfide, creating structural weaknesses. Similarly, lithium, sodium, and calcium in aluminium alloys can compromise casting integrity. Conversely, metals containing only unwanted impurities are termed "impure metals," not alloys. A significant concern is oxygen from air, which easily forms metal oxides, especially at high alloying temperatures. Consequently, processes like using fluxes or chemical additives are carefully employed to remove excess impurities through extractive metallurgy.

input: According to the 2002 Census, 4.6% of the Chilean population, including the Rapanui (a Polynesian people) of Easter Island, was indigenous, although most show varying degrees of mixed heritage. Many are descendants of the Mapuche, and live in Santiago, Araucanía and the lake district. The Mapuche successfully fought off defeat in the first 300–350 years of Spanish rule during the Arauco War. Relations with the new Chilean Republic were good until the Chilean state decided to occupy their lands. During the Occupation of Araucanía the Mapuche surrendered to the country's army in the 1880s. Their land was opened to settlement by Chileans and Europeans. Conflict over Mapuche land rights continues to the present.
rewrite: Based on the 2002 Census, indigenous peoples, among them the Rapanui of Easter Island, constituted 4.6% of Chile's population, with most having mixed heritage. A significant portion are Mapuche descendants, residing in Santiago, Araucanía, and the lake district. The Mapuche notably resisted Spanish conquest for centuries during the Arauco War. Relations with the nascent Chilean Republic were initially positive but deteriorated when the state moved to occupy their territories. In the 1880s, during the Occupation of Araucanía, the Mapuche yielded to the national army. Subsequently, their lands were made available for Chilean and European settlement. Disputes regarding these land rights persist today.

input: Temperature extremes are moderated by the adjacent Puget Sound, greater Pacific Ocean, and Lake Washington. The region is largely shielded from Pacific storms by the Olympic Mountains and from Arctic air by the Cascade Range. Despite being on the margin of the rain shadow of the Olympic Mountains, the city has a reputation for frequent rain. This reputation stems from the frequency of light precipitation in the fall, winter, and spring. In an average year, at least 0.01 inches (0.25 mm) of precipitation falls on 150 days, more than nearly all U.S. cities east of the Rocky Mountains. It is cloudy 201 days out of the year and partly cloudy 93 days. Official weather and climatic data is collected at Seattle–Tacoma International Airport, located about 19 km (12 mi) south of downtown in the city of SeaTac, which is at a higher elevation, and records more cloudy days and fewer partly cloudy days per year.
rewrite: The adjacent Puget Sound, greater Pacific Ocean, and Lake Washington help to moderate temperature extremes. Pacific storms are largely blocked by the Olympic Mountains, while the Cascade Range shields the region from Arctic air. Although the city lies on the edge of the Olympic Mountains' rain shadow, it is known for frequent rain. This reputation comes from the common light precipitation during fall, winter, and spring. On average, measurable precipitation of at least 0.01 inches (0.25 mm) occurs on 150 days annually—more than nearly all U.S. cities east of the Rocky Mountains. Skies are cloudy 201 days per year and partly cloudy another 93. Official climatic data is gathered at Seattle–Tacoma International Airport, situated approximately 19 km (12 mi) south of downtown in the city of SeaTac. This higher elevation location records more cloudy days and fewer partly cloudy days each year.

input: Norfolk Island is the only non-mainland Australian territory to have achieved self-governance. The Norfolk Island Act 1979, passed by the Parliament of Australia in 1979, is the Act under which the island was governed until the passing of the Norfolk Island Legislation Amendment Act 2015. The Australian government maintains authority on the island through an Administrator, currently Gary Hardgrave. From 1979 to 2015, a Legislative Assembly was elected by popular vote for terms of not more than three years, although legislation passed by the Australian Parliament could extend its laws to the territory at will, including the power to override any laws made by the assembly.
rewrite: Norfolk Island stands apart as the sole self-governing territory of Australia not on the mainland. Its governance was established by the Norfolk Island Act of 1979. This system remained in place until the 2015 Norfolk Island Legislation Amendment Act. During that period, a locally elected Legislative Assembly served terms of up to three years. However, the Australian Parliament always retained ultimate authority, able to extend its own laws to the island and override the assembly's legislation at any time. Today, the Australian government exercises control through an Administrator, a role currently held by Gary Hardgrave.

input: Richard Owen showed that fossils of extinct species Darwin found in South America were allied to living species on the same continent. In March 1837, ornithologist John Gould announced that Darwin's rhea was a separate species from the previously described rhea (though their territories overlapped), that mockingbirds collected on the Galápagos Islands represented three separate species each unique to a particular island, and that several distinct birds from those islands were all classified as finches. Darwin began speculating, in a series of notebooks, on the possibility that "one species does change into another" to explain these findings, and around July sketched a genealogical branching of a single evolutionary tree, discarding Lamarck's independent lineages progressing to higher forms. Unconventionally, Darwin asked questions of fancy pigeon and animal breeders as well as established scientists. At the zoo he had his first sight of an ape, and was profoundly impressed by how human the orangutan seemed.
rewrite: In March 1837, ornithologist John Gould made several key announcements regarding Darwin's specimens. He declared that the rhea Darwin found was a distinct species from the known variety, noted that Galápagos mockingbirds comprised three separate species each unique to an island, and identified several birds from those islands as finches. These findings, along with Richard Owen's earlier work showing fossils of extinct South American species were related to living ones there, prompted Darwin's speculation. In a series of notebooks, he began to consider that "one species does change into another." Around July, he sketched a genealogical branching tree from a single ancestor, rejecting Lamarck's idea of independent lineages progressing to higher forms. Darwin unconventionally sought insights from fancy pigeon breeders, animal breeders, and scientists. A visit to the zoo profoundly impressed him, as his first sight of an orangutan revealed how strikingly human an ape could seem.

input: Near-infrared is the region closest in wavelength to the radiation detectable by the human eye, mid- and far-infrared are progressively further from the visible spectrum. Other definitions follow different physical mechanisms (emission peaks, vs. bands, water absorption) and the newest follow technical reasons (the common silicon detectors are sensitive to about 1,050 nm, while InGaAs's sensitivity starts around 950 nm and ends between 1,700 and 2,600 nm, depending on the specific configuration). Unfortunately, international standards for these specifications are not currently available.
rewrite: The infrared spectrum is divided into regions based on proximity to visible light: near-infrared is closest, followed by mid- and far-infrared. Alternative definitions rely on physical properties like emission peaks or water absorption. More recent classifications consider technical factors, such as the sensitivity ranges of silicon detectors (to about 1,050 nm) and InGaAs detectors (from around 950 nm to between 1,700 and 2,600 nm). However, no universal standards for these definitions yet exist.

input: The Allied disaster at Austerlitz significantly shook the faith of Emperor Francis in the British-led war effort. France and Austria agreed to an armistice immediately and the Treaty of Pressburg followed shortly after on 26 December. Pressburg took Austria out of both the war and the Coalition while reinforcing the earlier treaties of Campo Formio and of Lunéville between the two powers. The treaty confirmed the Austrian loss of lands to France in Italy and Bavaria, and lands in Germany to Napoleon's German allies. It also imposed an indemnity of 40 million francs on the defeated Habsburgs and allowed the fleeing Russian troops free passage through hostile territories and back to their home soil. Napoleon went on to say, "The battle of Austerlitz is the finest of all I have fought." Frank McLynn suggests that Napoleon was so successful at Austerlitz that he lost touch with reality, and what used to be French foreign policy became a "personal Napoleonic one". Vincent Cronin disagrees, stating that Napoleon was not overly ambitious for himself, "he embodied the ambitions of thirty million Frenchmen".
rewrite: The Treaty of Pressburg, signed on 26 December following an immediate armistice, formally removed Austria from both the war and the Coalition. This agreement reinforced the earlier treaties of Campo Formio and Lunéville between the two powers. Its terms confirmed Austrian losses of lands in Italy and Bavaria to France, as well as cessions in Germany to Napoleon's allies. A substantial indemnity of 40 million francs was imposed on the defeated Habsburgs, and the treaty granted safe passage to fleeing Russian troops returning home. The Allied disaster at Austerlitz had profoundly shaken Emperor Francis's faith in the British-led war effort, leading to this settlement. Napoleon himself later declared, "The battle of Austerlitz is the finest of all I have fought." Historian Frank McLynn argues that this overwhelming success caused Napoleon to lose touch with reality, transforming French foreign policy into a "personal Napoleonic one." Conversely, Vincent Cronin disputes this, contending that Napoleon was not driven by excessive personal ambition but instead "embodied the ambitions of thirty million Frenchmen."

input: During the three years following its inception, the university bore three different names. The board first approved "Eliot Seminary," but William Eliot was uncomfortable with naming a university after himself and objected to the establishment of a seminary, which would implicitly be charged with teaching a religious faith. He favored a nonsectarian university. In 1854, the Board of Trustees changed the name to "Washington Institute" in honor of George Washington. Naming the University after the nation's first president, only seven years before the American Civil War and during a time of bitter national division, was no coincidence. During this time of conflict, Americans universally admired George Washington as the father of the United States and a symbol of national unity. The Board of Trustees believed that the university should be a force of unity in a strongly divided Missouri. In 1856, the University amended its name to "Washington University." The university amended its name once more in 1976, when the Board of Trustees voted to add the suffix "in St. Louis" to distinguish the university from the nearly two dozen other universities bearing Washington's name.
rewrite: In its first three years, the university was known by three distinct names. Initially, the board selected "Eliot Seminary," yet William Eliot objected, uneasy with the personal honor and opposed to the religious connotations of a seminary, preferring instead a nonsectarian institution. By 1854, the trustees had adopted "Washington Institute" to honor George Washington. This choice, made just seven years before the Civil War amid deep national divisions, was deliberate. Washington stood as a universally admired figure of unity, and the board hoped the university would act as a unifying force in a fractured Missouri. The name evolved to "Washington University" in 1856. A final change came in 1976, when the trustees voted to append "in St. Louis" to differentiate it from the many other schools bearing Washington's name.

input: According to the preamble in The Law of Treaties, treaties are a source of international law. If an act or lack thereof is condemned under international law, the act will not assume international legality even if approved by internal law. This means that in case of a conflict with domestic law, international law will always prevail.
rewrite: Treaties are recognized as a source of international law. Should an act be condemned internationally, it remains illegal even if domestic law permits it. Consequently, international law always takes precedence over domestic law in any conflict between the two.

input: The Farmington Canal Trail is a rail trail that will eventually run continuously from downtown New Haven to Northampton, Massachusetts. The scenic trail follows the path of the historic New Haven and Northampton Company and the Farmington Canal. Currently, there is a continuous 14-mile (23 km) stretch of the trail from downtown, through Hamden and into Cheshire, making bicycle commuting between New Haven and those suburbs possible. The trail is part of the East Coast Greenway, a proposed 3,000-mile (4,800 km) bike path that would link every major city on the East Coast from Florida to Maine.
rewrite: Eventually running continuously from downtown New Haven to Northampton, Massachusetts, the Farmington Canal Trail is a scenic rail trail. It traces the historic routes of the Farmington Canal and the New Haven and Northampton Company. A present 14-mile (23 km) continuous stretch enables bicycle commuting from New Haven through Hamden into Cheshire. This trail forms a segment of the proposed East Coast Greenway, a 3,000-mile (4,800 km) bike path intended to connect every major East Coast city from Florida to Maine.

input: According to the International Organization for Migration, Nigeria witnessed a dramatic increase in remittances sent home from overseas Nigerians, going from USD 2.3 billion in 2004 to 17.9 billion in 2007. The United States accounts for the largest portion of official remittances, followed by the United Kingdom, Italy, Canada, Spain and France. On the African continent, Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Chad, Libya and South Africa are important source countries of remittance flows to Nigeria, while China is the biggest remittance-sending country in Asia.
rewrite: Remittances to Nigeria surged from USD 2.3 billion in 2004 to 17.9 billion in 2007, as reported by the International Organization for Migration. The United States is the leading source of these official funds, with the United Kingdom, Italy, Canada, Spain, and France following. Within Africa, key sending nations include Egypt, Equatorial Guinea, Chad, Libya, and South Africa, while China stands as the primary source in Asia.

input: The islands are located about halfway between Hawaii and Australia, north of Nauru and Kiribati, east of the Federated States of Micronesia, and south of the U.S. territory of Wake Island, to which it lays claim. The atolls and islands form two groups: the Ratak (sunrise) and the Ralik (sunset). The two island chains lie approximately parallel to one another, running northwest to southeast, comprising about 750,000 square miles (1,900,000 km2) of ocean but only about 70 square miles (180 km2) of land mass. Each includes 15 to 18 islands and atolls. The country consists of a total of 29 atolls and five isolated islands.
rewrite: Situated roughly midway between Hawaii and Australia, the islands lie north of Nauru and Kiribati, east of the Federated States of Micronesia, and south of the U.S.'s Wake Island, which they claim. The nation is composed of 29 atolls and five isolated islands, organized into two parallel chains running northwest to southeast: the Ratak (sunrise) and Ralik (sunset) groups. Each chain contains 15 to 18 islands and atolls. Together, they encompass around 750,000 square miles of ocean, yet their total land area is only about 70 square miles.

input: The Caribbean initially provided England's most important and lucrative colonies, but not before several attempts at colonisation failed. An attempt to establish a colony in Guiana in 1604 lasted only two years, and failed in its main objective to find gold deposits. Colonies in St Lucia (1605) and Grenada (1609) also rapidly folded, but settlements were successfully established in St. Kitts (1624), Barbados (1627) and Nevis (1628). The colonies soon adopted the system of sugar plantations successfully used by the Portuguese in Brazil, which depended on slave labour, and—at first—Dutch ships, to sell the slaves and buy the sugar. To ensure that the increasingly healthy profits of this trade remained in English hands, Parliament decreed in 1651 that only English ships would be able to ply their trade in English colonies. This led to hostilities with the United Dutch Provinces—a series of Anglo-Dutch Wars—which would eventually strengthen England's position in the Americas at the expense of the Dutch. In 1655, England annexed the island of Jamaica from the Spanish, and in 1666 succeeded in colonising the Bahamas.
rewrite: England’s earliest efforts to colonise the Caribbean met with repeated failures before stable settlements took hold. An expedition to Guiana in 1604 collapsed within two years, having found no gold. Attempts in St Lucia (1605) and Grenada (1609) also quickly folded. Success finally came with colonies founded on St. Kitts (1624), Barbados (1627), and Nevis (1628). These settlements soon copied the Portuguese model from Brazil, building a sugar plantation economy that relied on slave labour, with Dutch ships initially handling both the slave trade and sugar exports. To keep the growing profits within English control, Parliament passed a 1651 law restricting trade with its colonies to English ships. This sparked hostilities with the United Dutch Provinces—the Anglo-Dutch Wars—which ultimately cemented England’s regional power while weakening the Dutch. Further expansion followed, with England seizing Jamaica from Spain in 1655 and successfully colonising the Bahamas in 1666. Thus, despite early setbacks, the Caribbean became England’s most vital and profitable colonial possession.

input: New York City has been a metropolitan municipality with a mayor-council form of government since its consolidation in 1898. The government of New York is more centralized than that of most other U.S. cities. In New York City, the city government is responsible for public education, correctional institutions, public safety, recreational facilities, sanitation, water supply, and welfare services.
rewrite: Since its consolidation in 1898, New York City has operated as a metropolitan municipality under a mayor-council system. Its government is more centralized than in most other U.S. cities. Responsible for numerous services, the city oversees public education, safety, sanitation, water supply, welfare, corrections, and recreational facilities.

input: Apple debuted the iTunes Wi-Fi Music Store on September 5, 2007, in its Media Event entitled "The Beat Goes On...". This service allows users to access the Music Store from either an iPhone or an iPod Touch and download songs directly to the device that can be synced to the user's iTunes Library over a WiFi connection, or, in the case of an iPhone, the telephone network.
rewrite: On September 5, 2007, Apple introduced the iTunes Wi-Fi Music Store at its "The Beat Goes On..." Media Event. This feature enabled iPhone or iPod Touch users to access the Music Store and download songs directly to their device. These downloads could then be synced to the user's iTunes Library via WiFi or, for iPhones, through the telephone network.

input: Society throughout Europe was disturbed by the dislocations caused by the Black Death. Lands that had been marginally productive were abandoned, as the survivors were able to acquire more fertile areas. Although serfdom declined in Western Europe it became more common in Eastern Europe, as landlords imposed it on those of their tenants who had previously been free. Most peasants in Western Europe managed to change the work they had previously owed to their landlords into cash rents. The percentage of serfs amongst the peasantry declined from a high of 90 to closer to 50 per cent by the end of the period. Landlords also became more conscious of common interests with other landholders, and they joined together to extort privileges from their governments. Partly at the urging of landlords, governments attempted to legislate a return to the economic conditions that existed before the Black Death. Non-clergy became increasingly literate, and urban populations began to imitate the nobility's interest in chivalry.
rewrite: The dislocations of the Black Death unsettled European society, prompting significant economic and social shifts. Survivors abandoned marginally productive lands in favor of more fertile areas. While serfdom waned in Western Europe, Eastern European landlords increasingly imposed it on formerly free tenants. Most Western peasants converted obligatory labor into cash payments to their landlords, reducing the serf population from about 90 percent to nearly 50 percent. Landlords, growing more aware of shared interests, collectively pressed governments for privileges. Partly due to this landlord pressure, governments tried to legislate a return to pre-plague economic conditions. Concurrently, literacy spread beyond the clergy, and urban populations adopted the nobility’s fascination with chivalry.

input: Muslim sects regarded as heretical, such as the Druze, Ismailis, Alevis, and Alawites, ranked below Jews and Christians. In 1514, Sultan Selim I, nicknamed "the Grim" because of his cruelty, ordered the massacre of 40,000 Anatolian Alevis (Qizilbash), whom he considered heretics, reportedly proclaiming that "the killing of one Alevi had as much otherworldly reward as killing 70 Christians."[page needed] Selim was also responsible for an unprecedented and rapid expansion of the Ottoman Empire into the Middle East, especially through his conquest of the entire Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt, which included much of the region. With these conquests, Selim further solidified the Ottoman claim for being an Islamic caliphate, although Ottoman sultans had been claiming the title of caliph since the 14th century starting with Murad I (reigned 1362 to 1389). The caliphate would remain held by Ottoman sultans for the rest of the office's duration, which ended with its abolition on 3 March 1924 by the Grand National Assembly of Turkey and the exile of the last caliph, Abdülmecid II, to France.
rewrite: Sultan Selim I, known as "the Grim" for his brutality, oversaw a dramatic expansion of the Ottoman Empire into the Middle East. His most significant achievement was the conquest of the entire Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt, which brought vast territories under Ottoman control. These victories greatly strengthened the Ottoman claim to leadership of the Islamic caliphate, a title its sultans had asserted since the 14th century under Murad I. Within the empire's religious hierarchy, Muslim sects deemed heretical—including the Druze, Ismailis, Alevis, and Alawites—were placed below Jews and Christians. Selim demonstrated profound hostility toward one such group, the Anatolian Alevis (Qizilbash). In 1514, he ordered the massacre of 40,000 of them, reportedly declaring that killing one Alevi brought as much spiritual reward as killing seventy Christians. The Ottoman sultans would continue to hold the caliphate until its abolition by the Grand National Assembly of Turkey on March 3, 1924, which also resulted in the exile of the final caliph, Abdülmecid II, to France.

input: The U.S. Census Bureau reported that in 2000, 24.0% of San Diego residents were under 18, and 10.5% were 65 and over. As of 2011[update] the median age was 35.6; more than a quarter of residents were under age 20 and 11% were over age 65. Millennials (ages 18 through 34) constitute 27.1% of San Diego's population, the second-highest percentage in a major U.S. city. The San Diego County regional planning agency, SANDAG, provides tables and graphs breaking down the city population into 5-year age groups.
rewrite: According to the U.S. Census Bureau, 24.0% of San Diego's population was under 18 in 2000, while 10.5% were 65 or older. By 2011, the median age was 35.6, with over a quarter under 20 and 11% over 65. Millennials (ages 18-34) represent 27.1% of residents, the second-highest share among major U.S. cities. Detailed tables and graphs from SANDAG, the county's planning agency, further break down the population into five-year age groups.

input: By the Middle Ages, large numbers of Jews lived in the Holy Roman Empire and had assimilated into German culture, including many Jews who had previously assimilated into French culture and had spoken a mixed Judeo-French language. Upon assimilating into German culture, the Jewish German peoples incorporated major parts of the German language and elements of other European languages into a mixed language known as Yiddish. However tolerance and assimilation of Jews in German society suddenly ended during the Crusades with many Jews being forcefully expelled from Germany and Western Yiddish disappeared as a language in Germany over the centuries, with German Jewish people fully adopting the German language.
rewrite: During the Crusades, a period of tolerance and assimilation for Jews in German society abruptly ceased, leading to many being forcibly expelled from Germany. Previously, by the Middle Ages, numerous Jews lived in the Holy Roman Empire and had assimilated into German culture. This group included many who had earlier adopted French culture and spoken a Judeo-French blend. Upon integrating into German society, these Jewish communities formed Yiddish, incorporating major parts of the German language along with elements from other European tongues. Over the following centuries, Western Yiddish vanished in Germany, and German Jews fully adopted the German language.

input: Inner and outer vestibules lead to the octagonal chapter house, which is of exceptional architectural purity. It is built in a Geometrical Gothic style with an octagonal crypt below. A pier of eight shafts carries the vaulted ceiling. To the sides are blind arcading, remains of 14th-century paintings and numerous stone benches above which are innovatory large 4-light quatre-foiled windows. These are virtually contemporary with the Sainte-Chapelle, Paris.
rewrite: Leading through inner and outer vestibules, the octagonal chapter house is a model of architectural purity in the Geometrical Gothic style. Beneath it lies an octagonal crypt. A pier of eight shafts supports the vaulted ceiling. Flanking the space are blind arcading, remnants of 14th-century paintings, and many stone benches. Above these benches are innovative large 4-light quatre-foiled windows, which are nearly contemporary with Paris's Sainte-Chapelle.

input: A new government was appointed on 31 March 2013, which consisted of members of Séléka and representatives of the opposition to Bozizé, one pro-Bozizé individual, and a number representatives of civil society. On 1 April, the former opposition parties declared that they would boycott the government. After African leaders in Chad refused to recognize Djotodia as President, proposing to form a transitional council and the holding of new elections, Djotodia signed a decree on 6 April for the formation of a council that would act as a transitional parliament. The council was tasked with electing a president to serve prior to elections in 18 months.
rewrite: On 31 March 2013, a new government was formed, comprising Séléka members, opponents of Bozizé, a single pro-Bozizé figure, and several civil society representatives. The following day, former opposition parties announced a boycott of this government. Meanwhile, African leaders in Chad rejected Djotodia's presidency, instead proposing a transitional council and new elections. In response, Djotodia issued a decree on 6 April to establish a council serving as a transitional parliament. This body was assigned the duty of electing an interim president to serve until elections could be held within eighteen months.

input: The bipolar junction transistor (BJT) was the most commonly used transistor in the 1960s and 70s. Even after MOSFETs became widely available, the BJT remained the transistor of choice for many analog circuits such as amplifiers because of their greater linearity and ease of manufacture. In integrated circuits, the desirable properties of MOSFETs allowed them to capture nearly all market share for digital circuits. Discrete MOSFETs can be applied in transistor applications, including analog circuits, voltage regulators, amplifiers, power transmitters and motor drivers.
rewrite: During the 1960s and 70s, the bipolar junction transistor (BJT) was the most prevalent type. Despite the later widespread availability of MOSFETs, BJTs continued to be favored for many analog circuits like amplifiers, owing to their superior linearity and simpler manufacturing. For digital integrated circuits, MOSFETs captured nearly the entire market due to their advantageous properties. Discrete MOSFETs, however, are also used in various transistor applications, such as analog circuits, voltage regulators, amplifiers, power transmitters, and motor drivers.

input: The centuries-long geopolitical and ideological rivalry between Safavid Iran and the neighboring Ottoman Empire, led to numerous Ottoman–Persian Wars. The Safavid Era peaked in the reign of Abbas the Great, 1587–1629, surpassing their Ottoman arch rivals in strength, and making the empire a leading hub in Western Eurasia for the sciences and arts. The Safavid Era saw the start of mass integration from Caucasian populations into new layers of the society of Iran, as well as mass resettlement of them within the heartlands of Iran, playing a pivotal role in the history of Iran for centuries onwards. Following a gradual decline in the late 1600s and early 1700s, which was caused by the internal conflicts, the continuous wars with the Ottomans, and the foreign interference (most notably the Russian interference), the Safavid rule was ended by the Pashtun rebels who besieged Isfahan and defeated Soltan Hosein in 1722.
rewrite: For centuries, a deep geopolitical and ideological rivalry existed between Safavid Iran and the neighboring Ottoman Empire, resulting in a series of Ottoman-Persian Wars. The empire reached its peak under Abbas the Great, who reigned from 1587 to 1629. During this period, Safavid strength surpassed that of their Ottoman rivals, establishing the state as a preeminent Western Eurasian center for science and art. This era also initiated the mass integration and resettlement of Caucasian populations into new societal layers and the heartlands of Iran, a pivotal development for the country's future history. A gradual decline began in the late 1600s and early 1700s, driven by internal conflicts, ongoing wars with the Ottomans, and foreign interference—most notably from Russia. Ultimately, Pashtun rebels ended Safavid rule by besieging Isfahan and defeating Sultan Husayn in 1722.

input: The president serves as a chief of state and commander in chief of the armed forces. A prime minister appointed by the president serves as head of government and in turn appoints the Council of Ministers. The unicameral National Assembly is Mali's sole legislative body, consisting of deputies elected to five-year terms. Following the 2007 elections, the Alliance for Democracy and Progress held 113 of 160 seats in the assembly. The assembly holds two regular sessions each year, during which it debates and votes on legislation that has been submitted by a member or by the government.
rewrite: As both chief of state and commander in chief of the armed forces, the president holds a key role. The head of government is a prime minister, appointed by the president, who then selects the Council of Ministers. Mali's sole legislative body is the unicameral National Assembly, where deputies serve five-year terms. After the 2007 elections, the Alliance for Democracy and Progress occupied 113 out of 160 seats. This assembly convenes for two regular sessions annually to debate and vote on legislation proposed by its members or the government.

input: Pope Paul VI knew the Roman Curia well, having worked there for a generation from 1922 to 1954. He implemented his reforms in stages, rather than in one fell swoop. On 1 March 1968, he issued a regulation, a process that had been initiated by Pius XII and continued by John XXIII. On 28 March, with Pontificalis Domus, and in several additional Apostolic Constitutions in the following years, he revamped the entire Curia, which included reduction of bureaucracy, streamlining of existing congregations and a broader representation of non-Italians in the curial positions.
rewrite: Having served in the Roman Curia from 1922 to 1954, Pope Paul VI possessed deep familiarity with its workings. He pursued reforms incrementally, not all at once. A regulatory process begun by Pius XII and advanced by John XXIII culminated in his regulation of 1 March 1968. Then, starting with *Pontificalis Domus* on 28 March and through later Apostolic Constitutions, he overhauled the entire Curia. This involved cutting bureaucracy, streamlining congregations, and ensuring broader representation for non-Italians in its positions.

input: A new approach to avoiding overhead wires is taken by the "second generation" tram/streetcar system in Bordeaux, France (entry into service of the first line in December 2003; original system discontinued in 1958) with its APS (alimentation par sol – ground current feed). This involves a third rail which is flush with the surface like the tops of the running rails. The circuit is divided into segments with each segment energized in turn by sensors from the car as it passes over it, the remainder of the third rail remaining "dead". Since each energized segment is completely covered by the lengthy articulated cars, and goes dead before being "uncovered" by the passage of the vehicle, there is no danger to pedestrians. This system has also been adopted in some sections of the new tram systems in Reims, France (opened 2011) and Angers, France (also opened 2011). Proposals are in place for a number of other new services including Dubai, UAE; Barcelona, Spain; Florence, Italy; Marseille, France; Gold Coast, Australia; Washington, D.C., U.S.A.; Brasília, Brazil and Tours, France.
rewrite: In Bordeaux, France, a "second generation" tram system introduced in December 2003—replacing an original system discontinued in 1958—employs a novel method to avoid overhead wires. Known as APS (alimentation par sol, or ground current feed), it uses a third rail set flush with the road surface, level with the running rails. This rail is divided into segments, each activated only when sensors on the lengthy articulated car pass over it; all other segments remain inert. Because each powered segment is entirely covered by the tram and de-energizes before being exposed, the system poses no risk to pedestrians. Similar APS technology has been implemented in sections of newer tram networks in Reims and Angers, both opened in 2011. Furthermore, proposals to adopt this system are underway for several other cities, including Dubai, UAE; Barcelona, Spain; Florence, Italy; Marseille, France; Gold Coast, Australia; Washington, D.C., U.S.A.; Brasília, Brazil; and Tours, France.

input: Beginning in first decade of the 15th century, Jan Hus—a Roman Catholic priest, Czech reformist and professor—influenced by John Wycliffe's writings, founded the Hussite movement. He strongly advocated his reformist Bohemian religious denomination. He was excommunicated and burned at the stake in Constance, Bishopric of Constance in 1415 by secular authorities for unrepentant and persistent heresy. After his execution, a revolt erupted. Hussites defeated five continuous crusades proclaimed against them by the Pope.
rewrite: In the early 15th century, the Roman Catholic priest and Czech reformer Jan Hus, inspired by John Wycliffe, established the Hussite movement to advance his Bohemian religious reforms. Declared an unrepentant heretic, he was excommunicated and burned at the stake in Constance in 1415. His execution sparked a revolt, during which the Hussites successfully repelled five consecutive papal crusades.

input: Efforts have been made to protect Guam's coral reef habitats from pollution, eroded silt and overfishing, problems that have led to decreased fish populations. (Since Guam is a significant vacation spot for scuba divers, this is important.) In recent years, the Department of Agriculture, Division of Aquatic and Wildlife Resources has established several new marine preserves where fish populations are monitored by biologists. Before adopting U.S. Environmental Protection Agency standards, portions of Tumon Bay were dredged by the hotel chains to provide a better experience for hotel guests. Tumon Bay has since been made into a preserve. A federal Guam National Wildlife Refuge in northern Guam protects the decimated sea turtle population in addition to a small colony of Mariana fruit bats.
rewrite: Guam's coral reefs face threats from pollution, silt, and overfishing, which have reduced fish numbers. As a major destination for scuba divers, protecting these habitats is crucial. The Department of Agriculture’s Division of Aquatic and Wildlife Resources now monitors fish in several new marine preserves. Tumon Bay, once dredged by hotels to enhance guest experiences before U.S. EPA standards were adopted, is among these protected areas. Additionally, a federal Guam National Wildlife Refuge in northern Guam safeguards a diminished sea turtle population and a small colony of Mariana fruit bats.

input: The Karabakh war ended after a Russian-brokered cease-fire was put in place in 1994. The war was a success for the Karabakh Armenian forces who managed to capture 16% of Azerbaijan's internationally recognised territory including Nagorno-Karabakh itself. Since then, Armenia and Azerbaijan have held peace talks, mediated by the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE). The status of Karabakh has yet to be determined. The economies of both countries have been hurt in the absence of a complete resolution and Armenia's borders with Turkey and Azerbaijan remain closed. By the time both Azerbaijan and Armenia had finally agreed to a ceasefire in 1994, an estimated 30,000 people had been killed and over a million had been displaced.
rewrite: A Russian-brokered ceasefire in 1994 ended the Karabakh war, which had resulted in an estimated 30,000 deaths and displaced over a million people. The conflict was a military success for Karabakh Armenian forces, who captured 16% of Azerbaijan's internationally recognized territory, including Nagorno-Karabakh itself. However, the region's final status remains undetermined. Since the war, peace talks mediated by the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) have continued. The unresolved conflict has damaged both nations' economies, and Armenia's borders with Turkey and Azerbaijan stay closed.

input: On 27 August 2007, Royal Dutch Shell and Reitan Group, the owner of the 7-Eleven brand in Scandinavia, announced an agreement to re-brand some 269 service stations across Norway, Sweden, Finland and Denmark, subject to obtaining regulatory approvals under the different competition laws in each country. On April 2010 Shell announced that the corporation is in process of trying to find a potential buyer for all of its operations in Finland and is doing similar market research concerning Swedish operations. On October 2010 Shell's gas stations and the heavy vehicle fuel supply networks in Finland and Sweden, along with a refinery located in Gothenburg, Sweden were sold to St1, a Finnish energy company, more precisely to its major shareholding parent company Keele Oy. Shell branded gas stations will be rebranded within maximum of five years from the acquisition and the number of gas stations is likely to be reduced. Until then the stations will operate under Shell brand licence.
rewrite: On August 27, 2007, an agreement was announced between Royal Dutch Shell and the Reitan Group, which holds the 7-Eleven brand rights in Scandinavia. This deal involved re-branding approximately 269 service stations across Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Denmark, pending necessary regulatory approvals under each nation's competition laws. By April 2010, Shell disclosed it was seeking a buyer for its Finnish operations and conducting similar market research for Sweden. In October 2010, Shell's gas stations and heavy vehicle fuel networks in Finland and Sweden, plus a refinery in Gothenburg, Sweden, were sold to the Finnish energy company St1, specifically to its major shareholder Keele Oy. These Shell-branded stations will operate under a brand license until they are re-branded within a maximum of five years, a process likely to reduce the total number of stations.

input: There are many different patterns of gas exchange demonstrated by different groups of insects. Gas exchange patterns in insects can range from continuous and diffusive ventilation, to discontinuous gas exchange.:65–68 During continuous gas exchange, oxygen is taken in and carbon dioxide is released in a continuous cycle. In discontinuous gas exchange, however, the insect takes in oxygen while it is active and small amounts of carbon dioxide are released when the insect is at rest. Diffusive ventilation is simply a form of continuous gas exchange that occurs by diffusion rather than physically taking in the oxygen. Some species of insect that are submerged also have adaptations to aid in respiration. As larvae, many insects have gills that can extract oxygen dissolved in water, while others need to rise to the water surface to replenish air supplies which may be held or trapped in special structures.
rewrite: Insects exhibit a variety of gas exchange patterns, which include continuous ventilation, discontinuous cycles, and diffusive processes.:65–68 Continuous gas exchange involves an unbroken cycle of oxygen intake and carbon dioxide release. A subset of this, diffusive ventilation, relies on diffusion instead of active physical intake. In contrast, discontinuous gas exchange occurs when the insect inhales oxygen primarily during activity, followed by minimal carbon dioxide release while at rest. Additionally, certain aquatic insects possess specialized respiratory adaptations. Many larval forms use gills to extract oxygen from water, while others must surface to access air, often storing it within unique bodily structures.

input: About 30 people have been indicted for participating in genocide or complicity in genocide during the early 1990s in Bosnia. To date, after several plea bargains and some convictions that were successfully challenged on appeal two men, Vujadin Popović and Ljubiša Beara, have been found guilty of committing genocide, Zdravko Tolimir has been found guilty of committing genocide and conspiracy to commit genocide, and two others, Radislav Krstić and Drago Nikolić, have been found guilty of aiding and abetting genocide. Three others have been found guilty of participating in genocides in Bosnia by German courts, one of whom Nikola Jorgić lost an appeal against his conviction in the European Court of Human Rights. A further eight men, former members of the Bosnian Serb security forces were found guilty of genocide by the State Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina (See List of Bosnian genocide prosecutions).
rewrite: Approximately thirty individuals have faced indictments for involvement in genocide or complicity in genocide during the Bosnian conflict of the early 1990s. To date, following several plea agreements and appealed convictions, two men—Vujadin Popović and Ljubiša Beara—stand convicted of committing genocide. Zdravko Tolimir has been found guilty of both genocide and conspiracy to commit genocide, while Radislav Krstić and Drago Nikolić were convicted for aiding and abetting genocide. Separately, German courts have convicted three others for participating in genocides in Bosnia; one of them, Nikola Jorgić, subsequently lost an appeal at the European Court of Human Rights. Additionally, Bosnia and Herzegovina’s State Court found eight former Bosnian Serb security force members guilty of genocide.

input: In 1713 Farrukhsiyar, the Mughal emperor, appointed Asif Jah I to be Viceroy of the Deccan, with the title Nizam-ul-Mulk (Administrator of the Realm). In 1724, Asif Jah I defeated Mubariz Khan to establish autonomy over the Deccan Suba, named the region Hyderabad Deccan, and started what came to be known as the Asif Jahi dynasty. Subsequent rulers retained the title Nizam ul-Mulk and were referred to as Asif Jahi Nizams, or Nizams of Hyderabad. The death of Asif Jah I in 1748 resulted in a period of political unrest as his sons, backed by opportunistic neighbouring states and colonial foreign forces, contended for the throne. The accession of Asif Jah II, who reigned from 1762 to 1803, ended the instability. In 1768 he signed the treaty of Masulipatnam, surrendering the coastal region to the East India Company in return for a fixed annual rent.
rewrite: Appointed Viceroy of the Deccan in 1713 by Emperor Farrukhsiyar, Asif Jah I received the title Nizam-ul-Mulk, meaning Administrator of the Realm. A decade later, in 1724, he defeated Mubariz Khan to secure autonomy for the Deccan Suba, renaming it Hyderabad Deccan and founding the Asif Jahi dynasty. His successors continued to hold the title Nizam ul-Mulk, becoming known as the Asif Jahi Nizams or the Nizams of Hyderabad. Following Asif Jah I's death in 1748, political turmoil ensued as his sons, supported by opportunistic neighbours and colonial powers, fought for succession. Stability was restored with the accession of Asif Jah II, whose reign lasted from 1762 to 1803. In 1768, he ceded the coastal region to the East India Company via the Treaty of Masulipatnam, in exchange for a fixed yearly payment.

input: Insects are the only invertebrates to have developed active flight capability, and this has played an important role in their success.:186 Their muscles are able to contract multiple times for each single nerve impulse, allowing the wings to beat faster than would ordinarily be possible. Having their muscles attached to their exoskeletons is more efficient and allows more muscle connections; crustaceans also use the same method, though all spiders use hydraulic pressure to extend their legs, a system inherited from their pre-arthropod ancestors. Unlike insects, though, most aquatic crustaceans are biomineralized with calcium carbonate extracted from the water.
rewrite: The success of insects is partly due to their unique ability among invertebrates to fly actively. Their wing muscles can contract multiple times per nerve impulse, enabling remarkably fast wingbeats. Additionally, attaching muscles directly to the exoskeleton improves efficiency and connectivity, a trait shared with crustaceans. However, spiders use hydraulic pressure to extend their legs, a legacy from pre-arthropod ancestors. Unlike insects, most aquatic crustaceans also incorporate calcium carbonate from the water to biomineralize their structures.

input: A liberal foreign investment law was approved in June 1994, and a law on privatisation was adopted in 1997, as well as a program of state property privatisation. Continued progress will depend on the ability of the government to strengthen its macroeconomic management, including increasing revenue collection, improving the investment climate, and making strides against corruption. However, unemployment, which currently stands at around 15%, still remains a major problem due to the influx of thousands of refugees from the Karabakh conflict.
rewrite: In June 1994, a liberal foreign investment law was approved, followed by a privatisation law and a corresponding state property program in 1997. Future progress relies on the government strengthening macroeconomic management through improved revenue collection, a better investment climate, and reduced corruption. A major ongoing issue, however, is unemployment—approximately 15%—exacerbated by the influx of thousands of refugees from the Karabakh conflict.

input: Due to the often political and cultural contours of blackness in the United States, the notion of blackness can also be extended to non-black people. Toni Morrison once described Bill Clinton as the first black President of the United States, because, as she put it, he displayed "almost every trope of blackness". Christopher Hitchens was offended by the notion of Clinton as the first black president, noting, "Mr Clinton, according to Toni Morrison, the Nobel Prize-winning novelist, is our first black President, the first to come from the broken home, the alcoholic mother, the under-the-bridge shadows of our ranking systems. Thus, we may have lost the mystical power to divine diabolism, but we can still divine blackness by the following symptoms: broken homes, alcoholic mothers, under-the-bridge habits and (presumable from the rest of [Arthur] Miller's senescent musings) the tendency to sexual predation and to shameless perjury about same." Some black activists were also offended, claiming that Clinton used his knowledge of black culture to exploit black people for political gain as no other president had before, while not serving black interests. They cite the lack of action during the Rwandan Genocide and his welfare reform, which Larry Roberts said had led to the worst child poverty since the 1960s. Others cited that the number of black people in jail increased during his administration.
rewrite: In the United States, the concept of blackness, shaped by political and cultural forces, can sometimes be applied to individuals who are not black. Nobel laureate Toni Morrison famously labeled Bill Clinton as the nation’s first black president, arguing he embodied “almost every trope of blackness.” This characterization drew sharp criticism. The writer Christopher Hitchens took offense, sarcastically summarizing Morrison’s implied criteria: a checklist including a broken home, an alcoholic mother, a marginalized existence, and—inferring from Arthur Miller’s work—propensities for sexual misconduct and perjury. Certain black activists were equally offended, accusing Clinton of leveraging his familiarity with black culture to secure political advantage without genuinely advancing black interests. They pointed to policy failures and consequences from his tenure as evidence. These included his administration’s inaction during the Rwandan Genocide and the welfare reform he signed into law. Critic Larry Roberts argued this reform precipitated the worst levels of child poverty since the 1960s. Further, critics noted a significant rise in the incarceration rate of black Americans during Clinton’s presidency. Thus, the extension of “blackness” to Clinton became a contentious point, revealing deep divides in perception and highlighting critiques of his political legacy regarding African American communities.

input: As of 2008[update], the population was 47.5% male and 52.5% female. The population was made up of 44,032 Swiss men (35.4% of the population) and 15,092 (12.1%) non-Swiss men. There were 51,531 Swiss women (41.4%) and 13,726 (11.0%) non-Swiss women. Of the population in the municipality, 39,008 or about 30.3% were born in Bern and lived there in 2000. There were 27,573 or 21.4% who were born in the same canton, while 25,818 or 20.1% were born somewhere else in Switzerland, and 27,812 or 21.6% were born outside of Switzerland.
rewrite: In 2008, the population comprised 47.5% males and 52.5% females. This included 44,032 Swiss men (35.4%) and 15,092 non-Swiss men (12.1%), alongside 51,531 Swiss women (41.4%) and 13,726 non-Swiss women (11.0%). Regarding birthplace, 39,008 people (30.3%) were born in Bern and resided there in 2000. Another 27,573 (21.4%) were born in the same canton, 25,818 (20.1%) elsewhere in Switzerland, and 27,812 (21.6%) outside the country.

input: Namibia is one of few countries in the world to specifically address conservation and protection of natural resources in its constitution. Article 95 states, "The State shall actively promote and maintain the welfare of the people by adopting international policies aimed at the following: maintenance of ecosystems, essential ecological processes, and biological diversity of Namibia, and utilisation of living natural resources on a sustainable basis for the benefit of all Namibians, both present and future."
rewrite: Namibia's constitution uniquely emphasizes conservation, making it one of the few nations to do so. Specifically, Article 95 commits the state to promote public welfare through policies that maintain ecosystems, essential ecological processes, and biological diversity. It further mandates the sustainable use of living natural resources for the benefit of all Namibians, both current and future generations.

input: After a series of test transmissions and special broadcasts that began in August, regular BBC television broadcasts officially resumed on 1 October 1936, from a converted wing of Alexandra Palace in London, which housed two studios, various scenery stores, make-up areas, dressing rooms, offices, and the transmitter itself, now broadcasting on the VHF band. BBC television initially used two systems, on alternate weeks: the 240-line Baird intermediate film system and the 405-line Marconi-EMI system, each making the BBC the world's first regular high-definition television service, broadcasting Monday to Saturday from 15:00 to 16:00 and 21:00 to 22:00.
rewrite: Regular BBC television broadcasts officially resumed on 1 October 1936 from Alexandra Palace in London, following a period of test transmissions and special broadcasts that had begun in August. The converted wing housed two studios, scenery stores, make-up areas, dressing rooms, offices, and the VHF transmitter. Broadcasting Monday to Saturday from 15:00 to 16:00 and 21:00 to 22:00, the service initially alternated weekly between two systems: the 240-line Baird intermediate film system and the 405-line Marconi-EMI system. This made the BBC the world's first regular high-definition television service.

input: Napoleon was born on 15 August 1769, to Carlo Maria di Buonaparte and Maria Letizia Ramolino, in his family's ancestral home Casa Buonaparte in Ajaccio, the capital of the island of Corsica. He was their fourth child and third son. This was a year after the island was transferred to France by the Republic of Genoa. He was christened Napoleone di Buonaparte, probably named after an uncle (an older brother who did not survive infancy was the first of the sons to be called Napoleone). In his 20s, he adopted the more French-sounding Napoléon Bonaparte.[note 2]
rewrite: Napoleon was christened Napoleone di Buonaparte, likely named for an uncle (an earlier son who died young had also been called Napoleone). He was born on 15 August 1769 in Ajaccio, Corsica, at the family home, Casa Buonaparte. His parents were Carlo Maria di Buonaparte and Maria Letizia Ramolino, and he was their fourth child and third son. His birth occurred a year after Genoa ceded Corsica to France. Later, in his twenties, he adopted the name Napoléon Bonaparte.

input: In the 9th century, the rise of the cult of the Apostle James in Santiago de Compostela gave Galicia a particular symbolic importance among Christians, an importance it would hold throughout the Reconquista. As the Middle Ages went on, Santiago became a major pilgrim destination and the Way of Saint James (Camiño de Santiago) a major pilgrim road, a route for the propagation of Romanesque art and the words and music of the troubadors. During the 10th and 11th centuries, a period during which Galician nobility become related to the royal family, Galicia was at times headed by its own native kings, while Vikings (locally known as Leodemanes or Lordomanes) occasionally raided the coasts. The Towers of Catoira (Pontevedra) were built as a system of fortifications to prevent and stop the Viking raids on Santiago de Compostela.
rewrite: During the 9th century, Galicia gained a unique symbolic importance for Christians through the rise of the Apostle James cult in Santiago de Compostela, a status maintained throughout the Reconquista. The 10th and 11th centuries saw Galician nobility intermarry with the royal family, and the region was at times ruled by its own native kings. In this era, Viking raiders, called Leodemanes locally, threatened the coasts. To protect Santiago de Compostela from these incursions, the defensive Towers of Catoira in Pontevedra were constructed.
