input: Strasbourg features a number of prominent parks, of which several are of cultural and historical interest: the Parc de l'Orangerie, laid out as a French garden by André le Nôtre and remodeled as an English garden on behalf of Joséphine de Beauharnais, now displaying noteworthy French gardens, a neo-classical castle and a small zoo; the Parc de la Citadelle, built around impressive remains of the 17th-century fortress erected close to the Rhine by Vauban; the Parc de Pourtalès, laid out in English style around a baroque castle (heavily restored in the 19th century) that now houses a small three-star hotel, and featuring an open-air museum of international contemporary sculpture. The Jardin botanique de l'Université de Strasbourg (botanical garden) was created under the German administration next to the Observatory of Strasbourg, built in 1881, and still owns some greenhouses of those times. The Parc des Contades, although the oldest park of the city, was completely remodeled after World War II. The futuristic Parc des Poteries is an example of European park-conception in the late 1990s. The Jardin des deux Rives, spread over Strasbourg and Kehl on both sides of the Rhine opened in 2004 and is the most extended (60-hectare) park of the agglomeration. The most recent park is Parc du Heyritz (8,7 ha), opened in 2014 along a canal facing the hôpital civil.
rewrite:
Strasbourg boasts numerous notable parks, many of cultural and historical significance. Among these is the Parc de l'Orangerie, originally designed as a French garden by André le Nôtre. It was later remodeled into an English garden for Joséphine de Beauharnais and today showcases fine French gardens, a neo-classical castle, and a small zoo. The Parc de la Citadelle surrounds impressive remnants of a 17th-century fortress built near the Rhine by Vauban. Another, the Parc de Pourtalès, is arranged in English style around a baroque castle—heavily restored in the 19th century—which now operates as a small three-star hotel; the park also includes an open-air museum of international contemporary sculpture.

Although the Parc des Contades is the city's oldest park, it was entirely redesigned following World War II. In contrast, the futuristic Parc des Poteries exemplifies European park design from the late 1990s. The Jardin des deux Rives, stretching across Strasbourg and Kehl on both banks of the Rhine, opened in 2004 and is the largest park in the area at 60 hectares. The most recent addition is the Parc du Heyritz (8.7 hectares), inaugurated in 2014 along a canal opposite the hôpital civil.

Also of note is the Jardin botanique de l'Université de Strasbourg. Established under German administration beside the 1881 Observatory of Strasbourg, it retains several greenhouses from that period.

input: Buddhism first entered China during the Eastern Han and was first mentioned in 65 AD. Liu Ying (d. 71 AD), a half-brother to Emperor Ming of Han (r. 57–75 AD), was one of its earliest Chinese adherents, although Chinese Buddhism at this point was heavily associated with Huang-Lao Daoism. China's first known Buddhist temple, the White Horse Temple, was erected during Ming's reign. Important Buddhist canons were translated into Chinese during the 2nd century AD, including the Sutra of Forty-two Chapters, Perfection of Wisdom, Shurangama Sutra, and Pratyutpanna Sutra.
rewrite: Buddhism arrived in China in the Eastern Han period, with its earliest record dating to 65 AD. Among its first Chinese followers was Liu Ying (d. 71 AD), a half-brother of Emperor Ming (r. 57–75 AD), though the faith was then closely linked to Huang-Lao Daoism. The White Horse Temple, China's earliest known Buddhist temple, was built under Emperor Ming. During the 2nd century AD, key scriptures like the Sutra of Forty-two Chapters, Perfection of Wisdom, Shurangama Sutra, and Pratyutpanna Sutra were translated into Chinese.

input: In the Church of England, the ecclesiastical courts that formerly decided many matters such as disputes relating to marriage, divorce, wills, and defamation, still have jurisdiction of certain church-related matters (e.g. discipline of clergy, alteration of church property, and issues related to churchyards). Their separate status dates back to the 12th century when the Normans split them off from the mixed secular/religious county and local courts used by the Saxons. In contrast to the other courts of England the law used in ecclesiastical matters is at least partially a civil law system, not common law, although heavily governed by parliamentary statutes. Since the Reformation, ecclesiastical courts in England have been royal courts. The teaching of canon law at the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge was abrogated by Henry VIII; thereafter practitioners in the ecclesiastical courts were trained in civil law, receiving a Doctor of Civil Law (D.C.L.) degree from Oxford, or a Doctor of Laws (LL.D.) degree from Cambridge. Such lawyers (called "doctors" and "civilians") were centered at "Doctors Commons", a few streets south of St Paul's Cathedral in London, where they monopolized probate, matrimonial, and admiralty cases until their jurisdiction was removed to the common law courts in the mid-19th century.
rewrite: Ecclesiastical courts in the Church of England, which date their separate status to the 12th-century Norman separation from earlier Saxon courts, retain jurisdiction over specific church matters. These include clergy discipline, alterations to church property, and issues concerning churchyards. Historically, these courts decided many civil matters like marriage disputes, divorce, wills, and defamation. Unlike other English courts, they operate under a legal system that is at least partially civil law, though heavily regulated by parliamentary statutes, rather than common law. Since the Reformation, these have been royal courts. The teaching of canon law at Oxford and Cambridge was abolished by Henry VIII; subsequently, practitioners were trained in civil law, earning either a Doctor of Civil Law (D.C.L.) from Oxford or a Doctor of Laws (LL.D.) from Cambridge. These lawyers, known as "doctors" or "civilians," were based at "Doctors Commons" near St Paul's Cathedral in London. There, they held a monopoly over probate, matrimonial, and admiralty cases until the mid-19th century, when their jurisdiction was transferred to common law courts.

input: Buddhism began to spread throughout Japan during the Heian period, primarily through two major esoteric sects, Tendai and Shingon. Tendai originated in China and is based on the Lotus Sutra, one of the most important sutras of Mahayana Buddhism; Saichō was key to its transmission to Japan. Shingon is the Japanese transmission of the Chinese Chen Yen school. Shingon, brought to Japan by the monk Kūkai, emphasizes Esoteric Buddhism. Both Kūkai and Saichō aimed to connect state and religion and establish support from the aristocracy, leading to the notion of 'aristocratic Buddhism'. An important element of Tendai doctrine was the suggestion that enlightenment was accessible to "every creature". Saichō also sought independent ordination for Tendai monks. A close relationship developed between the Tendai monastery complex on Mount Hiei and the imperial court in its new capital at the foot of the mountain. As a result, Tendai emphasized great reverence for the emperor and the nation. Kammu himself was a notable patron of the otherworldly Tendai sect, which rose to great power over the ensuing centuries. Kūkai greatly impressed the emperors who succeeded Emperor Kammu, and also generations of Japanese, not only with his holiness but also with his poetry, calligraphy, painting, and sculpture. Shingon, through its use of "rich symbols, rituals and mandalas" held a wide-ranging appeal.
rewrite: During the Heian period, Buddhism spread widely in Japan, chiefly through the two major esoteric sects of Tendai and Shingon. Tendai, which originated in China and is founded on the important Mahayana text, the Lotus Sutra, was transmitted to Japan largely through the efforts of Saichō. Shingon represents the Japanese lineage of the Chinese Chen Yen school, introduced by the monk Kūkai with a focus on Esoteric Buddhism. Both founders worked to link religion and the state, securing aristocratic backing and fostering what became known as 'aristocratic Buddhism'. A key doctrinal point of Tendai was its assertion that enlightenment could be attained by "every creature." Saichō further pursued independent ordination for Tendai monks. The Tendai monastic complex on Mount Hiei developed a close relationship with the imperial court, situated at the mountain's base in the new capital. This connection led Tendai to promote deep reverence for the emperor and the nation. Emperor Kammu himself notably patronized the otherworldly Tendai sect, which grew immensely powerful over the following centuries. Kūkai deeply impressed both the emperors following Kammu and generations of Japanese, not merely through his piety but also via his artistic achievements in poetry, calligraphy, painting, and sculpture. Meanwhile, Shingon held broad appeal through its employment of "rich symbols, rituals and mandalas."

input: When used with a load that has a torque curve that increases with speed, the motor will operate at the speed where the torque developed by the motor is equal to the load torque. Reducing the load will cause the motor to speed up, and increasing the load will cause the motor to slow down until the load and motor torque are equal. Operated in this manner, the slip losses are dissipated in the secondary resistors and can be very significant. The speed regulation and net efficiency is also very poor.
rewrite: A motor paired with a load whose torque rises with speed will run at the point where motor torque matches load torque. If the load decreases, the motor accelerates; if the load increases, it slows until equilibrium is restored. In this operating mode, substantial slip losses occur, dissipated through the secondary resistors. This results in very poor speed regulation and notably low net efficiency.

input: In 1988, Apple sued Microsoft and Hewlett-Packard on the grounds that they infringed Apple's copyrighted GUI, citing (among other things) the use of rectangular, overlapping, and resizable windows. After four years, the case was decided against Apple, as were later appeals. Apple's actions were criticized by some in the software community, including the Free Software Foundation (FSF), who felt Apple was trying to monopolize on GUIs in general, and boycotted GNU software for the Macintosh platform for seven years.
rewrite: Apple sued Microsoft and Hewlett-Packard in 1988, alleging copyright infringement of its graphical user interface, specifically targeting features like rectangular, overlapping, and resizable windows. Following four years of litigation, the ruling and subsequent appeals favored the defendants. This legal move drew criticism from segments of the software community, such as the Free Software Foundation, which accused Apple of seeking a GUI monopoly and consequently boycotted GNU software on Macintosh computers for seven years.

input: On the other hand, changes through the Phanerozoic correlate much better with the hyperbolic model (widely used in population biology, demography and macrosociology, as well as fossil biodiversity) than with exponential and logistic models. The latter models imply that changes in diversity are guided by a first-order positive feedback (more ancestors, more descendants) and/or a negative feedback arising from resource limitation. Hyperbolic model implies a second-order positive feedback. The hyperbolic pattern of the world population growth arises from a second-order positive feedback between the population size and the rate of technological growth. The hyperbolic character of biodiversity growth can be similarly accounted for by a feedback between diversity and community structure complexity. The similarity between the curves of biodiversity and human population probably comes from the fact that both are derived from the interference of the hyperbolic trend with cyclical and stochastic dynamics.
rewrite: In contrast to exponential and logistic models, changes throughout the Phanerozoic align more closely with the hyperbolic model, a framework common in population biology, demography, and macrosociology, as well as in studies of fossil biodiversity. Exponential and logistic models suggest diversity changes are driven by first-order positive feedback—where more ancestors lead to more descendants—or by negative feedback from limited resources. The hyperbolic model, however, involves a second-order positive feedback. This pattern in global population growth stems from such a feedback loop between population size and technological advancement rates. Similarly, biodiversity’s hyperbolic growth can be explained by feedback between diversity and the complexity of community structures. The resemblance between biodiversity and human population curves likely arises because both result from the interaction of hyperbolic trends with cyclical and stochastic dynamics.

input: Portugal has considerable resources of wind and river power, the two most cost-effective renewable sources. Since the turn of the 21st century, there has been a trend towards the development of a renewable resource industry and reduction of both consumption and use of fossil fuel resources. In 2006, the world's largest solar power plant at that date, the Moura Photovoltaic Power Station, began operating near Moura, in the south, while the world's first commercial wave power farm, the Aguçadoura Wave Farm, opened in the Norte region (2008). By the end of 2006, 66% of the country's electrical production was from coal and fuel power plants, while 29% were derived from hydroelectric dams, and 6% by wind energy.
rewrite: Portugal possesses significant wind and river power resources, which are among the most economical renewable options. The early 21st century saw a shift toward growing a renewable energy sector and decreasing fossil fuel consumption. Notably, the Moura Photovoltaic Power Station, then the world's largest solar plant, started operations in southern Portugal in 2006. Following this, the world's first commercial wave farm, the Aguçadoura Wave Farm, launched in the Norte region in 2008. Despite these advances, coal and fuel plants still generated 66% of the nation's electricity by the end of 2006, with hydroelectric dams providing 29% and wind energy contributing 6%.

input: The theories developed in the 1930s and 1940s to integrate molecular genetics with Darwinian evolution are called the modern evolutionary synthesis, a term introduced by Julian Huxley. Evolutionary biologists subsequently refined this concept, such as George C. Williams' gene-centric view of evolution. He proposed an evolutionary concept of the gene as a unit of natural selection with the definition: "that which segregates and recombines with appreciable frequency.":24 In this view, the molecular gene transcribes as a unit, and the evolutionary gene inherits as a unit. Related ideas emphasizing the centrality of genes in evolution were popularized by Richard Dawkins.
rewrite: The modern evolutionary synthesis, a term coined by Julian Huxley, refers to theories from the 1930s and 1940s that merged molecular genetics with Darwinian evolution. Later refinements included a gene-centric perspective, notably advanced by George C. Williams. He defined an evolutionary gene as "that which segregates and recombines with appreciable frequency,":24 proposing it as a unit of natural selection. In this framework, the molecular gene transcribes as a unit, while the evolutionary gene is inherited as one. Richard Dawkins further popularized related ideas emphasizing the central role of genes in evolution.

input: In the 10th century the establishment of churches and monasteries led to the development of stone architecture that elaborated vernacular Roman forms, from which the term "Romanesque" is derived. Where available, Roman brick and stone buildings were recycled for their materials. From the tentative beginnings known as the First Romanesque, the style flourished and spread across Europe in a remarkably homogeneous form. Just before 1000 there was a great wave of building stone churches all over Europe. Romanesque buildings have massive stone walls, openings topped by semi-circular arches, small windows, and, particularly in France, arched stone vaults. The large portal with coloured sculpture in high relief became a central feature of façades, especially in France, and the capitals of columns were often carved with narrative scenes of imaginative monsters and animals. According to art historian C. R. Dodwell, "virtually all the churches in the West were decorated with wall-paintings", of which few survive. Simultaneous with the development in church architecture, the distinctive European form of the castle was developed, and became crucial to politics and warfare.
rewrite: During the 10th century, the founding of churches and monasteries spurred advances in stone architecture, which expanded upon local Roman traditions—giving rise to the term "Romanesque." Builders often reused materials from existing Roman brick and stone structures where possible. Following its initial phase, known as First Romanesque, the style spread throughout Europe, achieving a notably uniform appearance. A major wave of stone church construction swept across the continent just before the year 1000. Characteristic features of Romanesque buildings include thick stone walls, openings capped by semi-circular arches, small windows, and, in France especially, arched stone vaults. Elaborately sculpted portals in high relief grew into a focal point of façades, again notably in France, while column capitals were frequently carved with narrative scenes featuring fantastic creatures and animals. Art historian C. R. Dodwell notes that "virtually all the churches in the West were decorated with wall-paintings," though few examples remain today. Parallel to these ecclesiastical developments, the distinctive European castle emerged, becoming a key element in political and military affairs.

input: Nasser's involvement in political activity increased throughout his school years, such that he only attended 45 days of classes during his last year of secondary school. Despite it having the almost unanimous backing of Egypt's political forces, Nasser strongly objected to the 1936 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty because it stipulated the continued presence of British military bases in the country. Nonetheless, political unrest in Egypt declined significantly and Nasser resumed his studies at al-Nahda, where he received his leaving certificate later that year.
rewrite: Throughout his school years, Nasser grew increasingly engaged in politics, missing all but 45 days of class in his final secondary year. He vehemently opposed the 1936 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty, despite its broad support among Egyptian political forces, due to its allowance of ongoing British military bases. As political unrest in Egypt subsided, he returned to his studies at al-Nahda, earning his leaving certificate later that same year.

input: Other sports clubs include Plymouth Albion R.F.C. and the Plymouth Raiders basketball club. Plymouth Albion Rugby Football Club is a rugby union club that was founded in 1875 and are currently competing in the third tier of Professional English Rugby . They play at the Brickfields. Plymouth Raiders play in the British Basketball League – the top tier of British basketball. They play at the Plymouth Pavilions entertainment arena and were founded in 1983. Plymouth cricket club was formed in 1843, the current 1st XI play in the Devon Premier League. Plymouth Devils are a speedway team in the British Premier League. Plymouth was home to an American football club, the Plymouth Admirals until 2010. Plymouth is also home to Plymouth Marjons Hockey Club, with their 1st XI playing in the National League last season.
rewrite: Plymouth hosts a variety of sports clubs. Plymouth Albion R.F.C., a rugby union club founded in 1875, competes in the third tier of Professional English Rugby and plays at the Brickfields. The city's basketball team, the Plymouth Raiders, was established in 1983 and plays in the top-tier British Basketball League at the Plymouth Pavilions. Cricket has a long history here, with Plymouth Cricket Club formed in 1843 and its first XI in the Devon Premier League.
