input: Meanwhile, Le Verrier by letter urged Berlin Observatory astronomer Johann Gottfried Galle to search with the observatory's refractor. Heinrich d'Arrest, a student at the observatory, suggested to Galle that they could compare a recently drawn chart of the sky in the region of Le Verrier's predicted location with the current sky to seek the displacement characteristic of a planet, as opposed to a fixed star. On the evening of 23 September 1846, the day Galle received the letter, he discovered Neptune within 1° of where Le Verrier had predicted it to be, about 12° from Adams' prediction. Challis later realised that he had observed the planet twice, on 4 and 12 August, but did not recognise it as a planet because he lacked an up-to-date star map and was distracted by his concurrent work on comet observations.
rewrite: At Berlin Observatory, Johann Gottfried Galle was urged by letter from Le Verrier to search for the predicted planet using the observatory's refractor. Upon receiving the letter on 23 September 1846, Galle, with the help of student Heinrich d'Arrest, acted that same evening. D'Arrest proposed comparing a recent sky chart of Le Verrier's specified region against the actual sky to detect the telltale motion of a planet versus a fixed star. Neptune was found by Galle within one degree of Le Verrier's calculated position, roughly twelve degrees from where Adams had predicted. Elsewhere, Challis later understood he had sighted the planet on two occasions in August but failed to identify it, hindered by an outdated star map and his simultaneous comet research.

input: According to the latest nationwide census, Roman Catholics constituted 30.8% of the total population of Germany, followed by the Evangelical Protestants at 30.3%. Other religions, atheists or not specified constituted 38.8% of the population at the time. Among "others" are Protestants not included in Evangelical Church of Germany, and other Christians such as the Restorationist New Apostolic Church. Protestantism was more common among the citizens of Germany. The North and East Germany is predominantly Protestant, the South and West rather Catholic. Nowadays there is a non-religious majority in Hamburg and the East German states.
rewrite: The latest nationwide census shows Roman Catholics made up 30.8% of Germany's population, with Evangelical Protestants at 30.3%. The remaining 38.8% included other religions, atheists, or unspecified affiliations. This "other" category encompasses Protestants outside the Evangelical Church of Germany and other Christian groups like the New Apostolic Church. Historically, Protestantism was more widespread among citizens, dominating the North and East, while the South and West were rather Catholic. Today, a non-religious majority exists in Hamburg and the East German states.

input: Many regions in Russia were affected by the Soviet famine of 1932–1933: Volga; Central Black Soil Region; North Caucasus; the Urals; the Crimea; part of Western Siberia; and the Kazak ASSR. With the adoption of the 1936 Soviet Constitution on December 5, 1936, the size of the RSFSR was significantly reduced. The Kazakh ASSR and Kirghiz ASSR were transformed into the Kazakh and Kirghiz Soviet Socialist Republics. The Karakalpak Autonomous Socialist Soviet Republic was transferred to the Uzbek SSR.
rewrite: The Soviet famine of 1932–1933 impacted numerous Russian regions, including the Volga, Central Black Soil Region, North Caucasus, Urals, Crimea, parts of Western Siberia, and the Kazak ASSR. Following the 1936 Soviet Constitution's adoption on December 5, the RSFSR's territory was greatly reduced. The Kazakh and Kirghiz ASSRs became full Soviet Socialist Republics, while the Karakalpak ASSR was moved to the Uzbek SSR.

input: On August 1, 2012, Windows 8 (build 9200) was released to manufacturing with the build number 6.2.9200.16384 . Microsoft planned to hold a launch event on October 25, 2012 and release Windows 8 for general availability on the next day. However, only a day after its release to manufacturing, a copy of the final version of Windows 8 Enterprise N (a version for European markets lacking bundled media players to comply with a court ruling) leaked online, followed by leaks of the final versions of Windows 8 Pro and Enterprise a few days later. On August 15, 2012, Windows 8 was made available to download for MSDN and TechNet subscribers. Windows 8 was made available to Software Assurance customers on August 16, 2012. Windows 8 was made available for students with a DreamSpark Premium subscription on August 22, 2012, earlier than advertised.
rewrite: Windows 8 reached the release to manufacturing stage on August 1, 2012, carrying the build number 6.2.9200.16384. Microsoft had scheduled a formal launch event for October 25, with general availability to follow the next day. However, leaks began almost immediately. Merely a day after the manufacturing release, the final version of Windows 8 Enterprise N—a European edition without bundled media players due to a legal ruling—appeared online. Leaks of the final Pro and Enterprise versions followed within days. Ahead of the public launch, the OS was released to specific groups: MSDN and TechNet subscribers gained access on August 15, Software Assurance customers on August 16, and DreamSpark Premium students on August 22, earlier than initially planned.

input: Bath Rugby play at the Recreation Ground in Bath, and the Somerset County Cricket Club are based at the County Ground in Taunton. The county gained its first Football League club in 2003, when Yeovil Town won promotion to Division Three as Football Conference champions. They had achieved numerous FA Cup victories over football League sides in the past 50 years, and since joining the elite they have won promotion again—as League Two champions in 2005. They came close to yet another promotion in 2007, when they reached the League One playoff final, but lost to Blackpool at the newly reopened Wembley Stadium. Yeovil achieved promotion to the Championship in 2013 after beating Brentford in the playoff final. Horse racing courses are at Taunton and Wincanton.
rewrite: The Recreation Ground in Bath hosts Bath Rugby, while the Somerset County Cricket Club is based at the County Ground in Taunton. Somerset acquired its first Football League club in 2003, when Yeovil Town earned promotion to Division Three as Football Conference champions. Over the preceding 50 years, Yeovil had secured numerous FA Cup victories against Football League sides. After joining the elite, they won promotion again as League Two champions in 2005. In 2007, they narrowly missed another promotion, losing to Blackpool in the League One playoff final at the newly reopened Wembley Stadium. Yeovil later achieved promotion to the Championship in 2013 by defeating Brentford in the playoff final. Horse racing courses are located at Taunton and Wincanton.

input: Despite this, the Austrians, under the command of General Laudon, captured Glatz (now Kłodzko, Poland) in Silesia. In the Battle of Liegnitz Frederick scored a strong victory despite being outnumbered three to one. The Russians under General Saltykov and Austrians under General Lacy briefly occupied his capital, Berlin, in October, but could not hold it for long. The end of that year saw Frederick once more victorious, defeating the able Daun in the Battle of Torgau; but he suffered very heavy casualties, and the Austrians retreated in good order.
rewrite: Under General Laudon, Austrian forces seized Glatz in Silesia. Frederick the Great, however, achieved a decisive victory at Liegnitz while outnumbered three to one. Later, in October, a combined Russian and Austrian army led by Generals Saltykov and Lacy briefly occupied Berlin before withdrawing. The year concluded with Frederick's costly victory at Torgau, where he defeated General Daun. Though the Austrians retreated in good order, Frederick's forces endured severe casualties.

input: Polarization is predictable from an antenna's geometry, although in some cases it is not at all obvious (such as for the quad antenna). An antenna's linear polarization is generally along the direction (as viewed from the receiving location) of the antenna's currents when such a direction can be defined. For instance, a vertical whip antenna or Wi-Fi antenna vertically oriented will transmit and receive in the vertical polarization. Antennas with horizontal elements, such as most rooftop TV antennas in the United States, are horizontally polarized (broadcast TV in the U.S. usually uses horizontal polarization). Even when the antenna system has a vertical orientation, such as an array of horizontal dipole antennas, the polarization is in the horizontal direction corresponding to the current flow. The polarization of a commercial antenna is an essential specification.
rewrite: While an antenna's polarization can often be predicted from its geometry, this is not always immediately clear, as with a quad antenna. Typically, linear polarization aligns with the direction of the antenna's currents from the receiver's viewpoint. For example, a vertical whip or Wi-Fi antenna operates with vertical polarization. Conversely, antennas with horizontal elements, like most U.S. rooftop TV antennas, are horizontally polarized, matching the standard for American broadcast TV. Notably, even a vertically mounted system, such as an array of horizontal dipoles, exhibits horizontal polarization due to the direction of current flow. This polarization characteristic is a crucial specification for any commercial antenna.

input: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, an Indian nationalist leader, declared Swaraj as the destiny of the nation. His popular sentence "Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it" became the source of inspiration for Indians. Tilak was backed by rising public leaders like Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai, who held the same point of view. Under them, India's three big provinces – Maharashtra, Bengal and Punjab, India shaped the demand of the people and India's nationalism. In 1907, the Congress was split into two factions: The radicals, led by Tilak, advocated civil agitation and direct revolution to overthrow the British Empire and the abandonment of all things British. The moderates, led by leaders like Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale, on the other hand wanted reform within the framework of British rule.
rewrite: For Indians, Bal Gangadhar Tilak’s declaration that “Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it” served as a profound inspiration, framing self-rule as the nation’s destiny. This radical nationalist leader found strong support in public figures like Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai, who shared his vision. Together, they galvanized the major provinces of Maharashtra, Bengal, and Punjab, shaping popular demand and fortifying Indian nationalism. This ideological divide culminated in the 1907 split of the Congress. Tilak’s faction, the radicals, pushed for civil agitation and direct revolution to overthrow British rule, rejecting all British influence. In contrast, the moderates, led by figures such as Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale, sought gradual reform under the existing British framework.

input: Swaziland derives its name from a later king named Mswati II. KaNgwane, named for Ngwane III, is an alternative name for Swaziland the surname of whose royal house remains Nkhosi Dlamini. Nkhosi literally means "king". Mswati II was the greatest of the fighting kings of Swaziland, and he greatly extended the area of the country to twice its current size. The Emakhandzambili clans were initially incorporated into the kingdom with wide autonomy, often including grants of special ritual and political status. The extent of their autonomy however was drastically curtailed by Mswati, who attacked and subdued some of them in the 1850s.
rewrite: The royal house of Swaziland bears the surname Nkhosi Dlamini, with "Nkhosi" meaning "king." The nation itself takes its name from a later ruler, Mswati II, its greatest fighting king who expanded its territory to twice the modern size. An alternative name, KaNgwane, references Ngwane III. Initially, the Emakhandzambili clans were integrated into the kingdom with considerable autonomy and special status. However, in the 1850s, Mswati drastically reduced this independence by attacking and subduing several of these clans.

input: Many Sanskrit dramas also indicate that the language coexisted with Prakrits, spoken by multilingual speakers with a more extensive education. Sanskrit speakers were almost always multilingual. In the medieval era, Sanskrit continued to be spoken and written, particularly by learned Brahmins for scholarly communication. This was a thin layer of Indian society, but covered a wide geography. Centres like Varanasi, Paithan, Pune and Kanchipuram had a strong presence of teaching and debating institutions, and high classical Sanskrit was maintained until British times.
rewrite: Sanskrit dramas reveal that the language coexisted with Prakrits, used by multilingual, educated speakers. Throughout the medieval era, it remained a spoken and written language, chiefly among learned Brahmins for scholarship. Though this group formed a thin layer of society, it was geographically widespread. Key centers such as Varanasi, Paithan, Pune, and Kanchipuram hosted vibrant teaching and debating institutions, preserving high classical Sanskrit until the British period.

input: By the end of the 5th century the western section of the empire was divided into smaller political units, ruled by the tribes that had invaded in the early part of the century. The deposition of the last emperor of the west, Romulus Augustus, in 476 has traditionally marked the end of the Western Roman Empire.[E] The Eastern Roman Empire, often referred to as the Byzantine Empire after the fall of its western counterpart, had little ability to assert control over the lost western territories. The Byzantine emperors maintained a claim over the territory, but none of the new kings in the west dared to elevate himself to the position of emperor of the west, Byzantine control of most of the Western Empire could not be sustained; the reconquest of the Italian peninsula and Mediterranean periphery by Justinian (r. 527–565) was the sole, and temporary, exception.
rewrite: By the close of the 5th century, the western portion of the Roman Empire had fragmented into smaller political entities governed by invading tribes from earlier in the century. Traditionally, the end of the Western Roman Empire is marked by the 476 deposition of its last emperor, Romulus Augustus. Following this fall, the Eastern Roman Empire—frequently termed the Byzantine Empire thereafter—possessed limited capacity to reimpose authority over the vanished western domains. Although Byzantine emperors continued to assert a formal claim to the territory, none of the new western monarchs risked assuming the title of western emperor. Sustained Byzantine control over most of the former Western Empire proved unfeasible. The sole, and brief, exception was the reconquest of the Italian peninsula and parts of the Mediterranean periphery under Emperor Justinian, who reigned from 527 to 565.

input: St. John's (/ˌseɪntˈdʒɒnz/, local /ˌseɪntˈdʒɑːnz/) is the capital and largest city in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada. St. John's was incorporated as a city in 1888, yet is considered by some to be the oldest English-founded city in North America. It is located on the eastern tip of the Avalon Peninsula on the island of Newfoundland. With a population of 214,285 as of July 1, 2015, the St. John's Metropolitan Area is the second largest Census Metropolitan Area (CMA) in Atlantic Canada after Halifax and the 20th largest metropolitan area in Canada. It is one of the world's top ten oceanside destinations, according to National Geographic Magazine. Its name has been attributed to the feast day of John the Baptist, when John Cabot was believed to have sailed into the harbour in 1497, and also to a Basque fishing town with the same name.
rewrite: Situated on the eastern tip of Newfoundland’s Avalon Peninsula, St. John's is the capital and largest city of Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada. Although incorporated as a city in 1888, it is often regarded as the oldest English-founded city in North America. The St. John's Metropolitan Area, with a population of 214,285 as of July 1, 2015, ranks as the second largest Census Metropolitan Area in Atlantic Canada after Halifax and the 20th largest in the country. National Geographic Magazine lists it among the world's top ten oceanside destinations. The city’s name is linked both to the feast day of John the Baptist—coinciding with John Cabot’s believed arrival in the harbour in 1497—and to a Basque fishing town sharing the same name.

input: Chemical communications in animals rely on a variety of aspects including taste and smell. Chemoreception is the physiological response of a sense organ (i.e. taste or smell) to a chemical stimulus where the chemicals act as signals to regulate the state or activity of a cell. A semiochemical is a message-carrying chemical that is meant to attract, repel, and convey information. Types of semiochemicals include pheromones and kairomones. One example is the butterfly Phengaris arion which uses chemical signals as a form of mimicry to aid in predation.
rewrite: Animals utilize chemical communications through taste and smell, a process known as chemoreception. This involves a sense organ's physiological response to chemical stimuli, which act as signals to modify a cell's state or activity. Message-carrying chemicals, called semiochemicals, serve to attract, repel, or convey information. Pheromones and kairomones are two types. For instance, the butterfly Phengaris arion employs chemical signals in a form of mimicry to assist in predation.

input: Distinctive and self-identified black communities have been reported in countries such as Iraq, with a reported 1.2 million black people, and they attest to a history of discrimination. African-Iraquis have sought minority status from the government, which would reserve some seats in Parliament for representatives of their population. According to Alamin M. Mazrui et al., generally in the Arabian Peninsula and neighboring countries, most of those of visible African descent are still classified and identify as Arab, not black.
rewrite: Reported in nations like Iraq, distinctive and self-identified black communities attest to a history of discrimination. African-Iraqis, for instance, have sought official minority status to reserve parliamentary seats for their population of about 1.2 million. However, as noted by Alamin M. Mazrui et al., across the Arabian Peninsula and neighboring areas, most people of visible African descent are still classified and identify as Arab rather than black.

input: Darwin's barnacle studies convinced him that variation arose constantly and not just in response to changed circumstances. In 1854, he completed the last part of his Beagle-related writing and began working full-time on evolution. His thinking changed from the view that species formed in isolated populations only, as on islands, to an emphasis on speciation without isolation; that is, he saw increasing specialisation within large stable populations as continuously exploiting new ecological niches. He conducted empirical research focusing on difficulties with his theory. He studied the developmental and anatomical differences between different breeds of many domestic animals, became actively involved in fancy pigeon breeding, and experimented (with the help of his son Francis) on ways that plant seeds and animals might disperse across oceans to colonise distant islands. By 1856, his theory was much more sophisticated, with a mass of supporting evidence.
rewrite: Darwin’s examination of barnacles reinforced his belief that variation occurred continuously, not merely as a reaction to altered environments. Shifting to full-time work on evolution in 1854 after finishing his Beagle writings, his views transformed. He moved from seeing species formation as solely happening in isolated groups, like on islands, to emphasizing speciation without isolation. Darwin now perceived increasing specialization within large, stable populations as a process that constantly opened new ecological niches. To address challenges to his theory, he engaged in empirical research. This included studying developmental and anatomical variations across domestic animal breeds, active participation in fancy pigeon breeding, and experiments—aided by his son Francis—on how seeds and animals could disperse over oceans to reach remote islands. By 1856, his theory had grown far more sophisticated, backed by substantial evidence.

input: On the whole, Eisenhower's support of the nation's fledgling space program was officially modest until the Soviet launch of Sputnik in 1957, gaining the Cold War enemy enormous prestige around the world. He then launched a national campaign that funded not just space exploration but a major strengthening of science and higher education. His Open Skies Policy attempted to legitimize illegal Lockheed U-2 flyovers and Project Genetrix while paving the way for spy satellite technology to orbit over sovereign territory, created NASA as a civilian space agency, signed a landmark science education law, and fostered improved relations with American scientists.
rewrite: Initially, Eisenhower offered only measured official backing to America's nascent space efforts. This changed after the 1957 Soviet launch of Sputnik, which bestowed significant global prestige on the Cold War rival. In response, Eisenhower initiated a sweeping national campaign. It dramatically increased funding for space exploration, scientific research, and higher education. His administration created NASA as a civilian agency, enacted a major science education law, and sought better ties with U.S. scientists. Furthermore, through the Open Skies Policy, he worked to justify surveillance flights and early spy balloon projects, thereby laying the groundwork for future reconnaissance satellites.

input: The Alps are split into five climatic zones, each with different vegetation. The climate, plant life and animal life vary among the different sections or zones of the mountains. The lowest zone is the colline zone, which exists between 500 and 1,000 m (1,640 and 3,281 ft), depending on the location. The montane zone extends from 800 to 1,700 m (2,625 to 5,577 ft), followed by the sub-Alpine zone from 1,600 to 2,400 m (5,249 to 7,874 ft). The Alpine zone, extending from tree line to snow line, is followed by the glacial zone, which covers the glaciated areas of the mountain. Climatic conditions show variances within the same zones; for example, weather conditions at the head of a mountain valley, extending directly from the peaks, are colder and more severe than those at the mouth of a valley which tend to be less severe and receive less snowfall.
rewrite: The Alps feature five distinct climatic zones, each supporting unique vegetation and animal life. At the lowest elevation lies the colline zone, ranging from 500 to 1,000 meters. Above it, the montane zone spans 800 to 1,700 meters, followed by the sub-Alpine zone from 1,600 to 2,400 meters. Next is the Alpine zone, stretching from the tree line to the snow line, and finally the glacial zone covering the mountains' glaciated areas. Climate, flora, and fauna differ across these sections. Notably, conditions can vary even within the same zone. For instance, weather at the head of a valley extending from the peaks is colder and more severe, while the valley mouth experiences milder conditions with less snowfall.

input: Han Chinese Banners were made up of Han Chinese who defected to the Qing up to 1644 and joined the Eight Banners, giving them social and legal privileges in addition to being acculturated to Manchu culture. So many Han defected to the Qing and swelled the ranks of the Eight Banners that ethnic Manchus became a minority, making up only 16% in 1648, with Han Bannermen dominating at 75% and Mongol Bannermen making up the rest. This multi-ethnic force in which Manchus were only a minority conquered China for the Qing.
rewrite: Composed of Han Chinese who defected to the Qing dynasty before 1644, the Han Chinese Banners were integrated into the Eight Banners system. This acculturation to Manchu ways came with social and legal advantages. Their defections were so numerous that by 1648, ethnic Manchus constituted a mere 16% of the Banners, while Han Bannermen dominated at 75%, and Mongols comprised the remainder. It was this multi-ethnic force, with Manchus as a minority, that ultimately conquered China for the Qing.

input: BBC Television is a service of the British Broadcasting Corporation. The corporation, which has operated in the United Kingdom under the terms of a Royal charter since 1927, has produced television programmes from its own since 1932, although the start of its regular service of television broadcasts is dated to 2 November 1936.
rewrite: BBC Television, a service of the British Broadcasting Corporation, began producing programmes in 1932. Its regular broadcasts started on 2 November 1936. The corporation has operated under a Royal charter in the UK since 1927.

input: The word madrasah derives from the triconsonantal Semitic root د-ر-س D-R-S 'to learn, study', through the wazn (form/stem) مفعل(ة)‎; mafʻal(ah), meaning "a place where something is done". Therefore, madrasah literally means "a place where learning and studying take place". The word is also present as a loanword with the same innocuous meaning in many Arabic-influenced languages, such as: Urdu, Bengali, Hindi, Persian, Turkish, Azeri, Kurdish, Indonesian, Malay and Bosnian / Croatian. In the Arabic language, the word مدرسة madrasah simply means the same as school does in the English language, whether that is private, public or parochial school, as well as for any primary or secondary school whether Muslim, non-Muslim, or secular. Unlike the use of the word school in British English, the word madrasah more closely resembles the term school in American English, in that it can refer to a university-level or post-graduate school as well as to a primary or secondary school. For example, in the Ottoman Empire during the Early Modern Period, madaris had lower schools and specialised schools where the students became known as danişmends. The usual Arabic word for a university, however, is جامعة (jāmiʻah). The Hebrew cognate midrasha also connotes the meaning of a place of learning; the related term midrash literally refers to study or learning, but has acquired mystical and religious connotations.
rewrite: Derived from the Semitic root د-ر-س (D-R-S), meaning "to learn" or "study," the term madrasah originates from the form *mafʻal(ah)*, which denotes a place where an action occurs. Thus, its literal meaning is "a place where learning and studying happen." In Arabic, مدرسة (madrasah) carries the same general sense as the English word "school," applicable to any educational institution—private, public, or parochial, and covering primary or secondary levels, regardless of being Muslim, non-Muslim, or secular. This word has been adopted into numerous languages influenced by Arabic, including Urdu, Bengali, Hindi, Persian, Turkish, Azeri, Kurdish, Indonesian, Malay, and Bosnian/Croatian, retaining its neutral meaning. Unlike the British English usage of "school," which typically excludes higher education, "madrasah" aligns more closely with American English, as it can refer to university-level or post-graduate institutions alongside primary and secondary schools. Historically, in the Ottoman Empire's Early Modern Period, madaris encompassed both lower schools and specialized advanced schools, with students in the latter known as danişmends. It should be noted that the standard Arabic word for a university is جامعة (jāmiʻah). Additionally, the Hebrew cognate *midrasha* similarly signifies a place of learning, while the related term *midrash* originally means study but has evolved to include mystical and religious dimensions.

input: In 2010, a number of workers committed suicide at a Foxconn operations in China. Apple, HP, and others stated that they were investigating the situation. Foxconn guards have been videotaped beating employees. Another employee killed himself in 2009 when an Apple prototype went missing, and claimed in messages to friends, that he had been beaten and interrogated.
rewrite: In 2010, multiple suicides occurred at a Foxconn facility in China, prompting investigations by Apple and HP. Guards were recorded beating employees. Separately, in 2009, an employee took his life after an Apple prototype was lost; he had messaged friends claiming beatings and interrogation.

input: Vietnam: The event was held in Ho Chi Minh City on April 29. Some 60 torchbearers carried the torch from the downtown Opera House to the Military Zone 7 Competition Hall stadium near Tan Son Nhat International Airport along an undisclosed route. Vietnam is involved in a territorial dispute with China (and other countries) for sovereignty of the Spratly and Paracel Islands; tensions have risen recently[when?] following reports that the Chinese government had established a county-level city named Sansha in the disputed territories, resulting in anti-Chinese demonstrations in December 2007 in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City. However to sustain its relationship with China the Vietnamese government has actively sought to head off protests during the torch relay, with Prime Minister Nguyễn Tấn Dũng warning government agencies that "hostile forces" may try to disrupt the torch relay.
rewrite: On April 29 in Ho Chi Minh City, approximately 60 torchbearers carried the flame from the downtown Opera House to the Military Zone 7 Competition Hall stadium near Tan Son Nhat International Airport, following an undisclosed route. This event occurred amid heightened regional tensions. Vietnam is engaged in a sovereignty dispute with China and others over the Spratly and Paracel Islands. Tensions increased following China's establishment of Sansha, a county-level city in the contested area, which sparked anti-Chinese demonstrations in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City in December 2007. To preserve its relationship with China, the Vietnamese government actively worked to prevent protests during the relay. Prime Minister Nguyễn Tấn Dũng cautioned government agencies that "hostile forces" might attempt to disrupt the proceedings.

input: Han Chinese make up the vast majority of the population, and the largest Han subgroup are the speakers of Wu varieties of Chinese. There are also 400,000 members of ethnic minorities, including approximately 200,000 She people and approximately 20,000 Hui Chinese[citation needed]. Jingning She Autonomous County in Lishui is the only She autonomous county in China.
rewrite: The vast majority of the population is Han Chinese, with the largest subgroup speaking Wu varieties. Ethnic minorities number 400,000, including about 200,000 She people and 20,000 Hui Chinese. China's only She autonomous county is Jingning She Autonomous County, located in Lishui.

input: The sensitivity of Earth-based infrared telescopes is significantly limited by water vapor in the atmosphere, which absorbs a portion of the infrared radiation arriving from space outside of selected atmospheric windows. This limitation can be partially alleviated by placing the telescope observatory at a high altitude, or by carrying the telescope aloft with a balloon or an aircraft. Space telescopes do not suffer from this handicap, and so outer space is considered the ideal location for infrared astronomy.
rewrite: Earth-based infrared telescopes face a major constraint: atmospheric water vapor absorbs much of the incoming infrared radiation, except within specific atmospheric windows. To partly overcome this, observatories can be built at high altitudes or mounted on balloons or aircraft. However, space telescopes operate completely free of this atmospheric interference, making outer space the optimal environment for infrared astronomy.

input: Dogs bear their litters roughly 58 to 68 days after fertilization, with an average of 63 days, although the length of gestation can vary. An average litter consists of about six puppies, though this number may vary widely based on the breed of dog. In general, toy dogs produce from one to four puppies in each litter, while much larger breeds may average as many as twelve.
rewrite: Gestation in dogs typically lasts about 63 days, ranging from 58 to 68 days. Litter size averages six puppies but varies considerably by breed. Smaller toy breeds often have one to four puppies per litter, whereas much larger breeds can average around twelve.

input: A UCLA research study published in the June 2006 issue of the American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry found that people can improve cognitive function and brain efficiency through simple lifestyle changes such as incorporating memory exercises, healthy eating, physical fitness and stress reduction into their daily lives. This study examined 17 subjects, (average age 53) with normal memory performance. Eight subjects were asked to follow a "brain healthy" diet, relaxation, physical, and mental exercise (brain teasers and verbal memory training techniques). After 14 days, they showed greater word fluency (not memory) compared to their baseline performance. No long term follow up was conducted, it is therefore unclear if this intervention has lasting effects on memory.
rewrite: A June 2006 study in the American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry, conducted by UCLA researchers, indicates cognitive function and brain efficiency can be enhanced with basic daily lifestyle adjustments. These include memory exercises, a healthy diet, physical activity, and stress management. The research involved 17 subjects averaging 53 years old, all with normal memory. Eight participants followed a regimen of mental exercise, a "brain healthy" diet, physical fitness, and relaxation techniques. After just 14 days, this group demonstrated improved word fluency, though not memory, from their baseline. Without long-term follow-up, however, the durability of these effects on memory remains uncertain.

input: In a WRIM, the rotor winding is made of many turns of insulated wire and is connected to slip rings on the motor shaft. An external resistor or other control devices can be connected in the rotor circuit. Resistors allow control of the motor speed, although significant power is dissipated in the external resistance. A converter can be fed from the rotor circuit and return the slip-frequency power that would otherwise be wasted back into the power system through an inverter or separate motor-generator.
rewrite: In a wound rotor induction motor (WRIM), insulated wire forms the rotor winding, which links to slip rings on the shaft. This setup allows external resistors or control devices to be added to the rotor circuit. While resistors enable speed control, they dissipate considerable power. Alternatively, a converter can harness the rotor circuit's slip-frequency power. Instead of being wasted, this energy is channeled back into the power system via an inverter or a separate motor-generator.

input: As civil wars engulfed several Central American countries in the 1980s, hundreds of thousands of Salvadorans fled their country and came to the United States. Between 1980 and 1990, the Salvadoran immigrant population in the United States increased nearly fivefold from 94,000 to 465,000. The number of Salvadoran immigrants in the United States continued to grow in the 1990s and 2000s as a result of family reunification and new arrivals fleeing a series of natural disasters that hit El Salvador, including earthquakes and hurricanes. By 2008, there were about 1.1 million Salvadoran immigrants in the United States.
rewrite: During the 1980s, widespread civil wars across Central America drove hundreds of thousands of Salvadorans to seek refuge in the United States. Their numbers surged from 94,000 to 465,000 between 1980 and 1990. Growth continued in the following decades, fueled by family reunification and new waves of migrants escaping earthquakes and hurricanes in El Salvador. Consequently, the Salvadoran immigrant population reached approximately 1.1 million by 2008.

input: Close to Richmond Park is Kew Gardens which has the world's largest collection of living plants. In 2003, the gardens were put on the UNESCO list of World Heritage Sites. There are also numerous parks administered by London's borough Councils, including Victoria Park in the East End and Battersea Park in the centre. Some more informal, semi-natural open spaces also exist, including the 320-hectare (790-acre) Hampstead Heath of North London, and Epping Forest, which covers 2,476 hectares (6,118.32 acres) in the east. Both are controlled by the City of London Corporation. Hampstead Heath incorporates Kenwood House, the former stately home and a popular location in the summer months where classical musical concerts are held by the lake, attracting thousands of people every weekend to enjoy the music, scenery and fireworks. Epping Forest is a popular venue for various outdoor activities, including mountain biking, walking, horse riding, golf, angling, and orienteering.
rewrite: Kew Gardens, home to the world's largest collection of living plants and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2003, lies near Richmond Park. London's borough Councils administer numerous parks, such as Victoria Park in the East End and Battersea Park in the centre. There are also more informal, semi-natural spaces, including the 320-hectare Hampstead Heath in North London and the vast, 2,476-hectare Epping Forest in the east, both managed by the City of London Corporation. Hampstead Heath features Kenwood House, a former stately home. In summer, classical concerts by its lake draw thousands weekly for music, scenery, and fireworks. Epping Forest is a popular venue for outdoor pursuits like walking, horse riding, mountain biking, golf, angling, and orienteering.

input: On 11 April 2006, Brian May and Roger Taylor appeared on the American singing contest television show American Idol. Each contestant was required to sing a Queen song during that week of the competition. Songs which appeared on the show included "Bohemian Rhapsody", "Fat Bottomed Girls", "The Show Must Go On", "Who Wants to Live Forever", and "Innuendo". Brian May later criticised the show for editing specific scenes, one of which made the group's time with contestant Ace Young look negative, despite it being the opposite. Taylor and May again appeared on the American Idol season 8 finale in May 2009, performing "We Are the Champions" with finalists Adam Lambert and Kris Allen. On 15 November 2009, Brian May and Roger Taylor appeared on the singing contest television show X Factor in the UK.
rewrite: During a 2006 episode of *American Idol*, Queen members Brian May and Roger Taylor appeared as the contestants performed songs from the band’s catalog, such as "Bohemian Rhapsody" and "The Show Must Go On." May later criticized the program for misleading editing, particularly in a segment with contestant Ace Young that portrayed their interaction negatively. The duo returned for the season 8 finale in May 2009, joining finalists Adam Lambert and Kris Allen for a performance of "We Are the Champions." Later that year, on 15 November 2009, May and Taylor also appeared on the UK television singing competition *The X Factor*.

input: Following a custom she maintained throughout her widowhood, Victoria spent the Christmas of 1900 at Osborne House on the Isle of Wight. Rheumatism in her legs had rendered her lame, and her eyesight was clouded by cataracts. Through early January, she felt "weak and unwell", and by mid-January she was "drowsy ... dazed, [and] confused". She died on Tuesday, 22 January 1901, at half past six in the evening, at the age of 81. Her son and successor King Edward VII, and her eldest grandson, Emperor Wilhelm II of Germany, were at her deathbed. Her favourite pet Pomeranian, Turri, was laid upon her deathbed as a last request.
rewrite: As was her tradition in widowhood, Victoria observed Christmas of 1900 at Osborne House on the Isle of Wight. Afflicted by lameness from rheumatism and clouded eyesight from cataracts, she felt “weak and unwell” in early January. By mid-month, she had become “drowsy ... dazed, [and] confused.” She passed away at age 81 on the evening of Tuesday, 22 January 1901. At her bedside were her son and successor, King Edward VII, and her eldest grandson, Emperor Wilhelm II of Germany. In accordance with her final wish, her favourite Pomeranian, Turri, was placed upon the deathbed.

input: Education is the process of facilitating learning, or the acquisition of knowledge, skills, values, beliefs, and habits. Educational methods include storytelling, discussion, teaching, training, and directed research. Education frequently takes place under the guidance of educators, but learners may also educate themselves. Education can take place in formal or informal settings and any experience that has a formative effect on the way one thinks, feels, or acts may be considered educational. The methodology of teaching is called pedagogy.
rewrite: Learning, or the gaining of knowledge, skills, values, beliefs, and habits, is facilitated through education. It can occur in formal or informal settings, often with educators guiding the process, though self-education is also possible. Methods like teaching, storytelling, discussion, training, and directed research are employed. Any experience that shapes how a person thinks, feels, or acts can be deemed educational. The methodology behind instruction is known as pedagogy.

input: Hayek disapproved of the notion of 'social justice'. He compared the market to a game in which 'there is no point in calling the outcome just or unjust' and argued that 'social justice is an empty phrase with no determinable content'; likewise "the results of the individual's efforts are necessarily unpredictable, and the question as to whether the resulting distribution of incomes is just has no meaning". He generally regarded government redistribution of income or capital as an unacceptable intrusion upon individual freedom: "the principle of distributive justice, once introduced, would not be fulfilled until the whole of society was organized in accordance with it. This would produce a kind of society which in all essential respects would be the opposite of a free society."
rewrite: Hayek rejected the concept of 'social justice' as essentially meaningless. He likened the market to a game, stating that labeling its results as just or unjust is pointless. In his view, "social justice is an empty phrase with no determinable content." Since individual efforts yield unpredictable outcomes, he argued that judging the resulting income distribution as fair or unfair is nonsensical. Hayek further saw state-led redistribution of wealth as a severe infringement on personal liberty. Introducing distributive justice, he warned, would demand a total societal reorganization, ultimately creating "a kind of society which in all essential respects would be the opposite of a free society."

input: While consulting for the Moore School of Electrical Engineering at the University of Pennsylvania on the EDVAC project, von Neumann wrote an incomplete First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC. The paper, whose premature distribution nullified the patent claims of EDVAC designers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, described a computer architecture in which the data and the program are both stored in the computer's memory in the same address space. This architecture is to this day the basis of modern computer design, unlike the earliest computers that were "programmed" using a separate memory device such as a paper tape or plugboard. Although the single-memory, stored program architecture is commonly called von Neumann architecture as a result of von Neumann's paper, the architecture's description was based on the work of J. Presper Eckert and John William Mauchly, inventors of the ENIAC computer at the University of Pennsylvania.
rewrite: While serving as a consultant for the University of Pennsylvania’s Moore School of Electrical Engineering on the EDVAC project, John von Neumann produced an unfinished First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC. This document outlined a stored-program computer architecture, where both data and instructions reside in the same address space within memory. That model, a foundational departure from earlier machines programmed via separate media like paper tape or plugboards, remains the cornerstone of modern computer design. The paper’s early circulation, however, invalidated potential patent claims by EDVAC engineers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly. Consequently, while the single-memory architecture is widely termed the “von Neumann architecture” due to his report, its conceptual origins are rooted in the prior work of Eckert and Mauchly, the inventors of the ENIAC.

input: In a factor analysis of the latest wave of World Values Survey data, Arno Tausch (Corvinus University of Budapest) found that Protestantism emerges to be very close to combining religion and the traditions of liberalism. The Global Value Development Index, calculated by Tausch, relies on the World Values Survey dimensions such as trust in the state of law, no support for shadow economy, postmaterial activism, support for democracy, a non-acceptance of violence, xenophobia and racism, trust in transnational capital and Universities, confidence in the market economy, supporting gender justice, and engaging in environmental activism, etc.
rewrite: In analyzing recent World Values Survey data, Arno Tausch of Corvinus University of Budapest identified Protestantism as closely aligning with a blend of religious faith and liberal traditions. His Global Value Development Index incorporates multiple dimensions from the survey. These include trust in the rule of law and market economy, rejection of the shadow economy, violence, xenophobia, and racism, alongside support for democracy, gender justice, environmental activism, and postmaterial values, as well as confidence in transnational capital and universities.

input: Russian Imperialism led to the Russian Empire's conquest of Central Asia during the late 19th century's Imperial Era. Between 1864 and 1885 Russia gradually took control of the entire territory of Russian Turkestan, the Tajikistan portion of which had been controlled by the Emirate of Bukhara and Khanate of Kokand. Russia was interested in gaining access to a supply of cotton and in the 1870s attempted to switch cultivation in the region from grain to cotton (a strategy later copied and expanded by the Soviets).[citation needed] By 1885 Tajikistan's territory was either ruled by the Russian Empire or its vassal state, the Emirate of Bukhara, nevertheless Tajiks felt little Russian influence.[citation needed]
rewrite: During the Imperial Era in the late 19th century, Russian expansionism drove the conquest of Central Asia. The territory of Russian Turkestan, including areas of present-day Tajikistan, was gradually annexed between 1864 and 1885. These lands had previously been under the control of the Emirate of Bukhara and the Khanate of Kokand. Motivated by a desire for cotton, Russia attempted in the 1870s to convert the region's agriculture from grain to cotton—a policy later intensified by the Soviets. By 1885, all of Tajikistan was governed either directly by the Russian Empire or through its vassal, the Emirate of Bukhara, yet Russian cultural influence on the Tajik population remained minimal.

input: In 2004, West had his first of a number of public incidents during his attendance at music award events. At the American Music Awards of 2004, West stormed out of the auditorium after losing Best New Artist to country singer Gretchen Wilson. He later commented, "I felt like I was definitely robbed [...] I was the best new artist this year." After the 2006 Grammy nominations were released, West said he would "really have a problem" if he did not win the Album of the Year, saying, "I don't care what I do, I don't care how much I stunt – you can never take away from the amount of work I put into it. I don't want to hear all of that politically correct stuff." On November 2, 2006, when his "Touch the Sky" failed to win Best Video at the MTV Europe Music Awards, West went onto the stage as the award was being presented to Justice and Simian for "We Are Your Friends" and argued that he should have won the award instead. Hundreds of news outlets worldwide criticized the outburst. On November 7, 2006, West apologized for this outburst publicly during his performance as support act for U2 for their Vertigo concert in Brisbane. He later spoofed the incident on the 33rd season premiere of Saturday Night Live in September 2007.
rewrite: The first of several public incidents involving West occurred in 2004 at music award ceremonies. After losing the Best New Artist award to country singer Gretchen Wilson at the 2004 American Music Awards, he stormed out of the auditorium. West later stated, "I felt like I was definitely robbed [...] I was the best new artist this year." Following the release of the 2006 Grammy nominations, he remarked he would "really have a problem" if he did not win Album of the Year, adding, "I don't care what I do, I don't care how much I stunt – you can never take away from the amount of work I put into it. I don't want to hear all of that politically correct stuff." His behavior escalated at the MTV Europe Music Awards on November 2, 2006. When his video for "Touch the Sky" lost Best Video to Justice and Simian's "We Are Your Friends," West walked onstage during the presentation to argue he deserved the award. This outburst was widely criticized by hundreds of global news outlets. Five days later, on November 7, West issued a public apology during his opening performance for U2's Vertigo tour in Brisbane. He later humorously referenced the incident on the September 2007 season premiere of *Saturday Night Live*'s 33rd season.

input: In 1993, to complement its own direct sales channel, Dell planned to sell PCs at big-box retail outlets such as Wal-Mart, which would have brought in an additional $125 million in annual revenue. Bain consultant Kevin Rollins persuaded Michael Dell to pull out of these deals, believing they would be money losers in the long run. Margins at retail were thin at best and Dell left the reseller channel in 1994. Rollins would soon join Dell full-time and eventually become the company President and CEO.
rewrite: In 1993, Dell aimed to supplement its direct sales by offering PCs through major retailers like Wal-Mart, a move projected to generate $125 million yearly. However, consultant Kevin Rollins convinced Michael Dell to abandon these agreements, arguing they would ultimately lose money due to the notoriously thin retail margins. Consequently, Dell exited the reseller channel in 1994. Rollins later joined the company full-time, eventually rising to the roles of President and CEO.

input: Avoidance of triggers is a key component of improving control and preventing attacks. The most common triggers include allergens, smoke (tobacco and other), air pollution, non selective beta-blockers, and sulfite-containing foods. Cigarette smoking and second-hand smoke (passive smoke) may reduce the effectiveness of medications such as corticosteroids. Laws that limit smoking decrease the number of people hospitalized for asthma. Dust mite control measures, including air filtration, chemicals to kill mites, vacuuming, mattress covers and others methods had no effect on asthma symptoms. Overall, exercise is beneficial in people with stable asthma. Yoga could provide small improvements in quality of life and symptoms in people with asthma.
rewrite: Improving control and preventing attacks relies significantly on avoiding triggers. Common examples are allergens, smoke from tobacco or other sources, air pollution, non-selective beta-blockers, and sulfite-containing foods. Notably, cigarette smoking and second-hand smoke can reduce medication efficacy, including corticosteroids, and laws restricting smoking have been shown to lower asthma hospitalization rates. While measures like air filtration, chemicals, vacuuming, and mattress covers for dust mite control do not affect asthma symptoms, exercise is generally beneficial for those with stable asthma. Additionally, yoga may offer modest improvements in symptoms and quality of life.

input: The Romans held off Hannibal in three battles, but then Hannibal smashed a succession of Roman consular armies. By this time Hannibal's brother Hasdrubal Barca sought to cross the Alps into Italy and join his brother with a second army. Hasdrubal managed to break through into Italy only to be defeated decisively on the Metaurus River. Unable to defeat Hannibal on Italian soil, the Romans boldly sent an army to Africa under Scipio Africanus to threaten the Carthaginian capital. Hannibal was recalled to Africa, and defeated at the Battle of Zama.
rewrite: After initially containing Hannibal in three engagements, the Romans saw several consular armies fall to him. Meanwhile, his brother Hasdrubal Barca attempted to bring a second army over the Alps to Italy. Though he succeeded in entering Italy, Hasdrubal was crushed at the Metaurus River. With Hannibal unbeatable in Italy, Rome dispatched Scipio Africanus to attack Carthage in Africa. This forced Hannibal’s recall, leading to his final defeat at the Battle of Zama.

input: During regular, day-to-day activities, Somali women usually wear the guntiino, a long stretch of cloth tied over the shoulder and draped around the waist. It is usually made out of alandi, which is a textile common in the Horn region and some parts of North Africa. The garment can be worn in different styles. It can also be made with other fabrics, including white cloth with gold borders. For more formal settings, such as at weddings or religious celebrations like Eid, women wear the dirac. It is a long, light, diaphanous voile dress made of silk, chiffon, taffeta or saree fabric. The gown is worn over a full-length half-slip and a brassiere. Known as the gorgorad, the underskirt is made out of silk and serves as a key part of the overall outfit. The dirac is usually sparkly and very colorful, the most popular styles being those with gilded borders or threads. The fabric is typically acquired from Somali clothing stores in tandem with the gorgorad. In the past, dirac fabric was also frequently purchased from South Asian merchandisers.
rewrite: In daily life, Somali women commonly wear the guntiino, a garment fashioned from a long piece of cloth. This cloth is typically draped over the shoulder and wrapped around the waist. Alandi, a textile prevalent in the Horn of Africa and parts of North Africa, is the usual material. However, other fabrics are also used, such as white cloth adorned with gold borders, and the garment can be styled in various ways. For formal occasions like weddings or Eid celebrations, the dirac is worn. This is a long, flowing dress made from light, diaphanous materials like silk, chiffon, taffeta, or saree fabric. It is worn over a full-length half-slip and a brassiere. The underskirt, known as the gorgorad, is a silk garment that forms an essential component of the ensemble. Typically very colorful and often sparkly, popular dirac styles feature gilded borders or threads. The fabric is generally bought from Somali clothing stores alongside the gorgorad, though historically it was also commonly sourced from South Asian merchants.

input: From 1889, when Guangxu began to rule in his own right, to 1898, the Empress Dowager lived in semi-retirement, spending the majority of the year at the Summer Palace. On November 1, 1897, two German Roman Catholic missionaries were murdered in the southern part of Shandong Province (the Juye Incident). In response, Germany used the murders as a pretext for a naval occupation of Jiaozhou Bay. The occupation prompted a "scramble for concessions" in 1898, which included the German lease of Jiazhou Bay, the Russian acquisition of Liaodong, and the British lease of the New Territories of Hong Kong.
rewrite: Beginning in 1889, as Emperor Guangxu assumed personal rule, the Empress Dowager entered a period of semi-retirement, primarily residing at the Summer Palace. This changed following the Juye Incident of November 1, 1897, where two German missionaries were killed in Shandong. Germany seized on this event to militarily occupy Jiaozhou Bay. This act triggered a broader "scramble for concessions" in 1898, leading to Germany leasing Jiazhou Bay, Russia acquiring Liaodong, and Britain securing a lease on the New Territories of Hong Kong.

input: The emperor was at the pinnacle of Han society. He presided over the Han government but shared power with both the nobility and appointed ministers who came largely from the scholarly gentry class. The Han Empire was divided into areas directly controlled by the central government using an innovation inherited from the Qin known as commanderies, and a number of semi-autonomous kingdoms. These kingdoms gradually lost all vestiges of their independence, particularly following the Rebellion of the Seven States. From the reign of Emperor Wu onward, the Chinese court officially sponsored Confucianism in education and court politics, synthesized with the cosmology of later scholars such as Dong Zhongshu. This policy endured until the fall of the Qing dynasty in AD 1911.
rewrite: At the pinnacle of Han society stood the emperor, who presided over the government yet shared power with the nobility and appointed ministers, the latter drawn largely from the scholarly gentry. The empire itself was divided into regions directly administered by the central government through commanderies—an innovation inherited from the Qin—and a number of semi-autonomous kingdoms. Following events like the Rebellion of the Seven States, these kingdoms gradually lost all remnants of independence. A lasting policy began under Emperor Wu, when the court officially sponsored Confucianism, synthesized with later cosmological thought like that of Dong Zhongshu, in education and politics. This endorsement endured until the Qing dynasty's fall in AD 1911.

input: North Carolina averages fewer than 20 tornadoes per year, many of them produced by hurricanes or tropical storms along the coastal plain. Tornadoes from thunderstorms are a risk, especially in the eastern part of the state. The western Piedmont is often protected by the mountains, which tend to break up storms as they try to cross over; the storms will often re-form farther east. Also a weather phenomenon known as "cold air damming" often occurs in the northwestern part of the state, which can also weaken storms but can also lead to major ice events in winter.
rewrite: Annually, North Carolina experiences fewer than twenty tornadoes, with many generated by hurricanes or tropical storms on the coastal plain. Thunderstorm-spawned tornadoes also pose a risk, particularly in the east. The western Piedmont is frequently shielded by mountains that disrupt storms attempting to cross; these storms commonly redevelop farther east. Additionally, the northwestern region often encounters "cold air damming," a phenomenon that can weaken storms but also cause significant winter ice events.

input: Bronx native Nancy Savoca's 1989 comedy, True Love, explores two Italian-American Bronx sweethearts in the days before their wedding. The film, which debuted Annabella Sciorra and Ron Eldard as the betrothed couple, won the Grand Jury Prize at that year's Sundance Film Festival. The CBS television sitcom Becker, 1998–2004, was more ambiguous. The show starred Ted Danson as Dr. John Becker, a doctor who operated a small practice and was constantly annoyed by his patients, co-workers, friends, and practically everything and everybody else in his world. It showed his everyday life as a doctor working in a small clinic in the Bronx.
rewrite: Nancy Savoca’s 1989 comedy True Love, set in the Bronx, follows two Italian-American sweethearts in the lead-up to their wedding. Starring Annabella Sciorra and Ron Eldard in their debut roles as the engaged couple, the film earned the Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Festival. In contrast, the CBS sitcom Becker (1998–2004) was more ambiguous. It featured Ted Danson as Dr. John Becker, a physician running a small Bronx clinic. The show depicted his daily life, highlighting his constant irritation with patients, colleagues, friends, and nearly every aspect of his world.

input: In December 2011, the system went into operation on a trial basis. It has started providing navigation, positioning and timing data to China and the neighbouring area for free from 27 December. During this trial run, Compass will offer positioning accuracy to within 25 meters, but the precision will improve as more satellites are launched. Upon the system's official launch, it pledged to offer general users positioning information accurate to the nearest 10 m, measure speeds within 0.2 m per second, and provide signals for clock synchronisation accurate to 0.02 microseconds.
rewrite: The Compass system began trial operations in December 2011, initiating free navigation, positioning, and timing services for China and surrounding regions on the 27th of that month. This initial phase provides positioning accuracy within 25 meters, which will be enhanced with additional satellite launches. Upon its official launch, the system is pledged to deliver 10-meter positioning precision, speed measurements within 0.2 meters per second, and clock synchronization signals accurate to 0.02 microseconds for general users.

input: In soil, microorganisms that reside in the rhizosphere (a zone that includes the root surface and the soil that adheres to the root after gentle shaking) carry out nitrogen fixation, converting nitrogen gas to nitrogenous compounds. This serves to provide an easily absorbable form of nitrogen for many plants, which cannot fix nitrogen themselves. Many other bacteria are found as symbionts in humans and other organisms. For example, the presence of over 1,000 bacterial species in the normal human gut flora of the intestines can contribute to gut immunity, synthesise vitamins, such as folic acid, vitamin K and biotin, convert sugars to lactic acid (see Lactobacillus), as well as fermenting complex undigestible carbohydrates. The presence of this gut flora also inhibits the growth of potentially pathogenic bacteria (usually through competitive exclusion) and these beneficial bacteria are consequently sold as probiotic dietary supplements.
rewrite: Within the rhizosphere—a region encompassing the root surface and the soil clinging to it—soil microorganisms perform nitrogen fixation, transforming atmospheric nitrogen into usable compounds. This process supplies an absorbable nitrogen form to numerous plants incapable of fixing nitrogen themselves. Meanwhile, many bacteria exist as symbionts in humans and other organisms. The normal human gut flora, comprising over 1,000 bacterial species, plays key roles: bolstering gut immunity, synthesizing vitamins like folic acid and biotin, converting sugars to lactic acid, and fermenting complex carbohydrates. Additionally, this microbial community suppresses pathogenic bacteria growth, often through competitive exclusion. Due to these benefits, such bacteria are marketed as probiotic supplements.

input: The possibility of unlikely victories in the earlier rounds of the competition, where lower ranked teams beat higher placed opposition, known as "giant killings", is much anticipated by the public, and is considered an integral part of the tradition and prestige of the competition, alongside that gained by teams winning the competition. Almost every club in the League Pyramid has a fondly remembered giant-killing act in its history. It is considered particularly newsworthy when a top Premier League team suffers an upset defeat, or where the giant-killer is a non-league club, i.e. from outside the professional levels of The Football League.
rewrite: The tradition and prestige of the competition are built not only by the ultimate winner, but also by the much-anticipated "giant killings"—unlikely early-round victories where lower-ranked teams defeat superior opponents. Nearly every club in the League Pyramid cherishes such an upset in its history. These events become especially newsworthy when a top Premier League team suffers a defeat or when the victor is a non-league club from outside the professional Football League tiers.

input: Although each institution is organized differently, nearly all universities have a board of trustees; a president, chancellor, or rector; at least one vice president, vice-chancellor, or vice-rector; and deans of various divisions. Universities are generally divided into a number of academic departments, schools or faculties. Public university systems are ruled over by government-run higher education boards. They review financial requests and budget proposals and then allocate funds for each university in the system. They also approve new programs of instruction and cancel or make changes in existing programs. In addition, they plan for the further coordinated growth and development of the various institutions of higher education in the state or country. However, many public universities in the world have a considerable degree of financial, research and pedagogical autonomy. Private universities are privately funded and generally have broader independence from state policies. However, they may have less independence from business corporations depending on the source of their finances.
rewrite: Universities typically feature a board of trustees, a head such as a president or chancellor, along with vice-presidents and deans, despite variations in their specific organization. Their structure commonly includes academic divisions like departments, schools, or faculties. For public university systems, government-run higher education boards hold authority. These bodies allocate funds after reviewing budgets, approve or modify instructional programs, and strategize for the coordinated growth of state or national institutions. Nevertheless, numerous public universities globally retain significant autonomy in financial, research, and teaching matters. In contrast, private universities are funded privately and usually enjoy greater freedom from state control. Their independence, however, can be influenced by corporate interests, depending on the origins of their financial support.

input: Various industrial businesses are located in Hannover. The Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles Transporter (VWN) factory at Hannover-Stöcken is the biggest employer in the region and operates a huge plant at the northern edge of town adjoining the Mittellandkanal and Motorway A2. Jointly with a factory of German tire and automobile parts manufacturer Continental AG, they have a coal-burning power plant. Continental AG, founded in Hanover in 1871, is one of the city's major companies, as is Sennheiser. Since 2008 a take-over is in progress: the Schaeffler Group from Herzogenaurach (Bavaria) holds the majority of the stock but were required due to the financial crisis to deposit the options as securities at banks. TUI AG has its HQ in Hanover. Hanover is home to many insurance companies, many of which operate only in Germany. One major global reinsurance company is Hannover Re, whose headquarters are east of the city centre.
rewrite: Hannover hosts a range of industrial enterprises. The largest employer in the area is the Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles Transporter (VWN) factory, situated in Hannover-Stöcken. This extensive plant lies at the city's northern border, adjacent to the Mittellandkanal and the A2 motorway. It shares a coal-fired power plant with a facility operated by Continental AG, a major tire and auto parts manufacturer founded in Hanover in 1871. Another key local company is Sennheiser. Since 2008, a takeover has been underway, with the Bavarian Schaeffler Group holding a majority of Continental's stock; due to the financial crisis, the group was required to deposit its options as bank securities. The headquarters of TUI AG are in Hanover, which also bases numerous insurance firms, many operating solely within Germany. A leading global reinsurance company, Hannover Re, is headquartered east of the city centre.

input: In matches with multiple competitors, an elimination system may be used. Any wrestler who has a fall scored against them is forced out of the match, and the match continues until only one remains. However, it is much more common when more than two wrestlers are involved to simply go one fall, with the one scoring the fall, regardless of who they scored it against, being the winner. In championship matches, this means that, unlike one-on-one matches (where the champion can simply disqualify themselves or get themselves counted out to retain the title via the "champion's advantag"), the champion does not have to be pinned or involved in the decision to lose the championship. However, heel champions often find advantages, not in champion's advantage, but in the use of weapons and outside interference, as these poly-sided matches tend to involve no holds barred rules.
rewrite: When multiple wrestlers compete, an elimination system is sometimes employed, where any competitor who suffers a fall is removed, and the contest proceeds until a single victor remains. More frequently, however, matches involving more than two participants are decided by a single fall; the first wrestler to score a pin or submission wins, irrespective of which opponent they defeat. This format alters the dynamics for championship bouts. Unlike in standard one-on-one contests, where a champion can exploit the "champion's advantage" by getting disqualified or counted out to retain the title, the titleholder in these multi-competitor matches can lose the championship without being pinned or directly involved in the deciding fall. Instead, heel champions often seek an edge through no-holds-barred tactics typical in such chaotic matches, like using weapons or relying on outside interference.

input: Immunology is strongly experimental in everyday practice but is also characterized by an ongoing theoretical attitude. Many theories have been suggested in immunology from the end of the nineteenth century up to the present time. The end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th century saw a battle between "cellular" and "humoral" theories of immunity. According to the cellular theory of immunity, represented in particular by Elie Metchnikoff, it was cells – more precisely, phagocytes – that were responsible for immune responses. In contrast, the humoral theory of immunity, held by Robert Koch and Emil von Behring, among others, stated that the active immune agents were soluble components (molecules) found in the organism’s “humors” rather than its cells.
rewrite: While immunology is a deeply experimental discipline in daily practice, it has also consistently maintained a theoretical dimension. From the late nineteenth century to today, numerous theories have been proposed. A major conflict emerged around the turn of the 20th century between the "cellular" and "humoral" theories of immunity. Proponents of the cellular theory, notably Elie Metchnikoff, argued that cells—specifically phagocytes—were the agents driving immune responses. Opposing this view, supporters of the humoral theory, such as Robert Koch and Emil von Behring, contended that soluble molecules within the body's fluids, not its cells, acted as the active immune agents.

input: Italy became a major industrialized country again, due to its post-war economic miracle. The European Union (EU) involved the division of powers, with taxation, health and education handled by the nation states, while the EU had charge of market rules, competition, legal standards and environmentalism. The Soviet economic and political system collapsed, leading to the end of communism in the satellite countries in 1989, and the dissolution of the Soviet Union itself in 1991. As a consequence, Europe's integration deepened, the continent became depolarised, and the European Union expanded to subsequently include many of the formerly communist European countries – Romania and Bulgaria (2007) and Croatia (2013).
rewrite: Following its post-war economic miracle, Italy re-emerged as a major industrialized nation. The division of powers within the European Union saw nation states retain control over taxation, health, and education, while the EU managed market rules, competition, legal standards, and environmental policy. The collapse of the Soviet system in 1989 ended communism in its satellite states, culminating in the USSR's dissolution in 1991. Consequently, European integration deepened amid a depolarized continent, enabling the EU's expansion to incorporate formerly communist nations like Romania and Bulgaria in 2007 and Croatia in 2013.

input: Major religious groups in the Republic of the Marshall Islands include the United Church of Christ (formerly Congregational), with 51.5% of the population; the Assemblies of God, 24.2%; the Roman Catholic Church, 8.4%; and The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormons), 8.3%; Also represented are Bukot Nan Jesus (also known as Assembly of God Part Two), 2.2%; Baptist, 1.0%; Seventh-day Adventists, 0.9%; Full Gospel, 0.7%; and the Baha'i Faith, 0.6%; Persons without any religious affiliation account for a very small percentage of the population. There is also a small community of Ahmadiyya Muslims based in Majuro, with the first mosque opening in the capital in September 2012.
rewrite: In the Republic of the Marshall Islands, the United Church of Christ (formerly Congregational) is the predominant faith, followed by 51.5% of the population. Other significant groups are the Assemblies of God at 24.2%, the Roman Catholic Church at 8.4%, and The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints at 8.3%. Smaller representations include Bukot Nan Jesus (2.2%), Baptist (1.0%), Seventh-day Adventists (0.9%), Full Gospel (0.7%), and the Baha'i Faith (0.6%). Those with no religious affiliation form a very minor segment. Additionally, a small Ahmadiyya Muslim community exists in Majuro, where the first mosque opened in September 2012.

input: The official policy became one of biological and cultural assimilation: "Eliminate the full-blood and permit the white admixture to half-castes and eventually the race will become white". This led to different treatment for "black" and "half-caste" individuals, with lighter-skinned individuals targeted for removal from their families to be raised as "white" people, restricted from speaking their native language and practising traditional customs, a process now known as the Stolen Generation.

Consequently, "black" and "half-caste" individuals were treated differently.
