Typically, the lower limit of the saturation speed is determined by the sensor itself, but with the gain of the amplifier between the sensor and the analog-to-digital converter, the saturation speed can be increased. The factor 78 is chosen such that exposure settings based on a standard light meter and an 18-percent reflective surface will result in an image with a grey level of 18%/√2 = 12.7% of saturation. The factor √2 indicates that there is half a stop of headroom to deal with specular reflections that would appear brighter than a 100% reflecting white surface.
rewrite: The saturation speed, which represents the maximum exposure before clipping or blooming occurs, is primarily limited by the sensor. However, this limit can be raised using the amplifier gain between the sensor and the analog-to-digital converter. The factor 78 is selected so that standard light meter readings from an 18-percent reflective surface produce a grey level at 12.7% of saturation, calculated as 18%/√2. This √2 factor provides half a stop of headroom to accommodate specular reflections, which can exceed the brightness of a perfectly white surface.

input: Gorbachev also radically expanded the scope of Glasnost, stating that no subject was off-limits for open discussion in the media. Even so, the cautious Soviet intelligentsia took almost a year to begin pushing the boundaries to see if he meant what he said. For the first time, the Communist Party leader had appealed over the heads of Central Committee members for the people's support in exchange for expansion of liberties. The tactic proved successful: Within two years political reform could no longer be sidetracked by Party "conservatives." An unintended consequence was that having saved reform, Gorbachev's move ultimately killed the very system it was designed to save.
rewrite: Gorbachev dramatically widened Glasnost, declaring that the media could openly discuss any topic. Despite this, the wary Soviet intelligentsia waited nearly a year before testing the sincerity of his promise. In a novel tactic, the Communist Party leader bypassed the Central Committee to seek public backing by offering greater freedoms. This approach succeeded; within two years, Party "conservatives" could no longer derail political reform. Yet an unforeseen result was that while saving reform, Gorbachev's maneuver ultimately destroyed the system it aimed to preserve.

input: Tiberius Gracchus was elected tribune in 133 BC. He attempted to enact a law which would have limited the amount of land that any individual could own. The aristocrats, who stood to lose an enormous amount of money, were bitterly opposed to this proposal. Tiberius submitted this law to the Plebeian Council, but the law was vetoed by a tribune named Marcus Octavius. Tiberius then used the Plebeian Council to impeach Octavius. The theory, that a representative of the people ceases to be one when he acts against the wishes of the people, was counter to Roman constitutional theory. If carried to its logical end, this theory would remove all constitutional restraints on the popular will, and put the state under the absolute control of a temporary popular majority. His law was enacted, but Tiberius was murdered with 300 of his associates when he stood for reelection to the tribunate.
rewrite: In 133 BC, Tiberius Gracchus was elected tribune and proposed a law to limit individual land ownership. This measure faced bitter opposition from aristocrats, who stood to lose substantial wealth. When Tiberius presented the law to the Plebeian Council, it was vetoed by another tribune, Marcus Octavius. In response, Tiberius used the Council to impeach Octavius, advancing a theory that a representative who acts against the people’s will ceases to represent them. This idea contradicted Roman constitutional principles, as it threatened to remove all restraints on popular will, placing the state under the absolute control of a temporary majority. Although his law was eventually enacted, Tiberius was murdered along with 300 supporters during his bid for reelection to the tribunate.

input: The city is also home to two large colleges. The City College Plymouth provides courses from the most basic to Foundation degrees for approximately 26,000 students. Plymouth College of Art offers a selection of courses including media. It was started 153 years ago and is now one of only four independent colleges of art and design in the UK.
rewrite: Two large colleges are located in the city. City College Plymouth serves around 26,000 students with courses ranging from basic to Foundation degrees. Meanwhile, Plymouth College of Art, founded 153 years ago, provides courses in areas like media and is one of just four independent art and design colleges in the UK.

input: Between 1853 and 1870, the Emperor Napoleon III and the city's first director of parks and gardens, Jean-Charles Alphand, created the Bois de Boulogne, the Bois de Vincennes, Parc Montsouris and the Parc des Buttes-Chaumont, located at the four points of the compass around the city, as well as many smaller parks, squares and gardens in the Paris' quarters. Since 1977, the city has created 166 new parks, most notably the Parc de la Villette (1987), Parc André Citroën (1992), and Parc de Bercy (1997). One of the newest parks, the Promenade des Berges de la Seine (2013), built on a former highway on the Left Bank of the Seine between the Pont de l'Alma and the Musée d'Orsay, has floating gardens and gives a view of the city's landmarks.
rewrite: From 1853 to 1870, Emperor Napoleon III and Jean-Charles Alphand, the inaugural director of parks and gardens, established major green spaces at the four compass points of Paris: the Bois de Boulogne, Bois de Vincennes, Parc Montsouris, and the Parc des Buttes-Chaumont. They also added numerous smaller parks, squares, and gardens throughout the city's quarters. Since 1977, an additional 166 parks have been created, including prominent ones like the Parc de la Villette (1987), Parc André Citroën (1992), and Parc de Bercy (1997). Among the newest is the Promenade des Berges de la Seine (2013), situated on a former Left Bank highway between the Pont de l'Alma and the Musée d'Orsay, featuring floating gardens and offering views of key landmarks.

input: PlayStation Network is the unified online multiplayer gaming and digital media delivery service provided by Sony Computer Entertainment for PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Portable, announced during the 2006 PlayStation Business Briefing meeting in Tokyo. The service is always connected, free, and includes multiplayer support. The network enables online gaming, the PlayStation Store, PlayStation Home and other services. PlayStation Network uses real currency and PlayStation Network Cards as seen with the PlayStation Store and PlayStation Home.
rewrite: Announced at the 2006 PlayStation Business Briefing in Tokyo, the PlayStation Network is Sony Computer Entertainment's unified online service for the PlayStation 3 and PlayStation Portable. This always-connected, free platform supports multiplayer gaming and digital media delivery. It facilitates online play, the PlayStation Store, and PlayStation Home, among other features. Transactions across the network, including in the Store and Home, utilize real currency and PlayStation Network Cards.

input: The Community Tool Box is a public service of the University maintained by the Work Group for Community Health and Development. It is a free, online resource that contains more than 7,000 pages of practical information for promoting community health and development, and is a global resource for both professionals and grassroots groups engaged in the work of community health and development.
rewrite: Maintained by the Work Group for Community Health and Development, the Community Tool Box is a University public service. This free, online resource offers over 7,000 pages of practical guidance for promoting community health and development. It serves as a global asset for professionals and grassroots groups alike.

input: According to the writer of Luke, Mary was a relative of Elizabeth, wife of the priest Zechariah of the priestly division of Abijah, who was herself part of the lineage of Aaron and so of the tribe of Levi.[Luke 1:5;1:36] Some of those who consider that the relationship with Elizabeth was on the maternal side, consider that Mary, like Joseph, to whom she was betrothed, was of the House of David and so of the Tribe of Judah, and that the genealogy of Jesus presented in Luke 3 from Nathan, third son of David and Bathsheba, is in fact the genealogy of Mary,[need quotation to verify] while the genealogy from Solomon given in Matthew 1 is that of Joseph. (Aaron's wife Elisheba was of the tribe of Judah, so all their descendants are from both Levi and Judah.)[Num.1:7 & Ex.6:23]
rewrite: The Gospel of Luke describes Mary as a relative of Elizabeth. Elizabeth was married to Zechariah, a priest from the division of Abijah, and was herself a descendant of Aaron, thus belonging to the tribe of Levi. [Luke 1:5;1:36] Interpretations of this familial link vary. Some scholars, believing the relationship was through the maternal line, hold that Mary—like her betrothed, Joseph—was of the House of David and the Tribe of Judah. From this perspective, the lineage in Luke 3, traced from David’s son Nathan, would be Mary’s, while Matthew 1 provides Joseph’s genealogy from David’s son Solomon. [need quotation to verify] Notably, Aaron’s wife Elisheba was from Judah, meaning their descendants combined lineage from both Levi and Judah. [Num.1:7 & Ex.6:23]

input: Each year, nearly $200 million in hunters' federal excise taxes are distributed to state agencies to support wildlife management programs, the purchase of lands open to hunters, and hunter education and safety classes. Since 1934, the sale of Federal Duck Stamps, a required purchase for migratory waterfowl hunters over sixteen years old, has raised over $700 million to help purchase more than 5,200,000 acres (8,100 sq mi; 21,000 km2) of habitat for the National Wildlife Refuge System lands that support waterfowl and many other wildlife species and are often open to hunting. States also collect money from hunting licenses to assist with management of game animals, as designated by law. A key task of federal and state park rangers and game wardens is to enforce laws and regulations related to hunting, including species protection, hunting seasons, and hunting bans.
rewrite: Annually, state agencies receive close to $200 million from federal excise taxes paid by hunters. These funds are allocated to wildlife management programs, acquiring public hunting lands, and providing education and safety courses for hunters. Additionally, revenue from hunting licenses, as mandated by law, aids states in managing game animal populations. Enforcement of hunting regulations, such as species protection, seasonal restrictions, and bans, falls to federal and state park rangers and game wardens. Separately, since 1934, the Federal Duck Stamp program has generated over $700 million from required purchases by migratory waterfowl hunters aged sixteen and older. This revenue has supported the acquisition of more than 5.2 million acres (21,000 km²) of habitat within the National Wildlife Refuge System, benefiting waterfowl and numerous other species, with these lands frequently available for hunting.

input: Morning (2008) looked at high school biology textbooks during the 1952-2002 period and initially found a similar pattern with only 35% directly discussing race in the 1983–92 period from initially 92% doing so. However, this has increased somewhat after this to 43%. More indirect and brief discussions of race in the context of medical disorders have increased from none to 93% of textbooks. In general, the material on race has moved from surface traits to genetics and evolutionary history. The study argues that the textbooks' fundamental message about the existence of races has changed little.
rewrite: Examining high school biology textbooks from 1952 to 2002, Morning (2008) observed a shift in how race is addressed. Direct discussion initially fell from 92% to 35% in 1983–92, later rising modestly to 43%. Conversely, indirect mentions of race regarding medical disorders surged from none to 93%. While the content has evolved from superficial traits to genetics and evolutionary history, the study concludes the textbooks' core message on the existence of races has remained largely unchanged.

input: FDR's New Deal programs often contained equal opportunity clauses stating "no discrimination shall be made on account of race, color or creed",:11 but the true forerunner to affirmative action was the Interior Secretary of the time, Harold L. Ickes. Ickes prohibited discrimination in hiring for Public Works Administration funded projects and oversaw not only the institution of a quota system, where contractors were required to employ a fixed percentage of Black workers, by Robert C. Weaver and Clark Foreman,:12 but also the equal pay of women proposed by Harry Hopkins.:14FDR's largest contribution to affirmative action, however, lay in his Executive Order 8802 which prohibited discrimination in the defense industry or government.:22 The executive order promoted the idea that if taxpayer funds were accepted through a government contract, then all taxpayers should have an equal opportunity to work through the contractor.:23–4 To enforce this idea, Roosevelt created the Fair Employment Practices Committee (FEPC) with the power to investigate hiring practices by government contractors.:22
rewrite:
Harold L. Ickes, then Interior Secretary, served as the true forerunner to affirmative action, despite New Deal programs often including equal opportunity clauses against racial, color, or creed discrimination. Ickes banned discrimination in hiring for Public Works Administration projects. Under his oversight, Robert C. Weaver and Clark Foreman implemented a quota system requiring contractors to hire a set percentage of Black workers. He also managed Harry Hopkins's proposal for equal pay for women.

President Franklin D. Roosevelt's most significant contribution was Executive Order 8802, which barred discrimination in the defense industry and government. This order advanced the principle that accepting taxpayer funds via a government contract should guarantee all taxpayers an equal chance to work for that contractor. To enforce this, Roosevelt established the Fair Employment Practices Committee (FEPC), empowering it to investigate the hiring practices of government contractors.

input: In 1579 the northern seven provinces signed the Union of Utrecht, in which they decided to join forces against Spanish rule. The Union of Utrecht is seen as the beginning of the Dutch Republic. In 1580 the new and predominantly Protestant state abolished the bishoprics, including the archbishopric of Utrecht. The stadtholders disapproved of the independent course of the Utrecht bourgeoisie and brought the city under much more direct control of the republic; which shifted the power towards its dominant province Holland. This was the start of a long period of stagnation of trade and development in Utrecht. Utrecht remained an atypical city in the new republic with about 40% Catholic in the mid-17th century, and even more among the elite groups, who included many rural nobility and gentry with town houses there.
rewrite: The Union of Utrecht, signed in 1579 by the northern seven provinces, marked the start of the Dutch Republic as these regions united against Spanish rule. The following year, this largely Protestant state eliminated the bishoprics, such as the archbishopric of Utrecht. Disapproving of the local bourgeoisie's independence, the stadtholders imposed stricter republican control over the city, shifting power toward the dominant province of Holland. Consequently, Utrecht entered a prolonged era of economic and developmental stagnation. Despite this, the city remained atypical within the republic, retaining a significant Catholic presence—about 40% in the mid-17th century, with an even higher proportion among its elites, including many rural nobles and gentry who maintained town houses there.

input: Genetic engineering is the modification of an organism's genome through biotechnology. Since the 1970s, a variety of techniques have been developed to specifically add, remove and edit genes in an organism. Recently developed genome engineering techniques use engineered nuclease enzymes to create targeted DNA repair in a chromosome to either disrupt or edit a gene when the break is repaired. The related term synthetic biology is sometimes used to refer to extensive genetic engineering of an organism.
rewrite: Using biotechnology to alter an organism's genome defines genetic engineering. Techniques for precisely adding, removing, or editing genes have evolved since the 1970s. Modern methods employ engineered nuclease enzymes to induce targeted DNA repair in a chromosome, disrupting or editing a gene upon repair. Extensive genetic modification is sometimes termed synthetic biology, a related concept.

input: Orthodox Judaism considers views on the part of Jews who depart from traditional Jewish principles of faith heretical. In addition, the more right-wing groups within Orthodox Judaism hold that all Jews who reject the simple meaning of Maimonides's 13 principles of Jewish faith are heretics. As such, most of Orthodox Judaism considers Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism heretical movements, and regards most of Conservative Judaism as heretical. The liberal wing of Modern Orthodoxy is more tolerant of Conservative Judaism, particularly its right wing, as there is some theological and practical overlap between these groups.
rewrite: Orthodox Judaism generally deems Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism heretical, and views most of Conservative Judaism the same way. This stems from the stance that any departure from traditional Jewish principles of faith is heretical. More right-wing Orthodox groups specifically label as heretics those Jews who reject the plain meaning of Maimonides's 13 principles. An exception is the liberal wing of Modern Orthodoxy, which shows greater tolerance toward Conservative Judaism, especially its right wing, due to certain theological and practical similarities.

The acute accent, present only in Croatian dialects, which Tito is perfectly pronouncing, is the strongest proof of Tito's belonging to Kajkavian dialect.

input: One of the most significant impacts To Kill a Mockingbird has had is Atticus Finch's model of integrity for the legal profession. As scholar Alice Petry explains, "Atticus has become something of a folk hero in legal circles and is treated almost as if he were an actual person." Morris Dees of the Southern Poverty Law Center cites Atticus Finch as the reason he became a lawyer, and Richard Matsch, the federal judge who presided over the Timothy McVeigh trial, counts Atticus as a major judicial influence. One law professor at the University of Notre Dame stated that the most influential textbook he taught from was To Kill a Mockingbird, and an article in the Michigan Law Review claims, "No real-life lawyer has done more for the self-image or public perception of the legal profession," before questioning whether, "Atticus Finch is a paragon of honor or an especially slick hired gun".
rewrite: Atticus Finch, from *To Kill a Mockingbird*, stands as a profound model of integrity for lawyers and judges. As scholar Alice Petry notes, he is regarded “almost as if he were an actual person” and has evolved into a folk hero within legal circles. His influence is vividly personal: Morris Dees, founder of the Southern Poverty Law Center, credits Atticus as his reason for becoming a lawyer. Similarly, federal judge Richard Matsch, who presided over the Timothy McVeigh trial, considers him a major judicial influence. A University of Notre Dame law professor even called the novel the most influential textbook he taught from. Yet this reverence is not without scrutiny. An article in the Michigan Law Review, while asserting that “no real-life lawyer has done more for the self-image or public perception of the legal profession,” also probes whether Atticus is “a paragon of honor or an especially slick hired gun.”

input: Roughly one quarter of all zinc output in the United States (2009), is consumed in the form of zinc compounds; a variety of which are used industrially. Zinc oxide is widely used as a white pigment in paints, and as a catalyst in the manufacture of rubber. It is also used as a heat disperser for the rubber and acts to protect its polymers from ultraviolet radiation (the same UV protection is conferred to plastics containing zinc oxide). The semiconductor properties of zinc oxide make it useful in varistors and photocopying products. The zinc zinc-oxide cycle is a two step thermochemical process based on zinc and zinc oxide for hydrogen production.
rewrite: In the United States (2009), approximately one quarter of total zinc output is consumed as zinc compounds, which serve numerous industrial purposes. Zinc oxide, for instance, is a common white pigment in paints and a catalyst in rubber manufacturing. It also disperses heat in rubber and protects its polymers from ultraviolet radiation, a benefit similarly applied to plastics containing it. Due to its semiconductor properties, zinc oxide is valuable in varistors and photocopying products. Additionally, the zinc zinc-oxide cycle, a two-step thermochemical process utilizing zinc and zinc oxide, is employed for hydrogen production.

input: Between the 8th and 18th centuries, the use of glazed ceramics was prevalent in Islamic art, usually assuming the form of elaborate pottery. Tin-opacified glazing was one of the earliest new technologies developed by the Islamic potters. The first Islamic opaque glazes can be found as blue-painted ware in Basra, dating to around the 8th century. Another contribution was the development of stone-paste ceramics, originating from 9th century Iraq. Other centers for innovative ceramic pottery in the Old world included Fustat (from 975 to 1075), Damascus (from 1100 to around 1600) and Tabriz (from 1470 to 1550).
rewrite: From the 8th to the 18th century, Islamic art widely featured glazed ceramics, often as intricate pottery. Among the earliest innovations was tin-opacified glazing, with the first opaque examples being blue-painted ware from 8th-century Basra. Islamic potters also pioneered stone-paste ceramics, beginning in 9th-century Iraq. Further centers of ceramic advancement included Fustat (975–1075), Damascus (1100–c. 1600), and Tabriz (1470–1550).

input: Paris today has more than 421 municipal parks and gardens, covering more than 3,000 hectares and containing more than 250,000 trees. Two of Paris' oldest and most famous gardens are the Tuileries Garden, created in 1564 for the Tuileries Palace, and redone by André Le Nôtre between 1664 and 1672, and the Luxembourg Garden, for the Luxembourg Palace, built for Marie de' Medici in 1612, which today houses the French Senate. The Jardin des Plantes was the first botanical garden in Paris, created in 1626 by Louis XIII's doctor Guy de La Brosse for the cultivation of medicinal plants.
rewrite: Paris boasts over 421 municipal parks and gardens, spanning more than 3,000 hectares and featuring in excess of 250,000 trees. Among its oldest and most renowned are the Tuileries Garden, established in 1564 and later redesigned by André Le Nôtre from 1664 to 1672, and the Luxembourg Garden, created in 1612 for the Luxembourg Palace. The latter now serves as the seat of the French Senate. The city's first botanical garden, the Jardin des Plantes, was founded in 1626 by Louis XIII's physician, Guy de La Brosse, to grow medicinal plants.

input: Saxophones appear in some scores from the late 19th century onwards. While appearing only as featured solo instruments in some works, for example Maurice Ravel's orchestration of Modest Mussorgsky's Pictures at an Exhibition and Sergei Rachmaninoff's Symphonic Dances, the saxophone is included in other works, such as Ravel's Boléro, Sergei Prokofiev's Romeo and Juliet Suites 1 and 2 and many other works as a member of the orchestral ensemble. The euphonium is featured in a few late Romantic and 20th-century works, usually playing parts marked "tenor tuba", including Gustav Holst's The Planets, and Richard Strauss's Ein Heldenleben.
rewrite: From the late 19th century, saxophones began appearing in orchestral scores. In some pieces, like Ravel's *Boléro* and Prokofiev's *Romeo and Juliet* suites, they function within the ensemble. Other works feature them as solo instruments, such as Ravel's orchestration of Mussorgsky's *Pictures at an Exhibition* and Rachmaninoff's *Symphonic Dances*. Separately, the euphonium is occasionally used in late Romantic and 20th-century music, often labeled "tenor tuba," as heard in Holst's *The Planets* and Strauss's *Ein Heldenleben*.

input: The record transfer fee for a Premier League player has risen steadily over the lifetime of the competition. Prior to the start of the first Premier League season Alan Shearer became the first British player to command a transfer fee of more than £3 million. The record rose steadily in the Premier League's first few seasons, until Alan Shearer made a record breaking £15 million move to Newcastle United in 1996. The three highest transfer in the sport's history had a Premier League club on the selling end, with Tottenham Hotspur selling Gareth Bale to Real Madrid for £85 million in 2013, Manchester United's sale of Cristiano Ronaldo to Real Madrid for £80 million in 2009, and Liverpool selling Luis Suárez to Barcelona for £75 million in 2014.
rewrite: Throughout the Premier League's history, the record fee for a player transfer has consistently climbed. Even before the competition's inaugural season, Alan Shearer set a benchmark as the first British player to move for over £3 million. This record continued to rise in the early years, with Shearer himself shattering it again in a £15 million transfer to Newcastle United in 1996. Notably, the three largest transfer fees ever recorded all involved Premier League clubs as sellers: Tottenham Hotspur sold Gareth Bale to Real Madrid for £85 million in 2013, Manchester United sold Cristiano Ronaldo to Real Madrid for £80 million in 2009, and Liverpool sold Luis Suárez to Barcelona for £75 million in 2014.

input: On 15 December 1944 landings against minimal resistance were made on the southern beaches of the island of Mindoro, a key location in the planned Lingayen Gulf operations, in support of major landings scheduled on Luzon. On 9 January 1945, on the south shore of Lingayen Gulf on the western coast of Luzon, General Krueger's Sixth Army landed his first units. Almost 175,000 men followed across the twenty-mile (32 km) beachhead within a few days. With heavy air support, Army units pushed inland, taking Clark Field, 40 miles (64 km) northwest of Manila, in the last week of January.
rewrite: On 9 January 1945, the initial units of General Krueger’s Sixth Army landed on the south shore of Lingayen Gulf, along Luzon’s western coast. This followed earlier landings on 15 December 1944 on Mindoro’s southern beaches, which met minimal resistance. Mindoro was a key position for the planned Lingayen operations, supporting the major assault on Luzon. Within days, nearly 175,000 men had come ashore across the twenty-mile beachhead. Supported heavily from the air, Army forces advanced inland, capturing Clark Field—40 miles northwest of Manila—by the final week of January.

input: In the later Imperial era, the burial and commemorative practises of Christian and non-Christians overlapped. Tombs were shared by Christian and non-Christian family members, and the traditional funeral rites and feast of novemdialis found a part-match in the Christian Constitutio Apostolica. The customary offers of wine and food to the dead continued; St Augustine (following St Ambrose) feared that this invited the "drunken" practices of Parentalia but commended funeral feasts as a Christian opportunity to give alms of food to the poor. Christians attended Parentalia and its accompanying Feralia and Caristia in sufficient numbers for the Council of Tours to forbid them in AD 567. Other funerary and commemorative practices were very different. Traditional Roman practice spurned the corpse as a ritual pollution; inscriptions noted the day of birth and duration of life. The Christian Church fostered the veneration of saintly relics, and inscriptions marked the day of death as a transition to "new life".
rewrite: During the later Imperial period, Christian and non-Christian burial and commemorative customs often intersected. Family tombs commonly included both Christian and non-Christian members, while traditional rites like the novemdialis feast found a partial parallel in the Christian Constitutio Apostolica. Practices such as offering wine and food to the deceased persisted; St. Augustine, influenced by St. Ambrose, warned this might encourage the "drunken" habits of the Parentalia, yet he approved of funeral feasts as a Christian act of providing alms to the poor. So many Christians participated in the Parentalia, along with the Feralia and Caristia, that the Council of Tours banned attendance in AD 567. However, other aspects sharply differed. Traditional Roman views saw the corpse as ritually impure, and inscriptions typically recorded the birth date and lifespan. In contrast, the Christian Church promoted the veneration of saintly relics, and inscriptions celebrated the day of death as an entry into "new life."

input: When infection attacks the body, anti-infective drugs can suppress the infection. Several broad types of anti-infective drugs exist, depending on the type of organism targeted; they include antibacterial (antibiotic; including antitubercular), antiviral, antifungal and antiparasitic (including antiprotozoal and antihelminthic) agents. Depending on the severity and the type of infection, the antibiotic may be given by mouth or by injection, or may be applied topically. Severe infections of the brain are usually treated with intravenous antibiotics. Sometimes, multiple antibiotics are used in case there is resistance to one antibiotic. Antibiotics only work for bacteria and do not affect viruses. Antibiotics work by slowing down the multiplication of bacteria or killing the bacteria. The most common classes of antibiotics used in medicine include penicillin, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, macrolides, quinolones and tetracyclines.[citation needed]
rewrite: Anti-infective drugs combat infections by suppressing the invading organisms. These agents are categorized based on their target: antibacterials (including antibiotics and antitubercular drugs), antivirals, antifungals, and antiparasitics (such as antiprotozoals and antihelminthics). Administration methods—oral, injectable, or topical—vary with the infection's type and severity. For serious brain infections, intravenous antibiotics are standard. To counter bacterial resistance, multiple antibiotics may be employed. It is important to note that antibiotics are specific to bacteria; they do not impact viruses. Their function involves either killing bacteria or inhibiting their reproduction. Common medical classes include penicillin, cephalosporins, aminoglycosides, macrolides, quinolones, and tetracyclines.

input: Tito's greatest strength, in the eyes of the western communists, had been in suppressing nationalist insurrections and maintaining unity throughout the country. It was Tito's call for unity, and related methods, that held together the people of Yugoslavia. This ability was put to a test several times during his reign, notably during the Croatian Spring (also referred as the Masovni pokret, maspok, meaning "Mass Movement") when the government suppressed both public demonstrations and dissenting opinions within the Communist Party. Despite this suppression, much of maspok's demands were later realized with the new constitution, heavily backed by Tito himself against opposition from the Serbian branch of the party.[citation needed] On 16 May 1974, the new Constitution was passed, and the aging Tito was named president for life, a status which he would enjoy for five years.
rewrite: Western communists viewed Tito's primary strength as his capacity to quell nationalist uprisings and preserve national unity. His appeals for solidarity, along with the tactics he employed, were crucial in binding Yugoslavia together. This unifying skill faced multiple challenges, most significantly during the Croatian Spring—known as *maspok*—when authorities curtailed public protests and internal party dissent. Although suppressed, many of the movement's aims were ultimately incorporated into a new constitution, which Tito personally championed despite resistance from the Serbian party faction. The constitution was adopted on 16 May 1974, granting the aging leader the title of president for life, a role he held until his death five years later.

input: The Great Plains is the broad expanse of flat land (a plain), much of it covered in prairie, steppe and grassland, that lies west of the Mississippi River tallgrass prairie states and east of the Rocky Mountains in the United States and Canada. This area covers parts, but not all, of the states of Colorado, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Texas, and Wyoming, and the Canadian provinces of Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. The region is known for supporting extensive cattle ranching and dry farming.
rewrite: West of the Mississippi tallgrass prairie and east of the Rocky Mountains lies the Great Plains, a broad expanse of flat land. Much of this plain is covered in prairie, steppe, and grassland. Encompassing parts of ten U.S. states and three Canadian provinces, the region supports extensive cattle ranching and dry farming. It includes areas within Colorado, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Texas, Wyoming, Alberta, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan, though not the entirety of these states and provinces.

input: Many of the crucial events of the American Revolution—the Boston Massacre, the Boston Tea Party, Paul Revere's midnight ride, the battles of Lexington and Concord and Bunker Hill, the Siege of Boston, and many others—occurred in or near Boston. After the Revolution, Boston's long seafaring tradition helped make it one of the world's wealthiest international ports, with rum, fish, salt, and tobacco being particularly important.
rewrite: Boston's central role in the American Revolution included events like the Boston Massacre, the Tea Party, Paul Revere's ride, and the battles of Lexington, Concord, and Bunker Hill, along with the Siege of Boston. Following the war, the city's maritime tradition enabled it to become a globally wealthy port, largely through trade in rum, fish, salt, and tobacco.

input: "Baseball's Sad Lexicon," also known as "Tinker to Evers to Chance" after its refrain, is a 1910 baseball poem by Franklin Pierce Adams. The poem is presented as a single, rueful stanza from the point of view of a New York Giants fan seeing the talented Chicago Cubs infield of shortstop Joe Tinker, second baseman Johnny Evers, and first baseman Frank Chance complete a double play. The trio began playing together with the Cubs in 1902, and formed a double play combination that lasted through April 1912. The Cubs won the pennant four times between 1906 and 1910, often defeating the Giants en route to the World Series.
rewrite: Penned by Franklin Pierce Adams in 1910, the baseball poem "Baseball's Sad Lexicon" is famously nicknamed "Tinker to Evers to Chance" for its recurring line. It features a single, lamenting stanza voiced by a New York Giants fan. This fan watches the skilled Chicago Cubs infield—shortstop Joe Tinker, second baseman Johnny Evers, and first baseman Frank Chance—execute a double play. This trio, whose double play partnership lasted from 1902 until April 1912, helped the Cubs secure four pennants from 1906 to 1910, frequently overcoming the Giants on their path to the World Series.

input: Orontid Armenia formally passed to empire of Alexander the Great following his conquest of Persia. Alexander appointed an Orontid named Mithranes to govern Armenia. Armenia later became a vassal state of the Seleucid Empire, but it maintained a considerable degree of autonomy, retaining its native rulers. Towards the end 212 BC the country was divided into two kingdoms, Greater Armenia and Armenia Sophene including Commagene or Armenia Minor. The kingdoms became so independent from Seleucid control that Antiochus III the Great waged war on them during his reign and replaced their rulers.
rewrite: Following the conquest of Persia, Orontid Armenia came under the empire of Alexander the Great, who appointed the Orontid Mithranes as its governor. Although Armenia later became a vassal of the Seleucid Empire, it preserved substantial autonomy under its native rulers. By around 212 BC, the region split into two kingdoms: Greater Armenia and Armenia Sophene, the latter encompassing Commagene or Armenia Minor. Their growing independence from Seleucid authority prompted Antiochus III the Great to wage war and install new rulers during his reign.

input: Chopin made his last public appearance on a concert platform at London's Guildhall on 16 November 1848, when, in a final patriotic gesture, he played for the benefit of Polish refugees. By this time he was very seriously ill, weighing under 99 pounds (i.e. less than 45 kg), and his doctors were aware that his sickness was at a terminal stage.
rewrite: On November 16, 1848, Chopin gave his final public performance at London's Guildhall for Polish refugees, a last patriotic act. He was gravely ill by then, weighing under 99 pounds (less than 45 kg), and his doctors recognized his condition was terminal.

input: The first attempts to use standard-frequency single-phase AC were made in Hungary as far back as 1923, by the Hungarian Kálmán Kandó on the line between Budapest-Nyugati and Alag, using 16 kV at 50 Hz. The locomotives carried a four-pole rotating phase converter feeding a single traction motor of the polyphase induction type at 600 to 1,100 V. The number of poles on the 2,500 hp motor could be changed using slip rings to run at one of four synchronous speeds. The tests were a success so, from 1932 until the 1960s, trains on the Budapest-Hegyeshalom line (towards Vienna) regularly used the same system. A few decades after the Second World War, the 16 kV was changed to the Russian and later French 25 kV system.
rewrite: Initial experiments with standard-frequency single-phase AC occurred in Hungary in 1923, led by engineer Kálmán Kandó on the Budapest-Nyugati to Alag route. This system employed 16 kV at 50 Hz. The locomotives featured a four-pole rotating phase converter, which supplied power to a single polyphase induction traction motor operating between 600 and 1,100 V. This 2,500 hp motor utilized slip rings to alter its number of poles, allowing it to run at one of four synchronous speeds. Following the successful tests, trains on the Budapest-Hegyeshalom line (toward Vienna) regularly operated with this same technology from 1932 through the 1960s. Decades after the Second World War, the original 16 kV system was replaced, first by the Russian and later by the French 25 kV standard.

input: The southern group (South Estonian language) consists of the Tartu, Mulgi, Võru (Võro) and Setu (Seto) dialects. These are sometimes considered either variants of a South Estonian language, or separate languages altogether. Also, Seto and Võro distinguish themselves from each other less by language and more by their culture and their respective Christian confession.
rewrite: South Estonian includes Tartu, Mulgi, Võro, and Seto dialects. They may be viewed as a single language or as distinct languages. Culturally and religiously, Seto and Võro differ more from each other than they do linguistically.

input: The desire to explore, record and systematize knowledge had a meaningful impact on music publications. Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Dictionnaire de musique (published 1767 in Geneva and 1768 in Paris) was a leading text in the late 18th century. This widely available dictionary gave short definitions of words like genius and taste, and was clearly influenced by the Enlightenment movement. Another text influenced by Enlightenment values was Charles Burney's A General History of Music: From the Earliest Ages to the Present Period (1776), which was a historical survey and an attempt to rationalize elements in music systematically over time. Recently, musicologists have shown renewed interest in the ideas and consequences of the Enlightenment. For example, Rose Rosengard Subotnik's Deconstructive Variations (subtitled Music and Reason in Western Society) compares Mozart's Die Zauberflöte (1791) using the Enlightenment and Romantic perspectives, and concludes that the work is "an ideal musical representation of the Enlightenment".
rewrite: The drive to explore, document, and organize knowledge significantly shaped music publications. A key example is Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s *Dictionnaire de musique* (Geneva 1767, Paris 1768), a widely circulated late-18th-century work offering concise entries for terms such as genius and taste, reflecting clear Enlightenment influences. Similarly informed by Enlightenment ideals was Charles Burney’s 1776 *A General History of Music: From the Earliest Ages to the Present Period*, which provided a historical overview aiming to rationally systematize musical elements across time. Modern musicology has seen a revived focus on Enlightenment concepts and their impacts. Scholar Rose Rosengard Subotnik, in *Deconstructive Variations: Music and Reason in Western Society*, analyzes Mozart’s *Die Zauberflöte* (1791) through both Enlightenment and Romantic lenses, ultimately declaring it an ideal musical embodiment of the Enlightenment.

input: In Islam, dogs are viewed as unclean because they are viewed as scavengers. In 2015 city councillor Hasan Küçük of The Hague called for dog ownership to be made illegal in that city. Islamic activists in Lérida, Spain, lobbied for dogs to be kept out of Muslim neighborhoods, saying their presence violated Muslims' religious freedom. In Britain, police sniffer dogs are carefully used, and are not permitted to contact passengers, only their luggage. They are required to wear leather dog booties when searching mosques or Muslim homes.
rewrite: In Islam, dogs are considered unclean due to their scavenging nature. This view has prompted various official responses. In The Hague, city councillor Hasan Küçük advocated in 2015 for a ban on dog ownership. Similarly, Islamic activists in Lérida, Spain, argued that dogs in Muslim neighborhoods infringed on religious freedom. British police adjust their procedures accordingly; sniffer dogs must wear leather booties in mosques or Muslim homes and are only permitted to examine luggage, not contact passengers directly.

input: The Acta Constitutiva de la Federación of January 31, 1824, and the Federal Constitution of October 4, 1824, fixed the political and administrative organization of the United Mexican States after the Mexican War of Independence. In addition, Section XXVIII of Article 50 gave the new Congress the right to choose where the federal government would be located. This location would then be appropriated as federal land, with the federal government acting as the local authority. The two main candidates to become the capital were Mexico City and Querétaro.
rewrite: Following the Mexican War of Independence, the political and administrative structure of the United Mexican States was established by the Acta Constitutiva de la Federación of January 31, 1824, and the Federal Constitution of October 4, 1824. Article 50, Section XXVIII granted the new Congress the authority to select the seat of the federal government. This chosen location would be designated as federal territory, governed directly by the federal authorities. The primary contenders for this capital were Mexico City and Querétaro.

input: During the late 1980s and early 1990s, Richmond experienced a spike in overall crime, in particular, the city's murder rate. The city had 93 murders for the year of 1985, with a murder rate of 41.9 killings committed per 100,000 residents. Over the next decade, the city saw a major increase in total homicides. In 1990 there were 114 murders, for a murder rate of 56.1 killings per 100,000 residents. There were 120 murders in 1995, resulting in a murder rate of 59.1 killings per 100,000 residents, one of the highest in the United States.
rewrite: From the late 1980s into the early 1990s, Richmond saw a significant surge in overall crime, most notably in its murder rate. The city recorded 93 murders in 1985, a rate of 41.9 per 100,000 residents. This figure climbed sharply over the following decade. By 1990, there were 114 murders, with a rate of 56.1 per 100,000. In 1995, the number reached 120 murders, yielding a rate of 59.1 per 100,000—among the highest in the nation at that time.

input: After the first two months of the conflict, South Korean forces were on the point of defeat, forced back to the Pusan Perimeter. In September 1950, an amphibious UN counter-offensive was launched at Inchon, and cut off many of the North Korean attackers. Those that escaped envelopment and capture were rapidly forced back north all the way to the border with China at the Yalu River, or into the mountainous interior. At this point, in October 1950, Chinese forces crossed the Yalu and entered the war. Chinese intervention triggered a retreat of UN forces which continued until mid-1951. After these dramatic reversals of fortune, which saw Seoul change hands four times, the last two years of conflict became a war of attrition, with the front line close to the 38th parallel. The war in the air, however, was never a stalemate. North Korea was subject to a massive bombing campaign. Jet fighters confronted each other in air-to-air combat for the first time in history, and Soviet pilots covertly flew in defense of their Communist allies.
rewrite: By September 1950, with South Korean forces having been pushed nearly to defeat into the Pusan Perimeter over the conflict's first two months, a UN amphibious counter-offensive was launched at Inchon. This maneuver cut off numerous North Korean attackers. Those troops avoiding envelopment and capture were then driven rapidly northward, either to the Chinese border at the Yalu River or into the mountainous interior. The war's dynamic shifted again in October 1950 when Chinese forces crossed the Yalu and entered the conflict. Their intervention prompted a prolonged UN retreat that lasted until mid-1951. Following these dramatic reversals—which included Seoul changing hands four times—the final two years settled into a war of attrition, with the front line stabilizing near the 38th parallel. The air war, however, never reached stalemate. North Korea endured a massive bombing campaign, jet fighters engaged in history's first air-to-air combats, and Soviet pilots flew covertly in defense of their Communist allies.

input: Boston's park system is well-reputed nationally. In its 2013 ParkScore ranking, The Trust for Public Land reported that Boston was tied with Sacramento and San Francisco for having the third-best park system among the 50 most populous US cities. ParkScore ranks city park systems by a formula that analyzes the city's median park size, park acres as percent of city area, the percent of residents within a half-mile of a park, spending of park services per resident, and the number of playgrounds per 10,000 residents.
rewrite: Nationally recognized for its parks, Boston earned third place in the 2013 ParkScore ranking by The Trust for Public Land, tying with Sacramento and San Francisco among the fifty most populous U.S. cities. This evaluation analyzes median park size, park acreage relative to city area, the percentage of residents living within a half-mile of a park, per capita park spending, and playgrounds per 10,000 residents.

input: Music, photos and videos can be played from standard USB mass storage devices, Xbox 360 proprietary storage devices (such as memory cards or Xbox 360 hard drives), and servers or computers with Windows Media Center or Windows XP with Service pack 2 or higher within the local-area network in streaming mode. As the Xbox 360 uses a modified version of the UPnP AV protocol, some alternative UPnP servers such as uShare (part of the GeeXboX project) and MythTV can also stream media to the Xbox 360, allowing for similar functionality from non-Windows servers. This is possible with video files up to HD-resolution and with several codecs (MPEG-2, MPEG-4, WMV) and container formats (WMV, MOV, TS).
rewrite: The Xbox 360 can play music, photos, and videos from various sources. These include standard USB drives, its own proprietary storage like memory cards or hard drives, and networked computers running Windows Media Center or Windows XP with Service Pack 2 or later. Streaming is also possible from alternative UPnP servers, such as uShare or MythTV, because the console uses a modified UPnP AV protocol. This allows non-Windows servers to provide similar functionality. Supported media includes video files up to HD resolution, with codecs like MPEG-2, MPEG-4, and WMV, as well as container formats including WMV, MOV, and TS.

input: Strasbourg also offers high-class eclecticist buildings in its very extended German district, the Neustadt, being the main memory of Wilhelmian architecture since most of the major cities in Germany proper suffered intensive damage during World War II. Streets, boulevards and avenues are homogeneous, surprisingly high (up to seven stories) and broad examples of German urban lay-out and of this architectural style that summons and mixes up five centuries of European architecture as well as Neo-Egyptian, Neo-Greek and Neo-Babylonian styles. The former imperial palace Palais du Rhin, the most political and thus heavily criticized of all German Strasbourg buildings epitomizes the grand scale and stylistic sturdiness of this period. But the two most handsome and ornate buildings of these times are the École internationale des Pontonniers (the former Höhere Mädchenschule, girls college) with its towers, turrets and multiple round and square angles and the École des Arts décoratifs with its lavishly ornate façade of painted bricks, woodwork and majolica.
rewrite: In the Neustadt, Strasbourg’s extensive German district, high-class eclecticist buildings stand as the primary surviving memory of Wilhelmian architecture. This is especially significant, as most major cities in Germany proper sustained intensive damage during World War II. The area features homogeneous streets, boulevards, and avenues that are surprisingly high—up to seven stories—and broad, exemplifying German urban layout. The architectural style itself summons and mixes five centuries of European design, alongside Neo-Egyptian, Neo-Greek, and Neo-Babylonian influences. Epitomizing the grand scale and stylistic sturdiness of the period is the former imperial palace, the Palais du Rhin, the most political and heavily criticized of all German buildings in Strasbourg. However, the two most handsome and ornate examples from these times are the École internationale des Pontonniers, the former girls' college (Höhere Mädchenschule), with its towers, turrets, and multiple angles, and the lavishly adorned École des Arts décoratifs, featuring a façade of painted bricks, woodwork, and majolica.

input: Models suggest that Neptune's troposphere is banded by clouds of varying compositions depending on altitude. The upper-level clouds lie at pressures below one bar, where the temperature is suitable for methane to condense. For pressures between one and five bars (100 and 500 kPa), clouds of ammonia and hydrogen sulfide are thought to form. Above a pressure of five bars, the clouds may consist of ammonia, ammonium sulfide, hydrogen sulfide and water. Deeper clouds of water ice should be found at pressures of about 50 bars (5.0 MPa), where the temperature reaches 273 K (0 °C). Underneath, clouds of ammonia and hydrogen sulfide may be found.
rewrite: According to scientific models, Neptune's troposphere features distinct cloud bands composed of different substances at specific altitudes. At the highest levels, where pressure falls below one bar, methane condenses into clouds. Deeper, within a range of one to five bars, clouds likely form from ammonia and hydrogen sulfide. Below this, above five bars of pressure, clouds may contain ammonia, ammonium sulfide, hydrogen sulfide, and water. At much greater depths, around 50 bars, water ice clouds exist where temperatures hit 273 K (0 °C). Beneath even these, further clouds of ammonia and hydrogen sulfide are anticipated.

input: At a certain temperature, (usually between 1,500 °F (820 °C) and 1,600 °F (870 °C), depending on carbon content), the base metal of steel undergoes a change in the arrangement of the atoms in its crystal matrix, called allotropy. This allows the small carbon atoms to enter the interstices of the iron crystal, diffusing into the iron matrix. When this happens, the carbon atoms are said to be in solution, or mixed with the iron, forming a single, homogeneous, crystalline phase called austenite. If the steel is cooled slowly, the iron will gradually change into its low temperature allotrope. When this happens the carbon atoms will no longer be soluble with the iron, and will be forced to precipitate out of solution, nucleating into the spaces between the crystals. The steel then becomes heterogeneous, being formed of two phases; the carbon (carbide) phase cementite, and ferrite. This type of heat treatment produces steel that is rather soft and bendable. However, if the steel is cooled quickly the carbon atoms will not have time to precipitate. When rapidly cooled, a diffusionless (martensite) transformation occurs, in which the carbon atoms become trapped in solution. This causes the iron crystals to deform intrinsically when the crystal structure tries to change to its low temperature state, making it very hard and brittle.
rewrite:
When steel is heated to a specific temperature—typically ranging from 1,500 °F (820 °C) to 1,600 °F (870 °C), with the exact point depending on carbon content—an allotropic change occurs in the base metal’s crystal structure. During this transformation, small carbon atoms diffuse into the iron matrix, occupying the interstices within the iron crystals. The carbon enters into solution, blending with the iron to create a uniform crystalline phase known as austenite.

If the cooling process is slow, the iron reverts to its low-temperature allotropic form. As a result, the carbon atoms lose their solubility and precipitate out of solution, gathering in the spaces between crystals. This leads to a heterogeneous material composed of two distinct phases: ferrite and the carbide phase cementite. Steel treated in this manner becomes relatively soft and malleable.

Conversely, rapid cooling prevents the carbon atoms from having sufficient time to precipitate. Instead, a diffusionless transformation takes place, producing martensite. Here, the carbon remains trapped in solution as the crystal structure attempts to shift to its low-temperature state, causing internal deformation of the iron crystals. This yields a steel that is exceptionally hard but also brittle.

input: Namibia extends from 17°S to 25°S: climatically the range of the sub-Tropical High Pressure Belt, arid is the overall climate description descending from the Sub-Humid (mean rain above 500 mm) through Semi-Arid between 300 and 500 mm (embracing most of the waterless Kalahari) and Arid from 150 to 300 mm (these three regions are inland from the western escarpment) to the Hyper-Arid coastal plain with less than a 100 mm mean. Temperature maxima are limited by the overall elevation of the entire region: only in the far south, Warmbad for instance, are mid-40 °C maxima recorded.
rewrite: Stretching from 17°S to 25°S, Namibia lies within the sub-Tropical High Pressure Belt, resulting in a predominantly arid climate. Conditions range from Sub-Humid inland, with over 500 mm of mean rainfall, down to the Hyper-Arid coast, receiving under 100 mm. In between are Semi-Arid and Arid zones, covering much of the interior west of the escarpment, including the dry Kalahari. Due to the region's high overall elevation, extreme temperature maxima are uncommon, with mid-40°C readings typically confined to areas like Warmbad in the far south.

input: In 1934 the Zagreb Provincial Committee sent Tito to Vienna where all the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia had sought refuge. He was appointed to the Committee and started to appoint allies to him, among them Edvard Kardelj, Milovan Đilas, Aleksandar Ranković and Boris Kidrič. In 1935, Tito travelled to the Soviet Union, working for a year in the Balkans section of Comintern. He was a member of the Soviet Communist Party and the Soviet secret police (NKVD). Tito was also involved in recruiting for the Dimitrov Battalion, a group of volunteers serving in the Spanish Civil War. In 1936, the Comintern sent "Comrade Walter" (i.e. Tito) back to Yugoslavia to purge the Communist Party there. In 1937, Stalin had the Secretary-General of the CPY, Milan Gorkić, murdered in Moscow. Subsequently Tito was appointed Secretary-General of the still-outlawed CPY.
rewrite: In 1934, Tito was dispatched by the Zagreb Provincial Committee to Vienna, where the entire Central Committee of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia had taken refuge. There, he gained appointment to the Committee and began placing allies like Edvard Kardelj, Milovan Đilas, Aleksandar Ranković, and Boris Kidrič into positions. The following year, he went to the Soviet Union, spending a year in the Comintern's Balkans section while also holding membership in the Soviet Communist Party and the NKVD secret police. His activities included recruiting volunteers for the Dimitrov Battalion to fight in the Spanish Civil War. By 1936, the Comintern directed him, under the alias "Comrade Walter," to return to Yugoslavia and purge the local Communist Party. After Stalin orchestrated the 1937 murder of CPY Secretary-General Milan Gorkić in Moscow, Tito was named the new Secretary-General of the still-outlawed party.

input: Since the Industrial Revolution some two hundred years ago, the food processing industry has invented many technologies that both help keep foods fresh longer and alter the fresh state of food as they appear in nature. Cooling is the primary technology used to maintain freshness, whereas many more technologies have been invented to allow foods to last longer without becoming spoiled. These latter technologies include pasteurisation, autoclavation, drying, salting, and separation of various components, all of which appearing to alter the original nutritional contents of food. Pasteurisation and autoclavation (heating techniques) have no doubt improved the safety of many common foods, preventing epidemics of bacterial infection. But some of the (new) food processing technologies have downfalls as well.
rewrite: Over two centuries following the Industrial Revolution, numerous technologies have emerged from the food processing industry. These innovations serve to extend freshness and modify the natural state of foods. While cooling remains the foremost method for preserving freshness, other techniques like pasteurization, autoclavation, drying, salting, and component separation have been developed to prevent spoilage. Such methods, however, often change the food's original nutritional makeup. Heating processes like pasteurization and autoclavation have undoubtedly enhanced safety and averted bacterial epidemics. Yet, some of these newer processing technologies also come with their own drawbacks.

input: An early advantage of AC is that the power-wasting resistors used in DC locomotives for speed control were not needed in an AC locomotive: multiple taps on the transformer can supply a range of voltages. Separate low-voltage transformer windings supply lighting and the motors driving auxiliary machinery. More recently, the development of very high power semiconductors has caused the classic "universal" AC/DC motor to be largely replaced with the three-phase induction motor fed by a variable frequency drive, a special inverter that varies both frequency and voltage to control motor speed. These drives can run equally well on DC or AC of any frequency, and many modern electric locomotives are designed to handle different supply voltages and frequencies to simplify cross-border operation.
rewrite: An AC locomotive avoids the need for power-wasting resistors employed in DC systems for speed control, as multiple transformer taps can provide various voltages. Lighting and auxiliary machinery motors are powered by separate low-voltage transformer windings. In more recent developments, the classic "universal" AC/DC motor has been largely supplanted by the three-phase induction motor, driven by a variable frequency drive. This special inverter adjusts both frequency and voltage to regulate motor speed. Capable of operating on either DC or AC of any frequency, such drives enable many modern electric locomotives to accommodate different supply voltages and frequencies, thereby simplifying cross-border operations.

input: Brigham Young University (often referred to as BYU or, colloquially, The Y) is a private research university located in Provo, Utah, United States. It is owned and operated by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church), and, excluding online students, is the largest of any religious university and the third largest private university in the United States, with 29,672 on-campus students. Approximately 99 percent of the students are members of the LDS Church, and one-third of its US students are from Utah.
rewrite: Located in Provo, Utah, Brigham Young University (BYU, or The Y) is a private research institution owned by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. With 29,672 on-campus students, it ranks as the largest religious university and the third-largest private university in the United States. Around 99% of its students are LDS Church members, and about one-third of its U.S. student body hails from Utah.

input: Habitat size and numbers of species are systematically related. Physically larger species and those living at lower latitudes or in forests or oceans are more sensitive to reduction in habitat area. Conversion to "trivial" standardized ecosystems (e.g., monoculture following deforestation) effectively destroys habitat for the more diverse species that preceded the conversion. In some countries lack of property rights or lax law/regulatory enforcement necessarily leads to biodiversity loss (degradation costs having to be supported by the community).[citation needed]
rewrite: Species diversity is systematically linked to habitat size, with larger species and those in forests, oceans, or lower latitudes being especially vulnerable to habitat reduction. Converting diverse ecosystems into simplified ones, like monocultures after deforestation, effectively destroys existing habitats. Furthermore, in certain nations, weak property rights or lax enforcement of laws and regulations inevitably results in biodiversity loss, imposing degradation costs on communities.

input: In the 2010s, American jurisdictions have experienced a shortage of lethal injection drugs, due to anti-death penalty advocacy and low production volume. Hospira, the only U.S. manufacturer of sodium thiopental, stopped making the drug in 2011. The European Union has outlawed the export of any product that could be used in an execution; this has prevented executioners from using EU-manufactured anesthetics like propofol which are needed for general medical purposes. Another alternative, pentobarbital, is also only manufactured in the European Union, which has caused the Danish producer to restrict distribution to U.S. government customers.
rewrite: During the 2010s, a shortage of lethal injection drugs emerged in American jurisdictions, driven by advocacy against the death penalty and limited production. In 2011, Hospira, the sole U.S. manufacturer of sodium thiopental, ceased its production. Furthermore, the European Union bans exports of any goods for use in executions, blocking access to EU-made anesthetics such as propofol, which are also essential for general medicine. Pentobarbital, another option, is produced only in the EU, leading its Danish manufacturer to limit sales to U.S. government buyers.

input: The bandolim (Portuguese for "mandolin") was a favourite instrument within the Portuguese bourgeoisie of the 19th century, but its rapid spread took it to other places, joining other instruments. Today you can see mandolins as part of the traditional and folk culture of Portuguese singing groups and the majority of the mandolin scene in Portugal is in Madeira Island. Madeira has over 17 active mandolin Orchestras and Tunas. The mandolin virtuoso Fabio Machado is one of Portugal's most accomplished mandolin players. The Portuguese influence brought the mandolin to Brazil.
rewrite: In the 19th century, the bandolim—Portuguese for mandolin—was especially popular among the bourgeoisie. Its influence quickly extended beyond Portugal, carried to other regions where it joined local musical traditions. Presently, the instrument remains vital to Portuguese folk culture, particularly within singing groups. The island of Madeira is the heart of Portugal's mandolin scene, home to more than 17 active Orchestras and Tunas. Virtuoso Fabio Machado stands as one of the country's most skilled players. Portuguese influence also introduced the mandolin to Brazil.

input: Florida i/ˈflɒrɪdə/ (Spanish for "flowery land") is a state located in the southeastern region of the United States. The state is bordered to the west by the Gulf of Mexico, to the north by Alabama and Georgia, to the east by the Atlantic Ocean, and to the south by the Straits of Florida and the sovereign state of Cuba. Florida is the 22nd most extensive, the 3rd most populous, and the 8th most densely populated of the United States. Jacksonville is the most populous city in Florida, and the largest city by area in the contiguous United States. The Miami metropolitan area is the eighth-largest metropolitan area in the United States. Tallahassee is the state capital.
rewrite: Located in the southeastern United States, Florida—a name derived from Spanish meaning "flowery land"—is bordered by the Gulf of Mexico to the west, Alabama and Georgia to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the east, and the Straits of Florida and Cuba to the south. It ranks as the 22nd largest state by area, the 3rd most populous, and the 8th most densely populated. While Tallahassee serves as the state capital, Jacksonville is its most populous city and the largest by area in the contiguous U.S. Additionally, the Miami metropolitan area is the nation's eighth-largest.

input: Various theories for the decline of the Native American populations emphasize epidemic diseases, conflicts with Europeans, and conflicts among warring tribes. Scholars now believe that, among the various contributing factors, epidemic disease was the overwhelming cause of the population decline of the American natives. Some believe that after first contacts with Europeans and Africans, Old World diseases caused the death of 90 to 95% of the native population of the New World in the following 150 years. Smallpox killed up to one third of the native population of Hispaniola in 1518. By killing the Incan ruler Huayna Capac, smallpox caused the Inca Civil War. Smallpox was only the first epidemic. Typhus (probably) in 1546, influenza and smallpox together in 1558, smallpox again in 1589, diphtheria in 1614, measles in 1618—all ravaged the remains of Inca culture.
rewrite: Scholars identify epidemic disease as the overwhelming cause of the Native American population decline, emphasizing it over other factors like conflicts with Europeans or intertribal warfare. Following initial contact, Old World illnesses are believed to have killed 90 to 95% of the New World's native inhabitants within 150 years. Smallpox alone killed up to a third of Hispaniola's population in 1518 and, by claiming the life of Incan ruler Huayna Capac, triggered the Inca Civil War. This was merely the first wave; a series of epidemics followed. These included typhus around 1546, combined influenza and smallpox in 1558, another smallpox outbreak in 1589, then diphtheria in 1614, and measles in 1618—each devastating the remnants of Inca society.

input: Other common forms include president of the council of ministers (for example in Italy, Presidente del Consiglio dei Ministri), President of the Executive Council, or Minister-President. In the Scandinavian countries the prime minister is called statsminister in the native languages (i.e. minister of state). In federations, the head of government of subnational entities such as provinces is most commonly known as the premier, chief minister, governor or minister-president.
rewrite: Common titles for a prime minister include president of the council of ministers, as in Italy, or President of the Executive Council. The Scandinavian nations use the term statsminister, meaning minister of state. Within federations, the leader of a provincial government is often titled premier, chief minister, governor, or minister-president.

input: On 7 April 1963, the country changed its official name to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Reforms encouraged private enterprise and greatly relaxed restrictions on freedom of speech and religious expression. Tito subsequently went on a tour of the Americas. In Chile, two government ministers resigned over his visit to that country. In the autumn of 1960 Tito met President Dwight D. Eisenhower at the United Nations General Assembly meeting. Tito and Eisenhower discussed a range of issues from arms control to economic development. When Eisenhower remarked that Yugoslavia's neutralism was "neutral on his side", Tito replied that neutralism did not imply passivity but meant "not taking sides".
rewrite: On 7 April 1963, the nation adopted the official name Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Accompanying reforms promoted private enterprise and significantly eased limits on speech and religion. Later, Tito embarked on a tour of the Americas. His visit to Chile prompted the resignation of two government ministers there. Earlier, in the autumn of 1960, Tito had met President Dwight D. Eisenhower at a UN General Assembly meeting. Their discussion covered arms control and economic development. When Eisenhower commented that Yugoslavia's neutralism seemed "neutral on his side," Tito responded that such a stance meant "not taking sides," not passivity.

input: Stout and porter are dark beers made using roasted malts or roast barley, and typically brewed with slow fermenting yeast. There are a number of variations including Baltic porter, dry stout, and Imperial stout. The name Porter was first used in 1721 to describe a dark brown beer popular with the street and river porters of London. This same beer later also became known as stout, though the word stout had been used as early as 1677. The history and development of stout and porter are intertwined.
rewrite: Dark beers known as stout and porter are brewed with roasted malts or barley and slow-fermenting yeast. Variations include Baltic porter, dry stout, and Imperial stout. First used in 1721, the name Porter described a dark brown beer favored by London's street and river porters. This same beverage later acquired the name stout, a term in use since 1677. Consequently, the histories of stout and porter are deeply interconnected.

input: Since 1066, when Harold Godwinson and William the Conqueror were crowned, the coronations of English and British monarchs have been held there. There have been at least 16 royal weddings at the abbey since 1100. Two were of reigning monarchs (Henry I and Richard II), although, before 1919, there had been none for some 500 years.
rewrite: Coronations for English and British monarchs have occurred there since 1066, starting with Harold Godwinson and William the Conqueror. Since 1100, the abbey has also hosted at least 16 royal weddings. Two involved reigning monarchs, Henry I and Richard II, though none took place for about 500 years prior to 1919.

input: After the Communist Party of China took power in 1949, the flag of China became a red flag with a large star symbolizing the Communist Party, and smaller stars symbolizing workers, peasants, the urban middle class and rural middle class. The flag of the Communist Party of China became a red banner with a hammer and sickle, similar to that on the Soviet flag. In the 1950s and 1960s, other Communist regimes such as Vietnam and Laos also adopted red flags. Some Communist countries, such as Cuba, chose to keep their old flags; and other countries used red flags which had nothing to do with Communism or socialism; the red flag of Nepal, for instance, represents the national flower.
rewrite: Following the establishment of Communist Party rule in 1949, China’s national flag was designed as a red field featuring a large star representing the Party, alongside smaller stars denoting workers, peasants, and the urban and rural middle classes. Similarly, the Communist Party of China’s own flag adopted a red banner with a hammer and sickle, echoing the Soviet emblem. During the mid-20th century, nations like Vietnam and Laos embraced red flags under their Communist governments. However, not all Communist states, such as Cuba, changed their banners, while other countries, like Nepal, fly red flags for non-ideological reasons—its crimson background symbolizes the national flower.

input: In the 1950 parliamentary elections, the Wafd Party of el-Nahhas gained a victory—mostly due to the absence of the Muslim Brotherhood, which boycotted the elections—and was perceived as a threat by the Free Officers as the Wafd had campaigned on demands similar to their own. Accusations of corruption against Wafd politicians began to surface, however, breeding an atmosphere of rumor and suspicion that consequently brought the Free Officers to the forefront of Egyptian politics. By then, the organization had expanded to around ninety members; according to Khaled Mohieddin, "nobody knew all of them and where they belonged in the hierarchy except Nasser". Nasser felt that the Free Officers were not ready to move against the government and, for nearly two years, he did little beyond officer recruitment and underground news bulletins.
rewrite: The Wafd Party, led by el-Nahhas, won the 1950 parliamentary elections. This victory was aided by a boycott from the Muslim Brotherhood, which viewed the party as a threat. Significantly, the Wafd's campaign promises echoed the demands of the Free Officers, making the party's success alarming to this clandestine military group. An environment of rumor and suspicion soon emerged, fueled by corruption accusations against Wafd politicians. This atmosphere ultimately propelled the Free Officers into a more prominent political role. Their organization had grown to approximately ninety members by this time, though, as Khaled Mohieddin noted, only Nasser knew everyone's identity and rank. Believing the group was unprepared for direct action, Nasser focused for nearly two years solely on recruiting officers and distributing underground bulletins.

input: At the request of the pope, he created an information office for prisoners of war and refugees, which in the years of its existence from 1939 until 1947 received almost ten million (9 891 497) information requests and produced over eleven million (11.293.511) answers about missing persons. Montini was several times openly attacked by Benito Mussolini's government as a politician, and meddling in politics, but each time he found powerful defenses by the Vatican. In 1944, Luigi Maglione died, and Pius XII appointed Tardini and Montini together as heads of the State Department. Montini's admiration was almost filial, when he described Pope Pius XII:
rewrite: Acting on the pope's initiative, he established an information bureau for prisoners of war and refugees. From 1939 to 1947, this office fielded nearly ten million inquiries (9,891,497) and issued over eleven million responses (11,293,511) concerning missing individuals. Although Benito Mussolini's government repeatedly denounced Montini as a political meddler, he consistently found robust defense from the Vatican. Following Luigi Maglione's death in 1944, Pius XII named Tardini and Montini joint heads of the State Department. Montini's regard for Pope Pius XII was nearly filial in nature, as reflected in his descriptions.

input: The Partisan Prohibitions were repealed during the Yellow Turban Rebellion and Five Pecks of Rice Rebellion in 184 AD, largely because the court did not want to continue to alienate a significant portion of the gentry class who might otherwise join the rebellions. The Yellow Turbans and Five-Pecks-of-Rice adherents belonged to two different hierarchical Daoist religious societies led by faith healers Zhang Jue (d. 184 AD) and Zhang Lu (d. 216 AD), respectively. Zhang Lu's rebellion, in modern northern Sichuan and southern Shaanxi, was not quelled until 215 AD. Zhang Jue's massive rebellion across eight provinces was annihilated by Han forces within a year, however the following decades saw much smaller recurrent uprisings. Although the Yellow Turbans were defeated, many generals appointed during the crisis never disbanded their assembled militia forces and used these troops to amass power outside of the collapsing imperial authority.
rewrite: During the Yellow Turban Rebellion and the Five Pecks of Rice Rebellion in 184 AD, the court repealed the Partisan Prohibitions. This decision was primarily driven by a desire to avoid further alienating a substantial segment of the gentry, who might otherwise have joined the revolts. These uprisings were led by two distinct hierarchical Daoist religious societies. The Yellow Turbans followed the faith healer Zhang Jue (d. 184 AD), while the Five-Pecks-of-Rice adherents were led by Zhang Lu (d. 216 AD). Zhang Jue's massive rebellion across eight provinces was crushed by Han forces within a year, though smaller recurrent uprisings followed for decades. Zhang Lu's rebellion, located in modern northern Sichuan and southern Shaanxi, persisted until 215 AD. Despite the Yellow Turban defeat, many generals appointed during the crisis retained their militia forces, using them to build power independent of the collapsing imperial authority.

input: Tort law covers the entire imaginable spectrum of wrongs which humans can inflict upon each other, and of course, partially overlaps with wrongs also punishable by criminal law.
