Although the American Law Institute has attempted to standardize tort law through the development of several versions of the Restatement of Torts, many states have chosen to adopt only certain sections of the Restatements and to reject others. Thus, because of its immense size and diversity, American tort law cannot be easily summarized.
rewrite: Tort law encompasses the full range of wrongs people can commit against one another, overlapping in part with criminal offenses. The American Law Institute has tried to standardize this area through multiple Restatements of Torts. However, many states selectively adopt only portions of these Restatements, rejecting others. Given its vast scope and variety, American tort law resists easy summarization.

input: In 1578 king Stefan Batory created the Crown Tribunal in order to reduce the enormous pressure on the Royal Court. This placed much of the monarch's juridical power in the hands of the elected szlachta deputies, further strengthening the nobility class. In 1581 the Crown Tribunal was joined by a counterpart in Lithuania, the Lithuanian Tribunal.
rewrite: To lessen the immense burden on the Royal Court, King Stefan Batory established the Crown Tribunal in 1578. This transferred significant judicial authority from the monarch to elected szlachta deputies, bolstering the nobility. A corresponding body, the Lithuanian Tribunal, was later added in 1581.

input: Tucson's largest park, Reid Park, is located in midtown and includes Reid Park Zoo and Hi Corbett Field. Speedway Boulevard, a major east-west arterial road in central Tucson, was named the "ugliest street in America" by Life magazine in the early 1970s, quoting Tucson Mayor James Corbett. Despite this, Speedway Boulevard was awarded "Street of the Year" by Arizona Highways in the late 1990s. According to David Leighton, historical writer for the Arizona Daily Star newspaper, Speedway Boulevard derives its name from an old horse racetrack, known as "The Harlem River Speedway," more commonly called "The Speedway," in New York City. The street was called "The Speedway," from 1904 to about 1906 before the word "The" was taken out.
rewrite: Reid Park, Tucson's largest park situated in midtown, contains both Reid Park Zoo and Hi Corbett Field. The name of Speedway Boulevard, a major east-west road in central Tucson, originates from an old New York City horse racetrack known as "The Harlem River Speedway" or simply "The Speedway." As historical writer David Leighton notes in the Arizona Daily Star, the street carried the name "The Speedway" from 1904 until roughly 1906, when the word "The" was removed. Ironically, this road was once labeled the "ugliest street in America" by Life magazine in the early 1970s, citing Mayor James Corbett. Yet, by the late 1990s, Arizona Highways had honored it as "Street of the Year."

input: The main mode of transportation, however, relies on Seattle's streets, which are laid out in a cardinal directions grid pattern, except in the central business district where early city leaders Arthur Denny and Carson Boren insisted on orienting their plats relative to the shoreline rather than to true North. Only two roads, Interstate 5 and State Route 99 (both limited-access highways), run uninterrupted through the city from north to south. State Route 99 runs through downtown Seattle on the Alaskan Way Viaduct, which was built in 1953. However, due to damage sustained during the 2001 Nisqually earthquake the viaduct will be replaced by a tunnel. The 2-mile (3.2 km) Alaskan Way Viaduct replacement tunnel was originally scheduled to be completed in December 2015 at a cost of US$4.25 billion. Unfortunately, due to issues with the worlds largest tunnel boring machine (TBM), which is nicknamed "Bertha" and is 57 feet (17 m) in diameter, the projected date of completion has been pushed back to 2017. Seattle has the 8th worst traffic congestion of all American cities, and is 10th among all North American cities.
rewrite: Seattle's streets form the primary transportation network, arranged in a grid aligned with cardinal directions. This pattern shifts in the central business district, where founders Arthur Denny and Carson Boren originally plotted the streets parallel to the shoreline instead of true north. Only two continuous north-south limited-access highways traverse the city: Interstate 5 and State Route 99. The latter runs through downtown on the Alaskan Way Viaduct, a structure built in 1953. Following damage from the 2001 Nisqually earthquake, this viaduct is being replaced by a tunnel. The 2-mile (3.2 km) Alaskan Way Viaduct replacement tunnel was initially planned for a December 2015 completion, with a budget of US$4.25 billion. However, significant delays involving "Bertha"—a 57-foot (17 m) diameter tunnel boring machine, the world's largest—have postponed the projected finish to 2017. Consequently, Seattle experiences substantial congestion, ranking 8th worst among U.S. cities and 10th in North America.

input: Studio producers Richard D. Zanuck and David Brown offered Spielberg the director's chair for Jaws, a thriller-horror film based on the Peter Benchley novel about an enormous killer shark. Spielberg has often referred to the gruelling shoot as his professional crucible. Despite the film's ultimate, enormous success, it was nearly shut down due to delays and budget over-runs. But Spielberg persevered and finished the film. It was an enormous hit, winning three Academy Awards (for editing, original score and sound) and grossing more than $470 million worldwide at the box office. It also set the domestic record for box office gross, leading to what the press described as "Jawsmania.":248 Jaws made Spielberg a household name and one of America's youngest multi-millionaires, allowing him a great deal of autonomy for his future projects.:250 It was nominated for Best Picture and featured Spielberg's first of three collaborations with actor Richard Dreyfuss.
rewrite: The thriller-horror film *Jaws*, based on Peter Benchley’s novel about a massive killer shark, was offered to Steven Spielberg by studio producers Richard D. Zanuck and David Brown. The production became a gruelling professional crucible for the director, nearly halted by delays and budget overruns. Yet Spielberg persevered. Upon release, the film was an enormous hit, grossing over $470 million worldwide and setting a domestic box office record that sparked “Jawsmania.” It won three Academy Awards for editing, original score, and sound, and was nominated for Best Picture. The success made Spielberg a household name and one of America’s youngest multi-millionaires, granting him significant future autonomy. It also marked his first collaboration with actor Richard Dreyfuss.

input: In sheer numbers, Kerry had fewer endorsements than Howard Dean, who was far ahead in the superdelegate race going into the Iowa caucuses in January 2004, although Kerry led the endorsement race in Iowa, New Hampshire, Arizona, South Carolina, New Mexico and Nevada. Kerry's main perceived weakness was in his neighboring state of New Hampshire and nearly all national polls. Most other states did not have updated polling numbers to give an accurate placing for the Kerry campaign before Iowa. Heading into the primaries, Kerry's campaign was largely seen as in trouble, particularly after he fired campaign manager Jim Jordan. The key factors enabling it to survive were when fellow Massachusetts Senator Ted Kennedy assigned Mary Beth Cahill to be the campaign manager, as well as Kerry's mortgaging his own home to lend the money to his campaign (while his wife was a billionaire, campaign finance rules prohibited using one's personal fortune). He also brought on the "magical" Michael Whouley who would be credited with helping bring home the Iowa victory the same as he did in New Hampshire for Al Gore in 2000 against Bill Bradley.
rewrite:
Entering the 2004 primaries, John Kerry’s campaign was widely perceived as troubled, especially following the dismissal of his campaign manager, Jim Jordan. While Howard Dean held a substantial lead in superdelegate endorsements ahead of the January Iowa caucuses, Kerry himself led in endorsements within several key states, including Iowa, New Hampshire, Arizona, South Carolina, New Mexico, and Nevada. Despite this, his main perceived weakness lay in his neighboring state of New Hampshire and in nearly all national polls. Most other states lacked updated polling data to accurately position Kerry’s campaign before Iowa.

Its survival hinged on critical interventions. Fellow Massachusetts Senator Ted Kennedy assigned Mary Beth Cahill to manage the campaign. Additionally, Kerry mortgaged his own home to lend funds to the effort—a necessary step, as campaign finance rules barred the use of his billionaire wife’s personal fortune. Another key move was enlisting the “magical” Michael Whouley, credited with securing the Iowa victory much as he had delivered New Hampshire for Al Gore against Bill Bradley in 2000.

input: On the other hand, certain financial techniques can reduce the impact of such purchases on the currency. One is sterilisation, in which highly valued assets are sold at the same time that the weaker assets are purchased, which keeps the money supply neutral. Another technique is simply to accept the bad assets as long-term collateral (as opposed to short-term repo swaps) to be held until their market value stabilises. This would imply, as a quid pro quo, adjustments in taxation and expenditure in the economies of the weaker states to improve the perceived value of the assets.
rewrite: Certain financial methods can mitigate the currency effects of these purchases. Sterilisation involves selling high-value assets while acquiring weaker ones, maintaining a neutral money supply. Alternatively, weaker assets may be accepted as long-term collateral—rather than through short-term repos—to be held until their market value recovers. This approach would require, in exchange, fiscal adjustments in the economies of the weaker states, such as changes to taxation and spending, to enhance the assets' perceived worth.

input: The Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi does not release any economic figures specifically for New Delhi but publishes an official economic report on the whole of Delhi annually. According to the Economic Survey of Delhi, the metropolis has a net State Domestic Product (SDP) of Rs. 83,085 crores (for the year 2004–05) and a per capita income of Rs. 53,976($1,200). In the year 2008–09 New Delhi had a Per Capita Income of Rs.1,16,886 ($2,595).It grew by 16.2% to reach Rs.1,35,814 ($3,018) in 2009–10 fiscal. New Delhi's Per Capita GDP (at PPP) was at $6,860 during 2009–10 fiscal, making it one of the richest cities in India. The tertiary sector contributes 78.4% of Delhi's gross SDP followed by secondary and primary sectors with 20.2% and 1.4% contribution respectively.
rewrite: Annually, the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi releases an economic report covering the entire capital, as it does not provide separate statistics for New Delhi alone. The Economic Survey of Delhi indicates the metropolis had a net State Domestic Product of Rs. 83,085 crores in 2004–05, with a per capita income of Rs. 53,976 ($1,200). By 2008–09, this per capita figure rose to Rs. 1,16,886 ($2,595) for New Delhi, then increased 16.2% to Rs. 1,35,814 ($3,018) in 2009–10. With a per capita GDP (PPP) of $6,860 in 2009–10, New Delhi ranks among India's wealthiest cities. Delhi's gross SDP is primarily driven by the tertiary sector at 78.4%, while secondary and primary sectors account for 20.2% and 1.4%, respectively.

input: On October 17, 1987, about 3,000 Armenians demonstrated in Yerevan complaining about the condition of Lake Sevan, the Nairit chemicals plant, and the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant, and air pollution in Yerevan. Police tried to prevent the protest but took no action to stop it once the march was underway. The demonstration was led by Armenian writers such as Silva Kaputikian, Zori Balayan, and Maro Margarian and leaders from the National Survival organization. The march originated at the Opera Plaza after speakers, mainly intellectuals, addressed the crowd.
rewrite: On October 17, 1987, a demonstration of roughly 3,000 Armenians commenced at Yerevan’s Opera Plaza. Following speeches by intellectuals, the march began, led by Armenian writers including Silva Kaputikian, Zori Balayan, and Maro Margarian, along with representatives from the National Survival organization. Protesters voiced concerns over Lake Sevan’s condition, the Nairit chemicals plant, the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant, and Yerevan’s air pollution. Although police attempted initial prevention, they took no action to halt the procession once it was underway.

input: An advantage of the universal motor is that AC supplies may be used on motors which have some characteristics more common in DC motors, specifically high starting torque and very compact design if high running speeds are used. The negative aspect is the maintenance and short life problems caused by the commutator. Such motors are used in devices such as food mixers and power tools which are used only intermittently, and often have high starting-torque demands. Multiple taps on the field coil provide (imprecise) stepped speed control. Household blenders that advertise many speeds frequently combine a field coil with several taps and a diode that can be inserted in series with the motor (causing the motor to run on half-wave rectified AC). Universal motors also lend themselves to electronic speed control and, as such, are an ideal choice for devices like domestic washing machines. The motor can be used to agitate the drum (both forwards and in reverse) by switching the field winding with respect to the armature.
rewrite: Universal motors offer the benefit of operating on AC power while maintaining key DC motor traits, notably high starting torque and a compact form at high speeds. However, the presence of a commutator leads to drawbacks like increased maintenance needs and a reduced lifespan. These motors are well-suited for intermittent-use appliances such as food mixers and power tools, which frequently require strong initial torque. Speed can be adjusted in steps, though not with high precision, through multiple taps on the field coil. For example, many household blenders achieve various speeds by using a tapped field coil along with a diode that can be switched to provide half-wave rectified AC. Furthermore, universal motors adapt readily to electronic speed control, making them a preferred option for applications like domestic washing machines. In such machines, the motor agitates the drum in both directions by reversing the connection between the field winding and the armature.

input: While the largest European-American population in Montana overall is German, pockets of significant Scandinavian ancestry are prevalent in some of the farming-dominated northern and eastern prairie regions, parallel to nearby regions of North Dakota and Minnesota. Farmers of Irish, Scots, and English roots also settled in Montana. The historically mining-oriented communities of western Montana such as Butte have a wider range of European-American ethnicity; Finns, Eastern Europeans and especially Irish settlers left an indelible mark on the area, as well as people originally from British mining regions such as Cornwall, Devon and Wales. The nearby city of Helena, also founded as a mining camp, had a similar mix in addition to a small Chinatown. Many of Montana's historic logging communities originally attracted people of Scottish, Scandinavian, Slavic, English and Scots-Irish descent.[citation needed]
rewrite: Montana's European-American population is predominantly German overall, yet distinct patterns emerge regionally. In the farming-focused northern and eastern prairies, significant Scandinavian ancestry is common, mirroring adjacent areas of North Dakota and Minnesota. Farmers of Irish, Scots, and English descent also settled across the state. The western mining towns, like Butte, present a broader ethnic tapestry. Here, Finns, Eastern Europeans, and notably the Irish made a lasting impact, alongside immigrants from British mining areas such as Cornwall, Devon, and Wales. Helena, another mining-founded city nearby, had a comparable mix and once featured a small Chinatown. Additionally, many historic logging communities drew early settlers of Scottish, Scandinavian, Slavic, English, and Scots-Irish backgrounds.

input: There are three primary shopping centers in the Bronx: The Hub, Gateway Center and Southern Boulevard. The Hub–Third Avenue Business Improvement District (B.I.D.), in The Hub, is the retail heart of the South Bronx, located where four roads converge: East 149th Street, Willis, Melrose and Third Avenues. It is primarily located inside the neighborhood of Melrose but also lines the northern border of Mott Haven. The Hub has been called "the Broadway of the Bronx", being likened to the real Broadway in Manhattan and the northwestern Bronx. It is the site of both maximum traffic and architectural density. In configuration, it resembles a miniature Times Square, a spatial "bow-tie" created by the geometry of the street. The Hub is part of Bronx Community Board 1.
rewrite: The Bronx features three main shopping centers: The Hub, Gateway Center, and Southern Boulevard. Serving as the retail core of the South Bronx, The Hub–Third Avenue Business Improvement District (B.I.D.) lies at the convergence of East 149th Street, Willis, Melrose, and Third Avenues. Primarily situated in Melrose, it also borders Mott Haven to the north. Often termed "the Broadway of the Bronx," it draws comparison to Manhattan's Broadway and the northwestern Bronx. This area experiences the highest traffic and architectural density. Its layout forms a spatial "bow-tie," reminiscent of a compact Times Square, shaped by the street geometry. The Hub falls within the jurisdiction of Bronx Community Board 1.

input: The economy has been growing quickly in recent years. In both 2010 and 2011, the metro area's gross domestic product (GDP) led 27 other metropolitan areas in the country, according to the Conference Board of Canada, recording growth of 6.6 per cent and 5.8 per cent respectively. At $52,000 the city's per capita GDP is the second highest out of all major Canadian cities. Economic forecasts suggest that the city will continue its strong economic growth in the coming years not only in the "oceanic" industries mentioned above, but also in tourism and new home construction as the population continues to grow. In May 2011, the city's unemployment rate fell to 5.6 per cent, the second lowest unemployment rate for a major city in Canada.
rewrite: Recent years have seen rapid economic expansion. According to the Conference Board of Canada, the metro area’s GDP growth led 27 other metropolitan areas in the country in both 2010 and 2011, with rates of 6.6 per cent and 5.8 per cent respectively. The city also boasts the second highest per capita GDP among major Canadian cities, at $52,000. With a declining unemployment rate that reached 5.6 per cent in May 2011—the second lowest for a major Canadian city—the outlook remains strong. Forecasts indicate continued robust growth, driven not only by established "oceanic" sectors but also by expanding tourism and new home construction as the population increases.

input: The last three years of Eisenhower's second term in office were ones of relatively good health. Eventually after leaving the White House, he suffered several additional and ultimately crippling heart attacks. A severe heart attack in August 1965 largely ended his participation in public affairs. In August 1966 he began to show symptoms of cholecystitis, for which he underwent surgery on December 12, 1966, when his gallbladder was removed, containing 16 gallstones. After Eisenhower's death in 1969 (see below), an autopsy unexpectedly revealed an adrenal pheochromocytoma, a benign adrenaline-secreting tumor that may have made the President more vulnerable to heart disease. Eisenhower suffered seven heart attacks in total from 1955 until his death.
rewrite: Following his departure from the White House, Dwight Eisenhower endured a series of debilitating heart attacks, having previously maintained relatively good health during the final three years of his presidency. A severe attack in August 1965 effectively concluded his public life. He experienced seven heart attacks in total from 1955 onward. In 1966, symptoms of cholecystitis led to gallbladder removal surgery, which uncovered sixteen gallstones. An autopsy after his 1969 death unexpectedly identified an adrenal pheochromocytoma, a benign tumor secreting adrenaline that likely increased his susceptibility to cardiac illness.

input: Qutb Shahi architecture of the 16th and early 17th centuries followed classical Persian architecture featuring domes and colossal arches. The oldest surviving Qutb Shahi structure in Hyderabad is the ruins of Golconda fort built in the 16th century. The Charminar, Mecca Masjid, Charkaman and Qutb Shahi tombs are other existing structures of this period. Among these the Charminar has become an icon of the city; located in the centre of old Hyderabad, it is a square structure with sides 20 m (66 ft) long and four grand arches each facing a road. At each corner stands a 56 m (184 ft)-high minaret. Most of the historical bazaars that still exist were constructed on the street north of Charminar towards Golconda fort. The Charminar, Qutb Shahi tombs and Golconda fort are considered to be monuments of national importance in India; in 2010 the Indian government proposed that the sites be listed for UNESCO World Heritage status.:11–18
rewrite: Emerging in the 16th and early 17th centuries, Qutb Shahi architecture drew from classical Persian styles, characterized by its massive arches and domes. The most ancient surviving example in Hyderabad is the 16th-century Golconda fort, now in ruins. This period also produced other enduring structures, including the Charminar, Mecca Masjid, Charkaman, and the Qutb Shahi tombs. Of these, the Charminar has become the iconic symbol of the city. Positioned at the heart of old Hyderabad, this square edifice measures 20 meters per side and features four grand arches, each opening onto a major roadway. Soaring 56 meters high, a minaret crowns each corner. Many historical bazaars still operate along the street stretching north from the Charminar toward Golconda fort. Recognized as monuments of national importance in India, the Charminar, Qutb Shahi tombs, and Golconda fort were proposed by the Indian government in 2010 for UNESCO World Heritage status.

input: In addition to limiting the total average power used by the device, the USB specification limits the inrush current (i.e., that used to charge decoupling and filter capacitors) when the device is first connected. Otherwise, connecting a device could cause problems with the host's internal power. USB devices are also required to automatically enter ultra low-power suspend mode when the USB host is suspended. Nevertheless, many USB host interfaces do not cut off the power supply to USB devices when they are suspended.
rewrite: Beyond restricting the device's overall average power consumption, the USB specification also caps the inrush current drawn upon initial connection to charge capacitors. This prevents potential disruptions to the host's internal power. Devices must automatically switch to an ultra low-power suspend mode if the host is suspended. However, it is common for host interfaces to continue supplying power to USB devices even during suspension.

input: The Western powers, largely unsatisfied with the Treaty of Nanjing, gave grudging support to the Qing government during the Taiping and Nian Rebellions. China's income fell sharply during the wars as vast areas of farmland were destroyed, millions of lives were lost, and countless armies were raised and equipped to fight the rebels. In 1854, Britain tried to re-negotiate the Treaty of Nanjing, inserting clauses allowing British commercial access to Chinese rivers and the creation of a permanent British embassy at Beijing.
rewrite: Grudgingly, the Western powers supported the Qing against the Taiping and Nian Rebellions, despite dissatisfaction with the Treaty of Nanjing. The conflicts devastated China, causing a sharp income drop as farmland was ruined, millions perished, and numerous armies were raised. Seeking further advantage, Britain attempted in 1854 to revise the treaty, demanding commercial access to inland rivers and a permanent embassy in Beijing.

input: The introduction of new or equivalent deities coincided with Rome's most significant aggressive and defensive military forays. In 206 BC the Sibylline books commended the introduction of cult to the aniconic Magna Mater (Great Mother) from Pessinus, installed on the Palatine in 191 BC. The mystery cult to Bacchus followed; it was suppressed as subversive and unruly by decree of the Senate in 186 BC. Greek deities were brought within the sacred pomerium: temples were dedicated to Juventas (Hebe) in 191 BC, Diana (Artemis) in 179 BC, Mars (Ares) in 138 BC), and to Bona Dea, equivalent to Fauna, the female counterpart of the rural Faunus, supplemented by the Greek goddess Damia. Further Greek influences on cult images and types represented the Roman Penates as forms of the Greek Dioscuri. The military-political adventurers of the Later Republic introduced the Phrygian goddess Ma (identified with Roman Bellona, the Egyptian mystery-goddess Isis and Persian Mithras.)
rewrite: Rome's major military campaigns, both offensive and defensive, were accompanied by the adoption of new or analogous deities. Following a recommendation from the Sibylline books in 206 BC, the aniconic Magna Mater (Great Mother) was brought from Pessinus and installed on the Palatine by 191 BC. Subsequently, the Senate suppressed the Bacchic mystery cult in 186 BC, deeming it subversive. Within the sacred pomerium, Greek deities were incorporated: temples were consecrated to Juventas (Hebe) in 191 BC, Diana (Artemis) in 179 BC, and Mars (Ares) in 138 BC. The cult of Bona Dea—equated with Fauna, the female counterpart of Faunus—was supplemented by the Greek goddess Damia. Greek influence also reshaped cult images, portraying the Roman Penates as forms of the Greek Dioscuri. Later, military-political adventurers of the Late Republic introduced deities like the Phrygian goddess Ma, identified with Bellona, as well as the Egyptian Isis and Persian Mithras.

input: These statistics point to the complexities surrounding the lack of health/nutrition literacy and reveal the degree to which they are embedded in the social structure and interconnected with other problems. Among these problems are the lack of information about food choices, a lack of understanding of nutritional information and its application to individual circumstances, limited or difficult access to healthful foods, and a range of cultural influences and socioeconomic constraints such as low levels of education and high levels of poverty that decrease opportunities for healthful eating and living.
rewrite: The lack of health and nutrition literacy is deeply embedded in social structures and linked to numerous issues. These include insufficient information on food choices, a poor understanding of nutritional data for personal use, and limited access to healthy foods. Cultural influences and socioeconomic constraints—like low education levels and high poverty—further reduce opportunities for healthy living. Together, these statistics highlight the profound complexity of the problem.

input: By the end of May, drafts were formally presented. In mid-June, the main Tripartite negotiations started. The discussion was focused on potential guarantees to central and east European countries should a German aggression arise. The USSR proposed to consider that a political turn towards Germany by the Baltic states would constitute an "indirect aggression" towards the Soviet Union. Britain opposed such proposals, because they feared the Soviets' proposed language could justify a Soviet intervention in Finland and the Baltic states, or push those countries to seek closer relations with Germany. The discussion about a definition of "indirect aggression" became one of the sticking points between the parties, and by mid-July, the tripartite political negotiations effectively stalled, while the parties agreed to start negotiations on a military agreement, which the Soviets insisted must be entered into simultaneously with any political agreement.
rewrite: Formal drafts were presented by the end of May, leading to the main Tripartite negotiations commencing in mid-June. These talks centered on potential guarantees for central and east European countries in the event of German aggression. A key point of contention emerged when the USSR proposed that a political shift toward Germany by the Baltic states should be considered an "indirect aggression" against the Soviet Union. Britain opposed this, fearing the proposed language could be used to justify Soviet intervention in Finland and the Baltic states or drive those nations closer to Germany. This definition became a major sticking point. By mid-July, the political negotiations had effectively stalled. The parties, however, agreed to begin talks on a military agreement, which the Soviets insisted must be concluded simultaneously with any political pact.

input: The pagan Slavic populations were Christianized between the 6th and 10th centuries. Orthodox Christianity is predominant in the East and South Slavs, while Roman Catholicism is predominant in West Slavs and the western South Slavs. The religious borders are largely comparable to the East–West Schism which began in the 11th century. The majority of contemporary Slavic populations who profess a religion are Orthodox, followed by Catholic, while a small minority are Protestant. There are minor Slavic Muslim groups. Religious delineations by nationality can be very sharp; usually in the Slavic ethnic groups the vast majority of religious people share the same religion. Some Slavs are atheist or agnostic: only 19% of Czechs professed belief in god/s in the 2005 Eurobarometer survey.
rewrite: Between the 6th and 10th centuries, the pagan Slavic peoples underwent Christianization. Today, the majority of religious Slavs are Orthodox Christians, with Catholics forming the second largest group, followed by a small Protestant minority; there are also minor Muslim communities. Orthodox Christianity predominates among East and South Slavs, whereas Roman Catholicism is more common among West Slavs and western South Slavs. These religious divisions largely correspond to the historical East-West Schism from the 11th century. Typically, within a given Slavic ethnicity, an overwhelming share of religious adherents practice the same faith, making religious borders quite sharp by nationality. However, some Slavs are atheist or agnostic, as illustrated by a 2005 survey where only 19% of Czechs professed belief in a god or gods.

input: Among all cities in the Mediterranean part of the European Union, Limassol has one of the warmest winters, in the period January – February average temperature is 17–18 °C (63–64 °F) during the day and 7–8 °C (45–46 °F) at night, in other coastal locations in Cyprus is generally 16–17 °C (61–63 °F) during the day and 6–8 °C (43–46 °F) at night. During March, Limassol has average temperatures of 19–20 °C (66–68 °F) during the day and 9–11 °C (48–52 °F) at night, in other coastal locations in Cyprus is generally 17–19 °C (63–66 °F) during the day and 8–10 °C (46–50 °F) at night.
rewrite: Limassol experiences some of the mildest winters in the EU Mediterranean. From January to February, its average daytime temperatures reach 17–18 °C (63–64 °F), cooling to 7–8 °C (45–46 °F) at night. This is slightly warmer than other Cypriot coastal areas, which typically see 16–17 °C (61–63 °F) by day and 6–8 °C (43–46 °F) after dark. The warmth continues into March, with Limassol averaging 19–20 °C (66–68 °F) during the day and 9–11 °C (48–52 °F) at night. Elsewhere along the coast, March averages are generally 17–19 °C (63–66 °F) by day and 8–10 °C (46–50 °F) by night.

input: The Ottoman Empire, believed to be about to collapse, was portrayed in the press as the sick man of Europe". The Balkan states, with the partial exception of Bosnia and Albania, were primarily Christian. Starting in 1894 the Ottomans struck at the Armenians on the explicit grounds that they were a non-Muslim people and as such were a potential threat to the Muslim empire within which they resided. The Hamidian Massacres aroused the indignation of the entire Christian world. In the United States the now aging Julia Ward Howe, author of the Battle Hymn of the Republic, leaped into the war of words and joined the Red Cross. Relations of minorities within the Ottoman Empire and the disposition of former Ottoman lands became known as the "Eastern Question," as the Ottomans were on the east of Europe.
rewrite: Portrayed in the press as "the sick man of Europe," the Ottoman Empire was widely believed to be nearing collapse. Within its borders, the Balkan states were primarily Christian, with the partial exceptions of Bosnia and Albania. Beginning in 1894, the Ottomans targeted Armenians explicitly because they were a non-Muslim people, seen as a potential threat to the Muslim empire. These Hamidian Massacres provoked indignation throughout the Christian world. In the United States, the aging Julia Ward Howe—author of the *Battle Hymn of the Republic*—joined the war of words and enlisted with the Red Cross. The issues of minority relations inside the empire and the fate of its former territories were termed the "Eastern Question," a reference to the Ottomans' position east of Europe.

input: On 23 November 1991, in a prepared statement made on his deathbed, Mercury confirmed that he had AIDS. Within 24 hours of the statement, he died of bronchial pneumonia, which was brought on as a complication of AIDS. His funeral service on 27 November in Kensal Green, West London was private, and held in accordance with the Zoroastrian religious faith of his family. "Bohemian Rhapsody" was re-released as a single shortly after Mercury's death, with "These Are the Days of Our Lives" as the double A-side. The music video for "These Are the Days of Our Lives" contains Mercury's final scenes in front of the camera. The single went to number one in the UK, remaining there for five weeks – the only recording to top the Christmas chart twice and the only one to be number one in four different years (1975, 1976, 1991, and 1992). Initial proceeds from the single – approximately £1,000,000 – were donated to the Terrence Higgins Trust.
rewrite: On his deathbed, Freddie Mercury issued a prepared statement on 23 November 1991, confirming he had AIDS. He died within a day from bronchial pneumonia, a complication arising from the disease. In accordance with his family's Zoroastrian faith, a private funeral was held in Kensal Green, West London, on 27 November. Following his death, "Bohemian Rhapsody" was re-released as a single, paired with "These Are the Days of Our Lives" as a double A-side. The video for the latter features Mercury's final filmed performance. This single reached number one in the UK for five weeks, becoming the only recording to top the Christmas chart on two separate occasions and to achieve the top spot across four different years (1975, 1976, 1991, and 1992). Initial proceeds, roughly £1,000,000, were directed to the Terrence Higgins Trust.

input: This article covers numbered east-west streets in Manhattan, New York City. Major streets have their own linked articles; minor streets are discussed here. The streets do not run exactly east–west, because the grid plan is aligned with the Hudson River rather than with the cardinal directions. "West" is approximately 29 degrees north of true west.
rewrite: This article discusses Manhattan's numbered east-west streets, focusing on minor ones, as major streets have separate articles. These streets do not align precisely east–west because the grid follows the Hudson River. Consequently, "west" points about 29 degrees north of true west.

input: Other important Venetian mosaics can be found in the Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta in Torcello from the 12th century, and in the Basilical of Santi Maria e Donato in Murano with a restored apse mosaic from the 12th century and a beautiful mosaic pavement (1140). The apse of the San Cipriano Church in Murano was decorated with an impressive golden mosaic from the early 13th century showing Christ enthroned with Mary, St John and the two patron saints, Cipriano and Cipriana. When the church was demolished in the 19th century, the mosaic was bought by Frederick William IV of Prussia. It was reassembled in the Friedenskirche of Potsdam in the 1840s.
rewrite: Significant Venetian mosaics also adorn the Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta on Torcello, dating to the 12th century. Another 12th-century example is the restored apse mosaic in Murano's Basilica of Santi Maria e Donato, which additionally features a beautiful mosaic pavement from 1140. The early 13th-century apse of Murano's San Cipriano Church once displayed a golden mosaic of Christ enthroned with Mary, St. John, and the patron saints Cipriano and Cipriana. Following the church's demolition in the 1800s, King Frederick William IV of Prussia purchased the work. It was subsequently reconstructed during the 1840s within Potsdam's Friedenskirche.

input: According to the Quran, God communicated with man and made his will known through signs and revelations. Prophets, or 'Messengers of God', received revelations and delivered them to humanity. The message has been identical and for all humankind. "Nothing is said to you that was not said to the messengers before you, that your lord has at his Command forgiveness as well as a most Grievous Penalty." The revelation does not come directly from God to the prophets. Angels acting as God's messengers deliver the divine revelation to them. This comes out in Quran 42:51, in which it is stated: "It is not for any mortal that God should speak to them, except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger to reveal by his permission whatsoever He will."
rewrite: The Quran teaches that God conveys His will to humanity through signs and revelations. These divine communications are delivered not directly, but via angels who serve as God's messengers to the prophets. These chosen individuals, known as 'Messengers of God', then relay the identical message to all of humankind. As stated in Quran 42:51, "It is not for any mortal that God should speak to them, except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger to reveal by his permission whatsoever He will." This universal message remains consistent, affirming that "Nothing is said to you that was not said to the messengers before you, that your lord has at his Command forgiveness as well as a most Grievous Penalty."

input: The first visible institution to run into trouble in the United States was the Southern California–based IndyMac, a spin-off of Countrywide Financial. Before its failure, IndyMac Bank was the largest savings and loan association in the Los Angeles market and the seventh largest mortgage originator in the United States. The failure of IndyMac Bank on July 11, 2008, was the fourth largest bank failure in United States history up until the crisis precipitated even larger failures, and the second largest failure of a regulated thrift. IndyMac Bank's parent corporation was IndyMac Bancorp until the FDIC seized IndyMac Bank. IndyMac Bancorp filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in July 2008.
rewrite: IndyMac, a Southern California–based spin-off of Countrywide Financial, was the first visible U.S. institution to encounter trouble. Before its collapse, it served as the largest savings and loan association in the Los Angeles market and the nation's seventh largest mortgage originator. Its failure on July 11, 2008, ranked as the fourth largest bank failure in U.S. history at the time, and the second largest for a regulated thrift. The FDIC seized IndyMac Bank, whose parent was IndyMac Bancorp. That parent corporation subsequently filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in July 2008.

input: In 1896, Patrick and Gilbert observed that during a prolonged period of sleep deprivation, sleepiness increases and decreases with a period of approximately 24 hours. In 1918, J.S. Szymanski showed that animals are capable of maintaining 24-hour activity patterns in the absence of external cues such as light and changes in temperature. In the early 20th century, circadian rhythms were noticed in the rhythmic feeding times of bees. Extensive experiments were done by Auguste Forel, Ingeborg Beling, and Oskar Wahl to see whether this rhythm was due to an endogenous clock.[citation needed] Ron Konopka and Seymour Benzer isolated the first clock mutant in Drosophila in the early 1970s and mapped the "period" gene, the first discovered genetic determinant of behavioral rhythmicity. Joseph Takahashi discovered the first mammalian circadian clock mutation (clockΔ19) using mice in 1994. However, recent studies show that deletion of clock does not lead to a behavioral phenotype (the animals still have normal circadian rhythms), which questions its importance in rhythm generation.
rewrite: In the early 20th century, researchers like Auguste Forel, Ingeborg Beling, and Oskar Wahl conducted extensive experiments on bees, noting circadian rhythms in their rhythmic feeding times and investigating if an endogenous clock was responsible. Earlier, in 1896, Patrick and Gilbert had documented that sleepiness fluctuates on a roughly 24-hour cycle during sleep deprivation. J.S. Szymanski further demonstrated in 1918 that animals could sustain 24-hour activity patterns without external cues like light or temperature changes. A key genetic breakthrough came in the early 1970s when Ron Konopka and Seymour Benzer isolated the first clock mutant in Drosophila, mapping the "period" gene as the initial genetic determinant of behavioral rhythmicity. Later, in 1994, Joseph Takahashi identified the first mammalian circadian clock mutation (clockΔ19) in mice. However, recent findings indicate that deleting this clock gene does not produce a behavioral phenotype, as animals maintain normal circadian rhythms, casting doubt on its critical role in rhythm generation.

input: In September 1982, Prime minister Margaret Thatcher travelled to Beijing to negotiate with the Chinese government on the future of Britain's last major and most populous overseas territory, Hong Kong. Under the terms of the 1842 Treaty of Nanking, Hong Kong Island itself had been ceded to Britain in perpetuity, but the vast majority of the colony was constituted by the New Territories, which had been acquired under a 99-year lease in 1898, due to expire in 1997. Thatcher, seeing parallels with the Falkland Islands, initially wished to hold Hong Kong and proposed British administration with Chinese sovereignty, though this was rejected by China. A deal was reached in 1984—under the terms of the Sino-British Joint Declaration, Hong Kong would become a special administrative region of the People's Republic of China, maintaining its way of life for at least 50 years. The handover ceremony in 1997 marked for many, including Charles, Prince of Wales, who was in attendance, "the end of Empire".
rewrite: In September 1982, British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher visited Beijing for negotiations concerning Hong Kong, Britain's final major and populous overseas territory. The future of the colony was complex: while Hong Kong Island had been permanently ceded to Britain under the 1842 Treaty of Nanking, the larger New Territories were held under a 99-year lease from 1898, set to expire in 1997. Initially, Thatcher, drawing a parallel to the Falkland Islands, hoped to retain British administration under Chinese sovereignty, a proposal China refused. Ultimately, a 1984 agreement, the Sino-British Joint Declaration, established that Hong Kong would revert to China in 1997 as a special administrative region, preserving its existing way of life for a minimum of fifty years. The 1997 handover ceremony, attended by figures such as Charles, Prince of Wales, was widely seen as symbolizing "the end of Empire."

input: The relationship between genes can be measured by comparing the sequence alignment of their DNA.:7.6 The degree of sequence similarity between homologous genes is called conserved sequence. Most changes to a gene's sequence do not affect its function and so genes accumulate mutations over time by neutral molecular evolution. Additionally, any selection on a gene will cause its sequence to diverge at a different rate. Genes under stabilizing selection are constrained and so change more slowly whereas genes under directional selection change sequence more rapidly. The sequence differences between genes can be used for phylogenetic analyses to study how those genes have evolved and how the organisms they come from are related.
rewrite: Sequence similarity between homologous genes, known as conserved sequence, serves as a measure of their relationship. This is assessed through DNA sequence alignment. Over time, genes typically accumulate mutations via neutral molecular evolution, as most sequence alterations do not impact function. However, selection pressures alter divergence rates. Genes under stabilizing selection are constrained and evolve more slowly, while those under directional selection change more rapidly. These sequence differences provide the basis for phylogenetic analyses, enabling the study of gene evolution and the relationships among the originating organisms.

input: The CBS Records Group was led very successfully by Clive Davis until his dismissal in 1972, after it was discovered that Davis has used CBS funds to finance his personal life, including an expensive bar mitzvah party for his son. He was replaced first by former head Goddard Lieberson, then in 1975 by the colourful and controversial lawyer Walter Yetnikoff, who led the company until 1990.
rewrite: Clive Davis led the CBS Records Group with great success until 1972, when he was dismissed for misusing company funds to pay for personal expenses, such as his son's lavish bar mitzvah. Goddard Lieberson, the former head, initially replaced him. Then, in 1975, the colorful and controversial lawyer Walter Yetnikoff took over, leading the company until 1990.

input: According to filings to the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) by Thunder Bay Electronics (owner of CBC's Thunder Bay affiliate CKPR-DT) and Bell Media (owner of CBC affiliates CFTK-TV in Terrace and CJDC-TV in Dawson Creek),[citation needed] the CBC informed them that it will not extend its association with any of its private affiliates beyond August 31, 2011. Incidentally, that was also the date for analogue to digital transition in Canada. Given recent practice and the CBC's decision not to convert any retransmitters to digital, even in markets with populations in the hundreds in thousands, it is not expected that the CBC will open new transmitters to replace its affiliates, and indeed may pare back its existing transmitter network. However, in March 2011, CKPR announced that it had come to a programming agreement with the CBC, in which the station will continue to provide CBC programming in Thunder Bay for a period of five years. On March 16, 2012, Astral Media announced the sale of its assets to Bell Media, owners of CTV and CTV Two, for $3.38 billion with CFTK and CJDC included in the acquisition. Whether the stations will remain CBC affiliates or become owned-and-operated stations of CTV or CTV Two following the completion of the merger is undetermined.
rewrite:
Based on documents submitted to the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC), the CBC notified certain private affiliates it would not continue their association past August 31, 2011. This date coincided with Canada's analogue-to-digital transition. The filings came from Thunder Bay Electronics, owner of CBC affiliate CKPR-DT, and Bell Media, owner of affiliates CFTK-TV in Terrace and CJDC-TV in Dawson Creek. Given the CBC's recent pattern of not converting retransmitters to digital—even in sizable markets—industry observers do not anticipate the CBC will launch new transmitters to replace these affiliates and suggest it may even reduce its existing transmitter network.

However, in March 2011, an exception emerged when CKPR announced a new five-year programming agreement to continue carrying CBC content in Thunder Bay. Subsequently, on March 16, 2012, Astral Media agreed to sell its assets, including CFTK and CJDC, to Bell Media for $3.38 billion. Bell Media also owns the CTV and CTV Two networks. Following this acquisition, it remains undetermined whether these stations will stay as CBC affiliates or transition into owned-and-operated stations of CTV or CTV Two.

input: Most samurai were bound by a code of honor and were expected to set an example for those below them. A notable part of their code is seppuku (切腹, seppuku?) or hara kiri, which allowed a disgraced samurai to regain his honor by passing into death, where samurai were still beholden to social rules. Whilst there are many romanticized characterizations of samurai behavior such as the writing of Bushido (武士道, Bushidō?) in 1905, studies of Kobudo and traditional Budō indicate that the samurai were as practical on the battlefield as were any other warrior.
rewrite: Guided by a strict code of honor, samurai were expected to model proper conduct. Their practices included seppuku, a ritual suicide permitting a disgraced warrior to regain honor through death. Although later romanticized, such as in the 1905 text *Bushidō*, studies of Kobudo and traditional Budō reveal that samurai were ultimately pragmatic fighters, as practical in warfare as any other warrior of their time.

input: In January 1920, Tito and his wife made a long and difficult journey home to Yugoslavia where he arrived in September. Upon his return, Broz joined the Communist Party of Yugoslavia. The CPY's influence on the political life of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia was growing rapidly. In the 1920 elections the Communists won 59 seats in the parliament and became the third strongest party. Winning numerous local elections, they gained a stronghold in the second largest city of Zagreb, electing Svetozar Delić for mayor. After the assassination of Milorad Drašković, the Yugoslav Minister of the Interior, by a young communist on 2 August 1921, the CPY was declared illegal under the Yugoslav State Security Act of 1921. During 1920 and 1921 all Communist-won mandates were nullified. Broz continued his work underground despite pressure on Communists from the government. As 1921 began he moved to Veliko Trojstvo near Bjelovar and found work as a machinist. In 1925, Broz moved to Kraljevica where he started working at a shipyard. He was elected as a union leader and a year later he led a shipyard strike. He was fired and moved to Belgrade, where he worked in a train coach factory in Smederevska Palanka. He was elected as Workers' Commissary but was fired as soon as his CPY membership was revealed. Broz then moved to Zagreb, where he was appointed secretary of Metal Workers' Union of Croatia. In 1928, he became the Zagreb Branch Secretary of the CPY. In the same year he was arrested, tried in court for his illegal communist activities, and sent to jail. During his five years at Lepoglava prison he met Moša Pijade, who became his ideological mentor. After his release, he lived incognito and assumed numerous noms de guerre, among them "Walter" and "Tito".
rewrite:
Following a lengthy and arduous journey that began in January 1920, Tito and his wife finally reached their home in Yugoslavia that September. He promptly joined the Communist Party of Yugoslavia (CPY), an organization whose political influence was expanding quickly within the kingdom. This growth was demonstrated in the 1920 elections, when the Communists secured 59 parliamentary seats to become the third-strongest party. They also achieved significant local success, establishing a stronghold in Zagreb, the nation’s second-largest city, where Svetozar Delić was elected mayor. However, this period of legal political activity was abruptly ended. After the assassination of Interior Minister Milorad Drašković by a young communist in August 1921, the government invoked the State Security Act to outlaw the CPY. All communist electoral mandates from 1920 and 1921 were subsequently nullified.

Forced underground, Broz continued his communist work under government pressure. Early in 1921, he relocated to Veliko Trojstvo near Bjelovar, finding employment as a machinist. By 1925, he had moved to Kraljevica to work at a shipyard, where he was elected a union leader. The following year, he led a strike that resulted in his dismissal. After being fired, Broz went to Belgrade, working at a train coach factory in Smederevska Palanka. His election as Workers' Commissary was short-lived; he was dismissed once his CPY membership was discovered. His next move was to Zagreb, where he was appointed secretary of the Metal Workers' Union of Croatia. In 1928, he rose to become the Zagreb Branch Secretary of the now-illegal CPY.

That same year, his clandestine activities led to his arrest, trial, and imprisonment. During his five-year sentence at Lepoglava prison, he met Moša Pijade, who became his ideological mentor. Upon his release, Broz lived incognito, adopting several aliases including "Walter" and the name he would make famous, "Tito."

input: With financial support from Sanders and Hubbard, Bell hired Thomas Watson as his assistant,[N 15] and the two of them experimented with acoustic telegraphy. On June 2, 1875, Watson accidentally plucked one of the reeds and Bell, at the receiving end of the wire, heard the overtones of the reed; overtones that would be necessary for transmitting speech. That demonstrated to Bell that only one reed or armature was necessary, not multiple reeds. This led to the "gallows" sound-powered telephone, which could transmit indistinct, voice-like sounds, but not clear speech.
rewrite: With the backing of Sanders and Hubbard, Bell employed Thomas Watson as his assistant to explore acoustic telegraphy. During experiments on June 2, 1875, Watson unintentionally plucked a reed. Bell, listening at the wire's end, heard its overtones—essential for speech transmission. This proved that a single reed, rather than multiple ones, was sufficient. The insight resulted in the "gallows" telephone, a sound-powered device capable of sending vague, voice-like noises, yet not intelligible speech.

input: On August 18, 1970, the NAACP filed suit against Michigan state officials, including Governor William Milliken, charging de facto public school segregation. The NAACP argued that although schools were not legally segregated, the city of Detroit and its surrounding counties had enacted policies to maintain racial segregation in public schools. The NAACP also suggested a direct relationship between unfair housing practices and educational segregation, which followed segregated neighborhoods. The District Court held all levels of government accountable for the segregation in its ruling. The Sixth Circuit Court affirmed some of the decision, holding that it was the state's responsibility to integrate across the segregated metropolitan area. The U.S. Supreme Court took up the case February 27, 1974. The subsequent Milliken v. Bradley decision had wide national influence. In a narrow decision, the Court found that schools were a subject of local control and that suburbs could not be forced to solve problems in the city's school district.
rewrite: On August 18, 1970, the NAACP initiated a lawsuit against Michigan state officials, such as Governor William Milliken, alleging de facto segregation within public schools. Their argument centered on the claim that policies enacted by Detroit and its surrounding counties maintained racial separation in schools, despite an absence of legal segregation mandates. The NAACP further contended that this educational segregation was directly linked to discriminatory housing practices, which created segregated residential patterns. A District Court ruling placed responsibility for the segregation on all levels of government. While the Sixth Circuit Court later affirmed portions of this judgment, stating the state had an obligation to pursue integration across the metropolitan area, the ultimate outcome was decided by the U.S. Supreme Court. Heard beginning February 27, 1974, the case resulted in the influential Milliken v. Bradley decision. In a narrow ruling, the Court determined that schools were primarily under local control and that suburban districts could not be compelled to address segregation issues originating in the city's school system.

input: During his brief majority reign, Murad IV (1612–1640) reasserted central authority and recaptured Iraq (1639) from the Safavids. The resulting Treaty of Zuhab of that same year decisively parted the Caucasus and adjacent regions between the two neighbouring empires as it had already been defined in the 1555 Peace of Amasya. The Sultanate of women (1648–1656) was a period in which the mothers of young sultans exercised power on behalf of their sons. The most prominent women of this period were Kösem Sultan and her daughter-in-law Turhan Hatice, whose political rivalry culminated in Kösem's murder in 1651. During the Köprülü Era (1656–1703), effective control of the Empire was exercised by a sequence of Grand Viziers from the Köprülü family. The Köprülü Vizierate saw renewed military success with authority restored in Transylvania, the conquest of Crete completed in 1669, and expansion into Polish southern Ukraine, with the strongholds of Khotyn and Kamianets-Podilskyi and the territory of Podolia ceding to Ottoman control in 1676.
rewrite: Murad IV (1612–1640), during his short reign as an adult, restored central power and retook Iraq from the Safavids in 1639. The subsequent Treaty of Zuhab that year formally divided the Caucasus and nearby areas between the neighboring empires, reaffirming boundaries established by the 1555 Peace of Amasya. A later phase, the Sultanate of women (1648–1656), saw mothers governing for their young sons. Its key figures, Kösem Sultan and her daughter-in-law Turhan Hatice, became political rivals, a conflict ending in Kösem’s assassination in 1651. Following this, the Köprülü Era (1656–1703) began, with a series of Grand Viziers from the Köprülü family holding effective power. This period brought military revival: authority was reasserted in Transylvania, Crete was fully conquered by 1669, and expansion into Polish southern Ukraine occurred. By 1676, the fortresses of Khotyn and Kamianets-Podilskyi, along with the Podolia region, had come under Ottoman control.

input: The two nations planned a joint mission to dock the last US Apollo craft with a Soyuz, known as the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP). To prepare, the US designed a docking module for the Apollo that was compatible with the Soviet docking system, which allowed any of their craft to dock with any other (e.g. Soyuz/Soyuz as well as Soyuz/Salyut). The module was also necessary as an airlock to allow the men to visit each other's craft, which had incompatible cabin atmospheres. The USSR used the Soyuz 16 mission in December 1974 to prepare for ASTP.
rewrite: In preparation for the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP), a joint mission to dock the final US Apollo with a Soviet Soyuz, the US developed a special docking module. This module was compatible with the Soviet docking system, enabling connections between various craft like Soyuz and Salyut. It also served as a crucial airlock, allowing crew transfers despite the incompatible cabin atmospheres of the two spacecraft. The USSR conducted its own preparatory work through the Soyuz 16 mission in December 1974.

input: In Canada, the largest Presbyterian denomination – and indeed the largest Protestant denomination – was the Presbyterian Church in Canada, formed in 1875 with the merger of four regional groups. In 1925, the United Church of Canada was formed by the majority of Presbyterians combining with the Methodist Church, Canada, and the Congregational Union of Canada. A sizable minority of Canadian Presbyterians, primarily in southern Ontario but also throughout the entire nation, withdrew, and reconstituted themselves as a non-concurring continuing Presbyterian body. They regained use of the original name in 1939.
rewrite: Canada's largest Protestant and Presbyterian denomination was originally the Presbyterian Church in Canada, established in 1875 from four regional groups. In 1925, most Presbyterians joined Methodists and Congregationalists to form the United Church of Canada. However, a significant minority across the country, especially in southern Ontario, withdrew. This group reestablished itself as a continuing Presbyterian church and reclaimed the original "Presbyterian Church in Canada" name in 1939.

input: Mexico City remains the only Latin American city to host the Olympic Games, having held the Summer Olympics in 1968, winning bids against Buenos Aires, Lyon and Detroit. (This too will change thanks to Rio, 2016 Summer Games host). The city hosted the 1955 and 1975 Pan American Games, the last after Santiago and São Paulo withdrew. The ICF Flatwater Racing World Championships were hosted here in 1974 and 1994. Lucha libre is a Mexican style of wrestling, and is one of the more popular sports throughout the country. The main venues in the city are Arena México and Arena Coliseo.
rewrite: Mexico City, which hosted the Summer Olympics in 1968 after outbidding Buenos Aires, Lyon, and Detroit, is still the sole Latin American city to have held the Olympic Games—a status set to change with Rio's 2016 hosting. It also staged the Pan American Games in 1955 and 1975, the latter after Santiago and São Paulo withdrew. The city welcomed the ICF Flatwater Racing World Championships in 1974 and 1994. Among popular local sports is lucha libre, a distinctive Mexican wrestling style, with Arena México and Arena Coliseo serving as its primary venues.

input: The Vietnam War is often regarded as a low point for the U.S. Army due to the use of drafted personnel, the unpopularity of the war with the American public, and frustrating restrictions placed on the military by American political leaders. While American forces had been stationed in the Republic of Vietnam since 1959, in intelligence & advising/training roles, they did not deploy in large numbers until 1965, after the Gulf of Tonkin Incident. American forces effectively established and maintained control of the "traditional" battlefield, however they struggled to counter the guerrilla hit and run tactics of the communist Viet Cong and the North Vietnamese Army. On a tactical level, American soldiers (and the U.S. military as a whole) did not lose a sizable battle.
rewrite: The U.S. Army's experience in the Vietnam War is frequently seen as a period of profound difficulty. This perception stems from several factors: reliance on a drafted force, deep domestic opposition to the conflict, and constraining rules of engagement imposed by political leadership. Although American personnel had been present in South Vietnam since 1959 in advisory capacities, a major troop deployment did not commence until 1965, following the Gulf of Tonkin Incident. Tactically, American forces consistently dominated conventional engagements, never losing a major battle. Yet, they faced immense challenges in combating the elusive guerrilla strategies employed by the Viet Cong and the North Vietnamese Army, which operated beyond the traditional battlefield.

input: A second New Haven gastronomical claim to fame is Louis' Lunch, which is located in a small brick building on Crown Street and has been serving fast food since 1895. Though fiercely debated, the restaurant's founder Louis Lassen is credited by the Library of Congress with inventing the hamburger and steak sandwich. Louis' Lunch broils hamburgers, steak sandwiches and hot dogs vertically in original antique 1898 cast iron stoves using gridirons, patented by local resident Luigi Pieragostini in 1939, that hold the meat in place while it cooks.
rewrite: Louis' Lunch, a small brick building on Crown Street, is another New Haven culinary landmark. Operating since 1895, it is famously credited—though debated—by the Library of Congress with inventing the hamburger and steak sandwich. The restaurant uses original 1898 cast iron stoves, broiling burgers, steak sandwiches, and hot dogs vertically. For this, they employ patented 1939 gridirons by local Luigi Pieragostini, which secure the meat during cooking.

input: Some examples of social and religious transition ceremonies that can be found in the U.S., as well as in other cultures around the world, are Confirmation, Bar and Bat Mitzvahs, Quinceañeras, sweet sixteens, cotillions, and débutante balls. In other countries, initiation ceremonies play an important role, marking the transition into adulthood or the entrance into adolescence. This transition may be accompanied by obvious physical changes, which can vary from a change in clothing to tattoos and scarification. Furthermore, transitions into adulthood may also vary by gender, and specific rituals may be more common for males or for females. This illuminates the extent to which adolescence is, at least in part, a social construction; it takes shape differently depending on the cultural context, and may be enforced more by cultural practices or transitions than by universal chemical or biological physical changes.
rewrite: Across various cultures, including the United States, numerous ceremonies mark social and religious transitions, such as Confirmation, Bar and Bat Mitzvahs, Quinceañeras, sweet sixteens, cotillions, and débutante balls. In many societies, initiation rites hold significant importance, signifying entry into adolescence or adulthood. These transitions are sometimes highlighted by visible physical alterations, ranging from new attire to tattoos or scarification. Additionally, the passage to adulthood often differs by gender, with specific rituals being more prevalent for males or for females. Such practices underscore that adolescence is, to a considerable degree, a social construct. Its form and recognition are shaped by cultural context, often dictated more by societal traditions and rites than by uniform biological or chemical changes.

input: At Maecenas' insistence (according to the tradition) Virgil spent the ensuing years (perhaps 37–29 BC) on the long didactic hexameter poem called the Georgics (from Greek, "On Working the Earth") which he dedicated to Maecenas. The ostensible theme of the Georgics is instruction in the methods of running a farm. In handling this theme, Virgil follows in the didactic ("how to") tradition of the Greek poet Hesiod's Works and Days and several works of the later Hellenistic poets. The four books of the Georgics focus respectively on raising crops and trees (1 and 2), livestock and horses (3), and beekeeping and the qualities of bees (4). Well-known passages include the beloved Laus Italiae of Book 2, the prologue description of the temple in Book 3, and the description of the plague at the end of Book 3. Book 4 concludes with a long mythological narrative, in the form of an epyllion which describes vividly the discovery of beekeeping by Aristaeus and the story of Orpheus' journey to the underworld. Ancient scholars, such as Servius, conjectured that the Aristaeus episode replaced, at the emperor's request, a long section in praise of Virgil's friend, the poet Gallus, who was disgraced by Augustus, and who committed suicide in 26 BC.
rewrite: At the urging of Maecenas, Virgil is said to have devoted the years approximately 37–29 BC to composing the Georgics, a lengthy didactic poem in hexameter whose title derives from the Greek for "On Working the Earth." He dedicated this work to Maecenas. Its apparent purpose is to offer instruction in agricultural management. In taking up this subject, Virgil places himself within a tradition established by Hesiod’s Works and Days and furthered by later Hellenistic poets. The poem is divided into four books: the first two address crop and tree cultivation, the third deals with livestock and horses, and the fourth focuses on beekeeping and the nature of bees. Among its celebrated sections are the Laus Italiae in Book 2, the prologue’s temple description in Book 3, and the account of a plague concluding Book 3. The final book ends with an extended mythological epyllion, vividly relating Aristaeus’s discovery of beekeeping and Orpheus’s descent into the underworld. According to ancient commentators like Servius, this Aristaeus narrative may have been inserted at the emperor’s behest to replace a lengthy tribute to Virgil’s friend Gallus, who fell from Augustus’s favor and died by suicide in 26 BC.

input: At times when a death sentence is affirmed on direct review, it is considered final. Yet, supplemental methods to attack the judgment, though less familiar than a typical appeal, do remain. These supplemental remedies are considered collateral review, that is, an avenue for upsetting judgments that have become otherwise final. Where the prisoner received his death sentence in a state-level trial, as is usually the case, the first step in collateral review is state collateral review. (If the case is a federal death penalty case, it proceeds immediately from direct review to federal habeas corpus.) Although all states have some type of collateral review, the process varies widely from state to state. Generally, the purpose of these collateral proceedings is to permit the prisoner to challenge his sentence on grounds that could not have been raised reasonably at trial or on direct review. Most often these are claims, such as ineffective assistance of counsel, which requires the court to consider new evidence outside the original trial record, something courts may not do in an ordinary appeal. State collateral review, though an important step in that it helps define the scope of subsequent review through federal habeas corpus, is rarely successful in and of itself. Only around 6 percent of death sentences are overturned on state collateral review. In 2010, the death sentences of 53 inmates were overturned as a result of legal appeals or high court reversals.
rewrite: When a death sentence is upheld on direct review, it becomes final. However, less familiar supplemental avenues to challenge the judgment still exist, known collectively as collateral review. This process allows for the overturning of otherwise final judgments. In the typical scenario where a prisoner receives a death sentence in state court, the initial step is state collateral review. (Federal death penalty cases move directly from direct review to federal habeas corpus.) While every state provides some form of collateral review, the specific procedures differ significantly. The general aim of these proceedings is to enable challenges based on claims that could not reasonably have been raised at trial or on direct appeal. Such claims often involve issues like ineffective assistance of counsel, which necessitate examining evidence outside the original trial record—an action not permitted in an ordinary appeal. Although state collateral review is a crucial stage that helps shape the scope of any subsequent federal habeas corpus review, it is seldom successful on its own. Only about 6 percent of death sentences are overturned during this state-level process. For instance, in 2010, the death sentences of 53 inmates were reversed through legal appeals or high court decisions.

input: Among the vast varieties of microorganisms, relatively few cause disease in otherwise healthy individuals. Infectious disease results from the interplay between those few pathogens and the defenses of the hosts they infect. The appearance and severity of disease resulting from any pathogen, depends upon the ability of that pathogen to damage the host as well as the ability of the host to resist the pathogen. However a host's immune system can also cause damage to the host itself in an attempt to control the infection. Clinicians therefore classify infectious microorganisms or microbes according to the status of host defenses - either as primary pathogens or as opportunistic pathogens:
rewrite: While only a small fraction of microorganisms cause illness in healthy people, infectious disease arises from the interaction between these pathogens and a host's defenses. The severity of any infection hinges on both the microbe's capacity to inflict harm and the host's ability to mount resistance. Notably, the immune response itself can sometimes damage the host in the process of fighting the invader. Consequently, medical professionals categorize microbes based on host immunity: as primary pathogens, which can sicken anyone, or opportunistic pathogens, which typically exploit weakened defenses.

input: The Somali Telecommunication Association (STA), a watchdog organization that oversees the policy development and regulatory framework of Somalia's ICT sector, reported in 2006 that there were over half a million users of internet services within the territory. There were also 22 established ISPs and 234 cyber cafes, with an annual growth rate of 15.6%.
rewrite: In 2006, the Somali Telecommunication Association (STA) reported over half a million internet users. This watchdog for Somalia's ICT policy and regulation also noted 22 ISPs and 234 cyber cafes, with an annual growth rate of 15.6%.

input: The major settlements in the ceremonial county are concentrated on the Fylde coast (the Blackpool Urban Area), and a belt of towns running west-east along the M65: Preston, Blackburn, Accrington, Burnley, Nelson and Colne. South of Preston are the towns of Leyland and Chorley; the three formed part of the Central Lancashire New Town designated in 1970. The north of the county is predominantly rural and sparsely populated, except for the towns of Lancaster and Morecambe which form a large conurbation of almost 100,000 people. Lancashire is home to a significant Asian population, numbering over 70,000 and 6% of the county's population, and concentrated largely in the former cotton mill towns in the south east.
rewrite: Within the ceremonial county, major settlements cluster along the Fylde coast, notably the Blackpool Urban Area, and in a west-east belt following the M65 corridor, encompassing Preston, Blackburn, Accrington, Burnley, Nelson, and Colne. South of Preston lie Leyland and Chorley; these three were included in the 1970 Central Lancashire New Town designation. The northern part is largely rural and sparsely populated, with the exception of the Lancaster-Morecambe conurbation, home to nearly 100,000 residents. Lancashire also has a significant Asian community, comprising over 70,000 people or 6% of the population, primarily concentrated in the former cotton mill towns of the south-east.

input: Romulus was credited with several religious institutions. He founded the Consualia festival, inviting the neighbouring Sabines to participate; the ensuing rape of the Sabine women by Romulus's men further embedded both violence and cultural assimilation in Rome's myth of origins. As a successful general, Romulus is also supposed to have founded Rome's first temple to Jupiter Feretrius and offered the spolia opima, the prime spoils taken in war, in the celebration of the first Roman triumph. Spared a mortal's death, Romulus was mysteriously spirited away and deified.
rewrite: Romulus established key religious foundations, including the Consualia festival. His invitation to the Sabines led to their women's abduction, weaving violence and assimilation into Rome's origin myth. A victorious general, he also founded the first temple to Jupiter Feretrius. There, he dedicated the spolia opima—the finest war spoils—during Rome's inaugural triumph. Ultimately spared a mortal end, Romulus vanished mysteriously and was later worshipped as a god.

input: According to the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Uniform Crime Reports, in 2010 the Raleigh Police Department and other agencies in the city reported 1,740 incidents of violent crime and 12,995 incidents of property crime – far below both the national average and the North Carolina average. Of the violent crimes reported, 14 were murders, 99 were forcible rapes and 643 were robberies. Aggravated assault accounted for 984 of the total violent crimes. Property crimes included burglaries which accounted for 3,021, larcenies for 9,104 and arson for 63 of the total number of incidents. Motor vehicle theft accounted for 870 incidents out of the total.
rewrite: In 2010, Raleigh police and city agencies reported crime statistics well below both national and North Carolina averages. The data, from the FBI's Uniform Crime Reports, detailed 1,740 violent crimes and 12,995 property crimes. Among violent incidents, there were 14 murders, 99 forcible rapes, and 643 robberies. Aggravated assaults made up the majority at 984 cases. For property crime, the 12,995 incidents consisted of 3,021 burglaries, 9,104 larcenies, 870 motor vehicle thefts, and 63 arson cases.

input: The earliest Greek philosophers, known as the pre-Socratics, provided competing answers to the question found in the myths of their neighbors: "How did the ordered cosmos in which we live come to be?" The pre-Socratic philosopher Thales (640-546 BC), dubbed the "father of science", was the first to postulate non-supernatural explanations for natural phenomena, for example, that land floats on water and that earthquakes are caused by the agitation of the water upon which the land floats, rather than the god Poseidon. Thales' student Pythagoras of Samos founded the Pythagorean school, which investigated mathematics for its own sake, and was the first to postulate that the Earth is spherical in shape. Leucippus (5th century BC) introduced atomism, the theory that all matter is made of indivisible, imperishable units called atoms. This was greatly expanded by his pupil Democritus.
rewrite: Seeking to explain how the ordered cosmos arose, the earliest Greek philosophers, or pre-Socratics, offered rival answers to a question present in neighboring myths. Thales (640-546 BC), called the "father of science," pioneered non-supernatural explanations. He proposed, for instance, that land floats on water and earthquakes result from this water's movement, not the god Poseidon. His student, Pythagoras of Samos, founded a school dedicated to mathematics and first suggested the Earth is spherical. Later, in the 5th century BC, Leucippus introduced atomism—the theory that all matter consists of indivisible, imperishable atoms. His pupil Democritus would later greatly expand this idea.
