input: The final chapter reviews points from earlier chapters, and Darwin concludes by hoping that his theory might produce revolutionary changes in many fields of natural history. Although he avoids the controversial topic of human origins in the rest of the book so as not to prejudice readers against his theory, here he ventures a cautious hint that psychology would be put on a new foundation and that "Light will be thrown on the origin of man". Darwin ends with a passage that became well known and much quoted:
rewrite: In the concluding chapter, Darwin revisits earlier points and expresses hope that his theory will revolutionize natural history. While he deliberately avoids human origins elsewhere to prevent bias, he now cautiously suggests psychology will gain a new foundation and "Light will be thrown on the origin of man." The book closes with a passage that would become widely celebrated and frequently cited.

input: Apple was initially reluctant to embrace mice with multiple buttons and scroll wheels. Macs did not natively support pointing devices that featured multiple buttons, even from third parties, until Mac OS X arrived in 2001. Apple continued to offer only single button mice, in both wired and Bluetooth wireless versions, until August 2005, when it introduced the Mighty Mouse. While it looked like a traditional one-button mouse, it actually had four buttons and a scroll ball, capable of independent x- and y-axis movement. A Bluetooth version followed in July 2006. In October 2009, Apple introduced the Magic Mouse, which uses multi-touch gesture recognition (similar to that of the iPhone) instead of a physical scroll wheel or ball. It is available only in a wireless configuration, but the wired Mighty Mouse (re-branded as "Apple Mouse") is still available as an alternative. Since 2010, Apple has also offered the Magic Trackpad as a means to control Macintosh desktop computers in a way similar to laptops.
rewrite: For many years, Apple maintained a firm commitment to single-button mice, resisting the industry trend toward multi-button and scroll-wheel designs. Even third-party pointing devices with extra buttons were not natively supported by Macs until the launch of Mac OS X in 2001. This policy persisted, with Apple offering only wired and Bluetooth single-button mice, until August 2005. That month saw the introduction of the Mighty Mouse, which retained a traditional one-button appearance but concealed four buttons and a unique scroll ball capable of independent movement on both axes. A Bluetooth version of this mouse was released in July 2006. A significant shift came in October 2009 with the Magic Mouse, which replaced physical scrolling mechanisms with multi-touch gesture recognition, technology akin to that of the iPhone. It is exclusively wireless, though a wired version of the Mighty Mouse, re-branded as the "Apple Mouse," remains an alternative. Since 2010, Apple has also provided the Magic Trackpad, offering desktop Mac users laptop-style gesture control.

input: The year 1789 brought the French Revolution and with it the first division of Alsace into the départements of Haut- and Bas-Rhin. Alsatians played an active role in the French Revolution. On 21 July 1789, after receiving news of the Storming of the Bastille in Paris, a crowd of people stormed the Strasbourg city hall, forcing the city administrators to flee and putting symbolically an end to the feudal system in Alsace. In 1792, Rouget de Lisle composed in Strasbourg the Revolutionary marching song "La Marseillaise" (as Marching song for the Army of the Rhine), which later became the anthem of France. "La Marseillaise" was played for the first time in April of that year in front of the mayor of Strasbourg Philippe-Frédéric de Dietrich. Some of the most famous generals of the French Revolution also came from Alsace, notably Kellermann, the victor of Valmy, Kléber, who led the armies of the French Republic in Vendée and Westermann, who also fought in the Vendée.
rewrite: In 1789, the French Revolution led to the initial division of Alsace into the départements of Haut-Rhin and Bas-Rhin. Alsatians were active participants in these transformative events. Notably, on July 21, 1789, upon learning of the Storming of the Bastille in Paris, a crowd stormed Strasbourg's city hall. This act forced the city administrators to flee and symbolically ended the feudal system in the region. Furthermore, Strasbourg was the city where, in 1792, Rouget de Lisle composed the revolutionary marching song "La Marseillaise." First performed in April of that year for the mayor of Strasbourg, Philippe-Frédéric de Dietrich, it was originally intended for the Army of the Rhine before becoming the French national anthem. The revolution also produced renowned generals from Alsace, including Kellermann, victor at Valmy; Kléber, who commanded republican armies in the Vendée; and Westermann, who also fought there.

input: As with most ancient civilizations, Rome's military served the triple purposes of securing its borders, exploiting peripheral areas through measures such as imposing tribute on conquered peoples, and maintaining internal order. From the outset, Rome's military typified this pattern and the majority of Rome's wars were characterized by one of two types. The first is the foreign war, normally begun as a counter-offensive or defense of an ally. The second is the civil war, which plagued the Roman Republic in its final century. Roman armies were not invincible, despite their formidable reputation and host of victories. Over the centuries the Romans "produced their share of incompetents" who led Roman armies into catastrophic defeats. Nevertheless, it was generally the fate of the greatest of Rome's enemies, such as Pyrrhus and Hannibal, to win early battles but lose the war. The history of Rome's campaigning is, if nothing else, a history of obstinate persistence overcoming appalling losses.
rewrite: Like most ancient civilizations, Rome employed its military to secure borders, exploit outlying regions by demanding tribute from conquered populations, and preserve internal stability. This pattern defined Roman military operations from the beginning, with wars generally falling into two categories. One was the foreign war, typically launched as a defensive response or in aid of an ally. The other was the civil war, which ravaged the Roman Republic in its last hundred years. Despite their fearsome reputation and many triumphs, Roman armies were not unbeatable. Across the centuries, Rome had its share of incompetent commanders who suffered disastrous losses. Even the most formidable adversaries, like Pyrrhus and Hannibal, often won initial battles only to ultimately lose the conflict. In essence, Rome’s military history is a chronicle of stubborn endurance prevailing over terrible setbacks.

input: The large magnitude of solar energy available makes it a highly appealing source of electricity. The United Nations Development Programme in its 2000 World Energy Assessment found that the annual potential of solar energy was 1,575–49,837 exajoules (EJ). This is several times larger than the total world energy consumption, which was 559.8 EJ in 2012.
rewrite: Solar energy's vast potential makes it an attractive electricity source. According to a 2000 UN assessment, its annual capacity ranges from 1,575 to 49,837 exajoules. This greatly exceeds global consumption, which was 559.8 exajoules in 2012.

input: A working group consisting of Leon van de Kerkhof (The Netherlands), Gerhard Stoll (Germany), Leonardo Chiariglione (Italy), Yves-François Dehery (France), Karlheinz Brandenburg (Germany) and James D. Johnston (USA) took ideas from ASPEC, integrated the filter bank from Layer 2, added some of their own ideas and created MP3, which was designed to achieve the same quality at 128 kbit/s as MP2 at 192 kbit/s.
rewrite: A team including Leon van de Kerkhof, Gerhard Stoll, Leonardo Chiariglione, Yves-François Dehery, Karlheinz Brandenburg, and James D. Johnston developed MP3. They combined concepts from ASPEC with Layer 2's filter bank, adding their own innovations. The result was designed to match MP2's 192 kbit/s quality at just 128 kbit/s.

input: Chanakya, 4th Century BC Indian political philosopher. The Arthashastra provides an account of the science of politics for a wise ruler, policies for foreign affairs and wars, the system of a spy state and surveillance and economic stability of the state. Chanakya quotes several authorities including Bruhaspati, Ushanas, Prachetasa Manu, Parasara, and Ambi, and described himself as a descendant of a lineage of political philosophers, with his father Chanaka being his immediate predecessor. Another influential extant Indian treatise on political philosophy is the Sukra Neeti. An example of a code of law in ancient India is the Manusmṛti or Laws of Manu.
rewrite: Chanakya, a 4th Century BC Indian political philosopher, is best known for the Arthashastra. This treatise details the science of politics for a wise ruler, covering foreign policy, warfare, a system of spies and surveillance, and economic stability. In it, Chanakya cites authorities like Bruhaspati, Ushanas, and Manu, presenting himself as part of a philosophical lineage begun by his father, Chanaka. Beyond this work, other influential texts include the Sukra Neeti on political philosophy and the ancient legal code known as the Manusmṛti, or Laws of Manu.

input: Sessions for West's sixth solo effort begin to take shape in early 2013 in his own personal loft's living room at a Paris hotel. Determined to "undermine the commercial", he once again brought together close collaborators and attempted to incorporate Chicago drill, dancehall, acid house, and industrial music. Primarily inspired by architecture, West's perfectionist tendencies led him to contact producer Rick Rubin fifteen days shy of its due date to strip down the record's sound in favor of a more minimalist approach. Initial promotion of his sixth album included worldwide video projections of the album's music and live television performances. Yeezus, West's sixth album, was released June 18, 2013 to rave reviews from critics. It became the rapper's sixth consecutive number one debut, but also marked his lowest solo opening week sales. Def Jam issued "Black Skinhead" to radio in July 2013 as the album's lead single. On September 6, 2013, Kanye West announced he would be headlining his first solo tour in five years, to support Yeezus, with fellow American rapper Kendrick Lamar accompanying him along the way.
rewrite: In early 2013, within the living room of his personal loft at a Paris hotel, the sessions for what would become Kanye West’s sixth solo album began to form. With a declared aim to “undermine the commercial,” West gathered trusted collaborators, weaving together elements of Chicago drill, dancehall, acid house, and industrial music. His perfectionism, heavily influenced by architecture, prompted a last-minute shift: just fifteen days before the deadline, he enlisted producer Rick Rubin to drastically strip back the sound, adopting a starkly minimalist approach. The album, titled *Yeezus*, was released on June 18, 2013, and met with widespread critical acclaim. Its promotion featured global video projections of its music and live TV performances. While it secured West his sixth consecutive number-one debut, it also represented his lowest solo first-week sales. In July, Def Jam serviced “Black Skinhead” to radio as the lead single. That September, West announced a headlining solo tour—his first in five years—to support *Yeezus*, with fellow rapper Kendrick Lamar set to join as support.

input: In addition to the Jazz Festival (described above), New Haven serves as the home city of the annual International Festival of Arts and Ideas. New Haven's Saint Patrick's Day parade, which began in 1842, is New England's oldest St. Patty's Day parade and draws the largest crowds of any one-day spectator event in Connecticut. The St. Andrew the Apostle Italian Festival has taken place in the historic Wooster Square neighborhood every year since 1900. Other parishes in the city celebrate the Feast of Saint Anthony of Padua and a carnival in honor of St. Bernadette Soubirous. New Haven celebrates Powder House Day every April on the New Haven Green to commemorate the city's entrance into the Revolutionary War. The annual Wooster Square Cherry Blossom Festival commemorates the 1973 planting of 72 Yoshino Japanese Cherry Blossom trees by the New Haven Historic Commission in collaboration with the New Haven Parks Department and residents of the neighborhood. The Festival now draws well over 5,000 visitors. The Film Fest New Haven has been held annually since 1995.
rewrite: Beyond the Jazz Festival, New Haven hosts the annual International Festival of Arts and Ideas. The city’s rich calendar includes Powder House Day, observed each April on the New Haven Green to mark New Haven’s entry into the Revolutionary War. Historic parades are a staple, with New Haven’s Saint Patrick’s Day parade—dating to 1842—standing as New England’s oldest such celebration and Connecticut’s largest single-day spectator event. In Wooster Square, the St. Andrew the Apostle Italian Festival has occurred yearly since 1900. That neighborhood also welcomes spring with the Wooster Square Cherry Blossom Festival, commemorating the 1973 planting of 72 Yoshino cherry trees by the New Haven Historic Commission, the Parks Department, and local residents; it now attracts over 5,000 visitors. Additional events include parish celebrations for the Feast of Saint Anthony of Padua and a carnival honoring St. Bernadette Soubirous. Since 1995, the city has also been home to the annual Film Fest New Haven.

input: The Palacio Taranco is located in front of the Plaza Zabala, in the heart of Ciudad Vieja. It was erected in the early 20th century as the residence of the Ortiz Taranco brothers on the ruins of Montevideo's first theatre (of 1793), during a period in which the architectural style was influenced by French architecture. The palace was designed by French architects Charles Louis Girault and Jules Chifflot León who also designed the Petit Palais and the Arc de Triomphe in Paris. It passed to the city from the heirs of the Tarancos in 1943, along with its precious collection of Uruguayan furniture and draperies and was deemed by the city as an ideal place for a museum; in 1972 it became the Museum of Decorative Arts of Montevideo and in 1975 it became a National Heritage Site. The Decorative Arts Museum has an important collection of European paintings and decorative arts, ancient Greek and Roman art and Islamic ceramics of the 10th–18th century from the area of present-day Iran. The palace is often used as a meeting place by the Uruguayan government.
rewrite: In the heart of Ciudad Vieja, facing Plaza Zabala, stands the Palacio Taranco. This early 20th-century palace was built as a residence for the Ortiz Taranco brothers, constructed upon the ruins of Montevideo’s first theatre from 1793. Its design reflects the period’s strong French influence, crafted by architects Charles Louis Girault and Jules Chifflot León, who also designed Paris’s Petit Palais and Arc de Triomphe. The city acquired the palace from the Taranco heirs in 1943, along with its valuable collection of Uruguayan furniture and draperies, deeming it an ideal museum site. It opened as the Museum of Decorative Arts of Montevideo in 1972 and was declared a National Heritage Site in 1975. The museum holds significant collections of European paintings, decorative arts, ancient Greek and Roman artifacts, and 10th–18th century Islamic ceramics from present-day Iran. Today, the palace also frequently serves as a meeting place for the Uruguayan government.

input: Mexico City offers an immense and varied consumer retail market, ranging from basic foods to ultra high-end luxury goods. Consumers may buy in fixed indoor markets, mobile markets (tianguis), from street vendors, from downtown shops in a street dedicated to a certain type of good, in convenience stores and traditional neighborhood stores, in modern supermarkets, in warehouse and membership stores and the shopping centers that they anchor, in department stores, big-box stores and in modern shopping malls.
rewrite: Mexico City presents a vast and diverse retail landscape, catering to all consumer needs from essential groceries to exclusive luxury items. Shoppers can explore numerous formats: traditional fixed and mobile markets (tianguis), street vendors, specialized downtown streets, local convenience stores, modern supermarkets, warehouse clubs, and large shopping centers. These centers often feature department stores, big-box retailers, and contemporary malls.

input: The territory now contained within Bronx County was originally part of Westchester County, one of the 12 original counties of the English Province of New York. The present Bronx County was contained in the town of Westchester and parts of the towns of Yonkers, Eastchester, and Pelham. In 1846, a new town, West Farms, was created by division of Westchester; in turn, in 1855, the town of Morrisania was created from West Farms. In 1873, the town of Kingsbridge (roughly corresponding to the modern Bronx neighborhoods of Kingsbridge, Riverdale, and Woodlawn) was established within the former borders of Yonkers.
rewrite: Originally part of Westchester County, the area now known as Bronx County was once included in the town of Westchester and sections of Yonkers, Eastchester, and Pelham. Westchester was divided in 1846 to form the town of West Farms, which then spawned the town of Morrisania in 1855. Later, in 1873, the town of Kingsbridge was established within old Yonkers boundaries, covering areas similar to today's Kingsbridge, Riverdale, and Woodlawn neighborhoods.

input: The cuisine of Switzerland is multifaceted. While some dishes such as fondue, raclette or rösti are omnipresent through the country, each region developed its own gastronomy according to the differences of climate and languages.  Traditional Swiss cuisine uses ingredients similar to those in other European countries, as well as unique dairy products and cheeses such as Gruyère or Emmental, produced in the valleys of Gruyères and Emmental. The number of fine-dining establishments is high, particularly in western Switzerland.
rewrite: Swiss cuisine is diverse, with nationwide staples like fondue, raclette, and rösti alongside distinct regional specialties shaped by climate and language. It features common European ingredients alongside unique local dairy products and cheeses, including Gruyère and Emmental from their namesake valleys. Fine-dining establishments are plentiful, especially in the western part of the country.

input: Extensive and diverse public spending is, in itself, inherently at risk of cronyism, kickbacks, and embezzlement. Complicated regulations and arbitrary, unsupervised official conduct exacerbate the problem. This is one argument for privatization and deregulation. Opponents of privatization see the argument as ideological. The argument that corruption necessarily follows from the opportunity is weakened by the existence of countries with low to non-existent corruption but large public sectors, like the Nordic countries. These countries score high on the Ease of Doing Business Index, due to good and often simple regulations, and have rule of law firmly established. Therefore, due to their lack of corruption in the first place, they can run large public sectors without inducing political corruption. Recent evidence that takes both the size of expenditures and regulatory complexity into account has found that high-income democracies with more expansive state sectors do indeed have higher levels of corruption.
rewrite: Public spending on a large and varied scale naturally creates opportunities for cronyism, kickbacks, and embezzlement. This risk is intensified by complex regulations and arbitrary actions from unsupervised officials, forming one rationale for privatization and deregulation. Critics, however, often view this argument as ideological. It is weakened by the example of nations, such as the Nordic countries, which maintain extensive public sectors yet exhibit very low corruption. These countries combine strong rule of law with straightforward, effective regulations, scoring highly on the Ease of Doing Business Index. Their inherent lack of corruption allows for large public sectors without spurring political graft. Nonetheless, recent studies considering both expenditure size and regulatory complexity indicate that high-income democracies with bigger state sectors do tend to have higher corruption levels.

input: Notre Dame's conference affiliations for all of its sports except football and fencing changed in July 2013 as a result of major conference realignment, and its fencing affiliation will change in July 2014. The Irish left the Big East for the ACC during a prolonged period of instability in the Big East; while they maintain their football independence, they have committed to play five games per season against ACC opponents. In ice hockey, the Irish were forced to find a new conference home after the Big Ten Conference's decision to add the sport in 2013–14 led to a cascade of conference moves that culminated in the dissolution of the school's former hockey home, the Central Collegiate Hockey Association, after the 2012–13 season. Notre Dame moved its hockey team to Hockey East. After Notre Dame joined the ACC, the conference announced it would add fencing as a sponsored sport beginning in the 2014–15 school year. There are many theories behind the adoption of the athletics moniker but it is known that the Fighting Irish name was used in the early 1920s with respect to the football team and was popularized by alumnus Francis Wallace in his New York Daily News columns. The official colors of Notre Dame are Navy Blue and Gold Rush which are worn in competition by its athletic teams. In addition, the color green is often worn because of the Fighting Irish nickname. The Notre Dame Leprechaun is the mascot of the athletic teams. Created by Theodore W. Drake in 1964, the leprechaun was first used on the football pocket schedule and later on the football program covers. The leprechaun was featured on the cover of Time in November 1964 and gained national exposure.
rewrite:
In July 2013, a major wave of conference realignment shifted the conference affiliations for all University of Notre Dame sports, with the exceptions of football and fencing. This move saw the Irish depart the Big East for the Atlantic Coast Conference, a change prompted by prolonged instability within the Big East. While Notre Dame maintains its historic independence in football, it has committed to playing five games annually against ACC opponents. The following year, in July 2014, the school’s fencing affiliation also changed, as the ACC announced it would sponsor fencing starting in the 2014–15 school year.

Separately, the hockey program was compelled to find a new conference home. This resulted from the Big Ten Conference’s 2013–14 decision to sponsor ice hockey, which triggered a series of moves leading to the dissolution of Notre Dame’s former league, the Central Collegiate Hockey Association, after the 2012–13 season. Consequently, the university moved its hockey team to Hockey East.

The athletics teams compete under the official colors of Navy Blue and Gold Rush. Reflecting the well-known Fighting Irish nickname, the color green is also frequently worn. This moniker, popularized in the early 1920s by alumnus Francis Wallace through his New York Daily News columns in reference to the football team, has several origin theories. Serving as the official mascot is the Notre Dame Leprechaun, created by Theodore W. Drake in 1964. It first appeared on the football pocket schedule and later on program covers. The leprechaun gained national exposure when it was featured on the cover of *Time* magazine in November 1964.

input: During colonial times, Edenton served as the state capital beginning in 1722, and New Bern was selected as the capital in 1766. Construction of Tryon Palace, which served as the residence and offices of the provincial governor William Tryon, began in 1767 and was completed in 1771. In 1788 Raleigh was chosen as the site of the new capital, as its central location protected it from attacks from the coast. Officially established in 1792 as both county seat and state capital, the city was named after Sir Walter Raleigh, sponsor of Roanoke, the "lost colony" on Roanoke Island.
rewrite: Edenton became North Carolina's capital in 1722 during the colonial era, followed by New Bern in 1766. In New Bern, construction on Tryon Palace—the governor's residence and offices for William Tryon—started in 1767, finishing in 1771. By 1788, Raleigh's more central, inland location was chosen for a new capital to avoid coastal threats. The city, officially founded in 1792 as both state capital and county seat, honors Sir Walter Raleigh, who sponsored the "lost colony" on Roanoke Island.

input: Carnivore and herbivore diets are contrasting, with basic nitrogen and carbon proportions vary for their particular foods. "The nitrogen content of plant tissues averages about 2%, while in fungi, animals, and bacteria it averages about 5% to 10%." Many herbivores rely on bacterial fermentation to create digestible nutrients from indigestible plant cellulose, while obligate carnivores must eat animal meats to obtain certain vitamins or nutrients their bodies cannot otherwise synthesize. All animals' diets must provide sufficient amounts of the basic building blocks they need, up to the point where their particular biology can synthesize the rest. Animal tissue contains chemical compounds, such as water, carbohydrates (sugar, starch, and fiber), amino acids (in proteins), fatty acids (in lipids), and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA). These compounds in turn consist of elements such as carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium, iron, zinc, magnesium, manganese, and so on. All of these chemical compounds and elements occur in various forms and combinations (e.g. hormones, vitamins, phospholipids, hydroxyapatite).
rewrite:
The diets of carnivores and herbivores differ fundamentally, reflected in the basic proportions of nitrogen and carbon within their respective foods. Animal tissue comprises chemical compounds like water, carbohydrates (including sugar, starch, and fiber), amino acids (found in proteins), fatty acids (in lipids), and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA). These compounds are themselves built from elements such as carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium, iron, zinc, magnesium, and manganese. All these chemicals and elements exist in diverse forms and combinations, such as hormones, vitamins, phospholipids, and hydroxyapatite.

A key distinction lies in nitrogen content: plant tissues average about 2% nitrogen, whereas fungi, animals, and bacteria average 5% to 10%. To meet their nutritional needs, many herbivores depend on bacterial fermentation to derive digestible nutrients from indigestible plant cellulose. Conversely, obligate carnivores must consume animal meat to acquire certain essential vitamins or nutrients their bodies cannot synthesize internally. Ultimately, every animal's diet must supply sufficient basic building blocks, up to the limit of what its own biology can produce.

input: The Theater District is a 17-block area in the center of downtown Houston that is home to the Bayou Place entertainment complex, restaurants, movies, plazas, and parks. Bayou Place is a large multilevel building containing full-service restaurants, bars, live music, billiards, and Sundance Cinema. The Bayou Music Center stages live concerts, stage plays, and stand-up comedy. Space Center Houston is the official visitors' center of NASA's Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center. The Space Center has many interactive exhibits including moon rocks, a shuttle simulator, and presentations about the history of NASA's manned space flight program. Other tourist attractions include the Galleria (Texas's largest shopping mall, located in the Uptown District), Old Market Square, the Downtown Aquarium, and Sam Houston Race Park.

Bayou Place itself is a multilevel building offering full-service restaurants, bars, live music, billiards, and the Sundance Cinema. Live concerts, stage plays, and comedy are staged at the Bayou Music Center. input: During the Age of Enlightenment, philosophers such as John Locke advocated the principle in their writings, whereas others, such as Thomas Hobbes, strongly opposed it. input: The strength of the Viking influence on Old English appears from the fact that the indispensable elements of the language - pronouns, modals, comparatives, pronominal adverbs (like "hence" and "together"), conjunctions and prepositions - show the most marked Danish influence; the best evidence of Scandinavian influence appears in the extensive word borrowings for, as Jespersen indicates, no texts exist in either Scandinavia or in Northern England from this time to give certain evidence of an influence on syntax. The change to Old English from Old Norse was substantive, pervasive, and of a democratic character. Old Norse and Old English resembled each other closely like cousins and with some words in common, they roughly understood each other; in time the inflections melted away and the analytic pattern emerged. It is most “important to recognize that in many words the English and Scandinavian language differed chiefly in their inflectional elements. The body of the word was so nearly the same in the two languages that only the endings would put obstacles in the way of mutual understanding. In the mixed population which existed in the Danelaw these endings must have led to much confusion, tending gradually to become obscured and finally lost.” This blending of peoples and languages happily resulted in “simplifying English grammar.”
rewrite: The profound impact of Viking settlers on Old English is unmistakably demonstrated through extensive lexical borrowings. As noted by Jespersen, the absence of contemporary texts from Scandinavia or Northern England limits definitive proof of syntactic influence, making these borrowed words the clearest evidence. This linguistic exchange was substantive, pervasive, and democratic in nature. Old Norse and Old English were closely related, akin to cousins sharing common words, which allowed for a rough mutual understanding. Over time, inflections faded and a more analytic structure emerged. Crucially, the two languages often differed mainly in their inflectional endings, while the core of many words remained nearly identical. In the culturally mixed Danelaw region, these differing endings inevitably caused confusion, leading them to gradually become obscured and eventually discarded. This process significantly contributed to simplifying English grammar. Furthermore, the most fundamental elements of the language—including pronouns, modals, comparatives, adverbs like "hence" and "together," conjunctions, and prepositions—reveal the most marked Danish influence, underscoring the depth of this transformation.

input: Another study of dogs' roles in families showed many dogs have set tasks or routines undertaken as family members, the most common of which was helping with the washing-up by licking the plates in the dishwasher, and bringing in the newspaper from the lawn. Increasingly, human family members are engaging in activities centered on the perceived needs and interests of the dog, or in which the dog is an integral partner, such as dog dancing and dog yoga.

input: The Ismailis differ from Twelvers because they had living imams for centuries after the last Twelver Imam went into concealment. They followed Isma'il ibn Jafar, elder brother of Musa al-Kadhim, as the rightful Imam after his father Ja'far al-Sadiq. The Ismailis believe that whether Imam Ismail did or did not die before Imam Ja'far, he had passed on the mantle of the imamate to his son Muḥammad ibn Ismail as the next imam. Thus, their line of imams is as follows (the years of their individual imamats during the Common Era are given in brackets):

input: Chopin's qualities as a pianist and composer were recognized by many of his fellow musicians. Schumann named a piece for him in his suite Carnaval, and Chopin later dedicated his Ballade No. 2 in F major to Schumann. Elements of Chopin's music can be traced in many of Liszt's later works. Liszt later transcribed for piano six of Chopin's Polish songs. A less fraught friendship was with Alkan, with whom he discussed elements of folk music, and who was deeply affected by Chopin's death.

input: Brood parasitism, in which an egg-layer leaves her eggs with another individual's brood, is more common among birds than any other type of organism. After a parasitic bird lays her eggs in another bird's nest, they are often accepted and raised by the host at the expense of the host's own brood. Brood parasites may be either obligate brood parasites, which must lay their eggs in the nests of other species because they are incapable of raising their own young, or non-obligate brood parasites, which sometimes lay eggs in the nests of conspecifics to increase their reproductive output even though they could have raised their own young. One hundred bird species, including honeyguides, icterids, and ducks, are obligate parasites, though the most famous are the cuckoos. Some brood parasites are adapted to hatch before their host's young, which allows them to destroy the host's eggs by pushing them out of the nest or to kill the host's chicks; this ensures that all food brought to the nest will be fed to the parasitic chicks.
rewrite: Brood parasitism, a reproductive strategy where an individual leaves her eggs with another's brood, is most prevalent among birds compared to other organisms. In this arrangement, a parasitic bird deposits her eggs in a host's nest, and these are frequently accepted and reared by the host, often to the detriment of the host's own offspring. Parasites are categorized as either obligate or non-obligate. Obligate brood parasites, such as the well-known cuckoos along with honeyguides, icterids, and ducks—totaling one hundred bird species—must use other species' nests, being unable to raise their own young. Non-obligate parasites, conversely, may lay eggs in the nests of their own species to boost reproductive success, despite being capable of raising their brood. Adaptations in some brood parasites include early hatching, enabling the parasitic chicks to eliminate host eggs or chicks by ejecting them from the nest, thereby monopolizing all food delivered by the host parents.

input: The area near the border with Cameroon close to the coast is rich rainforest and part of the Cross-Sanaga-Bioko coastal forests ecoregion, an important centre for biodiversity. It is habitat for the drill monkey, which is found in the wild only in this area and across the border in Cameroon. The areas surrounding Calabar, Cross River State, also in this forest, are believed to contain the world's largest diversity of butterflies. The area of southern Nigeria between the Niger and the Cross Rivers has lost most of its forest because of development and harvesting by increased population, with it being replaced by grassland (see Cross-Niger transition forests).
rewrite: Close to the coast near the border with Cameroon lies a rich rainforest, forming part of the Cross-Sanaga-Bioko coastal forests ecoregion. This area is a significant centre for biodiversity. It serves as habitat for the drill monkey, a species found in the wild exclusively here and in neighboring Cameroon. Within this forest, the regions around Calabar in Cross River State are thought to hold the world's greatest diversity of butterflies. However, in southern Nigeria between the Niger and Cross Rivers, development and harvesting by a growing population have replaced most forest with grassland (see Cross-Niger transition forests).

input: Lactase is an enzyme that breaks down the disaccharide lactose to its component parts, glucose and galactose. Glucose and galactose can be absorbed by the small intestine. Approximately 65 percent of the adult population produce only small amounts of lactase and are unable to eat unfermented milk-based foods. This is commonly known as lactose intolerance. Lactose intolerance varies widely by ethnic heritage; more than 90 percent of peoples of east Asian descent are lactose intolerant, in contrast to about 5 percent of people of northern European descent.
rewrite: Lactase, an enzyme, breaks down lactose into glucose and galactose, which the small intestine can absorb. Commonly called lactose intolerance, the inability to digest unfermented dairy affects about 65% of adults who produce minimal lactase. This condition varies significantly by ethnicity; over 90% of people of East Asian descent are lactose intolerant, compared to roughly 5% of those of northern European descent.

input: On August 24, 2006, Apple and Creative announced a broad settlement to end their legal disputes. Apple will pay Creative US$100 million for a paid-up license, to use Creative's awarded patent in all Apple products. As part of the agreement, Apple will recoup part of its payment, if Creative is successful in licensing the patent. Creative then announced its intention to produce iPod accessories by joining the Made for iPod program.

As part of the broad agreement, Apple paid Creative $100 million for a license to use Creative’s patent across all its products. Apple will recoup a portion of this payment should Creative successfully license the patent to others. Separately, Creative announced its plan to join the Made for iPod program to produce accessories for the iPod.

input: Next, Spielberg teamed with Star Wars creator and friend George Lucas on an action adventure film, Raiders of the Lost Ark, the first of the Indiana Jones films. The archaeologist and adventurer hero Indiana Jones was played by Harrison Ford (whom Lucas had previously cast in his Star Wars films as Han Solo). The film was considered an homage to the cliffhanger serials of the Golden Age of Hollywood. It became the biggest film at the box office in 1981, and the recipient of numerous Oscar nominations including Best Director (Spielberg's second nomination) and Best Picture (the second Spielberg film to be nominated for Best Picture). Raiders is still considered a landmark example of the action-adventure genre. The film also led to Ford's casting in Ridley Scott's Blade Runner.
rewrite: Following his collaboration with friend and Star Wars creator George Lucas on the action-adventure film *Raiders of the Lost Ark*, Steven Spielberg helped launch the Indiana Jones series. Harrison Ford, previously cast by Lucas as Han Solo, portrayed the archaeologist and adventurer hero. A tribute to the cliffhanger serials of Hollywood's Golden Age, the film was 1981's highest box office earner. It earned several Oscar nominations, including Best Picture (Spielberg's second film to receive this honor) and Best Director (his second nomination). Still regarded as a landmark in its genre, *Raiders* also led to Ford being cast in Ridley Scott's *Blade Runner*.

input: The indirect method of applying tesserae is often used for very large projects, projects with repetitive elements or for areas needing site specific shapes. Tiles are applied face-down to a backing paper using an adhesive, and later transferred onto walls, floors or craft projects. This method is most useful for extremely large projects as it gives the maker time to rework areas, allows the cementing of the tiles to the backing panel to be carried out quickly in one operation and helps ensure that the front surfaces of the mosaic tiles and mosaic pieces are flat and in the same plane on the front, even when using tiles and pieces of differing thicknesses. Mosaic murals, benches and tabletops are some of the items usually made using the indirect method, as it results in a smoother and more even surface.
rewrite: For projects that are very large, feature repetitive elements, or require site-specific shapes, the indirect application of tesserae is a common choice. In this technique, tiles are first adhered face-down to a backing paper. This assembly is later transferred as a whole onto the final surface, such as a wall, floor, or craft project. It is particularly advantageous for extensive works, as it permits sections to be reworked during the planning stage. The method also enables the rapid, single-step cementing of all tiles to the backing panel. A key benefit is that it ensures a perfectly flat, even front surface, even when incorporating pieces of varying thicknesses. Consequently, items like mosaic murals, benches, and tabletops—which benefit from a smooth finish—are typically created using this indirect approach.

input: Strict separation of powers did not operate in The United Kingdom, the political structure of which served in most instances[citation needed] as a model for the government created by the U.S. Constitution.[citation needed] Under the UK Westminster system, based on parliamentary sovereignty and responsible government, Parliament (consisting of the Sovereign (King-in-Parliament), House of Lords and House of Commons) was the supreme lawmaking authority. The executive branch acted in the name of the King ("His Majesty's Government"), as did the judiciary. The King's Ministers were in most cases members of one of the two Houses of Parliament, and the Government needed to sustain the support of a majority in the House of Commons. One minister, the Lord Chancellor, was at the same time the sole judge in the Court of Chancery and the presiding officer in the House of Lords. Therefore, it may be seen that the three branches of British government often violated the strict principle of separation of powers, even though there were many occasions when the different branches of the government disagreed with each other. Some U.S. states did not observe a strict separation of powers in the 18th century. In New Jersey, the Governor also functioned as a member of the state's highest court and as the presiding officer of one house of the New Jersey Legislature. The President of Delaware was a member of the Court of Appeals; the presiding officers of the two houses of the state legislature also served in the executive department as Vice Presidents. In both Delaware and Pennsylvania, members of the executive council served at the same time as judges. On the other hand, many southern states explicitly required separation of powers. Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina and Georgia all kept the branches of government "separate and distinct."
rewrite:
The United Kingdom’s political structure, often cited as a model for the framers of the U.S. Constitution, did not operate under a strict separation of powers. Its Westminster system was founded on parliamentary sovereignty and responsible government. In this system, Parliament—comprising the Sovereign (King-in-Parliament), the House of Lords, and the House of Commons—held supreme lawmaking authority. Both the executive and the judiciary acted in the name of the King, forming “His Majesty’s Government.” Typically, the King’s Ministers were drawn from one of the two Houses of Parliament, and the Government was required to maintain majority support in the House of Commons. A clear overlap of powers was exemplified by the Lord Chancellor, who simultaneously served as the sole judge in the Court of Chancery and as the presiding officer in the House of Lords. Thus, while the different branches of British government could and did disagree, the three branches frequently violated a rigid separation of powers.

Similarly, in 18th-century America, several states did not adhere to a strict division. In New Jersey, the Governor also sat on the state’s highest court and presided over one house of the legislature. Delaware’s President was a member of the Court of Appeals, while the presiding officers of the two legislative houses served as Vice Presidents in the executive department. Both Delaware and Pennsylvania saw members of the executive council serving concurrently as judges. By contrast, many southern states explicitly mandated separation. Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, and Georgia all maintained constitutions that required the branches of government to remain “separate and distinct.”

input: The settlement of Plympton, further up the River Plym than the current Plymouth, was also an early trading port, but the river silted up in the early 11th century and forced the mariners and merchants to settle at the current day Barbican near the river mouth. At the time this village was called Sutton, meaning south town in Old English. The name Plym Mouth, meaning "mouth of the River Plym" was first mentioned in a Pipe Roll of 1211. The name Plymouth first officially replaced Sutton in a charter of King Henry VI in 1440. See Plympton for the derivation of the name Plym.
rewrite: Located further up the River Plym than modern Plymouth, the settlement of Plympton was an early trading port. However, when the river silted up in the early 11th century, mariners and merchants were forced to move downstream to a village then called Sutton, meaning "south town." This site near the river mouth is now the Barbican area. The term "Plym Mouth," for the river's mouth, appears in a 1211 Pipe Roll. The name Plymouth officially replaced Sutton in a 1440 charter from King Henry VI. (The origin of "Plym" is detailed under Plympton.)

input: Through his actions and speeches, and because he was able to symbolize the popular Arab will, Nasser inspired several nationalist revolutions in the Arab world. He defined the politics of his generation and communicated directly with the public masses of the Arab world, bypassing the various heads of states of those countries—an accomplishment not repeated by other Arab leaders. The extent of Nasser's centrality in the region made it a priority for incoming Arab nationalist heads of state to seek good relations with Egypt, in order to gain popular legitimacy from their own citizens.
rewrite: Nasser became a symbol of the popular Arab will through his actions and speeches, inspiring multiple nationalist revolutions. He uniquely defined his generation's politics by communicating directly with the Arab public, circumventing their national leaders—a feat unmatched by others. His central role in the region meant that incoming Arab nationalist leaders prioritized strong ties with Egypt. This was essential for them to gain popular legitimacy and approval from their own citizens.

input: Conversely, most heat-treatable alloys are precipitation hardening alloys, which produce the opposite effects that steel does. When heated to form a solution and then cooled quickly, these alloys become much softer than normal, during the diffusionless transformation, and then harden as they age. The solutes in these alloys will precipitate over time, forming intermetallic phases, which are difficult to discern from the base metal. Unlike steel, in which the solid solution separates to form different crystal phases, precipitation hardening alloys separate to form different phases within the same crystal. These intermetallic alloys appear homogeneous in crystal structure, but tend to behave heterogeneous, becoming hard and somewhat brittle.
rewrite: In contrast to steel, most heat-treatable alloys use precipitation hardening, producing opposite effects. When rapidly cooled after being heated into a solution, they undergo a diffusionless transformation, becoming unusually soft. They subsequently harden during aging. Over time, solutes precipitate out, forming intermetallic phases that blend with the base metal. Unlike steel, where the solid solution separates into distinct crystal phases, these alloys form different phases within a single crystal. Though appearing homogeneous in structure, they behave heterogeneously, resulting in a hard and somewhat brittle material.

input: When the Frankish rulers established the system of feudalism, the Bishops of Utrecht came to exercise worldly power as prince-bishops. The territory of the bishopric not only included the modern province of Utrecht (Nedersticht, 'lower Sticht'), but also extended to the northeast. The feudal conflict of the Middle Ages heavily affected Utrecht. The prince-bishopric was involved in almost continuous conflicts with the Counts of Holland and the Dukes of Guelders. The Veluwe region was seized by Guelders, but large areas in the modern province of Overijssel remained as the Oversticht.
rewrite: Under the system of feudalism instituted by Frankish rulers, the Bishops of Utrecht gained worldly authority, becoming prince-bishops. Their territory encompassed the modern province of Utrecht (Nedersticht) and stretched northeast. Medieval feudal conflict deeply impacted Utrecht, with the prince-bishopric locked in nearly constant struggles against the Counts of Holland and the Dukes of Guelders. While Guelders seized the Veluwe region, extensive lands in what is now Overijssel were retained as the Oversticht.

input: Under the Qing dynasty (1644–1911), the Nanjing area was known as Jiangning (江寧) and served as the seat of government for the Viceroy of Liangjiang. It had been visited by the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors a number of times on their tours of the southern provinces. Nanjing was invaded by British troops during the close of the First Opium War, which was ended by the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842. As the capital of the brief-lived rebel Taiping Heavenly Kingdom (founded by the Taiping rebels in the mid-19th century, Nanjing was known as Tianjing (天京, "Heavenly Capital" or "Capital of Heaven").
rewrite: During the Qing dynasty (1644–1911), the region around Nanjing was called Jiangning and functioned as the administrative base for the Viceroy of Liangjiang. The Kangxi and Qianlong emperors visited it multiple times while touring the southern provinces. In the mid-19th century, as the capital of the short-lived Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, it was renamed Tianjing, meaning "Heavenly Capital." British forces invaded Nanjing near the end of the First Opium War, a conflict concluded by the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842.

input: General Ridgway was appointed Supreme Commander, Korea; he regrouped the UN forces for successful counterattacks, while General James Van Fleet assumed command of the U.S. Eighth Army. Further attacks slowly depleted the PVA and KPA forces; Operations Courageous (23–28 March 1951) and Tomahawk (23 March 1951) were a joint ground and airborne infilltration meant to trap Chinese forces between Kaesong and Seoul. UN forces advanced to "Line Kansas", north of the 38th parallel. The 187th Airborne Regimental Combat Team's ("Rakkasans") second of two combat jumps was on Easter Sunday, 1951, at Munsan-ni, South Korea, codenamed Operation Tomahawk. The mission was to get behind Chinese forces and block their movement north. The 60th Indian Parachute Field Ambulance provided the medical cover for the operations, dropping an ADS and a surgical team and treating over 400 battle casualties apart from the civilian casualties that formed the core of their objective as the unit was on a humanitarian mission.

In late March 1951, Operations Courageous (March 23–28) and Tomahawk (March 23) were executed as a combined ground and airborne infiltration, aiming to encircle Chinese forces between Kaesong and Seoul. Operation Tomahawk included the second combat jump of the 187th Airborne Regimental Combat Team, the "Rakkasans," at Munsan-ni on Easter Sunday. Their mission was to cut off the enemy's retreat north. Medical support was provided by the 60th Indian Parachute Field Ambulance, which dropped an Advanced Dressing Station and a surgical team. This humanitarian-focused unit treated more than 400 battle casualties, in addition to the civilian casualties that were central to its objective.

input: The European Revolutions of 1848, known in some countries as the Spring of Nations or the Year of Revolution, were a series of political upheavals throughout the European continent. Described as a revolutionary wave, the period of unrest began in France and then, further propelled by the French Revolution of 1848, soon spread to the rest of Europe. Although most of the revolutions were quickly put down, there was a significant amount of violence in many areas, with tens of thousands of people tortured and killed. While the immediate political effects of the revolutions were reversed, the long-term reverberations of the events were far-reaching.
rewrite: Beginning in France and spreading across the continent, the European Revolutions of 1848 formed a wave of political upheaval, also called the Spring of Nations. This period of widespread unrest, intensified by the French Revolution of 1848, involved significant violence; tens of thousands were tortured and killed as most revolts were swiftly suppressed. Though the immediate political changes were reversed, the events left profound and far-reaching long-term reverberations throughout Europe.

input: The term "Late Middle Ages" refers to one of the three periods of the Middle Ages, along with the Early Middle Ages and the High Middle Ages. Leonardo Bruni was the first historian to use tripartite periodization in his History of the Florentine People (1442). Flavio Biondo used a similar framework in Decades of History from the Deterioration of the Roman Empire (1439–1453). Tripartite periodization became standard after the German historian Christoph Cellarius published Universal History Divided into an Ancient, Medieval, and New Period (1683).
rewrite: Alongside the Early and High Middle Ages, the "Late Middle Ages" denotes one of three medieval periods. Tripartite periodization was first employed by historian Leonardo Bruni in his *History of the Florentine People* (1442). Flavio Biondo adopted a similar model in his work *Decades of History from the Deterioration of the Roman Empire* (1439–1453). This periodization became standard following the 1683 publication of *Universal History Divided into an Ancient, Medieval, and New Period* by German historian Christoph Cellarius.

input: The main industries are mineral based, agriculture based, and textile based. Rajasthan is the second largest producer of polyester fibre in India. The Pali and Bhilwara District produces more cloth than Bhiwandi, Maharashtra and the bhilwara is the largest city in suitings production and export and Pali is largest city in cotton and polyster in blouse pieces and rubia production and export. Several prominent chemical and engineering companies are located in the city of Kota, in southern Rajasthan. Rajasthan is pre-eminent in quarrying and mining in India. The Taj Mahal was built from the white marble which was mined from a town called Makrana. The state is the second largest source of cement in India. It has rich salt deposits at Sambhar, copper mines at Khetri, Jhunjhunu, and zinc mines at Dariba, Zawar mines and Rampura Aghucha (opencast) near Bhilwara. Dimensional stone mining is also undertaken in Rajasthan. Jodhpur sandstone is mostly used in monuments, important buildings and residential buildings. This stone is termed as "chittar patthar". Jodhpur leads in Handicraft and Guar Gum industry. Rajasthan is also a part of the Mumbai-Delhi Industrial corridor is set to benefit economically. The State gets 39% of the DMIC, with major districts of Jaipur, Alwar, Kota and Bhilwara benefiting.
rewrite:
Rajasthan holds a prominent position in India's quarrying and mining sectors. The state is a key producer of dimensional stone, with Jodhpur sandstone—often called "chittar patthar"—widely used in monuments, significant buildings, and homes. Rajasthan is also the nation's second largest cement source. Its mineral wealth includes rich salt deposits at Sambhar, copper mines at Khetri and Jhunjhunu, and zinc mines at Dariba, Zawar, and Rampura Aghucha near Bhilwara. Notably, the white marble mined from Makrana was used to construct the Taj Mahal.

The industrial landscape is diverse, anchored in mineral-based, agriculture-based, and textile-based sectors. Rajasthan ranks as India's second largest producer of polyester fibre. In textiles, the Pali and Bhilwara districts collectively produce more cloth than Bhiwandi in Maharashtra. Bhilwara is the leading city for the production and export of suitings, while Pali holds the same status for cotton and polyester blouse pieces and rubia. Beyond textiles, Kota in southern Rajasthan hosts several major chemical and engineering companies. Additionally, Jodhpur leads in the handicraft and guar gum industries.

Economically, the state is poised to benefit from the Mumbai-Delhi Industrial Corridor, set to receive 39% of the Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC) development. Major districts including Jaipur, Alwar, Kota, and Bhilwara will see significant advantages from this project.

input: Valerian's first religious edict singled out Christianity as a particularly self-interested and subversive foreign cult, outlawed its assemblies and urged Christians to sacrifice to Rome's traditional gods. His second edict acknowledged a Christian threat to the Imperial system – not yet at its heart but close to it, among Rome’s equites and Senators. Christian apologists interpreted his disgraceful capture and death as divine judgement. The next forty years were peaceful; the Christian church grew stronger and its literature and theology gained a higher social and intellectual profile, due in part to its own search for political toleration and theological coherence. Origen discussed theological issues with traditionalist elites in a common Neoplatonist frame of reference – he had written to Decius' predecessor Philip the Arab in similar vein – and Hippolytus recognised a “pagan” basis in Christian heresies. The Christian churches were disunited; Paul of Samosata, Bishop of Antioch was deposed by a synod of 268 for "dogmatic reasons – his doctrine on the human nature of Christ was rejected – and for his lifestyle, which reminded his brethren of the habits of the administrative elite". The reasons for his deposition were widely circulated among the churches. Meanwhile, Aurelian (270-75) appealed for harmony among his soldiers (concordia militum), stabilised the Empire and its borders and successfully established an official, Hellenic form of unitary cult to the Palmyrene Sol Invictus in Rome's Campus Martius.
rewrite: Valerian’s initial religious decree specifically targeted Christianity as a self-interested and subversive foreign cult, banning its gatherings and demanding that Christians offer sacrifices to Rome’s traditional gods. A subsequent edict recognized a Christian threat to the Imperial order—not yet at the core, but emerging among Rome’s equites and Senators. Christian apologists later viewed his ignominious capture and death as divine judgment. Following this, a forty-year period of peace allowed the Christian church to grow stronger. Its literature and theology achieved greater social and intellectual prominence, partly through its own pursuit of political toleration and theological consistency. Origen engaged traditionalist elites on theological matters within a shared Neoplatonist framework—having written similarly to Decius’ predecessor, Philip the Arab—while Hippolytus identified a “pagan” foundation in certain Christian heresies. Internally, the Christian churches were divided; for instance, Paul of Samosata, Bishop of Antioch, was deposed by a synod in 268 both for doctrinal reasons—his teaching on Christ’s human nature was rejected—and for a lifestyle that reminded his peers of the administrative elite. The grounds for his removal were widely disseminated among the churches. During this era, Emperor Aurelian (270–75) called for harmony among his soldiers (concordia militum), stabilized the Empire and its frontiers, and successfully instituted an official, Hellenic version of a unified cult to the Palmyrene Sol Invictus on Rome’s Campus Martius.

input: The United Kingdom has traditionally been governed as a unitary state by the Westminster Parliament in London. Instead of adopting a federal model, the UK has relied on gradual devolution to decentralise political power. Devolution in the UK began with the Government of Ireland Act 1914 which granted home rule to Ireland as a constituent country of the former United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. Following the partition of Ireland in 1921 which saw the creation of the sovereign Irish Free State (which eventually evolved into the modern day Republic of Ireland), Northern Ireland retained its devolved government through the Parliament of Northern Ireland, the only part of the UK to have such a body at this time. This body was suspended in 1972 and Northern Ireland was governed by direct rule during the period of conflict known as The Troubles.
rewrite: Traditionally, the United Kingdom has operated as a unitary state, with political authority centralized in London's Westminster Parliament. Rather than establishing a federal system, it has pursued a path of gradual devolution to decentralize power. This process originated with the Government of Ireland Act of 1914, which provided home rule to Ireland within the then United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. After the 1921 partition, the sovereign Irish Free State (later the Republic of Ireland) was formed, while Northern Ireland remained with a devolved government via its own Parliament—initially the UK's only region with such autonomy. This Parliament was suspended in 1972, leading to a period of direct rule from London during the era of conflict called The Troubles.

input: During up-peak mode (also called moderate incoming traffic), elevator cars in a group are recalled to the lobby to provide expeditious service to passengers arriving at the building, most typically in the morning as people arrive for work or at the conclusion of a lunch-time period. Elevators are dispatched one-by-one when they reach a pre-determined passenger load, or when they have had their doors opened for a certain period of time. The next elevator to be dispatched usually has its hall lantern or a "this car leaving next" sign illuminated to encourage passengers to make maximum use of the available elevator system capacity. Some elevator banks are programmed so that at least one car will always return to the lobby floor and park whenever it becomes free.
rewrite: In up-peak mode, often experienced during morning arrivals or after lunch, elevator groups are coordinated to efficiently handle incoming traffic. Cars are recalled to the lobby to provide quick service for passengers entering the building. Dispatching occurs individually once a car reaches a set passenger load or after its doors have remained open for a specific duration. To optimize capacity, the next elevator scheduled for departure typically signals with an illuminated hall lantern or a "this car leaving next" sign, guiding passengers to board. Additionally, many systems are programmed to ensure at least one car returns and parks at the lobby whenever it is unoccupied.

input: In 1922, Egypt, which had been declared a British protectorate at the outbreak of the First World War, was granted formal independence, though it continued to be a British client state until 1954. British troops remained stationed in Egypt until the signing of the Anglo-Egyptian Treaty in 1936, under which it was agreed that the troops would withdraw but continue to occupy and defend the Suez Canal zone. In return, Egypt was assisted to join the League of Nations. Iraq, a British mandate since 1920, also gained membership of the League in its own right after achieving independence from Britain in 1932. In Palestine, Britain was presented with the problem of mediating between the Arab and Jewish communities. The 1917 Balfour Declaration, which had been incorporated into the terms of the mandate, stated that a national home for the Jewish people would be established in Palestine, and Jewish immigration allowed up to a limit that would be determined by the mandatory power. This led to increasing conflict with the Arab population, who openly revolted in 1936. As the threat of war with Germany increased during the 1930s, Britain judged the support of the Arab population in the Middle East as more important than the establishment of a Jewish homeland, and shifted to a pro-Arab stance, limiting Jewish immigration and in turn triggering a Jewish insurgency.
rewrite:
Formal independence was granted to Egypt in 1922, despite its status as a British protectorate since the start of the First World War. It would remain a client state of Britain until 1954. British troops continued to be stationed there until the 1936 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty, which stipulated their withdrawal while permitting continued occupation and defense of the Suez Canal zone. As part of this arrangement, Egypt received assistance to join the League of Nations. Another Middle Eastern territory, Iraq, had been under a British mandate since 1920. Following its independence in 1932, it too gained League membership in its own right.

Meanwhile, in Palestine, Britain faced the complex task of mediating between Arab and Jewish communities. Incorporated into the mandate's terms was the 1917 Balfour Declaration, promising a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine and allowing Jewish immigration within limits set by the mandatory power. This policy fueled growing conflict, culminating in an open Arab revolt in 1936. During the 1930s, as the threat of war with Germany loomed, Britain began to prioritize the support of the Arab population across the Middle East over the establishment of a Jewish homeland. Consequently, British policy shifted to a pro-Arab stance, imposing limits on Jewish immigration. This restriction, in turn, triggered a Jewish insurgency.

input: Modern morphology recognizes a continuum between the major morphological categories of root, stem (caulome), leaf (phyllome) and trichome. Furthermore, it emphasizes structural dynamics. Modern systematics aims to reflect and discover phylogenetic relationships between plants. Modern Molecular phylogenetics largely ignores morphological characters, relying on DNA sequences as data. Molecular analysis of DNA sequences from most families of flowering plants enabled the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group to publish in 1998 a phylogeny of flowering plants, answering many of the questions about relationships among angiosperm families and species. The theoretical possibility of a practical method for identification of plant species and commercial varieties by DNA barcoding is the subject of active current research.
rewrite: Modern systematics seeks to reveal the phylogenetic relationships among plants. While modern morphology acknowledges a continuum between roots, stems (caulomes), leaves (phyllomes), and trichomes, it also focuses on structural dynamics. In contrast, modern molecular phylogenetics depends primarily on DNA sequences, largely setting aside morphological traits. Through analyzing such sequences from most flowering plant families, the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group produced a 1998 phylogeny that clarified numerous connections between angiosperm families and species. Concurrently, active research explores the potential for DNA barcoding to practically identify plant species and commercial varieties.

input: Many television shows and films have been produced which portray in-character professional wrestlers as protagonists, such as Ready to Rumble, ¡Mucha Lucha!, Nacho Libre, and the Santo film series. In the wildly popular Rocky series of films about the fictional boxer Rocky Balboa, Rocky III saw its hero fighting a "boxer vs. wrestler" exhibition match against the enormous and villainous wrestler "Thunderlips", portrayed by real-life soon-to-be wrestling icon Hulk Hogan. At least two stage plays set in the world of pro wrestling have been produced: The Baron is a comedy that retells the life of an actual performer known as Baron von Raschke. From Parts Unknown... is an award-nominated Canadian drama about the rise and fall of a fictional wrestler. The 2009 South Park episode "W.T.F." played on the soap operatic elements of professional wrestling. One of the lead characters on the Disney Channel series Kim Possible was a huge fan of pro wrestling and actually featured it on an episode (with two former WWE wrestlers voicing the two fictitious wrestlers featured in the episode). The 2008 film The Wrestler, about a washed-up professional wrestler, garnered several Oscar nominations.
rewrite: Professional wrestling has inspired diverse portrayals across television, film, and theater. The fictional boxer Rocky Balboa, for instance, faced the villainous wrestler "Thunderlips"—played by a pre-fame Hulk Hogan—in a "boxer vs. wrestler" exhibition match in *Rocky III*. Films like *Ready to Rumble*, *¡Mucha Lucha!*, *Nacho Libre*, and the *Santo* series have also featured in-character wrestlers as central figures. On stage, the comedy *The Baron* fictionalizes the life of real performer Baron von Raschke, while the Canadian drama *From Parts Unknown...*, an award-nominated play, traces the arc of a fictional wrestler's career. Television has explored the genre as well: the *South Park* episode "W.T.F." parodied wrestling's melodramatic traits, and the Disney Channel's *Kim Possible* dedicated an episode to the sport, with former WWE wrestlers voicing characters. Additionally, the 2008 film *The Wrestler*, which earned multiple Oscar nominations, offered a gritty look at an aging performer's struggles.

input: Some types of energy are a varying mix of both potential and kinetic energy. An example is mechanical energy which is the sum of (usually macroscopic) kinetic and potential energy in a system. Elastic energy in materials is also dependent upon electrical potential energy (among atoms and molecules), as is chemical energy, which is stored and released from a reservoir of electrical potential energy between electrons, and the molecules or atomic nuclei that attract them.[need quotation to verify].The list is also not necessarily complete. Whenever physical scientists discover that a certain phenomenon appears to violate the law of energy conservation, new forms are typically added that account for the discrepancy.
rewrite: Certain forms of energy represent a blend of potential and kinetic energy. Mechanical energy, for instance, combines the kinetic and potential energy within a system. Similarly, both elastic energy in materials and chemical energy rely on electrical potential energy at the atomic and molecular level. Chemical energy specifically involves stored electrical potential between electrons and the nuclei or molecules attracting them. The catalog of energy forms remains open; when observations seem to contradict energy conservation, scientists often introduce new forms to explain the difference.

input: Bern was the site of the 1954 Football (Soccer) World Cup Final, a huge upset for the Hungarian Golden Team, who were beaten 3–2 by West Germany. The football team BSC Young Boys is based in Bern at the Stade de Suisse Wankdorf, which also was one of the venues for the European football championship 2008 in which it hosted 3 matches.
rewrite: In 1954, Bern hosted the Football World Cup Final, where West Germany's 3–2 victory famously upset the Hungarian Golden Team. The city is home to BSC Young Boys, who play at the Stade de Suisse Wankdorf. This stadium also served as a venue for the 2008 European Championship, hosting three matches.

input: Since the start of the 1994–95 season, the FA Cup has been sponsored. However, to protect the identity of the competition, the sponsored name has always included 'The FA Cup' in addition to the sponsor's name, unlike sponsorship deals for the League Cup where the word 'cup' is preceded by only the sponsor's name. Sponsorship deals run for four years, though – as in the case of E.ON – one-year extensions may be agreed. Emirates airline is the sponsor from 2015 to 2018, renaming the competition as 'The Emirates FA Cup', unlike previous editions, which included 'The FA Cup in association with E.ON' and 'The FA Cup with Budweiser'.
rewrite: Sponsorship of the FA Cup began with the 1994–95 season. To preserve the competition's identity, the sponsored name always incorporates 'The FA Cup' alongside the sponsor, differing from the League Cup where only the sponsor's name precedes 'cup'. Deals typically span four years, with occasional one-year extensions, as seen with E.ON. Since 2015, Emirates airline has been the sponsor, using the title 'The Emirates FA Cup'. This contrasts with earlier formats like 'The FA Cup in association with E.ON' or 'The FA Cup with Budweiser'.

input: In July 2013, there were 41,000 non-Germans by citizenship living in Thuringia (1.9% of the population − among the smallest proportions of any state in Germany). Nevertheless, the number rose from 33,000 in July 2011, an increase of 24% in only two years. About 4% of the population are migrants (including persons that already received the German citizenship). The biggest groups of foreigners by citizenship are (as of 2012): Russians (3,100), Poles (3,000), Vietnamese (2,800), Turks (2,100) and Ukrainians (2,000). The amount of foreigners varies between regions: the college towns Erfurt, Jena, Weimar and Ilmenau have the highest rates, whereas there are almost no migrants living in the most rural smaller municipalities.
rewrite: Thuringia’s foreign population, while small relative to other German states, grew significantly in the early 2010s. In July 2013, 41,000 non-German citizens resided there, representing 1.9% of the population. This marked a 24% increase from just two years prior, when the figure was 33,000 in July 2011. Including those who have obtained German citizenship, migrants constitute about 4% of residents. The largest foreign groups in 2012 were Russians (3,100), Poles (3,000), Vietnamese (2,800), Turks (2,100), and Ukrainians (2,000). Distribution varies widely: university cities like Erfurt, Jena, Weimar, and Ilmenau have the highest concentrations, while rural smaller municipalities have almost none.

input: By the early 1970s, softer songs by artists like The Carpenters, Anne Murray, John Denver, Barry Manilow, and even Streisand, began to be played more often on "Top 40" radio and others were added to the mix on many AC stations. Also, some of these stations even played softer songs by Elvis Presley, Linda Ronstadt, Elton John, Rod Stewart, Billy Joel, and other rock-based artists.
