input: With the death of Zhengde and ascension of Jiajing, the politics at court shifted in favor of the Neo-Confucian establishment which not only rejected the Portuguese embassy of Fernão Pires de Andrade (d. 1523), but had a predisposed animosity towards Tibetan Buddhism and lamas. Evelyn S. Rawski, a professor in the Department of History of the University of Pittsburgh, writes that the Ming's unique relationship with Tibetan prelates essentially ended with Jiajing's reign while Ming influence in the Amdo region was supplanted by the Mongols.
rewrite: Following the death of Zhengde and the rise of Jiajing, court politics moved to favor the Neo-Confucian establishment. This group not only spurned the Portuguese embassy led by Fernão Pires de Andrade (d. 1523) but also held a deep-seated animosity toward Tibetan Buddhism and its lamas. As noted by University of Pittsburgh history professor Evelyn S. Rawski, the Ming dynasty's distinctive ties with Tibetan prelates largely concluded under Jiajing. Concurrently, Mongol influence replaced that of the Ming in the Amdo region.

input: St. John's served as the capital city of the Colony of Newfoundland and the Dominion of Newfoundland before Newfoundland became Canada's tenth province in 1949. The city now serves as the capital of Newfoundland and Labrador, therefore the provincial legislature is located in the city. The Confederation Building, located on Confederation Hill, is home to the House of Assembly along with the offices for the Members of the House of Assembly (MHAs) and Ministers. The city is represented by ten MHAs, four who are members of the governing Progressive Conservative Party, three that belong to the New Democratic Party (NDP), and three that belong to the Liberal Party. Lorraine Michael, leader of the NDP since 2006, represents the district of Signal Hill-Quidi Vidi.
rewrite: Before Newfoundland joined Canada as its tenth province in 1949, St. John's was the capital of both the Colony and Dominion of Newfoundland. Today, it remains the capital of the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, hosting the provincial legislature. The House of Assembly, along with offices for Ministers and Members of the House of Assembly (MHAs), is situated in the Confederation Building on Confederation Hill. Represented by ten MHAs, the city's current delegation includes four from the governing Progressive Conservative Party, three from the New Democratic Party (NDP), and three from the Liberal Party. Since 2006, the NDP has been led by Lorraine Michael, who represents the Signal Hill-Quidi Vidi district.

input: The Crimean War was a military conflict fought between October 1853 – March 1856 in which Russia lost to an alliance of France, the United Kingdom, the Ottoman Empire, and Sardinia. The immediate cause involved the rights of Christian minorities in the Holy Land, which was controlled by the Ottoman Empire. The French promoted the rights of Catholics, while Russia promoted those of the Eastern Orthodox Christians. The longer-term causes involved the decline of the Ottoman Empire and the unwillingness of the United Kingdom and France to allow Russia to gain territory and power at Ottoman expense. It has widely been noted that the causes, in one case involving an argument over a key, have never revealed a "greater confusion of purpose", yet led to a war noted for its "notoriously incompetent international butchery."
rewrite: Fought from October 1853 to March 1856, the Crimean War resulted in a Russian defeat by an alliance comprising France, the United Kingdom, the Ottoman Empire, and Sardinia. While the immediate trigger centered on disputes over the rights of Christian minorities in the Ottoman-controlled Holy Land—with France backing Catholics and Russia supporting Eastern Orthodox Christians—the longer-term causes were rooted in the Ottoman Empire’s decline. Britain and France were determined to prevent Russia from expanding its territory and influence at the Ottomans’ expense. Historians have observed that the causes, at times as trivial as a quarrel over a key, displayed a “greater confusion of purpose,” yet produced a conflict infamous for its “notoriously incompetent international butchery.”

input: Private CBC affiliates are not as common as they were in the past, as many such stations have been purchased either by the CBC itself or by Canwest Global or CHUM Limited, respectively becoming E! or A-Channel (later A, now CTV Two) stations. One private CBC affiliate, CHBC-TV in Kelowna, joined E! (then known as CH) on February 27, 2006. When a private CBC affiliate reaffiliates with another network, the CBC has normally added a retransmitter of its nearest O&O station to ensure that CBC service is continued. However, due to an agreement between CHBC and CFJC-TV in Kamloops, CFJC also disaffiliated from the CBC on February 27, 2006, but no retransmitters were installed in the licence area. Former private CBC affiliates CKPG-TV Prince George and CHAT-TV Medicine Hat disaffiliated on August 31, 2008 and joined E!, but the CBC announced it will not add new retransmitters to these areas. Incidentally, CFJC, CKPG and CHAT are all owned by an independent media company, Jim Pattison Group. With the closure of E! and other changes in the media landscape, several former CBC affiliates have since joined City or Global, or closed altogether.
rewrite: Private CBC affiliates have become less common over time, with many being acquired by the CBC itself, Canwest Global, or CHUM Limited, often rebranding as E! or A-Channel (later A, now CTV Two). When such a station switches to another network, the CBC typically ensures continued service by installing a retransmitter of its nearest owned-and-operated station. However, there have been exceptions. For instance, CHBC-TV in Kelowna joined E! (then CH) on February 27, 2006. That same day, CFJC-TV in Kamloops also ended its CBC affiliation under an agreement with CHBC, but no retransmitters were added in that licence area. Similarly, CKPG-TV in Prince George and CHAT-TV in Medicine Hat left the CBC on August 31, 2008, to join E!, with the CBC announcing it would not provide new retransmitters for these regions. Notably, CFJC, CKPG, and CHAT are all owned by the independent Jim Pattison Group. Following the closure of E! and broader industry shifts, several former CBC affiliates have since aligned with City or Global, or ceased operations entirely.

input: Available web browsers range in features from minimal, text-based user interfaces with bare-bones support for HTML to rich user interfaces supporting a wide variety of file formats and protocols. Browsers which include additional components to support e-mail, Usenet news, and Internet Relay Chat (IRC), are sometimes referred to as "Internet suites" rather than merely "web browsers".
rewrite: Web browsers vary from simple text-based interfaces with basic HTML support to feature-rich ones handling diverse formats and protocols. Some, equipped with extra components for email, Usenet news, and IRC, are called "Internet suites" instead of just "web browsers."

input: While West had encountered controversy a year prior when he stormed out of the American Music Awards of 2004 after losing Best New Artist, the rapper's first large-scale controversy came just days following Late Registration's release, during a benefit concert for Hurricane Katrina victims. In September 2005, NBC broadcast A Concert for Hurricane Relief, and West was a featured speaker. When West was presenting alongside actor Mike Myers, he deviated from the prepared script. Myers spoke next and continued to read the script. Once it was West's turn to speak again, he said, "George Bush doesn't care about black people." West's comment reached much of the United States, leading to mixed reactions; President Bush would later call it one of the most "disgusting moments" of his presidency. West raised further controversy in January 2006 when he posed on the cover of Rolling Stone wearing a crown of thorns.
rewrite: The rapper’s first major controversy erupted just days after the release of Late Registration, during a Hurricane Katrina benefit concert in September 2005. This followed an earlier incident a year prior, when West had stormed out of the 2004 American Music Awards after losing Best New Artist. At the televised NBC broadcast, A Concert for Hurricane Relief, West was a featured speaker. Presenting alongside actor Mike Myers, he deviated from the script. After Myers continued reading the prepared remarks, West again took his turn and declared, “George Bush doesn’t care about black people.” His comment reached a national audience, sparking mixed reactions; President Bush later called it one of the most “disgusting moments” of his presidency. Further controversy arose in January 2006, when West appeared on the cover of Rolling Stone wearing a crown of thorns.

input: Where old disc recordings are considered to be of artistic or historic interest, from before the era of tape or where no tape master exists, archivists play back the disc on suitable equipment and record the result, typically onto a digital format, which can be copied and manipulated to remove analog flaws without any further damage to the source recording. For example, Nimbus Records uses a specially built horn record player to transfer 78s. Anyone can do this using a standard record player with a suitable pickup, a phono-preamp (pre-amplifier) and a typical personal computer. However, for accurate transfer, professional archivists carefully choose the correct stylus shape and diameter, tracking weight, equalisation curve and other playback parameters and use high-quality analogue-to-digital converters.
rewrite: When old disc recordings hold artistic or historical value—particularly from before the tape era or when no tape master survives—archivists play them on appropriate equipment. The playback is typically recorded into a digital format. This digital copy can then be reproduced and enhanced to correct analog imperfections, preventing further harm to the original source. While anyone can attempt this with a standard record player, a suitable pickup, a preamp, and a computer, professional transfer requires precision. Experts meticulously select the proper stylus shape and size, tracking weight, equalization curve, and other parameters, employing high-quality analog-to-digital converters. For instance, Nimbus Records utilizes a custom-built horn record player to convert 78 rpm discs.

input: During her childhood, Madonna was inspired by actors, later saying, "I loved Carole Lombard and Judy Holliday and Marilyn Monroe. They were all incredibly funny ... and I saw myself in them ... my girlishness, my knowingness and my innocence." Her "Material Girl" music video recreated Monroe's look in the song "Diamonds Are a Girl's Best Friend", from the film Gentlemen Prefer Blondes (1953). She studied the screwball comedies of the 1930s, particularly those of Lombard, in preparation for the film Who's That Girl. The video for "Express Yourself" (1989) was inspired by Fritz Lang's silent film Metropolis (1927). The video for "Vogue" recreated the style of Hollywood glamour photographs, in particular those by Horst P. Horst, and imitated the poses of Marlene Dietrich, Carole Lombard, and Rita Hayworth, while the lyrics referred to many of the stars who had inspired her, including Bette Davis, described by Madonna as an idol. However, Madonna's film career has been largely received negatively by the film critic community. Stephanie Zacharek, critic for Time magazine, stated that, "[Madonna] seems wooden and unnatural as an actress, and it's tough to watch, because she's clearly trying her damnedest." According to biographer Andrew Morton, "Madonna puts a brave face on the criticism, but privately she is deeply hurt." After the box office bomb Swept Away (2002), Madonna vowed that she would never again act in a film, hoping her repertoire as a bad actress would never be discussed again.
rewrite:
Inspired by actors from a young age, Madonna once reflected, “I loved Carole Lombard and Judy Holliday and Marilyn Monroe. They were all incredibly funny ... and I saw myself in them ... my girlishness, my knowingness and my innocence.” This admiration manifested throughout her career. Her “Material Girl” video recreated Monroe’s iconic look from “Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend” in *Gentlemen Prefer Blondes* (1953). For the film *Who’s That Girl*, she studied 1930s screwball comedies, especially Lombard’s work. The visual for “Express Yourself” (1989) drew inspiration from Fritz Lang’s silent classic *Metropolis* (1927). Similarly, the “Vogue” video emulated Hollywood glamour photography, notably the style of Horst P. Horst, and mimicked poses of stars like Marlene Dietrich, Carole Lombard, and Rita Hayworth. Its lyrics also paid homage to inspirations such as Bette Davis, whom Madonna called an idol.

Despite these creative homages, Madonna’s film career has faced harsh criticism. Film critics have largely panned her acting. *Time* magazine critic Stephanie Zacharek noted, “[Madonna] seems wooden and unnatural as an actress, and it’s tough to watch, because she’s clearly trying her damnedest.” Biographer Andrew Morton revealed that while Madonna publicly braves the criticism, she is privately deeply hurt. Following the commercial failure of *Swept Away* (2002), she vowed never to act in a film again, hoping her reputation as a poor actress would be forgotten.

input: Another common application is the control of the throttle of an internal combustion engine in conjunction with an electronic governor. In this usage, the motor works against a return spring to move the throttle in accordance with the output of the governor. The latter monitors engine speed by counting electrical pulses from the ignition system or from a magnetic pickup and, depending on the speed, makes small adjustments to the amount of current applied to the motor. If the engine starts to slow down relative to the desired speed, the current will be increased, the motor will develop more torque, pulling against the return spring and opening the throttle. Should the engine run too fast, the governor will reduce the current being applied to the motor, causing the return spring to pull back and close the throttle.
rewrite: A frequent use involves managing an internal combustion engine's throttle alongside an electronic governor. Here, the motor operates against a return spring to adjust the throttle based on the governor's signal. The governor tracks engine speed by counting pulses from the ignition or a magnetic pickup. Depending on the speed, it slightly alters the current sent to the motor. Should the engine begin to slow below the target speed, current is raised, increasing the motor's torque to pull against the spring and open the throttle. Conversely, if the engine runs too fast, the governor decreases the current, allowing the return spring to close the throttle.

input: Sometimes people of mixed African-American and Native American descent report having had elder family members withholding pertinent genealogical information. Tracing the genealogy of African Americans can be a very difficult process, as censuses did not identify slaves by name before the American Civil War, meaning that most African Americans did not appear by name in those records. In addition, many white fathers who used slave women sexually, even those in long-term relationships like Thomas Jefferson's with Sally Hemings, did not acknowledge their mixed-race slave children in records, so paternity was lost.
rewrite: For many with African-American and Native American heritage, elder relatives have sometimes withheld key genealogical details. Tracing African-American ancestry is particularly challenging because pre-Civil War censuses did not name enslaved individuals, omitting most from official records. Furthermore, white fathers, such as Thomas Jefferson with Sally Hemings, often failed to acknowledge their children born to enslaved women, even in long-term relationships, thereby erasing paternity from historical documents.

input: Minute Maid Park (home of the Astros) and Toyota Center (home of the Rockets), are located in downtown Houston. Houston has the NFL's first retractable-roof stadium with natural grass, NRG Stadium (home of the Texans). Minute Maid Park is also a retractable-roof stadium. Toyota Center also has the largest screen for an indoor arena in the United States built to coincide with the arena's hosting of the 2013 NBA All-Star Game. BBVA Compass Stadium is a soccer-specific stadium for the Dynamo, the Texas Southern University football team, and Dash, located in East Downtown. In addition, NRG Astrodome was the first indoor stadium in the world, built in 1965. Other sports facilities include Hofheinz Pavilion (Houston Cougars basketball), Rice Stadium (Rice Owls football), and Reliant Arena. TDECU Stadium is where the University of Houston Houston Cougars football team plays. Houston has hosted several major sports events: the 1968, 1986 and 2004 Major League Baseball All-Star Games; the 1989, 2006 and 2013 NBA All-Star Games; Super Bowl VIII and Super Bowl XXXVIII, as well as hosting the 2005 World Series and 1981, 1986, 1994 and 1995 NBA Finals, winning the latter two. Super Bowl LI is currently slated to be hosted in NRG Stadium in 2017.
rewrite: Downtown Houston is home to Minute Maid Park, where the Astros play, and the Toyota Center, home of the Rockets. The city also features NRG Stadium, the NFL's first retractable-roof venue with natural grass, hosting the Texans. Notably, Minute Maid Park also features a retractable roof. For soccer, BBVA Compass Stadium in East Downtown serves the Dynamo, Dash, and the Texas Southern University football team. The historic NRG Astrodome, constructed in 1965, was the world's first indoor stadium. Additional facilities include Hofheinz Pavilion for Houston Cougars basketball, Rice Stadium for Rice Owls football, Reliant Arena, and TDECU Stadium, where the University of Houston football team competes. The Toyota Center boasts the largest indoor arena screen in the United States, installed for the 2013 NBA All-Star Game. Houston has a rich history of hosting major events, including MLB All-Star Games in 1968, 1986, and 2004; NBA All-Star Games in 1989, 2006, and 2013; Super Bowls VIII and XXXVIII; the 2005 World Series; and the NBA Finals in 1981, 1986, 1994, and 1995, with championships in the latter two. Looking ahead, Super Bowl LI is scheduled for NRG Stadium in 2017.

input: Numerous major American cultural movements began in the city, such as the Harlem Renaissance, which established the African-American literary canon in the United States. The city was a center of jazz in the 1940s, abstract expressionism in the 1950s, and the birthplace of hip hop in the 1970s. The city's punk and hardcore scenes were influential in the 1970s and 1980s. New York has long had a flourishing scene for Jewish American literature.
rewrite: The city has been the origin of many major American cultural movements. It launched the Harlem Renaissance, establishing the African-American literary canon, and was the birthplace of hip hop in the 1970s. Earlier, it served as a center for 1940s jazz and 1950s abstract expressionism. Its influential punk and hardcore scenes emerged in the 1970s and 1980s, and it has long fostered a flourishing scene for Jewish American literature.

input: Richard Phillips Feynman was born on May 11, 1918, in Queens, New York City, the son of Lucille (née Phillips), a homemaker, and Melville Arthur Feynman, a sales manager. His family originated from Russia and Poland; both of his parents were Ashkenazi Jews. They were not religious, and by his youth Feynman described himself as an "avowed atheist". He also stated "To select, for approbation the peculiar elements that come from some supposedly Jewish heredity is to open the door to all kinds of nonsense on racial theory," and adding "... at thirteen I was not only converted to other religious views, but I also stopped believing that the Jewish people are in any way 'the chosen people'." Later in his life, during a visit to the Jewish Theological Seminary, he encountered the Talmud for the first time, and remarked that he found it a "wonderful book" and "valuable".
rewrite: Born in Queens, New York City on May 11, 1918, Richard Phillips Feynman was the son of Melville Arthur Feynman, a sales manager, and Lucille (née Phillips), a homemaker. His parents, both Ashkenazi Jews with family roots in Russia and Poland, were not religious. Feynman himself became an "avowed atheist" in his youth. He rejected the notion of any special Jewish heredity, stating such selection "is to open the door to all kinds of nonsense on racial theory." By age thirteen, he had abandoned the belief that Jewish people were "the chosen people." Decades later, however, during a visit to the Jewish Theological Seminary, he encountered the Talmud for the first time and remarked on its value, calling it a "wonderful book."

input: In 118 BC, King Micipsa of Numidia (current-day Algeria and Tunisia) died. He was succeeded by two legitimate sons, Adherbal and Hiempsal, and an illegitimate son, Jugurtha. Micipsa divided his kingdom between these three sons. Jugurtha, however, turned on his brothers, killing Hiempsal and driving Adherbal out of Numidia. Adherbal fled to Rome for assistance, and initially Rome mediated a division of the country between the two brothers. Eventually, Jugurtha renewed his offensive, leading to a long and inconclusive war with Rome. He also bribed several Roman commanders, and at least two tribunes, before and during the war. His nemesis, Gaius Marius, a legate from a virtually unknown provincial family, returned from the war in Numidia and was elected consul in 107 BC over the objections of the aristocratic senators. Marius invaded Numidia and brought the war to a quick end, capturing Jugurtha in the process. The apparent incompetence of the Senate, and the brilliance of Marius, had been put on full display. The populares party took full advantage of this opportunity by allying itself with Marius.
rewrite: Upon the death of Numidia's King Micipsa in 118 BC, his kingdom, located in what is now Algeria and Tunisia, was divided among his two legitimate sons, Adherbal and Hiempsal, and his illegitimate son, Jugurtha. Jugurtha soon betrayed his brothers, murdering Hiempsal and forcing Adherbal to flee to Rome for aid. Rome initially mediated a partition of Numidia between the surviving brothers, but Jugurtha renewed his aggression, sparking a protracted and indecisive war. Throughout this conflict, he secured favor by bribing multiple Roman commanders and at least two tribunes. The war concluded when Gaius Marius, a legate from an obscure provincial family, returned from Numidia. Overcoming senatorial opposition, he was elected consul in 107 BC. Marius promptly invaded, swiftly ended the war, and captured Jugurtha. This sequence starkly revealed the Senate's apparent incompetence and Marius's brilliance, an opportunity the populares party seized by forming an alliance with the victorious consul.

input: The sixty-one year reign of the Kangxi Emperor was the longest of any Chinese emperor. Kangxi's reign is also celebrated as the beginning of an era known as the "High Qing", during which the dynasty reached the zenith of its social, economic and military power. Kangxi's long reign started when he was eight years old upon the untimely demise of his father. To prevent a repeat of Dorgon's dictatorial monopolizing of power during the regency, the Shunzhi Emperor, on his deathbed, hastily appointed four senior cabinet ministers to govern on behalf of his young son. The four ministers — Sonin, Ebilun, Suksaha, and Oboi — were chosen for their long service, but also to counteract each other's influences. Most important, the four were not closely related to the imperial family and laid no claim to the throne. However, as time passed, through chance and machination, Oboi, the most junior of the four, achieved such political dominance as to be a potential threat. Even though Oboi's loyalty was never an issue, his personal arrogance and political conservatism led him into an escalating conflict with the young emperor. In 1669 Kangxi, through trickery, disarmed and imprisoned Oboi — a significant victory for a fifteen-year-old emperor over a wily politician and experienced commander.
rewrite: The Kangxi Emperor’s sixty-one-year rule stands as the longest reign in Chinese imperial history, marking the start of the prosperous "High Qing" era when the dynasty attained peak social, economic, and military strength. His lengthy tenure began at age eight following his father’s sudden death. To avoid a recurrence of dictatorial regency like that of Dorgon, the Shunzhi Emperor, on his deathbed, quickly appointed four senior cabinet ministers—Sonin, Ebilun, Suksaha, and Oboi—to govern for his young heir. Selected for their extensive service and to balance each other’s power, these ministers held no close familial ties to the throne and posed no claim to it. Over time, however, Oboi, initially the most junior among them, maneuvered to achieve overwhelming political dominance, emerging as a potential threat. Though never accused of disloyalty, Oboi’s personal arrogance and conservative policies fueled growing tensions with the adolescent emperor. In a decisive move in 1669, the fifteen-year-old Kangxi used subterfuge to disarm and imprison Oboi, securing a major victory over the seasoned and cunning commander.

input: The FAA gradually assumed additional functions. The hijacking epidemic of the 1960s had already brought the agency into the field of civil aviation security. In response to the hijackings on September 11, 2001, this responsibility is now primarily taken by the Department of Homeland Security. The FAA became more involved with the environmental aspects of aviation in 1968 when it received the power to set aircraft noise standards. Legislation in 1970 gave the agency management of a new airport aid program and certain added responsibilities for airport safety. During the 1960s and 1970s, the FAA also started to regulate high altitude (over 500 feet) kite and balloon flying.
rewrite: Initially drawn into civil aviation security due to the hijacking epidemic of the 1960s, the FAA saw that responsibility shift primarily to the Department of Homeland Security following the events of September 11, 2001. The agency expanded its environmental role in 1968 by gaining authority to set aircraft noise standards. Further legislation in 1970 granted it management of a new airport aid program and additional airport safety duties. Throughout the 1960s and 1970s, the FAA also began regulating high-altitude kite and balloon flights above 500 feet, as it gradually assumed more functions.

input: In 1654, Otto von Guericke invented the first vacuum pump and conducted his famous Magdeburg hemispheres experiment, showing that teams of horses could not separate two hemispheres from which the air had been partially evacuated. Robert Boyle improved Guericke's design and with the help of Robert Hooke further developed vacuum pump technology. Thereafter, research into the partial vacuum lapsed until 1850 when August Toepler invented the Toepler Pump and Heinrich Geissler invented the mercury displacement pump in 1855, achieving a partial vacuum of about 10 Pa (0.1 Torr). A number of electrical properties become observable at this vacuum level, which renewed interest in further research.
rewrite: Otto von Guericke invented the first vacuum pump in 1654, demonstrating its power through the Magdeburg hemispheres experiment, where horses could not pull apart the evacuated spheres. Later improvements were made by Robert Boyle and Robert Hooke. Interest in partial vacuums then waned until the mid-19th century, when August Toepler created the Toepler Pump in 1850 and Heinrich Geissler developed the mercury displacement pump in 1855. These achieved a vacuum of around 10 Pa, a level at which various electrical properties become evident, reigniting scientific curiosity and driving further investigation.

input: The Han-era family was patrilineal and typically had four to five nuclear family members living in one household. Multiple generations of extended family members did not occupy the same house, unlike families of later dynasties. According to Confucian family norms, various family members were treated with different levels of respect and intimacy. For example, there were different accepted time frames for mourning the death of a father versus a paternal uncle. Arranged marriages were normal, with the father's input on his offspring's spouse being considered more important than the mother's. Monogamous marriages were also normal, although nobles and high officials were wealthy enough to afford and support concubines as additional lovers. Under certain conditions dictated by custom, not law, both men and women were able to divorce their spouses and remarry.
rewrite: Han-era families followed a patrilineal structure, usually comprising four to five nuclear members in a single household. Unlike in later dynasties, extended families spanning multiple generations did not typically cohabit. Confucian norms dictated distinct levels of respect and intimacy among relatives; for instance, mourning periods differed for a father compared to a paternal uncle. Marriages were ordinarily arranged, with the father’s opinion on a child’s spouse outweighing the mother’s. While monogamy was standard, nobles and high officials often maintained concubines. Custom, rather than law, permitted both men and women to divorce and remarry under specific conditions.

input: Part of the Russian resistance was credited[by whom?] to the deployment of newly invented blockade mines. Perhaps the most influential contributor to the development of naval mining was a Swede resident in Russia, the inventor and civil engineer Immanuel Nobel (the father of Alfred Nobel). Immanuel Nobel helped the Russian war effort by applying his knowledge of industrial explosives, such as nitroglycerin and gunpowder. One account dates modern naval mining from the Crimean War: "Torpedo mines, if I may use this name given by Fulton to self-acting mines underwater, were among the novelties attempted by the Russians in their defences about Cronstadt and Sevastopol", as one American officer put it in 1860.
rewrite: The deployment of newly invented blockade mines was credited[by whom?] with contributing to part of the Russian resistance. A key figure in advancing naval mining was Immanuel Nobel, a Swedish inventor and civil engineer residing in Russia, who was also the father of Alfred Nobel. He applied his expertise in industrial explosives like nitroglycerin and gunpowder to aid the Russian war effort. Modern naval mining is often dated to the Crimean War. As an American officer noted in 1860, "Torpedo mines, if I may use this name given by Fulton to self-acting mines underwater, were among the novelties attempted by the Russians in their defences about Cronstadt and Sevastopol."

input: In 1838, Claridge obtained patents in Scotland on 27 March, and Ireland on 23 April, and in 1851 extensions were sought for all three patents, by the trustees of a company previously formed by Claridge. This was Claridge's Patent Asphalte Company, formed in 1838 for the purpose of introducing to Britain "Asphalte in its natural state from the mine at Pyrimont Seysell in France", and "laid one of the first asphalt pavements in Whitehall". Trials were made of the pavement in 1838 on the footway in Whitehall, the stable at Knightsbridge Barracks, "and subsequently on the space at the bottom of the steps leading from Waterloo Place to St. James Park". "The formation in 1838 of Claridge's Patent Asphalte Company (with a distinguished list of aristocratic patrons, and Marc and Isambard Brunel as, respectively, a trustee and consulting engineer), gave an enormous impetus to the development of a British asphalt industry". "By the end of 1838, at least two other companies, Robinson's and the Bastenne company, were in production", with asphalt being laid as paving at Brighton, Herne Bay, Canterbury, Kensington, the Strand, and a large floor area in Bunhill-row, while meantime Claridge's Whitehall paving "continue(d) in good order".
rewrite: On March 27, 1838, Claridge secured a patent in Scotland, followed by another in Ireland on April 23. That same year, Claridge’s Patent Asphalte Company was established to bring natural asphalt from the Pyrimont Seysell mine in France to Britain. The company soon laid one of the nation’s first asphalt pavements in Whitehall. Initial trials in 1838 included sections of the Whitehall footway, the stable at Knightsbridge Barracks, and later the area at the base of the steps from Waterloo Place into St. James Park. This enterprise, supported by an impressive roster of aristocratic patrons and with Marc and Isambard Brunel serving as trustee and consulting engineer, provided a major boost to the British asphalt industry. By the close of 1838, at least two additional firms—Robinson’s and the Bastenne company—were also producing asphalt, which was used for paving in locations such as Brighton, Herne Bay, Canterbury, Kensington, the Strand, and a large floor in Bunhill-row. Meanwhile, Claridge’s original Whitehall pavement remained in good condition. In 1851, extensions for all three of Claridge’s patents were sought by the trustees of the company he had earlier founded.

input: In South Australia, initially a Liberal and Country Party affiliated party, the Liberal and Country League (LCL), mostly led by Premier of South Australia Tom Playford, was in power from the 1933 election to the 1965 election, though with assistance from an electoral malapportionment, or gerrymander, known as the Playmander. The LCL's Steele Hall governed for one term from the 1968 election to the 1970 election and during this time began the process of dismantling the Playmander. David Tonkin, as leader of the South Australian Division of the Liberal Party of Australia, became Premier at the 1979 election for one term, losing office at the 1982 election. The Liberals returned to power at the 1993 election, led by Premiers Dean Brown, John Olsen and Rob Kerin through two terms, until their defeat at the 2002 election. They have since remained in opposition under a record five Opposition Leaders.
rewrite: From the 1933 to 1965 elections, South Australia was governed by the Liberal and Country League (LCL), a party aligned with the Liberal and Country Party and predominantly led by Premier Tom Playford. This extended tenure was aided by an electoral gerrymander known as the Playmander. Following this period, the LCL's Steele Hall governed from 1968 to 1970 and initiated the dismantling of the Playmander. Later, David Tonkin, leading the state Liberals, became Premier after the 1979 election, serving one term until 1982. The Liberals regained power at the 1993 election, with Premiers Dean Brown, John Olsen, and Rob Kerin leading for two terms until their 2002 defeat. Since that loss, the party has remained in opposition under a record five consecutive Opposition Leaders.

input: The phrase "in whole or in part" has been subject to much discussion by scholars of international humanitarian law. The International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia found in Prosecutor v. Radislav Krstic – Trial Chamber I – Judgment – IT-98-33 (2001) ICTY8 (2 August 2001) that Genocide had been committed. In Prosecutor v. Radislav Krstic – Appeals Chamber – Judgment – IT-98-33 (2004) ICTY 7 (19 April 2004) paragraphs 8, 9, 10, and 11 addressed the issue of in part and found that "the part must be a substantial part of that group. The aim of the Genocide Convention is to prevent the intentional destruction of entire human groups, and the part targeted must be significant enough to have an impact on the group as a whole." The Appeals Chamber goes into details of other cases and the opinions of respected commentators on the Genocide Convention to explain how they came to this conclusion.
rewrite: Scholars of international humanitarian law have extensively debated the phrase "in whole or in part." This issue was addressed in the *Prosecutor v. Radislav Krstic* case before the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia. The initial Trial Chamber judgment in 2001 found that genocide had been committed. Later, the 2004 Appeals Chamber judgment, specifically in paragraphs 8 through 11, examined the meaning of "in part." It concluded that "the part must be a substantial part of that group," noting that the Genocide Convention aims to prevent the intentional destruction of entire human groups. Therefore, the targeted segment must be significant enough to impact the group collectively. To reach this determination, the Appeals Chamber detailed relevant precedents and considered the opinions of respected commentators on the Genocide Convention.

input: Iran received access to the Internet in 1993. According to 2014 census, around 40% of the population of Iran are Internet users. Iran ranks 24th among countries by number of Internet users. According to the statistics provided by the web information company of Alexa, Google Search and Yahoo! are the most used search engines in Iran. Over 80% of the users of Telegram, a cloud-based instant messaging service, are from Iran. Instagram is the most popular online social networking service in Iran. Direct access to Facebook has been blocked in Iran since the 2009 Iranian presidential election protests, due to organization of the opposition movements on the website; but however, Facebook has around 12 to 17 million users in Iran who are using virtual private networks and proxy servers to access the website. Around 90% of Iran's e-commerce takes place on the Iranian online store of Digikala, which has around 750,000 visitors per day and more than 2.3 million subscribers. Digikala is the most visited online store in the Middle East, and ranks 4th among the most visited websites in Iran.
rewrite: Internet access first became available in Iran in 1993. As of a 2014 census, approximately 40% of the nation's population were Internet users, ranking Iran 24th globally by this metric. The most visited websites in the country, according to Alexa, include the online store Digikala, which holds a dominant position in local e-commerce. Around 90% of Iran's online shopping occurs through Digikala, attracting about 750,000 daily visitors and boasting over 2.3 million subscribers. This makes it the most visited online store in the Middle East and the fourth most visited website within Iran. Regarding search engines, Google Search and Yahoo! are the most frequently used. In social networking, Instagram is the most popular service. The cloud-based messaging app Telegram has a user base comprising over 80% Iranian members. Although direct access to Facebook has been blocked since the 2009 presidential election protests—due to its use by opposition movements—an estimated 12 to 17 million Iranians still use the platform via virtual private networks and proxy servers.

input: The term "Kievan Rus'" (Ки́евская Русь Kievskaya Rus’) was coined in the 19th century in Russian historiography to refer to the period when the centre was in Kiev. In English, the term was introduced in the early 20th century, when it was found in the 1913 English translation of Vasily Klyuchevsky's A History of Russia, to distinguish the early polity from successor states, which were also named Rus. Later, the Russian term was rendered into Belarusian and Ukrainian as Кіеўская Русь Kijeŭskaja Rus’ and Ки́ївська Русь Kyivs'ka Rus’, respectively.
rewrite: Coined in 19th-century Russian historiography, the term "Kievan Rus'" (Ки́евская Русь) designated the period when Kiev was the centre. It entered English usage in the early 20th century, notably appearing in the 1913 translation of Vasily Klyuchevsky's *A History of Russia* to differentiate that early polity from later states also called Rus. The original Russian term was later adapted into Belarusian as Кіеўская Русь and into Ukrainian as Ки́ївська Русь.

input: The Melbourne rail network has its origins in privately built lines from the 1850s gold rush era, and today the suburban network consists of 209 suburban stations on 16 lines which radiate from the City Loop, a partially underground metro section of the network beneath the Central Business District (Hoddle Grid). Flinders Street Station is Melbourne's busiest railway station, and was the world's busiest passenger station in 1926. It remains a prominent Melbourne landmark and meeting place. The city has rail connections with regional Victorian cities, as well as direct interstate rail services to Sydney and Adelaide and beyond which depart from Melbourne's other major rail terminus, Southern Cross Station in Spencer Street. In the 2013–2014 financial year, the Melbourne rail network recorded 232.0 million passenger trips, the highest in its history. Many rail lines, along with dedicated lines and rail yards are also used for freight. The Overland to Adelaide departs Southern Cross twice a week, while the XPT to Sydney departs twice a day.
rewrite: Originating from privately constructed lines during the 1850s gold rush, the Melbourne rail network now features 209 suburban stations across 16 lines. These lines radiate from the City Loop, a partially underground metro section beneath the Central Business District's Hoddle Grid. The network serves both passengers and freight, with many lines and dedicated yards used for cargo. Flinders Street Station, the city's busiest railway station and a world leader in passenger traffic in 1926, endures as a major landmark and popular meeting place. For longer journeys, rail connections link Melbourne to regional Victorian cities. Direct interstate services to Sydney and Adelaide, along with other destinations, operate from the other major terminus, Southern Cross Station on Spencer Street. The Overland service to Adelaide runs twice weekly from Southern Cross, while the XPT to Sydney departs twice daily. Passenger use remains robust, with the network recording a historic high of 232.0 million trips in the 2013–2014 financial year.

input: The Universal Film Manufacturing Company was incorporated in New York on April 30, 1912. Laemmle, who emerged as president in July 1912, was the primary figure in the partnership with Dintenfass, Baumann, Kessel, Powers, Swanson, Horsley, and Brulatour. Eventually all would be bought out by Laemmle. The new Universal studio was a vertically integrated company, with movie production, distribution and exhibition venues all linked in the same corporate entity, the central element of the Studio system era.
rewrite: Incorporated in New York on April 30, 1912, the Universal Film Manufacturing Company saw Carl Laemmle become its president that July. He was the key partner among figures like Dintenfass, Baumann, Kessel, Powers, Swanson, Horsley, and Brulatour, eventually buying them all out. The resulting Universal studio was vertically integrated, a central element of the Studio System era, linking production, distribution, and exhibition within one corporate entity.

input: Kolmaš writes that, as the Mongol presence in Tibet increased, culminating in the conquest of Tibet by a Mongol leader in 1642, the Ming emperors "viewed with apparent unconcern these developments in Tibet." He adds that the Ming court's lack of concern for Tibet was one of the reasons why the Mongols pounced on the chance to reclaim their old vassal of Tibet and "fill once more the political vacuum in that country." On the mass Mongol conversion to Tibetan Buddhism under Altan Khan, Laird writes that "the Chinese watched these developments with interest, though few Chinese ever became devout Tibetan Buddhists."
rewrite: According to Kolmaš, Ming emperors displayed apparent unconcern as Mongol influence grew in Tibet, which culminated in its conquest by a Mongol leader in 1642. He notes this Ming indifference was a factor enabling the Mongols to seize the opportunity to reclaim their former vassal and again fill Tibet's political vacuum. Regarding the widespread Mongol conversion to Tibetan Buddhism under Altan Khan, Laird observes that while the Chinese monitored these events with interest, very few ever adopted Tibetan Buddhism devoutly.

input: From 2000 to 2010, the average cost per asthma-related hospital stay in the United States for children remained relatively stable at about $3,600, whereas the average cost per asthma-related hospital stay for adults increased from $5,200 to $6,600. In 2010, Medicaid was the most frequent primary payer among children and adults aged 18–44 years in the United States; private insurance was the second most frequent payer. Among both children and adults in the lowest income communities in the United States there is a higher rates of hospital stays for asthma in 2010 than those in the highest income communities.
rewrite: Between 2000 and 2010, the average expense for a child's asthma-related hospitalization in the U.S. held steady around $3,600. For adults, however, this cost rose from $5,200 to $6,600 per stay. In 2010, Medicaid served as the primary payer most often for both children and adults aged 18–44, with private insurance ranking second. Furthermore, individuals in the lowest-income communities—both children and adults—experienced higher rates of asthma hospitalizations compared to those in the highest-income communities that same year.

input: According to the scriptures, soon after the parinirvāṇa (from Sanskrit: "highest extinguishment") of Gautama Buddha, the first Buddhist council was held. As with any ancient Indian tradition, transmission of teaching was done orally. The primary purpose of the assembly was to collectively recite the teachings to ensure that no errors occurred in oral transmission. In the first council, Ānanda, a cousin of the Buddha and his personal attendant, was called upon to recite the discourses (sūtras, Pāli suttas) of the Buddha, and, according to some sources, the abhidhamma. Upāli, another disciple, recited the monastic rules (vinaya). Most scholars regard the traditional accounts of the council as greatly exaggerated if not entirely fictitious.[note 36]Richard Gombrich noted Sariputta led communal recitations of the Buddha's teaching for preservation in the Buddha's lifetime in Sangiti Sutta (Digha Nikaya #33), and something similar to the First Council must have taken place to compose Buddhist scriptures.
rewrite: Soon after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa (Sanskrit for "highest extinguishment"), the first Buddhist council was convened, as recorded in scripture. Since teachings in ancient India were transmitted orally, the assembly's main goal was a collective recitation to prevent errors. Ānanda, the Buddha's cousin and attendant, recited the discourses (sūtras), and possibly the abhidhamma. The monastic rules (vinaya) were recited by the disciple Upāli. However, most scholars view traditional accounts of this council as greatly exaggerated or even fictitious. Scholar Richard Gombrich observed that communal recitations for preservation, like those led by Sariputta during the Buddha's life in the Sangiti Sutta, likely occurred. Thus, an event similar to the First Council probably happened to compose the early scriptures.

input: His relationship with Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat of Fatah was strained, with Gaddafi considering him too moderate and calling for more violent action. Instead he supported militia like the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine – General Command, the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine, As-Sa'iqa, the Palestinian Popular Struggle Front, and the Abu Nidal Organization. He funded the Black September Organization who perpetrated the 1972 Munich massacre of Israeli athletes in West Germany, and had the killed militants' bodies flown to Libya for a hero's funeral. Gaddafi also welcomed the three surviving attackers in Tripoli following their release in exchange for the hostages of hijacked Lufthansa Flight 615 a few weeks later and allowed them to go into hiding.
rewrite: Gaddafi viewed Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat of Fatah as excessively moderate, straining their relationship as he advocated for more violent measures. Consequently, he extended his support to more militant factions, including the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, its General Command offshoot, the Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine, As-Sa'iqa, the Palestinian Popular Struggle Front, and the Abu Nidal Organization. He financed the Black September Organization, responsible for the 1972 Munich massacre of Israeli athletes. After the attack, Gaddafi had the slain militants' bodies returned to Libya for a hero's burial. Furthermore, following their release weeks later in a hostage exchange for the hijacked Lufthansa Flight 615, he welcomed the three surviving attackers in Tripoli and provided them sanctuary.

input: A major international priority for Tuvalu in the UN, at the 2002 Earth Summit in Johannesburg, South Africa and in other international fora, is promoting concern about global warming and the possible sea level rising. Tuvalu advocates ratification and implementation of the Kyoto Protocol. In December 2009 the islands stalled talks on climate change at the United Nations Climate Change Conference in Copenhagen, fearing some other developing countries were not committing fully to binding deals on a reduction in carbon emissions. Their chief negotiator stated, "Tuvalu is one of the most vulnerable countries in the world to climate change and our future rests on the outcome of this meeting."
rewrite: At the 2002 Earth Summit in Johannesburg and in other international forums, Tuvalu has made a major priority of raising concern about global warming and potential sea level rise. The nation strongly advocates for the ratification and implementation of the Kyoto Protocol. Fearing insufficient commitments from other developing nations to binding carbon emission reductions, Tuvalu stalled talks at the 2009 Copenhagen Climate Change Conference. Its chief negotiator emphasized the country's acute vulnerability, stating, "Tuvalu is one of the most vulnerable countries in the world to climate change and our future rests on the outcome of this meeting."

input: With the six consistories, Paul VI continued the internationalization policies started by Pius XII in 1946 and continued by John XXIII. In his 1976 consistory, five of twenty cardinals originated from Africa, one of them a son of a tribal chief with fifty wives. Several prominent Latin Americans like Eduardo Francisco Pironio of Argentina; Luis Aponte Martinez of Puerto Rico and Eugênio de Araújo Sales and Aloisio Lorscheider from Brazil were also elevated by him. There were voices within the Church at the time saying that the European period of the Church was coming to a close, a view shared by Britain's Cardinal Basil Hume. At the same time, the members of the College of Cardinals lost some of their previous influences, after Paul VI decreed, that not only cardinals but also bishops too may participate in committees of the Roman Curia. The age limit of eighty years imposed by the Pope, a numerical increase of Cardinals by almost 100%, and a reform of the regal vestments of the "Princes of the Church" further contributed to a service-oriented perception of Cardinals under his pontificate. The increased number of Cardinals from the Third World and the papal emphasis on related issues was nevertheless welcomed by many in Western Europe.
rewrite:
During his pontificate, Paul VI furthered the internationalization of the Church, a policy initiated by Pius XII in 1946 and advanced by John XXIII. This was evident across his six consistories. His 1976 consistory notably included five African cardinals, one of whom was the son of a tribal chief with fifty wives. He also elevated prominent Latin Americans such as Argentina's Eduardo Francisco Pironio, Puerto Rico's Luis Aponte Martinez, and Brazil's Eugênio de Araújo Sales and Aloisio Lorscheider. Many within the Church, including Britain's Cardinal Basil Hume, felt this signaled the end of the Church's traditionally European-dominated era.

Concurrently, Paul VI enacted reforms that shifted the role of cardinals. A decree allowed bishops, not just cardinals, to participate in Roman Curia committees, diminishing the exclusive influence of the College of Cardinals. An age limit of eighty for voting in conclaves, a near doubling of the cardinalate's size, and a simplification of their regal vestments all fostered a more service-oriented perception of these "Princes of the Church." While these changes reduced some traditional privileges, the increased representation from the Third World and the papal focus on global issues were broadly welcomed in Western Europe.

input: KU's Edwards Campus is in Overland Park, Kansas. Established in 1993, its goal is to provide adults with the opportunity to complete college degrees. Programs available at the Edwards Campus include developmental psychology, public administration, social work, systems analysis, information technology, engineering management and design.

With an average student age of 32, around 2,100 individuals attend. Available programs span fields such as developmental psychology, public administration, social work, systems analysis, information technology, engineering management, and design.

input: West demonstrated an affinity for the arts at an early age; he began writing poetry when he was five years old. His mother recalled that she first took notice of West's passion for drawing and music when he was in the third grade. Growing up in the city,[which?] West became deeply involved in its hip hop scene. He started rapping in the third grade and began making musical compositions in the seventh grade, eventually selling them to other artists. At age thirteen, West wrote a rap song called "Green Eggs and Ham" and began to persuade his mother to pay $25 an hour for time in a recording studio. It was a small, crude basement studio where a microphone hung from the ceiling by a wire clothes hanger. Although this wasn't what West's mother wanted, she nonetheless supported him. West crossed paths with producer/DJ No I.D., with whom he quickly formed a close friendship. No I.D. soon became West's mentor, and it was from him that West learned how to sample and program beats after he received his first sampler at age 15.

input: Other sources include fortified food and dietary supplements, which come in various forms. A 1998 review concluded that zinc oxide, one of the most common supplements in the United States, and zinc carbonate are nearly insoluble and poorly absorbed in the body. This review cited studies which found low plasma zinc concentrations after zinc oxide and zinc carbonate were consumed compared with those seen after consumption of zinc acetate and sulfate salts. However, harmful excessive supplementation is a problem among the relatively affluent, and should probably not exceed 20 mg/day in healthy people, although the U.S. National Research Council set a Tolerable Upper Intake of 40 mg/day.

Research from a 1998 review indicated that common supplements like zinc oxide and zinc carbonate are poorly absorbed due to their near insolubility. Supporting studies noted lower plasma zinc levels following intake of these compounds compared to more absorbable forms like zinc acetate and sulfate. Excessive supplementation, particularly a concern in wealthier populations, is harmful; for healthy individuals, intake should likely stay under 20 mg daily.
