input: The eastern shoreline of Funafuti Lagoon was modified during World War II when the airfield (what is now Funafuti International Airport) was constructed. The coral base of the atoll was used as fill to create the runway. The resulting borrow pits impacted the fresh-water aquifer. In the low areas of Funafuti the sea water can be seen bubbling up through the porous coral rock to form pools with each high tide. Since 1994 a project has been in development to assess the environmental impact of transporting sand from the lagoon to fill all the borrow pits and low-lying areas on Fongafale. In 2014 the Tuvalu Borrow Pits Remediation (BPR) project was approved in order to fill 10 borrow pits, leaving Tafua Pond, which is a natural pond. The New Zealand Government funded the BPR project. The project was carried out in 2015 with 365,000 sqm of sand being dredged from the lagoon to fill the holes and improve living conditions on the island. This project increase the usable land space on Fongafale by eight per cent.
rewrite: During World War II, the construction of an airfield—now Funafuti International Airport—altered the eastern shoreline of Funafuti Lagoon. To build the runway, fill material was taken from the atoll’s coral base, creating borrow pits that damaged the fresh-water aquifer. In Funafuti’s low-lying zones, seawater visibly bubbles up through the porous coral rock with each high tide, forming pools. A project to study the effects of using lagoon sand to fill these borrow pits and other low areas on Fongafale has been under consideration since 1994. Approved in 2014, the Tuvalu Borrow Pits Remediation (BPR) project aimed to fill ten borrow pits, excluding the natural Tafua Pond. Funded by the New Zealand Government and implemented in 2015, the project dredged 365,000 square meters of sand from the lagoon to fill the holes, enhancing island living conditions. This effort expanded Fongafale’s usable land area by eight percent.

input: Rebirth refers to a process whereby beings go through a succession of lifetimes as one of many possible forms of sentient life, each running from conception to death. The doctrine of anattā (Sanskrit anātman) rejects the concepts of a permanent self or an unchanging, eternal soul, as it is called in Hinduism and Christianity. According to Buddhism there ultimately is no such thing as a self independent from the rest of the universe. Buddhists also refer to themselves as the believers of the anatta doctrine—Nairatmyavadin or Anattavadin. Rebirth in subsequent existences must be understood as the continuation of a dynamic, ever-changing process of pratītyasamutpāda ("dependent arising") determined by the laws of cause and effect (karma) rather than that of one being, reincarnating from one existence to the next.
rewrite: In Buddhism, rebirth describes the cyclical process through which sentient beings experience successive lifetimes, each spanning from conception to death. Central to this understanding is the doctrine of anattā (or anātman), which denies the existence of a permanent self or an eternal soul, concepts found in traditions like Hinduism and Christianity. This teaching asserts that no independent self exists apart from the universe. Followers of this view are called Anattavadin or Nairatmyavadin. Crucially, rebirth is not the transmigration of a fixed entity but the ongoing flow of pratītyasamutpāda ("dependent arising"), shaped continuously by the laws of karma, or cause and effect.

input: New York City is situated in the Northeastern United States, in southeastern New York State, approximately halfway between Washington, D.C. and Boston. The location at the mouth of the Hudson River, which feeds into a naturally sheltered harbor and then into the Atlantic Ocean, has helped the city grow in significance as a trading port. Most of New York City is built on the three islands of Long Island, Manhattan, and Staten Island.
rewrite: Located in southeastern New York State, New York City lies roughly midway between Washington, D.C. and Boston in the U.S. Northeast. Its importance as a trading port stems from its position at the Hudson River's mouth, leading to a protected harbor and the Atlantic Ocean. The city is primarily built upon three islands: Manhattan, Staten Island, and Long Island.

input: In winter, the Piedmont is colder than the coast, with temperatures usually averaging in the upper 40s–lower 50s °F (8–12 °C) during the day and often dropping below the freezing point at night. The region averages around 3–5 in (8–13 cm) of snowfall annually in the Charlotte area, and slightly more north toward the Virginia border. The Piedmont is especially notorious for sleet and freezing rain. Freezing rain can be heavy enough to snarl traffic and break down trees and power lines. Annual precipitation and humidity are lower in the Piedmont than in the mountains or the coast, but even at its lowest, the average is 40 in (1,020 mm) per year.
rewrite: Winter in the Piedmont brings colder conditions than the coast, featuring daytime temperatures typically in the upper 40s to lower 50s °F (8–12 °C), while nights frequently fall below freezing. The region is particularly known for sleet and freezing rain, which can be severe enough to disrupt traffic and damage trees and power lines. Annual snowfall averages around 3–5 inches (8–13 cm) near Charlotte, increasing slightly toward the Virginia border. Compared to the mountains or coast, the Piedmont sees lower yearly precipitation and humidity, yet its average still reaches at least 40 inches (1,020 mm) annually.

input: The Neolithic 2 (PPNB) began around 8,800 BCE according to the ASPRO chronology in the Levant (Jericho, Israel). As with the PPNA dates, there are two versions from the same laboratories noted above. This system of terminology, however, is not convenient for southeast Anatolia and settlements of the middle Anatolia basin. This era was before the Mesolithic era.[citation needed] A settlement of 3,000 inhabitants was found in the outskirts of Amman, Jordan. Considered to be one of the largest prehistoric settlements in the Near East, called 'Ain Ghazal, it was continuously inhabited from approximately 7,250 – 5,000 B.
rewrite: According to the ASPRO chronology, the Neolithic 2 (PPNB) period commenced around 8,800 BCE in the Levant, as seen at Jericho, Israel. Laboratories have provided two dating versions, similar to those for the PPNA. However, this terminology is less suitable for southeast Anatolia and the settlements of the middle Anatolia basin. A major settlement from this pre-Mesolithic era was discovered near Amman, Jordan. Known as 'Ain Ghazal and inhabited from roughly 7,250 to 5,000 BCE, it housed around 3,000 people and is regarded as one of the Near East's largest prehistoric sites.

input: The American Civil War boosted the local economy with wartime purchases of industrial goods, including that of the New Haven Arms Company, which would later become the Winchester Repeating Arms Company. (Winchester would continue to produce arms in New Haven until 2006, and many of the buildings that were a part of the Winchester plant are now a part of the Winchester Repeating Arms Company Historic District.) After the war, population grew and doubled by the start of the 20th century, most notably due to the influx of immigrants from southern Europe, particularly Italy. Today, roughly half the populations of East Haven, West Haven, and North Haven are Italian-American. Jewish immigration to New Haven has left an enduring mark on the city. Westville was the center of Jewish life in New Haven, though today many have fanned out to suburban communities such as Woodbridge and Cheshire.
rewrite: Wartime industrial purchases, such as those from the New Haven Arms Company—later the Winchester Repeating Arms Company—stimulated the local economy during the American Civil War. Winchester produced arms in New Haven until 2006, and its former plant structures now constitute the Winchester Repeating Arms Company Historic District. Following the war, the population grew dramatically, doubling by the early 20th century, largely because of immigration from southern Europe, especially Italy. As a result, approximately half of the residents in East Haven, West Haven, and North Haven today are of Italian-American descent. Jewish immigration also left a lasting imprint on the city. While Westville was once the hub of Jewish life in New Haven, many families have since moved to suburbs like Woodbridge and Cheshire.

input: Most bacteria have a single circular chromosome that can range in size from only 160,000 base pairs in the endosymbiotic bacteria Candidatus Carsonella ruddii, to 12,200,000 base pairs in the soil-dwelling bacteria Sorangium cellulosum. Spirochaetes of the genus Borrelia are a notable exception to this arrangement, with bacteria such as Borrelia burgdorferi, the cause of Lyme disease, containing a single linear chromosome. The genes in bacterial genomes are usually a single continuous stretch of DNA and although several different types of introns do exist in bacteria, these are much rarer than in eukaryotes.
rewrite: Bacterial genomes typically consist of a single, continuous DNA stretch, with genes rarely interrupted by introns, which are far less common than in eukaryotes. While most bacteria possess a single circular chromosome—varying greatly in size from 160,000 base pairs in Candidatus Carsonella ruddii to 12.2 million in Sorangium cellulosum—there are exceptions. Notably, spirochaetes like Borrelia burgdorferi, responsible for Lyme disease, feature a single linear chromosome instead.

input: Daniel Gralath was the first to combine several jars in parallel into a "battery" to increase the charge storage capacity. Benjamin Franklin investigated the Leyden jar and came to the conclusion that the charge was stored on the glass, not in the water as others had assumed. He also adopted the term "battery", (denoting the increasing of power with a row of similar units as in a battery of cannon), subsequently applied to clusters of electrochemical cells. Leyden jars were later made by coating the inside and outside of jars with metal foil, leaving a space at the mouth to prevent arcing between the foils.[citation needed] The earliest unit of capacitance was the jar, equivalent to about 1.11 nanofarads.
rewrite: Daniel Gralath pioneered the concept of a "battery" by linking multiple jars in parallel, thereby boosting their overall charge storage capacity. The term "battery," originally referring to a row of artillery, was later adopted for groups of electrochemical cells. Benjamin Franklin, through his own investigations, determined that a Leyden jar's charge resided in the glass itself, contradicting the earlier belief that it was held in the water. Later designs involved coating the jar's interior and exterior with metal foil, while leaving an uncoated gap at the mouth to avoid arcing. Capacitance was first measured in "jars," a unit roughly equal to 1.11 nanofarads.

input: Cara Cusumano, director of the Tribeca Film Festival, stated in April 2014: "Piracy is less about people not wanting to pay and more about just wanting the immediacy – people saying, 'I want to watch Spiderman right now' and downloading it". The statement occurred during the third year that the festival used the Internet to present its content, while it was the first year that it featured a showcase of content producers who work exclusively online. Cusumano further explained that downloading behavior is not merely conducted by people who merely want to obtain content for free:
rewrite: In April 2014, Tribeca Film Festival director Cara Cusumano addressed the issue of piracy. She argued it stems less from an unwillingness to pay and more from a demand for instant access, exemplified by someone thinking, "I want to watch Spiderman right now." This statement came in the festival's third year of online content presentation, which for the first time included a showcase for producers working exclusively on the internet. Cusumano clarified that such downloading is not simply the act of those seeking free content.

input: As of the early 21st century, Christianity has approximately 2.4 billion adherents. The faith represents about a third of the world's population and is the largest religion in the world. Christians have composed about 33 percent of the world's population for around 100 years. The largest Christian denomination is the Roman Catholic Church, with 1.17 billion adherents, representing half of all Christians.
rewrite: With roughly 2.4 billion followers, Christianity is the world's largest religion, encompassing about one-third of the global population. This proportion has remained near 33 percent for approximately a century. The Roman Catholic Church is the biggest denomination, accounting for half of all Christians with 1.17 billion adherents.

input: In this respect, the counterpart of Ashkenazi is Sephardic, since most non-Ashkenazi Orthodox Jews follow Sephardic rabbinical authorities, whether or not they are ethnically Sephardic. By tradition, a Sephardic or Mizrahi woman who marries into an Orthodox or Haredi Ashkenazi Jewish family raises her children to be Ashkenazi Jews; conversely an Ashkenazi woman who marries a Sephardi or Mizrahi man is expected to take on Sephardic practice and the children inherit a Sephardic identity, though in practice many families compromise. A convert generally follows the practice of the beth din that converted him or her. With the integration of Jews from around the world in Israel, North America, and other places, the religious definition of an Ashkenazi Jew is blurring, especially outside Orthodox Judaism.
rewrite: Sephardic practice serves as the counterpart to Ashkenazi tradition, as most non-Ashkenazi Orthodox Jews adhere to Sephardic rabbinical authorities, regardless of ethnic Sephardic heritage. Custom dictates that a Sephardic or Mizrahi woman marrying into an Ashkenazi Orthodox family raises Ashkenazi children, while an Ashkenazi woman marrying a Sephardi or Mizrahi man typically adopts Sephardic customs, with children assuming a Sephardic identity—though families often find compromises. Converts generally follow the tradition of their converting beth din. However, the religious definition of an Ashkenazi Jew is becoming less distinct, particularly outside Orthodox circles, due to the global integration of Jewish communities in Israel, North America, and elsewhere.

input: Somerset is a rural county of rolling hills such as the Blackdown Hills, Mendip Hills, Quantock Hills and Exmoor National Park, and large flat expanses of land including the Somerset Levels. There is evidence of human occupation from Paleolithic times, and of subsequent settlement in the Roman and Anglo-Saxon periods. The county played a significant part in the consolidation of power and rise of King Alfred the Great, and later in the English Civil War and the Monmouth Rebellion. The city of Bath is famous for its substantial Georgian architecture and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
rewrite: With its varied landscape of rolling hills like the Blackdowns, Mendips, and Quantocks, along with the flat Somerset Levels and Exmoor National Park, Somerset is a distinctly rural county. Human presence dates to the Paleolithic era, with later Roman and Anglo-Saxon settlement. Historically, it was crucial to King Alfred the Great's consolidation of power and to later conflicts like the English Civil War and Monmouth Rebellion. The city of Bath, renowned for its extensive Georgian architecture, holds UNESCO World Heritage status.

input: Having initially announced a new album entitled So Help Me God slated for a 2014 release, in March 2015 West announced that the album would instead be tentatively called SWISH. Later that month, West was awarded an honorary doctorate by the School of the Art Institute of Chicago for his contributions to music, fashion, and popular culture, officially making him an honorary DFA. The next month, West headlined at the Glastonbury Festival in the UK, despite a petition signed by almost 135,000 people against his appearance. At one point, he told the audience: "You are now watching the greatest living rock star on the planet." Media outlets, including social media sites such as Twitter, were sharply divided on his performance. NME stated, "The decision to book West for the slot has proved controversial since its announcement, and the show itself appeared to polarise both Glastonbury goers and those who tuned in to watch on their TVs." The publication added that "he's letting his music speak for and prove itself." The Guardian said that "his set has a potent ferocity – but there are gaps and stutters, and he cuts a strangely lone figure in front of the vast crowd."
rewrite: Initially planning to release an album titled *So Help Me God* in 2014, Kanye West revealed in March 2015 that the project was tentatively renamed *SWISH*. That same month, he received an honorary doctorate from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, recognizing his impact on music, fashion, and popular culture, which formally granted him the title of honorary DFA. In the following month, West headlined the UK's Glastonbury Festival, even though a petition against his appearance had gathered nearly 135,000 signatures. During his set, he declared to the crowd, "You are now watching the greatest living rock star on the planet." Reaction to his performance was sharply divided across media and social platforms like Twitter. *NME* noted that booking West had been controversial from the start and that the show polarized both festival attendees and television viewers, while also observing that "he's letting his music speak for and prove itself." *The Guardian* described his set as having "a potent ferocity," but pointed out "gaps and stutters," adding that he cut "a strangely lone figure in front of the vast crowd."

input: Crystal Bowersox, who has Type-I diabetes, fell ill due to diabetic ketoacidosis on the morning of the girls performance night for the top 20 week and was hospitalized. The schedule was rearranged so the boys performed first and she could perform the following night instead; she later revealed that Ken Warwick, the show producer, wanted to disqualify her but she begged to be allowed to stay on the show.

To accommodate her, the schedule was rearranged for the boys to perform first, allowing her to take the stage the following night. input: During the Eastern Han, conscription could be avoided if one paid a commutable tax. The Eastern Han court favored the recruitment of a volunteer army. The volunteer army comprised the Southern Army (Nanjun 南軍), while the standing army stationed in and near the capital was the Northern Army (Beijun 北軍). Led by Colonels (Xiaowei 校尉), the Northern Army consisted of five regiments, each composed of several thousand soldiers. When central authority collapsed after 189 AD, wealthy landowners, members of the aristocracy/nobility, and regional military-governors relied upon their retainers to act as their own personal troops (buqu 部曲).
rewrite: In the Eastern Han, paying a commutable tax allowed one to avoid conscription, as the court preferred a volunteer army. This volunteer force was known as the Southern Army (Nanjun). Meanwhile, the standing army garrisoned in and around the capital was the Northern Army (Beijun). Organized into five regiments of several thousand soldiers each, the Northern Army was commanded by Colonels (Xiaowei). Following the collapse of central authority after 189 AD, wealthy landowners, aristocrats, and regional military-governors depended on their retainers to serve as private troops (buqu).

input: On 12 February 1912, after rounds of negotiations, Longyu issued an imperial edict bringing about the abdication of the child emperor Puyi. This brought an end to over 2,000 years of Imperial China and began an extended period of instability of warlord factionalism. The unorganized political and economic systems combined with a widespread criticism of Chinese culture led to questioning and doubt about the future. In the 1930s, the Empire of Japan invaded Northeast China and founded Manchukuo in 1932, with Puyi, as the emperor. After the invasion by the Soviet Union, Manchukuo collapsed in 1945.
rewrite: Following extended negotiations, an imperial edict issued by Longyu on 12 February 1912 mandated the abdication of the child emperor Puyi. This act concluded over two millennia of imperial rule in China, ushering in a prolonged era of instability marked by warlord conflicts. Widespread criticism of Chinese culture, alongside disorganized political and economic structures, fostered deep uncertainty about the nation's future. Decades later, in the 1930s, Japan invaded Northeast China, establishing Manchukuo in 1932 with Puyi installed as its emperor. This puppet state lasted until 1945, when it collapsed following Soviet invasion.

input: Valencia's port is the biggest on the Mediterranean western coast, the first of Spain in container traffic as of 2008 and the second of Spain in total traffic, handling 20% of Spain's exports. The main exports are foodstuffs and beverages. Other exports include oranges, furniture, ceramic tiles, fans, textiles and iron products. Valencia's manufacturing sector focuses on metallurgy, chemicals, textiles, shipbuilding and brewing. Small and medium-sized industries are an important part of the local economy, and before the current crisis unemployment was lower than the Spanish average.
rewrite: As the largest port on the western Mediterranean coast, Valencia leads Spain in container traffic and ranks second in total volume, managing 20% of the nation's exports. Foodstuffs and beverages are primary exports, alongside oranges, furniture, tiles, fans, textiles, and iron products. Key manufacturing areas include metallurgy, chemicals, textiles, shipbuilding, and brewing. Small and medium-sized industries are vital to the local economy, which historically maintained an unemployment rate below the national average before the recent crisis.

input: When a tree is very young it is covered with limbs almost, if not entirely, to the ground, but as it grows older some or all of them will eventually die and are either broken off or fall off. Subsequent growth of wood may completely conceal the stubs which will however remain as knots. No matter how smooth and clear a log is on the outside, it is more or less knotty near the middle. Consequently, the sapwood of an old tree, and particularly of a forest-grown tree, will be freer from knots than the inner heartwood. Since in most uses of wood, knots are defects that weaken the timber and interfere with its ease of working and other properties, it follows that a given piece of sapwood, because of its position in the tree, may well be stronger than a piece of heartwood from the same tree.
rewrite: A young tree’s limbs often extend nearly to the ground. As it ages, some or all of these limbs die, breaking or falling away. Later wood growth may hide the stubs, though they persist internally as knots. Even a log smooth on the outside will be knotty toward its center. Therefore, the sapwood of an old tree—especially one grown in a forest—tends to have fewer knots than the inner heartwood. Knots generally weaken timber and complicate its workability, making them defects in most wood applications. Consequently, due to its location in the tree, a section of sapwood can be stronger than a piece of heartwood from the same source.

input: Puritans were blocked from changing the established church from within, and were severely restricted in England by laws controlling the practice of religion. Their beliefs, however, were transported by the emigration of congregations to the Netherlands (and later to New England), and by evangelical clergy to Ireland (and later into Wales), and were spread into lay society and parts of the educational system, particularly certain colleges of the University of Cambridge. They took on distinctive beliefs about clerical dress and in opposition to the episcopal system, particularly after the 1619 conclusions of the Synod of Dort they were resisted by the English bishops. They largely adopted Sabbatarianism in the 17th century, and were influenced by millennialism.
rewrite: Blocked from reforming the established church internally and constrained by England's restrictive religious laws, the Puritans saw their beliefs spread through alternative channels. Congregations carried these ideas to the Netherlands and later New England, while evangelical clergy brought them to Ireland and Wales. From there, they permeated lay society and parts of the educational system, including certain colleges at Cambridge. The Puritans held distinctive views on clerical dress and opposed the episcopal system, a stance that drew resistance from English bishops, especially after the 1619 Synod of Dort. Additionally, they widely embraced Sabbatarianism and were influenced by millennialism during the 17th century.

input: Not all boys who pass the College election examination choose to become King's Scholars. If they choose instead to belong to one of the 24 Oppidan Houses, they are known as Oppidan Scholars. Oppidan scholarships may also be awarded for consistently performing with distinction in School and external examinations. To gain an Oppidan Scholarship, a boy must have either three distinctions in a row or four throughout his career. Within the school, an Oppidan Scholar is entitled to use the letters OS after his name.
rewrite: While passing the College election examination qualifies a boy as a King's Scholar, he may instead join an Oppidan House, becoming an Oppidan Scholar. This status, marked by the letters OS after one's name, can also be earned through academic distinction. Specifically, it requires either three consecutive distinctions or four total distinctions in School and external examinations throughout a student's career.

input: Some critiqued Paul VI's decision; the newly created Synod of Bishops had an advisory role only and could not make decisions on their own, although the Council decided exactly that. During the pontificate of Paul VI, five such synods took place, and he is on record of implementing all their decisions. Related questions were raised about the new National Bishop Conferences, which became mandatory after Vatican II. Others questioned his Ostpolitik and contacts with Communism and the deals he engaged in for the faithful.
rewrite: Paul VI faced criticism over the Synod of Bishops, which was merely advisory despite the Council's decision. He implemented all proposals from the five synods held under his pontificate. Further questions targeted the now-mandatory National Bishop Conferences. His Ostpolitik, involving contacts and deals with Communist regimes for the faithful, was also questioned by others.

input: By the late Middle Ages, Buddhism had become virtually extinct in India, although it continued to exist in surrounding countries. It is now again gaining strength worldwide. China and India are now starting to fund Buddhist shrines in various Asian countries as they compete for influence in the region.[web 20]
rewrite: Buddhism had largely disappeared from India by the late Middle Ages, surviving only in neighboring lands. Today, it is experiencing a global resurgence. Competing for regional influence, China and India are now funding Buddhist shrines across Asia.

input: The university's first chancellor was Joseph Gibson Hoyt. Crow secured the university charter from the Missouri General Assembly in 1853, and Eliot was named President of the Board of Trustees. Early on, Eliot solicited support from members of the local business community, including John O'Fallon, but Eliot failed to secure a permanent endowment. Washington University is unusual among major American universities in not having had a prior financial endowment. The institution had no backing of a religious organization, single wealthy patron, or earmarked government support.
rewrite: Joseph Gibson Hoyt served as the university's first chancellor. In 1853, Crow obtained the charter from the Missouri General Assembly, and Eliot was appointed President of the Board of Trustees. Eliot initially sought backing from local business figures like John O'Fallon but could not establish a permanent endowment. Unlike most major American universities, Washington University began without any prior financial endowment, religious organization support, a wealthy patron, or designated government funding.

input: European Dutch remained the literary language until the start of the 1920s, when under pressure of Afrikaner nationalism the local "African" Dutch was preferred over the written, European-based standard. In 1925, section 137 of the 1909 constitution of the Union of South Africa was amended by Act 8 of 1925, stating "the word Dutch in article 137 [...] is hereby declared to include Afrikaans". The constitution of 1983 only listed English and Afrikaans as official languages. It is estimated that between 90% to 95% of Afrikaans vocabulary is ultimately of Dutch origin.
rewrite: Until the 1920s, European Dutch served as the literary standard. Then, influenced by Afrikaner nationalism, the local "African" Dutch variant was favored over the European-based written form. This shift was formalized in 1925 when an amendment to the Union of South Africa's constitution declared that the term "Dutch" included Afrikaans. Later, the 1983 constitution recognized only English and Afrikaans as official languages. Approximately 90% to 95% of Afrikaans vocabulary is estimated to derive from Dutch origins.

input: Unarmed fox hunting on horseback with hounds is the type of hunting most closely associated with the United Kingdom; in fact, "hunting" without qualification implies fox hunting. What in other countries is called "hunting" is called "shooting" (birds) or "stalking" (deer) in Britain. Originally a form of vermin control to protect livestock, fox hunting became a popular social activity for newly wealthy upper classes in Victorian times and a traditional rural activity for riders and foot followers alike. Similar to fox hunting in many ways is the chasing of hares with hounds. Pairs of Sight hounds (or long-dogs), such as greyhounds, may be used to pursue a hare in coursing, where the greyhounds are marked as to their skill in coursing the hare (but are not intended to actually catch it), or the hare may be pursued with scent hounds such as beagles or harriers. Other sorts of foxhounds may also be used for hunting stags (deer) or mink. Deer stalking with rifles is carried out on foot without hounds, using stealth.
rewrite: In the United Kingdom, the term "hunting" without further detail specifically means the unarmed pursuit of foxes on horseback with hounds. This contrasts with other countries, where "hunting" is a broader term; in Britain, shooting birds or stalking deer are distinct activities. Fox hunting originated as necessary vermin control to safeguard livestock but evolved during Victorian times into a popular social pastime for the affluent upper classes and a traditional pursuit for rural participants on horseback and on foot. A comparable practice is the chasing of hares with hounds. This may involve coursing with sight hounds like greyhounds, where the dogs are judged on skill rather than a capture, or using scent hounds such as beagles. Beyond foxes, similar hounds can be used for stag or mink hunting. Separately, deer are pursued through stalking, a stealthy practice conducted on foot with rifles and without hounds.

input: The restoration of power to the patriciate was only temporary. After a period of unrest with repeated violent clashes such as the Züriputsch of 1839, civil war (the Sonderbundskrieg) broke out in 1847 when some Catholic cantons tried to set up a separate alliance (the Sonderbund). The war lasted for less than a month, causing fewer than 100 casualties, most of which were through friendly fire. Yet however minor the Sonderbundskrieg appears compared with other European riots and wars in the 19th century, it nevertheless had a major impact on both the psychology and the society of the Swiss and of Switzerland.
rewrite: The patriciate's return to power proved brief. Following unrest marked by events like the 1839 Züriputsch, a civil war—the Sonderbundskrieg—erupted in 1847 after several Catholic cantons formed a separate alliance (the Sonderbund). Lasting less than a month, the conflict resulted in fewer than 100 casualties, many from friendly fire. Though minor compared to other 19th-century European upheavals, the Sonderbundskrieg profoundly impacted Swiss society and national psychology.

input: A common application of a torque motor would be the supply- and take-up reel motors in a tape drive. In this application, driven from a low voltage, the characteristics of these motors allow a relatively constant light tension to be applied to the tape whether or not the capstan is feeding tape past the tape heads. Driven from a higher voltage, (and so delivering a higher torque), the torque motors can also achieve fast-forward and rewind operation without requiring any additional mechanics such as gears or clutches. In the computer gaming world, torque motors are used in force feedback steering wheels.
rewrite: In tape drives, torque motors often serve as the supply- and take-up reel motors. When operated at low voltage, their characteristics enable a relatively constant, light tension on the tape, regardless of whether the capstan is moving tape past the heads. These same motors, driven at a higher voltage to deliver increased torque, can perform fast-forward and rewind functions without needing extra mechanical components like gears or clutches. Additionally, within computer gaming, torque motors are utilized in force feedback steering wheels.

input: The Korean War was a conflict between the United States and its United Nations allies and the communist powers under influence of the Soviet Union (also a UN member nation) and the People's Republic of China (which later also gained UN membership). The principal combatants were North and South Korea. Principal allies of South Korea included the United States, Canada, Australia, the United Kingdom, although many other nations sent troops under the aegis of the United Nations. Allies of North Korea included the People's Republic of China, which supplied military forces, and the Soviet Union, which supplied combat advisors and aircraft pilots, as well as arms, for the Chinese and North Korean troops.
rewrite: Fought primarily between North and South Korea, the Korean War also drew in major global powers. The principal allies of South Korea were the United States, Canada, Australia, and the United Kingdom, with numerous other nations contributing forces under the United Nations banner. Opposing them, North Korea was supported by the People's Republic of China, which deployed military forces, and the Soviet Union. The Soviet Union, itself a UN member, provided combat advisors, pilots, arms, and other aid to the Chinese and North Korean troops. Thus, the conflict pitted U.S. and UN allies against communist powers influenced by the Soviet Union and China.

input: On 3 December, Chopin complained about his bad health and the incompetence of the doctors in Majorca: "Three doctors have visited me ... The first said I was dead; the second said I was dying; and the third said I was about to die." He also had problems having his Pleyel piano sent to him. It finally arrived from Paris in December. Chopin wrote to Pleyel in January 1839: "I am sending you my Preludes [(Op. 28)]. I finished them on your little piano, which arrived in the best possible condition in spite of the sea, the bad weather and the Palma customs." Chopin was also able to undertake work on his Ballade No. 2, Op. 38; two Polonaises, Op. 40; and the Scherzo No. 3, Op. 39.
rewrite: On 3 December, while in Majorca, Chopin lamented both his poor health and the inadequacy of local doctors, remarking that one declared him dead, another dying, and a third near death. His Pleyel piano, long delayed, finally reached him from Paris that same month. Writing to Pleyel in January 1839, Chopin noted he was sending his completed Preludes (Op. 28), which he had finished on that instrument despite its arduous journey by sea and through Palma customs. During this period, he also progressed on other compositions, including the Ballade No. 2, Op. 38; two Polonaises, Op. 40; and the Scherzo No. 3, Op. 39.

input: In the 1960s, Downtown Houston consisted of a collection of mid-rise office structures. Downtown was on the threshold of an energy industry–led boom in 1970. A succession of skyscrapers were built throughout the 1970s—many by real estate developer Gerald D. Hines—culminating with Houston's tallest skyscraper, the 75-floor, 1,002-foot (305 m)-tall JPMorgan Chase Tower (formerly the Texas Commerce Tower), completed in 1982. It is the tallest structure in Texas, 15th tallest building in the United States, and the 85th tallest skyscraper in the world, based on highest architectural feature. In 1983, the 71-floor, 992-foot (302 m)-tall Wells Fargo Plaza (formerly Allied Bank Plaza) was completed, becoming the second-tallest building in Houston and Texas. Based on highest architectural feature, it is the 17th tallest in the United States and the 95th tallest in the world. In 2007, downtown Houston had over 43 million square feet (4,000,000 m²) of office space.
rewrite: During the 1960s, Downtown Houston was characterized by a group of mid-rise office buildings. The area stood at the brink of a major expansion driven by the energy sector in 1970. Throughout the following decade, a series of skyscrapers rose, many developed by Gerald D. Hines. This period peaked in 1982 with the completion of the 75-story, 1,002-foot JPMorgan Chase Tower, formerly the Texas Commerce Tower, which remains Houston's tallest building. It holds the titles of tallest structure in Texas, the 15th tallest building in the United States, and the 85th tallest skyscraper globally, based on its highest architectural feature. The 71-story Wells Fargo Plaza, finished in 1983 at 992 feet, became the second-tallest in both Houston and Texas, ranking as the 17th tallest in the nation and 95th tallest worldwide by the same measure. By 2007, downtown Houston's office space exceeded 43 million square feet.

input: Symmetry groups are groups consisting of symmetries of given mathematical objects—be they of geometric nature, such as the introductory symmetry group of the square, or of algebraic nature, such as polynomial equations and their solutions. Conceptually, group theory can be thought of as the study of symmetry.t[›] Symmetries in mathematics greatly simplify the study of geometrical or analytical objects. A group is said to act on another mathematical object X if every group element performs some operation on X compatibly to the group law. In the rightmost example below, an element of order 7 of the (2,3,7) triangle group acts on the tiling by permuting the highlighted warped triangles (and the other ones, too). By a group action, the group pattern is connected to the structure of the object being acted on.
rewrite: Symmetry groups consist of the symmetries associated with specific mathematical objects, whether geometric like the symmetry group of a square, or algebraic such as polynomial equations and their solutions. Conceptually, group theory is essentially the study of symmetry. The presence of symmetry greatly simplifies the analysis of geometrical or analytical objects. When a group acts on another mathematical object X, each group element performs an operation on X in a manner consistent with the group's structure. For instance, in the rightmost example, an element of order 7 from the (2,3,7) triangle group acts on a tiling by rearranging the highlighted warped triangles along with the others. Through such group actions, the pattern inherent in the group becomes linked to the structure of the object it acts upon.

input: Currently, the Regular Force component of the Army consists of three field-ready brigade groups: 1 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group, at CFB Edmonton and CFB Shilo; 2 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group, at CFB Petawawa and CFB Gagetown; and 5 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group, at CFB Valcartier and Quebec City. Each contains one regiment each of artillery, armour, and combat engineers, three battalions of infantry (all scaled in the British fashion), one battalion for logistics, a squadron for headquarters/signals, and several smaller support organizations. A tactical helicopter squadron and a field ambulance are co-located with each brigade, but do not form part of the brigade's command structure.
rewrite: The Army's Regular Force currently fields three brigade groups ready for deployment. These include 1 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group based at CFB Edmonton and CFB Shilo; 2 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group at CFB Petawawa and CFB Gagetown; and 5 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group at CFB Valcartier and Quebec City. Every brigade is organized with one artillery, armour, and combat engineer regiment, three British-scaled infantry battalions, a logistics battalion, a headquarters/signals squadron, and various smaller support units. Although a tactical helicopter squadron and a field ambulance are stationed with each brigade, they operate outside its direct command.

input: The kingdom is mentioned in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea as an important market place for ivory, which was exported throughout the ancient world. Aksum was at the time ruled by Zoskales, who also governed the port of Adulis. The Aksumite rulers facilitated trade by minting their own Aksumite currency. The state also established its hegemony over the declining Kingdom of Kush and regularly entered the politics of the kingdoms on the Arabian peninsula, eventually extending its rule over the region with the conquest of the Himyarite Kingdom.
rewrite: According to the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, the kingdom was a key ivory market, exporting this commodity across the ancient world. At that time, Aksum was under the rule of Zoskales, who also controlled the port of Adulis. The kingdom minted its own currency to facilitate commerce. Furthermore, Aksum asserted its dominance over the declining Kingdom of Kush and frequently intervened in Arabian peninsula politics. This expansion culminated in the conquest of the Himyarite Kingdom, extending Aksumite rule over that region.

input: The abbey was restored to the Benedictines under the Catholic Mary I of England, but they were again ejected under Elizabeth I in 1559. In 1560, Elizabeth re-established Westminster as a "Royal Peculiar" – a church of the Church of England responsible directly to the Sovereign, rather than to a diocesan bishop – and made it the Collegiate Church of St Peter (that is, a non-cathedral church with an attached chapter of canons, headed by a dean.) The last of Mary's abbots was made the first dean.
rewrite: Under the Catholic Mary I of England, the Benedictines regained the abbey, only to be ejected again in 1559 under Elizabeth I. The following year, Elizabeth re-established Westminster as a "Royal Peculiar," a church directly responsible to the Sovereign instead of a diocesan bishop. It became the Collegiate Church of St Peter, a non-cathedral church with a chapter of canons led by a dean. The first dean appointed was the last abbot from Mary's reign.

input: This new approach liberated scientific speculation from the dogmatic restraints of Aristotelian science, and paved the way for new approaches. Particularly within the field of theories of motion great advances were made, when such scholars as Jean Buridan, Nicole Oresme and the Oxford Calculators challenged the work of Aristotle. Buridan developed the theory of impetus as the cause of the motion of projectiles, which was an important step towards the modern concept of inertia. The works of these scholars anticipated the heliocentric worldview of Nicolaus Copernicus.
rewrite: Breaking free from the rigid doctrines of Aristotelian science, this new method opened the door to innovative thinking. Significant progress in motion theory was achieved by scholars like Jean Buridan, Nicole Oresme, and the Oxford Calculators, who contested Aristotle's ideas. Buridan's impetus theory, explaining projectile motion, marked a key advancement toward the modern principle of inertia. Their collective work laid the groundwork for Nicolaus Copernicus's later heliocentric model.

input: Nasser remains an iconic figure in the Arab world, particularly for his strides towards social justice and Arab unity, modernization policies, and anti-imperialist efforts. His presidency also encouraged and coincided with an Egyptian cultural boom, and launched large industrial projects, including the Aswan Dam and Helwan City. Nasser's detractors criticize his authoritarianism, his government's human rights violations, his populist relationship with the citizenry, and his failure to establish civil institutions, blaming his legacy for future dictatorial governance in Egypt. Historians describe Nasser as a towering political figure of the Middle East in the 20th century.
rewrite: In the Arab world, Nasser is remembered as an iconic leader. He championed social justice, Arab unity, modernization, and anti-imperialism. His era saw a cultural boom and major industrial projects like the Aswan Dam and Helwan City. However, critics point to his authoritarianism, human rights violations, populist tactics, and failure to build lasting civil institutions, linking his rule to later dictatorships. Despite this, historians regard him as a towering political figure of the 20th-century Middle East.

input: Motorsport racecourses and events were banned in Switzerland following the 1955 Le Mans disaster with exception to events such as Hillclimbing. During this period, the country still produced successful racing drivers such as Clay Regazzoni, Sebastian Buemi, Jo Siffert, Dominique Aegerter, successful World Touring Car Championship driver Alain Menu, 2014 24 Hours of Le Mans winner Marcel Fässler and 2015 24 Hours Nürburgring winner Nico Müller. Switzerland also won the A1GP World Cup of Motorsport in 2007–08 with driver Neel Jani. Swiss motorcycle racer Thomas Lüthi won the 2005 MotoGP World Championship in the 125cc category. In June 2007 the Swiss National Council, one house of the Federal Assembly of Switzerland, voted to overturn the ban, however the other house, the Swiss Council of States rejected the change and the ban remains in place.
rewrite: Following the 1955 Le Mans disaster, Switzerland instituted a ban on motorsport racecourses and events, though exceptions like Hillclimbing were permitted. Despite this prohibition, the nation continued to cultivate accomplished racing drivers. Among them are Clay Regazzoni, Sebastian Buemi, Jo Siffert, and Dominique Aegerter, alongside successful World Touring Car Championship driver Alain Menu. Marcel Fässler, winner of the 2014 24 Hours of Le Mans, and Nico Müller, winner of the 2015 24 Hours of Nürburgring, also hail from Switzerland. The country secured the A1GP World Cup of Motorsport in 2007–08 with driver Neel Jani, while Swiss motorcycle racer Thomas Lüthi claimed the 2005 125cc MotoGP World Championship. In June 2007, the Swiss National Council voted to lift the ban, but the Swiss Council of States rejected the proposal, leaving the prohibition in effect.

input: While outer space provides the most rarefied example of a naturally occurring partial vacuum, the heavens were originally thought to be seamlessly filled by a rigid indestructible material called aether. Borrowing somewhat from the pneuma of Stoic physics, aether came to be regarded as the rarefied air from which it took its name, (see Aether (mythology)). Early theories of light posited a ubiquitous terrestrial and celestial medium through which light propagated. Additionally, the concept informed Isaac Newton's explanations of both refraction and of radiant heat. 19th century experiments into this luminiferous aether attempted to detect a minute drag on the Earth's orbit. While the Earth does, in fact, move through a relatively dense medium in comparison to that of interstellar space, the drag is so minuscule that it could not be detected. In 1912, astronomer Henry Pickering commented: "While the interstellar absorbing medium may be simply the ether, [it] is characteristic of a gas, and free gaseous molecules are certainly there".
rewrite: The heavens were once believed to be completely filled with a rigid, indestructible substance known as aether, a concept drawing from the Stoic idea of pneuma and named for the rarefied air it was thought to be. This notion provided a medium through which early theories suggested light traveled, and it later informed Isaac Newton’s explanations of refraction and radiant heat. In the 19th century, experiments sought to detect a slight drag on Earth’s orbit caused by this luminiferous aether. Although Earth does move through a medium denser than interstellar space, any resulting drag proved too minuscule to measure. Astronomer Henry Pickering noted in 1912 that while the interstellar medium might be the ether, it behaves like a gas, and free gaseous molecules are undoubtedly present. Thus, while outer space remains the most extreme natural partial vacuum, it was not originally conceived as such.

input: However, some scholars contest the idea of a Proto-Euphratean language or one substrate language. It has been suggested by them and others, that the Sumerian language was originally that of the hunter and fisher peoples, who lived in the marshland and the Eastern Arabia littoral region, and were part of the Arabian bifacial culture. Reliable historical records begin much later; there are none in Sumer of any kind that have been dated before Enmebaragesi (c. 26th century BC). Professor Juris Zarins believes the Sumerians were settled along the coast of Eastern Arabia, today's Persian Gulf region, before it flooded at the end of the Ice Age.
rewrite: The notion of a single Proto-Euphratean substrate language is disputed by certain scholars. They, along with others, propose instead that Sumerian originated with the hunter-fisher communities of the marshlands and the Eastern Arabian littoral, who belonged to the Arabian bifacial culture. Reliable historical records appear much later; no Sumerian records exist prior to Enmebaragesi (c. 26th century BC). Supporting a coastal origin, Professor Juris Zarins posits that the Sumerians were established along Eastern Arabia's coast—the present-day Persian Gulf region—before its flooding at the Ice Age's end.

input: In Arabic-speaking cultures, two words are commonly used for Christians: Naṣrānī (نصراني), plural Naṣārā (نصارى) is generally understood to be derived from Nazareth through the Syriac (Aramaic); Masīḥī (مسيحي) means followers of the Messiah. The term Nasara rose to prominence in July 2014, after the Fall of Mosul to the terrorist organization Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant. The nun or ن— the first letter of Nasara—was spray-painted on the property of Christians ejected from the city.
rewrite: In Arabic, Christians are often referred to by two terms: Naṣrānī (نصراني), derived from Nazareth via Syriac, and Masīḥī (مسيحي), meaning followers of the Messiah. The term Nasara gained widespread attention in July 2014 following the Fall of Mosul to ISIS. To mark the property of expelled Christians, the terrorist group spray-painted the nun (ن), the first letter of Nasara.

input: Yet the most impressive aesthetic works were done among the scholars and urban elite. Calligraphy and painting remained a central interest to both court painters and scholar-gentry who considered the Four Arts part of their cultural identity and social standing. The painting of the early years of the dynasty included such painters as the orthodox Four Wangs and the individualists Bada Shanren (1626–1705) and Shitao (1641–1707). The nineteenth century saw such innovations as the Shanghai School and the Lingnan School which used the technical skills of tradition to set the stage for modern painting.
rewrite: The most notable aesthetic achievements emerged from scholars and the urban elite, for whom calligraphy and painting were central pursuits. Both court painters and the scholar-gentry viewed these arts, part of the Four Arts, as integral to their cultural identity and status. Early dynastic painting featured masters like the orthodox Four Wangs and the individualists Bada Shanren (1626–1705) and Shitao (1641–1707). Later, the nineteenth century brought innovations such as the Shanghai and Lingnan Schools, which applied traditional techniques to pave the way for modern painting.

input: Many solar photovoltaic power stations have been built, mainly in Europe. As of July 2012, the largest photovoltaic (PV) power plants in the world are the Agua Caliente Solar Project (USA, 247 MW), Charanka Solar Park (India, 214 MW), Golmud Solar Park (China, 200 MW), Perovo Solar Park (Russia 100 MW), Sarnia Photovoltaic Power Plant (Canada, 97 MW), Brandenburg-Briest Solarpark (Germany 91 MW), Solarpark Finow Tower (Germany 84.7 MW), Montalto di Castro Photovoltaic Power Station (Italy, 84.2 MW), Eggebek Solar Park (Germany 83.6 MW), Senftenberg Solarpark (Germany 82 MW), Finsterwalde Solar Park (Germany, 80.7 MW), Okhotnykovo Solar Park (Russia, 80 MW), Lopburi Solar Farm (Thailand 73.16 MW), Rovigo Photovoltaic Power Plant (Italy, 72 MW), and the Lieberose Photovoltaic Park (Germany, 71.8 MW).
rewrite: Europe has been a primary location for the construction of numerous solar photovoltaic power stations. As of July 2012, the world's largest PV plants include the Agua Caliente Solar Project in the USA at 247 MW and India's Charanka Solar Park at 214 MW. Other major installations are China's Golmud Solar Park (200 MW), Russia's Perovo (100 MW) and Okhotnykovo (80 MW) Solar Parks, and Canada's Sarnia plant (97 MW). Significant German facilities are Brandenburg-Briest (91 MW), Solarpark Finow Tower (84.7 MW), Eggebek (83.6 MW), Senftenberg (82 MW), Finsterwalde (80.7 MW), and Lieberose (71.8 MW). Italy's contributions are Montalto di Castro (84.2 MW) and Rovigo (72 MW), while Thailand hosts the Lopburi Solar Farm at 73.16 MW.

input: Under a banner of "reducing public drunkenness" the Beer Act of 1830 introduced a new lower tier of premises permitted to sell alcohol, the Beer Houses. At the time beer was viewed as harmless, nutritious and even healthy. Young children were often given what was described as small beer, which was brewed to have a low alcohol content, as the local water was often unsafe. Even the evangelical church and temperance movements of the day viewed the drinking of beer very much as a secondary evil and a normal accompaniment to a meal. The freely available beer was thus intended to wean the drinkers off the evils of gin, or so the thinking went.
rewrite: Introduced in 1830, the Beer Act aimed to curb public drunkenness by creating a new class of licensed premises called Beer Houses. Beer was then considered a harmless, even nutritious beverage. Because local water supplies were often unsafe, young children frequently drank "small beer," a brew with low alcohol content. Contemporary evangelical and temperance movements largely regarded beer consumption as a normal part of a meal and only a secondary vice. The underlying logic was that making beer freely available would steer drinkers away from the greater perceived evil of gin.

input: Gagarin became a national hero of the Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc, and a worldwide celebrity. Moscow and other cities in the USSR held mass demonstrations, the scale of which was second only to the World War II Victory Parade of 1945. April 12 was declared Cosmonautics Day in the USSR, and is celebrated today in Russia as one of the official "Commemorative Dates of Russia." In 2011, it was declared the International Day of Human Space Flight by the United Nations.
rewrite: Yuri Gagarin was celebrated as a national hero across the Soviet Union and Eastern Bloc, achieving global fame. Following his flight, mass demonstrations swept Moscow and other Soviet cities, rivaled in scale only by the 1945 Victory Parade. The USSR established April 12 as Cosmonautics Day, a date still honored in Russia among its official commemorations. Later, in 2011, the United Nations designated it the International Day of Human Space Flight.

input: In June 1718 Blackbeard, aka Edward Teach, ran his flagship, the Queen Anne's Revenge, aground at Beaufort Inlet, North Carolina, in present-day Carteret County. After the grounding her crew and supplies were transferred to smaller ships. In 1996 Intersal, Inc., a private firm, discovered the remains of a vessel likely to be the Queen Anne's Revenge, which was added to the US National Register of Historic Places. In November, after losing his ship and appealing to the governor of North Carolina who promised safe-haven and a pardon, the notorious pirate, Blackbeard (Edward Teach) was killed in an ambush by troops from Virginia.
rewrite: In June 1718, the infamous pirate Blackbeard, also known as Edward Teach, deliberately grounded his flagship, the *Queen Anne's Revenge*, at Beaufort Inlet in present-day Carteret County, North Carolina. Following this, his crew and supplies were moved to smaller vessels. Later that November, after losing his ship and having sought a promised pardon from North Carolina's governor, Blackbeard was ambushed and killed by troops from Virginia. The likely remains of his ship were discovered in 1996 by the private firm Intersal, Inc., and the site was later listed on the US National Register of Historic Places.

input: QED vacuum has interesting and complex properties. In QED vacuum, the electric and magnetic fields have zero average values, but their variances are not zero. As a result, QED vacuum contains vacuum fluctuations (virtual particles that hop into and out of existence), and a finite energy called vacuum energy. Vacuum fluctuations are an essential and ubiquitous part of quantum field theory. Some experimentally verified effects of vacuum fluctuations include spontaneous emission and the Lamb shift. Coulomb's law and the electric potential in vacuum near an electric charge are modified.
rewrite: The QED vacuum possesses intriguing and complex characteristics. While average electric and magnetic fields are zero, their variances are not, leading to vacuum fluctuations—virtual particles appearing and disappearing—and a finite vacuum energy. These fluctuations are a fundamental and widespread aspect of quantum field theory. Their experimentally confirmed effects encompass spontaneous emission and the Lamb shift. Additionally, Coulomb's law and the electric potential near a charge in vacuum are altered as a result.

input: Transformation, unlike transduction or conjugation, depends on numerous bacterial gene products that specifically interact to perform this complex process, and thus transformation is clearly a bacterial adaptation for DNA transfer. In order for a bacterium to bind, take up and recombine donor DNA into its own chromosome, it must first enter a special physiological state termed competence (see Natural competence). In Bacillus subtilis, about 40 genes are required for the development of competence. The length of DNA transferred during B. subtilis transformation can be between a third of a chromosome up to the whole chromosome. Transformation appears to be common among bacterial species, and thus far at least 60 species are known to have the natural ability to become competent for transformation. The development of competence in nature is usually associated with stressful environmental conditions, and seems to be an adaptation for facilitating repair of DNA damage in recipient cells.
rewrite: Unlike transduction or conjugation, transformation is a complex process involving many bacterial gene products working together, making it a clear adaptation for DNA transfer. For a bacterium to bind, take up, and integrate donor DNA into its chromosome, it must first achieve a specialized physiological state known as competence (see Natural competence). In *Bacillus subtilis*, this requires about 40 genes. The amount of DNA transferred in *B. subtilis* can range from a third of a chromosome to an entire chromosome. At least 60 bacterial species are known to naturally develop this ability, indicating transformation is widespread. In nature, competence typically arises under stressful environmental conditions, serving as an adaptation that helps recipient cells repair damaged DNA.

input: On 1 July 1967, BBC Two became the first television channel in Europe to broadcast regularly in colour, using the West German PAL system that is still in use today although being gradually superseded by digital systems. (BBC One and ITV began 625-line colour broadcasts simultaneously on 15 November 1969). Unlike other terrestrial channels, BBC Two does not have soap opera or standard news programming, but a range of programmes intended to be eclectic and diverse (although if a programme has high audience ratings it is often eventually repositioned to BBC One). The different remit of BBC2 allowed its first controller, Sir David Attenborough to commission the first heavyweight documentaries and documentary series such as Civilisation, The Ascent of Man and Horizon.
rewrite: On 15 November 1969, BBC One and ITV simultaneously launched 625-line colour broadcasts. This followed BBC Two’s pioneering adoption of colour, as it became Europe’s first regular colour television channel on 1 July 1967, utilizing the West German PAL system. While this analogue standard remains in use, it is being gradually replaced by digital systems. BBC Two’s programming remit differs from other terrestrial channels, notably lacking soap operas and standard news. Instead, it offers an eclectic and diverse range of programmes, though highly popular shows are often moved to BBC One. This distinct mandate enabled its first controller, Sir David Attenborough, to commission seminal documentary series like *Civilisation*, *The Ascent of Man*, and *Horizon*.

input: On August 9, 2015, ESPN reported that the New Orleans VooDoo and Las Vegas Outlaws had ceased operations, effective immediately, a claim which was subsequently validated on the AFL website. On September 1, 2015, the Spokane Shock officially left the AFL and joined the IFL under the new name Spokane Empire, becoming the fifth active AFL/af2 franchise to leave for the IFL since bankruptcy (Iowa Barnstormers, Tri-Cities Fever, Green Bay Blizzard and Arkansas Twisters—now the Texas Revolution—left previously).
rewrite: On August 9, 2015, ESPN reported the immediate shutdown of the New Orleans VooDoo and Las Vegas Outlaws, a report later confirmed on the AFL website. Subsequently, on September 1, the Spokane Shock departed the AFL for the IFL, rebranding as the Spokane Empire. This move made it the fifth active AFL/af2 franchise to join the IFL following the league's bankruptcy, following the Iowa Barnstormers, Tri-Cities Fever, Green Bay Blizzard, and Arkansas Twisters (now the Texas Revolution).

input: Thousands more employees work in Midtown, north of the central business district. Midtown's anchors are the city's largest single employer Detroit Medical Center, Wayne State University, and the Henry Ford Health System in New Center. Midtown is also home to watchmaker Shinola and an array of small and/or startup companies. New Center bases TechTown, a research and business incubator hub that’s part of the WSU system. Like downtown and Corktown, Midtown also has a fast-growing retailing and restaurant scene.

Its major anchors include the city's largest single employer, the Detroit Medical Center, along with Wayne State University and the Henry Ford Health System in New Center. The area also hosts watchmaker Shinola and numerous small or startup companies. New Center is home to TechTown, a WSU-affiliated research and business incubator hub. input: The name Anabaptist, meaning "one who baptizes again", was given them by their persecutors in reference to the practice of re-baptizing converts who already had been baptized as infants. Anabaptists required that baptismal candidates be able to make their own confessions of faith and so rejected baptism of infants. The early members of this movement did not accept the name Anabaptist, claiming that since infant baptism was unscriptural and null and void, the baptizing of believers was not a re-baptism but in fact their first real baptism. As a result of their views on the nature of baptism and other issues, Anabaptists were heavily persecuted during the 16th century and into the 17th by both Magisterial Protestants and Roman Catholics.[aa] While most Anabaptists adhered to a literal interpretation of the Sermon on the Mount, which precluded taking oaths, participating in military actions, and participating in civil government, some who practiced re-baptism felt otherwise.[ab] They were thus technically Anabaptists, even though conservative Amish, Mennonites, and Hutterites and some historians tend to consider them as outside of true Anabaptism. Anabaptist reformers of the Radical Reformation are diveded into Radical and the so-called Second Front. Some important Radical Reformation theologians were John of Leiden, Thomas Müntzer, Kaspar Schwenkfeld, Sebastian Franck, Menno Simons. Second Front Reformers included Hans Denck, Conrad Grebel, Balthasar Hubmaier and Felix Manz.
rewrite: The label "Anabaptist," signifying "one who baptizes again," originated from their persecutors, highlighting the group's practice of re-baptizing adult converts previously baptized as infants. Central to Anabaptist belief was the requirement that candidates for baptism could personally confess their faith, leading them to reject infant baptism as invalid. Consequently, these early reformers refused the name Anabaptist, arguing that since infant baptism was without biblical foundation and void, their baptism of believers constituted a first genuine baptism, not a re-baptism. These views on baptism and other doctrines led to severe persecution throughout the 16th and into the 17th century by both Roman Catholics and Magisterial Protestants. The reformers of the Radical Reformation are categorized into the Radical stream and the so-called Second Front. Key Radical Reformation theologians included John of Leiden, Thomas Müntzer, Kaspar Schwenkfeld, Sebastian Franck, and Menno Simons. Second Front Reformers were figures such as Hans Denck, Conrad Grebel, Balthasar Hubmaier, and Felix Manz. Although most Anabaptists followed a literal interpretation of the Sermon on the Mount, rejecting oaths, military service, and civil government involvement, some who practiced believer's baptism dissented from these principles. Thus, while technically Anabaptists, these dissenters are often regarded as outside true Anabaptism by conservative Amish, Mennonites, and Hutterites, as well as by some historians.

input: The design architecture of USB is asymmetrical in its topology, consisting of a host, a multitude of downstream USB ports, and multiple peripheral devices connected in a tiered-star topology. Additional USB hubs may be included in the tiers, allowing branching into a tree structure with up to five tier levels. A USB host may implement multiple host controllers and each host controller may provide one or more USB ports. Up to 127 devices, including hub devices if present, may be connected to a single host controller. USB devices are linked in series through hubs. One hub—built into the host controller—is the root hub.
rewrite: USB employs an asymmetrical design architecture based on a tiered-star topology. This structure includes a host, numerous downstream USB ports, and various peripheral devices. The tiers can incorporate additional USB hubs, enabling branching into a tree structure that supports up to five levels. A single USB host may contain multiple host controllers, each offering one or more ports. As many as 127 devices, counting any hubs, can connect to one host controller. Devices are linked in series via hubs, with the root hub being integrated into the host controller.

input: Ozawa's "Northern Force" had four aircraft carriers, two obsolete battleships partly converted to carriers, three cruisers and nine destroyers. The carriers had only 108 planes. The force was not spotted by the Allies until 16:40 on 24 October. At 20:00 Toyoda ordered all remaining Japanese forces to attack. Halsey saw an opportunity to destroy the remnants of the Japanese carrier force. The U.S. Third Fleet was formidable – nine large carriers, eight light carriers, six battleships, 17 cruisers, 63 destroyers and 1,000 planes – and completely outgunned Ozawa's force. Halsey's ships set out in pursuit of Ozawa just after midnight. U.S. commanders ignored reports that Kurita had turned back towards San Bernardino Strait. They had taken the bait set by Ozawa. On the morning of 25 October Ozawa launched 75 planes. Most were shot down by U.S. fighter patrols. By 08:00 U.S. fighters had destroyed the screen of Japanese fighters and were hitting ships. By evening, they had sunk the carriers Zuikaku, Zuihō, and Chiyoda, and a destroyer. The fourth carrier, Chitose, and a cruiser were disabled and later sank.
rewrite: Ozawa's "Northern Force" comprised four aircraft carriers, two outdated battleships partially converted to carriers, three cruisers, and nine destroyers, equipped with only 108 planes. Allied forces did not detect this group until 16:40 on October 24. By 20:00, Toyoda had issued orders for all remaining Japanese units to attack. Recognizing a chance to eliminate the remaining Japanese carrier strength, Admiral Halsey mobilized the formidable U.S. Third Fleet, which included nine large carriers, eight light carriers, six battleships, 17 cruisers, 63 destroyers, and approximately 1,000 aircraft, vastly outgunning Ozawa’s fleet. Just after midnight, Halsey’s ships began pursuing Ozawa. U.S. commanders disregarded reports that Kurita had reversed course toward San Bernardino Strait, having taken Ozawa’s bait. On the morning of October 25, Ozawa launched 75 planes, most of which were shot down by U.S. fighter patrols. By 08:00, American fighters had eliminated the Japanese fighter screen and commenced attacks on ships. By day’s end, they had sunk the carriers Zuikaku, Zuihō, and Chiyoda, along with a destroyer. The fourth carrier, Chitose, and a cruiser were crippled and later sank.
